-> **[Marbled Endpaper]** <-

<note>This page contains no written text. It is a marbled endpaper, a decorative element frequently used in the binding of historical manuscripts. The patterns seen here—swirling veins of reddish-brown and tan—were created by floating pigments on a liquid bath and then transferring the design to paper. These papers served both to protect the manuscript and to provide an aesthetically pleasing transition from the cover to the internal pages.</note>

It served a dual purpose: it was an affordable decorative finish and it helped to mask the darkening caused by dust and frequent handling over the centuries.</note>

<meta>This is the title page of Johannes Kepler’s seminal 1619 work, "Harmonices Mundi." ### Johannes Kepler’s
# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

## FIVE BOOKS, OF WHICH:

The first is **GEOMETRICAL**, concerning the origin and demonstrations of Regular Figures <note>original: "Figurarum Regularium"; these are symmetrical shapes like squares or equilateral triangles</note>, which constitute Harmonic Proportions.

The second is **ARCHITECTURAL**, or **FROM SHAPED GEOMETRY**, concerning the Congruence <note>The way shapes fit together without gaps, like floor tilings</note> of Regular Figures in a plane or a solid:

The third is properly **HARMONIC**, concerning the origin of Harmonic Proportions from Figures; and concerning the Nature and Differences of things pertaining to song <note>or music</note>, in opposition to the Ancients:

The fourth is **METAPHYSICAL, PSYCHOLOGICAL, & ASTROLOGICAL**, concerning the mental Essence of Harmonies and their types in the World; especially concerning the Harmony of rays descending from celestial bodies to the Earth, and its effect on Nature or the sublunary <note>Earthly</note> and Human Soul:

The fifth is **ASTRONOMICAL & METAPHYSICAL**, concerning the most perfect Harmonies of celestial motions, and the origin of Eccentricities from Harmonic proportions.

The Appendix contains a comparison of this Work with Book III of the *Harmonics* of the distinguished Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note>, and with the Harmonic speculations of Robert Fludd, called "the Oxford Physician," which were inserted in his work on the Macrocosm and Microcosm.

---

*> NOW ADDED DUE TO THE KINSHIP OF THE SUBJECT is a book by the same Author published 23 years ago at Tübingen, titled The Forerunner, or The Cosmographic Mystery, concerning the causes of the Number of the Heavens, the Proportion and the Periodic motions [derived] from the five Regular Bodies <term>Platonic Solids: the five symmetrical 3D shapes (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron) that Kepler believed dictated the spacing of the planets</term>.*

### Johannes Kepler’s
# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD
## FIVE BOOKS

->Of Which<-

The first is **GEOMETRICAL**, concerning the origin and classes of Regular Figures <note>original: "Figurarum Regularium"; these are symmetrical shapes like squares or equilateral triangles</note>, which constitute Harmonic Proportions.

The second is **ARCHITECTURAL**, or **FROM SHAPED GEOMETRY**, concerning the Congruence <note>The way shapes fit together without gaps, like floor tilings</note> of Regular Figures in a plane or a solid:

The third is properly **HARMONIC**, concerning the origin of Harmonic Proportions from Figures; and concerning the Nature and Differences of things pertaining to song <note>original: "cantum"; referring here to music theory</note>, in opposition to the Ancients:

The fourth is **METAPHYSICAL, PSYCHOLOGICAL & ASTROLOGICAL**, concerning the mental Essence of Harmonies and their types in the World; especially concerning the Harmony of rays descending from celestial bodies to the Earth, and its effect on Nature or the sublunary <note>Earthly</note> and Human Soul:

The fifth is **ASTRONOMICAL & METAPHYSICAL**, concerning the most perfect Harmonies of celestial motions, and the origin of Eccentricities <note>the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note> from Harmonic proportions.

The Appendix contains a comparison of this Work with Book III of the distinguished Ptolemy’s <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note> *Harmonics*, and with the discourse of Robert Fludd <note>original: "Iohannis Roberti"; Kepler refers to the English physician and mystic Robert Fludd</note>, the Oxford physician...

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the front matter of Johannes Kepler’s "Harmonices Mundi" (1619). Having established the book’s contents on the previous page, Kepler now begins the formal dedication to King James I of England. He justifies why a work written in the service of the Holy Roman Emperor in Germany is being sent across the sea to the British monarch.</meta>

<image-desc>A wide decorative woodcut headpiece at the top of the page features ornate symmetrical scrolling foliage, floral motifs, and vines.</image-desc>

### TO THE
## Most Serene & Most Potent
## Prince and Lord,
# LORD JAMES,
## King of Great Britain, France, and
## Ireland, Defender of the
## Faith, etc.

->*My Most Merciful Lord.*<-

---

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring elaborate floral scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>

Why I should send these books of *Harmonics* <note>original: "Harmonices"; referring to the study of mathematical proportions in music, nature, and the heavens</note> to be published among men, away from the court of the most August Emperor <note>Ferdinand II, the Holy Roman Emperor</note>, my Lord—away from his Kingdoms and hereditary Austrian Provinces, and finally from Germany itself—sending them across the sea to present them to your most serene sight, O Illustrious King: I have had reasons partly present, and partly ancient.

First, I did not think this foreign to my duty; for since I earn the Emperor’s salary in the field of Mathematics, I wished to demonstrate even to those abroad how much care this Prince of the Christian Commonwealth <note>The Holy Roman Empire</note> bestows upon these most divine studies. It should be understood from the undisturbed progress of the "ornaments of Peace" <note>a reference to the arts and sciences</note> through these provinces, that the ominous rumor of internal war <note>The Thirty Years' War, which began in 1618, one year before this publication</note> will, along with the conflict itself, undoubtedly soon be extinguished. This current dissonance, though a little harsher than usual—just as in a moving Melody—is even now [resolving] into its plea- <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword "uem" indicates the next word is "suauem," meaning sweet or pleasant.</note>

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of Kepler's work to King James I of England. Kepler frames his scientific work as a sign of enduring peace and intellectual progress, despite the early stages of the Thirty Years' War in Germany.</summary>
<keywords>King James I, dedication, Emperor Ferdinand II, Thirty Years' War, harmony, mathematics, peace</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s dedication to King James I of England. Kepler is explaining why James is the ideal patron for "Harmonices Mundi," citing the King’s intellectual pedigree, his early interest in Tycho Brahe’s astronomy, and his public criticism of superstitious astrology. Kepler also reveals that he had intended to dedicate this work to James nearly twenty years earlier.</meta>

# DEDICATION.

...providence will find its closing clause <note>original: "prouidentiam Clausulam desituram"; this completes the sentence from the previous page suggesting that God's providence will eventually bring an end to the "dissonance" of the war</note>. For who could be a more worthy judge of Imperial Goodness than a great King? Whom could I have chosen as a more suitable Patron for a work on the **Harmonies of the Heavens**—which savors of **Pythagoras** and **Plato**—than that King who has testified to his study of Platonic wisdom through his own writings <note>original: "domesticis monumentis"; referring to King James’s published books and treatises</note>, which we even hold in public veneration among your subjects? Who, while still a boy, deemed the **Astronomy of Tycho Brahe**—upon which this work relies—worthy of the ornaments of his own genius? Who, finally, having become a man and handling the rudders of the kingdom, marked **Astrological vanity** with public censure? This vanity is clearly exposed in Book IV of this work, where the true foundations of planetary influences are uncovered: so that no one can doubt that you will be the most intelligent judge of this whole Work and all its parts.

But a greater cause for this dedication comes to me from long ago. When I first conceived the material for this work and announced its title a little less than twenty years ago—though the specific motions of the Planets were not yet known, in which the instinct of Nature nevertheless dictated that Harmonies were present—even then I destined the patronage of the work for your Majesty, should it ever succeed and be completed. I testified to this, as if it were my vow, to your Ambassadors at the Imperial court once and again.

The causes for thinking of this patronage of my *Harmonics* were supplied to me by that manifold **Dissonance** in human affairs, which is indeed so manifest that it cannot fail to offend; yet it is composed of harmonious and articulate intervals, the nature of which is to soothe the hearing in the midst of discord with the promise of a sweet concord to follow, and to sustain it with that same expectation. Truly, it was a persuasion worthy of a Christian man that it is God who moderates the entire **Melody of human life**; it is a patience worthy of the greatness of God not to be offended by the long duration of dissonances, nor to cast away hope; considering that it is not of God...

<summary>Kepler praises King James I as a philosopher-king capable of understanding the mathematical harmonies of the universe and reveals that he had intended to dedicate this book to him for nearly two decades.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Kepler, King James I, Tycho Brahe, Pythagoras, Plato, Harmonies of the Heavens, Astrology vs Astronomy, Dissonance, Providence</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to King James I. On the previous page, Kepler began a sentence explaining that while he had intended to dedicate this work to the King twenty years ago, he realized that God’s providence moves at a different pace than human life. This page completes that thought and praises James for uniting England and Scotland.</meta>

# DEDICATION.

...providence to move slowly, but the span of our individual lives to fly swiftly by. I was indeed taught by the sacred oracles <note>referring to Holy Scripture</note> that all things are destined by God for certain and beneficial uses: even these dissonant things, intended to illuminate and recommend the sweetness of Harmony. Why my desires commanded me to expect some beginning of restored harmony specifically from your **Davidic Harp**, <note>original: "Harpe Dauidica"; Kepler likens King James to the biblical King David, a musician and unifier</note> Illustrious King—although this is not the place to explain at length, lest I seem to disregard the warnings of the prudent—yet no one should prevent me from touching upon this part of your glory, long acknowledged by the whole world: that having obtained the kingdom of England by inheritance and the consent of the people, you shortly gave it the name of **Great Britain** common with the Kingdom of Scotland. From both provinces you tempered together one Kingdom and one **Harmony** (for what else is a kingdom, if not Harmony?); you most happily removed the hereditary discord of the most hostile nations; you utterly extinguished the memory of the frequent and bloodiest slaughters, which, like certain markers, punctuated the sequence of centuries.

This domestic work of yours seemed to me to contain a reliable omen (among other weightier matters) that even abroad, as a King among Kings, and as **Defender of the Faith** <term>Defender of the Faith (Fidei Defensor): A title held by the British monarch, here suggesting James's role as a peacemaker in Christendom</term> among Christ’s faithful, you would perform some greater and more excellent, and even more lasting work. This is what I pursued both with my silent prayers and with a public prophecy in my book on the **New Star** <note>Kepler refers to his 1606 work *De Stella Nova*, which discussed the supernova of 1604</note>, which burned like a Carbuncle (*a well-known Scottish verse* <note>original: "notus Scotiæ versiculus"; likely a reference to a poem or heraldic motto familiar to the King’s court</note>). Therefore, as if what I hoped for and predicted were already accomplished, I proposed all the more firmly to myself to eventually sing my **World Harmonies** to so praiseworthy an **Organizer of Harmony** <term>Harmost (Harmoste): from the Greek *harmostēs*, a term for a regulator or governor who brings order</term>.

I could wish here that the public **Dissonance**, consisting of three-fold clamoring voices <note>Kepler is likely referring to the religious strife between Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists during the early stages of the Thirty Years' War</note>, were a little milder toward me, so that I might be heard publicly according to my heart’s desire: in which matter, what outcome might have seemed to favor my prayers? What wounds of the head, what...

<summary>Kepler praises King James I for the peaceful unification of England and Scotland into Great Britain, viewing this political "harmony" as a terrestrial reflection of the celestial harmonies he describes in his book.</summary>

<keywords>King James I, Great Britain, Scotland, Harmony, Davidic Harp, Defender of the Faith, De Stella Nova, political unity, Thirty Years' War</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to King James I, picking up from the previous page's discussion of the King as a "Defender of the Faith" and a potential source of peace. The catchword "tibi" from the previous page likely combined with "quibus" to complete the phrase "by which Harmonies."</meta>

# DEDICATION.

...by which *Harmonies* <note>original: "Harmoniis"</note> was the attempt made, and by which *Physician*? <note>original: "Medico"</note> And how I even depicted this man in vivid colors long ago in my book on the *New Star*? <note>Kepler refers to his 1606 work *De Stella Nova*, which discussed the supernova of 1604 and its astrological/providential significance.</note> But what reward will there be if, while reaching for *Harmony* with my own private noise, I fail to overcome the public clamor due to the weakness of my lungs, and only increase the annoyance of this absurd concert in my own ears? It must indeed be confessed, alas, that the "crossed" wound—or if we prefer a more sacred and auspicious word, the **cruciform** <note>cross-shaped; Kepler is likely using the shape of a surgical incision as a metaphor for the religious divisions of the Reformation, symbolized by the Cross</note> wound—still swells with its many edges. None of them are closing, and the medicine has so far been ineffective and mocked by all sides. This is because the *Physician*, in order to slip a deceptive remedy to a delirious patient, adds many things at once that seem to stray far from sound reason.

I am refreshed, however, by this very thought: that the supreme *Healer* <note>original: "Curator"</note> of our wounds is certain of his art and applies nothing in vain. Therefore, He who has already begun the cure, who has already prepared and shown to the world these healing medicines; meanwhile, He makes use of the "corrosives" <note>substances used to eat away dead tissue</note> of public calamities until the putrid and wild flesh—the flesh of extinguished charity—is eaten away, and a sense of pain reaches down into the depths of the living flesh. Without a doubt, that same Healer will soon use soothing treatments to reduce the swelling, so that those healing medicines can finally take effect. At last, this long-lasting *Dissonance* (to return to my original example) will end in pure and lasting *Harmony*. 

I am confirmed in this hope, even against hope, not only by the success of my *Harmonic* speculations—where my good fortune has far exceeded my daring in the search—but also by this very fact: that among the other things necessary for the perfection of this Work that have remained in their original place for so many years, I have seen **Your Royal Majesty**, to whom I had destined the patronage of this work before it even began, remain safe and flourishing to this day. I shall not cease to petition the **God of Peace and Concord**, their author, with devoted prayers, so that...

<summary>Kepler uses medical and musical metaphors to describe the religious and political strife of Europe, expressing hope that God (the "Supreme Healer") will eventually resolve these dissonances into a lasting harmony, while praising King James I as a surviving symbol of that hope.</summary>
<keywords>Harmony, Physician, New Star, religious conflict, King James I, Divine Providence, Dissonance, medicine</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dedication of Kepler’s work. While the previous page discussed the religious and political turmoil of Europe (likely addressing King James I of England, as noted in the previous metadata), the signature block here identifies Kepler by his official title as the Mathematician to Holy Roman Emperor Matthias. The text transitions from a prayer for the King's safety to a formal closing and signature.</meta>

# DEDICATION.

...may He <note>Referring to God</note> guard both your life and Royal Majesty safely, even until that longed-for outcome.

Meanwhile, I humbly ask Your Most Reverend Majesty to look upon this work of *Harmony* <note>original: *Harmonices*, referring to the title of the book *Harmonices Mundi*</note>, dedicated to your Name, with a serene countenance, and to consider this expression of my most devoted affection toward you as just and good. Indeed, may you delight your royal mind in the contemplation of the Works of God, as much as the necessary occupations of the Kingdom permit. And by the examples of Harmony shining forth from the visible works of God, may you confirm and stir up within yourself a zeal for Harmony and for Peace, both Ecclesiastical and Political. Finally, may you deign to favor me and my studies with your most merciful Royal patronage. Given at Linz <note>original: *Lentiis Noricis*; Linz was the capital of Upper Austria where Kepler worked at the time</note> on the banks of the Danube, on the Ides of February <note>February 13th</note>, in the Year of the Western Era 1619.

->Your Most Serene Royal Majesty<-

->Venerating you with all submission,<-

->Mathematician to the Imperial Caesar Matthias,<-

## DEDICATION

...to you both life and the bright <unclear>course</unclear> of several of his mathematical works. 

Meanwhile, may Your Majesty see to it that I may appear [worthy], so that you do not close the way to this *Harmony* and <unclear>blending</unclear> <note>original: *Commixtionemque*; likely referring to the blending of musical and mathematical theory</note>, and that you might show such affection and favor toward me as is granted to good men: in the contemplation of the Works of God <note>Kepler viewed his astronomical work as a religious duty to uncover the "thoughts of God" through geometry</note> and in Royal service, as far as your kingly occupations will allow: and by these examples, a Partner in splendor from the venerable works in Partnership; and it belongs to [your] children and whoever else: to be practiced: and whoever [is] mine, in every way and proportion. DE FIGURARUM HARMON:
<note>original: "DE FIGURARUM HARMONIA" — On the Harmony of Figures</note>

# Preface.

<margin>Proclus on the intellectual essence of geometric things.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring ornate foliate designs and scrolled patterns in a square frame.</image-desc>Since we must seek the causes of Harmonic Proportions from the divisions of a circle into equal parts—divisions which are performed geometrically and scientifically (that is, from demonstrable regular plane figures)—I thought it necessary to point out at the start that the mental differences <note>Kepler means the conceptual or "intellectual" distinctions that exist in the mind rather than just physical properties.</note> of geometric things are, today, as far as can be seen from published books, entirely ignored. Thus, among the ancients, no one occurs to me who indicated that they exactly understood these specific differences of geometric things, except for Euclid and his commentator Proclus. To be sure, the distribution of problems into Plane, Solid, and Linear by Pappus of Alexandria <note>Pappus (c. 290–350 AD) was one of the last great Greek mathematicians; "Plane" problems used only a compass and straightedge, "Solid" used conic sections, and "Linear" used more complex curves.</note>, and the ancients whom he follows, is appropriate enough for explaining the mental habits arising around each <gloss>part</gloss> of the geometric subject; yet that distribution is both brief in words and applied to practice. No mention is made of theory. Truly, unless we occupy our whole mind with the theory of this matter, we will never be able to attain the harmonic ratios. Proclus the Successor <note>Diadochus, meaning "the Successor" to Plato’s Academy.</note>, in his four books on the first book of Euclid, acted professedly as a Theoretical Philosopher regarding mathematical subjects. If only he had also left us his commentaries on the tenth book of Euclid! <note>Book X of Euclid’s *Elements* deals with "irrational" lines, a notoriously difficult topic that Kepler found essential for his theories of harmony.</note> It would have freed our geometers from a neglected ignorance and relieved me of the heavy labor of explaining the differences of geometric things from the ground up. For it is easily apparent from his very introduction that those distinctions of Mental Beings <note>original: "Entium Mentalium" — things that exist as concepts in the mind.</note> were well known to him, since he establishes that the principles of the whole mathematical essence are the same ones that permeate all Beings and give birth to all things from themselves: namely, the Limit <gloss>that is</gloss> and the Infinite; or the Bound and the Unbounded. He recognizes the bound or the "circumscription" as the Form, and the "unbounded" as the Matter of geometric things.

For Configuration and Proportion are proper to quantities: configuration belongs to individual things, while proportion belongs to things joined together. Configuration is perfected by boundaries: for a line is bounded by points, a plane surface by lines, and a body is bounded, circumscribed, and shaped by surfaces. Therefore, those things which are finite, circumscribed, and shaped can also be grasped by the mind; but the infinite and indeterminate, insofar as they are such, can be narrowed down by no knowledge (which is compared to definitions) and by <gloss>no</gloss> barriers of demonstration. Furthermore, figures exist in the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" is the original divine blueprint or "idea" in the mind of God.</note> before they exist in the Work; they are in the divine mind before they are in creatures; though different in the manner of their subject, they are nonetheless the same in the form of their essence. Therefore, configuration is a certain Mental essence for quantities, or a "thought-process," which is their essential difference. This is much clearer from proportions. For since configuration is perfected by several boundaries, it happens that because of this plurality, configuration makes use of proportions. But what a proportion might be without the action of the mind can in no way be understood. And for this reason, he who gives boundaries to quantities as an essential principle posits that shaped quantities have an intellectual essence. But there is no need for argument; let the whole book of Proclus be read. It will be sufficiently apparent that the intellectual differences of geometric things were well known to him; even if he does not place this affirmation so separately and alone in the open as to warn even a drowsy reader. For his speech flows like a full river-bed, paved on all sides with the most abundant sentiments of the more abstruse Platonic philosophy, among which is also this unique argument of this book:

<meta>catchword: Verum (But/Indeed)</meta>

# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK 1.

<margin>Peter Ramus’s unfair and ignorant judgment of Euclid.</margin>
But our own age has not yet found the time to penetrate such hidden depths. Peter Ramus <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572) was a famous French scholar who sought to reform—and often simplify—the teaching of logic and mathematics, frequently attacking established authorities like Aristotle and Euclid.</note> did read the book of Proclus, but as far as the core of its philosophy is concerned, it was despised and thrown away, along with the tenth book of Euclid. Proclus, who had written a commentary on Euclid as if he were writing a defense for him, was rejected and ordered to be silent; indeed, the anger of that hostile Critic was turned against Euclid himself as if he were a criminal. Euclid’s tenth book was condemned with a harsh sentence so that it should not be read—even though, if read and understood, it could reveal the mysteries of philosophy. Please read Ramus’s own words, than which he never uttered anything more unworthy of himself: *Mathematical Schools, Book 21.* <note>original: "Scholarum Math. lib. 21"</note> *The subject matter,* he says, *presented in the tenth book, is handed down in such a way that I have never found similar obscurity in human literature or arts: I call it obscurity not in understanding what Euclid teaches (for that can be clear even to the unlearned and illiterate, who look only at what is right in front of them), but in perceiving deeply and exploring what the purpose and use of the work might be, or what the types, species, and differences of the subjects are; for I have never read or heard of anything so confused or tangled. Indeed, the Pythagorean superstition seems to have been led into this place like a cave, etc.* 

But by Hercules, Ramus, if you had not believed this book too easy to understand, you would never have slandered it with such talk of "obscurity." There is a need for greater labor, a need for quiet, a need for care, and a special attention of the mind, until you grasp the author's intent. When a noble mind has struggled toward that goal, then at last, seeing itself moving in the light of truth, it is bathed in incredible pleasure and exults; and from that watchtower, as it were, it perceives the whole World and all the differences of its parts most exactly. But as for you, who here act as the patron of ignorance and of the common mob—those who seek profit from everything, whether divine or human—to you, I say, let those things be "monstrous sophisms." To you, Euclid may have immoderately wasted your leisure; to you, those sharp points of logic may have no place in Geometry. Let it be your lot to pluck at what you do not understand. For me, who investigates the causes of things, no paths have opened toward them except through the tenth book of Euclid.

<margin>Lazarus Schoner.</margin>
Lazarus Schoner <note>A mathematician and contemporary of Kepler who edited some of Ramus’s works.</note>, following Ramus in his own *Geometry*, confessed that he could see absolutely no use for the five Regular solids in the World until he had read through my little book, which I titled *The Secret of the Universe* <note>original: "Mysterium Cosmographicum" — Kepler's 1596 work arguing that the distances between planets were determined by the five Platonic solids.</note>. In that book, I prove that the number and intervals of the Planets are derived from the five Regular solids. See how the teacher Ramus harmed his pupil Schoner! First, having read Aristotle—who had refuted the Pythagorean philosophy regarding the properties of the Elements being deduced from the five solids—Ramus immediately conceived a contempt for the whole of Pythagorean philosophy. Then, since he knew Proclus had belonged to the Pythagorean sect, he did not believe him when he affirmed what was most true: namely, that the ultimate goal of Euclid's work, to which absolutely all the propositions of all the books refer (except those leading to the Perfect Number), is the five regular solids. From this arose the most confident persuasion in Ramus that the five solids were to be removed from the goal of Euclid’s *Elements*.

Once the goal of the work was taken away—just as if the design of a building were removed—there remained in Euclid only a formless heap of propositions. Ramus attacks this heap, as if it were some ghost, throughout all twenty-eight books of his *Scholarum*, saying great—

->### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES###<-

...with a bitterness of speech and a great rashness, most unworthy of such a man. 
<margin>Lazarus Schöner’s opinion on the five solid figures.</margin>
Schöner <note>Lazarus Schöner (1543–1607) was a German mathematician and follower of Ramus.</note>, following this persuasion of Ramus, also came to believe that the regular bodies were of no use. Not only this, but he also neglected or despised Proclus, following the judgment of Ramus—the very Proclus from whom he could have learned the use of the five bodies both in Euclid’s *Elements* and in the construction of the World. Indeed, the student was more fortunate than the Master, because Schöner eventually welcomed with gratitude the use of these bodies in the Construction of the World that I revealed, which Ramus had rejected when Proclus urged it. For what does it matter if the Pythagoreans attributed these figures to the elements <note>The "four elements": Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>, and not, as I do, to the Spheres of the World? Ramus should have striven to remove this error of theirs regarding the true subject of the figures, just as I have done; he should not have abolished this entire philosophy with a single tyrannical word. What if the Pythagoreans taught the exact same thing as I do, but covered their meaning in a cloak of words?

<margin>A mystical interpretation of the Pythagoreans regarding the five figures.</margin>
Does not the Copernican form of the World exist in Aristotle himself, though wrongly refuted by him under other names? For they called the Sun "Fire," and the Moon the "Counter-earth" <note>original: "Antichthona". A hypothetical body in Pythagorean astronomy.</note>. For if the arrangement of the spheres was the same among the Pythagoreans as it is in Copernicus; if the five known Bodies were recognized, along with the necessity of their five-fold number; and if they all constantly taught that the five bodies are the Archetypes for the parts of the World—how much more should we believe that Aristotle read their opinion as a riddle, and refuted it as if the words held their literal sense? For example, Aristotle read "Earth," to which they gave the <term>Cube</term> <note>A six-sided regular solid.</note>, when they perhaps actually meant Saturn, whose orbit is separated from Jupiter by the insertion of a Cube. The common people ascribe "rest" to the Earth, but Saturn was allotted the slowest motion, which is closest to rest; for this reason, it even obtained its name from "Rest" among the Hebrews <note>The Hebrew name for Saturn is *Shabbathai*, sharing a root with *Shabbat* (Sabbath/Rest).</note>. 

Similarly, Aristotle read that the <term>Octahedron</term> <note>An eight-sided regular solid.</note> was given to "Air," when they perhaps meant Mercury, whose orbit is enclosed by the Octahedron; and Mercury is no less swift (being indeed the swiftest of all) than Air is considered mobile. By the word "Fire," perhaps Mars was implied, which otherwise is named *Pyroeis* <note>original: "Pyroeis", meaning "The Fiery One" in Greek.</note> from fire, and to it was given the <term>Tetrahedron</term> <note>A four-sided regular solid, or pyramid.</note>, perhaps because its orbit is enclosed by this figure. And under the cloak of "Water," to which the <term>Icosahedron</term> <note>A twenty-sided regular solid.</note> was attributed, the star of Venus could have been hidden (since its path is contained by the Icosahedron), because the bodily humors are subject to Venus, and she herself is said to have been born from the foam of the sea, which is the origin of the name *Aphrodite* <note>original: "Αφροδιτη". The name is traditionally derived from the Greek *aphros*, meaning "foam."</note>. Finally, the word "World" could have signified the Earth, and the <term>Dodecahedron</term> <note>A twelve-sided regular solid.</note> could be ascribed to the "World" because the Earth’s path is contained by this figure, distinguished by twelve parts of length <note>Likely referring to the twelve months or the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>, just as that figure is contained by twelve planes around its whole circumference. Therefore, the fact that in the Mysteries of the Pythagoreans the five figures were distributed in this way—not among the Elements, as Aristotle believed, but among the Planets themselves—is most strongly confirmed by Proclus. Among other things, Proclus teaches that the goal of Geometry is to show how the heavens received fitting shapes for their specific parts.

<margin>Willebrord Snell’s opinion on Binomials.</margin>
Nor is there yet an end to the damage Ramus has done us. Look at Snell <note>Willebrord Snell (1580–1626), the Dutch astronomer and mathematician famous for the law of refraction.</note>, the most skillful of modern Geometers, clearly supporting Ramus in his preface to the problems of Ludolph van Ceulen <note>Ludolph van Ceulen (1540–1610) was a mathematician famous for calculating pi to 35 decimal places.</note>. First, he says that the division of "irrationals" into thirteen species is useless for practice. I grant this, if he recognizes no use except in common life, and if no con...

### ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I. ###

...of whether physical contemplations have a use for life. But why does he not follow Proclus, whom he cites, who recognizes some greater good in Geometry than the arts necessary for survival? If he had, the use of the tenth book would indeed have appeared in evaluating the types of figures. Snellius <note>Willebrord Snellius (1580–1626), a Dutch mathematician famous for the law of refraction.</note> cites authors and geometers who do not use the tenth book of Euclid. Truly, all of them treat either linear or solid problems, and deal with figures or quantities of a kind that do not have their end within themselves, but clearly tend toward other uses, and would not be sought out without them. But **regular Figures** are sought for their own sake as **Archetypes**; they have their perfection within themselves. They are among the subjects of planar Problems, despite the fact that a solid is also enclosed by planar faces; similarly, the material of the tenth book pertains primarily to planes. Why then should heterogeneous things be cited? Or why is a cargo esteemed as worthless because Codrus <note>A stereotypical name for a poor man in Roman poetry.</note> does not buy it to feed his belly, but Cleopatra buys it to adorn her ears? *Is it merely a cross fixed for their wits?* <note>original: "Crux tantùm defixa est ingenijs?" Kepler is mocking those who find the study of irrational numbers to be a form of mental torture.</note> Certainly it is for those who vex the **Ineffables** <note>The "Ineffables" refers to incommensurable or irrational magnitudes, which cannot be expressed as simple ratios of whole numbers.</note> with numbers—that is, by trying to speak them. But I treat these species not with numbers, nor through **Algebra**, but by the reasoning of the Mind; indeed, because I have no need of them to calculate the accounts of markets, but to explain the causes of things. 

He <note>Snellius/Ramus</note> thinks these subtle matters should be separated from the *Elementary Arrangement* <note>original: "στοιχειώσεı" (stoicheiōsei), referring to the systematic building up of geometric principles.</note> and hidden away in Libraries. He acts entirely as a faithful disciple of Ramus, and spends his effort quite foolishly: Ramus took away the form from the **Euclidean Building**, he cast down the roof—the five [regular] bodies—and when these were removed, the whole structure was dissolved. The walls stand cracked, the arches threatening to ruin. Snellius therefore even takes away the Mortar, as if it has no use except for the solidity of a house joined together under the five figures. O happy understanding of a disciple! How skillfully he learned to understand Euclid from Ramus: namely, they think the *Elements* <note>original: "Στοιχεῖα" (Stoicheia).</note> are so named because there is found in Euclid an all-encompassing abundance of propositions, problems, and Theorems for every kind of Quantity and the arts occupied with them. Yet the book was called an *Elementary Arrangement* because of its **form**, because the following proposition always rests upon the preceding one, all the way to the last proposition of the last book (and partly the ninth book), which cannot do without any of the prior ones. They turn the Architect into a wood-cutter or a supplier of materials, thinking that Euclid wrote his book for the sake of serving all others, while he himself alone would have no house of his own. But enough of these matters in this place; I must return to the main point of the discourse.

<margin>The occasion for this Book I</margin>
For when I perceived that the true and genuine differences of geometric things (from which I must derive the causes of **Harmonic Proportions**) were generally ignored entirely; that Euclid, who had passed them down with great care, was being exploded and driven out by the quibbles of Ramus; and that, with the noise of the wanton disturbing him, he was heard by no one—or was telling the mysteries of Philosophy to the deaf; and that Proclus, who could have opened the mind of Euclid, unearthed hidden things, and made difficult concepts easy to grasp, was even a laughingstock and had not continued his Commentaries all the way to the tenth book: I saw that I absolutely had to do this. I decided that at the beginning, I would transcribe from the tenth book of Euclid those things which especially served my present purpose, and bring to light the series of matters in that book, with certain divisions cast between them...

->ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES<-

...I would show the reasons why certain parts of the divisions were omitted by Euclid; then, finally, I had to deal with the figures themselves. In those cases where matters were demonstrated very clearly by Euclid, I was content with a simple citation of his propositions. However, many things that were demonstrated by Euclid in another way had to be repeated here because of the goal I have set for myself—namely, for the **comparison of knowable and unknowable figures**—or separate things had to be joined, or the order changed. <note>Kepler distinguishes between "knowable" (constructible with a compass and straightedge) and "unknowable" (non-constructible) figures to explain why some shapes create "harmony" in the world and others do not.</note> I have embraced a sequence of Definitions, Propositions, and Theorems in a continuous numbering system, as I did in my *Dioptrics* <note>Kepler’s 1611 work on optics and the telescope.</note>, for the convenience of citation. I have not been overly precise even in the lemmas, nor too anxious about vocabulary, being more intent on the things themselves; for I am no longer acting as a **Geometer** in Philosophy, but as a **Philosopher** in this part of Geometry. And I wish that I could have discussed geometric matters even more popularly, provided it were clearer and more tangible. But I hope that fair-minded readers will think well of my labor in both respects: both that I hand down geometric matters in a popular way, and that I could not overcome the obscurity of the material through sheer industry. To those readers I also give this final piece of advice: if they are completely unskilled in mathematical matters, they should skip my explanations and read only the propositions, from number 30 to the end; and, having accepted the propositions themselves on faith without the demonstration, they should proceed to the remaining books, especially the last one; lest, frightened off by the difficulty of geometric arguments, they deprive themselves of the most delightful fruit of harmonic contemplation. Now let us approach the matter with God's help.

***

# On the demonstrations of Regular Figures.

## I. Definition.

A **regular plane figure** is called that which has all sides and all angles, facing outward, equal.

*As here in square QPRO, the sides OP, PR, RO, OQ, are equal, and the angles QPR, PRO, ROQ, OQP, are equal.*

<image-desc>A small diagram on the right side of the page depicting a square labeled with vertices Q (top-left), P (top-right), R (bottom-right), and O (bottom-left). A circle is inscribed within the square. A horizontal midline is drawn through the square, passing through the center L, with points M and N marked at the intersections with the circle or sides.</image-desc>

## II. Definition.

Of these, some are **primary and radical**, which do not exceed their own boundaries, to which the given definition properly applies. Others are **augmented**, which exceed their own sides, as it were, by extending the non-adjacent sides of some radical figure until they meet; these are called ***Stars***. <note>These are known today as star polygons or "Kepler-Poinsot" polyhedra in three dimensions.</note>

<meta>Catchword: As here</meta>

<summary>Kepler outlines his "philosophical" approach to geometry, prioritizing the comparison of constructible and non-constructible shapes over rigid Euclidean sequence, and defines regular and star polygons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the opening book of Kepler's *The Harmony of the World*, where he establishes the geometric foundations necessary for his later astronomical and musical theories. Having previously discussed the nature of quantity, he now moves into the formal definitions of regular and semi-regular polygons, specifically focusing on the pentagon and the pentagram.</meta>

->ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.<-

Just as A B C D E here is a perfect pentagon <note>original Latin: *quinquangulum*. Kepler uses this term for a five-sided polygon.</note>, it is a primary figure, not requiring any other perfect figure from which it might be produced by the extension of its sides.

<image-desc>Two circular geometric diagrams. The left circle contains an inscribed regular pentagon labeled A, B, C, D, E with a central point L. The right circle contains an inscribed five-pointed star (pentagram) with outer vertices labeled F, G, H, I, K and inner intersection points forming a pentagon labeled A, B, C, D, E.</image-desc>

On the other hand, F G H I K is a five-pointed star <note>original: *stella quinquangula*.</note>, an augmented figure formed by extending pairs of sides that are not adjacent to one another—for example, extending sides AB and DC until they meet at point K.

---

## III. Definition.

Semi-regular figures <note>original: *Semiregulares*.</note> are those which have four equal sides but varying angles, such as the Rhombuses <term>Rhombus: A four-sided shape where all sides are the same length, but the angles are not necessarily right angles (like a tilted square).</term> NMPO and GEKD.

<image-desc>Two rhombuses side-by-side. The left rhombus is labeled with vertices M, P at the top and N, O at the bottom. The right rhombus is labeled with vertices E, K at the top and G, D at the bottom.</image-desc>

---

## IV. Proposition.

All Regular figures can have all their angles rest upon the same circle at once.

For according to the 21st Proposition of the Third Book of Euclid <note>original: *21. Tertij Euclidis*. Kepler refers to Euclid's "Elements," the foundation of geometry.</note>, all equal angles can be inscribed in the same circle—and thus also in equal segments of the same circle. Since all angles of a Regular figure are equal, all the angles of a single figure can therefore be inscribed in equal segments of one circle. Furthermore, it is necessary that all angles are actually inscribed once a single one is inscribed. For all sides are equal; therefore, the segments of the circle cut off by the two sides of a single angle are also equal, according to the 24th Proposition of the Third Book of Euclid. Consequently, both the angle and the endpoints of the sides fit onto the same circle at the same time. The endpoints of the sides are, of course, the angles themselves. It would be otherwise if the sides were not equal, even if the angles were; in that case, the necessity of all points being inscribed would vanish.

---

## V. Definition.

To "describe" <note>In a geometric sense, "to describe" means to draw or construct a figure according to specific rules.</note> a Figure is to determine the proportion of the lines subtending the angles <term>Subtend: In geometry, this refers to a line segment that joins the two endpoints of an arc or an angle.</term> to the "legs" (sides) of the angle through a geometric act; from these determined parts, one constructs the elementary triangles of the figure, and from these triangles joined together, the figure itself is completed.

<image-desc>A diagram of a pentagon with vertices labeled A, B, C, D, E. Internal lines connect vertex A to vertices D and C, dividing the pentagon into three triangles labeled DAE, DAC, and CAB.</image-desc>

For given the proportion of the line DA to the sides AE and ED, the triangles DAE, DAC, and CAB are formed: the figure is composed of these.

### VI. Definition.

To **inscribe** a figure in a circle is to determine, through a geometric action, the proportion of the figure's side to the diameter of the circle in which it is to be inscribed; once this proportion is established, the proposed figure is easily drawn within the circle.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram. A circle is inscribed with a pentagon. Points on the circumference are labeled A, B, C, D, E. The center is labeled L. Dashed lines connect the center L to points A and D. A solid line connects L to D, labeled as the semidiameter (radius). Dashed lines also form the perimeter of the pentagon connecting A-B, B-C, C-D, D-E, and E-A.</image-desc>

*For example, if the radius <note>original Latin: *semidiameter*</note> LD (or its double, the diameter) is given, and if we know what steps to take with it to provide the side DE with its correct length, we then easily complete the figure by repeating that length DE around the circumference.*

### VII. Definition.

To **know** in geometric matters is to measure by a known measure; and in this business of inscribing figures into a circle, that "known measure" is the diameter of the circle.

### VIII. Definition.

A thing is said to be **knowable** <note>original: *scibile*</note> if it is either directly measurable by the diameter (if it is a line) or by its square (if it is a surface), or if it is formed at the very least from such quantities by a certain and geometric logic which, no matter how long the series of steps, ultimately depends on the diameter or its square. In Greek, this is called a *gnomon* <note>original: $\gamma\nu\acute{\omega}\mu\omega\nu$ — in geometry, this usually refers to the shape that remains when a smaller square is removed from a larger one, but Kepler uses it here to mean the "indicator" or "standard" of knowledge.</note>.

### IX. Definition.

**Demonstration** is the derivation of a quantity—whether it is to be drawn or known—from the diameter through possible intermediate steps. In Greek, it is called a *poiema* <note>original: $\Pi\acute{o}\epsilon\mu\alpha$, literally "a thing made" or "a creation."</note>.

*Thus, demonstration commonly produces either a description or knowledge. A description offers the bare quantity <note>i.e., just the physical drawing</note>, while knowledge further claims to understand its quality or its exact amount. However, a certain line can be geometrically determined—in Greek, *tache* <note>original: $\tau\acute{\alpha}\chi\eta$ — here used to mean a line that is "fixed" or "ordered."</note>—even if the mind does not yet know exactly what kind of line it is. Conversely, some quality of one or more lines might be known without that quality yet determining or necessitating the lines themselves—specifically if that quality is shared by many other things that differ in quantity. Furthermore, the description of certain lines is easy, while the knowledge of them is extremely difficult. Finally, many things can be drawn by some geometric action, yet they cannot be "known" by their own nature, according to the definition of "knowable" provided above.*

<summary>Kepler defines what it means to "know" a shape geometrically: it must be measurable in relation to the diameter of a circle. He distinguishes between the simple physical act of drawing a shape (description) and the intellectual understanding of its proportions (knowledge).</summary>

## X. Definition.

A **proper proof** occurs when the number of angles of a figure—either of the figure itself, or of one related to it by double or half the number of sides—serves as the "middle term" <note>In logic, the "middle term" is the link that connects two ideas to reach a conclusion.</note> to determine the proportion that the side has to the diameter.

For every regular figure is either a triangle itself or can be broken down into triangles by drawing diagonal lines. Since every such triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, the angle of a triangle <note>original: *Trigonico*</note> is one-third of two right angles; in the smallest elementary triangle of a square <note>original: *Tetragonici*</note>, it is one-fourth; in a pentagon <note>original: *Pentagonici*</note>, it is one-fifth; in a heptagon <note>original: *Heptagonici*</note>, one-seventh, and so on. The proof for any figure begins from this specific quantity of the angle.

## XI. Definition.

An **improper proof** occurs when the proportion of the side to the diameter cannot be determined geometrically from the number of angles directly, unless the side of a different figure is used—one that is not simply a double or half the number of sides.

## XII. Definition.

There are different **degrees of knowledge**: some are distant and others are close. The **first and closest degree** is when I know a certain line and can prove it is equal to the diameter, or a surface—though shaped differently—that is equal to the square of the diameter.

In this case, a known measure perfectly measures the object of study by itself and in a single act.

## XIII. Definition.

The **second degree** occurs when the diameter is divided into a certain number of equal parts (or its square is divided similarly), and the proposed line or surface is equal to one or more of those parts. In Greek, such a line is called <term>expressible in length</term> <note>original: ῥητὴ μήκει (*rhētē mēkei*); this refers to lines that have a whole-number ratio to the diameter.</note>. A surface of this kind is simply called <term>expressible</term> <note>original: ῥητόν (*rhēton*); often translated in geometry as "rational."</note>. For number is the language of Geometers.

We arrive at this degree of knowledge either through drawing and inscribing the figure, or through its relationship with some other quantity that was reached by those means. Therefore, this quality does not define one specific quantity; for it is not enough for a definition to know that something is related in this or that way for the sake of commensurability <note>The ability for two things to be measured by the same standard.</note>. One must also know *how* it is expressible—that is, by what specific number.

### XIV. Definition.

The **Third Degree** is this: when a line's length is **Inexpressible** <note>original: *Ineffabilis*; refers to a value that cannot be stated as a simple ratio or whole number relative to the diameter.</note>, but its square is **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabile*</note> and belongs to the second degree. It is called <term>expressible in power</term> <note>original: *ῥητὴ δυνάμει* (rhetē dynamei). This describes a line like the square root of 2, which is irrational as a length, but becomes a rational whole number when squared.</note>.

### XV. Definition.

<margin>What "Irrational" means to Latin Geometers.</margin>
The degrees that follow are all called <term>Inexpressible</term> <note>original: *Ἄλογοι* (Alogoi), literally "without speech" or "without ratio."</note>. Latin translators have rendered this as "Irrational," which risks great ambiguity and absurdity <note>Kepler argues that "irrational" implies something is against reason, whereas these geometric proportions follow strict logical laws.</note>. Let us bury this use of the word, because there are many lines which, although Inexpressible, are nonetheless contained within the best of ratios.
<margin>Surd Numbers.</margin>
Arithmeticians, using a similar metaphor, call these **surd numbers**—that is, numbers that "speak" no more than a deaf man hears <note>The term "surd" comes from the Latin *surdus* (deaf/silent). In Kepler’s time, this referred to roots that could not be expressed as integers or fractions.</note>. But under this name, they include both quantities expressible only in power and those that are truly inexpressible. Therefore, the fourth degree in order, but the first of the truly inexpressible ones, occurs when neither the line nor its square are Expressible; yet the square can be transformed into a rectangle whose sides are Expressible, at least in power. This line is called the <term>Medial</term> <note>original: *ΜΕΣΕ* (Mese), meaning "middle."</note> because it is the mean proportional between two lines that are expressible only in power and are commensurable <note>Commensurable means they can be measured by the same shared unit.</note>: as when one is Expressible in length and the other only in power; or if both are Expressible only in power, yet their powers are not in the ratio of one square number to another.

Such a line is not known or measured by the length of specific equal parts of the diameter, nor is its square measured by the square of the diameter. Furthermore, the two lines between which the <term>Medial</term> is the mean proportional are not both measured by the diameter; only the squares of those lines are eventually measured by the square of the diameter.

The square of a <term>Medial</term> line is itself called a <term>Medial Area</term> <note>original: *MESON*</note>, whether it is in the form of a square or transformed into a rectangle. This is the second type of Plane, after the Expressible plane. By these two planes—the Expressible and the Medial—the species that follow are distinguished from one another.

### XVI. Definition.

We now transition to other singular lines by coupling two lines together, which themselves introduce new degrees of knowledge. For let the diameter, or something commensurable to it (at least in power, and thus Expressible), or even a Medial line, be cut into two unequal parts. Or, let any two parts be compared from the sections of two such lines—either composed of parts, or having powers that are composed or diminished from such parts—two lines, I say, that are generally unequal. These will either be commensurable to each other in length, or they will be incommensurable in length but commensurable in power. Here, although the individual lines have clearly moved away from commensurability, some of them, when joined together—either by their squares being combined into one sum, or by a rectangle formed between them—constitute planes which thus far ex-

...[explained], no less than those do which are commensurable among themselves. Moreover, since the coupling of two such plainly incommensurable lines is manifold—one being less noble than another—we cannot place all pairs in the same rank.

## XVII. Definition.

Let there be, therefore, the **fifth degree of knowledge**: when two lines, which are neither both Expressible nor both Medial <note>original: *Mesæ*; a Medial line is the square root of a rectangle formed by two expressible lines commensurable only in power.</note>, and are furthermore plainly incommensurable with one another, produce an Expressible result in both cases: the sum of their squares and their shared Rectangle. They do this no less than two lines that are expressible in length (according to Euclid's *Elements*, Book X, Proposition 20), or even two lines expressible only in power but nevertheless commensurable in length with each other. For example, the side of a square of 2 <note>$\sqrt{2}$</note> and the side of a square of 8 <note>$\sqrt{8}$</note> are in a double proportion <note>1:2</note> to each other, because their squares are in a quadruple proportion <note>2:8, which is 1:4</note>. Therefore, they are indeed Inexpressible in length, yet commensurable with each other. Their squares, 2 and 8, joined together make the Expressible area 10. And when they are multiplied by each other (which is to form a Rectangle), they produce the rectangle 4, which is also expressible. This same thing, I say, is achieved by two lines that are neither Expressible nor Medial, and are further plainly incommensurable; and for that reason, they are not to be referred to the second or third degrees of knowledge like the former ones, but to the **Fifth**.

Note, therefore, that in this degree we measure neither the lines themselves nor their individual squares, but we measure both their shared Rectangle and the sum of both squares joined into one total; so that whatever one square lacks in being expressible is exactly compensated for by the other associated square.

## XVIIII. Definition. <note>Kepler's numbering skips XVIII or treats this as the 19th definition.</note>

The **sixth and more ignoble degree of knowledge** is when two lines are joined which are neither expressible nor Medial, and are also incommensurable with each other, but they produce at least one Expressible result, while the other is Medial <note>original: *Meson*</note>. This degree is twofold: for either the sum of the squares is expressible and the Rectangle is Medial; or the sum is Medial and the Rectangle is expressible.

*In the former effect, they are similar to two lines that are Expressible and commensurable only in power. For being commensurable in power, their squares are Expressible, and they also make the sum of both Expressible; but the Rectangle is Medial, according to Euclid, Book X, Proposition 22.*

*In the latter effect, they are similar to two Medial lines commensurable only in power, which are related to each other as two Expressible lines are, among which the first of the two Medials is the proportional Mean; according to Euclid, Book X, Propositions 26 and 28. For because they are commensurable in power, when the power is added, they produce a sum commensurable with the parts. But the parts are Medial, and that which is commensurable to a Medial is itself also Medial, according to Euclid, Book X, Proposition 24.*

## XIX. Definition.

The seventh, even more lowly <note>original: *ignobilior*; Kepler ranks geometric relationships by how "knowable" or "noble" they are; the more irrational a line, the more "ignoble" it is.</note> degree of knowledge is when, of two lines incommensurable with each other, neither result is expressible <note>original: *effabilis*; in geometry, this refers to a line whose square is rational or "knowable."</note>—neither the sum of the squares nor the shared Rectangle—but nevertheless both are still Medial. <note>original: *Meson*; a Medial line is the square root of an area formed by two lines that are commensurable only when squared.</note>

*These lines are similar in their effect: two Medial lines commensurable only in power, where one is to the other as one of those between which the MEDIAL is truly a Mean proportional—namely, those commensurable only in power—is to some third line commensurable only in power, according to Proposition 29 of Euclid's Tenth Book.*

*Euclid teaches how to find these three pairs, distinguished by two types of Areas, primarily because they contribute to the composition and construction of the species that follow.*

## XX. Definition.

Therefore, the Eighth Degree of knowledge is derived from the preceding intermediate steps. It concerns individual lines once again, but those which are formed by the composition of "two names"—that is, two lines joined from the preceding pairings—or by the subtraction of one (called the Fitting Line <note>original: *Epharmozusæ*; from the Greek for "fitting" or "coinciding," referring to the part subtracted from a whole to create an Apotome.</note>) from its partner, creating a new species. Thus, in these, we know or measure not the whole lines, nor the squares of the wholes, nor the two Names of each, but their joined squares and their shared Rectangle, as in the preceding XVIII and XIX. And although we could count as many degrees of knowledge as there will be species—of which the earlier is always more noble than the later—nevertheless, because any composition or subtraction refers back to its own degree, and no difference is established by the act of composition or subtraction itself (since they all relate equally to their pairs of Names or Elements), we shall therefore make only one degree for them: but let us recognize its species as being distinguished by their nobility.

## XXI. Proposition.

It must be understood, however, that from two lines commensurable with each other in length, nothing arises that ought to be taken into account here: whether they be Expressible, or Medial, or more Lowly.

*For if they are commensurable in length, the whole composed from them will also be commensurable with the parts. But that which is measured against an Expressible line is itself Expressible:*

Having passed over those lines that are commensurable in length, let us approach those that are commensurable only in power <note>Lines are "commensurable in power" when their squares can be measured by the same area, even if the lines themselves cannot be measured by a single ruler.</note>. Therefore, if two such Expressible <note>original: *Effabiles*; lines whose squares are rational.</note> lines are joined, the result is a BINOMIAL <note>original: *Binominis*; a line made of two parts or "names."</note>: but if they are subtracted, the remainder becomes an APOTOME <note>A line formed by subtracting a smaller rational line from a larger one.</note>: there are six subordinate species of each.

Here it is not permitted to join an Expressible line with a MEDIAL: for two such lines are simply incommensurable, a category that must be dealt with in what follows.

## XXIII. Proposition.

There remain, therefore, lines that are plainly incommensurable with one another. Of these, some pairs cannot provide the required effects, such as two Medials, or one MEDIAL with one Expressible line.

*The former is due to the lowliness <note>original: *ignobilitatem*</note> of the pair, while the latter is due to their conflicting Natures. Therefore, no species of composition can be derived from here; and we are left only with the Lowlier species, excluding both the Expressible and the Medial lines.*

## XXIV. Proposition.

From the first pair of such plainly incommensurable lines—namely, those knowable at the fifth degree in the preceding Proposition XVII—a new Expressible line is born again by adding or subtracting them; and these are necessarily the BINOMIAL and the APOTOME (see Propositions 112, 113, and 114 of Euclid’s Tenth Book). For example, if both the sum of the squares of the Binomial and Apotome, and the common Rectangle between them, are Expressible, then each Name <note>original: *Nomina*; the individual terms or segments of a compound line.</note> of the one must be commensurable with each Name of the other, which does not happen in all BINOMIALS and APOTOMES.

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES

The **Binomial** <note>original: *Binominis*; a line composed of two parts that are rational only in power, like $1 + \sqrt{2}$</note> and the **Apotome** <note>original: *Apotome*; a "cutting away," specifically a line formed by subtracting one rational part from another, like $1 - \sqrt{2}$</note> are demonstrated in the same manner as shown in Proposition 33 of Euclid’s tenth book; only here, instead of two lines that are rational in power only <note>original: *ῥηταῖς δυνάμει μόνον*</note>, lines that are rational in length <note>original: *ῥηταὶ μήκει*</note> are used. Wherever the word "medial" <note>original: *μέσον*</note> occurs, "expressible" <note>original: *ῥητὸν*</note> should be placed; and finally, the definitions of the Binomial and the Apotome should be compared.

However, it is clear why an **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabilis*; a line or area that can be expressed in terms of the initial unit</note> line is produced again from the composition (joining) and abstraction (subtraction) of the Binomial and Apotome, which perform the two required effects. For since the sum of the squares is Expressible, and the rectangle is Expressible; therefore, the square of the lines joined together into one will consist of the square of each part and two common rectangles—specifically, from two Expressible parts. For this reason, the whole square will be Expressible; and therefore, so is the composite line which is "powerful" over that square <note>original: *potens illud quadratum*; in geometry, a line is "powerful" over the area its square produces</note>. Let $λμ$ be the Binomial, and its square be $xο$; let $λθ$ be the Apotome, and its square be $θx$. When $θx$ and $xo$ are joined together, they are Expressible. Let the rectangle formed from $θλ$ and $λμ$ also be expressible; two such rectangles, $χμ$ and $νζ$, complete the square of the whole composite line $θμ$, which square is $θο$.

**A geometric diagram consisting of a square divided into several rectangular sections by horizontal and vertical lines. The vertices and intersection points are labeled with Greek letters: θ, λ, π, σ, and μ along the top edge; x and ν in the interior; and ζ and ο along the bottom edge.**

Regarding abstraction, it is proven in this way. If the line composed of $θλ$ and $μλ$ (that is, $θμ$) is expressible, then the half $θπ$ will also be Expressible as the "Greater Name" <note>original: *majus Nomen*; the larger of the two parts of a binomial</note>, and $πλ$ the "Lesser Name" <note>original: *Minus nomen*</note>, and the other half $πμ$. Subtract from it $μο$, which is equal to $θλ$; the remainder $πσ$ will also be Expressible, and the whole $λσ$ will be double that of $πσ$. But $πσ$ is what remains after the subtraction of the Apotome $μο$ from the Binomial $λμ$. Therefore, the remainder becomes Expressible.

---

->XXV. Definition.<-

Therefore, from the second pair of the sixth degree (previously mentioned in number XVIII), where the lines are completely incommensurable with one another and the sum of their squares is Expressible while their Rectangle is Medial: by joining them, the **GREATER** <note>original: *MIZON*</note> line is born; by subtraction, the **LESSER** <note>original: *ELASSON*</note> line. From the third pair, where the sum of squares is Medial and the Rectangle is Expressible: the line born by joining them is named **POWERFUL OVER AN EXPRESSIBLE AND A MEDIAL** <note>original: *POTENS EFFABILE ET MESON*</note>; the line born by subtraction is **MAKING WITH AN EXPRESSIBLE A MEDIAL AS A WHOLE** <note>original: *FACIENS CUM EFFABILI MESON TOTUM*</note>. Finally, from the fourth pair of the seventh degree (previously mentioned in number XIX), where both effects are Medial: by joining them comes the **POWERFUL OVER TWO MEDIALS** <note>original: *POTENS BINA MEDIA*</note>; by subtraction, the **MAKING WITH A MEDIAL A MEDIAL AS A WHOLE** <note>original: *FACIENS CUM MESO MESON TOTUM*</note>.

And behold the origin of the twelve species of Euclid, and the reasons for their number. For Euclid did not think he should proceed further to more remote species—those which produce either a sum of squares, a common rectangle, or both, that go beyond the Expressible and the Medial—into even lowlier <note>original: *ignobiliores*; Kepler classifies lines by "nobility," or how close they are to the perfection of a simple ratio</note> species.

# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

## XXVI. Definition and Comparison.

These points might have sufficed for us to establish the levels of Demonstrations by which the sides of figures—which are necessary for our **Harmonics** <note>original: *Harmonica*; the study of mathematical proportions in music, nature, and the cosmos</note>—are distinguished, were it not that certain other properties were added to those already reviewed; or rather, were it not that the properties reviewed so far were surpassed by other, nobler ones, which crown the levels of scientific Demonstrations.

We have come to composition and abstraction <note>In geometry, "composition" refers to adding line segments together, and "abstraction" refers to subtracting a shorter segment from a longer one.</note>; here we have taken the lines to be composed or subtracted loosely, with no necessity of a fixed quantity imposed upon them. But if we now tighten the laws by imposing a certain proportion on the pairs—not indeed given in such a way that those joined together form one of the twelve species [of irrational lines], but pairs given in another way: namely, where a straight line is given and its "greater part" is to be found. This occurs when the smaller part is to the larger as the larger is to the whole composed of both; or conversely, the larger is to the smaller as the smaller is to the residue <note>Kepler is describing the "Extreme and Mean Ratio" or Golden Ratio. If a line is divided this way, the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the larger segment to the smaller segment.</note>. What remains after the abstraction of the two parts will not always become some more remote degree; rather, as the situation arises, we fall back into one of the species already explained, and by making a return, we will compare the established line—which is of the **eighth degree** in itself—with lines of the **fourth degree**.

For just as in the fourth degree (Definition XV), two straight lines by their joint action formed a plane, from which (when reduced to a square) a line was born called the **Mese** <note>original: *Meſe*; the "middle" or Medial line, which is the square root of the product of two lines ($x = \sqrt{ab}$)</note>; so now two straight lines, the "Whole" and one "Part," form the other part itself by subtraction; or two parts form the whole by addition. In the former case, the lines forming the result were commensurable to each other only in power <note>Meaning their lengths are not simple ratios, but their squares are.</note>. Here, setting aside commensurability, there follows an **identity of proportion** between the whole and the parts. In the former case, there was a similarity of proportion between the smaller and the line to be produced, and between the line to be produced and the larger; here too there is a similarity of proportion between the two lines to be produced and between one of them and the proposed whole (in abstraction); or in composition, between the one to be produced and the proposed line, and between the proposed line and the other to be produced. In the former case, therefore, given two lines, a Rectangle was given equal to the square of the line to be produced, and thus the plane came before the line; here, on the contrary, once the two lines to be produced are made, there follows finally an equality between the Rectangle of the extremes and the square of the **Mean** <note>original: *Mediæ*</note>, according to Euclid, Book VI, Proposition 17, and Book II, Proposition 11.

In the former case, the forming lines had squares commensurable to the square of the proposed line. Here, Euclid teaches (Book VI, Prop. 30) to take a square that is **five-fourths** <note>original: *seſquintuplum*; literally "one and five-fold," but geometrically referring to the $5/4$ construction used to find $\sqrt{5}$</note> of the square of the proposed line, and from the side of this square to take away half of the proposed line, so that there remains the part to be established in the proposed line. Once this part is taken from the proposed line, the other required part is left (or, by adding it to the whole, a third required part is also made). By so many names, these parts seem to be reckoned in the fourth degree.

But at this point, the line is rendered nobler than the **Mese** itself, whatever position that proportion occupies: because the **Mese** depends on the proposed **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabili*; a rational/knowable starting line</note> line by a longer chain composed of four links; but the parts of this [proportion]...

rely on their own proportion, which they hold immediately to the **Rational** <note>original: *Effabilem*; literally "speakable," referring to lengths that can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers</note> line proposed. And so it happens that there can be many **Medial** lines <note>original: *Mesôn*; lines whose square is equal to a rectangle formed by two rational lines</note>, all distant from the Rational by the same degree; however, the "greater part" in this proportion of the Rational line itself is one and only one, and altogether for any line after the Rational, there is one singular part. By this name, its demonstration is equated in a certain way to the first level of certainty.

When, therefore, a proposed Straight line is ordered to be the whole, and two such parts of it are sought, then this is called by Geometers the section according to **Extremes and Mean** <note>The Golden Ratio. It is "Extreme and Mean" because the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the larger segment to the smaller segment</note>. This name effectively means that while a common section of a whole into two parts does not usually regard a specific proportion, here it is different. If, in a common section, some part is compared to the whole in the same proportion as the smaller part is to the larger, then four terms are created (two extremes and two means). In this section, by contrast, only three terms are created: the whole and the smaller part are the two extremes, while the larger part is the single mean term.

For the same reason, it is also called a proportional section. Modern authors call both the section and its proportion **Divine**, because of its admirable nature and manifold privileges. The chief of these is that if the larger part is always added to the whole, the newly composed line is again similarly sectioned; what was the larger part now becomes the smaller, and what was the whole now becomes the larger part of the new composite, according to Proposition 5 of the Thirteenth Book of **Euclid** <note>Euclid of Alexandria, the ancient Greek mathematician whose 'Elements' is the foundation of geometry</note>.

## XXVII. Proposition.

Since such a section has a place in all lines—in a line Rational in length, in a line Rational only in power, in a **Medial** line, in the twelve other species reviewed, and in all others—we have need in the present work of only two of its species, which coincide with the species explained so far, according to the two lines to be cut. For a line is either Rational in length, or it is **Greater** <note>original: *Mizon*; a specific type of irrational line defined in Euclid Book X</note>. If the line proposed for cutting is Rational in length, the larger part of the section becomes an **Apotome** <note>A type of irrational line formed by subtracting a smaller rational line from a larger one</note> of the fourth species; and a **Binomial** <note>A line formed by adding two rational parts</note> of the same fourth species corresponds to it, having common terms with it. But take care not to be confused: that part is called "greater" in relation to the proposed line; but the same line is called an "Apotome" here not in relation to the proposed line, but qualitatively. If you ask of what it is an apotome, the answer is that it is the apotome of something which is commensurable only in square to the proposed line—specifically, one that can produce five-fourths of the proposed line.
