which is as powerful <note>original: *potest*; in geometry, this refers to the area of a square formed by the line</note> as *GA*, as well as its half *AM*: so that if the power of *GA* itself is 4, the power of *AM* will be 1. And therefore, the power of *GM* will be 5. Insofar as *AO* or *AP* is an <term>Apotome</term> <note>A specific type of irrational line formed by subtracting one rational line from another when they are only "commensurable in power" (their squares share a common ratio, but their lengths do not).</note>, the <term>Binomial</term> <note>original: *binominis*; a line formed by the sum of two such rational parts.</note> *AX* corresponds to it: and their shared "names" <note>In Euclidean geometry, the "names" (nomina) are the two rational segments that make up a Binomial or Apotome.</note> are *MX*, or *MP*, or *MG*, and *AM*.

That *AP* is an Apotome, and *AX* a Binomial, both of the fourth species, is proved thus: For each name is <term>Rational</term> <note>original: *effabile*; a line that can be expressed in relation to a given standard. Here, Kepler uses it to mean lines whose squares are rational numbers.</note>, both *MX* and *MA*; yet they are commensurable only in power, because the square of *MX* (that is *MG*) is 5, while the square of *MA* is 1. But the ratio of 5 to 1 is not as a square number to a square number <note>Since 5 is not a perfect square, the lengths themselves cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers, only their squares can.</note>. Finally, the difference between the powers 1 and 5 is 4, which is a square number, whose side is 2—a length that is Rational, being equal to the proposed line *GA*. These indeed are the marks of the fourth species of Binomials, in the definitions before Proposition 74, and of Apotomes, before Proposition 85, of the tenth book of Euclid.

Finally, if the Rational line *GA* is cut <term>proportionally</term> <note>Cut according to the Golden Ratio (Extreme and Mean Ratio).</note>, its greater part *OA* and the line composed of both *OA* and *AG* fall into the fifth degree of knowledge. For their squares joined together make a Rational sum—namely, triple the square of the rational line *GA*, according to Proposition 4 of the thirteenth book of Euclid. The rectangle formed by them is also Rational, because it is equal to the square of the rational line *GA*, since *GA* is the mean proportional between the part *OA* and the composite line of *OA* and *AG*, through the preceding arguments.

## XXVIII. Proposition.

**Conversely, if any Rational line is cut proportionally in length, its smaller part shall be an Apotome of the first species.**

As if the Rational line were *GA*, as before, and its proportionally cut parts were the greater *AO* and the smaller *OG*: then *OG* will also be an Apotome, by Proposition 6 of the thirteenth book of Euclid.

Again, *OG* is called an Apotome qualitatively, not by its relation to the Rational length *GA* (of which it is the smaller part), nor by relation to *MG* or *MP* (of which *AO* or *AP* is an Apotome); rather, *GO* has its own peculiar "names." Since, by Proposition 97 of the tenth book of Euclid, the square of any Apotome—and likewise the square of *PO* extended to a Rational line (as here to *GT*, equal to *GA*)—creates a width *GO* that is an Apotome of the first species: conversely, *AO* itself was an Apotome of the fourth species. Therefore, the "greater name" of that *GO* is Rational in length; whereas the greater name of this *AO*, which was *MP*, was rational only in power. And conversely, because the names are commensurable only in power, it is necessary that the "lesser name," or the <term>Attached Part</term> <note>original: *prosharmozusa*; the segment added to or subtracted from the main line to complete the Euclidean definition of an irrational line.</note> of *GO* itself, be rational only in power; whereas the lesser name *AM* of *AO* was rational in length. Yet for both, this remains: that the difference of the squares described by the names is the square of some rational length.

However, as to what the names of this *GO* (the first Apotome) might be, I leave that for others to seek. Indeed, the Attached Part for *GO* as a First Apotome is unique according to Proposition 79 of the tenth book of Euclid. It must be such that its square is Rational but not a square number: and it, together with *GO*, must make one line that is Rational in length. And by Proposition 30 of the tenth book, if a diameter of a circle is made from this one whole—for example, *PX*—and if the Attached Part, a little longer than *PA* (if indeed the whole were equal to *PX*), is applied to the circumference *XG* from one end of the diameter *X*; then the line which connects the points *G* and *P* must be of a length commensurable to the whole *PX*.

## Proposition XXIX.

**When** a certain **Greater** line <note>original: *Mizon*; a specific type of irrational line defined in Euclid's *Elements*, Book X, Proposition 39</note> has been divided proportionally; and its square is equal to the rectangle formed by a length (composed of the proposed rational line and the line whose square is five-quarters of it) and a width whose square is five-quarters [of the same rational line]; then let the smaller part be the **Lesser** <note>original: *Elasson*; Euclid's term for an irrational line defined in Book X, Proposition 76</note>: here **Lesser** is a name indicating a specific mathematical quality, not merely a comparison of size: but let the larger part be another **Greater** line, again understood by its quality, whatever its component elements may be.

<margin>In the diagram on page 16.</margin>
As before, let the length of the proposed rational line be half $GA$, and let its own half be $AM$; so that in the same units where the square of $GA$ is 4, the square of $AM$ is 1. Let angle $GAM$ be a right angle; therefore, the square of $MG$ will be 5. Let $MA$ be extended on both sides, and with center $M$ and radius $MG$, let a semicircle $PGX$ be described. Thus $PX$ is double $GM$; for which reason the square of $PX$ will be five-quarters of the square of the line that is double $GA$. But since the squares of $PG$ and $GX$ joined together are equal to the square of $PX$ <note>By the properties of a semicircle, angle $PGX$ is a right angle, thus $PG^2 + GX^2 = PX^2$</note>, those squares are also five-quarters of the proposed rational square. Furthermore, if you combine $PG$ and $GX$ into a single line, its square will consist of the two squares of $PG$ and $GX$, plus two rectangles formed by $PG$ and $GX$. These are equal to two rectangles formed by $GA$ and $PX$—that is, one rectangle formed by the rational line (double $GA$) and the line $PX$. These two lines are rational but commensurable only in their squares <note>original: *solâ potentiâ commensurabilibus*; this means their lengths cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of one another, though their squares can</note>. For this reason, this rectangle will be **Medial** <note>original: *Meson*; a rectangle whose area is irrational, though it is formed by lines that are "rational in square"</note>, according to Euclid's *Elements*, Book X, Proposition 22. 

Since, therefore, the square of the whole line $PGX$ consists of the rational square $PX$ and a Medial rectangle of the same width $PX$: these two (the square $PX$ and the rectangle under the double of $GA$ and $PX$) are equal to a rectangle contained by $PX$ and the sum of $PX$ and the double of $GA$. These parts are commensurable only in square, and the square of the greater part $PX$ exceeds the square of the lesser (double $GA$) by a value commensurable with itself (for the square of $PX$ is 5 where the square of double $GA$ is 4; the difference of 1 is a square of a value that is incommensurable in length to $PX$, since 1 to 5 is not a ratio of a square number to a square number). For these reasons, the said composite of $PX$ and the doubled $GA$ is a **Binomial** of the fourth species. Since, I say, the square of the whole $PGX$ is equal to such a rectangle formed by a fourth **Apotome** <note>A line formed by subtracting one rational segment from another when they are only commensurable in power</note> and a rational line, the whole line $PGX$ will be a **Greater** line. The elements composing it are the parts $PG$ and $GX$. Because $PA$ is an Apotome and $AX$ a Binomial, they are incommensurable to each other in length. But as $PA$ is to $AX$, so is the square of $PG$ to the square of $GX$. Therefore $PG$ and $GX$ are incommensurable to each other in their squares and thus simply incommensurable; they produce a sum of squares that is rational (being equal to the square of $PX$), but the rectangle formed by $PG$ and $GX$ is Medial. 

Therefore, by Euclid X.39, the composite of $PG$ and $GX$ is a **Greater** line; and by Euclid X.76, if $PG$ is subtracted from $GX$, the remainder is a **Lesser** line. Furthermore, the whole $PGX$ is divided proportionally at $G$. For as $PA$ is to $AG$, so $PG$ is to $XG$. But $PA$ is the greater part of the proportionally divided $GA$ (labeled $OA$ elsewhere), because the square of $MP$ is five times the square of $MA$, and the Apotome $AP$ is equal to $AO$ by Euclid II.11. Therefore, $PG$ is also the greater part of the proportionally divided $GX$; and by Euclid XIII.5, if the greater part $PG$ is added to the whole $GX$, it creates a new whole $PGX$ which is itself proportionally divided at $G$. Thus, $PG$ is the smaller part of this composite, and $GX$ is the larger. In this way, $PGX$, being a **Greater** line, is divided at the same point $G$ both into its Euclidean elements and simultaneously into its parts of the <term>Divine Proportion</term> <note>The Golden Ratio, which Kepler identifies as the geometric key to cosmic harmony</note>.

### ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

I say that these same parts, when cut proportionally, are simultaneously the **Lesser** <note>original: *Elassona*; plural form of *Elasson*</note> and the **Greater** <note>original: *Mizona*; plural form of *Mizon*</note>. For since $AP$ is a fourth Apotome <note>A type of irrational line formed by subtracting one line from another, specifically defined in Euclid X.73-84</note>, then that which is under the Apotome $AP$ and the Rational line $PX$ <note>Kepler uses *Effabilis* for "Rational" or "Expressible"</note> is the "power" <note>In geometry, "power" often refers to the square of a line or the area of a rectangle representing its value</note> of a **Lesser** line, according to Proposition 94 of Euclid's tenth book. And because $AX$ is a fourth Binomial <note>A line composed of two rational parts</note>, that which is under this line and the Rational $PX$ is the power of a **Greater** line. But the squares of $PG$ and $GX$ are equal to the Rectangles $APX$ and $AXP$, each to each; therefore $PG$ is a **Lesser** line, and $GX$ is a **Greater** line.

Therefore, the names of qualities and the names of proportions meet here as one. For $PG$ is called the "smaller part" with respect to the whole $PGX$ proportionally cut at $G$; it is also called the "lesser line" or "lesser Element" of the whole $PGX$, just as the whole is a qualitative **Greater** line. Finally, it is called *Elasson* in Greek, which sounds like "minor" <note>smaller</note> in Latin, used qualitatively with respect to two other lines (not expressed here) from whose subtraction from one another it is constituted.

In the same way, $GX$ is first called the "larger part" of the whole $PGX$ cut proportionally; secondly, it is called the line or "greater Element" of the whole line $PGX$, as this is qualitatively a **Greater** line in its own right, no less than the whole $PGX$ is in its own. However, the lines that make up $GX$ itself as a **Greater** line through their composition are not expressed here.

Because of this convergence of the proportional section and the division of a **Greater** line into its Elements, I believe the qualitative names **Greater** <note>*Mizon*</note> and **Lesser** <note>*Elasson*</note> were bestowed upon these species.

However, we must be careful here not to confuse the distinctions between these things. A proportional section is an absolute proportion, not tied to any one specific line that is the first known (which is called the proposed Rational line). But those species of **Greater** and **Lesser** are formed by specific degrees of their distance from the first proposed Rational line. Thus, the "Divine Section" <note>The Golden Ratio</note> proceeds to infinity; but the attribute of being **Greater** or **Lesser** does not follow it. In that section, the part which was just now the larger becomes the smaller in the next step; but in this qualitative sense, the **Lesser** never—and in no respect—becomes the **Greater**, nor the **Greater** the **Lesser**. Thus, if the **Greater** line $GX$ is divided again proportionally, its larger part will be equal to $PG$, and so it will remain qualitatively a **Lesser** line; it will by no means become a qualitative **Greater** line, even though it becomes the larger part in quantity—as long as $GA$ is the proposed Rational line.

You may ask: if $PGX$ is a **Greater** line by quality, and $GX$ is also a **Greater** line by quality, why couldn't the larger Element of $GX$ itself also be some **Greater** line, just as the larger Element of the **Greater** line $PGX$ was $GX$, itself a **Greater** line? Because even though both $PGX$ and $GX$ are **Greater** lines, the formation of the former is different from the latter. For into the square of $PGX$ comes the whole square of $PX$ and the whole rectangle formed under double $GA$ and under $PX$. But into the square of $GX$ there enters only half of the square of $PX$ (namely, that under $MX$ and $XP$) and only a fourth part of the rectangle under double $GA$ and $PX$ (namely, that under $AM$ and $PX$). Therefore, the ratio of the Medial <note>original: *Mesi*; a line whose square is equal to a rectangle contained by two rational lines</note> to the Rational is one thing in that case, and another thing here. Our proposition strives to demonstrate this convergence of the "Divine Section" and qualitative composition in the same parts of a line only for the first line $PGX$ and its own proper ratio of the Medial to the Rational, but not likewise for the second.

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:</header>

...called PG, which is the greater part of GX itself in the divine section <note>The "Divine Section" refers to the Golden Ratio, where the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller.</note>: so on the contrary, PG, the **Lesser** <note>original: *Elasson*; a technical term from Euclid's Book X for a specific type of irrational line.</note> of this species, by the division of the divine proportion, gives PY, a somewhat smaller [line] than the **Lesser** itself—that is, the greater part of the cut PG, or the smaller part GV of the cut GX. Thus, just as the greatest line PGX falls by the divine section into the **Greater** <note>original: *Mizona*; Greek for "greater," another Euclidean irrational line type.</note> XG and the **Lesser** GP, so the second [line], the **Greater** GX, falls into two **Lessers** XV and VG, equal to GP and PY; and in this way two **Lessers** compose one **Greater**; while a **Greater** and a **Lesser** compose another, larger **Greater**.

### Proposition XXX.

Individual prime numbers of sides create individual classes of figures: and those that have a number of sides that is a continuous double of their prime number are counted in those same classes.

*This follows from Definition X of this book. For if the proper form of demonstration is the same for all figures that have numbers of sides that are continuous doubles of any one number, then the class of all of them is the same for the purpose of the demonstration. Indeed, bisection <note>The process of dividing an angle or arc into two equal parts using a compass and straightedge.</note> does not change the genus or class when associated with each of them, because of the simplicity and equality of the parts joined together: for from each individual arc of the previous figure, it makes only two parts, and those equal. But by trisection <note>Dividing into three parts.</note> or quinquisection <note>Dividing into five parts.</note>, or those that follow, you cannot avoid either designating unequal parts (if there must be only two), or many parts (that is, more than two) if they are to be equal. As in the trisection of an arc: it is either cut into 2 and 1 (two and unequal parts) or into 1, 1, and 1 (equal but many parts).*

*The antecedent is proved thus. The demonstration is sought from the number of sides, according to Proposition X of this book: Now prime numbers do not share any numerical part, for the unity by which they communicate does not admit division and is not a numerical part or a number. Therefore, even the demonstrations made through them do not communicate with one another. The classes of individual primes are therefore distinct. The first of these classes is that in which are the figures (or their like) with these numbers of sides: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and so on to infinity. The second class has 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, and so on to infinity. The third has 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, and so on to infinity. Other classes are infinite.*

### Proposition XXXI.

Individual classes of figures are created by the individual numbers that are the smallest multiples of two prime numbers of sides (excepting the number two).

*This follows from Definition XI of this book. For if such a figure does not use the number of its own angles for the demonstration of its side, then the form of its demonstration is different from all those mentioned above, and therefore it belongs to a different class. However, the number two was excepted from the generation of a new class when multiplied by some prime, because the bisection of an angle—since it is a geometric process—is that which extends the individual classes equally into infinity; if it were not so, there would be no classes, but only singular figures. The first of these [new classes] consists of 15, 30, 60, 120, 240, 480, etc., from the multiplication of 3 by 5. The second is 21, 42, 84, etc., from the multiplication of 3 by 7. Infinite others follow, such as when 5 is multiplied by 7, resulting in 35, 70, 140, etc.*

<summary>Kepler defines how regular polygons are categorized into "classes" based on their prime number of sides, arguing that doubling the number of sides through bisection maintains the same geometric family.</summary>

## Proposition XXXII.

But also the squares of Prime numbers, with the exception of the square of the number Two, and those formed from squares and another Prime, or the square of a Prime, produce individual classes, distinct from the previous ones.

*The reason that the square of a Prime number does not create the same class as the Prime itself is because, since the Prime itself creates a new class of figures by dividing the whole circle (according to Proposition XXX of this book), the square of that same Prime—now dividing not the whole, but a part of the circle—will produce an entirely different demonstration, provided that such a demonstration is even possible. For a Part of the circle differs greatly from the Whole in terms of its species and absolute configuration; it is this configuration we are now concerned with, as it is what forms the basis of the demonstration.* <note>Kepler is arguing that while a triangle (3 sides) is one class, a nonagon (9 sides, or $3^2$) belongs to a different family because the geometric construction used to find the side of a 9-sided figure is fundamentally different from that of a 3-sided one.</note>

*As for why the square of the number two <term>Binarius <gloss>the number two</gloss></term> is excepted: it is because a figure having twice two angles—that is, a Square <term>Tetragon <gloss>a four-sided figure</gloss></term>—falls into the first class. Indeed, the number Four multiplied by a Prime falls into the class of that Prime, because four is simply twice two; and every figure with a doubled number of sides is referred to the same class as the figure with the single number of sides.* <note>In Kepler’s system, doubling the sides of a polygon (like turning a square into an octagon) doesn't change the "class" because the construction is just a simple bisection of the existing arcs.</note>

The first of these [new classes] is that in which the figures have 9, 18, 36, 72, 144, 288 sides, and so on to infinity.
The second is that in which they have 25, 50, 100, 200, 400 sides, and so on to infinity.
The third is that in which they have 49, 98 sides, and so on to infinity.
There are infinite other classes derived from squares.
Thus 27, 54, 108, 216, 432, and so on to infinity, come from 3 and 9.
Thus 75, 150, 300, and so on to infinity, come from 3 and 25.
Thus 147, 294, and so on to infinity, come from 3 and 49.
Thus 45, 90, 180, 360, and so on to infinity, come from 5 and 9.
Thus 125, 250, 500, 1000, and so on to infinity, come from 5 and 25.
So also 225, 450, 900, and so on to infinity, come from 9 and 25, which are two squares.
There are infinite other classes, from Primes multiplied by squares, or from the squares of Primes multiplied by themselves.

## Proposition XXXIII.

If you subtract four from twice the number of a Figure’s angles, you will form the Numerator of the parts of a right angle that the figure's angle is worth; the Denominator of the parts is the number of the Angles itself.

*For example, in a Triangle <term>Trigon <gloss>3-sided figure</gloss></term>, twice three is six; subtract 4, and 2 remain. Therefore, the angle of a Triangle is worth two-thirds of a Right Angle.* <note>A right angle is $90^\circ$; $2/3$ of $90$ is $60^\circ$, which is indeed the interior angle of an equilateral triangle.</note> *Likewise, in a twenty-sided figure <term>Icosigon <gloss>20-sided figure</gloss></term>, twice 20 is 40; subtract 4, and 36 remain. Therefore, the angle of an Icosigon is worth 36/20, or 9/5, of one Right Angle.* <note>$9/5$ of $90^\circ$ is $162^\circ$.</note> *For the angles of any figure are distributed into as many triangles as it has sides, minus two. But the angles of any Triangle are worth two Right Angles; therefore, the angles of any figure are worth twice as many Right Angles as the Figure has sides, minus four. Since this total number of Right Angles must be distributed among the number of the figure's angles, that number serves as the denominator, and the result of the calculation serves as the numerator for the parts of a single Right Angle.*

## Proposition XXXIV.

A circle is divided into two equal parts by a geometric description; and the line bisecting it is known by knowledge of the first degree; for it is the Diameter itself.

> *For the beginning of forming figures in a circle is to draw a straight line through a specified point, as far as is necessary.*
>
> *The straight line bisecting the circle is the diameter, namely, drawn through the center, because the semicircle is the largest of the equal parts of the circle. Therefore, the line cutting it into two semicircles is also the longest itself, by Euclid’s Elements, Book III, Proposition 14, and it is the diameter by Proposition 15 and by definition.*
>
> *Furthermore, the diameter is that very Expressible <term>Effabilis <gloss>a magnitude that can be stated or compared rationally to others</gloss></term> line proposed as the measure of all others; it is equal to itself and is its own perfect measure, the starting point of geometric science.*

---

## Proposition XXXV.

The side of a Square <term>Tetragon <gloss>a four-sided figure</gloss></term> has a geometric description from its angles, outside the circle; and if it is inscribed in a circle, the side itself is in the third degree of knowledge, while its square is in the second, as is the area of the figure.

<image-desc>A circular diagram with an inscribed square. The square's vertices are labeled Q (top-left), P (top-right), O (bottom-left), and R (bottom-right). A horizontal diameter passes through the center, labeled with points M, L, and N, where L is the central point. A diagonal line connects vertices O and P.</image-desc>

> *Let OQPR be a Square. Its angle, by Proposition XXXIII of this book, is a right angle; wherefore by Euclid Book I, Proposition 46, a square is easily described once a side is given.*
>
> *And since it has four angles and just as many sides, two meeting sides intercept two-fourths of the circle—that is, half of the circle. Therefore, by Proposition XXXIV of this book, the diameter of the circle connects the endpoints of these contiguous sides. Just as QO and QP form the right angle OQP in the semicircle OQP, the extremes O and P are connected by the diameter of the circle OLP. Therefore, by Euclid Book I, Proposition 47 <note>the Pythagorean Theorem</note>, the squares of the two sides OQ and QP equal the square of the diameter. And if half of the square of the diameter is reduced into a square form, by Euclid Book II, Proposition 14, its side will be the side of the Square. Thus, the square of the side is Expressible.*
>
> *And because the square of the diameter OP is to the square of the side OQ as 2 is to 1, but not as a square number to a square number <note>meaning the ratio 2:1 is not a ratio of perfect squares like 4:1 or 9:4</note>; and since OP is expressible in length; therefore the side OQ is expressible only in power <term>Effabilis sola potentia <gloss>a line whose length is an irrational square root, but whose square is a rational number</gloss></term>, by Euclid Book X, Proposition 9. But the area of the square is the same in this figure as the square of the side; therefore, the area of the figure is also Expressible.*

## Proposition XXXVI.

The side of an Octagon has a geometric description from its angles, and no less the side of an octagonal star—or the chord subtended by three-eighths of the circle; and they are each in the eighth degree of knowledge... <meta>catchword: each</meta>

<header>OF THE DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.</header>

...taken individually, one is indeed a Minor line <term>Elasson <gloss>from the Greek 'elasson', a specific type of irrational line defined in Euclid's Book X</gloss></term>, while the other is a Major line <term>Mizon <gloss>from the Greek 'meizon', another specific Euclidean irrational line</gloss></term>; yet joined together they are in the sixth degree, and of a certain singular proportion. Finally, the area is Inexpressible <term>Ineffabilis <gloss>an irrational area that cannot be measured by a rational number</gloss></term>, because it is Medial <term>Meson <gloss>the geometric mean between two rational magnitudes</gloss></term>.

Let the octagon be VQTOXRSP, and the star be VOSQXPTRV: since two lines, for example QT and TO, which contain the octagonal angle QTO, are connected at their ends Q and O, the connecting line is the side of a Square <term>Tetragon <gloss>a four-sided figure</gloss></term>, because from O to T is half of four <note>original: "de O. to semis est quatuor" — Kepler is referring to the eight divisions of the circle; half of the four-fold division (square) results in the eight-fold division (octagon)</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a circle with a regular octagon (labeled V, Q, T, O, X, R, S, P) and an inscribed eight-pointed star (VOSQXPTRV). The center of the circle is labeled L. Therefore, once a Square is described in the circle (to omit other ways of describing an Octagon), let a perpendicular line be drawn from the center L to its side OQ, cutting the side at M and the arc at T, according to Proposition 11 of Euclid’s first book. By doing this, according to Proposition 30 of Euclid’s third book, the two parts of the quarter-circle OQ—namely, the arcs OT and TQ—will be equal. Thus, when points O and T are connected, the straight line OT will be the side of the Octagon, and when O and S are connected, OS will be the side of the star.

When the center L is connected with Q, because the angle QML is a right angle, QL is Expressible <term>Effabilis <gloss>rational in length</gloss></term> in its length; it has the power of the squares of <term>potest <gloss>a geometric term meaning the square of a line is equal to the sum of the squares of others</gloss></term> QM and ML. However, the radius QL has the power of double the square of the half-side of the Square, QM. Therefore, QM and ML are equal, and both are Expressible only in square <note>original: "Effabilis solâ potentiâ" — meaning the lines are irrational (surds), but their squares are rational numbers</note> according to Proposition 35 of this book. Thus, LQ has more power than LM by the power of MQ, which is incommensurable in length to LQ. But LQ, LS, and LT are all equal. Therefore, the combined line SM will be a Fourth Binomial <term>Binominis quarta <gloss>a compound line formed by adding two terms, specifically defined in Euclid X.48-53</gloss></term>, whose terms are SL and LM, according to the definition before Euclid X.48. But the remaining part MT will be a Fourth Apotome <term>Apotome quarta <gloss>a line formed by subtracting one rational magnitude from another, defined in Euclid X.85-90</gloss></term>, whose terms are TL and LM, according to the definition before Euclid X.85.

And because MS is a fourth binomial and TS is expressible, therefore by Euclid X.57, the line QS, which has the power of the rectangle contained under them, is a Major line <term>Mizon</term>. Likewise, because TM is a fourth apotome and TS is expressible, the side of the Octagon TQ, having the power of the rectangle under MT and TS, is a Minor line <term>Elasson</term>, by Euclid X.94.

Their elements are in this drawing: PA is the greater, and AT the lesser. For when AT is added to PA, it makes PT, the side of the star; conversely, when TA is taken away from PA or PT, it leaves AT, which is the side of the Octagon QV. That is to say, the Minor line TQ has the power of double the Annex <term>Prosharmozusa <gloss>the 'fitting-core' or the part subtracted to form an apotome in Euclid's terminology</gloss></term> TA; and the side of the Square QP has the power of both elements PA and AQ (which is AT).

And just as the Major line PX relates to the greater element PA, so the Minor line TQ relates to the lesser element TA; and conversely, as the greater element PA is to the lesser AT, so is the Major line PX to the Minor TQ: As the greater part is to the lesser, so is the whole to the difference.

Furthermore, these sides SQ and QT are not only Major and Minor lines themselves; they are also the kind of lines from which others of the same kind are made by adding or subtracting. For first, they are incommensurable with each other; second, the squares of TQ and QS joined together are equal to the expressible square of TS. Third, the rectangle under TQ and QS is Medial <term>Meson</term>, for it is equal to the rectangle under the half-side of the square QM (which is expressible only in square) and the length TS (which is expressible in length). For this reason, they are also joined in the sixth degree of knowledge. Therefore, by Euclid X.39, the lines TQ and QS combined into one line TQS become a Major line; and by Euclid X.76, when TQ (which is QZ) is taken away from QS, it leaves ZS as a Minor line. And so it can happen that the Minor and Major lines of one pair become the elements...

# OF THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.
<meta>catchword: Triangle</meta>

...of the other pair, and the **Minor** <term>Elasson <gloss>a specific Euclidean irrational line</gloss></term>, taken away from its own **Major** <term>Mizon <gloss>another specific Euclidean irrational line</gloss></term>, leaves the **Minor** of the other.

As far as the area of the **Octagon** is concerned, it consists of eight such triangles as is *LQT*. But the Rectangle *QTRS* consists of four such triangles; it is therefore half of the Area. And it is **Medial** <term>Meso <gloss>from the Greek 'meson', the geometric mean between two rational magnitudes</gloss></term>, as was proved a little earlier; therefore also its double, namely the Area of the **Octagon**, is **Medial**, by the corollary of Proposition 24 of the tenth book of Euclid. From this, Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who led the Gregorian calendar reform.</note> in his *Practical Geometry*, Book VIII, Prop. 31, demonstrates that its area is the mean proportional between the area of the inscribed **Square** <term>Tetragon <gloss>a four-sided figure</gloss></term> and the area of the circumscribed **Square**, which are to each other as 1 to 2; which certain determination of quantity implies the same quality of the **Medial**.

### XXXVII. Proposition.

The side of the **Hexakaidecagon** <term>Hekkædecagon <gloss>a sixteen-sided polygon</gloss></term> has a geometric description from its angles, but the knowledge of its side wanders further off into degrees more ignoble <note>Kepler considers shapes "ignoble" if they are harder to construct or express mathematically, as they are further removed from simple, "noble" proportions.</note> than all those previously mentioned; and much more so for the sides of its stars, or the chords <term>subtensæ <gloss>lines connecting two points on a circle's circumference</gloss></term> subtending three, five, or seven sixteenths.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram containing an eight-pointed star (octagon) inscribed within a circle. The outer vertices are labeled clockwise from the top-left: A, u, P, R, Q, T, S, M. Several interior points of intersection are labeled L, N, and Z. Lines connect the vertices to form both the star and various internal geometric shapes.</image-desc>

Because twice eight is sixteen, therefore by the side of the **Octagon**, this figure is described from the same foundations by which the **Octagon** was previously described by the side of the **Square**.

Let *QO* be the side no longer of a **Square**, but of an **Octagon**, and let *QT* and *TO* be the sides now of a sixteen-sided figure, and let *QP* be the side of the **Octangular** star: it was previously a **Major** line <term>Mizon <gloss>original Greek: meizon</gloss></term>; therefore also its half *LM* was a **Major** line. Therefore the rectangle under the **Expressible** <term>Effabilis <gloss>a line whose length can be expressed as a rational number</gloss></term> line *ST* and the **Major** line *LM* is of a clearly new species, of which no mention is made among the more noble degrees explained above. Indeed, such a new thing, taken away from that which is contained under the lines *LT* and *TS*, which are **Expressible** in length, leaves again some more remote species, namely the rectangle under *MT* and *TS*, equal to the square <note>original: "quadrato," literally the power/area of the square formed by the side</note> of *TQ*, the side of the **Hexakaidecagon**. This is much more true for polygons of this Class: such as those of 32, 64, 128 angles, etc.

Since it is thus with one side, or the chord subtending one sixteenth, now its square, taken away from the square of the diameter, leaves the chord for seven sixteenths; it is therefore of a more remote degree.

Indeed, three sixteenths have a chord derived from the chord of three eighths by bisection: they are therefore in a more remote degree than those. And the square of the chord of three sixteenths, taken away from the square of the diameter, leaves the square of the chord of five sixteenths. This is therefore again of a more remote degree.

### XXXVIII. Proposition.

The sides of the **Triangle** <term>Trigonus <gloss>the equilateral triangle</gloss></term> and the **Hexagon** have a geometric description from the angles of the figures, and when inscribed in a circle, they are knowable—the former in the third degree, the latter in the second; but the planes, or areas of the figures, are **Medial** <term>Mesa <gloss>plural of meson</gloss></term>, in a double proportion to each other.

<header>ON DEMONSTRATION. Book I.</header>

*The construction of a **Triangle** <term>Trigon <gloss>an equilateral triangle</gloss></term> outside a circle is very easy by Proposition 1 of Book I of Euclid. Its*
*inscription into a circle is most efficiently achieved—to say nothing of other methods—by means of the **Hexagon's** side.*
*Because three halves of six make three.* <note>Kepler is using a simple wordplay to explain that a triangle (3 sides) is derived from a hexagon (6 sides).</note> *And the*
*description and inscription of the **Hexagon** are indeed proposed in Proposition 15 of Book IV of*
*Euclid. But the following must be shown:*
*the quantity of the side, based on the ratios of the angles.*

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram showing an inscribed hexagon and triangle. Points labeled include B at the top, H at the upper left, C at the middle left, G at the bottom, D at the middle right, and center A. A line segment CD is horizontal, with point E marked on it. A triangle BCD and parts of a hexagon BHCGDF are visible.</image-desc>

*Let BHCGDF be a **Hexagon**. Since there are, therefore,*
*6 angles, the plane of the Hexagon is also divided into*
*six **Triangles**, meeting with their vertices at the center A; such as the one*
*which is CAG. Therefore, the sum of the four Right angles* <note>360 degrees</note> *surrounding the*
*center A, divided into six vertices, gives to one*
*vertical angle CAG four-sixths, or two-thirds*
*of one Right angle.* <note>60 degrees</note> *And yet, all three angles of the triangle CAG joined together are equal to two*
*right angles, or six-thirds of one Right angle: therefore, by subtracting the angle at A (of 2 thirds) from the sum*
*of 6 thirds, there remains for the two at C and G a sum of 4 thirds. But they are all equal;*
*therefore, for each at C and G there remain 2 thirds of one Right angle, no less than for the*
*vertical angle at A. And yet, if three angles are equal, the sides must also be equal in*
*the **Triangle**. Therefore, the side CG—the same for both the Hexagon and the triangle that is its*
*sixth part—is equal to the semi-diameter* <term>radius</term> *of the circle CA or AG. Therefore, the side of the Hexagon is **Expressible** <term>Effabile <gloss>Kepler’s term for a rational magnitude</gloss></term> in*
*length, being exactly half of the diameter. This is truly **Degree II** according to Proposition XIII of this book.*

*Now for the **Triangle**, let it be BCD; the side BC connects two sides of the Hexagon, CH*
*and HB, meeting at H. Since BHC is therefore 2 thirds of a semicircle,* <note>120 degrees</note> *and CG is one third,* <note>60 degrees</note> *the*
*arc BCG is therefore a semicircle, and BG is the diameter, passing through A. Therefore, the angle BCG*
*is a Right angle, by Proposition 31 of Book III of Euclid. The squares of BC and CG are therefore equal to*
*the square of BG, by Proposition 47 of Book I of Euclid.* <note>The Pythagorean Theorem.</note> *But CG is the semi-diameter, and its square*
*is a fourth part of this square [of the diameter]; therefore, by taking away a fourth part from the square of BG, there*
*remains the square of the side of the triangle* <note>original: *tetragonici*; likely a typo for *trigonici* (triangle) or a reference to the "square" of the side.</note> *BC. This square is therefore **expressible**;*
*but because it does not have the same ratio to the square of BG as a square number to a*
*square number, but rather as 3 to 4, BC is therefore **Expressible in power** only.* <note>This means the side BC is the square root of a rational number, what we would call an irrational number like √3.</note> *This is indeed*
*the **Third Degree**, by Proposition XIV of this book.*

*And because BC and CD are equal, and the angles BCD and BDC are equal: therefore the perpendicular BE,*
*dropped onto CD, will cut it at E into equal parts CE and ED. But the whole of CD was **Expressible***
*in power only; therefore its half CE is also so. Therefore, the Rectangle formed by CE*
*and AG (being magnitudes commensurable in power only, of which the latter is Expressible in length) is*
*a **Medial** <term>Meson <gloss>a specific Euclidean irrational area</gloss></term>. But this Rectangle is equal to the area of two triangles equal to CG A*
*(of which there are six in the Hexagon) and is thus a third part of the Area of the Hexagon.*
*The Area of the Hexagon is therefore a **Medial** plane. And because the triangles BCA and BCH*
*have sides BA and BH, CA and CH that are equal, and share one common side BC: they*
*therefore have equal areas. But BCH, BDF, and CDG are parts of the Hexagonal area by*
*which it exceeds the area of the Triangle BCD—consisting of the same number of equal triangles: BAC,*
*CAD, DAB. Therefore, the Hexagonal area is double the Triangular area; therefore the Triangular area*
*is also **Medial**, because it is commensurable (namely, half) with the Hexagonal area, which was Medial.*

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

...extended parts can be geometrically described by five-twelfths of a circle, and when inscribed in the same circle, they are knowable, each in the eighth degree of the more noble knowledge, joined in the fifth degree; but the plane <note>The area</note> of the Dodecagon is <term>Effable <gloss>rational or expressible in square units</gloss></term>.

Let the Dodecagon be BMHLCKGQDPFN, and the Dodecagonal star BKFLDMGNCPHQB.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram showing a dodecagon inscribed in a circle. Within the circle, a twelve-pointed star (stella dodecagonica) is formed by lines connecting the vertices. Vertices are labeled B, N, F, D, Q, G, K, L, H, M. The center of the circle is labeled A. A vertical diameter connects L and P. Various internal points and intersections are labeled R, S, O, P. A side of a hexagon HC is marked with O as its midpoint on the radius AO.</image-desc>

Therefore, because twice six are twelve, the figure is described from the same foundations through the side of the Hexagon as the Octagon was previously through the side of the <term>Tetragon <gloss>a square</gloss></term>, by drawing a perpendicular from the center A to the side of the Hexagon HC, cutting the side at O and the circle at L and P; and by connecting LH for the side of the Dodecagon, and HP for the side of the star.

Since, therefore, the side HC of the hexagon is **Effable** in length; its half HO will also be such; but AC, being equal to HC itself, is equal in power <note>original: "potest" – meaning its square is equal to</note> to the sum of the squares of its half OC and of AO. Therefore, the square of AO relates to the square of AC or AP as 3 to 4, which is not a ratio of a square number to a square number.

Therefore, PA and AO are commensurable with each other only in power <note>Their squares have a rational ratio, but their lengths do not</note>, as are LA and AO. And CA (which is PA or AL), the greater **Effable** line, is greater in power than OA, the lesser, by the square of CO, which is commensurable to it. Therefore, by the definition before Proposition 48 of Book 10 of Euclid: the combined line PO is a <term>Binomial <gloss>a line composed of two parts commensurable only in square</gloss></term>, and by the definition before Proposition 85, the remaining part OL is an <term>Apotome <gloss>the "remainder" of a rational line from which a rational line commensurable only in square has been subtracted</gloss></term>, both being of the "First" type. The names <note>The two parts of the line</note> are AP, which is **Effable** simply, and AO, which is **Effable** only in power. But through Proposition 54 of Book 10 of Euclid, HP—being the side of a square equal to the rectangle contained by the First Binomial OP and the **Effable** line PL—is itself a **Binomial**; and through Proposition 91 of the same book, HL, the side of the Dodecagon—being the side of a square equal to the rectangle contained by the First Apotome OL and the **Effable** line LP—is an **Apotome**. Thus, each falls into the eighth, more noble degree of knowledge.

The names of this composite line PH and the diminished line HL are PS and SH. And since HB is the side of the hexagon, KP the side of the Triangle, and BP the side of the Quadragon <note>Square</note>; the first indeed is equal in power to double the lesser Name, namely HS and SB; the second to double the greater, namely KS and SP; but this last one is equal in power to both together, and each once, namely BS and SP.

The binomial PH is also composed of PR, the side of the square, and RH, the side of the Dodecagon: but because of this composition it is not called a **Binomial**: because through Proposition 42 of Book 10 of Euclid, besides the one sign, which here was S, no other can be given that divides it into its Names.

And since HO and LP are **Effable** in length, the rectangle under them (that is, under LH and HP) will be **Effable**, and the sum of the squares of LH and HP is likewise **Effable**, being equal to the square of LP itself. Therefore, by this name, the joined lines LH and HP are in the fifth degree of knowledge. Nor do they create anything new when joined, nor again a Binomial or Apotome: for LH added to HP makes a line **Effable** in power only, namely one whose square is one-and-a-half times the square of LP; while LH (or HR) subtracted from HP constitutes again a line **Effable** in power, PR, the side of the square: whose square is half of the square of LP.

And since the Area of the Dodecagon consists of 12 Triangles, such as LAC, and four of these are contained in the **Effable** rectangle LHPD, which is a third of the whole area; therefore the whole area is also **Effable**, to such an extent...

## XL. Proposition.

A Regular Figure of twenty-four sides, and all those derived from it by continuously doubling the number of sides, indeed have Geometric inscriptions, but the knowledge of their sides wanders further, into more remote degrees than those that were previously established: as do the sides of its stars or the **chords** <term>subtensarum <gloss>lines connecting two points on a circle's edge</gloss></term> of five, seven, and eleven twenty-fourths of the circle.

*It is proven as before in Proposition 37 regarding the sixteen-sided figure; however, with this difference: that here the side of the Dodecagonal star and its half are **First Binomials** <note>A term from Euclid’s Elements, Book X, referring to a specific type of irrational number composed of the sum of two rational parts</note>, wherefore the rectangle formed by the half and the diameter, as if from an **Effable** <gloss>rational or expressible</gloss> quantity, does not yet become a new species, because the square root of it (by Proposition 54) is again a Binomial. But now this rectangle, subtracted from the **Effable** quantity formed by the whole and half diameter, leaves something new, of which no mention has yet been made, and more **ignoble** <note>In Kepler's hierarchy, "ignoble" refers to numbers that are more complex and further removed from the simple "nobility" of whole numbers or simple roots</note>, since it is more composite; and this is formed by the **square** <note>original: "potentiâ" — meaning the area produced by the side</note> of the side of the 24-angled figure.*

*This is much more true for figures with more angles in this class; such as the forty-eight-sided figure, the ninety-six-sided figure, etc.*

<image-desc>A circular diagram of an icositetragon (24-sided regular polygon) inscribed within a circle. Radials connect the center to each of the 24 vertices, and various internal chords connect vertices to form a complex geometric star pattern.</image-desc>

The **chord** <gloss>subtensa</gloss> of five twenty-fourths of the circle is revealed by the bisection of the arc containing five-twelfths; its square <note>original: "potentiâ"</note> subtracted from the square of the diameter leaves the square of the chord of seven twenty-fourths: thus the square of the side or chord of one twenty-fourth forms, by the same method, the square of the chord of eleven such parts. They are therefore all in a more remote degree of knowledge.

## XLI. Proposition.

The sides of the **Decagon** <gloss>10-sided figure</gloss> and the decagonal star, or the chord of three-tenths of the Circle, have a Geometric description from their angles and an inscription into a circle; and they are knowable, individually in the eighth degree of knowledge, but joined together, in the fifth degree; and joined with the semi-diameter, in the fourth degree.

Let the Decagon be BCDEFG HIKL, and its star BEHLDGKCFIB. Since, therefore, there are ten angles, the plane of the figure will be composed of ten triangles meeting at the center A, one of which is FAG. It distributes, therefore, the sum of four right angles, which is around the single point A, into [the angles of] those ten triangles...

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram containing an inscribed ten-pointed star (decagon). The vertices on the circumference are labeled B, L, K, I, H, G, F, E, D, C in clockwise order. The center point is labeled A. Various internal lines connect the vertices, and intersection points are marked with the letters R, S, and T.</image-desc>
four-tenths or two-fifths of one **Right angle** <gloss>90 degrees</gloss>. Now, the sum of the three angles of this triangle is ten-fifths, which is two **Right angles** <note>original: "2. Recti"; Kepler is using a system where 5/5 equals 90 degrees, so 10/5 equals 180 degrees</note>; therefore, by taking away two-fifths for the vertical angle at A, eight-fifths remain for the two angles at the base. Since these are equal, each one is four-fifths. Thus, each angle at the base is double the angle at the vertex. This is the bond of the following demonstration.

For by bisecting angle AFG into two equal parts by the line FO (following Euclid, Book I, Proposition 9), the angles AFO and OFG will be equal to each other, and each will be two-fifths of a **Right angle**; therefore, each is equal to the angle FAO itself.

Wherefore, by Euclid, Book VI, Proposition 3, as side AF is to FG, so is AO to OG.

<image-desc>A geometric construction diagram featuring a horizontal baseline P-A-M-X. Above it is a circular arc with points G and T. Vertical and diagonal lines connect points on the baseline to the arc and internal points Y, O, and U. Lines include vertical P-G and M-T, and diagonals P-Y-G, G-O-A, A-U-T, and T-X.</image-desc>
But because angle OFG is two-fifths, and OGF (which is AGF) was four-fifths, then FOG will also be four-fifths. Therefore, since the angles at O and G are equal, the sides FG and FO opposite them are also equal.

In the same way, in triangle AOF, because AFO is two-fifths—the same as FAO—then AO and FO (which is the side FG) will be equal. Now, as AF is to FG, so AO is to OG, as has already been demonstrated; therefore, as AG is to the part AO, so is AO to the remainder OG. Thus, the leg AG is cut at point O **proportionally** <note>This refers to the "Golden Ratio" or "Extreme and Mean Ratio," where a line is divided such that the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller one.</note>.

Therefore, by Euclid, Book XIII, Proposition 5: if OA or OF is continued to I, so that OI is equal to the whole AG, then FI is also cut proportionally at O. When the points AI are connected, triangle AIO will be congruent to the initial triangle FAG; thus angle OAI is double FAO, and FAI is six-fifths. Wherefore, with center A and the interval AG describing the circle FGI, FG will be the side of the **decagon** <note>a 10-sided polygon</note>, the greater part of the semi-diameter AG when proportionally cut; and FI will be the side of the **star** <note>a decagram</note>, or the **chord** <gloss>subtensa</gloss> of three-tenths of the circle, composed of FO and OI (the side of the decagon and the semi-diameter).

For this reason, these sides, when joined to the semi-diameter, can be reckoned in the **fourth degree** of knowledge, according to Proposition XXVI of this book.

And since AG is **Effable** <term>Effabilis <gloss>a magnitude whose square is commensurable with a rational area; essentially "expressible" in geometric terms</gloss></term> in length, and the side of the decagon is its greater part; the side of the star is composed of the whole and the greater part. Wherefore, by Proposition XXVII of this book, the former is an **Apotome** and the latter is a **Binomial** <note>These are technical terms from Euclid’s Elements, Book X, for specific types of irrational lines</note>, both of the fourth species. In this respect, they are in the **eighth degree** of knowledge, immediately following the side of the Dodecagon and its star, and clearly in the same order as the side of the Octagon and its star.

And by Proposition XXIII of this book, the remainder OG, and thus also its half NG, is an **Apotome of the first species**. But beware of thinking its "Names" <note>The two parts of a binomial or apotome</note> are the greater AG and the lesser AN.

Finally, by the same Proposition XXVII, the sides GF, or OF and FI—not joined with the semi-diameter, but with themselves—are in the **fifth degree** of knowledge, because they have both the sum of their squares and their common rectangle as **Effable**.

Thus, the side of the Decagon combined with the side of its star makes a line that is **Effable in power only** <note>meaning its square is rational, even if the line itself is not</note>, having the power of five-fourths of the power of the semi-diameter. In the preceding diagram, by Proposition XXVII, this is PX, composed of PA (equal to OA) and AX; between which the **Effable** mean proportional is GA.

Conversely, subtracting the side of the Decagon OF from the side of the star FI leaves the **Effable** OI, namely the semi-diameter. Thus, nothing new is created by those operations.

### Proposition XLII.

The sides of the Pentagon and the Pentagonal Star, or the chord subtending two-fifths of the Circle, have a geometric description based on angles, and are knowable, each joined at the eighth degree, both from the sixth and fourth degrees of knowledge. <note>Kepler categorizes polygons into "degrees" based on how they can be constructed and understood through geometry.</note>

As here FB and BH are the legs, and FH is the base.

<margin>
As here FDB is upon FB and BKH is upon BH.

*The description outside the circle is as follows: if the length of the intended side is given, we shall cut it proportionally (by Euclid, Book II, Proposition 11 or Book VI, Proposition 30), and we shall add to it the larger part of that section. Having made two legs, each composed of the proposed side and the larger section, and using the proposed side itself as the Base, we shall establish the internal triangle of the Pentagon. Since the composite leg consists of the whole proposed side and its larger part from the <term>divine section<note>The "divine section" refers to the Golden Ratio, a mathematical proportion where the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller.</note></term>, the composite line will also be cut in this way, and its larger part will be the proposed side. Therefore, the angle of this triangle at the base will be double the angle at the vertex, as stated above regarding the Decagon. Upon these two legs as Bases, we shall add two exterior triangles, whose legs are equal to the proposed side.*

*The inscription into a circle is very easy by means of the side of a Decagon <note>A ten-sided figure</note>. Since five is half of ten, we shall connect the endpoints F and H of two contiguous Decagon sides, FG and GH (meeting at G); the line FH will be the side of the Pentagon, and likewise HK. By connecting the endpoints F and K, the line FK will be the side of the star. Therefore, let the Pentagon be BDFHK, and its star BFKDHB.*

*Euclid demonstrates in Book XIII, Proposition 10, that the square of the side of the Pentagon FH is equal to the squares of the side of the Hexagon FA and the side of the Decagon FG combined—that is, the radius AG and the larger part of the cut section AO together. This demonstration in Euclid is difficult to grasp; I will therefore attempt an easier one here.*

*From the endpoints of the Pentagonal side B and D, let straight lines BG and DI be drawn through the center A. Just as DB <term>subtends<note>To "subtend" means to be the chord that connects the two ends of an arc.</note></term> two-tenths <note>original: "duas decimas"; 2/10 or 1/5 of the circle</note>, so let the next chord DL subtend three-tenths, and DK subtend four-tenths, intersecting BG at points S and R. Therefore, the angle LDI, which is SDA, is two-fifths of one Right angle; because the arc LI is one-fifth part of the circle, just as FH is. Indeed, equal angles stand upon equal arcs at the circumference (by Euclid Book III, Proposition 21 or 27). However, the angle DAB (which is DAS) is four-fifths of one right angle, because DB is a fifth part of the circle, which measures four right angles around the center A. Therefore, the combined angles SAD and ADS are six-fifths of one right angle. But all three angles of a triangle together equal ten-fifths <note>Kepler is using fifths of a right angle; 10/5 equals two right angles, or 180 degrees</note>. Thus, the remaining angle DSA is also four-fifths. Therefore, angle DSA is equal to angle DAS; thus side DS is equal to side DA, the radius. Therefore, by the previous arguments, the larger part of the proportionally cut radius DA equals SA. Thus SA is equal to the side of the Decagon, as stated. And DA is the radius, namely the side of the Hexagon. I say that the side of the Pentagon DB squared is equal to the squares of both SA and AD.*

*...[the squares of the smaller sides] are less than the combined squares of DA and AB by twice the rectangle of RA and AB, which is the same as once the rectangle of SA and AE. However, the two rectangles formed by SA and AB, and by SB and BA, together constitute the whole square of BA. Therefore, when the rectangle of SA and AB is removed, the square of DA and the rectangle of SB and BA remain, and when joined they are equal to the square of DB. Since the radius BA is cut <term>proportionally<note>Meaning according to the Golden Ratio, or "extreme and mean ratio."</note></term> at S, and AS is the larger part: the rectangle of SB and BA is therefore equal to the square of SA. Thus, the square of the side of the Pentagon is equal to the sum of the squares of DA and AS; namely, the squares of the sides of the Hexagon and the Decagon.* <note>Kepler is proving Euclid's Theorem XIII.10: that the square of the side of a regular pentagon equals the square of the side of the hexagon plus the square of the side of the decagon, all inscribed in the same circle.</note>

*As for the side of the Pentagonal star BF: it is composed of BD (or BQ), which is the side of the Pentagon, and QF, which is the larger part of its proportional section: according to Book 13, Proposition 8 [of Euclid’s Elements]: which can also be proven from the pentagonal triangle FBH, as mentioned above.*

*Since the side of the Pentagon is equivalent to the square of the radius, which is <term>Expressible<note>Original: *Effabilis*. In geometry, this refers to a line whose square is rational relative to a starting area.</note></term> in length, and the square of the larger part of its proportional section, as in the previously shown semicircular diagram: PG is equivalent to the squares of PA and AG. And just as PA is to AG, so the side of the Pentagon PG is to the side of its star. Let GX be that side of the star. Therefore, GX is equivalent to the squares of the radius GA of the circle around the Decagon, and AX (composed of PA and AG). For this reason, by the proofs there, GX is a <term>Greater<note>Original: *Mizon*. A specific type of irrational line defined in Euclid's *Elements*, Book X.</note></term> line, and GP is a <term>Lesser<note>Original: *Elaßon*. An irrational line whose square is the difference between two areas that cannot be expressed as a simple ratio.</note></term> line. Each is therefore in the eighth degree of knowledge, and in its second order. Because the joined lines PG and GX create a sum of squares that is Expressible—specifically, equal to the square of PX, which is five times the Expressible square of GA—and because these same lines PG and GX form a <term>Medial<note>Original: *Meson*. An irrational line that is the mean proportional between two rational lines.</note></term> rectangle; by this name the joined lines PG and GX are in the sixth degree of knowledge, which is discussed in Proposition XVIII. Finally, because the side of the Pentagon and the side of its star are as the larger part and the whole of the <term>divine section<note>The Golden Ratio.</note></term>; they are also in the fourth degree of knowledge when joined together: see Proposition XXIX of this book. It follows from these properties that just as the side of the Pentagon is a Lesser line and the side of the Star is a Greater line, so also the line composed of both is again a Greater line. The side of the Pentagon becomes the "lesser element" of this composite Greater line, while the side of the star becomes the "greater element." Furthermore, the difference between the two sides is also a Lesser line, namely DQ or QF, according to the same Proposition XXIX.*

# XLIV. Proposition.

The sides of the <term>Pentekaedecagon<note>A fifteen-sided polygon.</note></term> and its stars—namely those subtending two, or four, or seven fifteenths of the circle—have a geometric description indeed, but not outside the circle; and within the circle also not from angles, and therefore they are improper, and belong to a heterogeneous knowledge of a more remote degree than all the preceding. The Thirty-sided polygon and others of this class are still more remote.

## Proposition XLV.

The Heptagon <note>A seven-sided polygon.</note> and all figures derived from it which have a number of sides that is one of the Prime numbers (so-called), and their stars, and thus the entire classes derived from them, lack a Geometric description outside of a circle; within a circle, although the quantity of their sides is necessary, it is equally necessary that this quantity remains unknown.

> *A great matter is at stake here; for it was by this effect that the Heptagon and other figures of this kind were prevented from being employed by God to adorn the World, whereas the knowable figures explained above were indeed employed.*

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram of a regular heptagon inscribed within a circle. A central vertical diameter is labeled BAP, where A is the center of the circle and P is the point on the circumference at the bottom. A radius connects center A to vertex E. Additional points within the figure are labeled I and K.</image-desc>

> *Let there be, then, a Heptagon BCDEFGH, and let all the angles be connected with all others, and let A be the center of the circle, and BAP the Diameter, and let A be connected with E.*

> *First, then, such figures obtain no "improper" demonstration as mentioned above: for the number of their sides and angles is one of the Primes. But no pair of the preceding figures divides the whole circle into parts numerable by any Prime Number; rather, they obtain a Number that is a Multiple of the numbers of both figures.*

But such figures do not even have a "proper" demonstration from the number of angles: because whatever is elicited from this is vague, multiple, and least of all determined.

For let the Heptagon be cut into its five triangles: two outer <term>obtuse-angled isosceles triangles<note>original: "æquicrura Obtusangula". Triangles where all three sides are of different lengths.</note></term> *BED* and *BFG* placed between them. Since, therefore, the arc upon which the legs of an angle stand (made at the opposite part of the circumference) measures the quantity of the angle, the angle *BEF* stands upon three parts of the circumference, *BH*, *HG*, and *GF*; the angle *BFE* similarly stands upon three [parts], *BC*, *CD*, and *DE*; but *EBF* stands upon one, *EF*. Therefore, *BEF* is such a triangle that has both angles at the base triple to that which is at the vertex. In the same way, it is proved that the scalene *BED* has angles...

<margin>Cardano’s Reflexive Heptagonal Proportion.</margin>
If this figure has a fixed description of its own outside the circle, no less than the pentagon had above, it is necessary (as <note>Campanus of Novara (13th century), Girolamo Cardano (16th century), and François de Foix-Candale (also known as Candalla Flussas, 16th century) were prominent mathematicians who studied the construction of regular polygons.</note>Campanus, Girolamo Cardano, and Candalla Flussas once advised) that first of all, such triangles must be able to be given. Just as before the pentagon, a triangle was given in which each angle at the base was double the angle at the vertex. However, while in that <term>Pentagonal Triangle<note>A triangle with angles of 72, 72, and 36 degrees, used to construct a regular pentagon.</note></term> a certain proportion of the sides was given based on the angles, in this <term>Heptagonal Triangle<note>A triangle related to the seven-sided figure, which Kepler argues cannot be formally defined.</note></term>, no certain proportion is given. For let *I* and *K* be the marks by which *BF* is cut by *EH* and *EG*, which <gloss>trisect</gloss> the angle *BEF*. Therefore, in triangle *FEI*, because angle *FEI* has been bisected: as *FE* is to *EI*, so is *FK* to *KI*. But *EF* is equal to the whole of *FI*. For *FEI* is 4-sevenths of a right angle, of which *EFI* is 6-sevenths; therefore *EIF* is also 4-sevenths. Thus the legs *FE* and *FI*, being opposite equal angles, are equal. For the same reason, *EI* and *IB* are also equal; therefore, as *FI* is to *IB*, so is *FK* to *KI*. Furthermore, in triangle *KEB*, because angle *KEB* is bisected by *EIH*: as *KE* is to *EB*, so is *KI* to *IB*. But *KE* and *FE* are equal, because triangle *KEF* is isosceles and similar to *EBF*; and truly *EF* was equal to *IF*, and *EB* is equal to *FB*; therefore, as *IF* is to *FB*, so is *KI* to *IB*. In the same line *BF* (which subtends three-sevenths of the circle), two proportions of three parts have been found. First: as the middle segment *KI* is to the smallest *KF*, so is the largest *IB* to *IF* (which is composed of both smaller segments, that is, the side of the heptagon *FE*). Second: as the largest *IB* is to the middle *IK*, so is the whole *BF* to *FI* (composed of the two smallest). This proportion puts on a show of necessary determination to a fixed and single proportion of *EF* to *FB*. It deceived Cardano, who—having noticed something of this kind in the sides of the <term>Scalene triangle<note>A triangle with three unequal sides.</note></term> *BED*, which he called a **Reflexive Proportion**—vainly boasted of having discovered the side of the heptagon. For no certain quantity follows for *EF* or *IF*; because what we think we obtain as something new the second time around actually coincides with the first. Whenever there are four proportionals in which the first two equal the third, it also happens that as the first is to the third, or the second to the fourth, so is the third to the sum of the third and fourth (which sum becomes the fifth in number). There are infinite cases of this, both in <term>commensurable<note>Quantities that have a common measure; rational numbers.</note></term> and incommensurable terms. Specifically, there are as many cases of commensurable terms as there are <term>superparticular ratios<note>original: "proportiones superparticulares". Ratios of the form (n+1)/n, where the numerator is the denominator plus one (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note></term>—namely, as many as there are odd square numbers.

### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

For as 15 is to 9, so 40 is to 24 (which is the sum of 15 and 9). And as 40 is to 15, so 64 (consisting of 40, 15, and 9) is to 24 (the sum of 15 and 9).
Behold a common property of many proportions, which necessarily follows from the established <term>septangle<note>A seven-sided polygon, now more commonly called a heptagon.</note></term>; but from this property alone being given, the heptagonal triangle cannot be constructed. The reason why in the Pentagon the certain proportion of the side depends on the angles, even outside of a circle, while in the Heptagon and other such figures it does not, is easily clear from what has been said. In the pentagonal

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram with an inscribed pentagon and a star-like pattern of chords. The center is labeled A. triangle *BFK*, by the bisection of the angle *BKF*, one immediately arrives at the isosceles triangles *BKT* and *KTF*, its two elements. From this follows the equality of their angles *BFK* and *BKT*, and the equality of the sides *BK*, *KT*, and *TF*. But in the Heptagonal triangle, through the trisection of the angle, three elements of the triangle are formed: two isosceles triangles *BEI* and *KEF*, and one scalene triangle *IEK*. Nor does the proportion of the angles follow from it, as is well known in Geometry. Since, therefore, the angles of this figure do not teach anything further outside the circle, the required triangle cannot be constructed outside the circle. Therefore, this figure is not inscribable in a circle by means of anything prior to it in knowledge or description; rather, only by the inscription itself (of whatever kind it may be) is that wandering proportion forced into the narrow constraints of a single case. Thus, the principle is "begged" <note>original: "principium petitur" — a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premises.</note>: for in order to find that by which the inscription is completed, we are ordered to employ the inscription itself, as if it were already possible beforehand.

The proportion of the Side *EF* to the side of the star *FB* therefore lies hidden—it lies hidden, I say, in "quantitative matter." Thus, by the cause of the material principle of quantities (which is "indeterminate magnitude"), it is indeed possible to establish the side of a septangle in a just proportion to the diameter of the circle. This is because there is something certainly larger than the side of the septangle and something smaller within the Circle itself; and further, as the division proceeds toward infinity, something always larger than side *EF* or something smaller than it can be given. But by the cause of that which is "formal" in quantities, it is simply impossible. This is because the figure of the septangle and its like lacks all means by which any certain proportion of the side might be demonstrated or found; and thus it utterly lacks knowable formation or determination. Since this is so, the figure of 14 angles cannot be inscribed in a circle (where the semi-diameter is *AP*) by the side *EP*, nor can its two contiguous sides be spanned by one straight line *EF*, which would be the side of the Heptagon in that circle. Nor can this side be compared with the diameter, since it is by its own nature of an unknown comparison to the Diameter.

Therefore, no **Regular Septangle** was ever constructed by anyone knowing and willing and acting by design; nor can it be constructed by design. It might well be constructed by chance, and yet it must necessarily remain unknown whether it has been constructed or not.

For it seems that in that art, the sides of all kinds of Polygons can be determined.

For example, in the case of the Septangle <note>Heptagon</note>, Jost Bürgi—the mechanician to the Emperor and the Landgrave of Hesse, who invented many ingenious and unexpected things in this field—proceeds in this way. First, he assigns the number 2 to the diameter of the circle B$\circ$, so that AB is a total unit; by dividing this into infinite parts by sectioning, the length of the side BC may be numbered through them. Next, he assumes that the proportion of AB to BC is known, even though it is this very proportion that is ultimately being sought. He imagines a continuity in this proportion: just as 1 (AB) is to 1 $\dot{\text{j}}$ (BC), so 1 $\dot{\text{j}}$ is to 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$, and 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ to 1 $\dddot{\text{iij}}$, and 1 $\dddot{\text{iij}}$ to 1 $\text{iv}$, and so on perpetually. We shall mark these more conveniently with indices like this: 1, 1 $\dot{\text{j}}$, 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$, 1 $\dddot{\text{iij}}$, 1 $\text{iv}$, 1 $\text{v}$, 1 $\text{vj}$, 1 $\text{vij}$, etc. <note>These symbols represent powers of the unknown variable: $x^0, x^1, x^2, x^3, x^4$, etc.</note>

With these values established, the quadrilateral BEDC is considered first. Now, it has been demonstrated by Ptolemy, Copernicus, Regiomontanus, Pitiscus, and others who have written on the doctrine of sines <note>Trigonometry</note>, that in any quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, the rectangle of the two diagonals CE and DB equals the two rectangles of the opposite sides joined together—namely, the product of DC and EB added to the product of CB and DE. Furthermore, since <margin>Place O at the mutual intersection of CH and BP.</margin> it is certain from Geometry that CO (half of the chord CH) and OB (the <term>sagitta<note>The "arrow" or height of the arc segment.</note></term>), when their squares <note>original: "potentijs"</note> are joined, equal the square of the side CB.

Let BP therefore be 2 and CB be 1 $\dot{\text{j}}$. Its square is 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$; divide this by BP, and BO will be 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ divided by 2. The square of BO is 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ divided by 4; subtract this from the square of CB (which is 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$), and there remains 4 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 1 $\text{iv}$ divided by 4, which is the square of CO. However, since CH is double CO, the square of CH will be 16 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 4 $\text{iv}$ divided by 4, which is 4 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 1 $\text{iv}$.

Since we now have the square of CH or BD (that is, the rectangle formed by BD and CE), multiply CB by DE so that the rectangle between them is 1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$. Subtract this from the rectangle formed by BD and CE (4 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 1 $\text{iv}$), and there remains the rectangle of CD and BE (3 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 1 $\text{iv}$). Divide this by $\dot{\text{j}}$ (that is, by CD), and BE results as 3 $\dot{\text{j}}$ minus 1 $\dddot{\text{iij}}$.

We proceed further to the Quadrilateral DBHE. Because BE is 3 $\dot{\text{j}}$ minus 1 $\dddot{\text{iij}}$, the rectangle of BE and DH (the square of BE) will be 9 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 6 $\text{iv}$ + 1 $\text{vj}$. Subtract the rectangle of BH and DE (1 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$), and there remains the rectangle of BD and EH (8 $\ddot{\text{ij}}$ minus 6 $\text{iv}$ + 1 $\text{vj}$). # ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES
<meta>Catchword: easier</meta>

In a new quadrilateral, the diagonal, whose sides subtend three parts <note>referring to segments of the circle's circumference</note>, and thus their rectangle <note>the product of the sides</note> is 9 squared – 6 fourths + 1 sixth, which when subtracted from the rectangle 16 squared – 20 fourths + 8 sixths – 1 eighth, leaves the rectangle of the remaining sides as 7 squared – 14 fourths + 7 sixths – 1 eighth. Bürgi uses this chord, comparing it either with a number by which the chord of a certain arc to be divided into seven is expressed, or with the figure of zero, if the entire circle (as in this case) is to be divided into seven. And then, these quantities are equal either to that number or to the figure of zero:

-> 7 squared – 14 fourths + 7 sixths — 1 eighth, or 7 – 14 squared + 7 fourths – 1 sixth. <-

The value of the root produced for him from the equation—which he helps along mechanically <note>likely referring to numerical approximation or use of instruments</note>—is not just one. In a **Pentagon** <note>original: "Quinquangulo"</note> there are two; in a **Heptagon** <note>original: "Septangulo"</note> there are three; in a **Nonagon** <note>a nine-sided figure</note> there are four, and so on. For one value is the side *BC*, another is *BD*, and the third is *BE*.

Therefore, so that it may appear that this way of investigating the sides of a figure has absolutely nothing in common with our **Definitions** I, II, and III premised above, you will first note: what does this algebraic <term>cossic<gloss>from the Italian 'cosa' (thing), the early name for algebra where the unknown variable was called 'the thing'</gloss></term> chord of Bürgi actually declare? It declares this: if seven continuous proportionals are established in that ratio which the side of the heptagon has to the radius of the circle—the first of these proportionals being the side of the heptagon itself—then seven of the first plus seven of the fifth will produce as much as fourteen of the third plus one of the seventh.

This statement is indeed geometric and demonstrable, no less than in the previous sections when it was demonstrated that the plane of an Octagon is a <term>Meson<gloss>A Greek term from Euclid's Elements for a specific type of irrational area</gloss></term>, or that the side of a **Dodecagon** <note>twelve-sided figure</note> is the <term>Apotome<gloss>A Euclidean term for a line segment formed by subtracting one rational line from another</gloss></term> of some line. For in those cases, something was stated about a plane or a line; here, something is stated about the proportion of lines.

But just as it does not suffice for my knowledge and for the measurement of a plane to know that it is a *Meson*, nor for the measurement of a line to know it is some kind of *Apotome*—since there are many of this kind, and no construction or certain, determined quantity of the plane or line is drawn from this general knowledge, but rather these properties only follow after the quantities have already been established and described—so also here, it is not enough for me to know what will happen once seven continuous proportionals are made in the ratio I desire. Since I do not yet have that proportion described by any geometric act, I was therefore waiting for someone to teach me how to establish that proportion first. For in all the previously mentioned figures, there preceded a description, an inscription, the determination of a certain quantity, and a specific geometric act by which this determination was perfected; only then followed the knowledge of those properties which allowed for the comparison of figures among themselves.

To make the difference between these two things clearer, let us look at the side of the **Pentagon**. Our method for describing it above was this: having joined two squares—one of the radius, the other of half its length—into a single square shape, we would subtract half the radius from the side of this square. We would then form a square from the remaining line combined with the square of the radius; the side of this resulting square would be the side of the Pentagon. All these things were possible to do, and even easier to do than to say, as those who handle compasses know. For what is easier
