### OF THE DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

...easier than making a right angle *GAM*, and marking upon its legs as you please *AM*, and its double *AG*; and, having placed one foot of the compass at *M* and the other extended to *G*, drawing a circle *GP*, continuing the line *MA* to *P*; and finally, grasping *GP* with the compass and applying it into another circle, whose semi-diameter is *GA*?

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle with a horizontal diameter. Points labeled P, A, M, and G are marked along this baseline. From the center point A, two radii are drawn to points X and u on the circular arc. Additional construction lines are drawn from point P to X and from M to u, illustrating a trigonometric or algebraic construction related to pentagons or septagons.</image-desc>

But see now what **Bürgi’s Algebra** <note>original: *Cossa Byrdiana*; "Cossic" math was the early name for algebra</note> tells us about the side of the **Pentagon**. Once that method has been previously derived, it produces the number 5 roots – 5 cubes + 1 fifth-power <note>original: *5 i -- 5 iij + 1 v*; in early algebra, these Roman numerals indicated the power of the unknown variable x</note> equal to no chord <note>meaning the equation equals zero</note>; that is: if five quantities are made proportional in a continuous order, of which the first is the side of the Pentagon, and the proportion is that which exists between the Pentagonal side and the semi-diameter, then the five first powers together with one fifth power will be equal to five third powers.

Again, as in the **heptagon** <note>original: *septangulo*; a seven-sided figure</note>, it does not teach how to establish the continuous proportion in which this occurs, nor does it express the length of the proportionals through things known before; rather, it teaches what relationship <note>original: *affectio*</note> follows once it has been established. I am commanded, therefore, to represent the relationship, for it is supposed to follow that I shall also have the proportion. But how shall I represent the relationship—by what **Geometric** act? I am taught to do it by no other way than by using the very proportion I am seeking; the principle is begged <note>a "begging of the question" or circular reasoning</note>: and the poor **Calculator**, destitute of all the protections of Geometry, sticking fast among the thorns of Numbers, fruitlessly looks back to his algebra. This is the one distinction between **Algebraic** <note>original: *Cossicas*</note> and **Geometric** determinations.

The second distinction is that this entire Bürgian reasoning rests upon the essence of discrete quantity, or numbers; and it divides the diameter into certain small particles as often and as long as it wishes, generally into two parts; the whole process rests on this number, and would be changed if another name or another number were given to the **Diameter**. But the Geometry of figures, delivered above, is not like this; it marks those sides that are **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabilia*; commensurable lengths</note> in length indeed by Numbers; but it by no means pursues **Inexpressible** <note>original: *ineffabilia*; irrational lengths</note> things with numbers. Instead, having distributed them through its own certain species, it declares them in such a way that it appears we are dealing not with discrete quantities, but with continuous quantities—with lines and surfaces.

Thirdly, up to this point, both the side of a Figure and the side of a star-polygon of the same name each had its own certain description; in this **Algebraic Analysis**, this is most marvelous (although it especially frightens the Geometer): that what is commanded cannot be performed by a single way. Although that is not free from all law, but, as was begun to be said above, there are as many numbers performing the command as there are chords—or **Diagonals**—in the figure differing in length; just as in a pentagon there are two, and in a heptagon three: one for the side, the others for the chords of the angles. Therefore, whatever is finally pronounced concerning the proportion proper to the figure, that is common to the proportions of all its lines to the diameter.

Fourthly, granted that a single proportion performs what is commanded; nevertheless, I am not taught to solve it, but only to hunt it from afar. For since the species of lines, for the sake of science, are occupied with the genus of **Inexpressibles** <note>that is, non-countable things, or things that reject numbers</note>, and for that reason the ratio is never exhausted by any multitude <note>of digits</note>, something always remains in uncertainty...

### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.

left behind: on the contrary, this method—as was said in the second place—does not take up other supports besides numbers, but always divides the diameter in various ways into many tens of thousands of tens of thousands <note>original: *Myriadas Myriadum*</note> so that the ratio might become more exact. Yet in this way, it never becomes perfectly exact. Briefly put: this is not to know the thing itself, but at least to know something nearly greater or lesser; and some later calculator can always approach more closely. To arrive at the point itself is given to no one. Such, indeed, are all things that lie hidden in the sole possibility of quantitative matter; they do not have a knowable formation by which they might eventually be established in an act of human knowledge.

Fifthly, to deal specifically with the **heptagon** <term>septangulo; a seven-sided polygon</term> and the figures of this kind that follow: since continuous proportionality is extended along with the number of sides through those figures following each other in their order, it follows that even if the last term were known as much as possible—as in the heptagon, the seventh proportional—the intermediate terms still could not be obtained through it. For between two quantities which do not have a proportion between them like two numbers of a continuous proportionality (such as cubes, fifth-powers, etc.), any number of intermediate continuous proportionals cannot be established **geometrically**; rather, only one, or three, or seven, or fifteen, etc. <note>Kepler refers to the fact that one can find means by repeated bisection (2, 4, 8...), which allows for $2^n - 1$ intermediates</note> can be found. But two, four, five, six, eight, nine, etc., cannot then be established in a plane—since we are here dealing with plane figures.

Now, between the radius 1 and the seventh proportional $1^{vii}$ of the heptagonal proportion, there are six mean proportionals; and the ratio of 1 to $1^{vii}$ is not as a number to a number of a continuous proportion of the same length. That is, the proportion of the radius to the side of the heptagon is not according to two numbers; it is, in other words, **Ineffable** <note>original: *non Effabilis*; meaning it cannot be expressed as a rational ratio of whole numbers</note>. For if it were **Effable**, it would fall into the types previously explained in the earlier classes, and the seven angles would not be seven, but three or four, which involves a contradiction. For the proportion of the sides was derived from the angles of the primary figures. It would therefore be necessary for all six mean proportionals to be established—namely, between 1 and $1^{vii}$. Conversely, if $1^{vi}$ were given in quantity, then five means would fall between 1 and $1^{vi}$. But if 1 to $1^{vi}$ were then as a cubic number to a cubic number, then first $1^{ii}$ and $1^{iv}$ could be established in one act, and then between 1, $1^{ii}$, $1^{iv}$, and $1^{vi}$, three mean proportionals could be found in three acts. But if $1^{v}$ were given in quantity, again all four intermediates would have to be established in a single act; which could not happen except in an **Effable** proportion, as before. Let the rest be understood according to these principles.

We conclude, therefore, that these **Cossic Analyses** <term>Analyses Cossicas; early algebra, named from the Italian 'cosa' (thing) for the unknown variable</term> are foreign to the present contemplation; nor do they constitute any degree of knowledge comparable to those which we have explained above.

### ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

<margin>
It is more negatively [held] among theologians that those things are impossible which contain a contradiction in
</margin>
the eternally simple: because by its own nature it is among the unknowables. And yet, there are some scientific properties of this non-being; just like **conditional beings** <term>Entia conditionalia; things that would exist only if a certain condition were met</term>. For IF there WERE a heptagon <term>Septangulum; a seven-sided polygon</term> described in a circle, the proportion of its sides would have such properties. Let it suffice to have warned: they should consider that God’s knowledge does not extend to such impossibilities, especially since these formal ratios of geometric things are nothing other than the very Essence of God; because whatever is in God from eternity, that is one individual divine essence. It would therefore be, in a way, for Him to know Himself otherwise than He is, if He knew as communicable <note>capable of being shared or created</note> those things which are incommunicable. And what a flattery this would be—to defraud the rest [of the readers] for the sake of the unskilled who will not even read the book.

There are also other false propositions of geometers concerning the sides of figures of this kind, which even a more skillful **mechanical method** <term>Mechanica; practical geometry using tools and approximations rather than pure logic</term> would refute; yet they are thrust upon the youth for the sake of practical application. An example is when the side $AC$ of a heptagon is set by **Albrecht Dürer** <note>The famous German Renaissance artist who wrote a manual on geometry for artists</note> as equal to half the side of a triangle $AB$ of the same circle. But that this is too short, even the mechanical experiment itself teaches. Nevertheless, lest a too-crude manual experimentation deceive anyone, one can detect the falsehood by this reasoning alone before even setting hand to tools. The side of a triangle is proved to be **expressible in power** <term>Effabile potentiâ; a side whose square can be expressed as a rational number or ratio</term> by the number of its angles; therefore, its half is the same. But the side of a heptagon is not expressible in power, by the very fact that it is a heptagon, and because seven is neither six, nor five, nor three. For prime numbers produce distinct species; and species are incommensurable among themselves, nor is one the same as another.

The eleven-sided figure.

For the side of a **hendecagon** <term>Undecanguli; an 11-sided polygon</term>, such a description is circulated: In a circle, from the same point $A$, let the side of a square $AC$ be drawn to one part of the circumference, the side of a triangle $AD$ to the opposite part, and the side of a hexagon $AB$ and $AF$ to both sides. Let the angle $FAB$ of those two hexagon sides be subtended by another triangle side $BF$, which will cut the first triangle side $AD$ at $G$. Also, from the end of the square side $C$, let the diameter $CE$ be drawn through the center $I$. From the other end of the diameter $E$, through the intersection of the triangle sides $G$, let the straight line $EG$ be drawn, cutting the square side $AC$ at $H$. The line $GH$ between these two intersections is said to be the side of the hendecagon. In truth, it is too long, as even the mechanical method teaches. But a skillful Geometer...

[the geo]metry considers the appearance of the line, which necessarily shares something from the **Triangular** <term>Trigonico; three-sided</term> and **Quadrangular** <term>Tetragonico; four-sided</term> sides, however remote the degree. ## Proposition XLVI.

The division of any arc of a circle into three, five, seven, etc., equal parts, and in any ratio which is not a continuous doubling of those previously demonstrated, is not within a Geometric possibility of the kind that produces scientific knowledge.

*The division of an arc into two, four, eight, etc.—that is, by continuous doubling—is indeed Geometric, and has been used until now. Division into three happens to occur in the whole Circle by means of the **Triangle** <term>Trigonum</term>; in the Semicircle, as in the **Hexagon**; in a quarter part, as in the **Dodecagon** <term>12-sided polygon</term>; in a fifth part, as in the **Pentadecagon** <term>Pentekadecagono; 15-sided polygon</term>; in an arc of 135 Degrees, as in the **Octagon**; and in an arc of 108 degrees, as in the **Decagon** <term>10-sided polygon</term>. In five parts, however, it happens to be divided similarly: the whole circle by the **Pentagon**; the semicircle, as in the Decagon; a third part of the circle, as in the Pentadecagon; and an arc of 150 degrees, as in the Dodecagon. The same is true for the halves, quarters, and other parts of these arcs in a continuous sub-double proportion. But this does not occur because of the inherent nature of **Trisection** <term>division into three</term> and **Quinisection** <term>division into five</term>, but by accident, and because of other properties of the figures, which have been discussed until now.*

*But that a general trisection, or a division in any other proposed ratio that is not continuously doubled, is impossible, is clear from a comparison with possible bisection <note>dividing in two</note>. In bisection, the "means" to the arc and the angle to be bisected (which the arc measures) is a straight line, the **chord** <term>subtenſa; a line segment connecting two points on a curve</term> of the arc, which can be divided into two equal parts Geometrically. Since the equality of these linear parts results in the equality of the parts of any arc—whether small or large—with respect to the whole circle: from this source it also follows that in a Triangle, from the equality of the sides, one may argue for the equality of the opposite angles. This "means," however, deserts us in other divisions. For even if a straight line subtended to an arc can be divided into any number of parts, and that Geometrically; yet it does not follow that any proportion of the parts of the chord (after the proportion of equality) results in the same proportion of the parts of the arc. Just as in a Triangle one cannot argue from any proportion of the sides (except for the case of equality) to the same proportion of the opposite angles. For if the chord of an arc, for example, is divided into three equal parts: if the lines that divide it were perpendicular to the chord, the middle part of the arc would be smaller than the side parts; if the dividing lines started from the center of the arc <note>as radii</note>, the middle part of the arc would be larger than the side parts. Therefore, between the distance in-*

# BOOK I. ON THE DEMONSTRATION

...finite and the center of the circle, is a point from which two cutting lines, when drawn, would divide both the chord <term>subtensam; a straight line connecting two points on a curve</term> and its arc into three equal parts. In truth, that point is always further removed from the arc of the circle the smaller the arc to be trisected is, yet the proportion is not constant. Since the arcs of a circle can be diminished toward infinity, the distance of this point also runs out toward infinity. Truly, there is no scientific knowledge of the infinite, or of infinite variety. And this difficulty holds back Trisection, which is even simpler and closer to equality. A much greater difficulty arises in the subsequent divisions of any arc—for example, into 5, 7, 9, 11, etc., equal parts. For then, it is no longer even possible for there to be an identical point from which straight lines could be drawn that cut the chord into the commanded equal parts while also cutting the arc into equal parts.

Whatever support we can bring to universal division <note>the "promiscuous" or general division of any arc</note> derived from the number that names the division, it must be general and common to the chords of any arc, whether of a large arc that differs greatly from its chord, or a small one that differs little. However, to leave the proportion of the parts of the chord to the parts of its arc vague is not to determine it scientifically. And let this be said especially regarding Trisection or Quinisection <note>division into five parts</note> etc., by the "Byrgian Analytic" <note>Referring to the algebraic methods of Jost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who developed early logarithms and algebraic techniques</note> which we discussed copiously in the preceding Proposition. 

<margin>The nature of Bürgi’s method for dividing an arc into equal parts.</margin> Even though everything said there also applies here, certain things said there are more appropriate to this place, and they become more illustrious and admirable in the division of arcs than in the division of the whole circle. For I will pass over those common points: that the starting principle is begged (by ordering us to do the very thing whose method of doing was being sought); that the properties of continuous quantity are not produced scientifically through discrete quantities or Numbers; and that whatever number is elicited for the side determining the commanded part of the arc, it can teach nothing more than that the result is either greater or less than what is required. Therefore, just as raw and undigested matter relates to something formed, or as indeterminate and undefined quantity relates to a figure, so too does that Analytic method relate to Geometric determinations. 

That "semi-mechanical" Cossic art <term>Cossâ; the early modern name for Algebra, from the Italian 'cosa' meaning 'the thing' or the unknown variable</term> is especially excellent and noble in its own right, yet it is degenerate and lowly within scientific Geometry. This is because, while every chord smaller than the diameter is associated with two unequal arcs of the circle (one smaller than a semicircle, the other larger), and thus the equal part of the smaller arc has a smaller chord while the equal part of the larger arc has a larger chord, this Byrgian Analytic prescribes a general rule—not only for these two unequal arcs but also for many other chords of the circle—which is useful for expressing all of them closely in numbers. 

For example, in trisection, the law is this: If an arc is given (let it be 48 degrees) and its chord, and that arc is to be divided into three parts, each of 16 degrees—that is, the chord of this part must be found, or its ratio to the chord of the whole 48 degrees—then I am instructed to make the chord of the whole to the sought chord of the part as the latter is to a second proportional, and the second to a third proportional. Now I am instructed to triple the chord of the part and from it subtract the third proportional; what remains is said to equal the chord of the whole. That is, from the given chord, the third part is multiplied cubically as a fraction, and the resulting number is added to the whole. Thus increased, the third part is a little smaller than the sought chord. For if this itself is again multiplied cubically and added to the whole, the third part thus increased comes closer to the truth; and this continues on to infinity. By this process, one gradually arrives very close to the chord of 16 Degrees.

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

But if you set a larger number *n* to be multiplied cubically <note>Kepler is referring to solving a cubic equation, which corresponds to the trisection of an angle</note>, and nearly as much as the compass indicates should be owed to the third part of the remainder of the circle after 48° has been removed—namely 312°, of which a third is 104°—then you will also complete the chord <term>subtensam; the straight line connecting the ends of an arc</term> of an arc of 104°, and of its complement 256°, in this same way. Nor is this all; but if you also add a full circle <note>360 degrees</note> to 48 and to 312, you will also find, through that same <term>Cossic Name; "Cossic" comes from the Italian 'cosa' (thing), an early term for algebra</term>, another chord for the thirds of those sums (namely 136 and 224). And in general, for as many units as remain in the number of the division after two are removed, so many times is it permitted to add a full circle or a second arc as proposed, so that the chords of the new arcs may be tracked down by the same algebraic name. From this, the huge difference appears between these algebraic names and the "scientific" degrees <note>referring to the geometric constructibility explained in the previous chapters</note> which I explained above.

But can some nobler art not be found by which the divisions of arcs might be performed in every possible way? I respond: if all the chords of the arcs to be divided are considered under a common notion, and if we only have those aids which are common to all sought-after chords (such as any number of continuous proportionals in the sought-after ratio), then no one will ever devise anything nobler. Anyone who strives here is merely repeating what has already been done; they have established a contradiction in terms, having become confused. For from common principles, nothing specific to any individual case can be concluded.

However, if we start a discussion about the "specific differences" of the lines that are stretched under the arcs to be divided, the state of the question changes. In place of a universal division of an arc, there is substituted a division of the whole circle through a **Regular figure**, which grants its own specific property to the proposed chord. We have already dealt with these Regular figures above, and we shall deal with them more fully in what follows. Indeed, in this very question, we were seeking a means by which we could describe some of those figures. Since, therefore, such a means must by its nature be prior to the thing itself that is to be produced through this means, we would certainly be begging the principle <note>using circular reasoning</note> if we sought aid from the Regular figures to provide our means.

<margin>The universal arc divisions of Pappus and Clavius.</margin>
But here, some adversary might object to me: that *Pappus of Alexandria*, in the fourth book of his *Mathematical Collections*, Proposition 31, provides a three-part division of an angle <note>trisection</note> by means of a **Hyperbola**; and in Proposition 35, shows how to cut an angle in any given ratio by means of the **Quadratrix** and the **Helix**. And *Clavius*, in Book 13, Proposition 25 of his *Practical Geometry*, performs the same thing by means of the **Conchoid of Nicomedes** <note>a "shell-like" curve used to solve problems that simple geometry cannot</note>.

Truly, the inventions of those authors establish no possibility of a "Scientific Geometric" universal division. To make this clear, I will first explain Pappus's mechanisms regarding trisection; then, I will bring to light the difference between those and "scientific" descriptions.

<margin>Pappus’s trisection of an angle.</margin>
First, *Pappus* himself, in the preamble before Proposition 31, divides problems (which he calls "Geometric" in the more general sense of the word, whereas for us "Geometric" has a special meaning) into **Plane, Solid, and Linear**. He admits that the **Trisection** of an angle cannot be solved by **Plane** means (which to me are "Geometric" in the special sense, being scientific and belonging to the degrees I have explained). For that reason, he rebukes the ancient Geometers for their ill-advised efforts, who sweated here in vain.

He himself, therefore, performs his trisection through **Solids** <note>using conic sections like the hyperbola</note>, and performs universal division through "figured lines" <note>complex curves like the quadratrix</note>.

# DEMONSTRATION OF BOOK I.

*The method of trisection is as follows. Having proposed an angle to be trisected, let a perpendicular be dropped from a point on one leg <note>original: "cruris"</note> onto the other leg, which is understood to determine the length of the legs; and to that other leg, now made shorter, and to the perpendicular, let parallel lines be drawn—to the former from the first point, and to the latter from the proposed angle—so that where they meet they form a right angle. Now, through the point where the perpendicular was dropped, he makes the surface of a Cone (a solid figure) pass; then, he inclines the Cone thus applied, or makes it "nod," until it designates on the plane, with that same surface of its own, the section called a **Hyperbola**, which is characteristic of the drawn parallels as its **Asymptotes**. Then, from that point where the perpendicular was dropped, with a distance that is double the first leg, he describes an arc in the plane, cutting the line of the conic section; and having connected the center of the arc with this common section, he draws a line parallel to it from the proposed angle; and once this is done, he demonstrates that a third part has been cut away from the angle.*

<margin>Pappus, Book 4, Proposition 34</margin>
*Pappus* indeed makes this a **Solid problem** <term>Problems solvable using conic sections (like the hyperbola or parabola) rather than just a ruler and compass</term> in this way, through the use of a *Cone*, a solid figure. But insofar as a Conic section, called a **Hyperbola**, can be delineated in a plane even without a *Cone*—between given **Asymptotes** <term>Lines that a curve approaches but never reaches</term> forming a right angle, through a given point within them—the same problem seems to belong also among **Linear problems** <term>In classical geometry, "linear" problems involved curves more complex than circles and conic sections, often called "mechanical" curves</term>. For such a line is produced by Geometric motion and a continuous change of intervals; that is, it is represented by any number of points, an indeterminate number of them; and this is no less true than for the **Quadratrix** and the **Helix** <note>The Spiral of Archimedes</note>; by which lines *Proposition 35* accomplishes both a **Triple** <note>Trisection</note> and an **All-varying** <note>Dividing into any number of parts</note> section. Such is the mechanism of *Pappus*.

What then shall we say? Is it not true that between given *Asymptotes*, through a given point, only one single *Hyperbola* is traced, whether that happens by the "nodding" of a *Cone* or by the continuation of infinite points? Is there not only one single section of a circle with a *Hyperbola* in the outer region? Is there not only one single and certain inclination of the line connecting the points of the *Hyperbola* to the diameter of the figure?

Indeed, I confess that all these things are necessary and certain, provided that the *Hyperbola* has already been described. For even previously, in the analytical trisection of *Bürgi* <note>Jost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss mathematician and clockmaker</note>, there was a certain and necessary length or proportion of the chord <note>original: "subtensæ"</note> of the established third part to the chord of the whole arc. But because we are not asking about this—what the thing is once it is already done—but rather how the thing, not yet done, is finally to be made so that it may exist: for that reason, we have nothing more from the **Solid** and **Linear Problems** of the ancients that might lead to the sought-after science of lines than we previously had from the Analytical doctrine of the moderns. To be sure, there is only one single *Hyperbola* line drawable in the plane of the positioned *Asymptotes* through the proposed point. But since it is not yet drawn, I am ordered to incline the *Cone* over the point of application for just so long until the curve exists and has been drawn; or without a *Cone*, I am ordered to change the lines which delineate the *Hyperbola* through continuous points for just so long until the *Hyperbola* is sufficiently prolonged; and those intermediate parts which fall between the established points, I am ordered to imagine as having been made. On both sides, I am ordered to pass through—by a single act or motion—that which exists by the power of infinite division; so that by this transition, that which lies hidden in that potential infinity might also be reached, though without the perfect light of science, such as those problems named **Plane problems** <term>Problems solvable using only a straightedge and compass</term> by the ancients possess.
<margin>(solid problems)</margin>

*François Viète the Frenchman* and the *modern Belgian Geometers* <note>Likely referring to Simon Stevin or Adriaan van Roomen</note> frequently use postulates of this kind in their solutions of those problems which, by their own nature, are not solvable except "inartificially"—either through numbers or through Geometric motions governed by a certain infinity of changes.

For when everything has been made ready that is thought to serve in making the mind certain: we shall hold the determination of that which is sought, whether it be closer to being greater or smaller, and always moving nearer—just as we had said before regarding Analytical trisection.

<margin>
There is no **scientific** <note>original: "scientificus"; here meaning a rigorous, logical proof following the rules of Euclidean geometry</note> transition from planes to solids.
</margin>

<margin>
It is impossible to find two mean proportionals **scientifically**.
</margin>

That what I say is true regarding this **solid problem** <term>A "solid problem" in classical geometry is one that cannot be solved with only a ruler and compass, requiring instead the use of conic sections</term> of Trisection is suggested by the very word "solid" itself. *For unless the proportion of the solids is given as that which exists between two cubic numbers, we cannot measure the proposed solid by another known solid to inform the mind. This is because **two intermediate proportionals** <note>original: "duæ intermediæ proportionales"; a classic geometric problem involving finding two values between two given lengths to form a geometric progression</note> cannot be established exactly in a plane. Although they can exist in cubes, there is no passage from planes to the formation of any such cubes without those two means; it is like a broken bridge.* Others teach how to find two mean proportionals through **Geometric motion** <note>original: "motum Geometricum"; referring to mechanical methods or "sliding" rulers that go beyond static geometry</note>, commanding what is impossible regarding the certainty of a proper Geometric act. Pappus himself also teaches this through **Conic sections**, to be expedited by the benefit of two proportionals, since even a Cone is a solid thing. Thus, the principle is always "begged" <note>original: "principium petitur"; a logical fallacy where the proof assumes the thing it is trying to prove</note>, and the bridge lies on the opposite bank.

## XLVII. Proposition.

Figures with an odd number of sides greater than 5 (except for the **Pentadecagon** <note>15-sided figure</note>), along with the chords of some of their parts and even their entire classes, are held in the same status as the **Heptagon** <note>7-sided figure</note> and other figures with a **Prime** number of sides.

*For if the number of sides is odd and not one of the Primes: it is either the smallest multiple of two odd Primes; or the square of some Prime; or a multiple of one Prime and the square of another; or a multiple of squares and multiples separately or joined together.*

*If these figures were describable, inscribable, and **knowable** <note>original: "scibiles"; Kepler uses this to mean figures that can be constructed using only a straightedge and compass</note>, then they would have either a proper demonstration based on their angles, or an improper one based on a comparison with the figures they share traits with. But they have no proper demonstration, because their number of sides is not a Prime from which a demonstration could be formed. Nor do the primary ones—for example, the **Icosihenagon** <note>original: "Unetvigintangulum"; a 21-sided figure</note>—have an improper one, because the figures communicating with them (either both or one or the other, such as the Heptagon here, after the Triangle and Pentagon from which the Pentadecagon is formed) have no proper demonstration themselves, according to Proposition 45. Nor do the secondary ones, such as the **Nonagon** <note>9-sided figure</note>, because there is no way to cut a portion of an arc—say, a third—into as many equal parts as the whole circle took, according to Proposition 46. Neither the third nor the fourth types have demonstrations, because the earlier figures they relate to are themselves indemonstrable.*

<margin>
The side of a **Nonagon** is not knowable.
</margin>

Regarding the **Enneagon** <note>another term for a 9-sided figure</note>, whose number 9 is the square of the first odd Prime (namely 3), geometers have struggled until now. Most have exerted themselves to demonstrate the side of this figure, yet all were in vain. They would never have even attempted this problem if they had paid attention to the distinction between knowable and unknowable things.

<margin>
**Campanus** on the Nonagon.
</margin>

**Campanus** <note>Johannes Campanus (1227–1296), a mathematician famous for his commentary on Euclid</note> wished to demonstrate the Nonagon through the **Trisection of an angle**, which Proposition 46 showed to be unknowable. And while it is true that it is necessarily trisected by the method of **Pappus** and **Clavius** <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician</note>, assuming **Geometric motion**: what is that to the plane figures we are dealing with here, since solid objects are needed to create the aids for trisection?

...curves, such as the Hyperbola, the Quadratrix, the Spiral, and the Conchoid? Indeed, Campanus himself, when attempting trisection, did not notice that he was taking a third part of the angle as if it were already a certainty, which was the very thing that remained to be found. There is a passage in my own copy at the end of Euclid's work on page 586, pertaining to the end of Book IV.

<margin>
Giordano Bruno's **Nonagon** <note>original: "Nonangulum"; a nine-sided polygon</note>.
</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with points A, B, C, D, E, F marked on its circumference, forming a hexagon. A rectangle GHIK is drawn around the circle, tangent at points A and D. A diagonal line runs from H to I, passing through the circle. Points M and N are marked where this diagonal intersects the circle. A perpendicular line AO is dropped from point A to the line LH (the radius).</image-desc>

Giordano Bruno of Nola, in the opposite sides BC and EF of a hexagon ABCDEF, continued in both directions, draws perpendiculars GH and IK, touching the circle at A and D. Then, having drawn the diagonal IH of the resulting parallelogram, he thought the circle was cut in such a way that between the points of contact AD and the intersections M and N, there existed **ninth parts** of the circle, AN and DM. Yet it is demonstrated from the diagram that since the square of that semi-diagonal LH is **expressible** <term>original: "effabile"; in Euclidean geometry, this refers to a magnitude that can be expressed as a rational number or its square root (a "surd"), making it geometrically constructible</term>—specifically 7/16ths of the square of the diameter—(for ABH is 60 degrees; therefore BH is half of AB, or AL; and its power, therefore, is a quarter of the power of AL; thus the power of AH is three-quarters of the power of AL; but the power of LH equals the powers of LA and AH combined). Therefore, the **sine** <note>original: "sinus"; here used in the sense of a half-chord</note> of 40 degrees—that is, half the chord of two-ninths of the circle—would have been **expressible in power** <note>original: "Effabilis potentiâ"; meaning the square of the value is a rational fraction of the square of the diameter</note>, namely the square root of 3/28ths of the square of the diameter. For if a perpendicular AO is dropped from A onto LH, then as the power of LH (7/16) is to the power of HA (3/16), so the power of LA (4/16) is to the power of AO, which is 12/7ths of 1/16, or 3/28ths. Thus, the chord of this nonagonal angle would be "nobler" than some of the previously mentioned ones and would share a common measure with them. However, since it has an odd number of sides—specifically a number derived from the first number 3 squared (9)—it shares nothing with the **Square** <note>original: "Tetragono"</note> and **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigono"</note> through the bisection of arcs, which are the figures to which this degree of "nobility" properly belongs.

## XLVIII. Corollary.

**I**t follows, therefore, that the boundaries of Insight, Science, Determination, Description, and Demonstration consist within the first orders of figures: so that there are no more than four classes of knowable figures. Three of these have their own proper demonstrations, in which the heads of the families are: in the first, the **Square** <note>original: "Tetragonus"</note>, following the diameter of the circle, whose characteristic number is 2; in the second, the **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigonus"</note>, whose characteristic is 3; and in the third, the **Pentagon** <note>original: "Pentagonus"</note>, [whose characteristic is 5]. There is, however, one class of improper demonstrations, whose number is a multiple of two of these (3 and 5), namely 15; for the first figure of that class is the **Fifteen-sided figure** <note>original: "Pentekædecagonus"</note>.

## XLIX. Proposition.

**M**oreover, since bisection (which the first class uses as its own) is common to both the second and third classes, it is clear that the first class exists by one right, and the two remaining classes by another; so that the first has a familiarity with each of the others, while those two are distinguished from each other by their shapes...

...are distinguished, so much so that among those which have their own formal demonstrations, there are, in a sense, only two Families.

*For the **Square** and **Octagon** immediately join themselves to the **Triangular** family, as if they were entirely part of it: because a sixth and a twelfth part of a circle joined together make a fourth part <note>1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4; connecting the Hexagon and Dodecagon to the Square</note>; and a twelfth and a twenty-fourth part, when combined, make an eighth part. Likewise, the **Square** accommodates itself to the **Pentagonal** family to some extent: because a fifth part of the circle added to a twentieth part constitutes a fourth part. The reason is that the numbers 3 and 5 can be divided into numbers of a continuously double proportion: for the parts of 3 are 1 and 2; the parts of 5 are 1 and 4. Truly, such a fellowship does not exist between the classes of Three and Five themselves. For although a sixth part of the circle added to a thirtieth constitutes a fifth, the thirtieth belongs to the class of the **Fifteen-sided polygon** <note>original: "Pentekadecagonicæ"</note>, which does not have its own demonstration. In the same way, a tenth of a circle added to a fifteenth—see here the mixing in of the fourth class—makes a sixth. Because of this duality of Families, the characteristic numbers are 12 in the first, and 20 (or its half, 10) in the second. These matters must therefore be referred to and recorded below in Book III for the distinction of the types of musical song.*

# 50. Comparison of Figures

->or divisions of the circle,<-

The **diameter** holds the first rank; for it is **expressible** <term>original: "effabilis"; a magnitude that can be stated as a rational number or its square root, making it "knowable" in Euclidean geometry</term> in length. Second is the side of the **Hexagon**, which is equal to the semi-diameter, and thus likewise expressible in length. In the third place stand the **Square** <note>original: "Tetragonus"</note> and the **Triangle** <note>original: "Trigonus"</note>, because they have sides expressible only in **power** <term>original: "potentiâ"; meaning the square of the side is a rational number, even if the side itself is a square root</term>. The fourth rank is held by the sides of the **Dodecagon**, the **Decagon**, and the sides of their associated stars; for they arise from an inexpressible power and from **Composites of the first species**—specifically, they are **Binomials** and **Apotomes** <term>specific types of irrational lines defined in Euclid's Book X</term>; those of the Dodecagon are of the first species, while those of the Decagon are of the fourth. In the fifth place follow the sides of the **Pentagon** and its star, as well as the sides of the **Octagon** and its star; for they are of the fourth species of composites, called the **Greater** <note>original: "Mizon"</note> and the **Lesser** <note>original: "Elasson"</note>.

Lest any good quality in the **Decagon** should prejudice the **Pentagon** <note>original: "Quinquangulo"</note>; or lest the same species of the **Octagonal** side should equate its figure to the Pentagon or Decagon; a new virtue is added to the Pentagon at its very origin: through this Family, which communicates with the number Ten, the **Divine Proportion** <note>The Golden Ratio</note> reigns everywhere. This proportion is immediately present in the sides of the Pentagon and its star; yet it does not fit the Decagon and its star except by the mediation of the side of the Hexagon; and to the Octagon, it plainly does not fit at all.

Beyond these properties of the sides, there is yet another assessment of nobility: that figures are distinguished by the suitability and perfection of the **area** which the figure encloses. Here, after the diameter (which has no area, and which alone cuts the area of the circle into two equal parts—as Ptolemy notes—no less than it cuts the circumference), the **Square** and the **Dodecagon** hold the principal place, for they have an **Expressible** area. The Square has an especially high prerogative: for its area is the same as the square of its side, since the species of the area is itself square; thus it encloses half of the square of the diameter. The **Dodecagon**, however, stands after these principles, enclosing three-quarters of the square of the diameter. In the next place follow the **Triangle**, the **Hexagon**, and the **Octagon**, whose area is of the **Medial** <note>original: "Meson"; a type of irrational area in Euclidean geometry</note> species. The areas of the **Pentagon** and **Decagon** do not yet have specific names.

IO. KEPLER'S HARMONIES OF THE WORLD

# BOOK II.
## On the Congruence of Harmonic Figures.

---

### Preface.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut floral band separates the title from the preface heading.</image-desc>

I have thus far explained the mental—or, one might say, the **intellectual** <note>original: νοερῶν (noerōn)</note>—essence of individual regular figures. What follows is a study of their properties when joined together, and their effect, as it were, within the realm of Geometry: this is **Congruence** <note>The ability of shapes to fit together perfectly without gaps, like floor tiles.</note> or, conversely, Incompatibility. For **Demonstrability** <note>The ability to construct a shape using only a compass and straightedge.</note> and **Congruence** do not cover the same ground. While demonstrability applies to individual figures and extends to infinity—simply by the continuous doubling of a single figure's sides—congruence is restricted by specific laws. In congruence, several figures are called into a single fellowship, and because the angles increase as sides are added, the process quickly hinders itself and comes to an end.

And although there are different levels of knowledge and demonstration, and those shapes we have explained differ greatly in "nobility" from those we dismissed as nameless, **Congruence** does not walk exactly in step with this nobility of demonstration. Thus, one is not the cause of the other; rather, both depend on the same common cause—the suitability of the figure’s angles—yet each follows its own laws.

One can see how necessary this part of our inquiry is from the very purpose of the entire work. Since we have taken it upon ourselves to explain the origin of **Harmonics** <note>The mathematical study of musical intervals and universal proportions.</note> and its most excellent effects in the whole world, how could we say nothing about the congruence of figures? For these figures are the very springs from which harmonic proportions flow. Indeed, the Latin word for "to fit together" (*Congruere*) and **Congruence** (*Congruentia*) means the same thing as the Greek terms **to harmonize** <note>original: ἁρμόττειν (harmottein)</note> and **harmony** <note>original: ἁρμονία (harmonia)</note>. 

Furthermore, this effect of figures within Geometry—and within that part of Architecture concerned with **Archetypes** <note>The original "blueprints" or divine ideas used by God to create the universe.</note>—is a kind of image and prelude to the effects found outside of Geometry and beyond the concepts of the mind, occurring in natural and celestial things themselves. This property of congruence, which results in a structure or a physical body, is such that it invites the contemplative Mind to do something similar: to act, to create, and to embody things in the world. This idea has been hidden from eternity in the most-blessed divine mind, within the ranks of Ideas; and like the "Highest Good," which by its nature must communicate itself, it could not be contained within your abstract thought...

<meta>catchword: but that [quin]</meta>

<summary>Kepler introduces the concept of "congruence"—how geometric shapes fit together—as the mathematical equivalent of musical harmony. He argues that this geometric fitting-together is a physical manifestation of divine "archetypes" that God used to structure the universe.</summary>

# On the Congruence of Regular Figures
->Congruence.<-

## I. DEFINITION.

One kind of congruence belongs to the plane, and another to the solid. In a Plane, Congruence is when the individual angles of several figures meet at a single point in such a way that no gap is left.

## II. DEFINITION.

This is called **perfect** when all the angles of every meeting figure meet in the same way, so that all the meetings are similar to one another, and the pattern of meetings can be continued to infinity.

## III. DEFINITION.

**Most perfect**, when even the figures meeting in the plane are of the same species <note>original: "speciei"—meaning they are all the same type of polygon, such as all squares or all hexagons.</note>.

## IV. DEFINITION.

**Imperfect**, when a larger figure is indeed surrounded on all sides by similar meetings, yet a continuation to infinity is not possible; or it is possible, but not without a mixture of different types of meetings. It is an imperfect congruence of a **lower degree** when the larger figure is not suited to meet with a similar type at all its angles.

## V. DEFINITION.

**Solid congruence** occurs, and a solid figure is formed, when the individual angles of several plane figures constitute a solid angle <note>A vertex where three or more faces meet in 3D space.</note>; and with the regular or semi-regular figures fitted together, no gap remains between the sides of the figures—which meet each other on the opposite part of the solid figure—that cannot be closed by a figure of one of the types used, or at least by Regular ones.
*Note that there is another congruence, not of plane figures to form a solid figure, but of the solid figures themselves with each other, to fill a solid space around a single point: of this kind, the three-dimensional figures are only*

<meta>The catchword "duæ" indicates the sentence continues on the next page: "only two."</meta>

<summary>Kepler defines the geometric principles of "congruence," explaining how regular polygons can fit together to tile a 2D plane or form 3D solids. He distinguishes between perfect congruences (uniform tilings) and imperfect ones.</summary>

# CONGRUENCE, BOOK II.

...urs, namely, the **Cube** and the **Rhombic Dodecahedron** <note>original: "Rhombus Dodecahedricus." This is a 12-sided solid where every face is a rhombus; Kepler was one of the first to describe its ability to tile space perfectly.</note>. For the eight angles of a Cube meet at a single point and fill the space entirely on all sides. The Rhombus, however, has two kinds of angles: eight three-lined obtuse angles, and six four-lined acute angles <note>Kepler is describing the vertices: some are formed by the meeting of three faces, others by four.</note>. Therefore, four obtuse angles fit together to fill a space, or six acute ones: <margin>The Geometry of Bees in hexagonal cells with Rhombic bases.</margin> such is the structure that Bees build with contiguous cells, so that three cells from the bottom surround one by their opposing bases, and six surround it from the sides; three others could also surround it from the front to complete the figure, were it not necessary for the doors to remain open. However, we are not dealing here with this congruence of solid figures <note>Kepler moves from 3D space-filling back to the geometry of individual polyhedra.</note>.

### VI. DEFINITION.

The **most perfect** solid Congruence, and solid figure, is when even the Plane congruences are all of the same figure.

### VII. DEFINITION.

This is either entirely regular, when the Planes are regular; it has all its angles on the same spherical surface <note>i.e., all vertices touch the surface of an imaginary sphere</note>, and they are similar to one another.

### VIII. DEFINITION.

Or it is semiregular, when the Planes are semiregular (see Book I, Def. III), and it has solid angles distinguished and dissimilar by the number of lines; yet of no more than two kinds; nor arranged on more than two spherical surfaces described from a single center; and it has as many angles of each kind as one of the Regular figures has.

> It is no obstacle that this solid Congruence is called "most perfect"; for whatever imperfection exists in its planes should not be blamed on the "solidification" <note>The process of forming a 3D object from 2D parts.</note>, but happens to it by chance. Nevertheless, this semiregular type is called "most perfect" only in an equivocal sense.

### IX. DEFINITION.

**Perfect** of a lower degree is when the Planes are regular, and all angles are on the same spherical surface and similar to each other; yet the Planes are of different species, though of each kind there are as many as there are in one of the most perfect figures—that is, no fewer than four, since a solid figure is bounded by at least four planes.

### X. DEFINITION.

**Imperfect** congruence or figure is when, other things remaining the same, the larger figure is found no more than once or twice.

For in that case, the figure becomes more like a part than a whole, and here more like a plane than a solid; since every solid must be bounded by at least four surfaces. This is seen in the following copper engravings <note>original: "typis ex ære"—referring to the printed illustrations.</note> at letters A and B, where the larger figure is a Heptagon <note>A seven-sided polygon.</note>. These two classes, along with the <margin>A. B. page 13 and following.</margin> number of the sides of the larger figure itself, run out into infinity; starting from the Triangle on both sides, which in class A is among the most perfect regular congruences; then passing through the tetragon <note>A square.</note>: then in class B, we encounter once again a most perfect regular congruence: all the others are imperfect.

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

### XI. DEFINITION.

A **semi-solid** is that which does not satisfy all the parts of the fifth definition; as when, with plane figures fitted together, the congruence <note>The way shapes fit together without gaps.</note> does not fully return upon itself, but leaves gaps; otherwise, it maintains what was prescribed in Definitions VI and VII.

### XII. DEFINITION.

**Congruent plane figures** are those which either enclose a solid figure or fill a plane surface without a gap, being themselves regular or semiregular figures.

### XIII. DEFINITION.

**Incongruent** shall be the name for those regular plane figures inscribed in a circle (if indeed they are inscribable) which form neither a solid figure inscribable in a sphere by themselves, or with others of their own or another class, except only an imperfect one; nor do they pave a plane, either by themselves individually, or with the stars of their class, or with the figures and stars of another class all around.

<margin>A. B.</margin>
*Where note that the heptagon <note>A seven-sided polygon; original: "septangulum"</note> and such things are excluded, notwithstanding that two parallel heptagons, assisted by seven squares or fourteen regular triangles, completely enclose a solid; because only two heptagons meet, a figure is formed that is disk-shaped and similar to a plane, and by no means a globe-like spheroid. See the letters A. B. in the figure on the copperplate <note>original: "ex ære," referring to an engraving</note> on folio 53 and following. Thus also the quindecagon <note>A fifteen-sided polygon; original: "Quindecangulum"</note> is excluded, notwithstanding that at some of its angles it fills a space in the plane with related figures; for it does not do this at all angles all the way around.*

### XIV. PROPOSITION.

**At least three** plane angles must meet in a plane congruence.
*For around any point of meeting, the sum of the angles is four right angles <note>i.e., 360 degrees</note>: but the angle of no figure equals the sum of two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>, therefore two angles of any size are still less than four right angles: therefore two do not fill a plane surface, by Definition I.*

### XV. PROPOSITION.

**At least three** plane angles must meet or rise up to form a solid angle.
*For two would coincide not only by their sides but by their whole planes, and would encompass nothing of a solid body: which is contrary to the definition of a solid angle in Euclid.*

### XVI. PROPOSITION.

**The sum** of angles meeting in a plane is always four right angles, never greater: the sum of those meeting in a solid is less than this sum.
*For in a plane, no more than four right angles surround a single point: therefore, when the sum equals four right angles, then no gap is left, and by Definition I, the congruence is then in a plane. If the angles pave a plane, they do not rise to solidity. And conversely, if angles fitted together in a plane leave a gap—that is, when they are less than four right angles—then*

### XVII. PROPOSITION.

<margin>C.</margin> **A**n odd-sided figure, to whose sides figures of two different species are fitted, cannot meet with the same form at all angles, whether in a plane or in a solid.
For let it be that in one of its angles, figures of the same species stand on both sides, which does not happen in the other angles. For the reason of this matter, see figure C of the following copperplate.

### XVIII. PROPOSITION.

**O**nly three types of plane figures perfectly fill a flat space: six <term>Triangles</term><note>original: "Trigoni"; Kepler uses 90-degree "right angles" as his unit of measurement. A triangle's angle is 60 degrees, or 2/3 of a right angle.</note>, four <term>Quadrangles</term><note>original: "Tetragoni"; a square's angle is 90 degrees.</note>, and three <term>Hexagons</term><note>original: "Hexagoni"; a hexagon's angle is 120 degrees.</note>.
<margin>D.</margin> For by Proposition XXXIII of the first book of this work, the angle of a Triangle is two-thirds of one right angle; therefore, six angles of six Triangles are 12 thirds, which is 4 whole right angles <note>In Euclidean geometry, angles around a point must sum to 360 degrees, or 4 right angles, to tile a plane.</note>. See D.
<margin>E.</margin> Likewise, the angle of a Quadrangle is one right angle; therefore, the four angles of four Quadrangles make four right angles. See E. <margin>F.</margin> Likewise, the angle of a Hexagon is eight-sixths of one right angle; therefore, three angles of three figures make 24 sixths, which is 4 right angles; see F. But the angle of a Pentagon is smaller than that of a Hexagon; therefore, three are less than 4 right angles, so three leave a gap. The same is larger than a Quadrangle: therefore, four pentagonal angles are greater than 4 right angles, and thus they cannot be contained in one flat place, by Proposition XVI of this book. <margin>H.</margin> For this reason, see H, with a fourth pentagon marked with points. <margin>I.</margin> Likewise for the <term>Heptagon</term><note>A seven-sided polygon</note> and all larger figures, the angle is larger than that of a Hexagon; therefore, three heptagonal angles exceed 4 right angles. See I, where parts of two Heptagons cover the same place on a plane.
<margin>G.</margin> Refer here to <term>Rhombs</term>, each consisting of two regular Triangles. For they fit together perfectly, like regular Hexagons, even though they themselves are semi-regular figures. See this congruence in the following diagram from the copperplate, at Letter G.
<margin>K.</margin> Refer here also to the six-angled stars made from a <term>Dodecagon</term><note>A twelve-sided polygon</note>, with six rays cut out: at letter K: for in the place of a cut-out ray comes a hollow angle, equal to a right angle. Therefore, three quadrangular angles and three rays of such stars fill the space. For a Hexagon is divided into such a star and six half-Quadrangles.

**A** flat space is filled by the planes of two different figures in six ways; twice from five angles, once from four, and three times from three angles.
For six plane figures cannot meet so that one of their angles is larger than a triangular one: because the quantity of the first triangular angle is two-thirds of one right angle: thus, this taken six times makes 12 thirds, or 4 right angles. Therefore, if one of these six were larger, that is, if the figure had more...

### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

...many-sided figures exceed 4 right angles: and then the plane is not paved <note>Tiled or covered without gaps or overlaps</note>, according to Proposition XVI of this book.

<margin>1. L.</margin>
*Indeed, five plane figures meet if one **Hexagon** is joined to four **Triangles**; they equal two Triangles <note>original: "æquant duos Trigonicos"; Kepler means the 120-degree angle of the hexagon is equal to two 60-degree triangle angles</note>, and such is the Hexagonal form; the shape is like the letter L.*

<margin>2. M. N. O.</margin>
*Or if two **Quadrangles** <note>Squares</note> are joined to three **Triangles**; because they equal three other Triangles <note>The two 90-degree angles of the squares (180°) equal three 60-degree triangle angles (180°)</note>. The form is as in M, or as in N, which is continuously uniform; or finally as in O, which is of a non-uniform continuation.*

*But if you take two **Triangles** and three **Quadrangles**, these will now exceed four right angles: and much more so if two larger angles are brought to join two Triangles.*

<margin>3. P. R.</margin>
*Four figures of two species meet if two **Hexagons** are joined to two **Triangles**. The form is as in P, or as in R.*

*Otherwise, however you join groups of four: you will always produce either more or less than four right angles; and therefore you will not pave the plane space.*

*If we therefore join groups of three, taking care that there are no more than two species; first, there cannot be two **Triangles**, nor two **Quadrangles**, for they would not exceed two right angles, and there would be a gap left for a third figure which no single shape could fill alone.*

<margin>4. S.</margin>
*Now with one **Triangle** placed among three figures, two **Dodecagons** <note>12-sided polygons</note> fit together: and continuation is possible; nor is any other meeting point mixed in. The form of this tiling can be seen at letter S.*

<margin>T.</margin>
*Refer here to the twelve-pointed **Star**, based on the principle that its hollow angle <note>The interior, re-entrant angle of the star</note> equals a **Triangle**: and thus the **Dodecagon** is divided into a star and 12 Triangles; therefore five **Triangles** and two points <note>original: "radii," literally rays</note> of two stars meet: this form can be continued, as seen at letter T.*

<margin>5. V.</margin>
*And with one **Quadrangle** assumed among three figures, two **Octagons** <note>8-sided polygons</note> fit together, and this form is also capable of continuation: see letter V.*

<margin>X. T.</margin>
*Refer here to the **Octagonal Star**, based on the principle that its hollow angle equals a **Quadrangle**: and thus the **Octagon** is divided into a star and eight quadrangular triangles <note>Isosceles right triangles</note>, two of which make a **Quadrangle**. And so three **Quadrangles** and two points of two stars fill the space: a mixed form, as at letter X: or also mixed in another way, as at letter T.*

<margin>6. Z.</margin>
*Now leaving aside the **Triangle** and **Quadrangle** in fitting groups of three, if we come to the **Pentagon**, two of them can be taken because joined they exceed two right angles: and one **Decagon** <note>10-sided polygon</note> fits into the remaining space: for the Decagon is crowned by ten Pentagons: but this form cannot be continued purely. See the diagram at letter Z on the inside.*

<margin>Z.</margin>
*Refer here therefore to the **Pentagonal Star**, when there are three **Pentagons** and the point of one star; because the hollow angle of the star also holds one pentagonal angle, just as the gap between three Pentagons holds the point of the star. See the same letter Z on the outside.*

<margin>Aa.</margin>
*Although not even in this way does the continuation succeed to infinity; for the rule of this "sect" <note>Kepler personifies the pentagonal shapes as a "sect" or group that does not play well with others</note> is unsociable, which, having admitted a few of its own kind, immediately fortifies itself. Behold these two forms also in another way, at letter Aa.*

*But if you wish to continue it entirely, certain "monsters" <note>Irregular or non-standard composite shapes</note> must be admitted: two **Decagons** joined together, with two sides worn away <note>overlapping or removed</note> in each; and let there be a series of five Decagons in a pentagonal arrangement, with no monster in between. In a second, looser arrangement, linear series of Decagons are mediated by single couplings of two Decagons joined together; In a third, the locations of individual angles...*

### HARMONY [OF FIGURES] BOOK II.

<margin>Aa.</margin>
Each pair of **Decagons** <note>10-sided polygons</note> joined together occupies a specific place, with a single **Decagon** placed between them. In the fourth arrangement, whole **Decagons** stand again at the corners, and two **Decagons** mediate between two angles, arranged at equal intervals. In the fifth, stars <note>star-polygons</note> stand with their individual outer rays in each corner, while two whole **Decagons** fill the lines, and in the middle are two joints of **Decagons**. Consequently, every five-angled form brings something new. This structure is most laborious and artistic; it is to be seen at the same letter **Aa**.

<margin>Bb.</margin>
Here also refer to the **Decagonal star**, into whose concave angle the angle of a **Pentagon** <note>5-sided polygon</note> fits; and in turn, two "Tridecile" rays <note>Kepler's term for the points of a decagonal star</note> join with two **Pentagonal** angles and fill a solid place. This form accepts unequal **Pentagons**; and although it can be continued, it leaves empty, gaping **Decagons** in the middle. The form is to be seen at letter **Bb**.

A single **Pentagon** cannot be taken into a joining of three planes <note>A vertex where three shapes meet</note>, for its angle is six-fifths of a right angle <note>108 degrees</note>, according to Proposition XXXIII of Book I. Therefore, fourteen-fifths <note>252 degrees</note> would be left for the remaining two angles, or seven-fifths each <note>126 degrees</note>; no regular figure has such an angle. Nor can two **Hexagons** <note>6-sided polygons</note> be taken; for the remainder would also be the angle of a **Hexagon** <note>120 degrees</note>, and that produces the form reported above, whereas we are seeking here for structures made from two species, not from figures of a single species. Regarding those figures that have more sides and larger angles than a **Hexagon**, once two angles are subtracted from four right angles <note>360 degrees</note>, the remainder is less than what a **Hexagon** possesses; but if only one is subtracted, the remainder is less than what two **Hexagons** possess. However, we have already dealt with those figures that have fewer and smaller angles than a **Hexagon**, determining which and how many they can be when three of them pave a flat surface.

->XX. PROPOSITION.<-

**A flat space is congruently filled in four ways by the plane angles of three species <note>three different types of polygons</note>.**

Three or more **Triangles** <note>Trigonici</note> are not tolerated here; for three triangular angles make two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>; what remains is less than the sum of the smallest angles following them—namely, those of the **Square** <note>Tetragonici</note> and the **Pentagon**. For this reason, two **Squares** or larger shapes cannot be joined to two **Triangles**, because not enough space would remain for the angle of a third species.

<margin>1. Cc. Dd. Ee.</margin>
Therefore, if there are two **Triangles** and one **Square**, a **Dodecagon** <note>12-sided polygon</note> will be joined to them; however, the form is not continued <note>uniformly</note>. See letters **Cc, Dd, Ee** for three forms, all pertaining to this first case.

<margin>Ff. Gg. Hh.</margin>
Here also the **Dodecagonal star** should be referred, as mentioned above. For four **Triangles**, one **Square**, and one star-ray will fill the space. Behold forms **Ff, Gg, Hh**.

If one **Pentagon** is joined to two **Triangles**, the remainder will be incongruous—thirty-two fifteenths <note>Original: "32 decimæ quintæ". This appears to be a mathematical error or misprint for 22/15 of a right angle (132°), which is the remainder when two 60° angles and one 108° angle are subtracted from 360°</note>—for no regular angle has sixteen-fifteenths <note>again, likely a misprint for 11/15, or 66°</note>. But if one **Hexagon** is added to two **Triangles**, the remainder will also be a **Hexagon**, and the form will be one of those mentioned above. Therefore, there can be no more pairs of **Triangles**.

Thus, if there is only one **Triangle**, three **Squares** cannot be added to it, for too much is used up; nor is enough space left for the angle of a third species.

<margin>2.</margin>
Let two **Squares** be added to one **Triangle**; into the remainder of the four right angles, there fits—

### ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

<margin>Ii. Kk.</margin>
The **Hexagonal** <note>original: *Hexagonicus*; 6-sided</note> form fits: it is a double form, able to be continued in the style of Letter Ii, but Letter Kk cannot be continued without mixing shapes. This is the second case.

One **Triangle** <note>60°</note> cannot be joined with two **Pentagons** <note>108° each</note>, for there remains a gap of 14 fifteenths of one right angle <note>84°; a right angle is 90°, so 14/15 of 90° = 84°</note>, which is foreign to Regular figures. Nor can it be joined with a single **Pentagon**; for again there remain 32 fifteenths <note>192°</note>, while no regular figure has an angle of 18 fifteenths <note>108°—Kepler is noting that if one shape is a triangle and one is a pentagon, the remaining space is too large for a single regular shape</note>. Nor can it be joined with one **Hexagon** <note>120°</note>; for together they make 2 right angles <note>60° + 120° = 180°</note>, and no single angle of a figure is that large. Indeed, half of this would be the size of a **Square** <note>90°</note>, which has already been discussed. Nor can it be joined with a single **Heptagon** <note>7-sided</note>, **Octagon** <note>8-sided</note>, or **Enneagon** <note>9-sided</note>; for there would remain for the third type of figure an angle of either 40 twenty-firsts, 11 sixths, or 16 ninths of a right angle, none of which any Regular figure possesses.

Therefore, one **Triangle** <note>60°</note> joined with one **Decagon** <note>144°</note> leaves a gap of 26 fifteenths <note>156°</note>, which is the size of a **15-gon** <note>original: *Pentekædecagonicus*</note>. This is indeed a case of congruence, but at least in an incomplete way. For the **15-gon** has an odd number of sides; therefore, by Proposition XVII, different types of meetings are mixed at the angles of the same figure. A **Decagon**, having an even number of sides, could be surrounded by alternating **Triangles** and **15-gons**; but immediately two such **15-gons** would run into each other and obstruct the pattern.

Furthermore, a **Triangle** cannot be joined with an **11-gon** <note>original: *Hendecagonico*</note>, for there would remain 56 thirty-thirds of a right angle, an angle which no Regular figure has.

Finally, a **Triangle** <note>60°</note> with a **12-gon** <note>150°</note> leaves a gap for another **12-gon** <note>150°</note>, a form which has already been mentioned.

If a **Triangle** were joined to larger shapes, the gap would become smaller, and we have already dealt with the smaller shapes. And so we have finished with the **Triangle** being admitted among three species of shapes.

When more than one **Square** angle <note>90° each</note> is taken away from 4 right angles <note>360°</note>, they do not leave enough space for two angles of two different species, because those joined together would be larger than two right angles.

<margin>3. Ll.</margin>
One **Square**, joined to one **Pentagon**, leaves a gap for a **20-gon** <note>original: *Icosigonico*; 162°</note>. Therefore, the **20-gon** associates with all the angles and fits legitimately; but this order cannot be continued toward the outside. It is, therefore, an imperfect congruence. Behold the figure at letter **Ll**. This is the third case.

<margin>4. Mm.</margin>
A **Square** joined to a **Hexagon** leaves a gap for a **12-gon** <note>original: *Dodecagonico*; 150°</note>. Behold the figure at letter **Mm**: This is the fourth and final case.

<margin>Nn</margin>
To this, refer the **12-pointed star** <note>original: *stella Dodecagonicam*</note>, which twelve **Triangles** fill: so that here four angles meet to fill the solid space: two **Triangles**, a **Square**, a **Hexagon**, and the ray of the star. Behold the figure at letter **Nn**.

A **Square** added to a **Heptagon** leaves a gap of 11 sevenths of a right angle, an angle which no Regular figure has. Added to an **Octagon**, it leaves an **Octagonal** gap: a form discussed above. Thus we have finished with the **Square**.

A **Pentagon** with a **Hexagon** leaves a gap of 22 fifteenths; with a **Heptagon**, 48 thirty-fifths; with an **Octagon**, 13 tenths, since no regular figure has an angle that large. And now the gap begins to be smaller than the angle of an **Octagon**, which is 15 tenths <note>135°</note>. But we have already completed those which have smaller angles. Thus we have finished with the **Pentagon**.

Three **Hexagons** together fill a flat place <note>120° x 3 = 360°</note>, therefore they cannot be mixed with two shapes larger than themselves. And thus we have finished with the mixing of three figures.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on how plane figures (polygons) can be joined at a single point (vertex). <header>CONGRUENCE BOOK II.</header>

## XXI. PROPOSITION.

<margin>see figure q 1. below</margin>
Plane figures of four or more species <note>original: *specierum*; meaning different types of polygons, such as a triangle, a square, a pentagon, and a hexagon combined</note> do not fit together at individual angles to fill a solid space.

*For the four smallest angles are these: the Triangular <note>60°</note>, the Tetragonal <note>Square, 90°</note>, the Pentagonal <note>108°</note>, and the Hexagonal <note>120°</note>. But the first and last of these together equal two right angles <note>60° + 120° = 180°</note>, the second is a right angle <note>90°</note>, and the third exceeds a right angle by one fifth of a right angle <note>108° is 90° + 18°</note>. Therefore, joined together, they are greater than four right angles <note>360°</note>; wherefore, by Proposition XVI, they do not fit together. Much more, then, will four right angles be exceeded by even larger angles.*

## XXII. AXIOM.

<margin>see p 7. below</margin>
When two plane angles are not together greater than a third, they do not form a solid angle with it. <note>In modern geometry, for a vertex to "fold" into 3D space, the sum of any two angles must be greater than the third, and the sum of all angles must be less than 360°.</note>

## XXIII. PROPOSITION.

<margin>see figure 2. a. below</margin>
Two plane angles of an unequal-sided figure <note>original: *figurae imparilaterae*; likely referring to polygons with an odd number of sides, like pentagons</note>, meeting with one of another species, do not form any regular solid.

*For by Proposition XVIII, the solid angles become irregular <note>original: *difformes*</note>, which is against the definitions from V to X.*

## XXIV. PROPOSITION.

<margin>Number 1. of the following figure.</margin>
Three plane angles of three distinct species of figures, one being unequal-sided, meeting together, do not complete a perfect solid figure.

*For again, by XVII, the solids become diverse in form, which is contrary to the definitions.*

<image-desc>A faint geometric diagram, likely a triangular pyramid or tetrahedron, is sketched between Proposition XXIV and Proposition XXV.</image-desc>

## XXV. PROPOSITION.

The most perfect and regular congruences of plane figures for forming a solid figure are five. <note>These are the five "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>

*This is a commentary <note>original: *scholion*</note> on the final part of the last book of Euclid. For by Proposition XV of this book, we begin with three angles, and by XVI we conclude that they cannot meet in groups of six Triangles, four Squares, or three Hexagons, because by XVII these would equal four right angles <note>360°, thus lying flat rather than forming a corner</note>.*

<margin>Number 2. of the following figure.</margin>
*Therefore, three Triangles, fitting together at individual angles, make less than 4 right angles—that is, they make two right angles <note>3 × 60° = 180°, which is 2 × 90°</note>; thus, when three triangles are fitted together, the gap <note>original: *hiatus*</note> is filled by a fourth Triangle. From this comes the Tetrahedron, or Pyramid.*

<margin>Oo. & Nn. 5. on the following leaf.</margin>
*Four Triangles, fitting together at individual angles, make 8 thirds of a right angle <note>4 × 60° = 240°</note>, which is less than 12 thirds, or 4 right angles <note>360°</note>. When the sides of the triangles are joined, a Pyramid is formed with a gaping quadrilateral base; to this, another such Pyramid from the opposite side fits into the same gap to close the figure on all sides. From this comes the Octahedron.*

<margin>Pp. & qq. 4. on the following leaf.</margin>
*Five Triangles, fitting together at individual angles, make 10 thirds of a right angle <note>5 × 60° = 300°</note>, which is less than 12 thirds. When ten sides are fitted to a common angle, a Pyramid with a pentagonal base is formed. In order for the angles at the base to also become five-planed <note>having five faces meet at each vertex</note>, two planes in that base must meet three other plane angles, and thus fifteen others must fit those ten, and as many must be extended on the other side. **Three Tetragonal angles** <note>original: *Tetragonici anguli*; the 90° angles of a square</note> are three right angles, *which is less than four plane right angles* <note>360°</note>: they therefore fit together to form a solid angle. The joined squares <note>tetragons</note> leave a gap of three plane right angles; conversely, there are three angles of those three planes that project outward. Therefore, three other Squares, fitting together with their individual angles into one solid, are suitable and fitting to fill those gaps with their projections, and to receive those projections into their own gaps. From this comes the **Hexahedron** or **Cube**.

**Four Tetragonal angles** equal four right angles, wherefore by Proposition XVI they do not form anything solid <note>Four 90° angles lie perfectly flat (360°), so they cannot "fold up" into a 3D corner</note>. *So we have finished with pure Squares.*

<margin>
See figure R. r. and here number 3.
</margin>
**Three Pentagonal angles** <note>Each 108°</note> are eighteen-fifths of one plane right angle <note>18/5 * 90° = 324°</note>, which is less than twenty-fifths, or four right angles <note>360°</note>: they therefore fit together to form one solid. If one Pentagon is surrounded at its base in this way by five others, the figure gapes upwards with five pentagonal plane angles, and has five projecting pentagonal plane angles. Therefore, another figure is to be built opposite this one, similar to it; and the five projecting plane angles of either one will fit into the five gaps of the other, and vice versa. From this is born the **Dodecahedron** <note>A 12-sided solid made of regular pentagons</note>. *So we have finished with pure Pentagons, and at the same time with all the figures of only one species that can be fitted together: because three Hexagonal angles, by Proposition XVI, do not rise to form a solid.* <note>Three 120° angles of a hexagon equal 360°, creating a flat tiling rather than a solid</note>
