*Pythagoreans* and *Plato*, and Euclid's commentator *Proclus*, were accustomed to call the **World-Figures** <note>original: *figuras mundanas*; more commonly known today as the Platonic Solids</note>. I have said in the preamble to Book I that it is uncertain how they were applied to the bodies of the world. To be sure, there is a common persuasion, derived from *Aristotle*, that those philosophers looked toward the five simple Bodies of the World <note>the elements</note> according to the fivefold number of these figures—namely to the four Elements: **Fire**, **Air**, **Water**, **Earth**, and to the so-called **Fifth Essence** <note>original: *Quinta Essentia*; the ether or celestial matter</note>, or celestial Matter; comparing the properties of the figures with the qualities of those simple bodies. For in the **Cube**, its uprightness upon a square base has a certain shadow of stability, which is the same property as that of earthly Matter: seeking the bottom by the weight of its gravity, since even the whole globe of the Earth is commonly believed to rest in the middle of the World. ...a four-sided plane <note>original: *quadrilaterum*, completing the word from the previous page</note> dividing the body of the figure into two equal parts, just as the great circle divides a globe suspended from two poles; this is a certain image of mobility, just as **Air** is the most mobile of elements through both the speed and the variety of its directions. 

In the **Tetrahedron** <note>a four-sided pyramid</note>, the small number of planes seems to signify the dryness of **Fire**, since the definition of dry things is *to be contained by their own limits*; in the **Icosahedron** <note>a twenty-sided solid</note>, conversely, the multitude of planes seems to signify the moisture of **Water**, since moisture is defined as *being contained by the limits of others* <note>Kepler is quoting Aristotle's definitions of the qualities of the elements</note>. For a small number of planes indicates what is one’s own, while a multitude indicates what is adopted or foreign. And in another way, the plane Triangle is proper to the Tetrahedron, because the whole Tetrahedral figure is a solid triangle; but that same Triangle is not proper to the Icosahedron, but borrowed, because the solidity of the Icosahedron is more like a Pentagon <note>five-sided shape</note> than a Triangle <note>likely referring to the five triangles meeting at each vertex</note>. Again, in the sharp point of the Tetrahedron pressing from one base, the *penetrating and dividing power of Fire* seems to be sketched; in the blunt and five-lined angle of the Icosahedron, the *filling power of humors* <note>liquids</note>, that is, the power of moistening. In the smallness and thinness of the Tetrahedron is the nature of fire; in the globe-like mass of the Icosahedron is the nature of water, even having a shape like a drop. In the Tetrahedron there is the most surface area and the least body; in the Icosahedron the corporeal mass is much greater than the surface: just as in **Fire** form excels, while in **Water** matter excels.

<margin>
3. The **Dodecahedron** is the symbol of **the Heavens**.
</margin>
The **Dodecahedron** <note>a twelve-sided solid made of pentagons</note> indeed is left for the celestial body, having the same number of planes as the celestial Zodiac has signs; and it is demonstrated to be the most capacious of the remaining figures: just as the **Heavens** contain all things.

Although this analogy is plausible—not indeed to Aristotle (who, since he denied the World was created, could not acknowledge an Archetypal power in quantitative figures, since no such power resides in them to make anything corporeal without an Architect)—but to me, and to all Christians, who hold by faith that the World, when it did not previously exist, was created by God *in weight, measure, and number* <note>original: "in pondere mensura & numero", a reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20</note>, namely according to Ideas co-eternal with Himself; although, I say, this analogy is plausible in general, yet shaped in this specific way it is held by no necessity. It suffers from objections, not only because of the discrepancy of certain properties in the same analogy, but also because of a greater suitability of the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron with Fire; and finally because the dispute over the number of Elements and the rest of the Earth is much greater than that over the number of these figures.

But if the Pythagoreans stopped here, I do not blame Ramus <note>Petrus Ramus, a 16th-century philosopher</note> or Aristotle for rejecting this analogy when it was shaken by their disputes. But twenty-four years ago, I investigated these five bodies in the fabric of the world in a far different way. I said in the preamble of Book I that it seemed likely to me that the teaching of the ancients was the same, but hidden in the manner of their sect. For since **Copernican Astronomy** (or that of the ancient **Aristarchus of Samos**, the Pythagorean) holds the arrangement of the moving World to be such that there are six Orbs or paths in it, drawn around the body of the sun which is immobile in the center, and separated by large and unequal intervals—that of **Saturn** the outermost, then **Jupiter**, then **Mars**, then **Earth** with the **Moon**, then **Venus**, and finally **Mercury** the innermost; and since for these five figures, the inscription into a Spherical surface with their angles, and the circumscription around a spherical surface with the centers of their planes, is proper and essential; and so a certain interval is fixed for each figure between its two orbs: nothing could seem more plausible than that those six celestial orbs...

This distribution can be tested by numbers; it introduces a necessity of form and does not anxiously search for the number of bodies but occupies them once found. Finally, it is so constructed that in these past twenty-two years, it has not only found no attacker, but has even drawn in the very followers of the thoughtless master Ramus and the "scourgers of Euclid" <note>original: "Euclideomastigis." Kepler is likely referring to critics of classical geometry or followers of Petrus Ramus who questioned Euclidean proofs</note>; and today it draws so many that mathematicians have long since demanded a second edition. But to deal with this matter in more detail is not the purpose of this second book; you, the reader, will find more below in the fifth book, and some also in Book IV of the *Epitome of Astronomy*, where the genuine origin of these five solid figures is explained metaphysically. For that origin through the formation of angles is not their true origin, but follows them once they have arisen, as something posterior in nature.

### PROPOSITION XXVI.

<margin>
Similarly and below in Book V, chapter I. Translated in the copperplates provided.
</margin>
**A**dded to the most perfect regular congruences <note>In this context, "congruence" refers to the way geometric shapes fit together to fill space or create tilings</note> can be two other congruences: those of the twelve planar pentagonal stars; and two semi-solid ones: the octangular and decangular stars.

For the pentagonal ones enclose pointed solid figures on all sides: one of which has twelve five-lined angles, the other twenty three-lined angles. The former stands upon three angles at once, the latter upon five; the former is more beautifully raised upon an angle, while the latter sits more squarely, resting upon five. In these, although a regular plane does not appear on the outside, but rather a pentagonal isosceles triangle in its place, nevertheless, five of this kind always fit into one and the same plane, surrounding a pentagon hidden beneath the solidity, like its own heart. They create with it the aforementioned pentagonal star, or in the German language, the *Druid's foot* <note>original: "pedem Trutta" (likely a Latinization of "Drudenfuß"), a pentagram used as a protective symbol</note>, which Theophrastus Paracelsus <note>A famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541)</note> called the sign of health. The "Idea" of the body is in some way the same as that of its plane; for just as in this—that is, in the five-angled star—the sides of two triangles always meet in a single straight line (which in its inner part becomes the base for an outer triangle, and a side for the innermost pentagon), so too in the solid, the individual isosceles triangles of the five solid angles always meet in a single plane. The pith and heart of these five triangles, or the innermost star—the pentagon—becomes the base for one solid angle standing above it, or in the other case, for the five solids standing beneath it. Indeed, the kinship of these figures is so great—one with the Dodecahedron, the other with the Icosahedron—that these latter two (especially the Dodecahedron) seem in a way truncated and mutilated when compared to those pointed stars.

Regarding the octangular and decangular stars: their sides or rays (which always meet in a single straight line at the first and fourth points, with two passed over) always fit together in pairs. These create a certain kind of cube, and the others a certain kind of Dodecahedron—not angled figures, but "eared" ones, because when two plane angles are joined, a gap must necessarily be created that cannot be closed. Therefore, according to Proposition XI, it is only a semi-solid congruence.

These solid ones are called the most perfect congruences, and these others semi-solid, because the sixth definition of this book applies to them regarding their solidity. Regarding their planes, however, the definition of a perfect figure applies to them (which is the second definition in Book I); that is, they are secondarily perfect. Nor do we say "most perfect semi-solid" absurdly, for we imply that something is begun to which the sixth definition would apply—rather than the ninth or tenth—if it could be perfected.

# BOOK II. ON CONGRUENCE.

## PROPOSITION XXVII.

**C**ongruence <term>Congruence: In geometry, this refers to how shapes fit together perfectly without gaps or overlaps.</term> also serves to solidify figures; semi-regular figures, namely plane Rhombi, do this most perfectly, and in only two ways.

<margin>Look here for the smaller figure.</margin>
*For from twelve plane Rhombi of a specific proportion of diagonals, a solid Rhombus is created, possessing the shape of a honeybee cell <note>Kepler is describing the Rhombic Dodecahedron. He famously observed that the bottom of a bee's hexagonal honeycomb cell is composed of three rhombi meeting at a point.</note>, at least regarding its six sides and its solid triangular base. For when six rhombi are joined so that obtuse angles meet obtuse ones and acute meet acute, they create three obtuse-angled gaps, with three pairs of acute angles projecting above and three below. Therefore, the three projections of the three rhombi on each side, joined at their obtuse angles, fit into these gaps, and their own gaps receive the projections of the others.*

<image-desc>Two geometric woodcuts of polyhedra composed of rhombic faces. The left figure shows a rhombic dodecahedron (a 12-sided solid where every face is a diamond). The right figure shows a rhombic triacontahedron (a 30-sided solid where every face is a diamond).</image-desc>

<margin>Regarding this, see also above on folio 49, in Definition V. XX. and here for the larger figure.</margin>
*Similarly, thirty plane rhombi, of a different proportion of diagonals, form a solid Rhombic Triacontahedron <note>A thirty-sided solid. Kepler was the first to fully describe this shape in print.</note>. For when five rhombi at a time are joined by their acute angles to form two solid points standing on opposite sides, they leave gaps where they are joined at their obtuse angles; these gaps are filled by the other obtuse angles of the groups of five. Finally, in the middle of each "shell," so to speak, a zone composed of ten rhombi circles around, joining the two shells together.*

*The proof that there are no more perfect congruences of rhombi is as follows. There are two acute plane angles in a rhombus and two obtuse; one acute and one obtuse together always make two right angles. No more than three obtuse angles can meet, lest they exceed four right angles <note>In 3D geometry, the sum of the face angles meeting at a vertex must be less than 360 degrees (four right angles) to form a "corner."</note>. If you join only three acute angles, as in a Cube, you get a Rhombic Hexahedron <note>A cube is technically a rhombus where the angles are 90 degrees.</note> with only two acute solid angles placed very far apart; the other solid angles in the middle of the body are not so distant. Therefore, the laws of Definition VIII are not kept, which does not allow for only two [such] angles on the same sphere. Furthermore, of the six obtuse solid angles, each is enclosed by two obtuse planes and one acute; this irregularity is again against the definitions. Therefore, it is not only three plane acute angles that must meet. But neither can six acute angles (of as many rhombi) meet. For if each had a value of two-thirds of one right angle, the obtuse ones would have double that value, namely four-thirds; thus, both three obtuse and six acute angles would form four right angles, and neither would form a solid angle, but would instead spread out into a continuous flat surface, as in Figure G <margin>G. folio 53.</margin>. If the acute angles are made smaller, the obtuse ones will be larger, and three of them will exceed four right angles. Therefore, there are only two most perfect rhombic congruences: one in which four acute rhombic angles meet in a solid; the other in which five meet. To these, however, the Cube is associated as the origin of all rhombi, because its plane has four equal sides, just like the rhombic ones.*

<margin>See the thirteen Archimedean numbers regarding these.</margin>

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

Since different figures are mixed at this level, according to Proposition XXI, figures of either two or three species were mixed. If they are of two species, then either triangles are among them or they are not.

<margin>801</margin>
Therefore, from triangles <term>Trigonis: Three-sided polygons, or triangles.</term> and squares <term>Tetragonis: Four-sided polygons, or squares.</term>, three solids are created which satisfy Definition IX. For that definition rejects these three forms in which the following planes enclose a solid angle <note>A "solid angle" refers to a vertex where multiple faces meet in three dimensions.</note>: one square plane with either two or three triangular planes; or one triangular plane with two square planes. In the first case, there is only a single square, which results in something like half an Octahedron, and the solid angles become differently shaped. In the second case, there are only two squares, and in the third, only two triangles; according to Proposition X, these are imperfect congruences <note>Kepler is explaining why certain combinations of shapes cannot form a "uniform" solid where every corner looks the same.</note>.

<margin>
I. The Snub
Cube.
</margin>
The remaining modes, therefore, are those in which planes enclose a solid angle as follows: First, four triangles and one square. These are less than four right angles <note>Kepler measures angles in "right angles" (90°). To form a solid corner, the sum of the angles meeting at the point must be less than 360° (four right angles); if they equal 360°, the surface is flat.</note>. Thus, six squares and thirty-two (that is, 20 and 12) triangles fit together, and a thirty-eight-sided figure is created, which I call the **Snub Cube** <note>original: "Cubum simum". The word "simus" literally means "flat-nosed" or "snub." In geometry, this process involves pulling the faces of a cube apart and filling the gaps with a ribbon of triangles.</note>. This is illustrated in the following diagram at Number 12.

For five triangular planes and one square plane exceed four right angles, whereas to enclose a solid they ought to be less than four right angles, according to Proposition XVI. So also do four triangles and two squares. Indeed, three triangles and two squares make exactly four right angles.

<margin>
II. The Cub-
octahedron:
</margin>
Secondly, two triangles and two squares have less than four right angles. Here, therefore, eight triangles and six squares fit together to form one fourteen-sided solid <note>original: "Tessareskadecaëdron", from the Greek for fourteen-sided.</note>, which I call the **Cuboctahedron**. It is illustrated here at number eight. However, two triangles with three squares exceed four right angles.

<margin>
III. The Rhom-
bic Cubocta-
hedron.
</margin>
Thirdly, one triangle and three squares have less than four right angles. Here, therefore, eight triangles and eighteen (that is, 12 and 6) quadrangles fit together into one twenty-six-sided solid <note>original: "Icosihexaëdron", from the Greek for twenty-six-sided.</note>, which I call the cut Rhombicuboctahedron, or simply the **Rhombicuboctahedron**. It is illustrated here at number 10.

<margin>
IV. The Snub
Dodecahedron
</margin>
In these three, therefore, squares are placed next to triangles; it follows that we should also separately associate pentagons with them. Five triangular planes do not stand next to one pentagonal plane, because they could not even stand next to a square, which is smaller than it. Therefore, four triangles with one pentagon produce less than four right angles, and eighty (that is, 20 and 60) triangles fit together with twelve pentagons to form a ninety-two-sided solid <note>original: "Ennenacontakadyhedron", from the Greek for ninety-two-sided.</note>, which I call the **Snub Dodecahedron**. It is illustrated here at number 13. And in this order of "snub" solids, the Icosahedron could be the third, as it is effectively a "Snub Tetrahedron."

# CONGRUENCE BOOK II.

<margin>Pp.</margin>
If you associate three triangular planes with one pentagonal plane, the result is as stated above: only two pentagons come together in the solid. If you associate two triangular planes with one pentagonal plane, only one pentagon comes into the solid. In the former case, a "Zone" or middle column is formed; in the latter, a Pyramid is formed—both of which are parts of an *Icosahedron* <note>The Icosahedron is the regular 20-sided solid made of triangles.</note>. Nor are the solid angles of the same type here, because one is surrounded by five triangles, as in the *Icosahedron*. This concludes the possibilities for a single pentagonal plane.

<margin>*V. Icosidodecahedron.*</margin>
However, three triangular planes with two pentagonal planes create a sum greater than four right angles <note>Kepler measures the sum of angles at a vertex. For a solid to be convex, the sum must be less than 360° (four right angles). If it is more, the shapes cannot meet at a point.</note>. Therefore, we have finished considering three triangles in partnership with pentagons. 

Two triangular planes with two pentagonal planes create a sum less than four right angles. Therefore, twenty triangles and twelve pentagons join together into one *thirty-two-sided solid* <note>original: "Triacontakädyhedron"</note>, which I call the *Icosidodecahedron*. It is depicted here as Number 9. Since we have already rejected the pairing of one pentagon with two triangles, we are finished with the case of two triangles.

One triangular plane with three pentagonal planes creates a sum greater than four right angles; but with two pentagonal planes, by Proposition *XXIII*, nothing regular is produced because the pentagon is an odd-sided figure <note>Kepler argues that if a vertex has an odd-sided shape like a pentagon, the arrangement of surrounding shapes must follow specific symmetry rules to close the solid.</note>. Thus, we are finished with pentagons in partnership with triangles.

Four triangular planes with one hexagonal plane, and two triangles with two hexagonal planes, both fill a flat surface <note>The angles sum to exactly 360°, meaning they lie flat and cannot form a 3D corner.</note>. However, three triangles with two hexagons are greater than four right angles. With one hexagonal plane, they only receive two hexagons into the figure; but since three triangles are equal to one hexagon, they are rejected by Proposition *XXII*. It remains for one triangular plane to be coupled with two hexagonal planes. Thus, four triangles and four hexagons join into one *eight-sided solid* <note>original: "Octaëdron"</note>, which I call the *Truncated Tetrahedron*. It is depicted as Number 2 on the following leaf.
<margin>*VI. Truncated Tetrahedron.*</margin>

Four triangular planes with one heptagonal plane <note>A seven-sided figure.</note> or larger, exceed four right angles; therefore, no further mention need be made of four triangles. Nor of three, for the reasons often cited. Two triangles with two planes of any figure larger than a hexagon also exceed four right angles; therefore, no further mention of two triangles with two larger planes is needed. Nor can two triangles be paired with one larger plane, because they are excluded by the logic of Proposition *XXII*. There remains to be examined the case where one triangular plane is coupled with two planes of a figure larger than a hexagon. However, one triangle with two heptagonal planes is rejected by Proposition *XXIII*, as is the case with two of any odd-sided figure. But with two octagonal planes, a body is formed in which eight triangles and six octagons join into a *fourteen-sided solid* <note>original: "Tessarakadecahedron"</note>, which I call the *Truncated Cube*. You have its figure marked as Number 1 on the following leaf. With two decagonal planes <note>ten-sided figures</note>, a body is formed in which twenty triangles and twelve decagons join into one *thirty-two-sided solid*, which I call the *Truncated Dodecahedron*. This is marked among the following figures as Number 3. With two dodecagonal planes <note>twelve-sided figures</note>, a flat surface is filled and no solid angle is made, much less with larger figures. And so, we have finished entirely with triangles in the pairing of two species.
<margin>*VII. Truncated Cube.*</margin>
<margin>*VIII. Truncated Dodecahedron.*</margin>

Since, therefore, triangles are no longer used between two species of planes, the next smallest figure will be the square <term>Tetragonus: A four-sided regular polygon, or square.</term>. Now, three squares with one angle of a larger plane exceed four right angles. Two squares with one larger plane are not permitted by Definition IX, because only two planes of the larger species would be received into the solid. One square with two pentagonal planes is rejected by Proposition *XXIII*; but with two hexagonal planes it combines, and six squares and eight hexagons join into one *fourteen-sided solid*, which I call the *Truncated Octahedron*. It is depicted as number 5 in the following diagram. One square with two heptagonal planes and others...
<margin>*IX. Truncated Octahedron.*</margin>

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

...which is rejected for odd-sided figures <note>Kepler refers to a rule established in his Proposition 23: for certain solids to be uniform, the faces surrounding a polygon with an odd number of sides must alternate in a specific way.</note>, with two octagons, it fills a flat surface. With larger shapes, it even exceeds four right angles <note>Kepler measures the total degrees at a vertex using "right angles." 4 right angles = 360°. To form a 3D corner, the sum must be less than 360°.</note>; thus it does not rise to form a solid angle. This concludes the cases involving the **Square**; since only two types of planes should be present.

Two pentagons with one hexagon or any other single shape begin a rejected arrangement <note>Again, per Proposition XXIII</note>, which we also observed above regarding triangles and squares paired with two pentagons. Moreover, with one decagon <note>A 10-sided polygon.</note>, they spread out into a flat plane, and they do not rise into a solid with that or any larger shapes.

<margin>X. The Truncated Icosahedron.</margin>
Therefore, one pentagon with two hexagons makes less than four right angles; and twelve pentagons with twenty hexagons fit together into one **thirty-two-sided solid** <note>original: "Triacontaka-dyhedron"</note>, which I call the **Truncated Icosahedron**.

<image-desc>Seven numbered geometric diagrams of polyhedra (numbered 1 through 7) showing various arrangements of polygons (pentagons, hexagons, triangles, etc.) forming solid figures. Figure 4 shows a truncated icosahedron (the familiar soccer ball shape), and Figure 7 is a more complex polyhedron with many facets.</image-desc>

You see the form marked with the number 4. No more can be expected from the **Pentagon**. For one pentagon with two heptagons <note>7-sided polygons</note> already exceeds four right angles.

A **Hexagon** with two others fills a flat plane; with larger shapes, it exceeds four right angles. Thus, this is the end of mixtures composed of only two species of shapes.

But what if planes of *three* species can meet at one solid angle? First, two plane angles—one of a **Square**, the other of a **Pentagon**—together exceed two right angles; larger shapes exceed it by much more. Three angles of three **Triangles** equal exactly two right angles. However, three triangles cannot be admitted into a three-species mixture, lest the sum of all angles exceed four right angles. Furthermore, two triangles with one square and one pentagon (or a hexagon or anything larger) are rejected by Proposition XXIII, because a triangle—being an odd-sided figure—would have to be surrounded by both a square and a pentagon (or hexagon, etc.), which is not possible in this arrangement.

<margin>XI. Rhombicosidodecahedron.</margin>
Therefore, one **Triangle** with two **Squares** and one **Pentagon** create a sum less than four right angles; twenty triangles, thirty squares, and twelve pentagons fit together into one **sixty-two-sided solid** <note>original: "Hexacontadyhedron"</note>, which I call the **Rhombicosidodecahedron**, or the *cut icosidodecahedral rhombus*. It is pictured as number 11 on the preceding leaf.

One triangle and two squares with one **Hexagon** equal exactly four right angles; with any larger shape, they exceed it; thus they do not rise to form a solid. Let us therefore dismiss the use of two squares.

One triangle, one square, and two pentagons exceed four right angles; much more so if two larger plane angles were mixed. Thus, the mixing of four plane angles to form one solid comes to an end; and so too does the **Triangle** cease to enter into a triple mixture. For one triangle, one square...

# THE CONGRUENCE OF FIGURES BOOK II.

...[a] square and one pentagonal shape, or whatever other shape is used in its place, are rejected by Proposition XXIV, because a triangle is an odd-sided figure <note>Kepler's rule states that if an odd-sided polygon is used, the polygons surrounding it must alternate, which becomes impossible in certain geometric clusters.</note>.

Therefore, since there are furthermore only three plane angles <note>meaning three faces meeting at a single corner</note>: no odd-sided figure is tolerated among the figures, by the same Proposition XXIX.

<margin>XII. The truncated Cuboctahedron.</margin>
Therefore, a square, with the smallest possible hexagon and octagon, sum to less than 4 right angles <note>4 right angles = 360°. If the sum is less than 360°, the shapes can "fold" up from a flat sheet to form a 3D corner.</note>; and 12 Squares, 8 Hexagons, and 6 Octagons fit together into one **twenty-six-sided solid** <note>original: "Icosihexaëdron"</note>, which I call the **truncated Cuboctahedron**: not because it can be produced by literal truncation <note>the slicing off of corners</note>; but because it is similar to a truncated Cuboctahedron. It is depicted as number 6.

<margin>XIII. The truncated Icosidodecahedron.</margin>
A square with a hexagon and a decagon <note>a 10-sided polygon</note> create less than 4 right angles: and 30 Squares, 20 Hexagons, and 12 Decagons fit together into one **sixty-two-sided solid** <note>original: "Hexacontadyhedron"</note>, which I call the **truncated Icosidodecahedron**, for a similar reason as the previous one. It is depicted as number 7.

If a dodecagon <note>a 12-sided polygon</note> were to join the partnership in place of the decagon, 4 right angles would be filled exactly, and no solid would be formed; likewise, if an octagon joins in place of the hexagon, and some shape larger than an octagon is the third, 4 right angles are exceeded. No less is this the case if the square is absent and three larger distinct even-sided figures are joined. Therefore, the entire family of <term>Archimedean solids|The 13 semi-regular polyhedra composed of two or more types of regular polygons meeting in identical vertices.</term> stands at exactly 13; which was to be demonstrated.

### XXIX. COROLLARY.

There are twelve congruent figures in total: eight **Radical** or **Primary** figures; and four **Augmented** figures or **Stars**.

| | |
|----------|----------|
| 1. Triangle | 7. Dodecagon |
| 2. Square | 8. Icosagon <note>A 20-sided polygon.</note> |
| 3. Pentagon | 9. Pentagonal Star |
| 4. Hexagon | 10. Octagonal Star |
| 5. Octagon | 11. Decagonal Star |
| 6. Decagon | 12. Dodecagonal Star |

The degrees of congruence <note>how well they fit together</note> are distinct. In the **first degree** are the Triangle and the Square, because they fit together both in a solid and in a plane, both with those of their own kind and when joined with others.

In the **second degree** stand the Pentagon and its star. For they fit together with their own kind in a solid, and they lend mutual service in a plane: but the Pentagon is superior, because it also fits with several others both in a plane and in a solid.

The **third degree** belongs to the Hexagon, because figures of this type fit together in a plane, but with others they fit in both solids and planes.

The **fourth degree** is held by the Octagon and the Decagon with their stars. For those Radical shapes fit with several others in a solid, while the stars fit with figures of their own specific kind to some extent; in a plane, however, all four fit with others, though the octagonal division does so with more variety and perfection.

The **fifth degree** has the Dodecagon with its star; because they fit with others least of all in a solid, but in many ways in a plane; in a solid, therefore, they are hindered by size alone. Because of its performance in a plane, this group is to be preferred over the fourth degree.

The **last degree** belongs to the Icosagon, because it fits together only in a plane, only with other shapes, and even then, imperfectly.

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES

*But if we consider the Plane surface alone, the order of the figures will be as follows: 1. Hexagon. 2. Square <note>original: "Tetragonus"</note>. 3. Triangle <note>original: "Trigonus"</note>. 4. Twelve-sided polygon <note>original: "Dodeca-gonus"</note>. 5. Its star. 6. Octagon. 7. Its star. 8. Pentagon. 9. Its star. 10. Ten-sided polygon <note>original: "Decagonus"</note>. 11. Its star. 12. Twenty-sided polygon <note>original: "Icosigonus"</note>.*

<margin>Fifteen-sided</margin>
*All other figures are incongruent <note>meaning they cannot tile a flat surface or form regular 3D corners</note>. However, the next closest to being congruent is the **fifteen-sided polygon** <note>original: "Pentekædecagonus"</note>, because it begins to fit with others in a plane; but it is excluded <margin>XXIII.</margin> by Proposition XXIII, which prevents it—unlike the twenty-sided polygon—from being surrounded on all sides equally. After that comes the 16-sided figure and similar ones, which clearly do not fit with other regular figures because the size of their angles is an obstacle. But the <margin>Heptagon.</margin> **heptagon** <note>a seven-sided polygon</note> and similar figures are incongruent for a much different reason: neither their total angles, nor any aliquot parts of their angles <note>fractions of an angle that divide into 360°</note> that are proper to those figures, fit with other regular figures.*

*Thus, in the three classes of shapes that can be demonstrated in themselves <note>referring to shapes constructible with a compass and straightedge</note>, congruence ends with the Octagon, the Twelve-sided polygon, and the Twenty-sided polygon; in the fourth, "spurious" class, it does not even begin. These have their use in Book IV in the selection of **Aspects** <note>the specific angular distances between planets in astrology</note>.*

### XXX. COROLLARY.

From these things, the true distinction appears between **demonstration** <note>theoretical geometric proof</note> and **congruence** <note>the practical ability of shapes to fit together</note> for the sake of width.

*For: 1. The degrees of proper demonstration extend to infinity beyond the Octagon, Decagon, and Twelve-sided polygon into figures with double the number of sides; whereas congruence stops at the Octagon, Twenty-sided polygon, and Twelve-sided polygon. 2. The Pentagon with its star is considered less "noble" than the Twelve-sided polygon for the sake of demonstration and knowledge; yet for the sake of congruence in a solid, it is much more noble. 3. The Octagon follows the Pentagon in the former case, but precedes it here. 4. The 16-sided polygon held a more important place there than the Twenty-sided polygon; and yet the former is an incongruent figure, while the latter is congruent to a certain extent. 5. But in the fifteen-sided polygon, there is a beautiful agreement of both factors, preserving the same analogy; because among demonstrations none occurs that is proper to it, but only accidental; and among congruences, none is perfected, but some are at least begun, though not occupying the whole figure. These things should be noted below in Book III regarding the origin and use of the **semitone** <note>Kepler relates the geometric properties of the 15-sided polygon to the musical interval of the semitone</note>.*

->PROCLUS DIADOCHUS<-
<note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentaries on Euclid deeply influenced Kepler's belief that mathematics is the link between the human mind and the divine.</note>
->Book I: Commentary on Book I of Euclid’s Elements<-

> *Since philosophy encompasses many faculties, and many that are Mathematical, he writes these things concerning one part of it called Harmonics <note>original: "Harmonice"</note>, and concerning Number (which are believed to be the principles of Harmonies).*

**It prepares the efforts of the Mind for Theology.** For those things concerning the truth of divine matters which seem difficult to grasp and too sublime for the uninitiated, those things are demonstrated by Mathematical Reasons to be trustworthy, manifest, and beyond controversy, through certain Images. For they show the evidence of superessential <note>In Neoplatonism, "superessential" refers to things that exist beyond or above the level of physical "being."</note> properties in Numbers: and they bring into the light of reasoning what the Powers of Intellectual Forms may be. Therefore, Plato teaches us many wonders concerning the Nature of the Gods through the types of mathematical objects: and the Pythagorean Philosophy uses these as veils to shroud the instruction of divine matters. For of this kind is that entire SACRED DISCOURSE <note>original: "SERMO SACER," referring to the *Hieros Logos*, a lost Pythagorean or Orphic text</note>, and Philolaus in his *Bacchics*, and Pythagoras’s whole method of teaching about God.

Again, it perfects us for Moral philosophy, implanting in our character Order, decency, and harmonic living; it also teaches which figures, which Songs <note>original: "Cantilenæ"</note>, and which Movements are fitting for virtue: with which doctrine Athenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Greek rhetorician and grammarian who wrote on music and ethics.</note> also wants those who will devote themselves to Moral virtues from youth to be refined and perfected. Furthermore, it explains the proportions of Numbers familiar to the virtues—some arithmetic, some Geometric, others Harmonic: it shows both the Excesses and Defects of Vices, by all of which we are guided toward a moderation <note>original: "mediocritatem," referring to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean" or middle path between extremes</note> of character and decency.

BOOK III.

# ON THE ORIGIN OF HARMON-
## ICAL PROPORTIONS, AND ON THE
### Nature & differences of things
->pertaining to<-
->Song.<-

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'H' containing floral patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>

Hitherto, following the Nature of things, we have first spoken of Regular Plane Figures; then we passed to their Congruences <note>original: "Congruentias." In geometry, this refers to the way regular polygons fit together to fill a surface without gaps.</note>. In what follows, it will be necessary to depart somewhat from the Natural Method, so that the understanding of the human mind—which not infrequently uses a different path—may be all the more assisted. For the nature of the matter required this: that now, in the third place, we should explain those proportions in the abstract which are established between a circle and a part cut off from any side; and what other types of things arise from the composition and division of such proportions. Then, in the fourth place, we would pass to the works of the world, which either God the Creator himself attuned to such proportions, or which sublunary <note>Referring to the Earth and its atmosphere, situated "below the moon."</note> Nature practices daily in the angles of the starlight rays, according to the rule of such proportions. Lastly, we would subjoin human Music, showing how the human Mind, informing the judgment of hearing, imitates the Creator by a natural instinct, through the choice and approval of those same proportions in sounds which pleased God in the tempering of the celestial motions. 

But because it is difficult to abstract the differences, Genera <note>Technical categories of musical scales</note>, and Modes of Harmonic Proportions in the mind from musical voices and sounds—since no other vocabulary is available to us for explaining these things than that of Music—therefore, in this book, we must join the third topic with the fifth and last. We must speak not only of abstract Harmonic Proportions but also anticipate this human imitation of creation in song. The work of the creation of the heavens, however, must be deferred to the final place because of its sublimity and difficulty of belief, following that order prescribed in the title of the book. And so much for the order of things to be said.

Certainly, just as it is arranged in all human affairs—that in those things granted to us by Nature, use precedes the knowledge of causes—so also it happened to the human race regarding Song: that from its very origin, it used those same melodies and intervals of voices without speculation or knowledge of causes which we commonly use today, in-

ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.

...by the singing of melodies, not only in temples and choirs of musicians, but everywhere without any training in the art, even at crossroads and in fields.

<margin>Genesis 4:21</margin>This antiquity of song is apparent from the first book of *Genesis*. For there must have been great delight in the singing of the human voice (when I say delight, I mean harmonic and melodious intervals) which moved *Jubal*, the eighth in descent from *Adam*, to learn and teach how to imitate the songs of men with inanimate instruments. Unless I am mistaken, this *Jubal* is *Apollo* <note>Kepler suggests that the biblical Jubal and the Greek god Apollo are the same historical figure, noting the phonetic similarity of their names.</note>, with a slight change of letters; he surpassed his brother *Jabal*, the father of animal husbandry who delighted in the rustic pipe (believed by the Greeks to be the *God Pan*), with the invention of the lyre and its clear ringing, having borrowed the material for the strings from his brother *Tubal-cain*, who for us—by an allusion of the name—shall be *Vulcan* <note>Tubal-cain was a biblical "forger of all instruments of bronze and iron." Kepler links him to Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and smithing.</note>.

However ancient the form of human song may be, composed of consonant or melodious intervals, the causes of these intervals remained hidden from men; so much so that before *Pythagoras* they were not even sought; and having been sought for two thousand years, I—unless I am mistaken—shall be the first to set them forth most accurately.

*Pythagoras* is indeed said to have been the first who, while passing by a blacksmith’s shop and noticing the harmonically tempered sounds of the hammers, discovered that the difference in sounds came from the size of the hammers, such that the large ones produced deep sounds and the small ones sharp sounds. Since proportion is properly observed between sizes, having measured the hammers, he easily noticed the proportions by which harmonic intervals of voices were formed, and by which dissonant ones; which were melodious, and which unmelodious. For he immediately passed from hammers to the lengths of strings, where the ears indicate more exactly which parts of a string harmonize with the whole, and which are dissonant from it.

Once certain proportions were found as the "fact of the matter" <note>original Greek: τὸ ὅτι (to hoti). The observation that something is true.</note>, there remained the task of investigating the causes, or the "reason why" <note>original Greek: τοῦ διότι (tou dioti). The underlying explanation for the observation.</note>, as to why these proportions defined melodious, sweet, and consonant intervals of voices, while other proportions defined dissonant ones, abhorrent to the ears and unfamiliar. And for two thousand years, the opinion was held that the causes must be sought from the properties of the proportions themselves, as they are contained under the terms of discrete quantity—namely, Numbers. For the *Pythagoreans* saw that perfect harmonies are established if strings of equal tension have a ratio between their lengths of double, triple, or quadruple, among the numbers 1:2, 1:3, and 1:4. These proportions are called *Multiples* in *Arithmetic*. Conversely, they saw that the consonances of strings which make a ratio of one-and-a-half, the *Hemiholia* <note>original: "Hemiholiam." A 3:2 ratio, known in modern music as a perfect fifth.</note>, and one-and-a-third, the *Epitriton* <note>original: "Epitriton." A 4:3 ratio, known in modern music as a perfect fourth.</note>, were a little less perfect: namely, between the numbers 2:3 and 3:4. These two proportions joined together make a double proportion between the numbers 2:4 or 1:2; while the smaller, between 3:4, subtracted from the larger, 2:3, left the sesquioctave <note>original: "sesquioctavam." A 9:8 ratio, the mathematical definition of a whole tone.</note> between 8:9. And they detected that there was so much in—

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
1.
2. 3.
4. 6. 9.
8, 12, 18, 27.
</margin>
...the interval of a Whole Tone <note>The ratio of 9:8, a standard interval in musical scales.</note>, which is very common in every song. And yet, the number 8 is the cube of 2, and the number 9 is the square of 3. Thus, these numbers were already at hand: 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9. Since the same unity <note>The number 1.</note> is both its own square and its own cube; and the number two has 4 as its square and 8 as its cube; they also added the cube of the number three, which is 27, alongside its square, 9. They did this because they believed one must progress as far as cubes, for the reason that the entire World and all things capable of sound do not consist of empty surfaces, but of solid bodies. Finally, from this beginning, such a great opinion of these numbers grew—because they were the Primes, along with their squares and cubes—that the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that the universe was structured according to mathematical ratios.</note> judged that the whole of Philosophy should be composed from them.

For them, unity represented the Idea, the Mind, and the Form, because just as unity is indivisible and remains the same whether multiplied as a square or a cube, so too are Ideas <note>In the Platonic sense, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal, unchanging patterns of all things.</note> indivisible and universal, and always the Same. Therefore, they made unity the symbol of the Nature of Identity, while they made the other numbers symbols of the Nature of Alterity <note>original: "Alteritatis," meaning "Otherness" or "Difference."</note>. Thus, the number two signified otherness and Matter, because it admits division, just as matter does; and as two becomes 4 when squared and 8 when cubed—which are numbers distinct from 2—so too can matter be unstable and multi-formed. Alternatively, the number two also signified the soul, because while the Mind is immobile (or enjoys a uniform circular motion), the Soul, by contrast, receives multiple movements from the body, and feels more at home with rectilinear movements, which exist in a six-fold difference <note>Up, down, left, right, forward, and backward.</note>. Finally, the number three denoted for them the body, composed of Form and Matter, just as 3 is composed of 2 and 1; and because mundane bodies have as many dimensions as the number three has units.

<margin>
To the Pythagoreans, the Soul is Number and Harmony.
</margin>
Nor were numbers merely symbols of the three principles; rather, they believed the Soul itself was composed of these very numbers, and all their proportions, and the subdivisions of proportions into <term>sesquialteras</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2, representing a perfect fifth in music.</note>, <term>sesquitertias</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3, representing a perfect fourth.</note>, and <term>sesquioctavas</term> <note>A ratio of 9:8, representing a whole tone.</note>: so that the Soul, the bond between Mind and Body, was in its essence nothing but Harmony, and composed of harmonies. Without a doubt, they were led to this dogma by the observation that the human soul is so greatly delighted by voices which, by their magnitude, form and contain these harmonic proportions.

## Digression on the Pythagorean Tetractys.

From the principles explained just a moment ago, it seems we must draw out that <term>Tetractys</term> <note>The Tetractys is a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows, a sacred symbol for Pythagoreans representing the organization of the universe.</note>, the perennial spring of the human Soul, by which the Pythagoreans used to swear; in my opinion, it is because between the two cubes of 1, 8, and 27—for example, between 1 and 8—there are two proportional means: 2 and 4. Therefore, the four numbers 1, 2, 4, 8 (whose sum is 15) or 1, 3, 9, 27 (whose sum is 40) make up that Tetractys. For two cubic numbers possess two proportional means, just as two plane <note>Two-dimensional</note> numbers possess one proportional mean, as is well known from geometry.

### ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.

Whether this was that *Tetractys* <note>A mystical symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle of four rows (1, 2, 3, and 4).</note> [consisting of] 1, 2, 3, 4: 1. that principle of Numbers; 2. the first of Numbers and of Even numbers; 3. the first of composite and Odd numbers; when 1 is multiplied by 3, a rectangle of 3 is made, as if from an odd number; but when 2 is multiplied by itself, a square of 4 is made, as if from an even number, for which it is also fitting that the length and width in its making be even, just as in the other's rectangle they are unequal. Therefore, the sum of 1, 2, 3, and 4 is 10, and the human soul is accustomed to count to 10. And just as there are four Numbers—namely, as many as there were units in the fourth—so also through them, four species of harmonies exist: between 1 and 2 is the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, as also between 2 and 4; and between 1 and 4 is the Double Octave <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note>, which they consider as one; between 1 and 3 is the Octave-plus-Fifth <note>original: "Diapason Epidiapente"</note>, which they held to be the greatest harmony of the system, and this is the second here; the third is between 2 and 3, the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; and the fourth is between 3 and 4, the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. Nor did they themselves recognize any more Harmonies than these.

*These things are from my own mind. But Joachim Camerarius <note>A prominent German classical scholar (1500–1574) and friend of Melanchthon.</note> speaks a little differently about the same Tetractys, and perhaps not a little more correctly, unless he was misled by his wide reading of ancient authors. In his Greek commentaries on the "Golden Verses of Pythagoras," he writes: "They designated the number Ten uniquely by the name of 'Number.' In this sense Plato said in the Phaedo that the whole half of Numbers is odd." For let two ranks of numbers be described from unity to ten in an alternating series—one rank of Odds, the other of Evens—in this manner:*

->*1, 3, 5, 7, 9. (Sum 25, odd, the square of five.*<-
->*2, 4, 6, 8, 10. namely, as many as there were odds.)*<-

*Or, omitting unity as the principle, and Ten as the Number uniquely so-called, thus:*

->*2, 4, 6, 8.*<-
->*3, 5, 7, 9. (Sum 24, even.)*<-

*This is that enigma: that Odds are Evens. For each of 3, 5, 7, 9 are odd, yet all together they are four in number, which is even (and the Sum 24 is even).*

Therefore, the number Ten, called "Number" peculiarly by the Pythagoreans, has this property: it is collected from unity and its continuous multiples up to four. For it makes an equilateral numeral Triangle, whose base is Four and whose vertex is unity. From this, the Pythagoreans called every [such] number a *Tetractys*. For by doubling the sides of the first Tetractys, another Pythagorean Tetractys is made, the number 36. This was most celebrated and useful in every way among them—namely, a numerical Triangle <note>A "triangular number" formed by the sum of integers: 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8 = 36.</note> whose base is Eight. And so, in many demonstrations they used the number 36, especially in Harmonics. For in the arrangements of the figures of this Number, these numbers are found: 12, 9, 8, 6. With these numbers, they demonstrated that all Harmonic Consonances were comprised according to the proportions of the Intervals. For the number 36 is a square, and its side is 6. It is Triangular, its side being 8. It is an Oblong Rectangle, whose length is 9 and its other length 12. (For nine times four, and twelve times three, both make 36.) Finally, when these—6, 8, 9, 12—are cast into one sum, the result is the number 35, called "Harmony" by the Pythagoreans; to which unity added again completes the Number 36. Furthermore, among the numbers which are collected from the preceding ones in natural order (that is, from the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28), 36 is the first (and the only one within 1225) that is a square; and it has 6 as its side, the first perfect number <note>A perfect number is equal to the sum of its divisors: 1+2+3 = 6.</note>.

One may indeed behold the Worldly *Tetractys* more accurately in this manner: that starting from unity, produced through a triple ratio, with a unit taken into the middle to fill the interval, and enclosed by fourfold lines around it like straight lines, so finally that *Tetractys* makes up the *Denary* <note>The number ten.</note>: since it is in this way the third of the *Trigons* <note>Triangular numbers, formed by the sum of consecutive integers (1, 3, 6, 10...).</note> in its generation: (For after unity, the first triangle is 3, whose base is 2; the second is 6, whose base is 3; if you draw the three outer lines through those two points there, and three here, shadowing the triangle, nothing is left in the middle. But the third triangle, 10, with a base of 4, if it receives single lines going around the outside instead of the four points, one point will be left in the middle, which belongs to none of the shaping lines but shadows the interior space, like a heart or a kernel.) For this reason, the Pythagoreans called the *Decad* <note>The number ten.</note>:

->The all-containing Mother, who hedges all things around,<-
->Unyielding, Untamed, and Chaste,<-

as Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who wrote extensively on mathematics and Plato.</note> says. And the fulfillment of the ten units itself—namely the *Denary* gathered from this *Tetractys*—was handed down by the Pythagoreans (whom Plato also follows) as containing and completing, or fulfilling, the adornment of the entire universe. For 1. the universe was made corporeal and sensible; 2. it contains all things that are in it, indissolubly, through the bond of Analogy or commensuration; 3. it is a whole, indeed made from whole Elements; 4. its body is round; 5. it is that which suffers within itself, and from itself, all passions; 6. it moves in a circle; 7. its body is animate; 8. it is the bringer of time through the revolutions of the stars; 9. it has certain sacred stars counted among the number of the Gods, which complete the Great Year <note>The period of time in which all the planets and stars return to the same relative positions.</note> as something perfect; 10. the universe of things is perfect in every way, having within itself all living creatures, likened to four forms (stars to the heavens, birds to the air, fish to the water, quadrupeds to the earth). In this way, starting from unity (as the Pythagoreans say, "from the cave of the *Monad*" <note>original: "Munadis", the fundamental indivisible unit.</note>), the progression goes up to Four (until one comes to the divine *Tetrad* <note>original: "Tetrada"</note> itself), and thus it gives birth to the *Denary*, the mother of all things, as we said. The progress of unity is of this kind: For the World is one. The *Binary* <note>The number two.</note> signifies the first multiplicity contained within it. The *Ternary* <note>The number three.</note> signifies the bond and knot necessary for the fitting together of things; for it is not possible for two things alone to come together into one, separate from a third.

The sum of these (namely 1, 2, 3, and 4) is the Decad <note>The number ten.</note>, of which we have spoken thus far. from the ancients: with whom Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretic combination of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient wisdom.</note> (whoever he was) instills many agreeing things in his son Tatius: whose words are these: *Unity, according to reason, embraces the Decad, and again the Decad embraces Unity.* Next, he composes the desiring faculty of the Soul from 12 vices, or ethical faults, according to the number of the signs of the Zodiac, to which he subjects the Body and this power of the Soul tending toward the body; but the rational faculty of the Soul he himself composes from a Decad of Ethical Virtues. All things are also conducted through Harmonies; there is much insistence on *Silence*, much mention of *Mind and Truth*; there is proposed also a Cave, a Foundation, an Inner Sanctuary, a Bowl of Souls, and many other things: so that there can be no doubt that either Pythagoras "Hermeticizes," or Hermes "Pythagoricizes."

<margin>The error of the Pythagoreans concerning the Number of Harmonies.</margin>
The Pythagoreans were so devoted to this form of philosophizing through Numbers that they no longer stood by the judgment of the ears, even though it was by the evidence of the ears that this Philosophy was first reached in the beginning. Instead, they defined what was Concordant or discordant, what was Consonant or dissonant, from their Numbers alone, doing violence to the natural instinct of hearing. And that Harmonic tyranny stood until Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the astronomer and music theorist.</note>; who first, fifteen hundred years ago, asserted the sense of hearing against the Pythagorean Philosophy. ...[a val]ue for the semitone; nor did he only add other superparticular <note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 4:3.</note> ratios approved by the ears, such as the *sesquiquarta* <note>The ratio 5:4, which forms a major third.</note> and *sesquiquinta* <note>The ratio 6:5, which forms a minor third.</note>; but he even adopted some from the superpartient <note>A ratio where the numerator is more than one unit larger than the denominator, such as 5:3.</note> ratios: such as between 3 and 5, and between 5 and 8, and others.

<margin>
Ptolemy's error concerning the Number of Harmonies and Concords.
</margin>
In this way, Ptolemy corrected the Pythagorean speculation regarding the origin of harmonic proportions as if it were stumbling, yet he did not remove it entirely as false. Although he restored the judgment of the ears to its proper dignity in his words and teachings, he nonetheless abandoned it again, himself clinging to the contemplation of abstract numbers. For the cause of the number and of each harmonic proportion is not adequate to its effect even in this way; instead, it falls short in defining Consonances and exceeds in other Concords. Ptolemy still denies that the major and minor Thirds and Sixths (which are contained in these ratios: 4:5, 5:6, 3:5, and 5:8) are consonant—something all modern musicians with good ears affirm. On the other hand, he accepts the ratios 6:7 and 7:8 and others among the musical intervals as "concords," so that in a song proceeding from **VT** <note>The syllable "Ut," the ancestor of "Do" in the solfège system.</note> to **FA**, a middle note would be placed between **RE** and **MI**, in the proportion where 7 is the middle between 6 and 8. For the sake of notation, this becomes **RI**, and now one could sing **VT**. **RI**. **FA**. just as one can sing **VT**. **RE**. **MI**. **FA**. This is utterly abhorrent to the ears and singing habits of all men, however much strings might be tuned that way; for since strings are inanimate, they do not offer their own judgment, but follow the hand of an unskilled theorist without any resistance.

<margin>
The error of the same author in taking a non-cause for a cause.
</margin>
Furthermore, even if those causes sought from abstract numbers and these effects (the Consonances) were perfectly equal in breadth, and it might not seem absurd to see it as an archetypal cause—testifying that the Father of things, the Eternal Mind, having contemplated those numbers, took from them the Idea of voices and intervals which He then had to provide for through the conformation of Souls so that they would please human minds—the matter would still not be entirely clear. Why do these numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, etc., coincide with musical intervals, while 7, 11, 13, and the like do not? Numbers, as numbers, do not show the cause of this in themselves. For that cause regarding the Trinity <note>original: "Ternario"; the number three.</note> of principles and the family of squares and cubes derived from it is no cause at all, since the number five <note>original: "quinarius"</note> is excluded from it—yet five will not allow its right of citizenship to be snatched away from the origin of musical intervals.

Nor does it satisfy the theorist to know that the numbers 1, 2, 3 are symbols of the Principles of which natural things consist. For an interval is not a natural thing, but a geometric <note>Kepler argues that music is governed by geometry (shapes), not just arithmetic (numbers).</note> one; unless, therefore, these numbers count something else that is more related to intervals, the philosopher will be unable to place any faith in this cause, but will suspect it of being a "non-cause."

For these reasons, therefore, I decided twenty years ago that I must work on this: to make this part of mathematics and physics more illustrious by discovering such causes which, on the one hand, [correspond] to the judgment of the ear...

...so that they might satisfy the requirements in establishing the Number of Consonances and other Concordant intervals; nor should they run beyond what the ears can tolerate. On the other hand, they should establish a clear and open distinction between the Numbers that form Musical intervals and those that are foreign to this business. Finally, these numbers, with respect to both the Archetype <note>The original "blueprint" or ideal pattern used by God to create the universe.</note> and the Mind (which uses the archetype to shape things accordingly), should have a kinship with the intervals and thus shine with the clearest probability. 

Since the boundaries of Consonant intervals are continuous quantities <note>Kepler refers to geometry—lines and shapes—rather than "discrete" or individual numbers.</note>, the causes that separate them from Dissonances must also be sought from the family of continuous quantities, not from abstract Numbers, which are discrete quantities. Furthermore, since it is the Mind that has shaped human Souls so that they are delighted by a particular interval (which is the genuine definition of consonant and dissonant), the differences between one and another, and the causes by which these intervals become harmonic, must possess a mental and intellectual essence. Specifically, this essence is that the boundaries of consonant intervals are properly "knowable" <note>original: *scibiles*. In Kepler's geometry, this refers to proportions that can be constructed using a straightedge and compass.</note>, while those of dissonant intervals are either improperly knowable or unknowable. 

For if they are knowable, they can enter the Mind and be adopted to form the archetype; but if they are unknowable (in the sense explained in Book I), they remain outside the Mind of the eternal Creator and in no way contribute to the Archetype. But enough on these matters for now; we shall hand down this teaching itself through its own chapters, which we begin with God's guidance. We shall speak everywhere of Song—that is, of harmonic intervals not as abstract concepts, but as they are realized in sound. However, for those with ears trained by the mind, we will always understand these intervals as being abstract from sounds; for they produce their beauty not only in sounds and human Song, but also in other things that lack sound entirely, as we shall hear in the fourth and fifth books.

# CHAPTER I.
## On the causes of consonances.

### DEFINITION.

Since the ancients used these terms: Single-sounding <note>original: *Μονόφωνον* (Monophonon)</note>, Counter-sounding <note>original: *Ἀντίφωνον* (Antiphonon)</note>, Same-sounding <note>original: *Ὁμόφωνον* (Homophonon)</note>, Divergent-sounding <note>original: *Διάφωνον* (Diaphonon)</note>, Concordant <note>original: *Σύμφωνον* (Symphonon)</note>, and Discordant <note>original: *Ἀσύμφωνον* (Asymphonon)</note>; for us, **Dissonant** shall mean the same as Discordant, and **Consonant** the same as Concordant. The categories of Consonant are: *Identical*, which we shall use in place of Same-sounding, and *Non-Identical*, which we use for Divergent-sounding. Of the Identical, there will be two species: the unison, and the "Identical-by-opposition" <note>This likely refers to the octave, which sounds like the same note but at a different pitch level.</note>.

### DEFINITION.

In Geometry, the terms *Part* and *Parts* differ. A **Part** is said to be that of which the Whole is a multiple according to a certain proportion—for example, double, triple, or quadruple. However, **Parts** (plural) is used when a multitude of Wholes (rather than just one) is a multiple of them. For example, one-seventh is called a *Part*, because the whole circle is seven times this part. But three-sevenths are called not a *Part* but *Parts*, because the sum of three circles is seven times this arc.

Here, however, we shall not use this distinction; instead, we shall call both types of portions a **Part**. That is, every portion whose length is "effable" <term>effable: from the Latin *effabilis*, meaning a length that can be expressed or constructed through specific geometric rules, such as those forming regular polygons</term> shall be called a *Part* by us; yet with this restriction: that it be no larger than a semicircle.

The **Remainder** <note>original: *residuum*</note> shall be that which remains of the Whole after an "effable" portion has been taken away, being itself no less than a semicircle.

*The distinction between the Remainder and the Part is highly necessary, because a Part can be consonant while its Remainder is dissonant, as we shall see.*

### DEFINITION.

A **String** <note>original: *chorda*. While this means "chord" in geometry (a line segment touching two points on a circle), in music it refers to the physical string of an instrument like a monochord.</note> is taken here not as a line segment subtending the arc of a circle, as in Geometry, but as any length that is fit for producing a sound. And because sound is drawn out through motion, in the abstract a "string" is to be understood as the length of any motion whatsoever, or any other length, even one conceived only in the mind.

<summary>Kepler establishes the foundational vocabulary for his musical theory, redefining ancient Greek musical terms into geometric concepts and distinguishing between "Parts" and "Remainders" of a circle. He expands the definition of a musical "string" to include any measurable length or motion capable of representing a ratio.</summary>

<header>ON HARMONY, BOOK III.</header>

# AXIOM I.

**The diameter of a circle, and the sides of the Fundamental Figures** <note>original: *figurarum Radicalium*. These are the regular polygons—like the triangle, square, and pentagon—that Kepler discussed in Book I.</note> explained in Book I, which possess their own geometric demonstration, determine a part of the circle that is consonant with the whole circle.

*How a circle might be stretched so that it gives off a sound, and how it ought to be attached to a hollow body so that resonance occurs—whether from a single point so that the whole sounds, or from two points to sound its parts—would be a long matter to explain here. Nevertheless, it was necessary to begin in this way, because we are not only dealing with song (which is harmony embodied in sounds), but we must also understand the abstract interval apart from the sounds. As far as song is concerned, it is enough that a string stretched in a straight line can be divided in the same way as a string curled into a circle is divided by the side of an inscribable figure.* <note>Kepler is arguing that the mathematics of a vibrating string are identical to the geometry of polygons drawn inside a circle.</note>

---

## Corollary.

Consonances are infinite, because the number of demonstrable <term>demonstrable: in geometry, this refers to shapes that can be perfectly constructed using only a compass and a straightedge.</term> figures is infinite. *However, it is not yet time to speak of the selection of concords, which will be presented much further on. Here, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed the universe was governed by whole numbers.</note> sought the limits of the size of consonant intervals in their numbers as causes; yet it is the human sense of hearing alone which fixes these limits, for the ear is not of infinite power. Therefore, that narrowing down of the number of concords is merely incidental to abstract Harmonic intervals, not their primary cause. Even modern musicians go beyond the Pythagorean limits—to say nothing of the celestial harmonies.*

# AXIOM II.

**To the same degree** that the geometric demonstration of a side differs from the first and simplest demonstration; to that same degree the consonance of the part of the circle (cut off by that side) with the whole circle recedes from the most perfect consonance of the unison. In other words: whatever the "rank" of a figure is among other figures, that same rank belongs to its corresponding consonance among others.

*This axiom will be used below to help us select concords based on how sweet they sound.*

# AXIOM III.

**The sides** of Regular and Star Figures that are "indemonstrable" <note>Shapes that cannot be perfectly constructed with a compass and straightedge, such as a heptagon (7-sided figure).</note> determine a part of the circle that is dissonant from the whole circle. This also applies to the side of a figure that is demonstrable, but not through its own nature or its own unique demonstration. Or, if a unique demonstration is lacking, consider the "lack of congruence" from Book II. By both measures, the Fifteen-sided figure <note>original: *Quindecangulum*</note> is excluded.

## AXIOM IV.

**Figures that have related demonstrations <note>original: *cognatas... demonstrationes*. In geometry, this refers to shapes that share a mathematical lineage, such as a square and an octagon.</note> of their sides also produce related Harmonies.**

*Through this axiom, the origin and cause of Harmonic Proportions will be proved from the remainder.* <note>The "remainder" refers to what is left of a circle's circumference after the side of a polygon has been "cut" from it.</note>

## AXIOM V.

**Strings or arcs of a circle, under equal tension, which have between them—on account of their length—the same proportion that exists between a Part or Remainder of a circle and the Whole circle; these also possess the same Consonance or dissonance, even if they are contained between different limits or sounds.**

*In an abstract sense, let it be understood this way: that a circle, along with its part, constitutes certain Harmonic proportions; wherever these are found in other contexts—whether in sounds or in silent motions <note>By "silent motions," Kepler is referring to the orbits and velocities of the planets, which he believed followed these same harmonic laws.</note>—they are always harmonic.*

*However, this Axiom is added because not all Harmonic Proportions arise immediately from the circle itself by the very first division of it by a <term>Regular figure: a shape where all sides and angles are equal, like an equilateral triangle or a square.</term>; rather, some come about having been propagated from those preceding them, up to a certain limit: as we shall see in the propositions.*

*The use of this Axiom is in Propositions VII and VIII.*

...a third note, if it is consonant with one of them, will also be consonant with the other; if it is dissonant with one, it will also be dissonant with the other, regardless of how different those various consonances or dissonances may be.

Note that in this logical statement, "Identity-sound" <note>original: *Identifoni*. Kepler uses this term for intervals like the octave where the two notes sound like the same "identity," just higher or lower.</note> is the specific subject, while "Consonance" is the general category. We should understand two things from this. First, it does not follow that if any two notes are consonant in any way, a third note must also be consonant or dissonant with both. This is false regarding the general category of consonance, but true for the specific type of "Identity-sounds." Second, it also does not follow that if a third note is consonant with one Identity-sound by a specific interval, it will be consonant with the other by that *same* interval. This is not always true, which I will demonstrate with an example, even if I am getting ahead of myself. Let there be two voices making an octave <note>original: *diapasõ*</note>, G and g. Let there be a third note, d. This d makes a fifth <note>original: *diapente*</note> with the lower G; therefore, it also harmonizes with the higher g, but not as a fifth, but as a fourth <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>.

<margin>The Metaphysical Cause of Harmonies.</margin>
Regarding these Axioms, then, and especially the first five, there is a sublime speculation—Platonic in nature and analogous to the Christian Faith—pertaining to Metaphysics and the doctrine of the Soul. For Geometry (the part of which relevant here was covered in the first two books) is co-eternal with God and shines forth in the Divine Mind. As stated in the preamble to this book, it provided God with the patterns for decorating the World, so that the World might become the Best and Most Beautiful, and finally, most like the Creator. Indeed, all Spirits, Souls, and Minds are images of God the Creator; each is placed in charge of its own body to govern, move, grow, preserve, and even propagate it.

Since, therefore, these Minds encompass a certain pattern of Creation in their duties, they also observe the same laws of work as the Creator, which are drawn from geometry. They delight in the same proportions that God used, wherever they find them—whether through pure contemplation, through the intervention of the senses in physical things, or even without the Mind's active reasoning, through a hidden and innate instinct. This is true whether God himself expressed these proportions invariably in bodies and motions, or whether, by a certain Geometric necessity of infinitely divided matter and motions through the quantity of matter, these harmonic proportions occurred at their own times among infinite non-harmonic proportions, thus existing not in **BEING** but in **BECOMING**. <note>original: *non in ESSE sed in FIERI*. A philosophical distinction: "Being" refers to permanent existence, "Becoming" refers to things that happen through motion or time.</note> Nor do Minds only delight...

# ON PROPORTIONS

...Images of God, according to these proportions; but they also use them as laws to carry out their duties, and to express those same proportions in the movements of their bodies as far as they are able. The following books will provide two brilliant examples: one of the Creator God Himself, who distributed the movements of the heavens by harmonic proportions; the other of that Soul which we are accustomed to call sublunary Nature <note>In Kepler’s cosmology, the "sublunary" sphere refers to the Earth and its atmosphere—everything below the orbit of the moon—which was believed to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note>, which rouses meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> according to the prescription of the proportions that occur in the radiation of the stars. Therefore, let the third example, and the one proper to this book, be that of the human soul, and even to some extent that of cattle. For these, having perceived the harmonic proportions of voices, rejoice in them, but are saddened by those that are not harmonic; from these feelings of the Soul, the former are called Consonances and the latter Dissonances. If another harmonic proportion is added—that of long and short sounds and voices for the sake of time <note>Kepler is referring here to rhythm and musical meter.</note>—then they move their bodies in dances and their tongues in pronunciation according to these same laws. To this, the craftsmen accommodate the blows of their hammers, and soldiers their stride; all things live while harmonies endure, but grow sluggish when they are disturbed.

Whether these and similar things are the work of Purpose or Instinct—that is, the work of the Mind—or whether it happens by the necessity of the Elements of Nature and Matter, so that no temperament <note>original: *temperies*. In this context, it refers to a balanced mixture or arrangement of physical qualities.</note> can be pleasant to the senses unless it consists of harmonic proportions of figures; this has been variously disputed by philosophers. All of them seek the origin of that sweetness which flows into the ears from the proportion of voices, by which sweetness we define Consonances. Those who lean toward the Matter and Motion of the Elements bring forward this example—truly wonderful in itself—that 
<margin>A wonderful experiment with strings.</margin> 
a string when struck draws another string that was not struck into sound with it, if it has been stretched in consonance with it, but leaves a string that is stretched dissonantly unmoved. Since this cannot happen through the service of any Mind (because the sound caused by this has no Mind or intellect), it follows that we must say it happens through the tempering of motions. For the sound of a string has highness or lowness from the speed or slowness of the vibration by which the whole free length of the string vibrates. These differences of sounds are not present primarily and immediately in the length or shortness itself, but secondarily; because, naturally, when the length is decreased, the slowness of the vibration is decreased and the speed is increased. This is why, while the free length of the string remains the same, the tension itself sharpens the sound; for by leaving the string less slack, it also decreases the space through which it can be vibrated in a reciprocal motion.

Therefore, when there is the same tension in two strings, so that they can produce a unison, then the sound of one—that is, the immaterial species <note>In the Aristotelian and Renaissance tradition, a "species" was an invisible form or image that traveled from an object to the senses or to other objects.</note> of the body of the string, established in the vibration—having glided from its own string, strikes the other string. It is as if someone were to let out a shout toward a lyre <note>original: *Chelyn*, from the Greek word for a tortoise-shell lyre.</note> or another hollow object; by that shout he strikes that hollow space and makes all its strings resonate. That species of vibration strikes the other string with the same rhythm of speed with which it also moves, because it is equally stretched; so that in this way, individual blows (into which the vibration is understood to be divided) into individual...
