### ON HARMONICS BOOK III.

...of the struck second <term>string<note>original: "chorda"</note></term> fall continuously into the pauses of the first. Thus it happens that the string moved most of all is the one tuned to a <term>unison<note>The same pitch; a 1:1 ratio.</note></term> with the first. However, that string which is of double or half speed also moves, because two strokes of vibration are completed within one pause of the string, and so every third stroke from the previous one always matches at the end of each pause. Finally, even that string which is of <term>one-and-a-half speed<note>original: "sesquialteræ"; this refers to the musical interval of a fifth (a 3:2 ratio).</note></term> moves somewhat, because three little strokes occur within two of its pauses. But now those strokes and these pauses begin to get in each other's way more frequently and hinder one another; while two of its strokes stray from the end of this pause, only one falls in harmony. By this encounter, the motion of the other strings is stopped, just as if someone had placed a finger on a vibrating string. This seems to me the cause of this wonderful experiment; to whoever is more fortunate than I in the search of the mind, I shall grant the prize.

<margin>What is the cause of pleasure from harmonies?</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;What then? If the speed of one string is enough to move another proportioned string, which, to the eye, remains untouched; will not these same speeds of two strings relative to each other be enough to create a sweet "tickling" of the hearing? Is it because the hearing is moved, in a certain way, uniformly by both strings, and two strokes from two sounds or vibrations fall at the same moment? Not at all, I say; this matter is not settled so easily. I wonder that such an explanation regarding the cause of this thing could satisfy <note>original: "Porphyrio"</note> Porphyry, the commentator on <note>original: "Ptolemæi"</note> Ptolemy's *Harmonics*, since he is a philosopher of the deepest investigation. Unless it is likely that he was held back by the difficulty of searching for the cause, preventing him from penetrating as far as he wished; and he thought it better to put something forward than to remain entirely silent, which they say is a disgrace for a Philosopher.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For what, I ask, is the proportion of a "tickling" of the hearing—a bodily thing—to that incredible pleasure which we perceive most deeply within the soul from harmonic <term>consonances<note>Intervals that sound pleasing and stable, like the octave or fifth.</note></term>? If there is any pleasure from tickling, does not the part of the body that endures the tickling hold the primary place in that pleasure? <margin>What is sense?</margin> For it seemed to me that every sense must be defined thus, in my book <note>original: "Dioptricis"</note> *Dioptrics*, that it is only a complete sensation, producing pleasure or pain, when the "image" of the organ destined for sensation—as it is affected by an external thing—comes inward to the "tribunal of common sense" by the passage of the <term>spirits<note>In 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were believed to be very fine fluids that traveled through the nerves to carry sensory information to the brain.</note></term>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Now, in the hearing of consonant voices or sounds, what parts of the pleasure remain stuck in the ears? Do we not sometimes feel pain in our ears while we long for this hearing, and place our hand against sounds that are too loud? Nevertheless, we continue to perceive the consonances, and our heart leaps within us.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Add to this that this reasoning based on motion is strongest in a unison; yet the greatest sweetness is not found in a unison, but in other Consonances and their arrangement.

<margin>The cause of the sweetness of Harmonies must be sought from the approval of the Mind.</margin>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Many things could be brought forward to destroy this proposed reasoning for the sweetness of Consonances; I refrain from writing them down more carefully for the present. I emphasize this one point, which I have already touched upon above and which can stand in place of all others: that the Works and Movements of bodies, which imitate harmonic proportions, belong to the parts of the Soul and Mind; it is these that assign the cause for why Consonances delight us. Nor does authority shrink...

# ON PROPORTIONS

Of the ancients; who, defining the Soul now as Motion, now as Harmony, did not speak so much absurdly as they were clumsily understood: since in difficult matters, mystical senses often lie hidden, concealed beneath the bark of words. Indeed, the philosophy of Timaeus of Locri <note>Timaeus of Locri was a Pythagorean philosopher; Kepler refers to the "Timaeus" dialogue by Plato which discusses the mathematical composition of the soul.</note> regarding how the soul is composed of harmonic proportions (which I mentioned in the preamble) was refuted by Aristotle in the sense that the words literally sound: yet I would not dare to affirm that nothing lies hidden in those pages beyond what the words sound like. On the contrary, I think no one would deny that this author holds at the very least what I am asserting here: that it is the Mind and the human Soul by whose judgment or instinct the sense of hearing distinguishes sweet (that is, <term>consonant<note>Sounds that "sound well" together, like a perfect fifth or an octave.</note></term>) proportions from the unpleasant and <term>dissonant<note>Clashing or harsh sounds.</note></term>. For he who considers this diligently knows that proportions are <term>Entities of Reason<note>original: "Rationis Entia"; things that exist in the mind or through logic rather than as physical objects.</note></term>, perceptible by reason alone and not by sense, and that it is the work of the Mind to distinguish the proportions as the "form" from the proportioned thing as the "matter."

<margin>From the scientific demonstration of figures.</margin>
Since we have explained two properties of <term>Regular Figures<note>Geometric shapes with equal sides and angles, like squares or equilateral triangles.</note></term>—the scientific demonstrability of the sides in each, and the <term>congruence<note>Kepler's term for how shapes fit together to fill a space or relate to one another.</note></term> of their entire joints among themselves—though both are not of clearly the same breadth: our axioms ring out most especially regarding Demonstration, because this is more familiar to the proportions of motions, from which sounds also arise.

For Congruence is in figures as they are wholes: but motions (to which harmonic proportions happen) extend the sides of the figure from which they are derived into a straight line (since almost all are considered as rectilinear) and thus, just as serpents destroy their mother, they ruin and destroy their own figure. <note>A common ancient belief was that baby vipers ate their way out of their mother's womb, killing her.</note> A figure, insofar as it is congruent, divides a whole circle into parts: harmonic proportions extend the divided circle into a straight line, and they erase the act of division made by the figure. Thus, harmonies associated with demonstrable figures run out into infinity; but Congruent Figures are limited to the number twelve. Finally, any figure makes only one division of the circle; yet the parts established in the circle always create two harmonies with the Whole.

<margin>And congruence.</margin>
Even though in this third book the reasoning of scientific demonstration of the sides will be more important than the Congruence of the whole figures: nevertheless, because of their great kinship, this must not be neglected in its place. For first, if you examine everything, the Latin meaning of the word "Congruence" <note>original: "Congruentia"</note> sounds the same as the Greek word "Harmony" <note>original: "Harmonia"</note>, which we deal with in this book: except that usage has slightly distinguished these words according to their subject matter. Secondly, the Congruence of figures procures some Congruence for motions (about which we treat in this and the fifth book). Thirdly, although we do not look so much at the whole figure as at one of its sides, and the part it cuts off—that part is consonant. But it is also true at the same time that we do not consider so much how great a part of the circle is intercepted, as by what kind of figure it was done—whether demonstrable and congruent, or the opposite. For any figure, from its angles (from which it obtained Congruence in Book II), also attained demonstration in Book I. Therefore, the respect for the Congruence of figures must not be taken away from Harmonies.

## PROPOSITION I.

->**The Consonance of the Half with the Whole, after the unison,**<-
->**is the only one in the first degree that is simple, perfect, and Identical; namely, from the Opposite.**<-

---

For that which is shaped <note>original: "figuratum"; referring to geometric polygons</note> is composed of diverse elements; therefore, it is neither simple nor Identical. For a figure has an area, parts related to that area, and angles differing in position. However, that which is not shaped—where the area lacks width, and consisting of parts and angles, exists as one mere straight line equal to the proposed Measure—is, for these very reasons, both simple and the same as the Measure; that is, Identical. Of the former kind are the Regular Figures inscribed in a circle; of the latter kind is the Diameter of the circle.

1. For all sides of the figures deviate equally from the center; the Diameter is drawn through the center itself. 
2. The measurer <note>the geometrician or the act of measuring</note>, dividing the circle from one point with the side of a figure, when he has proceeded by doing this several times, finally returns to the first point with the other end of the side; the Diameter, however, passing through the center itself, returns to the initial point at the very first repetition. 
3. The other figures have both a length of sides<gloss>sides</gloss> and a surface area which they surround; the diameter, surrounding or enclosing no part of the plane, coincides entirely with itself on the second pass through repeated rotations. 
4. Other figures dividing the circle create many parts; the Diameter creates the smallest number of all, namely, only two: for it could not divide the whole at all with fewer than two. 
5. And since the Diameter is that measure to which the sides of figures must be compared for the sake of understanding and demonstration: the sides of the other figures are described with more effort and are brought into the state of knowledge through a more imperfect degree of demonstration. But the diameter of the circle is described by the simplest law: a path through the center, from one point of the circle to the opposite, and it equals itself and is the measure of itself. 
6. Also, the sides of figures in one division of a circle (or in the cutting away of a part) create unequal portions, making the Part smaller than the Remainder; the diameter leaves the cut part equal to the Remainder. This proportion of equality is pure, simple, and perfect: because parts that are equal to each other are the same for the purpose of Measurement. 
7. Finally, the other figures divide the circumference of the circle into several equal parts, but they divide the area of the circle into unequal parts, because one remains in the middle—namely, the area of the figure—which is larger than any of the segments. The diameter divides not only the circumference but also the area into two equal parts at the same time.

But according to Axiom II, the character of a side or line which divides a circle consonantly passes into the consonance itself. Therefore, the Consonance of the Part which the diameter cuts from the circle—that is, of the semicircle with the whole circle—is simple, perfect, and Identical <note>By "Identical," Kepler refers to the Octave (2:1 ratio), where the two notes sound so similar they are often given the same name.</note>. And according to Axiom V, all other lengths which are related to each other as the Whole circle is to its half create the same Identical, perfect, and simple consonance. And in Numbers (not purely abstract and counting numbers, but numbered lengths), the Double Proportion <note>The ratio of 2:1</note>—namely between 1 and 2, as well as between their equal multiples—generates the Identical Consonance.

Note here that although the diameter, through all its simplicities and perfections, is still not as simple as a point; rather, it remains a line, [bounded] by two circum-

He argues that because the diameter is the simplest way to divide a circle's area and circumference equally, its harmonic equivalent must be the most "identical" consonance.</summary>

# ON PROPORTIONS

terminated by points, cutting the circle in opposite places and forming two parts; and just as these parts, though equal to each other, are each smaller than their whole, so too an **Identical Consonance** is not the same as a unison. Although the voices are identically consonant, one is nonetheless smaller and the other larger; the former being high <note>original: "acuta"</note> and the latter deep <note>original: "gravis"</note>, answering the other as if from the opposite side. For this reason, it is called **Identical Consonance from the Opposite**.

Thus, you have the genuine cause, derived from the diameter of the circle, as to why the sound of a whole string and the sound of a half-string—though different from one another—are nonetheless perceived by the ear as somehow the same compared to other concords.

Others seek the cause of this **Identity of Sound** <note>original: "Identisonantia"</note> in vain from the number of eight notes <note>The "octave" name comes from the eight notes of the scale, but Kepler argues the physical harmony exists before we ever name the scale</note>, since the identity of sound is by nature prior to the division of this interval into the seven tuneful steps by which the eight sounds are designated.

However, it is not yet time to give a name to this consonance, nor to the others; for this must be deferred to Chapter V.

Note also this: other parts that are not established by the diameter may also be identically consonant, but not in the first degree, nor through geometric figures, but through "propagation," which is the subject of the following propositions.

## PROPOSITION II.

->*If, of two parts of a circle, the smaller relates to the larger as the larger relates to the whole circle, in any continuous proportion other than double: then while the larger part harmonizes with the whole circle, the smaller part will be dissonant from the whole.*<-

For after the double [1:2] comes the triple [1:3]. A continuous triple proportion, however, establishes in the third place a *ninth* part of the whole circle; a quintuple [1:5] establishes a *twenty-fifth* part. A sextuple [1:6] implies a ninth, and a decuple [1:10] implies a twenty-fifth, because 6 times 6 is 36 (which is four times nine) and 10 times 10 is 100 (which is four times 25). The same follows for the rest. Yet the ninth, the twenty-fifth, and similar parts are dissonant from the whole, according to Axiom III. See Book I, Proposition XLVII.

## PROPOSITION III.

->*Strings in a continuous double proportion all harmonize identically with one another, though those further apart do so at a more remote degree.*<-

For any three adjacent strings in this sequence relate to each other as the whole circle, the half, and the quarter part relate to each other. Now, both the half and the quarter harmonize with the whole circle, according to Axiom I. Furthermore, the quarter harmonizes with the half, according to Axiom V. Therefore, all three adjacent strings harmonize with each other. Moreover, the consonance of the quarter part with the whole circle is also "identical," because the whole and its half harmonize identically according to Proposition I. So too does the quarter part with the half, by the same logic. Therefore, by Axiom VII, the quarter part also harmonizes identically with the whole circle; and by Axiom V, any quadruple relates to the single.

Now, truly, whatever the ratio is for the first, second, and third proportions, the same...

<meta>catchword: will be [erit]</meta>

<summary>Kepler explains that the octave (1:2 ratio) is an "identical" consonance because it arises from the circle's diameter, the simplest division. He argues that this mathematical relationship precedes the musical scale and proves that only double proportions (1:2, 1:4, 1:8) maintain this harmonic identity.</summary>

# ON HARMONICS BOOK III.

...it will also be of the second, third, and fourth; and so on continuously for any three adjacent ones. All proportional values in a continuous double proportion <note>The 1:2, 1:4, 1:8 ratio series</note>, therefore, harmonize identically with one another.

Note, therefore, in such cases, the distinction between **Consonance** in general and **Identical Consonance** <note>original: *Identisonantia*</note> specifically. The Parts of the Fourth, Eighth, Sixteenth, and similar divisions harmonize because of Axiom I and the figures—the Square, the Octagon, etc.—but they harmonize *identically* because of the additional derivation <note>original: *propagationem*</note> of this family of figures from the bisection of the circle. For if it had been without this derivation, their consonances would not have been identical. Since all figures create either many parts of a circle, if equal; or unequal, if only two; since they encompass an area; and they do not divide the area of the circle into equal parts; nor are their sides drawn through the center; nor do they return upon themselves; nor are they equal to the diameter: Consonances arising from the figures of the Square family would have, in a way, expanded themselves in the hearing, and would have strained the mind with a manifest variety and diversity of voices; as do those consonances which are from other figures consisting of a number of sides that is not "even-even" <note>original: *numero non pariter pari*; a Pythagorean term for numbers that are powers of two, like 4, 8, 16</note>: through Prop. I.

However, this family of figures has not been entirely deprived of the power to vary consonances and deflect them from the purity of Identical Consonance (just as they themselves have receded from the simplicity of the Diameter). First, although the Consonance of the part of the circle cut off by a figure is converted into mere Identity of Sound (because of the said derivation of the parts of the circle from the very first bisection); nevertheless, the degrees of Identity of Sound become more remote. For the smaller part, harmonizing identically from the opposite side with the larger part closest to it, always becomes sharper <note>Higher in pitch</note> as the instances of opposition are multiplied; thus the intervals of the voices are always increased. Secondly, Identity of Sound remains in the Part (as in the section through the diameter): but by no means in the Remainder; for this Remainder in subsequent figures is always worse than itself regarding its Harmonic Nature. But concerning such Remainders, specific Propositions follow.

And conversely, it is not only the Square family that produces identical consonances; but also other families, in so far as they participate in bisection, to that extent they also make identical consonances; for the part of the circle cut off by the side of a later figure always harmonizes identically with the part cut off by the side of a previous figure; as the remaining propositions teach. Thus the Analogy stands firm in all its members.

The use of this Proposition is in the following one.

## PROPOSITION IV.

->A string which is consonant with either of the Multiples of a<-
->continuous double proportion, is also consonant with the rest: and if it<-
->is dissonant from one; it is also dissonant from the other.<-

For by Prop. III, the sounds of continuous doubles are identical to one another. What harmonizes with one of the identical strings, also harmonizes with the other: and so on, by Axiom VI.

Axiom VI was established for the sake of this proposition, and this proposition now serves for examining the Parts and Remainders of circles. Let the "know-it-alls" <note>original: *sciolj*; those with superficial or pretentious knowledge</note> beware of a contradiction between Propositions and Axioms: for there is no Tautology here, everything is necessary; anyone who wishes to settle the matter more briefly will only entangle himself.

He also introduces the principle that a note in tune with one octave is necessarily in tune with all its octave multiples.</summary>

## PROPOSITION V.

Even if the sides of Star-polygons <note>original: *Stellarum*; Kepler uses the geometry of stars to explain complex musical ratios</note> are otherwise constructible <note>original: *demonstrabilia*; meaning they can be drawn with a compass and straightedge</note>, and by the same right determine parts of a Circle that are consonant with the Whole (just as their primary figures do according to the first Axiom): nevertheless, those sides are excepted which cut off a part of the circle consisting of a number of parts that is characteristic of some non-constructible <note>original: *indemonstrabilis*</note> figure; this occurs when the numbers of the Part and the Whole are Prime to each other <note>meaning they share no common factors, such as 9 and 20</note>.

*The first part of this proposition is an axiom; however, to prevent it from being too general, it had to be restricted by the second part. It is proven as follows: Suppose a circle is divided by a constructible figure, for example, by an Icosagon <note>a 20-sided polygon</note>. Now consider an Icosagon-star whose side spans nine of the twenty parts made by the Icosagon, so that 9 and 20 are prime to each other. Since the Part cut off is from the circle, it will certainly be smaller than the Whole; yet it could be larger than a half, a quarter, or an eighth of the whole. We can continue dividing the whole by two <note>creating a "sub-double" series: 10, 5, 2.5...</note> until some part of the whole is less than half of the Part we are discussing. In our example, since the Whole is 20 and the Part is 9, take half the whole (10), then half of that (5), and finally 2 1/2 (the eighth of the Whole). This 2 1/2 is now less than half of 9. Therefore, our part (9) relates to the eighth of the circle (2 1/2) just as a circle divided by a non-constructible figure relates to one of its parts—specifically, as 18 relates to 5 <note>9 divided by 2.5 is the same ratio as 18 divided by 5</note>. Now, the Corollary to Axiom III declared that five-eighteenths is dissonant from the whole of 18. Therefore, by Axiom V, our part (9) will be dissonant from the Eighth of the circle (the 2 1/2 parts). Consequently, by Proposition IV, our part (9) will also be dissonant from the whole circle (20), even though its spanning chord is constructible; it is, however, of the most remote degree, and its star-polygon is among the incongruent ones.*

## PROPOSITION VI.

The Remainders <note>original: *Residua*; the "leftover" arc of a circle after a section is removed</note> of circles or chords, after consonant Parts have been cut off from the Whole, are also consonant both with the part cut off and with the whole circle or chord, provided they are continuous doubles of their own consonant part.

*Consonant with the part cut off by Proposition I, and with the whole by Proposition IV.*

## PROPOSITION VII.

If such a Remainder has the same proportion to the half or quarter of the circle or chord as the Whole circle has to some other of its consonant Parts, it will also be consonant with the Whole circle; if it relates to a dissonant portion, it will be dissonant.

*For the whole circle, its half, and its quarter part are in a continuous double proportion <note>1 : 1/2 : 1/4</note>; therefore (by Prop. IV) those remainders which are consonant to such a part of the circle are also consonant to the whole; and those which are dissonant from that part will also be dissonant from the whole. But those Remainders are consonant to such a Part if they have the same proportion to it as the Whole...*

The Whole is dissonant to any consonant part from such a Part which has the same proportion to it as the circle has to any dissonant part; and this is by Axiom V.

->*Therefore, such Remainders <note>original: "Residua"; the portion of the circle left over after a specific arc or "part" is removed</note> are consonant with the Whole circle; conversely, others are dissonant from the whole circle.*<-

This proposition exists for the sake of the following Proposition VIII.

## PROPOSITION VIII.

**Indeed, if the Remainder has the same proportion to the cut-off Part as the Whole circle has to any consonant Part, it is also consonant with that cut-off part, just as in the previous proposition it was consonant with the Whole; but if it has the proportion which the Whole has to some dissonant Part, it will be dissonant from both the cut-off part and from the Whole.**

*The first part relies on Axiom V, as does one small detail of the second part—namely, that the Remainder is dissonant from the cut-off Part. But that such a Remainder is also dissonant from the Whole is proved as follows:*

In the stated proportion, it takes the place of a whole circle divided by an unconstructible figure <note>original: "figura indemonstrabili"; a polygon that cannot be drawn using only a compass and straightedge, such as a heptagon (7-sided)</note>. Therefore, although such a Remainder is smaller than the whole circle of which it is a Remainder, it is nevertheless larger than a semicircle, according to the definition of a Remainder. But if it is larger than its own semicircle, then a fourth part of its circle (being half of the semicircle) is smaller than half of this Remainder. Therefore, just as the Remainder is to a fourth of its circle, so will some circle divided by an unconstructible figure be to some part of that division. But such a whole circle is dissonant from such a part by Axiom III. Therefore, the said Remainder will also be dissonant from a fourth of its circle by Axiom V. Consequently, it will also be dissonant from its own whole circle, by Proposition VII.

# CHAPTER II.

## On the Harmonic Section of a String.

So far, we have taught the origin of harmonic proportions, and shown it to be twofold: one is immediate, derived from demonstrable <note>original: "demonstrabilibus"; referring to regular polygons that can be constructed with a compass and straightedge</note>, congruent figures; the other is by means of the double proportion <note>the 2:1 ratio of the octave</note>, upon which the identity of consonances rests. However, since harmonic proportions are infinite—and, as far as our knowledge goes, still unrefined, unpolished, inconspicuous, and unnamed, or rather piled up and scattered like a heap of rough stones and timber—it follows that we must proceed to polish them, to assign names to them, and finally to construct from them the most beautiful edifice of the Harmonic System, or Musical Scale. The constitution of this system is not arbitrary, as someone might think, nor is it a human invention that could be changed; rather, it is most rational and natural, so much so that God the Creator himself expressed it in the adjustment of the celestial motions. Harmonic proportions are joined together into a single System through harmonic sections of a string; how many of these there are must be investigated in this chapter.

## DEFINITION.

<margin>
<image-desc>A vertical diagram using brackets to define terms for the harmonic division of a string:
- 1. The Whole (Tota)
- 2. The Larger Part (Pars Major)
- 3. The Smaller Part (Pars Minor)
A bracket links "2. The Larger Part" to the label "Mean" (Med:).
A larger bracket links "1. The Whole" and "3. The Smaller Part" to the label "Extremes" (Extrema).</image-desc>
</margin>

**When the whole string is cut into such parts which are consonant both among themselves and each with the whole: that division shall be called by us a Harmonic Section. Furthermore, the Mean <note>original: "Medium"; the middle term in a proportional relationship</note> of this section, proportioned musically (that is, consonantly), is one of the two equal parts; or if they are unequal, it is the Larger of them. The Extremes <note>original: "extrema"</note> of the consonant proportion shall be the remaining or smaller part, and the whole string.**

> *Let the Geometer observe the analogy of the "Divine Proportion" <note>The Golden Ratio, or "Extreme and Mean Ratio"</note>: in which the Whole has the same proportion to the Larger part as the Larger has to the Smaller. For what is the "same Proportion" in that geometric section is, in our musical section, the "same Quality"—which is called Consonance, Concordance, Congruence, or Harmony. Yet, be careful not to assume the consonance is of the same specific type, just as the proportion there is unique.*
>
> *The Ancients made no mention of this section in this sense, because they were ignorant of the true causes of Consonances; however, we shall deal with their own section of the string <note>likely referring to the Pythagorean monochord division</note> further below.*

## PROPOSITION IX.

**The section of a string into two equal parts is Harmonic.**

Thus, there are three consonances; therefore, by definition, the string is divided harmonically.

## PROPOSITIO X.

->*The section of a string into two parts in a double proportion is Harmonic.*<-

<margin>3 2 1</margin>
For the parts of this proportion <note>a 2:1 ratio</note> are in identical consonance, by *Prop. I*. And because the larger part is double the smaller, the whole is therefore triple the smaller <note>1 + 2 = 3</note>. The whole is therefore to the smaller part as a circle is to a segment cut off by the side of an inscribed triangle <note>the "trigon," which divides a circle into 1/3 and 2/3 sections</note>, and it is consonant, by the *final Corollary of the previous chapter*. Wherefore the Whole itself is consonant to the smaller part, by *Axiom V*. Consequently, its double—that is, the **Remainder**—is also consonant, by *Proposition IV*. Thus, three consonances are established by this division. Therefore [it is harmonic].

<image-desc>A musical staff with three notes aligned vertically, labeled from top to bottom as 1, 2, and 3, representing the whole and the two parts of the string.</image-desc>

---

## PROPOSITIO XI.

->*The section of a string into two parts in a triple proportion to each other is Harmonic.*<-

<margin>4 3 2 1</margin>
For since parts 1 and 3 are related to each other as a Consonant part of a Circle is to the whole, they will be in consonance with each other, by *Axiom V*. And because 1 and 3 make 4, part 1 will be in consonance with the whole string, 4, by *Axiom I* and *Prop. III*.

<margin>1</margin>
Finally, because the **Remainder** 3 resonates with part 1, it will also resonate with its quadruple, 4—that is, with the whole string. Therefore, here too there are three consonances.

<image-desc>A musical staff showing notes labeled 1, 3, and 4, illustrating the harmonic intervals created by a 1:3 division.</image-desc>

---

## PROPOSITIO XII.

->*The section of a string into two parts in a quadruple proportion to each other is Harmonic.*<-

<margin>5 4 3 2 1</margin>
For since the parts are in a quadruple proportion <note>a 4:1 ratio</note>, they are in identical consonance with each other, by *Prop. III*. And because 1 and 4 make 5, part 1 resonates with the whole string, 5, by *Axiom I* and the previously mentioned *Corollary*. Wherefore the whole 5 also resonates with the quadruple of part 1 (which is 4), by *Prop. IV*. Thus, three consonances are produced. Therefore, etc.

## PROPOSITION XIII.

*The section of a string into two parts in a five-fold proportion <note>original: "quintuplæ"; a 5:1 ratio</note> is Harmonic.*

<image-desc>A small marginal diagram consisting of numerical labels 1, 6, and 5 arranged vertically, each associated with a horizontal line and symbols resembling musical notation (a flat 'b' and a square notehead).</image-desc>
*For since the part is 1 and the remainder is 5, they therefore have the same proportion as the whole circle has to a consonant part, according to Axiom I and the stated Corollary. For this reason, these parts are consonant with each other, according to Axiom V. And because part 1 joined with the Remainder 5 makes the whole 6: therefore (by Axiom I and the Corollary) part 1 is consonant with the whole 6 <note>a ratio of 6:1 is an octave plus a fifth</note>. And because the Remainder 5 is to the fourth part of the whole Circle 6 (namely to 1 ½ of this division) as the whole Circle 10 is to the consonant part 3, by the Corollary: therefore the Remainder 5 will also be consonant with the whole 6, by Proposition VII. Or, what comes to the same thing, because the Remainder 5 is to the double of the whole Circle 6 (which is 12) as a consonant part is to the whole, by the Corollary: therefore this Remainder 5 will also be consonant with 12, the double of the whole, by Axiom V. It will therefore also be consonant with the single, namely with the whole 6 itself, by Proposition IV. Thus, three consonances are created. Therefore, etc.*

---

## PROPOSITION XIV.

*The section of a string into two parts in a sesquialterate proportion <note>original: "sesquialteræ"; a 3:2 ratio, which produces the interval of a perfect fifth</note> is Harmonic.*

<image-desc>A marginal diagram similar to the previous one, showing the numbers 2, 5, and 3 vertically aligned with horizontal line segments and musical note symbols.</image-desc>
*For since part 2 with the Remainder 3 constitutes a sesquialterate proportion, the Part is related to the Remainder as a certain consonant Remainder 2 is related to the circle 3, by the Corollary; wherefore this part 2 will also be consonant with its Remainder 3, by Axiom V. And because part 2 with the remainder 3 makes the whole 5, and indeed part 1 and its remainder 4 are consonant with their whole 5 by the Corollary: therefore the whole 5 will also be consonant with the double of the consonant Part 1, which is 2 (our Part in this case), or with the half of the consonant Remainder 4, which is 2, according to Proposition IV. The same also follows simply from the first axiomatic part of Proposition V: because the chord subtending <note>original: "subtensa"</note> two-fifths is demonstrable, and therefore it is Consonant. Finally, because the Remainder 3 of part 2 is to the fourth part of the whole 5, as the whole circle 12 is to the consonant part 5, by the Corollary: therefore our Remainder 3 will also be consonant with the whole 5, according to Proposition VII. Thus, three consonances exist. Therefore <note>the section is harmonic</note>.*

And because part 3 with the remainder 5 makes the whole 8, by the Corollary, part 3 will be consonant with the whole 8. Finally, because the Remainder*

# PROPOSITION XVI.

**If a string is cut into two expressible <note>original: "Effabiles"; in this context, it refers to lengths that can be expressed as rational numbers or whole units</note> parts, and among those and the whole—that is, among three terms—there is one dissonance; it must be that the other dissonance is also among them.**

*For the cause of dissonance will be that either the whole or the part has a number of portions from that division which is characteristic of an undemonstrable figure <note>Kepler believed that only "constructible" polygons—those drawable with a compass and straightedge—could create harmonious musical intervals. Figures like the seven-sided heptagon were "undemonstrable" and thus caused dissonance</note>. Now, such a number is neither consonantly joined to any larger number that is characteristic of a demonstrable figure, nor to any number smaller than itself, by Axioms III and V and Propositions V and VII. Therefore, that term which consists of such a number of portions is dissonant from the two remaining terms of that section: thus two dissonances exist at once.*

To this proposition, there is a similar one in geometry: if a straight line is cut into expressible parts, and one of them is incommensurable <note>meaning they share no common measure; they cannot be expressed as a simple ratio</note> to some third line (not to the Whole composed of both as here); then it is necessary that the other part is also incommensurable to that same third line.

Or, if a straight line is cut into parts incommensurable to each other: both will be incommensurable to the Whole.

# PROPOSITION XVII.

**If a string is cut into two parts expressible <note>original: "Effabiles"</note> in length, and among these and the whole—that is, among three terms—there are two consonances; it is necessary that the third be a consonance as well.**

*For if there are two consonances, since there are no more than three proportions possible <note>the proportions between the whole and part A, the whole and part B, and part A and part B</note>: there cannot, therefore, be two dissonances. If there are not two dissonances, then there is not even one, by the converse of Proposition XVI: Therefore all three proportions will be consonant.*

So in Geometry, if a straight line is cut into parts commensurable to each other, the whole will be commensurable to each of the parts.

# PROPOSITION XVIII.

**A section of a string into two parts expressible in length, in which either the Whole or one of the Parts acquires a number of portions characteristic of an undemonstrable figure (provided the numbers of both the Whole and the Parts are prime to each other), is not Harmonic.**

*This is demonstrated as in Proposition XVI. For out of those three proportions of the terms, at least two become dissonant, contrary to the previous Definition.*

## PROPOSITION XIX.

**After the Octagonal <note>original: "Octogonicam"; referring to the division of a string into 8 equal parts</note>, no harmonic division of a string is possible.**

For the following divisions are either made through unconstructible <note>original: "indemonstrabiles"; figures that cannot be drawn using only a compass and straightedge, such as a 7-sided heptagon</note> figures and their star-polygons, and in that case, even if the parts might be consonant with each other, they are nevertheless dissonant with the whole, according to Axiom III. Or, they are made through figures that are demonstrable only by an "improper" demonstration, such as the fifteen-sided polygon <note>original: "Pentekedecagonum"</note>; and the proper parts of that division are dissonant with the whole, according to the Corollary to Axiom III. Or, they are made through figures demonstrable by "proper" demonstration: all of which, after the Pentagon, are many-sided polygons <note>original: "plurilatera"</note>; see Book I. Therefore, it is necessary to constitute the proper parts of such divisions by an odd number of portions; for if they were taken in an even number, the Part would not belong to this division but to a prior one. For example: if a string is divided into 10 parts, if you take 4 or 6 portions, it is exactly the same as if you divided it into 5 parts and took 2 or 3 portions <note>Kepler is explaining the reduction of fractions: 4/10 reduces to 2/5, which he already covered under the pentagon</note>. Since, therefore, the Part is an odd number and the Whole is an even number, the Part itself could be consonant with the Whole if it were not greater than five (by Proposition V); but one consonance is not sufficient for a harmonic division, as is clear from the definition. In that case, the Remainder <note>original: "Residuum"</note> will be dissonant: for the whole is set at more than 8 portions, and the definition of a Remainder is that it must be greater than half—that is, greater than 4. The smallest Remainder in an eight-fold division is 5; in divisions with more parts, it is greater than 5. In all divisions of the String after the eight-fold <note>original: "octonariam"</note>, the Remainders are odd numbers greater than 5. But odd numbers greater than 5 are characteristic of unconstructible figures, according to Propositions 45 and 47 of Book I. Therefore, by Proposition XVIII of this book, these Remainders cause the divisions to be non-harmonic.

I. The harmonic divisions of a single string are seven in number, and no more. <note>Kepler limits the "pure" harmonic ratios to those derived from the circle divided by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8.</note>
II. The generation <note>original: "Propagatio"</note> of the numbers which characterize the divisions occurs in this way: At the beginning, the Whole is placed in the form of a fraction—namely, unity [1] over...

<margin>The causes of this sevenfold set were discovered successively.</margin>

I first discovered these seven sections of the string by using my hearing as a guide—specifically, as many as there are Harmonies no larger than a single Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. Afterward, not without great effort, I unearthed the causes of both the individual sections and the total Number of them from the deepest springs of Geometry. Let the curious reader look at what I wrote about these sections twenty-two years ago in *The Secret of the Universe* <note>original: "Mysterio Cosmographico"; Kepler’s first major work, published in 1596</note>, Chapter XII; and let him consider how much I was deluded <note>original: "hallucinatus"</note> in that place regarding the causes of the sections and Harmonies. I had wrongly struggled to derive their number and proportions from the number of the five regular solid bodies <note>The "Platonic Solids": tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note>. In truth, it is more accurate to say that the five solid figures, the musical Harmonies, and the sections of the string all share a common origin in the regular plane figures. <margin>Unknown to Ptolemy and Porphyry.</margin> Through the generosity of Johann Georg Herwart <note>Herwart von Hohenburg, a Bavarian Chancellor and patron of Kepler</note>, the Chancellor of Bavaria, I have finally obtained the manuscripts of Ptolemy's *Harmonics* along with the commentary by Porphyry, both of which I mentioned in the passage cited above. I have translated the greater part of the third book of their work into the Appendix for Books IV and V of this current volume. However, I did not find the genuine causes of the Harmonies in their writings; indeed, there is no mention at all of the number of these sections, nor of their sevenfold set <note>original: "septenarij"</note>.

And although I noticed early enough that the causes must be sought from plane figures—as you can see the seeds of this idea already scattered in the aforementioned Chapter XII of *The Secret*—nevertheless, these problems tormented me for a very long time before every doubt in my mind was satisfied. First, the constructible <note>original: "demonstrabiles"</note> figures had to be separated from the unconstructible ones. Next, a cause had to be found for why, since these sections were derived from figures, the sections themselves should stop at seven, while the figures run on to infinity. Third, a distinction had to be established between the fifteen-sided figure <note>original: "Pentekædecagonum"</note> and the other constructible figures; for I saw that this figure was excluded from the creation of Harmonies, as my hearing testified. Each of these points had its own difficult hurdles, any one of which kept me occupied for a long time. Take, for example, Proposition V, which was the very last thing I realized needed to be added while I was already writing this work, and which I had been ignorant of until then. For unless that proposition were among the principles, then—to use an example—if seven-twentieths were fit to establish a harmony because they are constructible through the three-twentieths (with which they form a semicircle), then seven-tenths, five-sevenths, and even two-sevenths or one-seventh would be proven to create harmonies. Yet, the ears and our own Axioms reject this in every way.

Therefore, by the testimony of my book *The Secret of the Universe* alone, the sense of hearing is sufficiently fortified against the carping of the Sophists...

# CHAPTER III.
## On Harmonic Means,
### & the Trinity of Concordant
->sounds.<-

The definition of a <term>harmonic proportion</term> <note>A sequence of three numbers where the ratio of the two extremes is the same as the ratio of the differences between the numbers.</note> is hollow if it is merely said to be that where, with three Numbers placed in their natural order, the Excesses <note>The differences between the numbers.</note> of the two neighbors are in the proportion of the Extremes: as in the numbers 3, 4, 6, the largest (6) is double the smallest (3), and thus also the difference of 2 between the two larger neighbors (4 and 6) is double the difference of 1 between the two smaller neighbors (4 and 3).

<image-desc>A mathematical diagram illustrating the harmonic mean. On the right, the numbers 3, 4, and 6 are stacked. On the left, the differences are shown: the difference between 6 and 4 is 2; the difference between 4 and 3 is 1. Dashed lines indicate that the ratio of the extremes (6:3 or 2:1) is equal to the ratio of the differences (2:1).</image-desc>

<margin>
The method of establishing any Musical Mean according to the opinion of the ancients.
</margin>
I will, however, insert the method for finding the numbers containing such a proportion, called "Musical" by authors, because it is frequently transferred from <term>Harmonic</term> doctrine into Ethics and Politics. The method is as follows: *Having proposed two numbers that are Prime to each other <note>Numbers that have no common divisor other than 1.</note>, which contain the proportion of both the Extremes (from the three to be musically tempered according to the opinion of the ancients) and of the differences of each from the Middle; multiply each by itself and both by each other: of the three products, add the two smaller for the Minimum of the numbers to be found, add the two larger for the Maximum, and double the Middle for the Musical Mean of the ancients.* *For example*, let three numbers be found in the ancient Musical proportion such that the Extremes have between them the proportion which is between 3 and 5. Three times 3 are 9. Three times 5 are 15. Five times 5 are 25. Thus the products are 9, 15, and 25. Add 9 and 15, which are 24. Add 15 and 25, which are 40. Double 15, which becomes 30. These three sought numbers are 24, 30, and 40, whose differences (of the Extremes from the middle) are 6 and 10. For as 3 is to 5, so 24 is to 40, and so also 6 is to 10. In their lowest terms <note>original: "minimis inter se Primis"</note>, these are 12, 15, and 20.

<margin>
A refutation of this sort.
</margin>
This indeed is truly a harmonic proportion even to me, because not only is the proposed proportion between 3 and 5 harmonic (by Proposition 8, Corollary), but also the found Middle number 15 makes consonant proportions with the Extremes 12 and 20 by the same Corollary. But this does not always happen. For as often as the <term>Arithmetic Mean</term> <note>The simple average of two numbers.</note> between two numbers proposed in this way determines proportions that are dissonant with the extremes...

He provides a mathematical demonstration of how to calculate a "harmonic mean" while warning that these numerical patterns do not always result in pleasing musical sounds.</summary>

...as many times there also arise from this operation three numbers in a proportion that is not truly <term>Harmonic</term> <note>Kepler defines a "harmonic" proportion not just by math, but by whether the resulting sounds are pleasing to the ear.</note>, even though the two numbers originally proposed contain a harmonic proportion on their own. This happens in the ratios 1:6, 1:8, 3:4, 4:5, 5:6, 2:5, 3:8, and 5:8. For example, between 2 and 5—that is, between 4 and 10—the <term>Arithmetic mean</term> <note>The middle value in a sequence where the difference between numbers is constant (e.g., 4, 7, 10, where the difference is 3).</note> is 7, which is not harmonic; for 7 concords neither with 4 nor with 10, according to Proposition V. Therefore, if you work according to the Rule, the numbers 14, 20, and 35 will be produced, with differences of 6 and 15. In this case, according to the ancients, 20 should be called the harmonic mean, because as 14 is to 35 (that is, 2 to 5), so the difference 6 is to the difference 15. And yet, the ears completely reject the ratios 20:35 (which is 4:7) and 14:20 (which is 7:10).

<margin>See page 86. Nor yet because of this, etc.</margin>
In the harmonic sections of Chapter II, therefore, as many means present themselves as there are sections, minus one. In those sections, the "Mean" is taken in a stricter sense: it is the <term>major part</term> of a string that has been harmonically divided into two unequal parts, or the number representing that part. Thus, 2 is the harmonic mean between 1 and 3; likewise 3 is the mean between 1 and 4, and between 2 and 5; 4 is between 1 and 5; 5 is between 1 and 6, and between 3 and 8.

Besides these, however, there are also other Means, which are released from this law of dividing a whole string into two parts, yet are still encompassed by our general definition. These do not divide a single string, as in the previous chapter, but rather divide a *proportion* of strings into smaller consonant proportions.

<image-desc>A musical notation diagram integrated into the right side of the text. It features a five-line staff with multiple clefs (including C and F clefs) and diamond-shaped notes. Numerical annotations indicate harmonic proportions: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24 are written above the staff, while 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 are written below, illustrating the mathematical division of intervals into octaves and fifths.</image-desc>

First, all proportions greater than a <term>double proportion</term> <note>original: "dupla"; the 2:1 ratio, or an octave.</note> are resolved into their principles by removing the double proportion. For instance, the ratio 1:24 consists of four doubles (that is, a <term>sixteen-fold ratio</term> <note>original: "sedecupla"; $2^4 = 16$.</note>) and a <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>original: "sesquialterâ"; the 3:2 ratio, or a perfect fifth. $16 \times 1.5 = 24$.</note>. Therefore, Harmonic Means exist between 1 and 24 under this name: either these 2, 4, 8, 16 (with the sixteen-fold ratio placed above) or these 12, 6, 3, 2 (with one double placed above and three below, for this can be done in various ways). Next, the Double proportion (the octave) is resolved into these concords: 3:4 and 2:3; or into 3:4, 4:5, and 5:6; or into 4:5 and 5:8; or into 5:6 and 3:5. Finally, the <term>sesquialtera</term> (the 2:3 ratio) is resolved into 4:5 and 5:6; likewise 3:5 is resolved into 3:4 and 4:5.

<image-desc>Two segments of musical notation side-by-side at the bottom of the page. The left segment shows a bass clef with notes and vertical numbers 3, 4, 6, 8, 10. The right segment shows a C-clef with notes and numbers 4, 5, 6, 8.</image-desc>

Therefore, those three proportions—3:4, 4:5, and 5:6—are the smallest among the concords; that is, they are immediate, or lacking a Harmonic mean. They are, in fact, the <term>consonant elements</term> of the others.

<margin>Two Harmonic Means.</margin>
From this it follows that a single double proportion (octave) can have two harmonic means that are also consonant with each other, and this can happen in six ways. For because the octave has three minimal consonant elements, their order can be varied six times. The 3:4 ratio <note>the perfect fourth</note> is either in the first place from the smaller string, in the middle, or in the last; and in each case, of the remaining elements, either the larger 4:5 <note>the major third</note> is toward the smaller string, or the smaller 5:6 <note>the minor third</note> is.

Each of these cases is to be expressed by individual <term>sets of four numbers</term> <note>original: "Numerorum Quadrigis"; literally "chariots of four numbers."</note>, as follows in the table:

But out of these six pairs of <term>harmonic means</term> <note>A harmonic mean is a specific mathematical way to find a middle value between two others; in music, it helps define the notes that "fit" between the top and bottom of an octave.</note>, only one—represented by the numbers 10, 12, 15, 20—satisfies the definition of the ancients. For 12 is the musical mean (in their sense) between 10 and 15; likewise, 15 is the musical mean between 12 and 20. Indeed, the differences <note>original: "excessus"</note> are 2, 3, and 5. Just as the outer terms of the first triad <note>original: "trigae"</note>, 10 to 15, are in a ratio of 2 to 3, so too the outer terms of the second triad, 12 to 20, are in a ratio of 3 to 5.

<margin>On the Trinity of concords.</margin>
**Therefore, since the strings of a double proportion sound identically;** <note>Kepler is referring to "octave equivalence," the phenomenon where two notes an octave apart sound like the "same" note, just higher or lower.</note> and since there cannot be more than two <term>means</term> at one time between them that are consonant both with each other and with the doubles themselves: from this arises that famous observation of musicians, who marvel that all harmonies are completed by three voices. For however many voices may be added besides these, each one returns to one of those three through the identical consonance of the double proportion.

<image-desc>A vertical musical diagram consisting of a single staff with ten diamond-shaped notes arranged in a series, representing a scale or harmonic sequence. The notes are labeled with the numbers 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24, indicating their proportional relationships across multiple octaves.</image-desc>

> For although one consonance exists from all these string lengths—3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24—whatever exists beyond the strings 3, 4, and 5 returns to one of these through <term>identical sound</term> <note>original: "identisonum"</note>: just as 6 reduces to 3, and 8 to 4, and 10 to 5; likewise 12 reduces to 6 and 3; 16 to 8 and 4; 20 to 10 and 5; and 24 to 12, 6, and 3.

In vain do others seek the cause of this fact elsewhere: some from the triple dimension of a perfect quantity or body (which extends in length, width, and depth); others from the perfection of the number three; still others from the adorable <term>Trinity</term> itself within the Godhead.

In vain, I say, do they all seek it: for neither does solid quantity enter into this business (since we have shown the origin of harmonic proportions to come from plane figures), and the cause of science is very different for solid quantity than for plane quantity—since the former uses two mean proportionals, which are known...

<header>ON HARMONICS BOOK III.</header>

...to be known indiscriminately is impossible; nor can there be any power in number, insofar as it is considered merely as the act of counting. Nor is the origin of this <term>Trinity</term> <note>original: "Trinitatis"; here Kepler refers to the musical triad or the grouping of three notes that form a complete harmony</note> derived immediately from the divine essence through "exemplary causation" <note>A philosophical concept where God's nature serves as the direct blueprint for physical things</note>. For it appeared above that the cause of a thing is composed from the principles already explained, which by no means intend any specific number of voices for its own sake. Rather, by harmonically fitting the individual voices together—and thus, as it were, doing something else by accident—they produce something similar to divine things because of that same number; this same occurrence happens frequently in many other things. 

Briefly, this number three <note>original: "ternarius"</note> is not the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary source of change or rest; the "maker" of the thing</note> of harmonies, but its effect, or a companion to the harmony already produced. It does not give form to harmonies, but is a reflection of the form; it is not the matter of harmonic voices, but an offspring born from material necessity. It is not the "purpose" <note>original: "οὕ ἕνεκα" (hou heneka) - the final cause or the end for which a thing exists</note>, but the completion of the work. Finally, it is nothing of the harmonic thing itself, but is a secondary "being of reason" <note>original: "Ens rationis"; a concept that exists only in the mind rather than in physical reality</note> and a concept of the mind, a "second intention" <note>A logical term for a concept that classifies other concepts, like 'species' or 'number'</note>. 

For one should no more ask why only three voices sound harmonically together (while the fourth and all others return, in a way, to the same sound through the <term>octave</term> <note>original: "duplæ proportionis"</note>), than why there are only six pairs in any octave, or six forms of triple concords. For just as that number six <note>original: "Senarius"</note> does not come from the six days of creation, so too that number three is not there because of the Trinity of persons in the Godhead. But since the number three is common to both divine and worldly things, wherever it occurs, the human mind—ignorant of the true causes—marvels at this "conspiracy" or agreement.

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the origin of the <term>concinnous</term> intervals, which are smaller than concords.
<note>Concinnous intervals are "fitting" or melodic intervals, like whole steps and half steps, which are used to build scales but are not themselves "concords" (stable chords).</note>

<margin>What is Deep/Low?</margin>
<margin>What is High/Sharp?</margin>
<margin>What is Profound?</margin>
<margin>What is High?</margin>

Since the senses testify that among strings of equal tension, those that are longer produce lower sounds and those that are shorter produce higher sounds, these joined words **High** and **Low** <note>original: "Acutum & Grave"</note> are the proper distinctions of Harmonics. Individually, these terms belong to other separate sciences where they are paired with different opposites: "High/Sharp" with "Blunt/Obtuse" in Geometry, and "Heavy" with "Light" in Physics. Furthermore, in Mechanics, "High/Sharp" sounds like something subtle and penetrating; in the realm of the senses, "Heavy" is used for smells which, like heavy weights, are less tolerable due to a certain magnitude. 

But when paired as **High** and **Low** and placed in opposition to one another, they are understood only in reference to voices. Yet they retain something of their original meaning. For just as in Geometry a "Sharp" <note>Acute</note> angle is smaller than an "Obtuse" one, so too in Harmonics, a "high" voice sounds small, and thus penetrating and "high" (using the German idiom <note>original: "idiotismo Teutonico"</note>), and flying as if in the heavens because of a certain lightness. And just as in Physics "Heavy" things have great weight and "Light" things have little, so also here: a "Low" voice sounds "large." And as "Heavy" things on a scale seek the bottom and the lower regions, while "Light" things leap upward, so also in Harmonics, the "Low" voice, because of its magnitude, is considered "ponderous" and therefore "inferior" or "profound" (**bass**); while the "high" voice, as was said, is considered "high."

<summary>Kepler argues that the appearance of the number three in music is a mathematical consequence rather than a direct mystical imprint of the Trinity. He then defines the physical and linguistic origins of musical pitch, explaining why we describe sounds as "high" or "low/bass."</summary>

<keywords>triad, Trinity, efficient cause, being of reason, pitch, bass, high and low, geometry of sound, musical terminology</keywords>

# ON PROPORTIONS

For the fact that on the <term>Testudo</term> <note>original: "Testudine"; referring to the lyre, which was traditionally made from a tortoise shell</note> the <term>Hypatē</term> <note>The "Highest" string in terms of physical position on the instrument, but the "Lowest" in pitch</note>—that is, the "Highest"—produced a deep sound, was solely because of its physical position on the instrument, as is still the case today, and not because of any similarity of the voice to light things that fly above. The physical placement of the strings on the instrument has a mechanical reason: the <term>Nētē</term> <note>The "Lowest" string physically, which produced the "Highest" pitch</note>—that is, the "Last" or "Lowest"—produced the sharpest sound and had to be struck most frequently. Since swift motion is suited to small things, and because of the shape of the thumb, we strike downward more easily than upward. Added to these causes is the experience of the human throat. For men are generally taller than women, and adults taller than children, and they emit a deeper voice as if it were sought from a greater depth. Individual humans, taught by the sense of touch itself, draw out a deeper voice from further down and a higher voice from further up. Those who sing with the deepest pitch extend their bodies so the voice may come out from as deep as possible. To be sure, those who sing high also stretch their necks, but not to make the neck long, but rather to more tightly constrict the topmost rings of the throat.

<margin>What an Interval or Diastema is.</margin>
For these reasons, the concept of "High" and "Deep" was born in <term>Harmonics</term> <note>The science of sounds and their proportions</note>, for which we frequently use the terms "Sharp" and "Grave." Since "High" and "Deep" are otherwise words denoting location, the custom of speech, following these principles, also accommodates to voices that which belongs to locations: namely, **Intervals**, or in Greek <term>diastēmata</term> <note>original: "διασήματα"; literally "spaces between"</note>. For locations are said to "stand apart" <note>original: "διϊσάσαι" (diistasai)</note>. Finally, the discipline of Harmonics transferred this word even into its pictures or diagrams (discussed below), which consist of high and deep lines; in this way, its geometric sense was restored.

Therefore, what have until now been called "proportions of strings" will henceforth mostly be called "intervals of voices," which are emitted by strings of unequal length. For voices sounding the same—to which correspond strings of equal length and equal tension—do not create an **Interval**, since they are of the same height.

However, in Book V, we must refrain from this musical sense of the word "Interval." This is because there, the word must be used frequently in its astronomical sense, referring to the straight line between the body of a planet and the Sun, and likewise to the space that exists between different orbits.

<margin>What is a superior and inferior interval.</margin>
Furthermore, just as in the preceding chapter proportions were considered in two ways—namely, either individually by themselves, or compared to each other for the sake of order (which extended from the smaller term or string of a compound proportion to the larger or longer, and vice versa)—so now **Intervals** are considered either individually or compared to each other for the sake of their harmonic place. In a continuous ordering of several intervals (where two adjacent ones always share a common term, which is the major term of one and the minor term of the other tending toward deeper voices), that interval is always called **inferior** which is between deeper voices, and **superior** which is between sharper voices.

<margin>Which Intervals are equal.</margin>
In Geometry, proportions are recognized as equal even if the terms of one are unequal to the terms of the other, and if the difference between the terms of one is unequal to the difference of the terms of the other. For instance, if there are three strings in the proportion of the numbers 4, 6, and 9, the proportion is considered the same...

He distinguishes between the musical use of "interval" and the astronomical use he will employ later in the book.</summary>

<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>
The ratio of 4 to 6 is the same as the ratio of 6 to 9 <note>In both cases, the ratio is 2:3, the "Sesquialter" or Perfect Fifth</note>, notwithstanding that both the terms themselves and the differences between them—2 and 3—are unequal. Similarly in Music, all vocal intervals arising from strings that have the same proportion are considered equal and are written with the same numerical sign; they are even drawn as equal spaces between lines on a musical diagram. Thus, we completely forget the inequality that exists between the actual physical differences of the various strings.

<image-desc>Three musical ratios: 4/3 (the Perfect Fourth), 5/4 (the Major Third), and 6/5 (the Minor Third).</image-desc>

It follows, therefore, that we call intervals of a smaller proportion "smaller" and those of a larger proportion "larger," without regard for the magnitude or smallness of the numbers that represent them.

<margin>What are consonant and dissonant intervals?

What are concinnous and inconcinnous intervals, and why are they named so?</margin>
With these definitions established, we must now look further into the differences between intervals. Thus far, all proportions that we have demonstrated to be consonant (except for the proportion of equality) are to be regarded as consonant intervals; likewise, proportions we have called dissonant are to be regarded as dissonant intervals. However, among the dissonant intervals, there is a great difference. Some are taught by Nature and approved by the ear's instinct, while other smaller intervals are also established by that same sense. Although these latter ones are technically dissonant <note>meaning they do not form a stable harmony like a Fifth or Third</note>, they are still suitable for building a melody. Music, following Nature, gives them the name <term>Concinnous</term> <note>original: "Concinnorum"; meaning well-joined or fit for song</note> and distinguishes them from <term>Inconcinnous</term> ones, which never enter into the flow of an ordered song. In Greek, these are called *melodic* <note>original: "ἐμμελῆ" (emmele)</note> and *unmelodic* <note>original: "ἐκμελῆ" (ekmele)</note>.

When the Ancients saw this natural talent for distinguishing between the Concinnous and Inconcinnous, they thought they should search for some common, smallest element shared by all. They believed that by taking a certain number of these "atoms" of sound, any consonant or concinnous interval could be composed. It seemed necessary for such a "minimum interval" to exist as a simple building block, existing before the harmonies themselves, which seemed to be composed of such small units since some intervals are larger than others.

<margin><insert>These things and what follows, not being sufficiently aptly composed, the author corrects on page 235.</insert></margin>
But the matter is quite different, as can be shown by many examples. For if individuals of every species that differ in size were made of one common minimum unit, there would have to be one minimum quantity for the human species. Then, every human would be composed of a certain number of these "atoms"—a tall man from many, a dwarf from few. But in music, the quality of "consonance" shapes the proportion of the strings (or the interval of the voices) just as the form of a man shapes that mass of matter contained within his skin. Why have they forgotten Geometry? In geometry, there are many examples of all kinds of <term>incommensurable</term> quantities—those that have no common measure at all, and which cannot be built from a single certain element.

<margin>Most musical intervals are incommensurable.</margin>
Thus, it must be held that consonant intervals (except those where one is a multiple of the other, like the octave) are, like those very proportions themselves, incommensurable.

<summary>Kepler defines musical intervals through mathematical proportions rather than physical differences and introduces the concept of "concinnous" intervals—dissonances that are nonetheless useful in melody. He argues against the ancient Greek idea that all music is built from a single "minimum" unit, comparing musical intervals to incommensurable geometric shapes.</summary>

...miraculous things, so that although their differences are expressed by numbers—which in simple numbers is a sign of commensurability—these differences, because they are not simple numbers but fractions, are not actually commensurable. 

<margin>VI</margin>
<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>
For example, two ratios, 1:2 <note>The Octave</note> and 1:4 <note>The Double Octave</note>, are related to each other as the number 1 is to the number 2. They are therefore **commensurable** <term>commensurable: having a common measure, like 1 and 2 are both measured by 1</term>; for the ratio 1:4 is the double of 1:2. This relationship only holds true in a series of continuous doubles. For in the series of triples <note>1:3, 1:9, etc.</note> and other **multiples**, there are not two consonant ratios that relate this way. For instance, while 1:9 is indeed the triple of 1:3, only 1:3 is among the **consonant** <note>original: "consonas"</note> intervals, while 1:9 is among the **dissonant** intervals, according to **Axiom III**. The same can be seen even in non-multiples: in the **sesquialter** <note>The ratio 2:3, or the Perfect Fifth</note>, which is consonant, there is indeed a multiple of it that is commensurable (for 4:9 is to 2:3 as the number 2 is to 1), but 4:9 is not among the consonant intervals. On the other hand, take two other consonances that are not from the series of continuous doubles, such as 1:4 and 2:3; these two ratios are not commensurable with each other—that is, they do not relate as one whole number to another. For the difference between them, the ratio 3:8, measures neither 1:4 nor 2:3.

Therefore, **Consonant Intervals** are prior by nature to the smaller intervals which we call **concinnous** <term>concinnous: from "concinnus," meaning musically "neat" or "apt"; these are smaller melodic steps like tones and semitones that are pleasing but not primary harmonies</term>. The primary harmonies are not "composed" of these smaller ones as if from elements or from some smaller quantity; rather, on the contrary, these smaller ones arise from the harmonies as if from their causes.

Here we must note the ambiguous word "**composition**." Sometimes it denotes the natural origin of a thing, and other times it denotes the quantitative division of a thing—which is not its origin, but rather its destruction. For instance, when we say a circle "consists" of three thirds, we are first mentally dividing the circle into three; or when we say the human body is "composed" of limbs, we do not mean that the limbs existed before the body and the body was collected and built from them like a house is from stones and wood. Instead, we mean that because of its bulk, the body is divisible into these limbs—which, once separated, are no longer organic bodies themselves.

In the first sense of the word, we must deny that consonant intervals are "composed" of either other consonances or concinnous steps. In the second sense, they certainly "consist" of them, and are thus "composed" (as we ourselves used the term above). Larger consonant intervals consist of smaller consonant ones, and the smallest consonant intervals consist of concinnous ones, etc., because they can be dissolved into these as if into elements. However, different intervals do not all consist of a certain number of some "common smallest species" of interval, nor can they be dissolved into such a thing.

Furthermore, although consonant intervals have related causes, they do not all share the *same* cause; rather, each has its own peculiar cause, distinct from the causes of the others, as explained previously. For **consonance** belongs to the intervals themselves not simply as quantities, nor simply as relations, but as **qualitative** (that is, in a way, shaped or formal) relations. Therefore, wanting to establish a "smallest common interval" for them is irrelevant. Smallest and largest are considered in bare quantities and their proportions; but to divide a consonance *as a consonance* is to abolish its "species" <note>its unique character or form</note>, and to substitute for it either other species of consonance, or concinnous dissonances, or even plainly **inconcinnous** intervals. It does not therefo—

<summary>Kepler argues that musical harmonies (consonances) are primary qualitative forms that exist before the smaller melodic steps (concinnous intervals) that divide them. He uses the metaphor of a human body to explain that while a harmony can be divided into parts, it is not "built" from those parts like a house made of bricks.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>
CHAPTER IV.
</margin>

Therefore, an Interval possesses the causes or elements of its own consonance from its parts as if from principles—just as **commensurable quantities** <term>commensurable: quantities that can be measured by the same unit</term> increase by the multiplication of a common measure and exist with this measure under one and the same genus. But on the contrary, those things which the ancients held to be the "principles" of consonances (namely **Tones**, **semitones**, and **dieses** <note>original: "Tonos puta & ſemitonia & dieſes" — a diesis is a very small melodic interval, smaller than a semitone</note>) actually arise from Consonances as their own genuine principles.

<margin>
The form of a Consonance as such does not arise from the number of melodic intervals as parts.
</margin>

For although these Consonances consist of those **melodic intervals** <term>melodic intervals: Kepler uses "concinna," meaning intervals like tones and semitones that are "apt" for melody but not necessarily consonant when played together</term> which are not themselves Consonances (if not from one common unit, then at least from several combined in various ways), this should not be attributed to the consonance of the Interval itself. For if melodic intervals bestowed their own consonance upon a larger interval composed of them, this would always happen in any multiplication of melodic intervals, and a consonance would be better the more melodic intervals it contained. But this is false; for as we shall hear below, two tones joined together create a consonance <note>A Major Third</note>, but three joined together constitute a dissonant interval <note>A Tritone</note>.

Moreover, the fact that a consonance can be resolved into dissonant melodic intervals (as follows) is entirely accidental to that consonance considered in itself; and it happens only insofar as several consonances are compared with one another, each having arisen from its own principles.

<margin>
Definition of a Melodic Interval.
</margin>

Therefore, **Melodic intervals** are defined as being all the differences between consonances that are smaller than the **double interval** <note>The Octave, 1:2</note>; and the natural faculty of hearing accepts no other melodic intervals than those arising from this subtraction. Thus, consonant intervals have their origin in **Geometry** and demonstrable figures, while melodic intervals arise from the consonances themselves. Melodic intervals are related to consonances just as in Geometry the **Apotomes** <term>Apotome: in Euclidean geometry, an "irrational" line segment formed by subtracting one rational line from another</term> (ineffable lines) are "expressible in power," because they too are defined by the subtraction of one Expressible line from another Expressible line.

<margin>
The origin of Melodic Intervals from consonances.
</margin>

Furthermore, one method of comparison or abstraction is general or **arithmetic**, while the other is special, proper to **Harmonics**. In the Arithmetic method, Consonances smaller than the double are chosen, provided one is not such a part of the other as designated by some **harmonic mean** <note>original: "Medietas harmonica"</note> mentioned in the previous chapter.
