# An arithmetic corollary
->quite beautiful in its numbers and the following diagram.<-

<image-desc>An arithmetic diagram (typus) illustrating the ratios of squares (n²) to rectangles of adjacent numbers (n²-1) for integers 1 through 10. For even numbers 2, 4, 6, and 8, the diagram shows squares (4, 16, 36, 64) and products (3, 15, 35, 63) above the main line of integers. For odd numbers 3, 5, 7, and 9, it shows squares (9, 25, 49, 81) and products (8, 24, 48, 80) below the main line. Brackets connect these values to visualize the proportion n² : n²-1.</image-desc>

Namely, the square of every number below ten, along with the **rectangle** <note>In this context, the product of two numbers</note> of the two numbers immediately surrounding it, constitutes either a consonant, a melodic, or a "Third-order" interval—except for the square of seven (49) and its two rectangles (35 and 63). But here the melodic interval 9:10 is excluded, as are most consonances except for 3:4. Therefore, it is accidental with respect to the order of numbers and the structure of this diagram.

In vain will the arithmetician seek causes here; in vain will the follower of Pythagoras be occupied with the superstition of the number seven, as if it were a **counting number** <note>original: "numeri numerantis"; Kepler is distinguishing between pure abstract numbers and numbers applied to reality</note>. The matter must be traced back more deeply to Geometry, and to **numbered and figured numbers** <note>original: "Numeris numeratis & figuratis"; numbers that correspond to physical shapes</note>, namely from the very **indemonstrable figures** themselves, the first of which is the **heptagon** <note>original: "septangulum"; a seven-sided figure</note>. For what prevents this diagram from being continued beyond ten is no longer the number seven, but other numbers related to indemonstrable figures—9 and 11—which produce the product 99. This, when compared with the square of ten (100), constitutes an interval utterly abhorrent to the nature of song. So great is the difference between **axioms of opinion** and **axioms of knowledge** <note>original: "Axiomata doxastica & epistemonica"; Kepler distinguishes between Pythagorean numerology and his own geometric proofs</note>.

# The order of melodic intervals in perfection, and their names.

Thus far we have spoken of the origin and order of intervals that are smaller than consonances. We must now also speak of their differences and their names, which we cannot retain as exactly the same as those used by the ancients, since we have had to depart from them both in the matters themselves and in their causes.

It is therefore consistent with what was said above—especially with Axiom II—that any of these intervals belonging to the nature of a melodic interval should retain the nature of those consonances from which it is constituted. Since, therefore, among those consonances smaller than a **double interval** <note>The octave (2:1)</note>, the most perfect are 2:3 <note>The perfect fifth</note> and 3:4 <note>The perfect fourth</note>...

He introduces a new classification system for melodic intervals based on the consonances that form them.</summary>

Let us therefore call this interval by the name common among the ancients, the **TONE**, and because of this excellence, the "perfect Tone," but because of the size of its proportion, the "Major Tone."

Conversely, if you compare the larger perfect interval 2:3 <note>the perfect fifth</note> with the larger imperfect interval 3:5 <note>the major sixth</note> above, or if you compare the smaller of the perfects 3:4 <note>the perfect fourth</note> with the smaller of the imperfects 5:6 <note>the minor third</note> below, there will be born from this union a less perfect melodic interval, 9:10, which is smaller than 8:9. Since this interval was hardly

<margin>Minor tone.</margin>

<image-desc>A musical staff snippet showing two notes (A and B). Above the notes are the numbers 9 and 10, the symbol "O", and a square bracket. This represents the 9:10 ratio of the Minor Tone.</image-desc> noticed in ancient music before Ptolemy—for the theorists used to demonstrate everything through the full tones defined earlier—we shall give it the name **Minor or Small Tone**, so that this may be a mark of its imperfection. At this point, let the reader be warned in a word that some others have given that name to a different interval; this is so that if he should happen to read them, he will not be confused by a lack of attention.

But if you have associated the larger perfect 2:3 with the smaller imperfect 5:8 <note>the minor sixth</note> above, or the smaller perfect 3:4 with the larger imperfect 4:5 <note>the major third</note> below; the melodic interval arising from the comparison, namely 15:16, again draws something of imperfection from this origin of its own, and it shall be called a **semitone**,

<margin>Semitone.</margin>

Some have repeatedly called this the "Minor Tone," against whom the reader should be on his guard, lest he be confused.

Therefore, these three intervals derived from the perfect harmonies, compared either with each other or with the imperfect ones, shall have obtained this quality: that they are melodic in themselves and always.

On the other hand, if you have compared the imperfect intervals with each other (those derived from the Pentagon or the Decagon), either the upper 3:5 with 5:8, or the lower 4:5 with 5:6; the interval arising from this, namely 24:25, is of such great imper-

<margin>Diesis.</margin>

<image-desc>A musical staff snippet with three notes: G, a sharped/flatted note, and A. Above them are the numbers 24 and 25, the symbol "O", and a square bracket. This represents the 24:25 ratio of the Diesis.</image-desc> fection that it almost ceases to be among the melodic intervals. This interval we shall call the **Diesis**, using the ancient word <note>Greek: δίεσις</note> as if to say, a "loosening of the string." I do not strive to propose the same quantity for the interval under this word as the ancients did, which it suffices to have mentioned again. There are three causes for its imperfection: its origin; its smallness (since it does not equal even a third part of a perfect tone); and because it is also numbered among the "Third-order" intervals mentioned above—those which serve the specialized tuning of different musical scales—for it also arises from the comparison of a minor tone and a semitone. For this interval is not melodic in itself, nor always; for the human voice is not accustomed to move through this interval in one and the same **musical progression** <note>original: "αγωγή" (agoge)</note> as it does through other intervals. Instead, the voice neglects and skips over it, except only in the variation of a song, for the sake of "seasoning": then it becomes extraordinarily melodic, but in such a way that it starts almost a new type of song. It is a matter of skill and no small labor to achieve this with the human voice without the aid of an organ. Therefore, this interval only serves to distinguish the different types of melodic intervals, and in that way it serves them.

He emphasizes that while the first three are naturally melodic, the Diesis is so small that it is mostly used as a "seasoning" or to transition between musical genres.</summary>

# On Harmonics, Book III.

<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>
We began to speak about intervals of the third type; for the first of these, 24:25 or the *diesis* <term>diesis: the smallest interval in ancient Greek music, often representing a quarter-tone or a small semitone</term>, was also the last of the melodic intervals <term>concinna: intervals that are pleasing to the ear and suitable for use in a melody</term>. The names of the remaining ones now follow. For the ratio 128:135, which arises from [the difference between] 15:16 and 8:9, can be called the "major and irregular diesis"; as was said a little above <image-desc>A small horizontal diagram consisting of two pairs of boxes stacked vertically. The left boxes contain diagonal crosses (X) with dots in the triangular segments, while the right boxes are empty.</image-desc> <margin>Major Diesis or Limma.</margin> (namely in the quantity of 2025:2048), it is smaller than the melodic interval of a semitone and can hardly be distinguished from it by the ear. It is included among the melodic intervals under this name because it takes the place of a "legitimate" diesis, especially in the changing of a song <note>original: "mutatione cantus"</note>. For its origin is not so much natural as it is necessary for practical use, so that semitones and dieses may be available everywhere for the various seasonings of a song. For this reason, since a "legitimate" semitone is cut away from a Major Tone, leaving this interval as a remainder, we can also call it by the Greek word *Limma* <note>original: "Limma"</note> or "Remainder" <note>original: "Residuum"</note>.

<margin>Comma</margin>
Finally, the difference occurring between the melodic intervals 8:9 and 9:10, which is 80:81, can be called by us a **Comma**, or in Latin a "segment" or "cutting" <note>original: "segmentum seu concisio"</note>. For the ancients used to cut their *diesis* into four parts, and they called those "commas," believing this to be the common element of all harmonies. However, this interval is a little larger than a fourth part of our *diesis*, and smaller than a third part. For 24:25 is [the same as] 72:75 or 96:100. Therefore, a third part would be 74:75, and a fourth part roughly 96:97; the ratio 80:81 falls between the two. With a closer number, we could define it as the eighth part of a Major Tone (8:9). This is also clear here: here the Major Tone (8:9) is divided into a diesis (72:75), a semitone (75:80), and a comma (80:81). But since a comma <image-desc>A numerical diagram showing ratios: 75 . 15 . 25 above a line, and 80 . 16 below it.</image-desc> [associated with] 8:9 was just now about a third part of a diesis, therefore about four commas equal half a Tone, and eight equal a whole Tone—at least approximately, not in every way. This interval, therefore, is clearly not among those melodic intervals that are sung in succession, because its smallness is hardly perceptible to the ear, let alone expressible by the human voice on its own as two distinct pitches.

<margin>Double Semitone.</margin>
But it does not for that reason cease to be considered melodic, like 11:12 and similar ratios, because we also compare those which are distant in place and time. A "Double Semitone" must be established because, in the division of tones arranged in sequence, two semitones are sometimes placed one after another; those who affect variety and novelty <note>original: "insolentiam"</note> to express grave emotions of the mind sometimes use these fused into one in place of a tone.

<margin>Double Comma.</margin>
<margin>Triple Comma.</margin>
<margin>Diminished Diesis.</margin>
<margin>Platonic Limma.</margin>
<margin>Augmented Semitone.</margin>
<margin>Plato’s Apotome.</margin>
Note that between the semitone 15:16 and the *diesis* 24:25 there is [the ratio] 125:128, which is almost 42:43, or a "double comma." If you add the Comma 80:81 to this, it becomes 625:648, almost 27:28, or a "triple comma." Truly, the same 80:81 taken away from the diesis 24:25 leaves 243:250, which is very close to 35:36 <note>this is the diminished diesis mentioned in the margin</note>. The same comma taken away from the semitone 15:16 leaves the "Platonic Limma" 243:256, which is almost 19:20; but added to 15:16 it makes 25:27, which is between 12:13 and 13:14 <note>this is the augmented semitone mentioned in the margin</note>. In this way, two Major Tones (8:9) added together make 64:81; by taking this interval away from the fourth (3:4), Plato established his *Limma*. With this 243:256 (the *limma*) taken away from the Major Tone, there remained for Plato the ratio 2048:2187, which he called the *Apotome* <note>original: "Apotomen"</note>; it is larger than our *limma* 128:135 by exactly one comma (80:81), and it exceeds the semitone 15:16 by only a very small amount.

Although these are unusual intervals, some of them will be mentioned below in Book V.

# CHAPTER V.
## On the natural division of consonant intervals into melodic intervals, and the names arising from this.

What melodic intervals <term>concinna: musical intervals that are pleasing to the ear and suitable for use in a melody, as opposed to purely mathematical ones</term> were—that is, those observable to human ears in the performance of a song and imitable by the voice of a singer—was discussed in the preceding chapter. Now, we must investigate with singular care into which melodic intervals each of the consonants is naturally dissolved, with Nature as our guide.

Therefore, taking up again those same numbers through which all the natural harmonic divisions of a single string were placed into one view: it will appear to us that the interval between the numbers 75 and 100, with 80 and 90 placed in between, has split into these three melodic intervals: the semitone 75:80 (or 15:16), the Major Tone 80:90 (that is, 8:9), and the Minor Tone 90:100 (that is, 9:10).

<image-desc>A horizontal line diagram representing musical intervals and numerical proportions. Above the line, curved brackets indicate specific ratios: 15 to 16 (Semitone), 9 to 8 (Major Tone), and 10 to 9 (Minor Tone). Below these are the base numbers 75, 80, 90, and 100. A large bracket spanning the entire length from 75 to 100 is labeled with the ratio 3 to 4 (a Fourth). A musical G-clef and fraction-like notation appear to the left.</image-desc>

The same thing also occurs with the interval between the numbers 72 and 96 when the same 80 and 90 are placed between them. For 72:80 is a 9:10 Minor Tone; 80:90, as above, is an 8:9 Major Tone; and finally, 90:96 is a 15:16 Semitone. In both cases, however, between the outer limits—both 75 to 100 and 72 to 96—an interval of 3:4 <note>original: "intervallum 3. 4."</note> is found.

<image-desc>A second line diagram showing the same 3:4 total span (a Fourth) but divided differently. Above the line, the ratios are 9 to 10 (Minor Tone), 9 to 8 (Major Tone), and 15 to 16 (Semitone). Below the line, the points are marked 72, 80, 90, and 96. Musical clefs (a C-clef and G-clef) and notation symbols appear to the left.</image-desc>

Therefore, since Nature has taught us to fit these numbers together because of the division of the circle through demonstrable figures: Nature has thus divided two sesquitertial intervals <term>sesquitertia: the ratio 4:3, where the larger number contains the smaller once plus one-third of it</term>, situated in a certain position between the two boundaries of a double proportion <note>original: "proportionis duplæ"; the 2:1 ratio or octave</note>, by the very act of the divisions, into three perfect melodic intervals: the Major Tone, the Minor Tone, and the Semitone. Furthermore, for three contiguous intervals, there must be four locations, or voices, or strings.

<margin>The Fourth or Diatessaron</margin>
Hence, this 4:3 interval began to be called the **Fourth**—understand this as the "fourth voice" from the first, whether moving to a higher or lower note. For the same reason, the Greeks call this interval *Diatessaron* <note>original: "Διὰ τεσσάρων", meaning "through four"</note>, which we also express in Latin letters, writing it in the customary way as **Diatessaron**.

<margin>The Fifth or Diapente</margin>
It follows, then, that because the 3:2 interval <note>original: "intervallum sesquialterum"</note> adds one full Major Tone (since the difference between 2:3 and 3:4 was 8:9), for this very reason it is called the **Fifth**, or, in imitation of the Greek pronunciation, **Diapente** <note>original: "Diapente", from the Greek meaning "through five"</note>. This is despite the fact that 3:2 intervals are not actually divided into that many melodic intervals by our harmonic divisions; for that reason, one number necessary for this full division is still lacking to us. God the Creator himself expressed this deficiency even in the motions of the planets, as we shall hear in Book Five.

Furthermore, because in this way both 5:8 and 3:5 add to the 3:2 ratio...

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS

### CHAPTER V
## On the natural division of consonant intervals into melodic intervals, and the names arising from this.

The ratio 2:3 <note>the Fifth</note>, when combined with one of the elements already mentioned—either the semitone 15:16 or the minor tone 9:10—results in what are called the Sixths; the former combination produces the Major Sixth, and the latter the Minor Sixth.

<image-desc>Three musical staves arranged horizontally. The first is titled 'Diapente' (The Fifth) with the ratio 2:3 and numbers 60, 72, 80, 90. The second is 'Diatessaron' (The Fourth) with the ratio 3:4 and numbers 72, 80, 90, 96. The third is 'Dia hex' (The Sixth) with the ratio 5:3 and numbers 60, 72, 80, 90, 96, 120.</image-desc>

Conversely, because both the 4:5 <note>Major Third</note> and the 5:6 <note>Minor Third</note> subtract from the <term>sesquitertia: the 4:3 ratio, or the musical Fourth</term> one of the elements mentioned—the former subtracting the semitone 15:16 and the latter the minor tone 9:10, as shown in the preceding chapter—there remain for them only two melodic elements. For the Major Third, these are the Major and Minor Tones; for the Minor Third, these are the Major Tone and the semitone.

<margin>
What the Major and Minor Thirds are.
</margin>

For this reason, some call these intervals by the Greek word <term>Ditonos: literally 'two tones,' referring to the Major Third</term>, major and minor, or the "semi-ditone." Since these two intervals require three terms or notes to be expressed, they are called the Major and Minor Thirds. Of these intervals established by the natural divisions of a string, the others are actually divided in this way, but the highest and lowest are not yet actually divided.

<margin>
Galileo uses the word "Ditonos" to signify something else from the oldest music <note>referring to Pythagorean tuning</note>, which differs from the Major Third consonant. See Chapter XII.
</margin>

<image-desc>Four musical staff diagrams showing intervals. Top left: ratio 4:5 (Major Third). Bottom left: ratio 5:6 (Minor Third). Top right: ratio 5:8 (Minor Sixth). Bottom right: ratio 3:5 (Major Sixth). Brackets show how the notes 60, 72, 80, 90, 100, and 120 relate to these spans.</image-desc>

<margin>
The origin of the terms Third or Sixth, "Hard" and "Soft."
</margin>

Since the harmonics 3:5 and 4:5 <note>the Major Sixth and Major Third</note> are derived from the Pentagon, whose side is "ineffable" <note>irrational in relation to the diameter</note>, and the ratios 5:8 and 5:6 also share something of this Pentagonal nature, it follows that both pairs are considered imperfect consonances. Whichever is the "minor" interval sounds softer and more pleasant to the ears. The "minor" quality exists in the 5:6 and 5:8 ratios because they divide the whole circle, or a "perfect" figure (namely the Hexagon, whose side is of a rational length), into parts of a continually doubling proportion (which is identical to itself), specifically into 6 and 8. Therefore, 5:8 and 5:6 are held to be the **Soft** Sixth and Third; whereas 3:5 and 4:5 are the **Hard** or "harsh" Sixth and Third, and they are so named.

<margin>What the eighth or Diapason is.</margin>
It follows, therefore, that the last note in the counting of the sequence is the eighth in number. And from this, the interval obtained the name of the "Octave." The Greeks, looking to the identity of its consonance, call it **Diapason** <note>original: "Διὰ πασῶν," meaning "through all"</note>; it is written in Latin letters as *Diapason*, as if, once all the different sounding notes have been exhausted, the singer’s voice returns to its starting point on the eighth sound. From there, a new beginning and a new series of <term>Melodic Intervals: "concinnorum," meaning intervals suitable for melody</term> arises, similar in all respects to the first: see Proposition I.

<image-desc>A musical staff with three sections of notes. The first section is labeled "The Fifth" (Diapente), showing a five-note interval. The second is labeled "The Fourth" (Diatessaron) showing a four-note interval. The third is labeled "System of the Octave" (Systemadiapason) showing an eight-note scale spanning the full octave.</image-desc>

In vain do people philosophize about the Number here—namely, why the eighth voice exhausts all the others and returns to the same sound. For the true answer must be given by "begging the question" <note>Kepler suggests the answer is inherent in the definition</note>: because nature dictates that the interval of the double proportion (2:1), which by Chapter I is <term>Identifonum: sounding the same, or unisons in different registers</term>, is divided into seven melodic intervals, which are determined by eight sounds, as has been proven in this chapter. They <margin>What is a System?</margin> think this happens because the number 8 is the first Cube and the first "Tessera" <note>a square or solid block</note>. But what does the division of a musical string have to do with solid shapes? And why does the twenty-seventh voice (which is the second cube, 3x3x3) not also return to the same sound?

For this reason, the name **System** <note>from the Greek "systema," a standing together</note> properly and primarily applies to the interval of the double proportion (the octave), divided into its seven melodic steps, described by its eight voices or strings, and expressed on instruments: concerning which, see Chapter IX below.

<margin>The Double Octave.</margin>
In those intervals that exceed the Octave or *Diapason*, specifically the multiples of the Octave, the double octave is usually called **Disdiapason** in Greek <note>original: "Δὶς διὰ πασῶν"</note>; the triple is called *Trisdiapason*, and so on. In others, the *Diapason* (or its multiple) is expressed and the excess is added, in this manner: "the Fifth above the octave," or "the Octave above the Fifth," the *Diapason epidiapente*, or **The Fifth upon the Diapason** <note>original: "Διὰ πέντε ἐπὶ διὰ πασῶν"</note>. Sometimes we also continue by number, calling them the Ninth, Tenth, Twelfth, etc.

This division of consonant intervals into melodic ones is natural. This quantity and the number of melodic elements is no greater than three <note>referring to the three types of melodic steps: the major tone, minor tone, and semitone</note>. It does not rely solely on the ears becoming accustomed to it; rather, the hearing possesses this by a natural instinct. No other intervals besides these, nor any other number of them, can be taken as melodic steps into which any of the consonances may be divided. For if you wished, for example, to add the <term>Diesis: a very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</term>, firstly, that is the offspring of dissonant melodic intervals; secondly, even if you specifically wanted to add it because it is an "offspring" of consonances, you could not do so alone. It would drag with it the *Limma* or "minor semitone," which arises only from dissonances. But it is fitting for the hearing to distinguish that from the offspring of consonances; while admitting the latter during singing and among the secondary intervals, the ear rejects the former as if it were spurious.

->Therefore, the Diesis shall not be among the principal intervals of the Octave.<-

ON HARMONY, BOOK III.

# CHAPTER VI.
## On the types of song, the Hard and the Soft.

**Regarding** the types of figures, it was spoken of in Book I, Proposition 49. Since the sections of the string itself also imitate these figures (according to Axiom II of this book), it follows that because the section of the continuous double proportion <note>original: "continuè duplæ," referring to the 1:2 ratio of the octave</note>, the Trigonal section <note>Derived from the triangle</note>, and its continuous double are from figures with expressible sides—at least the primary ones, the Triangle and the Quadrilateral—the Pentatonic section, however, is made from an inexpressible side <note>Kepler refers to the "inexpressible" or irrational proportions, like the Golden Ratio, found in the pentagon</note>. Therefore, those [first] sections, according to Axiom IV, produce one genus of song, while the latter produces another genus. To this latter genus, the bisection <note>The division of the string into two equal parts</note> is also added—not because of the Tetragonal <note>Square</note> figure, but solely because of the identical consonance of the bisection itself.

From this, two Genera of sections are born; one indeed has these sections:

->ON PROPORTIONS<-

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
These are those two commonly celebrated types of Song; the first is called the **Soft Song** <note>original: "cantus mollis," the ancestor of the minor key</note>, because in it are found intervals arranged from the lowest voice—the Third and Sixth—which are **Soft** <term>mollis: minor</term>; the latter is called the **Hard Song** <note>original: "cantus durus," the ancestor of the major key</note>, from intervals of the same name <note>the major third and major sixth</note> arranged in the same place in the octave system, the reason for these names was given in the preceding Chapter V.

For just as in that previous case, the 5:6 ratio <note>the minor third</note> in the lowest position did not allow for a 3:5 <note>the major sixth</note>, so now here the 4:5 ratio <note>the major third</note> does not allow for a 5:8 <note>the minor sixth</note>. This is because the nature of a harmonious song requires that a third combined with a sixth makes a perfect fourth, or *diatessaron* <term>diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth, with a ratio of 3:4</term>.

From this, therefore, the natural boundary of each type appears. For since in the Soft Song the 5:6 is in the lowest position, and in the Hard Song the 4:5 is there, and the difference between the two—namely the *diesis* 24:25—does not arise from standard harmonious intervals (according to Chapter IV), they cannot stand together in the same natural song series in the lowest position: the 4:5 and 5:6. But if the major third 4:5 is assumed, it must on that occasion exile the 5:6 from the lowest position; or if the latter is received, the former is pushed out. In this arrangement, the 4:5 pulls with it the 3:5 <note>the major sixth</note>, and the 5:6 pulls with it the 5:8 <note>the minor sixth</note>.

Moreover, God himself expressed this distinction of both types of harmony in the motions of the planets, as we shall hear in Book V.

Concerning those three Genera of the Ancients, whose names are **Diatonic**, **Chromatic**, and **Enharmonic**, I deliberately refrain from speaking here, lest I confuse the reader. You might, however, interpret the **Diatonic** as the **Hard Song**, the **Chromatic** as the **Soft Song**, or perhaps the **Diatonic** as the individual types while the **Chromatic** is a mixture of Hard and Soft. The **Enharmonic**, however, has nothing corresponding to it in natural song; in practical Music, the vibrations of the human voice, the tremolo of Organs, the *mordents* <note>ornamental rapid alternations between notes</note> on the strings of the lute <note>original: "panduræ," a long-necked lute</note>, and similar things correspond to it to some extent.

<margin>There the reader will find nothing.</margin>
See what we discuss concerning these Genera below in the Appendix to the text of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist whose work *Harmonics* deeply influenced Kepler</note>.

# CHAPTER VII.
## On the complete division of one Octave
### in both types of song, and on the natural order
### of all harmonious intervals.

Therefore, thus far Nature herself has shown that in the **Soft Song**, the third harmonious interval from the bottom is the **Minor Tone** 9:10, the fourth is the **Major Tone** 8:9, and the fifth is the **semitone** 15:16. In the **Hard Song**, however, the third from the bottom is 15:16, the fourth is 8:9, and the fifth is 9:10.

There remain in both types of Song two pairs of thirds, one minor and one major, which have not yet been actually divided into the smallest harmonious elements by the natural sections of the string.

First let us see into which harmonious elements those can be divided, then in what order each should be placed.

Nature teaches enough, if we can divide those into the same elements of which we have seen them consist so far, with nature showing the way, the Diatessa- <meta>catchword: Diatessa-</meta>

# BOOK III. ON HARMONICS.

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
...the consonances of the fourth <term>diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth, with a ratio of 3:4</term>; we ought not to use others whose examples nature does not demonstrate. Arithmetic teaches us, therefore, that the ratio 4:5 <note>the major third</note> consists of 8:9 <note>a major tone</note> and 9:10 <note>a minor tone</note>; likewise, 5:6 <note>the minor third</note> consists of 8:9 and 15:16 <note>a semitone</note>. Behold the same elegant proportions as before.

But if you do not arrange the **Major Tone** <term>Major Tone: the larger of the two whole-step intervals, with a ratio of 8:9</term> in the lowest position of each lower third, it will be impossible to have a single shared string <note>meaning a single fixed pitch for a note</note> in both types of song. For if in the **soft song** <note>original: "cantus mollis," the minor mode</note> you could not place the major tone in the lowest position, it would be necessary to place the semitone 15:16 there instead, because only these two intervals exist within the undivided 5:6 ratio. Conversely, in the **hard song** <note>original: "cantus durus," the major mode</note>, the **Minor Tone** <term>Minor Tone: the smaller whole-step interval, with a ratio of 9:10</term> would have to be placed in the lowest position, because that undivided consonance—the major third (4:5)—does not contain the semitone that would have been placed at the bottom in the soft song. Thus, there would be two different strings: the longer one forming a semitone with the lowest note for the soft song, and the other forming a <insert>lowest</insert> major tone for the hard song.

Secondly, it is added that it seems consistent with nature that, wherever we have a free choice in dividing a section, the larger intervals should gravitate toward the deeper <note>grave</note> sounds, because the deep sounds themselves are "smaller" <note>in terms of frequency or tension, though produced by longer strings</note> than the high <note>acute</note> ones.

By the same primary reasoning, we shall also prove that the upper third (undivided until now) must be divided so that the major tone is in the highest position, lest the seventh string <note>the seventh note of the scale</note> becomes doubled. For in the soft song, the upper interval is 4:5, and in the hard song it is 5:6, according to the natural method handed down in the previous sections. Therefore, if we were to arrange the perfect tone (the other element of the Third) in the lower position of this upper Third, then the same interval rising from notes of different heights would also reach notes of different heights, making two notes where there should be one. These reasons are demonstrative and clearly necessary; they suffice against the authorities of Ptolemy, Zarlino, and Galilei <note>Kepler is citing the famous theorists Claudius Ptolemy, Gioseffo Zarlino, and Vincenzo Galilei, mother of the astronomer Galileo</note>, who place the minor tone in the lowest position of the octave.

Therefore, the eight strings are explained by these numbers, reduced to the same lowest common denominator.

You see expressed here in the smallest possible numbers not only the proportions of all eight lengths, but also those of the four highest and four lowest notes in even smaller numbers. Most importantly, you see the three highest and three lowest notes, regarding which I have a dispute with other authors in this chapter concerning their "middle" values and their corresponding numbers. For the 7th position in both types of song is 405, and the 2nd position is 640 in both.

Remember, however, that only the eight principal strings of each type of song are placed in this chapter. Regarding the "accessory" strings—one of which the Hard Song adopts near the very top—we shall examine them in the following chapter. For our goal here is to see how the penultimate and second-to-last strings should be established so that they can be the same in both types of song.

Because these eight principal strings of both songs are joined together, it happens that two of them are doubled on musical instruments. Therefore, in the common system, there are ten principal strings in one <term>octave: the interval of an eighth, or "diapason"</term>, though no more than eight "Positions" are recognized (and are so named). See the origin of this term in Chapter IV. **

# CHAPTER VIII.

## On the number and order of the smallest
## intervals of one Octave.

The lowest and highest intervals, as well as the fourth, are by nature (or by the imitation of nature) made into **Major Tones** <note>ratio 8:9</note>. From these, again by the imitation of nature—which cuts a **Minor Tone** <note>ratio 9:10</note> into a semitone and a diesis—the **semitones** 15:16 are likewise cut away for the sake of greater variety, especially in the turnings or windings of a song; this occurs in the upper part of the interval. There remain, therefore, in the lower part, **Limmata** <term>Limma: a "leftover" interval, here defined as a major diesis</term>, or **Major Dieses** with a ratio of 128:135, which exceeds the **diesis** <note>ratio 24:25</note> by one **comma** <term>Comma: the tiny mathematical difference between two nearly identical intervals, such as 80:81</term>.

These are Greek terms for the ratio 4:3, or a Perfect Fourth.</note> 3 to 4 with the fourth (namely 405 with 540 from the previous chapter), so also this extraordinary seventh loves to make a perfect fifth <note>original: "diapente perfectum," the ratio 2:3.</note> or 2 to 3 with the third. CHAPTER VIII.
The Lack of Scientific Method among Organists.

You see that in two places, two semitones meet below the diesis <note>A diesis is a very small musical interval, specifically the difference between a major and minor semitone in just intonation.</note>, which is what we said would happen above. And the craftsmen seize upon this in organs, and they use two semitones for a whole tone whenever they set up some unusual modulation. Although, according to the principles of their craft, they temper <term>Temperament</term> <note>The practice of slightly adjusting the tuning of intervals so they sound acceptable in all keys, rather than having some perfectly pure and others completely unusable.</note> all the intervals so that they leave none pure; rather, they adjust and soften the imperfection of the others so that the intervals that ought to have been perfect suffer the least loss of perfection. By this method, it happens that all whole tones are equal for organists, and the limma <note>A "limma" is a small semitone (roughly 256:243).</note> is also equal to the semitone, and thus two semitones make a whole tone for them by an exact bisection. So that this may succeed more easily, not even the diesis retains its proven mathematical perfection among them.

## A Quick Division of the Monochord for the Lute, and its Rejection by the Sense of Hearing.

This place requires that I fulfill what I promised above toward the end of the second chapter: namely, that I compare the division of the Monochord for the Lute <note>original: "Teſtudinariam," referring to the lute, which was traditionally compared to a tortoise shell (testudo).</note>—brought forward by Vincenzo Galilei <note>An influential Italian lutenist and the father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note>, if I am not mistaken, following the theories of Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher who argued that music should be judged by the ear rather than by strict mathematical ratios.</note>—with my own findings. I shall also question the ears concerning it, though in such a way that Reason may speak what it would be natural for the ears themselves to say.

Since the Octave <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> consists of seven harmonious intervals, from which it takes the name "OCTAVE," as was said in the previous chapter; among these intervals are five whole tones and two semitones. Since any of these tones can be bisected into parts closest to a semitone, so that twelve intervals are created as defined in this chapter—represented by the letters G, G♯, A, B♭, c, c♯, d, d♯, e, f, f♯, g—taking this opportunity, instrumental musicians themselves established twelve intervals within one Octave. They did this not by a laborious path, but by one entirely easy and quick, as is proper for most mechanical tasks. The method is as follows: The entire length of the neck of the lute, between the two bridges <note>original: "Ephippia" or "magadia," the nuts or bridges that mark the ends of the vibrating string.</note> upon which the string rests and obtains its free vibration, they divide into 18 equal parts. And they place the first fret <term>Fret</term> <note>original: "ligaturam ſeu Tactum." These are the gut strings tied around a lute's neck to mark where the fingers press.</note> starting from the tuning pegs <note>original: "Verticillis"</note> so that 1 part is above and 17 parts are below. Then, having cleared the division points, they divide these remaining 17 parts again into another 18, and cut off one part with a second fret as before, and they repeat this twelve times. With the twelfth cut, they say such a portion of the string remains that there is an Octave consonance between it and the whole. Suppose, then, the length of the string is 100,000. If 18 parts make 100,000, what is 17? The result is 94,444. Again, if 18 are worth 94,444, what is 17? The result is 89,198. And if 18 are worth 89,198, what is 17? The result is 84,242, and so on. In this way, twelve numbers are produced for the same number of intervals, alongside which are placed the numbers required by the true ratio demonstrated thus far, within the total quantity of the string.

If this ratio were exact, then surely the proportion repeated twelve times would be equal to the double proportion <note>The ratio 1:2, which defines an octave.</note> between 1 and 2. However, good mathematicians know this to be false, since 1:2 and 17:18 are incommensurable. This...

<meta>The text cuts off here, continuing the mathematical proof of why the "Rule of 18" for lute fretting is an approximation rather than a perfect geometric division.</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
Nevertheless, the mechanical division of the string satisfies the hearing well enough; this is because the individual numbers approach the true ones placed beside them, and because the strings of lutes <note>original: "chelyum," referring to the lute or lyre family</note> are flexible, and their sounds are in a certain way varied: they are sharper in the beginning when their motion is still great, having just been released by the finger; and they are deeper and more relaxed when the width of the vibration is narrowed into a small space as the string returns to itself. Furthermore, there is a difference between a lighter or stronger touch, and in a more extended or restricted plucking, according to the skill of the Musician.

But if you examine the judgment of the hearing with the skillful investigation of Reason, the disagreement <term>dissensus</term> will immediately appear; which I prove in this way: The ears certainly recognize the harmony between 100,000 and 50,363, as the Craftsman <note>original: "Mechanicus," referring to practitioners like Galilei who used mechanical/approximate divisions</note> asserts; they also recognize the same harmony between 100,000 and 50,000, as I assert. The question is: do the ears notice no difference at all, and does this harmony possess such a wide range of latitude? I answer, based on my harmonic divisions in Chapter II, that it does not.

<column-break/>

For just as they discern nothing between two <term>Consonances</term> <note>intervals that sound stable and pleasant together</note>—namely, between the strings of 100,000 and 50,000, and the strings of 100,000 and 50,363—in the same way they will not discern between the two consonances of 100,000 to 50,000 and 100,000 to 49,637; because the difference between the two consonances is equal in both directions.

But if it is not against the whole 100,000 that this or that part is struck, but the parts themselves—here 50,363 and there 49,637—are struck against each other, then it is absolutely necessary that the shorter part emit a higher sound and the longer part a deeper one. This difference of sounds is easily detected by the ears in an examination of <term>unison</term> <note>notes that are supposed to be the same pitch</note> parts. It is clear, therefore, that the ears judge it to be the same consonance between 50,363 and 100,000 as between 49,637 and 100,000 for no other reason than that 50,363 and 49,637 appear to be equal; that is, they do not differ sensibly from 50,000. Therefore, if the ears respond according to the questions of Reason, they will say that the exact Harmony lies between 100,000 and 50,000—that is, in the ratio of 2 to 1. Wherefore it is false that there is an exact Consonance between 100,000 and 50,363.

The same judgment applies to the Harmony between 100,000 and 67,025; for although at first the ears do not discern it from 66,667 (the correct length of the truly consonant part), yet the remainder of that, 32,975, is not half of 67,025 itself. Therefore, the double of that, 65,950, will sound one way, and 67,025 will sound another, since these strings make a different sound when compared to each other. Therefore, the fact that the ears do not discern these in Harmony happens because they approve the middle number—if the sense is sharpened by reason—namely 66,667, so that its complement is 33,333, which is exactly half of it.

Having now established the sharpness of the sense in judging the Harmony of 2 to 3, and likewise...

G
<meta>catchword: and likewise...</meta>

<summary>Kepler compares Vincenzo Galilei's practical, equal-tempered string divisions with his own "true" geometric ratios, arguing that while the ear might tolerate slight inaccuracies in lute tuning due to the physical properties of strings, Reason proves that only perfect mathematical ratios create true harmony.</summary>
<keywords>equal temperament, Vincenzo Galilei, monochord division, lute tuning, consonance, harmonic ratios, auditory perception vs reason</keywords>

...and likewise from 1 to 3, it follows that we should judge similarly regarding 2 and 3 with 5, and regarding 1 and 3 with 4. For if 59,785 <note>This value represents the note 'E' in Galilei’s system, as seen in the table on the previous page.</note> were to sound with 100,000, and thus the remainder were 40,215, this is certainly not a *bes* <note>original: "bes"; a Latin term for the fraction two-thirds (2/3), here referring to a specific harmonic ratio</note> of that number. However, the consonance of the *Bes* <term>Major Sixth (5:3 ratio)</term> has already been justified as perfect: namely, 60,000 with 40,000. In this way, the sense of hearing—if sharpened by reason—is transferred from one division to another, beginning from the unison (the recognition and judgment of which is easiest) until it pervades them all, approving the parts which my numbers signify and rejecting those "Mechanical" ones of the first order.

See another very clever temperament of this kind in the work of Vincenzo Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (1520–1591), father of Galileo Galilei, was a music theorist who advocated for equal temperament on fretted instruments</note>. It was produced not from an ignorance of the demonstration of the quantity of sounds, but from singular study. And indeed, I acknowledge its mechanical use, so that we may use instruments with almost the same freedom of tension as is found in the human voice; but for the sake of theory—indeed, for discerning the very Nature of song—I consider it destructive. It causes the Organ to never truly attain the nobility <note>original: "ingenuitatem," meaning naturalness or frankness</note> of human singing.

# CHAPTER IX.
## Concerning the Diagram—that is, the modern notation of strings or voices by lines, letters of the Alphabet, and Notes—and concerning the System.

<margin>Lines</margin>
This matter is not without dispute, but I follow necessary reasons. Musicians of our age depict the strings <note>the notes of the scale</note> differently in Lute diagrams than in singing diagrams. In the former, the individual lines of the diagram denote individual strings, each of which provides different sounds for different touches if they are plucked. In the printed singing diagrams <note>the musical staff</note>, not only do individual lines signify individual voices or strings, but the very intervals <note>spaces</note> between two lines also signify an intermediate string.

<margin>Strings</margin>
In this way, 4 transverse lines with 3 spaces denote 7 strings, and 5 lines with 4 spaces denote nine strings. Next, they express the voices of the singing System either by specific Notes placed in their proper location on the diagram (which notes simultaneously suggest the measure of time), or by the first seven letters of the alphabet, or finally by six syllables: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. Or, as the Belgians do today, by these seven: *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni* <note>A system of solmization known as "Bebization," used in the late 16th and 17th centuries.</note>.

<image-desc>A technical musical diagram showing the relationship between lines and chords (notes). Four horizontal lines are drawn. To the right, Roman numerals label the positions: I is the space below the first line, II is the first line, III is the space between the first and second line, IV is the second line, V is the space between the second and third line, VI is the third line, VII is the space between the third and fourth line, VIII is the fourth line, and IX is the space above the fourth line. On the left, brackets and text distinguish between "Lineæ" (the four horizontal lines) and "Chordæ" (all nine positions including spaces).</image-desc>

<margin>Notes</margin>
Because there are two kinds of song, "hard" and "soft" <term>cantus durus and cantus mollis</term> <note>These terms roughly correspond to the modern concepts of Major and Minor, though they specifically refer to the use of B-natural (durus) versus B-flat (mollis) in the hexachord system.</note>, which start from one common lowest voice, the difference is this: the third and the sixth in "hard" song are one diesis <term>semitone</term> higher than in "soft" song. Therefore, the strings for the third and sixth cannot remain stable in both kinds of song; they must either be made as pairs on instruments and organs (as was done in the numbers in Chapter VII) or be varied by touch, as I believe was done of old on the lyre and the pan-pipes <note>original: "syringibus"</note>. The same things must be said regarding the Diagram and the human voice. For since only one diagram is made for the octaves of both kinds rising from the same root, and in it there are only eight places for eight sounds...

It happens that two sounds, separated by a *Diesis* <term>a very small interval, smaller than a semitone</term> or a *Limma* <term>a "leftover" interval, often a minor semitone</term>, are depicted in the same place on the diagram, whether that be on a line or in the space between lines. This is because *dieses* and *limmata* are not sung in succession like Tones and semitones; for which reason I have also refused, unlike some others, to call them "minor semitones." For this reason, certain Marks had to be prefixed to the lines and intervals—the images of the strings—by which "hard" song <note>original: "cantus durus"; music using B-natural, often associated with the hexachord starting on G</note> could be distinguished from "soft" <note>original: "molli"; music using B-flat, associated with the hexachord starting on F</note>, and by which the location of the semitone would be clear, whether it be the ordinary one or those others cut away from the major tones. There is also another more hidden necessity, arising not from the diversity of the Genera, but within any song whatever, from the inequality of the major and minor Tones; so that they may be distinguished against each other in the diagrams. For the syllables *Ut, Re, Mi* <note>The traditional solfège syllables used to learn and sing scales</note> must be general and applicable to both the major and the minor Tone. Therefore, however much these names satisfy those learning to sing and practical organists, they by no means satisfy the Theorists. On account of this function, these letters, when they are prefixed to the Diagrams, are usually called *Keys* <note>original: "Claves"; Kepler is playing on the double meaning of "clef" (notation) and "key" (instrument)</note>, because without them, the entrance into the diagram does not lie open to the singer.

Indeed, these same letters are also employed in musical organs; for they are inscribed on the handles of the plectra in stringed instruments, or on the stops <note>original: "Epistomiorum"</note> in wind instruments. From this inscription, those handles are called "Keys" <note>original: "Claves"</note> in their own right, and the order itself, or the System of all the handles, is called the Keyboard <note>original: "Clavarium", and the German "das Clavier"</note>, and the type of instrument is the *Clavichord*; because the strings are struck by "keys" <note>original: "clavibus"</note>—that is, by handles depressed from the outside and by plectra jumping up from within.

Furthermore, there are diagrams usually written for Organists, in which, instead of black lines, there are series of letters indicating which Keys ought to be touched: here letters stand for the Notes which the singing-diagrams used to place on lines or in intervals.

Concerning these letters, some things come to our observation which are quite pleasing. First, not all letters are placed upon their own lines and intervals, but only these: *F, G, C*, whenever the place for one of them is on a line; and *B* as well, even when it takes its place in an interval.

Next, the letter *C* has a sign far different [from the letter itself], such as the one depicted here at the side. However, so that the horns would be bounded, they drew small lines parallel to the first one, like this: <image-desc>A vertical line with two shorter horizontal bars</image-desc>. When, however, there is no place for the letter *C* on a line (because in the past there were usually only four lines), then the place is for the letter *F* on one of the lines. This is written in other higher voices with its own natural note-mark, but in the Bass with a curved semicircle and two dots nearby. For Vincenzo Galilei <note>an influential Italian music theorist and father of Galileo Galilei</note> provides evidence that this method of marking the sounds of the System through the letters of the Alphabet flowed down from the Greeks, by bringing forth very ancient examples of Greek songs. Then, on every black Key is inscribed the letter of the neighboring Key, but with a tail added for distinction (except for $\text{\hslash}$, in whose place a simple $b$ is placed on the black key). But between d-flat <gloss>e</gloss> and d-sharp <gloss>d</gloss> <note>Kepler uses superscript letters to indicate accidentals: 'e' for flat (soft) and 'd' for sharp (hard/durum)</note> e, there is a semitone; so that these two letters, although the same, are not actually assigned to the same place, but to the succeeding ones. However, a Diesis <term>a very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone</term> exists between d-flat <gloss>e</gloss> and e-sharp <gloss>d</gloss>, and these different letters fall into the same place: a diversity which must be granted to ancient custom and softened by practical use. Therefore, caution must be applied here, lest we presume anything about the identity of the interval based on some analogy from the same style of writing.

That which is also particularly strange, and similarly to be forgiven as an ancient custom, is that in some Clavichords and organs (in which the octaves are continued), although the same letters are deservedly repeated because of the identity of the Octave <term>original: "Diapason"</term> resonance, this does not start from the first letter *A*, but from the second, *b*. For here is the order of the characters: *C. D. E. F. G. A. b. c. d. e. f. g. a. bb. cc. dd. ee. ff. gg. aa. bbb. ccc. ddd. eee. fff. ggg. aaa.* etc.

<margin>
The System.
</margin>
Furthermore, what the diagram is on paper, the System is in the organ; specifically, the System is the series of all the strings dividing a single consonant interval. As was said in Chapter V, this primarily suits the interval of the octave, and from that, all larger intervals that any instrument may encompass.

<margin>
Ancient names of the strings.
</margin>
Even though it is not my purpose to dwell much on the music of the ancients, since it is full of obscurity, I nevertheless decided that the names by which they designated those eight sounds in the System of a single octave should not be passed over; for that naming has a kinship with the letters we have dealt with so far.

Thus, the ancients in the time of Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher who wrote extensively on music and acoustics</note> numbered the strings as follows: *Hypate, Parhypate, Lichanos, Mese, Paramese, Trite, Paranete, Nete*. The voice of the *Hypate* was the lowest, and it seems to have been named so from its position on the instrument when held taut and applied for playing; for it still occupies that same position today on the Lyre <note>original: "Chely"</note>, the Lute <note>original: "Pandura"</note>, and the Cittern <note>original: "Cythara"</note>.

And since Aristotle affirms that there was a diesis between the *Hypate* and the *Parhypate* (this is the Platonic semitone which, when two major tones are subtracted from a Fourth <term>original: "Diatessaron"</term>, leaves 243:256, which he called a Diesis): Therefore, the *Hypate* was the same as what we mark with the letter *A*. The *Parhypate*, that which he marks with the letter *b*. Therefore, the *Lichanos* (so named from the index finger) is *c*. The *Mese* <note>meaning "Middle"</note> is indeed *d*: and it was called by this name because it was the middle among seven, at the time when there were only seven strings on the Psaltery, and the first was struck for the eighth. The *Paramese* has the letter d-flat <gloss>e</gloss> or e; the older Greeks used to omit this. The *Trite* has the letter *f*; it is so called because it was third in order from the high end, just as we call it the sixth from the low *A*. The *Paranete* is marked with the letter *g*. And the *Nete*, as if it were the last to be touched by the plectrum drawn downward, returns to the letter *a*. This distribution is also confirmed by the fact that a Fifth <term>original: "Diapente"</term> is said to have existed between the *Nete* and the *Mese*.

However, such a System of eight strings could not serve both types of singing unless either the *Parhypate* were shortened by the touch of a finger...

# ON PROPORTIONS

CHAPTER IX.
Which pitches <note>original: "phthongi"</note> were stable to the ancients, and which were movable?
</margin>

...b. and paramese d-sharp/e-flat <gloss>de</gloss>, so that they might be created, that is, either tightened by tuning pegs <note>original: "verticillis"</note> for a "hard" song <note>original: "duro... cantu"</note>, or loosened for a "soft" song. On this occasion, the distinction was born between stable and movable pitches, and even the name "Diesis" <term>a very small interval</term>, which comes from the loosening <note>original: "remissione"</note> of the movable strings.

<margin>
Proslambanomenos <term>the lowest note in the ancient Greek scale, literally the "added note"</term>.
</margin>

In the arrangement of multiple Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> systems, the method of the ancients was rather intricate. One must observe, however, that they added one note lower than the *Hypate* <note>the lowest note of the traditional Greek tetrachord</note> itself, which for this very reason was called the *Proslambanomenos*. A trace of this remains in the Musical Scale that our children learn, which adds a note below the Latin letter *A*; it signifies a lower sound and is marked out of the ordinary by the Greek letter *Gamma* (Γ). For the scale begins thus: *Gammut, A-re*, and so on.

Let it suffice to have touched upon the ancient names of the strings in this place. For below in Chapter XI, all fifteen strings of the composite system will be explained using ancient terms, but according to the later musicians.

Now at last, let us approach our "Natural System" of a single Octave, and apply the letters used in common Music to it.

<margin>
The natural system begins from G.
</margin>

I establish, therefore, that the lowest voice of this natural and demonstrative system is that which the ancients called the *Proslambanomenos* and the musical scale usually calls *Gammut*; to this, the letter G must certainly be assigned. The reasons are these: because the voices established through harmonic sections determine such intervals within the octave—relative to the sound of the whole string—as musicians ordinarily establish between G and b-flat, b-natural, c, d, d-sharp/e-flat, and e.

Someone might say that the same intervals could be understood between D and F, F-sharp, G, A, b-flat, and b-natural; or even between c and d-sharp/e-flat, e, f, g, g-sharp, and a. I do not deny that instrumental musicians <note>original: "Musici organicos"</note> use these letters generally, and do not distinguish between the Major (8:9) and Minor (9:10) tones. For what is to stop them from transposing a song from G to D? On their organs, they take the two Tones—the Major (8 to 9) and the Minor (9 to 10)—conflated into a single interval (4 to 5) <note>Kepler refers to the Major Third</note>, and afterward precisely bisect them into two "common" tones that are equal to each other. Although Galileo <note>Vincenzo Galilei, father of the astronomer, who wrote on music theory</note> is more accurate in this comparison. We, however, look here not at the lack of skill <note>original: "atechnian"</note> of the Empiricists, but at the precision <note>original: "akribeian"</note> of Nature; therefore, we cannot imitate them.

As for the letter C, they themselves might reject it as the starting point of the natural octave system by this argument: for between their g and a is a Semitone; and this interval is in the fifth place, because a is the sixth from c. But in the Natural System, we need a Diesis before the sixth. Instrumentalists themselves place the Diesis only between b-flat and b-natural, and between d-sharp and e. Therefore, even by the assent of the instrumentalists, our system must arise from either D or G so that a purely natural system is expressed.

Yet the natural system cannot begin from D either. For it is their custom to place a Semitone between d and d-sharp/e-flat; but in my Natural System, the first interval is a Limma <term>a small ancient semitone</term>, which is less than a Semitone.

<meta>This page follows Chapter IX, where Kepler explained the ancient "stable" and "movable" notes and the origin of the "Gamma-ut" scale. BOOK III OF THE HARMONICS.

# CHAPTER X.
## On Tetrachords and the use of syllables,
## Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. <note>The syllable "Ut" was the original name for the note we now call "Do."</note>

It was common practice for the ancients to divide the system of the octave <note>original: "Systema octavae"</note> into two tetrachords <term>a scale of four notes spanning the interval of a fourth</term>, and they did so in different ways according to the various intentions of the musicians. For they were either "joined" <note>original Greek: *synemmena*</note>, with one sound placed in the middle which produced a fourth <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> both with the lowest note below it and with the highest note above it. In this way, the outer notes produced a dissonant interval, a "dis-seventh" <note>original: "Diheptà"</note>, and one whole tone was understood to be added above them. For whenever the order required the sounding of the octave **a**, they would strike the first **A**, which produced an identical sound from the opposite side, an antiphonal <note>original Greek: *antiphōnon*, meaning "sounding in response"</note> note. In this arrangement, there were not truly two tetrachords, but rather two intervals of a fourth forming a single seven-stringed scale <note>original: "Heptachordum"</note>. Or, the tetrachords were "separated" <note>original Greek: *diezeugmena*</note> by the interval of one major whole tone. This is what the very nature of things suggests even in our own division of the system, in which the lower tetrachord contains **G, A, B, C** and the upper contains **D, E, F-sharp, G**, where a major tone exists between **C** and **D**. Perhaps even by their physical position, the four lowest strings were separated from the four higher ones, leaving a larger gap between the two boundary strings.

<image-desc>A musical staff showing two types of tetrachord structures. On the left, "Conjunct Tetrachords" (joined by a shared middle note). On the right, "Disjunct Tetrachords" (separated by a whole tone gap).</image-desc>

The reason they thought in terms of a tetrachord system was because they saw that in a single consonant fourth <note>original: "diateſſaron"</note>, there were two and a half tones. We also have a major tone, a minor tone, and a semitone in a perfect fourth—all the fitting elements in a minor concord (for they did not even consider the ratios 4:5 and 5:6 to be concords). Thus, the semitone could be placed at the very bottom, in the middle, or at the top. Therefore, every song seemed to them to be comprised of these three forms of tetrachords.

<margin>Three types of tetrachord.</margin>

<image-desc>A musical staff presenting three variations of tetrachordal patterns based on the placement of the semitone: "Tone, Tone, Semitone," "Tone, Semitone, Tone," and "Semitone, Tone, Tone."</image-desc>

<margin>
The use of syllables.
A short line marks a medium-sized minor tone; a slightly longer line marks a major tone.
</margin>

For me, the forms of tetrachords are multiplied because of the distinction between the minor and major tones; for instead of three, there become six, and in a single octave <note>original: "Diapaso"</note> most are doubled. Thus, we also have a certain testimony from Nature for distinguishing the tetrachords, for the upper is in some way [different] from the lower—

<image-desc>A set of six musical examples labeled I to VI. Each shows a four-note tetrachord with horizontal lines of different lengths above the notes to indicate the specific interval types: a tick for a semitone, a medium line for a minor tone, and a long line for a major tone. Example I: G-A-B-C; II: A-B-C-D; III: B-C-D-E; IV: C-D-E-F; V: D-E-F-G; VI: E-F-G-A.</image-desc>

And these are only the forms of the perfect fourth <note>original: "diateſſaron"</note>; regarding the imperfect ones we shall treat in Chapter XII.

But if we ignore the difference between the major and minor tone, as the instrumentalists <term>original: "Organici," referring to those who play fixed-pitch instruments like the organ</term> do, then these subsequent disjointed tetrachords <note>original: "Tetrachorda diſjuncta"</note> are entirely similar.

| | |
|:---|:---|
| G A b c | & d e f g |

| ->These lowest<- | ->& these highest.<- |

On both sides the semitone is in the same place, either at the highest or middle point; the only difference is that the semitone is one comma <term>a tiny interval representing the difference between a major and minor tone</term> higher in the lower tetrachord than in the upper; this difference is not greatly perceived during singing.

<margin>Transposition.</margin>

Therefore, the transposition <note>original: "Transpoſitio"</note> of a song from key to key, common among musicians, is supported by this similarity of tetrachords; it is all the more convenient because the instrumentalists have removed the distinction between major and minor tones and other such things. <note>Kepler is referring to the move toward temperament, where the small mathematical differences between intervals are averaged out for keyboard instruments.</note>

<margin>The use of the syllables Ut, Re, Mi, fa, Sol, la.</margin>

Again, this similarity of tetrachords and their triple variety gave birth, in more recent music, to those six syllables *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*: by which the memory of students is aided. Because if only a single octave were sung, composed of two similar tetrachords, we could be content with only four syllables, *ut, re, mi, fa*, while ignoring the distinction between major and minor tones.

But because there are three possible positions for the semitone in a tetrachord, so that these syllables would not be too general, but rather that the semitone would always be denoted by *Mi Fa* or *Fa Mi*: it was necessary for two other syllables to be added. Thus, in these [*Ut, re, mi, fa*] the semitone would be in the highest place; in these [*Re, mi, fa, sol*] the semitone would be in the middle place; and finally, in these [*Mi, fa, sol, la*] the semitone would be in the lowest place. And this is the reason why they used six syllables discov—

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
...inventors of Music, not eight. And so, let that Belgian <note>likely referring to Hubert Waelrant (c. 1517–1595), who proposed a seven-syllable system called "Bebization"</note> see what profit he gains from this increase, who made seven syllables instead of six—*bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni*. For if he judged that syllables ought to be used in a number equal to the strings of one octave, minus one; why, I ask, does he miss the letters *a. b. c. d. e. f. g.* which have long since been accepted for this purpose?

<margin>Mutation of the song.</margin>
Since, therefore, the six syllables were born in this way on account of the triple form of the tetrachord <term>a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</term>: from there was born the doctrine of Mutations <note>the practice of changing between hexachords to reach different pitches</note> through the modern musical scale. This doctrine is occupied solely with these syllables, which are to be fitted to the letters explained above. It shows that the redundant syllables *sol* and *la* are sometimes equivalent to the first syllables *ut* and *re*, and sometimes to the succeeding ones *re* and *mi*, so that occasionally, out of the usual order and without a formal mutation, *fa* can be introduced after *sol* or *la*. <gloss>ut re mi fa mi</gloss>

-> 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 6. <-
-> *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, fa, la,* <-
-> *Ut, re, mi, ut, re, mi, fa, mi* <-

<image-desc>A musical staff containing two sequences of notes. The first sequence follows the syllables 'ut re mi fa sol la fa la' and the second 'ut re mi fa mi'. The notation uses the square neumes common in the 17th century.</image-desc>

There is, however, another kind of "dissimilar similarity" of tetrachords, which is the foundation for the assimilation of different melodies harmonizing among themselves, which they are accustomed to call Fugues and Fantasias <note>early forms of imitative polyphony where one voice follows another</note>. For if you take contiguous tetrachords, separated by no interval from each other, just as a major tone remains to fill the octave above or below: in certain systems of the octave there will occur on both sides the same series of elementary intervals—that is, of Semitones, Diesis <term>a very small interval, often a quarter-tone in ancient theory</term>, and Limmas <term>a "leftover" interval, slightly smaller than a semitone</term>. To one tetrachord a major tone is added, so that instead of a fourth <note>original: "quartâ"</note> a fifth <note>original: "quinta"</note> is produced, somewhat similar to the other fourth; and two melodies—the first earlier in time, running through the interval of a fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> above, and the other later in time, running through the interval of a fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> below—the latter follows the former and, as far as is permitted, imitates its pattern as if it were its rival.

<image-desc>A complex structural chart of intervals. On the left, it is labeled 'Family of Tetrachords'. It lists the 'Semito.' (Semitone), 'Limma', 'Tonus adjunctus' (Added tone), 'Diesis', 'Semitonium', 'T. major' (Major tone), and 'T. minor' (Minor tone). These are grouped into 'Superioris' (Higher) and 'Inferioris' (Lower) categories to show how a fifth and a fourth are constructed to mirror one another.</image-desc>

# CHAPTER XI.
## On the composition of Systems.

Although the voice of a single human is usually turned within the system of a single octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>, the harmony of several melodies nevertheless teaches us to arrange several contiguous octaves. Therefore, the Ancients, defining all things by the properties of numbers, defined the "perfect system" as the octave-plus-fifth <note>original: "Diapason epidiapente"</note> by the numbers 1, 2, 3. For us, the individual harmonic sections above have each given back individual systems, the greatest of which was the double-octave-plus-major-sixth <note>original: "Disdiapason-epidiapente," here using a 1:5:6 ratio</note>, represented by the numbers 1, 5, 6. Although for our Composers, as they are called, the limit...

# CHAPTER XII.
## Concerning Adulterated Consonances.

From the continuation of two octaves <term>diapason: the interval of an octave</term>, imperfect consonances result. For in the joining of both, two major tones <note>A major tone is a whole step with a ratio of 9:8</note> follow in succession between *f-g* and *g-a*. Thus, in the interval *f-a*, the ratio is 64:81, which is one comma <note>A comma is a tiny musical interval, specifically the syntonic comma (81:80), which is the difference between a pure major third and four perfect fifths</note> greater than a true major third (which is 4:5 or 64:80). Following Galileo <note>Likely referring to Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), a lutenist and music theorist who famously challenged traditional Pythagorean tuning</note>, we call this a <term>ditone: an interval consisting of two major tones</term>.

<margin>Ditone.</margin>
<image-desc>A musical diagram showing two staves with notes for F, A, and the octave F. Numerical values are aligned above the notes: 64 above the first F, 81 above the A, and 128 above the upper F. A bracket connects the 64 and 81 markings and is labeled as a Ditonus. Mathematical symbols are placed next to the notes.</image-desc>

The same interval exists between *e* and *g-sharp* <note>Original: "ge"</note>, because there is the same semitone interval on both sides: between *e-f* and between *g-sharp-a* <note>Original: "ge. a"</note>.

Thus, between *f* and *b-flat* <note>Original: "bb"</note>, if a semitone is added to the excessive ditone *f-a*, it creates the interval 60:81 (or 20:27). This is one comma (80:81) larger than a perfect fourth (3:4 or 60:80).

Judge the same for the interval *e-a*, because just as *e* is a semitone lower than *f*, so too is *a* lower than *b-flat* <note>Original: "b"</note>.

If these imperfect or "excessive" consonances are subtracted from the interval of an octave <term>diapason</term>, they leave behind imperfect remainders that are deficient by one comma. For in the span of an octave from *a* to the *f* above <note>Original: "aff"</note>, the ratio will be 81:128, which is a deficient minor sixth <note>Original: "sextâ mollis," literally "soft sixth"</note>.

The same occurs between *g-sharp* and *e* if you subtract the interval *e-g-sharp* from the octave.

Likewise, in the octave between *b-flat* and the *f* above <note>Original: "bb ff"</note>, after subtracting the imperfect fourth *f-b-flat* (20:27) from the octave, there remains a diminished fifth of 27:40 (which is the same as 81:120).

The same happens between *a* and the *e* above <note>Original: "a ee"</note>, when the interval *e-a* is subtracted from the octave.

<image-desc>A musical diagram consisting of a single staff with notes marked for F, C, and the octave F. Above the staff, numerical values 160, 243, and 320 are aligned with the notes. Brackets indicate the ratios between 160 to 243, and 243 to 320.</image-desc>

Furthermore, when the excessive ditone *f-a* is added to the minor third *a-c* (5:6), it produces the ratio 160:243. This is a fifth <term>diapente: the interval of a fifth</term> that is excessive by one comma. For 160:240 is a perfect 2:3 ratio, and 240:243 is the comma 80:81. <gloss>From which if you take away, etc. See page 233, Proposition 43.</gloss>

And when this excessive fifth *f-c* <note>Original: "f cc"</note> is removed from the interval of an octave, there remains the fourth *c-f* (243:320), which is deficient by one comma.

### Table of the Six Imperfect Consonances.

| | |
|----------|----------|
| For 5:6 | 27:32 (deficient) |
| For 4:5 | 64:81 (excessive) | |
| For 3:4 | 60:81 (excessive) or 20:27 | & 243:320 (deficient) |
| For 5:8 | 81:128 (deficient) | |
| For 2:3 | 81:120 (deficient) or 27:40 | & 160:243 (excessive) |

Nor, however, is there a need for the semitone or <term>Platonic Limma: a small interval (256:243) used in Pythagorean tuning to represent a semitone</term> of 243:256. Plato called this a "limma" for a different reason than I do. For when two major tones (the ditone 64:81) are removed from the interval of a fourth (3:4), he was left with this "Limma" (243:256) in place of a semitone. But I have no need for this subtraction; rather, for me, the 3:4 interval is increased, becoming 20:27.

H

### CHAPTER XIV.
## What constitutes a Naturally Harmonious and Fitting Song.

We shall say nothing of that shrill manner of singing which the Turks and Hungarians are accustomed to use for their battle signals <note>original: "classico suo," referring to a trumpet call or war-cry</note>; they imitate the unformed voices of brute animals rather than human nature.

It seems altogether likely that the first author of such unformed melody derived it from an ill-suited instrument, and through long habit, along with the construction of the instrument itself, transmitted it to posterity and the entire nation. I was present in Prague at the prayers which the priest of the Turkish Legation used to chant at fixed hours, kneeling down and frequently striking the ground with his forehead. It was easily apparent that he sang from training, and that he had acquired skill and readiness through labor, for he never hesitated; yet he used strange, unusual, clipped, and discordant intervals, such that no one, guided by their own nature and of their own accord, would seem able to consistently devise anything similar. I shall attempt to express something close to it using our musical notation.

<image-desc>A line of musical notation depicting a single melody. It features unusual accidentals, including cross-like symbols (asterisks) and flats, used to transcribe the "strident" Turkish melody mentioned in the text.</image-desc>

A harmonious song <note>original: "Concinnus," meaning well-put-together or elegant</note>, therefore, and one fitting in the judgment of human ears, is one which, having begun from a certain sound, proceeds from it through harmonious intervals toward sounds consonant both with the first one and, for the most part, with each other. It skims over dissonant intervals but dwells upon consonant ones, whether by the measure of time and the length of syllables, or by frequent return to them, as if striving for the consonance of two voices with each other by the transition of a single voice from one place in the system to another. For example:

<image-desc>Musical notation for the sequence "Victimae paschali laudes" using square neumes on a four-line staff. The Latin text is printed below the music.</image-desc>

> Let Christians offer praises to the Easter Victim <note>original: "Victimæ paschali laudes immolent Christiani"</note>. The Lamb has redeemed the sheep; the innocent Christ has reconciled sinners to the Father.

<margin>This initial sound is in the key of G, with which b-flat, c, d, and g agree in the soft song <term>soft song: "cantus mollis," the hexachord system that uses B-flat</term>.</margin>
The song therefore runs (first making a downward turn) to the consonant key of *c*, and skips over the clearly dissonant position of *a*; it would have been the same if it had touched it, but only with a brief pause. However, the entire remaining series sounds most especially in the positions of *b-flat*, *d*, and *g*, expressing a kind of skeleton of the octave—returning most frequently to *d*, then to *b-flat*, and occasionally lifting itself to the higher *g*, distinctly to all these positions. It does not do so in *a* or in *f*, which are positions initially dissonant; and finally, it returns to *G* and ends there.
<image-desc>A small snippet of musical notation on a staff, positioned to the right of the paragraph text.</image-desc>

Regarding the provided definition of song, many things must be noted by us.

I. The parts of a song, from which all songs consist in whole or in part, Euclid <note>Referring to the "Introduction to Harmonics" traditionally attributed to Euclid, though now often attributed to Cleonides</note> names these four: <term>Agoge: direction or melodic motion</term>, <term>Tone: tension or pitch</term>, <term>Petteia: the choice or "gaming" of which notes to use</term>, and Interlacing—
