<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of melody, moving from the comparison of "barbaric" music to defining the specific Greek terms for melodic movement (agoge, ploke, tone, and petteia) and how they relate to the underlying harmonic structure of the octave.</meta>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin> The terms **Interweaving** <note>original: "Πλοκή" (Ploke)</note> and the others indicate by their names what they are. For **Melodic Progression** <note>original: "ἀγωγή" (Agoge)</note> is the movement of the voice from a proposed root to a place consonant with that root, or from one consonant to another consonant with it or with the first root. **Sustaining** <note>original: "τονή" (Tone)</note> is the lingering in a place, whether it be the first place or one consonant to it—or even one consonant to a previous note, though not necessarily consonant with the first. **Interweaving**, or "implication," is a certain species or "color" of Melodic Progression, just as **Variation** <note>original: "πεττεία" (Petteia)</note>, or "game-playing," is a species of Sustaining. As Melodic Progression relates to Sustaining, so Interweaving relates to Variation; for while Progression moves, as it were, directly, Interweaving wanders during the passage around the Progression, like a dog around a traveler.

Thus, Progression is like a direct movement, while Interweaving is a varied movement. Sustaining, however, is like the boundary of movement, or a rest in a sought-after place in the System; Variation consists of many boundaries of smaller movements, acting like brief rests. In our example, the syllables [*Christ redeems the sheep*] <note>original: "demit Oves Christus in," from the Easter sequence "Victimae Paschali Laudes"</note> are a certain perpetual Sustaining, with only two syllables excepted; but the syllables [*reconciled sinners*] <note>original: "cens rec li peccat"</note> express Variation. If you look at the ligatures <note>musical symbols connecting two or more notes</note> of the syllables in this song, such as [*praise, to the, father, of the*] <note>original: "laud an patr tor"</note> and consider them as two-toned, then there would be no pure or unmixed Progression in it. But if you consider that it was done in a rustic manner—so that from a sound that was meant to be sung longer, a two-toned sound was made rising at the end—and if you restore the simple long sound (which is the first note of the ligature) to these syllables, you will find pure Progression in these: [*To the Easter praises*] <note>original: "Paschali laudes"</note>, likewise [*Christians*], likewise [*The innocent to the Father*], and a brief one in [*sinners*] <note>original: "catores"</note>. Pure Interweaving, though not a natural kind, is found in the Turkish example.

Therefore, just as the skeleton relates to the body in the study of anatomy, so do the Octaves—the sounds consonant both with each other and with the root or base of the octave—relate to the melody or song itself within a single System. For just as flesh fills the hollows of the bones and clothes them for beauty, so do these reviewed parts fill the skeleton of the octave—especially Melodic Progression and Variation—wandering through the dissonant places cast between the consonant sounds, they shape and, as it were, give a body to the Melody.

II. When a song is defined as starting from a certain sound, 
<image-desc>A fragment of musical notation on a five-line staff using an alto C-clef. It contains several diamond-shaped notes (semibreves or minims) and two ligatures (connected notes), illustrating a melodic line within a specific range.</image-desc>
which serves as the basis of the System of the octave, this is not always to be understood as being the actual first note <note>original: "de actu," in actuality</note>. Since variety is pleasing and serves to add emphasis, a melody very often begins abruptly from another key or place; nevertheless, by the power of the music <note>original: "potestate," in potentiality</note>, a certain fixed beginning is understood, which shines forth from the entire course of the Melody on all sides. As in this very ancient German song, it is easily understood that even though the start is actually on D, the root is nevertheless G.

III. There is a similar exception regarding the rule that a regular song, with its Sustaining or Variation, should aim toward places consonant with the root of the Octave. For frequently these parts, in the middle of a longer stretch of melody, concern themselves with...

### ON THE BOOK OF HARMONICS, BOOK III.

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
...those places dissonant from the first root; but this is done for the sake of variety. It is exactly as if a new melody were mixed into the previous one, in which a new beginning is fixed in that dissonant note, or a new **octave skeleton** <note>Kepler uses "skeleton" to describe the essential framework of notes—the 1st, 4th, 5th, and 8th—that define a scale.</note> is marked out. It is like an excursion or a digression in a speech; therefore, we do not linger in such places, but quickly return to the principal skeleton. And as long as **Sustaining** <note>original: "tonē"</note> and **Variation** <note>original: "petteia"</note> are occupied with dissonant notes, we understand that the song is not yet finished. For at the very end, one must return not only to the consonant notes—as is regular—but to the very root of the proper octave. From this articulation of song and the striving for consonances, the ancients also seem to have called simple song "Harmony." In the same way, a decent and suitable correspondence of the limbs, which is the form of the soul, might be called harmony, as if it were "beauty"; for **Harmony** <note>Harmonia, in Greek mythology, was the daughter of Ares and Aphrodite.</note> was also a woman's name.

<margin>Leaps.</margin>
IV. Regarding **Melodic Progression** <note>original: "Agogēn"</note>, it is again varied; for it does not always actually pass through all the intervening places, but often jumps over some and is carried by a leap from one note to another consonant to it. In that case, the **progression** exists only by potential; it is almost pure **Variation** or **Sustaining**. This is the habit of our modern **Trumpeters** <note>original: "Tubicinum"</note> when they play a fanfare or a cavalry call; for then, almost nothing is heard except the skeleton of the octave. Consider whether the ancient **"Upright Strain"** <note>original: "Nomos orthios," an ancient Greek musical style known for being high-pitched and stirring.</note> was of this kind.

V. Since a **Fitting** <note>original: "Concinnus"; often translated as "concinnous," meaning musically suitable or melodic.</note> song consists of its own Elements, which are fitting intervals, those must first be defined more accurately.

<margin>How many ways intervals are unfitting.</margin>
For intervals are called "fitting" or "unfitting" in two senses. First, individual intervals are called fitting or unfitting separately, with respect to their origin. The fitting ones are those which nature admits in the divisions of consonant intervals; the unfitting ones are those that do not result from the comparison of Consonances and are entirely foreign to Harmonics, as explained in Chapter IV. Secondly, with respect to the Song or Melody itself, there is this distinction even among Musical (or sensibly fitting) intervals: certain of them, when considered together, though they are naturally fitting (having arisen from the comparison and abstraction of harmonies), are nevertheless rejected by Melodies in a certain respect as being unfitting in use. **Sustaining** and **Variation** presuppose and look toward the first sense; but **Melodic Progression** (both actual and jumping) looks chiefly toward the latter. Therefore, these become unfitting for two reasons: either with respect to the **Genre** or the skeleton of the Octave (because they are simply not used in it or do not form it), or if they are arranged in an order other than what nature taught in Chapter VII. For example, if someone wanted to arrange three semitones in a row: a semitone is indeed fitting in the first sense, but this order of semitones is not fitting in this second sense. Likewise, a **Diesis** <note>A very small interval, smaller than a semitone.</note>, while naturally fitting, is nonetheless unfitting when considered separately in either the "Hard" or "Soft" genre of song; or finally, they are not sung in succession, nor are they allowed for a leap of the melodic voice, nor are they suitable for **Melodic Progression**.

<summary>Kepler explains how melodies can deviate into dissonant "digressions" but must return to the octave's structural "skeleton" to feel complete. He also distinguishes between intervals that are theoretically harmonious and those that are practically "fitting" for use in a melody.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the rules of melodic composition. Having established that some notes are used only for variety, the author now lists specific technical "laws" or prohibitions for melodic intervals that were considered "unfitting" (inconcinna) in the musical practice of the time.</meta>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
Therefore, in this second sense, there are **unfitting** <term>inconcinna; intervals that do not sound harmonious or pleasing when sung in sequence</term> and forbidden intervals, comprised by these as the principal laws.

I. A **diesis** <note>original: "diesis"; a very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone, often associated with a sharp or flat</note> is not regularly sung before or after a semitone.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a sequence of notes with sharps (diesis) and natural/flat signs, illustrating the prohibited interval described in the text.</image-desc>

II. Although two semitones may be arranged in succession in the order of the smallest intervals discussed in Chapter VII, they cannot be sung successively across three sounds; instead, they must coalesce with two other elements into two whole tones.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff illustrating a sequence of semitones with accidentals.</image-desc>

III. Two semitones within the compass of a single fourth or fifth—placed thus in the lower part of the **skeleton of the octave** <note>The structural "frame" of a scale, usually the 1st, 4th, 5th, and 8th notes.</note>—are not ordinarily sung.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff illustrating intervals of two semitones within the structure of a fourth or fifth.</image-desc>

For the result would be that the voice would not harmonize with the first note, neither perfectly nor imperfectly; therefore, it would not truly be a fourth or a fifth.

IV. Four whole tones are not sung in a row, except in the highest part of the Octave, when the skeleton is changed for the sake of **color** <note>The use of chromaticism or melodic variety to add "flavor" to a piece.</note> and variety; therefore, this is not done ordinarily.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a sequence of notes with the labels "T. T. Tō. Tō." written underneath, indicating four consecutive tones.</image-desc>

V. The seventh and all dissonances above the octave are not ordinarily sung using sounds arranged in succession after the root note; unless the preceding note has, in a way, the character of an ending, and the following note the character of a new beginning.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing various melodic intervals exceeding an octave.</image-desc>

VI. Even though they are consonant, we admit **sixths** more rarely, and only the minor ones.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing examples of minor sixth intervals.</image-desc>

->They have passed over me.<-
<note>original: "In me transierunt." This is a reference to Psalm 88:16 ("Thy terrors have cut me off"), a text often set to mournful music using minor intervals.</note>

VII. Two **tetrachords** <note>A scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note> within one octave are more rarely sung if the semitone is not located in the same relative position in both; this is done for the sake of color or **Syncopations** <note>Shifting the rhythmic accent so that a note begins on a weak beat and lasts through a strong beat.</note> (which are discussed in Chapter XVI). However, there is no mere freedom in placing the semitone, for it is restricted to that place which the **Type of Song** <note>original: "Genus Cantus"; referring to the specific musical mode or scale structure being used.</note> admits.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff divided into two sections, each illustrating different tetrachord arrangements within an octave.</image-desc>

VIII. Related to this is the rule that three whole tones in a row are not sung in the lower part of the octave; yet they are admitted in the upper part by the laws already stated.

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a melodic sequence of three consecutive tones.</image-desc>

IX. Two semitones do not naturally melt together into one whole tone, although the difference is small to the ear. For example, if the octave begins from E, the interval between C and D would result in a ratio of 225:256 from the composition, which is naturally unfitting (see Chapter IV).

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff illustrating complex chromatic intervals that do not naturally resolve into single tones.</image-desc>

X. In general, every system of an **Octave** is **unfitting** <term>inconcinnum; lacking proper musical proportion or pleasing sequence</term> if it does not establish both a **fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> and a **fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> within its structure.
<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
<image-desc>A small musical staff with a C-clef on the middle line. It shows two intervals in white mensural notation: a perfect fifth from middle C to the G above, and a perfect fourth from that G to the high C.</image-desc>

Most of these laws will serve us now in establishing the number of **Tones** <term>Toni; here referring to the musical modes or scales used in composition</term> in the following chapter.

<margin>On Measures.</margin>
VI. Regarding that part of the definition which states: "*skimming quickly through dissonances, lingering on consonances*": although it is not my purpose in this work to dispute concerning **measures** <note>original: "mensuris"; the rhythmic duration of notes</note>, I nevertheless advise in general that the chief grace of harmonic song lies in its measurement. For what was said very generally—*skimming through dissonances*, etc.—is made true in this specific way. First, the Latins have a distinction between long and short syllables, of which they make the latter one **unit of time** <note>original: "Temporum"</note> and the former two times, and thus of double length.

<margin>In Prose.</margin>
Although today not only poems but also prose is sung, in which modern musicians completely neglect the distinction between long and short syllables, they look solely to the custom of pronunciation, even though it is corrupted today. Whatever syllable is usually uttered with an **acute accent** <note>a stressed or higher-pitched syllable</note> is held as a long syllable, and whatever has a **grave accent** <note>an unstressed or lower-pitched syllable</note> is held as short.

It is no wonder this happens in the Latin language, since the later Greeks did the same. Although they wrote in a pure style, they embraced a most flawed pronunciation in which there is no longer any distinction between an acute accent and syllable length, or a grave accent and brevity, even though they abound in signs for this purpose which are not in such frequent use among the Latins.

<margin>Greek Political Verses.</margin>
Therefore, the Greeks, having abolished the old custom of composing verse, began several centuries ago to write so-called **Political Verses** <note>original: "versus Politici"; a form of medieval Greek poetry based on word stress rather than the classical length of vowels</note>. In these, syllables are counted but not measured by duration; the verse maintains its stress on the second-to-last syllable, not because it is long by nature, but because it is sharpened by accent in popular speech. Our musicians imitate this even in Latin.

<margin>In Meters.</margin>
They do this to such an extent that they do not spare even poems, except very rarely, and never entirely. I believe this is because a perpetual double and triple rhythm is accepted in songs, while poems mix these rhythms unequally—except for the **Hexameter** <note>the standard meter of epic poetry, such as Virgil’s Aeneid</note>, which is content with the proportion of equality in the **spondee** <note>two long beats</note> and the perfect double in the **dactyl** <note>one long and two short beats</note>. Therefore, musicians assign a short syllable (or one in the place of a short, such as when a spondee follows an iamb), and in general any syllable to be uttered with an accent, to a **dissonant sound** if it must be passed through quickly, but a long syllable to **consonances**, or things similar to them.

<margin>In modern Meters.</margin>
Second, the **vernacular languages** <note>original: "lingue Ionice"; Kepler refers to the Western European languages</note> which use **Rhythm**—namely German, French, Spanish, and Italian—make either the last syllable of a poem "sharp" or the second to last. They deliver the whole verse as if alternating sharp or grave syllables follow one another in turn, whether this is suitable (as in a proper German verse) or not (as is frequent in French). Therefore, every one of their verses is either like a **Trochee** <note>a stressed beat followed by an unstressed one</note> or an **Iamb** <note>an unstressed beat followed by a stressed one</note>. These are either **acatalectic** <note>having a complete final foot</note>, such as "*Creator of Heaven and Earth*" <note>original German: "Schöpffer Himmels und der Erden"</note> or "*Now we pray to the Holy Spirit*" <note>original German: "Nun bitten wir den Heyligen Geiſt"</note>, or **catalectic** <note>missing a final syllable</note>, such as "*At which all the world wonders*" <note>original German: "Deß ſich wundert alle Welt"</note> or "*He is the Morning Star*" <note>original German: "Er iſt der Morgenſterne"</note>. Thus, musicians fix the seat of dissonant sounds on the "grave" or shortened syllables, and consonances on the "sharp" ones.

<margin>In the Beat.</margin>
Third, when a song receives its measure not from the syllables of the text but from the **Beat** <note>original: "Tactu"; the physical motion of the hand marking time</note>, and it follows either a double or triple proportion, they reserve the first part of the beat for consonances. The later part—which in a triple proportion is shorter and signified by the raising of the hand—is reserved primarily for dissonances.

# CHAPTER XIV.
## On the Modes of Melodies, which
## they call Tones.

As I am about to speak of modes, I first advise modern musicians that regarding those things they are accustomed to calling **Modes**—namely, the double or triple proportion of the beat and the like (the sort of "Modes" perhaps once played on pipes in the comedies of the Romans)—I will have nothing further to say beyond what has already been mentioned. By "Modes," I mean those which they, along with the ancients, are accustomed to calling **Tones** <term>Toni</term>, as when it is asked which Tone a song belongs to. For there are certain qualities or species of melodic song, set apart from one another by the two highest differences of **Genders** <term>Genera</term>: the **Hard** <note>original: "Duri"; corresponding roughly to the major quality</note> and the **Soft** <note>original: "Mollis"; corresponding to the minor quality</note>.

The Greeks called them **Tropes** <note>original: "Τρόπους"</note> and **Ethoi** <note>original: "ἤθη"</note>; the former name comes from the form of the system, the latter from the **effect** of the song upon a person, because many legislators believed that the Modes of songs served to shape **character** <term>Mores</term>.

Regarding the number and distinctions of these Tones, there are not only great controversies among musicians today, but there were already in ancient times: some of these can be seen in **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist whose "Harmonics" heavily influenced Kepler</note>, and many in **Vincenzo Galilei** <note>A 16th-century Italian theorist and the father of Galileo Galilei</note>. It is not my purpose to examine or refute everyone's opinions; therefore, the musician should expect nothing else from me on this question than that single conclusion to which my principles, explained thus far, lead me. For although the "Tones" seem to be named from the fact that one Mode begins either higher or lower than another by the interval of a single **Tone** (or semitone), I myself do not distinguish Tones by the pitch or depth of the song itself—which Vincenzo Galilei testifies was the only thing some observed—but instead, following Ptolemy, I define their number according to the number of species of a single **Octave** <term>Diapason</term>. 

I say that there are just as many Tones as there can be legitimate and **consonant** <term>concinna; pleasingly proportioned</term> "skeletons" <note>Kepler uses the word "sceleta" to refer to the basic structural framework of a scale</note> of the Octave system, differing among themselves in their **Genders**, the **order of melodic intervals**, and the **position of the tetrachords** <term>tetrachordum; a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</term>—or the choice of the two harmonic means. Indeed, there are three things that vary the Tones and distinguish them from one another: the **Gender**, the **sequence of melodic intervals**, and the **articulation of the skeleton** from the smaller consonances.

First, the two **Genders** established in Chapter VI for the division of the Octave system provide us with the two primary and naturally first Tones, arising with the system of a single Octave itself. Then, in both genders of the system, both **Hard** and **Soft**, from the composition of two Octaves into one larger and **perfect system**—as we described in Chapter XI—individual Octave systems are produced, differing in their "roots" or the boundaries by which they are enclosed; these boundaries are the places of the **natural system**...

<summary>Kepler transitions from discussing rhythmic measures to defining musical Tones (modes), arguing that they should be classified by the mathematical structure of the Octave species rather than just pitch height.</summary>
<keywords>Tones, Modes, Genders, Hard and Soft, Ptolemy, Vincenzo Galilei, Octave species, Tetrachords, musical skeletons</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of musical "Tones" or modes from the previous page. Kepler is moving from the general definition of modes (based on character and "Genders" like Hard and Soft) to the technical construction of these scales relative to a "Natural" system and the mathematical placement of intervals.</meta>

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS.

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin>
...various natural systems, or in today’s vocabulary, different **Keys** <note>original: "Claves"</note>, which necessarily result in a different pitch relative to the natural system that begins from G; and through this, a different position for the **semitone**, which is located in either the third, the second-to-last, or the very last place of the **Octave**. For as far as the pitch itself is concerned, considered in isolation, it changes nothing about the **species** <term>the specific pattern of intervals</term> of the song, since the same species can be intoned either high or low. Nor are we bound to follow **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note> in taking half of the remaining Tones lower than the principal and natural G-system, and the other half higher. For we can take either all of them higher or all of them lower, since the same **Order of Concordances** <term>the arrangement of harmonious intervals</term> follows in both cases—provided, of course, that the system of the double octave, naturally composed, begins from the key of G. But if we make some lower and some higher, as Ptolemy does, the natural system must be composed so that we add a **Fifth** <term>Diapente</term> below and a **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron</term> above; thus, the composed system of the double octave will begin from C.

<image-desc>A musical diagram featuring two musical staves enclosed in a single bracket. Each staff has five lines and contains several diamond-shaped notes (punctum) indicating a sequence of pitches, with the top staff containing four notes and the bottom staff containing three.</image-desc>

Thirdly and finally, in systems constructed in this way, there is a choice of two **Harmonic Means** <term>mathematical center points</term> toward which the **tension** <note>original Greek: "τονή" (tonē)</note> and the **completion** <note>original Greek: "τελεία" (teleia)</note> of the parts of the song aim; or, what amounts to the same thing, there is a placement of the **Tetrachord** <term>a scale of four notes spanning a fourth</term> either in the highest or lowest place of the Octave, or in the middle of two **Thirds**.

Therefore, for the sake of this diversity, we must first of all subjoin here the **Square Net** arranged from Chapter XI, consisting of twelve orders of the twelve smallest natural intervals. This is not done so that we may create just as many Tones according to their number (following **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek theorist who favored human hearing over mathematical ratios</note>), beginning each one a single such tiny interval higher; rather, it is so that when these smallest intervals are contracted into the usual concordant ones, it may appear whether any new **species of the Octave** can begin from any one of these smallest parts.

->Net of intervals in the Systems, for investigating the<-
->different species of Tones.<-

S is the Semitone.
D is the Diesis <term>a tiny interval, smaller than a semitone</term>.
L is the Limma <term>a "remainder" interval in Pythagorean tuning</term>.
</margin>

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
CHAPTER XIV.

**The Origin of 14 species of differing Octave systems.**
</margin>

You see that among the twelve distinctions of Octave pitches, there is not one that agrees with another in the order of its elements.

Let us now see how many species of Octave systems arise from this if the first difference of Octaves—which is that of **Genus** <term>the classification of scales as "Hard" (major-like) or "Soft" (minor-like)</term>—is mixed in; that is, whether the 12 smallest intervals of all 12 Orders can be harmoniously contracted into the seven usual intervals of a single Octave, distinguished by eight positions, and in how many ways each can be done.

Note here that *LS* or *SL* is the sign for a **Major Tone** <note>original: "Toni Majoris"; the interval of a 9:8 ratio</note>, *DS* or *SD* is the sign for a **Minor Tone** <note>original: "Toni Minoris"; the interval of a 10:9 ratio</note>, and *S* is the sign for a **semitone** <note>the 16:15 ratio</note>. Our descriptions will proceed from the Grave to the Acute, or from the bottom to the top.

It is certain, therefore, that in the Octave of G, two species exist due to the double placement of the semitone in either the second or third position from the bottom.

->The First, of the Soft Genus.<-
<image-desc>A five-line musical staff in bass clef showing a scale from G to G. Above the notes are the interval labels: LS. S. DS. LS. S. SD. LS. Below the first segment is an alternative: or SD. S. LS.</image-desc>

->The Second, of the Hard Genus.<-
<image-desc>A five-line musical staff in bass clef showing a scale from G up to G with sharp accidentals. Above the notes are the labels: LS. SD. S. LS. SD. SL. S. Below the first segment is an alternative: or S. LS.</image-desc>

But in G# as well as in C#, since two semitones do not compose a single harmonious interval, nor can they be sung in succession **melodically** <note>original: "ἐμμελῶς"</note>; therefore, the lowest semitone stands alone, according to laws 9 and 2 of the previous Chapter. The distribution would therefore be:
Either such as *S. SD. SL. S. SD. SL. SL.* which is unharmonious according to law 3.
Or in G# specifically, such as *S. SD. SL. SS. DS. etc.* and this is unharmonious according to law 9. Therefore, no harmonious species of the Octave begins from G#.

In the octave of A, due to the triple possible placement of the lower semitone, the elements are contracted into Tones in three ways: for it is either thus *S. DS. LS. S. DS. etc.* which coincides with what has already been rejected; or it is such that from here is born:

III. <image-desc>Musical staff in bass clef showing an A scale.</image-desc> **Third:** *S. DS. LS. SD. S. LS. LS.*

IV. <image-desc>Musical staff in bass clef showing an A scale.</image-desc> **Fourth:** *SD. S. LS. SD. S. LS. LS.*

V. <image-desc>Musical staff in bass clef showing an A scale with accidentals.</image-desc> **Fifth:** *SD. SL. S. SD. SL. SL. S.*

V. <image-desc>Musical staff in bass clef showing a scale starting on B-flat, indicated by a flat symbol on the staff.</image-desc> In the Octave of Bb <note>original: "b"</note>, there can be only a single contraction of elements, which coincides with the fifth form, nor is any other given—namely, *DS. LS. S. DS. LS. LS. S.*—because the semitone can only hold the third position from the bottom.

<margin>CHAPTER XIV. I.</margin>
<image-desc>Two musical staves showing octaves in white mensural notation. The first staff is labeled "I." and shows a scale from G to G. The second is labeled "XIV." and shows a scale from F to F. The notes are diamond-shaped.</image-desc>
<margin>XIV.</margin>

Finally, in the Octave of F <note>original: "fe"; in Kepler's notation, this likely refers to the F-scale, though "e" sometimes denotes a specific pitch quality</note> there are two possible places for the semitone: either in the penultimate seat, or in the last. If, therefore, you arrange them thus: *SL. S. SD. SL, S. SD. SL.* <note>These abbreviations represent specific musical ratios: S for semitone, SL/LS for various types of tones</note> it will be the first species, as appears from the comparison. But if arranged otherwise, it will be the fourteenth: *S. LS. SD. SL. S. SD. SL.*

The reason is therefore apparent why in the Second, Fourth, Fifth, Seventh, and Ninth orders—namely, in the Octaves of G, B-flat, B-natural, C, and D <note>original: "Gg. b. h. cc. dd."</note>—no unique species begins.

It appears secondly, that no genuine transposition can occur while keeping the same species of the Octave, except for these: I. from F to G. II. from G to A, but with the forms rejected. III. from A to B-flat. IV. from B-natural to C. V. from C to D. VI. from D to E-flat <note>original: "de"</note>, with the forms rejected. VII. from E to F.

But if we comply with the common practice of instrumental musicians <note>original: "Musicorum Organicorum"; referring to those who play the organ or other keyboard instruments</note>, who neglect the <term>comma</term> <note>a tiny interval representing the difference between a major and minor tone</note> and do not distinguish between the major and minor tones, then all fourteen of our octave species will constitute no more than three Modes, based on the triple placement of the semitone. As Vincenzo Galilei <note>a famous music theorist and father of the astronomer Galileo</note> says of ancient times, there were no more than three Tones: *Dorian, Phrygian, and Lydian*. These are multiplied into more only through their pitch.

For as far as the third cause is concerned—the articulation of the "skeleton" of the Octave <note>the fundamental structural intervals like the fourth and fifth</note>—that remains common between us and them; because of this, even for us, more than fourteen species will arise.

->Behold the three common orders of Octaves.<-

Therefore, according to the common opinion regarding the Major and Minor Tone, many transpositions of melodies from one letter to another can occur by using the mediating signs of the flat (♭) and sharp (♯).

It remains for us to examine which of our fourteen species of the Octave can be made multiple <note>meaning they can appear in different forms</note> through the articulation of fitting elements. For a fivefold distinction of species arises from the proximity of the Tones; for either three tones follow one another in succession, or only two. If three tones follow, they must either stand unnaturally in the middle of the octave, having single tones and single semitones on either side; or they must lean toward one or the other end of the System, and then a semitone is necessarily at that end, according to laws 8 and 3. But if only two Tones follow each other, with semitones intervening, then there is no place for a semitone at the ends; and two pairs of tones stand either above or below, with a third "soft" tone <note>Kepler likely refers to the "movable" or minor tone</note> at the opposite end—this being "upright" <note>original: "recta"</note> when lower, having a semitone above it, and "inverted" when higher, having a semitone below it.

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin>

In this way, among our 14 species, ten others are found interspersed, coinciding with the former in the first four places, or even five; but where they begin to differ, the word *or* <note>original: "vel"</note> is placed before them.

But if the final cause is now added, which distinguishes the Modes <note>Kepler uses "Toni" (Tones) here to mean musical modes or keys</note>, namely the **division** and the **compositional use** <note>original: "τομὴ & πετεία" – technical terms from ancient Greek music theory referring to how a scale is divided and how its notes are used in practice</note>: the number will be tripled, and there will be 72 species. For every "skeleton" <note>the underlying structural framework</note> of the Octave out of all 24 has both a third and a fourth concordant with the first, and a fifth and a sixth. If, therefore, these parts of the song are occupied chiefly around the fourth and sixth, then they place the **fourth** <term>Diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth</term> in the lowest position. But if they are around the third and sixth, the fourth is in the middle; if finally they are around the third and fifth, the fourth is in the highest position.

[The image shows three musical staff segments illustrating the placement of a Diatessaron at the lowest, middle, and highest positions of a scale fragment.]

I do not say these things because such a minute division is necessary, since I know that usually three forms are mixed in one song; but so that from this number a judgment can be made regarding the distinctions of the Modes which the **Moderns** <note>Kepler refers to contemporary music theorists of the 16th and 17th centuries</note> teach. Some of these are such that it seems to me as many modes could be established as there are songs, while others are all of a single Mode. But if we observe these principles, the number of Modes, however large, is nonetheless finite. In short, the Modes distinguished by real boundaries and differences—not with respect to the pitch of the instrument <note>original: "in Organo"</note>, but even in the human voice itself, which can begin a natural system from any voice, high or deep—are either only 3, or 14, or 24, or 72.

With these principles of mine, I thus reconcile the eight common Modes, which they call **Ecclesiastical** <note>The "Church Modes" used in Gregorian chant</note>; and they were to the ancients, in the opinion of some:

## I. Dorian
## II. Hypodorian

[Two musical scales representing the Dorian and Hypodorian modes, with notes written in square notation on a five-line staff.]

->Adam the first Man.<-
->Noah the second.<-

These are two species of "soft song" <term>Cantus mollis: music utilizing the "soft" hexachord, typically characterized by a B-flat</term>, from the species of the octave which is my First among the 14. Nor do I see any other difference than in mere pitch, of which the first has more and the second less: unless you wish to distinguish them by the "final cause" <note>the melodic purpose or structure</note>, in that the first observes this skeleton: [Small musical snippet showing the interval C to F], and the second observes this: [Small musical snippet showing the interval B-flat to F].

# BOOK III OF THE HARMONICS
K
<meta>catchword: more</meta>

<margin>
CHAPTER XV.
\*
There are three types of pitch <note>original: "altitudo"</note> for a Tone. 1. The absolute and, in a sense, material pitch, such as in the human voice; or on an Organ, if the root of the System rises from *G* in the "hard" genus <note>original: "ing." likely for "in g."</note>, where the form of the System does not change. I shall say nothing more of this here. 2. The formal pitch of the root itself for each Tone in a natural System composed of two octaves <note>original: "diapason"</note>. This is also not what is meant here, for it implies a change of Tone when the root Key <note>original: "Clavi radicali"</note> of the System is swapped. 3. Again a formal pitch, being the height of a Melody in respect to its own root key. While the key remains the same, the Tone stays the same, but it puts on a different, as it were, "schema" <note>shape or appearance</note>. For instance, if the melody does not rise to the Octave of the root but stays below the sixth, fifth, or fourth, or frequently sinks below the root, yet returns to the root at the end. Therefore, these skeletons <note>the basic structural notes of a scale</note> are not to be understood as if the Melody must traverse every joint or note depicted here; it is enough if it touches some of them, or their lower octaves. Thus, we could call those that sink below the root "Plagal" <note>original: "Plagios"</note> according to the ancients, and the others "Authentic" <note>original: "Authentas"</note>.
</margin>

Nothing is more obvious than that these two of the "Hard" genus <term>Genus durum: scales using natural or sharp notes, often associated with a "harder" or brighter sound</term> belong to our eleventh species and should be written starting from *e*. Again, there is almost no difference other than pitch, unless you wish to adapt these skeletons to them separately.

->Common Fifth: Lydian.<- ->Common Sixth: Hypolydian.<-

->The five books of Moses<- ->The six water jars placed there<-

Similarly, these are most obviously to be written starting from *f*. They are of the "Soft" genus <term>Genus molle: scales using flats (like B-flat), often associated with a "softer" or more somber sound</term> and are distinguished by pitch or by these skeletons, from our thirteenth species.

->Common Seventh: Mixolydian.<- ->Common Eighth: Hypomixolydian.<-

->The seven liberal arts<- ->And there are eight parts.<-

Although the intention of the inventors is clear—that they wished to write the First and Second modes from *d*, the Third and Fourth from *e*, the Fifth and Sixth from *f*, and the Seventh and Eighth from *G*—it is certain from what we discussed above that even those of the Hard genus, along with the First and Second, ought to be written from the same key of *G*. These skeletons from our second species are suitable for them.

[The image shows a musical staff with two pairs of notes: G to C and D to G.]

Therefore, by this application of the eight common Tones to my octave species I, XI, XIII, and II, I can show a much more evident distinction between these Tones than our musicians can, because they ignore the comma <term>Comma: a very small musical interval resulting from the difference between two types of whole tones; Kepler argues that ignoring it leads to tuning inaccuracies</term>. For those written from *G* all have four legitimate consonances: the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth with the first note. But those that use *F* and *e* employ "adulterated" <note>imperfect or out-of-tune</note> consonances: below the major fourth *e–a* and *f–b-flat*, and the major fifth *e–b* and *f–c'*.

You may ask: what then of the remaining ten species, since all the commonly used Tones are reduced to four? Surely they serve this purpose: so that Musicians may know that if we tune the Systems of the principal Octave described from *G* as nature suggests, then the song cannot be transposed so easily and variedly without losing its purity <note>original: "sinceritatis"</note>, as they are accustomed to doing. It is therefore free for them either to reject all the remaining ten species, and with them their transpositions, or to admit that more Forms of Melodies—namely more Modes or Tones—can exist, and that these are different from the ones established here, others...

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>CHAPTER 14</margin> ...some more, others less; as you see the equivalences noted in the margin above. For if we take no account of the ratio of the intervals of one of the upper octaves <note>original: "Octavæ"</note>; certainly some transpositions are possible from $G$ to $c$, and from $A$ to $d$, and others.

<margin>*</margin> Lastly, you might ask, what prevents those transpositions that I have so often rejected? For they seem not to offend the ears, since it is admitted that the excess of a Comma <term>Comma: Kepler refers here to the "Syntonic Comma," a tiny mathematical difference (ratio 81:80) between two types of whole steps. In pure tuning, not all whole steps are the same size.</term> in intervals that are separated by different locations in the System <note>The "System" refers to the overall scale or tuning map</note> is not judged by the ears. Suppose the system is tuned as well as possible according to the laws of nature explained thus far. Let $G$ to $a$ and $a$ to $b$ <note>Kepler writes "h," the traditional German/Latin notation for B-natural</note> be struck. Ask all people hearing them which of these intervals is larger; they will say they do not know. Nor will they discern the difference until the intervals are joined in the same place in the Octave—that is, where a space of the string is marked off by a compass, and an eighty-first part of the string is cut off, so that two lengths of 80 and 81 are struck in close succession and compared to each other.

I respond that although the hearing does not distinguish the difference when only three strings of the Octave are struck (the boundaries of two intervals), yet when all the strings of one Octave are struck, it finally distinguishes the "first-born" and natural Octave of $G$ from the Octaves of other keys. For in all species of the Octave, there are the same seven harmonious <note>original: "Concinna"</note> intervals, which, once expressed by the striking of the strings, immediately stick in the memory. Thus, it is easily apparent to the hearing at what place in the natural Octave any Tone begins. In this way, the sense of the Comma will be implicit in the distinction of Octaves. Just as the hearing approves the Consonances themselves and all the harmonious intervals by their effect—even if it does not count the lengths of the strings that cause the chords—so the same hearing notices even the effect of the Comma (80:81), even if it does not count it, and thus does not grasp it as a separate, distinct sensation.

# CHAPTER 15

## Which Modes or Tones serve which Affects.

<note>The term "Affects" refers to the Renaissance and Baroque theory that different musical structures could trigger specific emotional states in the listener, such as joy, sadness, or courage.</note>

Thus far we have dealt with the principles from which the Tones consist and are distinguished from one another; now I shall say a few things about their effect, consistent with my principles.

First, the reader must be warned that we are not dealing here with the difference in the dispositions of the soul which cause a person to sing rather than use plain and calm speech; nor with those things that follow from singing on the one hand and simple speech on the other in the listener. For just as it is the alacrity of the soul that precedes every kind of singing in the singer and, as it were, dictates the melody to them; so also a pleasure for the listeners follows every kind of harmonious song.

We must separate this general disposition of the soul, or rather...

## CHAPTER XV.

Since all the parts of tuneful and natural song <note>original: "Cantus"</note> are designed to stir the emotions by imitating the sounds that animals produce to express their desires, it is clear that this discussion is varied, complex, and seemingly infinite. Because this subject exceeds my own strength <note>Kepler uses the idiom "surpasses my biceps"</note>, it would be more properly handed over entirely to the practitioners—that is, the performing musicians. Without formal rules, and guided by nature alone, they frequently create wonderful melodies; it is far easier for them to compose than to explain in a long and eloquent speech what a song is, what it consists of, or how it was made.

For just as prose and poetry represent speech, so voices and gestures represent a living person through song—as if painting a portrait of them. Certainly, the ability to compose music, like the art of poetry, must be learned through use and practice, provided that a person's nature is already suited for it.

However, because it is one of the most honorable recreations of the Soul to investigate the causes of things—or to look closely at what others have discovered—even Aristotle dedicated a large portion of his *Problems* to harmonic contemplations. Therefore, I must also attempt something here to extend the boundaries of Philosophy. By applying the laws of Method, I will try to restrain this "infinite" discussion and bring it back under general headings, so that by looking at specific examples, the same judgment can later be applied to similar cases.

I. The elements of the song itself and the emotions that follow the specific types of song are proportional; they are almost equal in number on both sides. Even the very terms for the parts of a song—**melodic motion**, **pitch**, **note selection**, and **weaving** <note>original Greek: "αγωγή, τονή, πετεία, πλοκή"</note>—allude to certain emotions. The first (motion) serves simplicity, while the last (weaving) serves luxury; one is like the body, the other like the colors. The equality of the **pitch** moves our attention; **note selection** <note>original: "Pettia," a term derived from a Greek board game, referring here to the "moves" or choices a composer makes in a melody</note>, or the scouring of notes, is designed for delight and recreation. These are general principles across all musical Modes.

II. Regarding **Melodic Motion** <note>original: "Agôge"</note>, Galileo <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), a famous music theorist and the father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei</note> notes this specific point: there are two types, one moving upward and the other downward. The former serves joy, while the latter serves sadness and weeping. The cause is natural: a low voice is produced with slow motion, while a high voice is produced with sharp, agitated motion. Therefore, when a voice descends, it approaches rest; when it ascends, it advances in motion. For this reason, in choral singing, we usually finish at the bottom. There the voice faints; here it flourishes. So too in sorrow the mind and all its functions languish, while in cheerfulness it lives and is active.

III. There is also great power in the **leap** <note>original: "saltûs"</note>, which is like a concentrated form of melodic motion. It possesses boldness, movement, and audacity; it is military, masculine, and—if frequent—impudent. This is especially true of the leap of a **Fifth** <term>Diapente: An interval of a perfect fifth (e.g., C to G)</term>, whose geometric figure, the Triangle, consists of sharp angles and consumes the whole circle in only three lines. Conversely, a single ascending **minor Sixth** <note>original: "sextam mollem"</note> followed by a downward motion expresses great pain; it is suited for wailing because of its resemblance to the human voice, as seen in the work *In Me Transierunt* <note>A famous penitential motet by the composer Orlande de Lassus (1532–1594)</note> by Orlando.

IV. It also matters a great deal how much height the main part of the song occupies within the **Octave system** <note>the range of eight notes</note> from the lowest root. For if it runs through or exceeds the entire Octave, the song is spirited. If it stays within a **Fourth** <term>Diatessaron: An interval of a perfect fourth (e.g., C to F)</term>, it is modest and pleasant. The **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> holds a middle ground. A minor **Third**...

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
...humility and low-spiritedness. Some attribute this to the descent below the root by a perfect fourth <note>original: "per diatessaron"</note>; they call tones of this form "plagal," or the side-modes of their "authentic" <note>In traditional music theory, "Authentic" modes generally move upward from a starting note, while "Plagal" modes move both above and below it, which Kepler associates with a more subdued or humble character</note> originals.

V. Among the general elements, the most important to consider are the speed and slowness of the rhythm, or beat <note>original: "tactûs"</note>. Speed is suited to anger, movement, fighting, and joy; slowness is suited to the emotions we enjoy in stillness: sorrow, love, longing, and the pleasure of possession.

VI. Add to this the mode, that is, the Rhythm itself. There is one power in "triple" time and another in "double" time. This perhaps draws much of its force from the imitation of dancing; for since the alternating variety of movements in dances is known to everyone, it immediately prompts the listeners, bringing them as if into the present event. Triple rhythm <note>similar to a waltz or jig</note> is thus more turbulent and active; double rhythm <note>similar to a march</note> is quieter, more peaceful, and more modest. But regarding Rhythms and their signs, there is nothing more in this book; therefore I shall let them pass.

<margin>Aristotle writes about the Enharmonic genus, saying it fills minds with a "divine fury." Conversely, the Spartan magistrates—because they considered this type of singing to be effeminate and artificial—expelled its creator from the city, branding him with disgrace.</margin>

VII. We must now come to those things by which we said Tones are properly distinguished; the chief of these is the diversity of the "genera" or types of Song. And here a most abundant crop of disputes will arise: which of the three ancient genera <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic scales of ancient Greece</note> was assigned to which emotion? We shall pass over this untouched, since the distribution of song into exactly three genera is not natural, nor are the ancients consistent with themselves on this subject. I shall speak instead of the two *natural* types of song, namely the Hard <note>original: "Duri," which we now call Major</note> and the Soft <note>original: "Mollis," which we now call Minor</note>; the very names reveal which emotions they stir. For just as a woman is made chiefly for enduring and a man for acting—especially in the business of procreation—so the Soft genus is suited to feminine passions of the soul, and the Hard to masculine actions. The distinctions between these things will shine more brightly from what follows.

VIII. For not only the Genera of song, but even the Tones in general, differ by the position of the semitone <note>the smallest interval in the scale</note>. This position of the semitone animates and affects both the Genus and the Mode or Tone. However, this position must be discussed differently regarding the genera than regarding all the tones. For we have said that the genera arise first of all in the principal Octave, which begins from G; in this, placing the semitone at the lowest position forms the Soft genus, while placing it at the third-from-last position forms the Hard genus. In the former, there is a minor third <note>original: "tertia mollis"</note> at the bottom; in the latter, a major third <note>original: "tertia dura"</note>. What, then, is the connection of this position with the emotions? What does the minor third have in common with women, passions, and softness; or the major third with masculinity, hardness, actions, and efficacy?

First, remember that the Major Third arose from the Pentagon; the pentagon uses a sectioning according to the "Extremes and Mean," which forms the "Divine Proportion" <note>Now known as the Golden Ratio. Kepler believed this mathematical ratio was the blueprint for biological growth and beauty</note>. In this proportion, there is a beautiful idea of Generation. For just as a father begets a son, and the son another, each similar to himself, so also in that mathematical section: when the larger part is added to the whole, the proportion continues. The composite takes the place of the Whole, and what was previously the whole takes the place of the larger part. Although this ratio cannot be expressed in whole numbers, a certain series of numbers is given <note>The Fibonacci sequence: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, etc.</note> which continually approaches the truth. In this series, the very difference of the numbers from the genuine terms (which are not countable but ineffable) produces "males" and "females" by a wonderful alternation, distinct in the members that indicate their sex. For example, if the larger part is first 2, the smaller 1, the total is 3. Here, 1 is not exactly to 2 as 2 is to 3; for the difference is one unit, which prevents the rectangle of the extremes (1 times 3) from equaling the square of the mean (2 times 2).

Since this is the nature of this "section" <note>Kepler refers to the Golden Ratio or "Divine Proportion"</note> which converges in the demonstration of the pentagon; and since God the Creator has conformed the laws of generation to it; then the seminal ratios of plants—each commanded to have its own seed within itself—belong to that genuine proportion of inexpressible terms <note>irrational numbers</note> which is perfect in itself. However, the union of male and female belongs to these joined pairs of numerical proportions (where the unit deficiency of one is compensated by the excess of the other). What wonder is it, then, if the offspring of the pentagon—the major <note>original: "Tertia dura," literally "hard third"</note> (or 4:5) and the minor <note>original: "mollis," literally "soft third"</note> (or 5:6) thirds—move the souls (which are images of God) to emotions comparable to the business of generation? Here we must recall from Chapter III that although the ratio 1:6 arises from the hexagon, the remaining ratio 5:6 <note>the minor third</note> does not create consonance because of the hexagon, but because of its derivation from the three tenths of a circle through the doubling and halving of terms; thus, this remainder and its offspring, the minor third, belongs to the pentagonal class of figures.

Having established, therefore, that the partnership of the two thirds represents the partnership of male and female, it is no trouble at all to assign each sex its own third. For the major third turns out to be virile, and the minor third feminine; since the same proportion exists in their very bodies, and in their strengths of both body and mind. And since the major third arises from an odd-sided figure (namely the pentagon) while the minor third originally arises from an even-sided figure (the decagon), this is also consistent with the decrees of Pythagoras, who said odd numbers were male and even numbers were female. This is confirmed by that observation of excesses and deficiencies: since the odd is that which exceeds <note>Kepler links the "male" Fibonacci rectangle, which exceeds the square, to the major third</note>, let it be considered of the masculine sex, and the other of the feminine.

To these reasons, let us add the contemplation of the melodic intervals, of which the smallest is the semitone <note>the half-step</note>. For a following semitone always invites the voice to overcome it because of its smallness; it is like a ridge on a softening slope. Whenever a semitone occurs moving toward the higher notes, it is held as a kind of goal for the song, toward which it strives; from there, as if the ridge has been crested and the effort completed, the song often tends to return to the lower notes. Certainly, if we sing RE, MI, the hearing is not satisfied, but expects FA to be added <note>In the hexachord system, the semitone occurs between MI and FA</note>. Since the major third—which holds the lowest position in the Eighth Tone <note>Mode 8</note>—lacks a semitone (which only arrives later to complete the <term>Diatessaron</term> <gloss>a perfect fourth</gloss>), it is rightly considered active and full of effort. Its power is <term>γόνιμος</term> <gloss>fruitful</gloss> and <term>ἀκάμητος</term> <gloss>tireless</gloss>, seeking its end—namely the Fourth—whose semitone is for it like an <term>ἔκχυσis</term> <gloss>outpouring or climax</gloss>, sought with total effort. But the minor third, standing in the lowest place of the First Tone, since it has already embraced the semitone (after the overcoming of which a return usually occurs), is as if content with itself; and by its nature, being made for submission and passion <note>or "being acted upon"</note>, it always spreads itself on the ground like a hen, ready for the rooster that mounts her. And behold, here are the causes of the emotions in the Genera, and in the Tones of the primary system rising from G.

</margin>

Now let us consider the position of the semitone <note>the smallest interval in the standard scale</note> with respect to all the modes <note>original: "Tonorum"; here referring to the musical scales or "tones"</note> indiscriminately. Here I will adjust my discussion, as I have done so far, to the common modes as I have distinguished them based on my own principles. As for the other ten species of the octave that I added for the sake of comparison, it will be up to the judgment of musicians whether they truly deserve to be called "modes."

It has often been said that, in the order of nature, among harmonious intervals, the larger ones demand the lowest position so that "great things are joined with great things." For low sounds <note>original: "soni graves"</note>, which are at the bottom of the scale, are determined by magnitude—that is, by long strings—while high sounds are determined by short ones. Or, to put it another way, a low sound is produced by a large and slow motion, and a high sound by a small and swift one. Therefore, the natural series occurs when, in a perfect tetrachord <note>a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</note>, the first and lowest place is held by a Major Tone, the second by a Minor Tone, and the third and highest by a semitone. 

Since we are joyful when all things follow the order of nature, it follows that the "Joyful Modes" are those which have their lower tetrachord divided in this way. This occurs in the Seventh and Eighth modes, which some believe were called Phrygian or Mixolydian by the ancients—though with strange inconsistency. However, I am more inclined to believe the ancients called these "Lydian," for they testify that their Lydian mode fills the mind with a divine fury—that is, with alacrity and a military spirit—qualities found in our Seventh and Eighth modes.

Thus, when this ratio is overturned and the semitone occupies the lowest place—as happens in the Third and Fourth Ecclesiastical modes, which were the Phrygian of the ancients—it is natural that the sound produced is something plaintive, broken, and mournful <note>original: "querulum, fractum, & lamentabile"</note> due to this inversion of nature’s order. 

But when the semitone is in the middle position, the "affect" <note>the emotional character</note> is likewise moderate: one of tranquility, humanity, and the pleasantness found in conversation and storytelling. The First and Second modes are suited to this, being of a "soft and feminine" nature; these are thought to have once been called the Dorian. Indeed, Vincenzo Galilei <note>A prominent Italian music theorist and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei</note> describes the Dorian as being stable by nature, quiet, without violence, and fit for gravity and severity. This is more or less true of these two modes. For modes designated by an even number must always be softer, as they are "plagal" <note>modes that share the same final note but have a lower range</note> to their "authentic" <note>primary</note> counterparts designated by odd numbers, for the reason provided a little earlier in Number IV. 

Thus, Galilei also characterizes the Plagal of the First [the Second mode] as "languid, tearful, and timid," for he argues that motion toward the low notes suggests languor, while motion toward the high suggests vigor. However, I would prefer to moderate these descriptions and distinguish the cause. Languor, weeping, and fear are not properties unique to the Dorian modes, but belong generally to passages that descend frequently into the low notes below the "root" <note>the fundamental starting note of the mode</note>.

**IX.** Thus far we have discussed the position of the semitone; yet we have not yet assigned properties to all the modes. It follows, therefore, that we must also speak of the "imperfect and false consonances" <note>original: "consonantijs imperfectis & adulterinis"; intervals that deviate slightly from pure mathematical ratios</note> by which the "skeletons" of the octaves are articulated. We must first examine their essence, and then their location within the system.

When the arrangement of the octave system is natural and primal—where the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth intervals harmonize perfectly with the lowest note—such a mode arouses all those things in the soul that follow nature: soft passions, hard actions, or affects suited to them. This property belongs to the First and Eighth modes rising from G; for which reason Galilei rightly claimed that the Eighth coincides with the First. Understand, however, that the property of the "sixth" or of the musical genus is preserved for each. In this way, the Seventh and Eighth modes surpass the others on two counts: both because of the position of the semitone, and also because of the perfection...

On the contrary— <note>catchword: E contra-</note>

**CHAPTER XV.**
</margin>

On the contrary, the Fifth and Sixth modes, and the Third and Fourth, use intervals below that are altered or augmented; the former use the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> and the latter the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>. This quality provides them with a power to evoke sadness and emotions that depart from a balanced human temperament.

In the Fifth and Sixth modes, the Fourth is indeed high-pitched <note>original: **ὄρθιον** (*orthion*)</note>, with the semitone <note>the smallest interval in the scale</note> naturally situated at the top, just as in the Seventh and Eighth modes. However, two major tones are placed at the very bottom, followed by the semitone; from these, a Fourth is constructed that is "wide" by a comma <note>a "comma" is a tiny mathematical discrepancy in tuning; here it suggests the interval feels slightly "too big" or strained</note>.

Therefore, these modes promote emotions of great magnitude, such as Devotion, Admiration, Amplification, and Grief; and conversely, Hope and Confidence—as if the mind is being lifted above its present lot.

In the Third and Fourth modes, however, in addition to the inverted form of the Fourth itself, there is a certain agitation <note>original: "fermentatio"</note> of the harmonies which increases sadness and the languors of the soul.

But if we may follow this analogy beyond the usual modes to a third species of "soft song" <note>minor key</note> that I described starting on the note A: because it has a semitone at the bottom and a perfect Fourth, I would assign it to "pleasant sadness." This is the feeling we have when we indulge in a soft state of mind, in Love and Longing, or when joy is so intense it brings tears.

These observations concern the harmonies by their own nature; now let us see what effect they have based on their position within the musical system.

When the "tension" <note>original: **τονή** (*tonē*)</note> and "sinking" <note>original: **πελεία** (*peleia*); these are ancient terms for melodic movement</note> are primarily occupied around the fourth and sixth strings, so that the Fourth interval is placed at the very bottom, this structure invites the song toward humility. This is for the same reason I used above in section IV. But if these parts of the song are occupied around the third and fifth strings, placing the Fourth higher up, the song is excited and elevated, especially if it runs up to the octave. This seems to be the nature of the High-Pitched Song <note>original: **Νόμο ὄρθιο** (*Nomos Orthios*), a famous melody of ancient Greece</note> of the ancients. Finally, if it is around the third and sixth strings, so that the Fourth is reduced to the middle—which happens more frequently in the First and Second modes than in the Seventh and Eighth—then a middle emotion will be promoted. Often, however, these articulations are mixed together, so that different parts of the song have different qualities to suit the variety of the text and the skill of the composer who "paints" the text with music.

X. If it is true, as some say, that the odd-numbered modes (I, III, V, VII) are higher in pitch, and the even-numbered (II, IV, VI, VIII) are lower—even in respect to the "root" of the octave—then surely height corresponds to the excitement of the soul and depth to its lowering. In that case, we can distribute the four classes of emotions into eight classes, according to the eight modes:
*   **Seventh:** Anger, violence, and strength.
*   **Eighth:** Cheerfulness, alacrity, and sharp pleasure.
*   **Third:** Sharp grief and longing.
*   **Fourth:** Weeping and love.
*   **First:** Festivity, weddings, and banquets.
*   **Second:** Modest cheerfulness, conversation, and storytelling.
*   **Fifth:** Public assemblies <note>original: "Panegyres"</note>, exclamations, confidence, and hope.
*   **Sixth:** Devotion and great sorrow, etc.

->ON PROPORTIONS<-

And now it is time for my discourse to return to the beginning. For the philosophical reader must be reminded of this: that all our modern musicians express all kinds of emotions <note>original: "affectus"</note> indiscriminately in all the Modes <note>original: "Tonis," referring to the church modes or scales</note>. They do so because every song, without distinction, brings pleasure to the listener and requires a certain spiritedness in the author. They are able to do this because the instruments used to stir the emotions are numerous—as I listed some at the beginning—and these can be applied generally across all the Modes. Nevertheless, if they were to strive to use every available resource to achieve a specific goal, they would not so easily neglect the choice of Modes that are naturally suited to a particular emotional premise. But let them see to what is permitted in their practice; for me, it is enough to have proceeded this far in theory.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## What Polyphonic or "Figured" Song Is.

Although the word **Harmony** <note>original: "Harmonia"</note> was used by the ancients to mean a "Song" or "Melody," it should not be understood by this name as a modulation through several voices sounding together in harmonic consonance. For it requires little proof to show that the "Concert" of multiple voices in a perpetual exchange of harmonies is a recent invention, and was entirely unknown to the ancients. On this matter, one should consult Vincentio Galilei <note>An Italian lutenist and music theorist, father of Galileo Galilei</note> in his Italian work on music. It is true that some object, citing the banishment of "Song through Harmony" from Plato's Republic as if it were already in use back then; but that passage is understood to refer to **Instruments**—to the **Pan-pipes** <note>original: "Syringe"</note>, the **Bagpipe** <note>original: "Utriculo"</note>, and the **Lute** <note>original: "Testudine"</note>—where one voice either sounds a continuous tone or pauses, giving way to an approaching dissonance. In that ancient custom, there was no greater artifice than what is found among our modern bagpipers.

In these recent centuries, this method of singing began to be called **"Figured"** <note>original: "Figurata," meaning ornate or florid</note> because the first authors did not make their diagrams as simple as they are in **Plainchant** <note>original: "Choral," the monophonic chant of the church</note>. Instead, they used various figures, colors, and points <note>referring to "counterpoint"</note>; some of these signs command silence, others sound; some indicate a long duration, others a short one. Some are applied to distinguish the Tones, others the measured Modes, and others for Fugues, repetitions, and similar techniques.

Let us, therefore, define **Harmonic Concert** <note>polyphony</note> thus: it consists of two, three, four, or more voices or **Pleasant and Fitting Melodies**, such as we described in **Chapter XIII**, all of the same <term>Genus<gloss>The classification of scales, such as Diatonic</gloss></term>, and of the same or related Modes, moving together in such a way that they create concords that are either pure or "leavened" <note>original: "fermentatas," suggesting the dissonances act like yeast to animate the music</note> by the briefest interruption of fitting dissonances. These harmonies are not identical in a perpetual drone, nor are they always the same in succession; rather, they are varied for delight by the very alternation of their sequences.

For just as the consonance of two voices is to a <term>Unison<gloss>Two voices singing the exact same pitch</gloss></term> in terms of proportion, so is Harmonic Song to the simple melody of a single 

<meta>catchword: VOICE</meta>

I. First, concerning the plurality of voices, a point must be noted that artisans have established as most agreeable to Nature: although many voices may often sing together, they are all called by only four names, according to the number of perfect harmonic mediation in one perfect octave <note>original: "diapason"</note> system. For they call the highest voice the **Discant** <note>Also known as the Soprano</note>, the one next to it the **Alto**, the higher of the low voices the **Tenor**, and the lowest the **Bass**. For between two voices sounding an octave apart, there are only two means <note>Intermediate notes</note> that are harmonically consonant at the same time with the identical-sounding extremes, as was explained in Chapter III.

<image-desc>A small musical staff showing four notes stacked vertically as a chord, representing the four voice parts.</image-desc>

<margin>Chapter XIII, from Euclid.</margin>
Although the origin of these Italian terms seems to refer more to a composite musical system—such that the Alto and Bass hold opposite parts in it—the Alto is not indeed the highest voice; rather, these two frequently (though not at the end) form an octave, the former being superior and sharper, the latter inferior and deeper. Thus, the origin of the word **Tenor** <note>from Latin 'tenere', to hold</note> provides the "Idea" and simple modulation of the song. The name **Discant** [Soprano] seems to have been given by its perpetual agility and its wandering from the region opposite the Tenor by an octave. Therefore, if we compare these to the parts of song cited by Euclid, even though those roles apply to all voices, the Tenor is primarily occupied with **melodic motion** <note>original: Αγωγῆ (Agogē)</note>, the Discant with **interweaving** <note>original: Πλοκῆ (Plokē)</note>, the Alto with **prolongation** <note>original: Τονῆ (Tonē)</note>, and the Bass with leaping through harmonic intervals; yet **compositional choice** <note>original: Πεττεία (Petteia), the art of deciding which sounds to use and where</note> is common to all four, though more notable in the Alto.

<image-desc>A small musical staff with four notes plotted horizontally and vertically, labeled to the right as: Disc, Alt, Ten, Bass.</image-desc>

These properties of the four voices are taken from the very Nature of things. For since, by the definition provided, the harmony must be perpetually changed from one to another, it was necessary for this to occur so that one of the middle voices, compared to the rest, is kept within a narrow space of the System. For if an equal, loose freedom were granted to all, it would necessarily follow that the lower voice would frequently wander into the space of the higher, and vice versa; an insane confusion would result, and the distinction of the four voices would be rendered void. One of the middle voices (the **Alto** or **Tenor**) should occupy these narrow bounds rather than the extremes, the **Discant** or **Bass**.

For if such a thing were done in the extreme parts, every variation of intervals would turn toward only one region—either the high or the low. It was therefore better for the Harmony to be fixed or bound in a narrow place by some intermediate voice, like a single boundary for the parts themselves; and for the variation of intervals to proceed from there, partly upward and partly downward. However, the lower of the middle voices should not be restricted; because the "Idea" of the song, assigned to the **Tenor** (the lower of the middle parts), must be both free and proceed through the middle quantity of the entire System, so that the surrounding voices are nothing other than its colors, ornaments, or emblems. Indeed, the lower intervals are always larger than their higher namesakes. So that the Tenor might hold the middle position of quantity, it was necessary for it to be the lower of the middle parts; and thus the Alto in an-

...it was necessary for [the Alto] to be compressed into a narrow range, but not the Tenor. There remain, therefore, the wanderings for the Discant and the Bass, but with this distinction: the Bass, which sounds deep <note>original: "grave"</note>, is expressed with great movement and long strings, and it wanders through slow and large measures and large harmonic intervals. The Discant, which sounds sharp <note>original: "acutum"</note> and flies above the rest, is drawn out from short strings and with a swift movement in a narrow space; it wanders through everything with short and therefore more frequent measures, and with the smallest fitting intervals. This, therefore, is the property of the voices. Now I shall also explain the remaining parts of the definition.

<margin>Dissonances.</margin>
II. Now, as pertains to that primary and chief seasoning of Melodic Song, Dissonance: First, it is necessary that these be taken not from just any unharmonious <note>original Greek: "ἀναρμόστῳ" (anarmosto); refers to intervals that do not fit into a musical scale</note> interval, but from fitting <note>original: "concinnis"</note> intervals. For because individual voices, meeting in a common harmony, admit no intervals between successive sounds unless they are fitting—and they are indeed of the same genus and Tone, as stated in the previous definition—it is easily seen that if any harmony is established among such voices (since all harmony is dissolved into fitting elements), it can never happen through any wandering of the individual voices from the root of their Octave that two voices together produce anything other than a fitting interval, even if it is not always a consonant one.

<margin>
See Book II of *On the Art of Counterpoint* by Giovanni Maria Artusi of Bologna, which is entirely about dissonances.
</margin>
Secondly, although excellent craftsmen sometimes use larger dissonances—such that the dissonant voice is a whole tone distant from the one that would create a consonance—this does not happen except to express and draw out the deepest emotions of the soul. However, the ordinary dissonance, joined with pleasantness and therefore in a certain way natural, is created by a semitone.

<margin>
The power of the Quindecagon <note>A 15-sided polygon</note> in the selection of dissonances.
</margin>
The cause of this matter, so that the last things may correspond to the first, must be sought again from the innermost foundations of Geometry, from Chapter I, Axioms II and III, and from the first book and the contemplation of the Quindecagon. For since the semitone is contained in the numbers 15 and 16, and since not only the sixteen-sided figure has a geometric demonstration <note>meaning it can be constructed with a compass and straightedge</note>, but also the fifteen-sided figure, it was very nearly the case that 15:16 defined a harmonic proportion for us. No less so were those derived from it: 15:8, 15:4, 15:2, 15:32, and 15:64, and especially 15:1—those, namely, which composers most frequently admit to shape legitimate dissonances. We had no other exception than this: that the demonstration of the Quindecagon <note>original Greek: "Pentekædecagoni"</note> was not formed by the number of the figure's angles immediately, like the others, and thus it is not its own property but is borrowed from different figures, the Triangle and the Pentagon, and is thus a borrowed thing of the most remote degree. Likewise, although the angle of the Quindecagon might fit with others to fill a flat space, the whole figure with all its angles would not admit such a fitting <note>tessellation</note>. Since, therefore, the ratio 15:16 and its companions approach Consonances so closely by reason of their shaping cause, it is no wonder that they are also mixed among the consonances by frequent use. On the other hand, the Tones 8:9 and 9:10 participate in the Nonagon <note>A 9-sided polygon</note> through their other terms, a figure that is entirely unconstructible <note>original: "indemonstrabili"</note>. Therefore, the dissonances admitted through them and their related proportions (4:9, 2:9, 1:9, 9:16, 9:32, as well as 9:5, 18:5, 36:5, 9:20, 9:40, etc.) are not sweet but altogether harsh. Much harsher still are those which are produced from the Tritone <note>An interval of three whole tones</note>, and the "mutilated" Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"; refers to a diminished fifth</note>, and similar intervals; regarding which see Artu—
