# BOOK III ON THE HARMONIES

Artusi <note>original: "Artusium"; Giovanni Maria Artusi (c. 1540–1613) was a music theorist famous for his defense of traditional counterpoint against the modern style of Monteverdi.</note>: for they arise after the Tones, Major and Minor, and the Semitone—namely, from a composition of these as Elements that is not natural. For as much as one departs from Nature, one departs just as much from sweetness.

<margin>CHAPTER XVI. Syncopation</margin>
Thirdly, the other name for dissonances suggests their remaining laws, as they are called **Syncopations**: though this is a common occurrence for both dissonances and imperfect consonances, we are now dealing here with dissonances. For composers normally hold this rule: that they use dissonance like leaven, salt, or vinegar in side-dishes; that is, just as these do not make for whole courses, so here too entire songs do not overflow with dissonances (unless for the sake of great emphasis). Nor does any single voice, starting at the very beginning of the <term>tactus</term> <note>The pulse or beat in Renaissance and Baroque music.</note>, run into the other consonant voices while being dissonant itself. Instead, it admits dissonance stealthily and as if turning away. 

While in one place of the musical system which it occupied when the beat was raised—and thus starting a certain sound in the latter and less principal part of the beat—with the remaining voices in agreement, after they have finished, the voice itself lingers longer and beyond the start of the following beat. Thus, all the other voices—mostly lower than it (so that it, being high-pitched, might obstruct less with its smallness, weakness, and speed)—move by common harmony at the start of the next beat into a place dissonant from that voice's position, before the voice has left that spot. From there, they expel it as if it were sluggish, and usually push it down to a lower note. It is by this occasion that the name **Cadences** <margin>Cadences.</margin> <note>original: "Cadentiæ", literally "fallings."</note> seems to have been born for the concords and endings <note>original: "clausulis"</note> that consume and resolve the dissonances.

Furthermore, they observe this: that the battle of Dissonants is normally engaged not so often from a close interval (such as between seconds) as it is between sevenths. Thus, the upper voice, having been driven from its place in this way, flows down through a Semitone or Tone to a sixth, or flies up to be marked with the preceding voices as an Octave.

<margin>Common Dissonances.</margin>
There are also other very frequent dissonances, less artistic, when a low voice continues its sound, remaining on a unison, but the high voice runs out from the Octave <note>original: "diapason"</note> of that low sound with swift notes toward some note consonant to it through a Fifth <note>original: "diapēte"</note> or Fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>, flying through all the fitting intermediate places. Thus, it alternates between sounding consonant and dissonant; however, the one prior in the order is always consonant. The dissonance is both brief (occurring in passage) and on the sound which is later in the order: as if a beat of double proportion should couple five sounds of the Discant (Soprano) with one of the Bass, the first, third, and fifth sounds of the Discant will be consonant, while the second and fourth will be dissonant, or more imperfectly consonant. Behold:

<margin>Alternation of consonances.</margin>
III. Therefore, the natural reason for this rarer mixture is the same as for that other most frequent and perpetual one: while the Consonances are varied. For just as in a simple Melody, the movement of a single individual voice from the root of the system tends through dissonant (but still fitting <note>original: "Concinna"</note>) intervals toward places harmonically tempered to the Root, and lingers in them: so the melodic harmony, beginning almost from a unison, tends through minor Concords (commonly called "imperfect") or even through these dissonances, toward the major

Imperfect consonances.

IV. Again, just as in simple songs of those languages which consist of Rhythm and the length or brevity of syllables, not much account is taken of the short ones; but we direct the long syllables, and the ends of verses, to places consonant with the first sound. So also in harmony <note>original: "concentu"</note>, there are consonances called minor and imperfect, which we pass over quickly; and there are perfect ones toward which we strive, which are therefore called **Cadences** <term>Clausulæ</term> <note>literally "closings"; the musical formulas used to end a phrase or piece</note>.

<margin>Cadences.</margin>
<margin>Perfect [consonances] are not to be placed in succession.</margin>

V. Furthermore, just as individual consonances considered separately are pleasing for the reason that they do not sound exactly identical, but are shaped in a certain way and diverse in sound, occupying a certain qualitative breadth in hearing, drawing their nature from regular plane figures from which they also arise: so now Harmonic Music <note>original: "Concentus Harmonicus"</note>, or the perpetual sequence of several Harmonies, loses all its grace without their variety.

<margin>Why two Fifths <note>original: "diapente"</note> etc. [are forbidden] in succession.</margin>

From this explanation of the definition, the reasons can be given for the laws that composers observe in arranging concords. For it may be asked: What is the natural cause why they think it permissible to arrange several natural **Thirds** and **Sixths** in succession, but do not admit several similar **Fourths**, **Fifths**, and **Octaves** of the same species in succession?

I answer that the cause is this: that Thirds or Sixths following one another in pitch are usually truly diverse—one being major and the other minor. And although sometimes two minor Thirds may follow each other closely, they are nonetheless the smallest and most imperfect consonances. For example, let the first voice sing *Ut Re Mi Fa*, and the second at the same moments in time sing *Mi Fa Sol La* <note>These are solmization syllables used to name notes; the example shows two voices moving in parallel thirds</note>. Four Thirds follow each other: the first, *Ut Mi*, is a Major Third; the second, *Re Fa*, and the third, *Mi Sol*, are minor; the fourth, *Fa La*, is again a Major Third.

<image-desc>Two musical staves showing examples of parallel singing. Each staff contains four diamond-shaped notes (semibreves) in an ascending scale. The upper staff represents the voice singing "Mi Fa Sol La" and the lower staff "Ut Re Mi Fa", illustrating the intervals of a third between the two voices as discussed in the text.</image-desc>

On the contrary, all **Fourths** are commonly held to be intervals of the same size, as are **Fifths**, and most especially **Octaves**. Therefore, if several of these perfect concords of the same species were arranged in succession, differing only in pitch, the song would not be varied in its consonances.

But another principal cause prevents several Fifths from being sung in order going upward, which does not prevent Octaves from being sung; about which **Aristotle** thought he should inquire in his *Problems*: "Why do they modulate Octaves (for example, men with women, men with boys), but do not modulate Fifths and Fourths?" The cause, therefore, is this: since two Thirds [together make] the consonance of a **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, and two Octaves [make] the consonance of a **Double Octave** <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note>; conversely, two Fifths make a **Ninth**, and two Fourths a **Seventh**—intervals that are dissonant. Thus, the voice running through Octave and Third consonances stays equally within the Tone or mode, observing the same species of Octave; but here, if it should run through equal intervals [like fifths], it changes the mode or Tone significantly, which is against the definition.

VI. Regarding the choice of concords, some things must also be noted: first, that in general, large intervals express great emotions of the soul (as in those works by **Orlando** <note>original: "Orlandicis"; referring to Orlando di Lasso (1532–1594), a prolific Franco-Flemish composer</note>, *Where is Abel?* <note>original: "Ubi est Abel"</note> and *My soul is sorrowful* <note>original: "Tristis est Anima mea"</note>); small and high intervals express joyful emotions; low and small ones express sad ones.

It also touches on how different musical intervals can evoke specific emotional states.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK III

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>

Furthermore, since harmonic song usually ends in identity of sound <note>original: "Identisonantiam"; the state of two notes sounding like the same pitch, such as a unison or octave</note>: in order that we may embrace a large interval at the end, as the text requires, it is necessary not only for the Bass to descend, but also for the Soprano <note>original: "Discantum"</note> to ascend—contrary to the usual nature of ending a song—in imitation of pipes and the strings of the Pandura <note>a long-necked, lute-like string instrument</note>. And it is then that the power of the semitone, explained in the previous chapter, shines forth most clearly: because the natural and ordinary ending of a song by ascent loves to overcome a semitone at the finish—at least in those Tones <note>musical modes</note> that do not already have a semitone immediately above the root of their Octave.

<margin>
Why large
intervals are
more pleasing.
</margin>
Thirdly, Galileo <note>Vincenzo Galilei (1520–1591), father of the famous astronomer, who wrote influential works on music theory</note> judged it a question worthy of study: why a Fifth over an Octave <term>Diapente epi diapason</term> <note>an interval of a twelfth</note> sounds more pleasing than a simple Fifth <term>Diapente</term>; and so consequently, why one Harmony is always more pleasing than another. It is not worth the effort to examine the causes he himself brought forward, as they are obscure and uncertain. From my own principles, however, the causes of this matter appear very clearly: For because, by Axiom II of the first chapter, the degrees of knowledge by which the sides of figures differ from each other are also transplanted into the proportions themselves (the offspring of the figures), it is indeed consistent that those degrees by which the demonstration of the Part of the circle and the Remainder <note>original: "Residui"</note> are distant should also distinguish the sweetness of both the Part and the Remainder. Therefore, those Harmonies which exist immediately through the section of the circle itself—namely, those between the Whole and the Part cut away—are more perfect and more pleasing than those between the Remainder and the Whole. These latter are ultimately derived from the former through the admixture of identities of sound <note>octave equivalents</note> from the bisection or doubling of strings. Thus 1:3 holds the first rank and is therefore more pleasing than 2:3; and 1:6 more than 5:6; and 1:5 more than 4:5; and 1:4 more than 3:4; and 2:5 more than 3:5; and 3:8 more than 5:8. For first, the Part becomes consonant through itself, not because of the Remainder; later, and thus more imperfectly, the Remainder is demonstrated to be consonant because of its allied or foreign Part.

<margin>
The goal of
this whole
work.
</margin>
The remaining rules of the art of Composition I leave to the craftsmen themselves to prove or to give the reason for them. For what I have discussed so far is abundantly sufficient for me, both to illustrate the nature of Song (having shown at least its first and general foundations in Nature) and especially for the speculations of the following Book V. The subject matter of that book is proposed as my only goal in this entire work. For as an Astronomer, I discuss regular figures not so much geometrically (except where that geometry seemed incomplete) as astronomically and metaphysically. So also I write about the proportions of song not so much musically as geometrically, physically, and finally, as before, astronomically and metaphysically. For just as I have need of the five regular solids from Geometry, so also do I need the Proportions and the whole Harmonic apparatus from Music to explain the causes of the proportions of the celestial spheres, the eccentricities, and the movements in the Apsides <note>the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the sun</note>. But as for the art of composing song, which is the practice of Music, I by no means profess it; he who wishes to seek it more correctly will do so from the books on the art of musical composition published by the aforementioned Artusi <note>Giovanni Maria Artusi (c. 1540–1613), an Italian theorist</note> and by Seth Calvisius <note>Sethus Calvisius (1556–1615), a German musician and astronomer</note>, a former friend of mine. I name these men not because I think they are the best, but because I have not seen others.

# On the Three Means
## A Political Digression.

<margin>See the most beautiful passage in Bodin’s *On the Republic* <note>Jean Bodin (c. 1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher. His work *The Six Books of the Republic* argued for "harmonic justice" in the state.</note></margin>
The following paragraph was excluded from its proper place at Folio 29, line 9, because the printers had incautiously distributed the leaves of the manuscript (specifically pages 7 and 10). However, those authors who admit proportions of this kind into the State under the title of "Harmonic" should not be blamed on that account. For even if few proportions formed in this way define pure Harmonies <note>In the musical sense of consonant intervals</note>, and all the rest are foreign to Harmonies, they all nevertheless share this definition: they are tempered from both proportions, the Arithmetic and the Geometric. It is from this tempering that they possess their suitability within a State. Conversely, if there is any power of Harmonies within a State, *as* Harmonies, then our harmonic means cannot be scorned, which I provide here under a broader definition:

<margin>What a Harmonic mean truly is.</margin>
> It is everything that lies between two consonant voices, being itself consonant with each of them. Therefore, in sections, etc.

*Hitherto omitted.* Since I have mentioned Bodin in the margin, and having now finished the third book and added the above paragraph, I judged that enough work has been done on mathematical speculations. This thorny material being finished, I decided to transcribe the principal heads of this political dispute from Bodin himself, with the words and order mostly shaped by my own understanding of that passage. I do this both to bring some light to a place that is obscure in itself—for Bodin did not bring enough support from mathematical disciplines to this speculation—and to soften the tedium of the peevish mathematical demonstrations of which this entire book consists by interposing pleasant, popular material, and to offer a taste of its non-negligible use in understanding the State. I shall begin, however, with a fuller mathematical explanation of the matter, adapted to the grasp of the non-mathematical reader.

When equals are added to several numbers without regard for their magnitude, that is an Arithmetic proportion. For example:

| | | | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | 3. | 9. | 5. | 10. | 17. | 38. | |
| **Add** | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | *For just as 6 is greater than 3,* |
| | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | *so too (by just as many units) 12* |
| | 6. | 12. | 8. | 13. | 20. | 41. | *is greater than 9.* |

In this example, the proportion is "disjunct" <note>Meaning the pairs of numbers are separate rather than a continuous sequence</note>. Therefore, a "conjunct" proportion or arithmetic progression occurs when, starting from any number at all, equals are added to it continuously, such as:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **3** | or | **38** | |
| 3 | | 3 | Since, therefore, between 3, 6, 9, 12, and likewise between 38, 41, 44, 47, |
| --- | | --- | there is a continuous arithmetic progression, it happens that the |
| **6** | | **41** | middle of three such numbers placed in sequence is called |
| 3 | | 3 | an Arithmetic mean <term>medietas</term>; just as between 6 and 12, the |
| --- | | --- | Mean is 9; between 38 and 44, the Arithmetic mean is 41. |
| **9** | | **44** | |
| 3 | | 3 | |
| --- | | --- | |
| **12** | | **47** | |

However, when similar things are added to several numbers with regard for their magnitude, then it is a Geometric proportion <note>Kepler is about to explain that geometric proportions involve ratios or multiplication rather than simple addition</note>.

->As for example:<-

| 3. | 9. | 5. | 10. | 17. | 38. |
|----|----|----|-----|-----|-----|
| 9. | 27. | 15. | 30. | 51. | 114. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12. | 36. | 20. | 40. | 68. | 152. |
<note>The OCR provided "35" in the second column, but the subsequent text confirms the intended value is 36, maintaining the triple proportion (9 + 27 = 36).</note>

For just as the triple, 9, is added to 3, so the triple, 27, is added to 9. This sum <note>36</note> is as much greater than 9 as 9 is greater than 3; and as 15 is greater than 5, and so on. Therefore, as 3 is to 12, so 9 is to 36. And as 3 is to 9, so 12 is to 36.

Again, this proportion in this example is "disjunct" <term>disjunct proportion | where the four terms are distinct, a:b and c:d</term>. Therefore, a "conjoined" <term>conjoined proportion | a continuous progression where the end of one ratio is the start of the next, a:b:c</term> Geometric proportion or progression occurs when, starting from any number, either a similar part or a similar multiple is always added to it.

->As for example:<-

| 3 | 10 | 8 |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 30 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 12 | 40 | 12 |
| 36 | 120 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 48 | 160 | 18 |
| 144 | 480 | 9 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 192 | 640 | 27 |

To the initial number, the triple is added in the first two examples, and the half in the third. Again, to the number produced from this, the same multiple or part is added. Therefore, just as 8 is to 12, so this same 12 is further to 18; and so also is 18 to 27. Here, 12 is the Geometric mean <term>Geometric mean | The middle value in a geometric progression, calculated as the square root of the product of two numbers</term> between 8 and 18. Likewise, 18 is the Geometric or proportional mean between 12 and 27, and so on.

These things must be understood first, so that it may be understood what a Harmonic proportion is. For it is defined by Bodin in this way: that in it, *the ratios of equals and similars are moderately mixed* <note>original: "Rationes æqualium & similium sint modicè confusæ"</note>, that is, the earlier ratios are Arithmetic, and the later are Geometric.

Furthermore, this definition is not true. **1.** For there are many ways, even in non-harmonic numbers, by which the ratios of equals and similars can be "moderately mixed"; nor is this sufficient for it to be a harmonic proportion. For other relationships of numbers must also be added, which must be sought from Chapters I, II, and III. **2.** Conversely, there are many harmonic pairings of numbers in which the ratios of neither equals nor similars are contained. **3.** Indeed, there are harmonic proportions in which there is a simple Geometric proportion, such as 1, 2, 4. Even if these are identical <note>in their internal ratios</note>, they do not by themselves produce a particularly pleasing effect—so much so that Bodin denies they create any concord <term>concentus | a sounding together or musical harmony</term> on their own (understand this as "figured" or complex harmony). Conversely, there are other harmonic proportions in which there is a simple Arithmetic proportion, such as 1, 2, 3, and likewise 2, 3, 4, which Bodin—forgetting his own rules—acknowledges as harmonic, even though they have no mixture of Geometric analogy. So too 3, 4, 5; 4, 5, 6; 1, 3, 5; 2, 5, 8; etc. These latter ones Bodin wrongly denies create harmonic concords, rising up against the evidence of the sense of hearing by relying on the authority of ancient writers.

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
However, the assertion is true to some extent regarding that proportion which the ancients, through a false persuasion, called Harmonic. I say "to some extent" if you understand the *Ratios of equals* to be Arithmetic Means <term>Arithmetic Mean | A sequence where the difference between numbers is constant, such as 4, 7, 10 (where the difference is always 3)</term> transformed into other numbers, in which the actual equality of the differences (which existed in the first three numbers) is no longer explicitly shown. For the Harmonic Mean <term>Harmonic Mean | A sequence where the ratio of the differences between the numbers is the same as the ratio of the outer numbers</term> of the ancients is most properly defined as follows: *that the proportion of the differences between the three numbers is the same as the proportion of the outer terms*, as in 3, 4, 6. <note>In the sequence 3, 4, 6, the difference between 3 and 4 is 1, and between 4 and 6 is 2. The ratio of these differences (1:2) is the same as the ratio of the outer terms (3:6).</note> Whatever three numbers are of this kind, whether they are truly harmonic or not, it is always true of them that the ratios of *equals* (or rather *arithmetic*) and *similars* (or *geometric*) are combined in one certain way. 

The method is this: Given the outer terms, like 2 and 5, an arithmetic mean is found. To avoid using fractions, let the doubles of the outer terms be taken: 4 and 10. Their arithmetic mean is 7. Now, in such an arithmetic mediation—4, 7, 10—where the differences are an equal 3 and 3, two proportions are always established: one larger, between the smaller terms 4 and 7; the other smaller, between the larger terms 7 and 10. <note>In ratios, 7/4 (1.75) is a "larger" proportion than 10/7 (approximately 1.43).</note> He who now wants to produce a Harmonic mediation from this Arithmetic one, and mix into it something of a Geometric mediation, should place 

<margin>* 7:10, 4:7 *</margin>

the smaller proportion in the first place and the larger proportion in the second place, and seek a number that has the same relationship to 10 as 4 has to 7. This results in three numbers: 7, 10, and 17 ½. To express these as whole numbers, we use 14, 20, and 35. To this trio, something of an Arithmetic progression has been mixed, though its explicit equality no longer remains. For both proportions of the Arithmetic mediation (between 4, 7, and 10) have been brought here, only with their positions swapped: for just as the first terms there were 4 to 7, here the last terms are 20 to 35. And just as the last terms there were 7 to 10, here the first terms are 14 to 20. In turn, something of a Geometric mediation is also mixed in. For the smaller proportion, 7 to 10, is applied to the smaller terms 14 and 20; the larger, 4 to 7, to the larger terms 20 and 35. Finally, it results that just as the smallest term 14 is to the largest 35, so the smaller difference (6) is to the larger difference (15). <note>14/35 reduces to 2/5, and 6/15 also reduces to 2/5.</note> All these things carry a certain similarity familiar to Geometric proportion; because in a geometric sequence, the ratio of the smallest term to the middle is the same as the middle to the largest.

These mathematical points must be kept in mind, which Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist whose work "The Six Books of the Republic" Kepler is critiquing here.</note> does not seem to have understood sufficiently. He proposes a "Harmonic proportion" using five numbers—3, 4, 6, 8, 12—and claims of them *that equal and similar spaces exist tempered in a certain way*. For when he saw the differences between them were 1, 2, 2, and 4, he recognized an "expressed equality" in the 2 and 2, and a "similarity" <note>A geometric doubling</note> in the 1, 2, and 4. Yet, in the definition provided by the ancients, three terms are sufficient; and that definition contains no such "tempering" of explicit equality mixed with similarity. In the sequence 3, 4, 6, there is no explicit equality of differences at all.

Now it is worth the effort to see how Bodin, who is very wordy on this subject, applies these ideas to Morals and Politics in various ways. It usually happens to him that instead of true Harmonic mediations (whether those of the ancients or the true ones), he seizes upon mere combinations of Arithmetic and Geometric proportions, leaning on his own faulty definition. As this had to be stated at the very beginning, so it will have to be repeated more often in what follows.

I. Since there are three forms of Government: Popular, Aristocratic, and Royal; the popular...

# ON HARMONICS. BOOK III.

<margin>POLITICS.</margin>
[The popular state] he compares to Arithmetic proportion, that of the Aristocracy to Geometric, and the Royal state to Harmonic. For just as in Arithmetic the increments of all numbers are equal, whether they are large or small, so in a Republic <note>Latin: *Respublica*; here referring specifically to a popular or democratic state.</note> the people want the burdens, benefits, honors, and magistracies to be equal for everyone. They do not wish to tolerate any "respect of persons" <note>An idiom meaning favoritism based on social status.</note>; they want, for example, the right of hunting to belong to all, whether they are noble or ignoble, rich or poor. If there is something that cannot be divided among many, the people want it to be decided by lot; for fate is blind, not distinguishing the noble from the ignoble, the rich from the poor, the well-deserving from the undeserving, the virtuous from the vicious, or the ingenious from the stupid. For a person only thinks himself equal to others if he takes his chances with them in such matters, whether he then obtains a good or bad lot. In place of a lot, other means of acquisition can also be used, such as if the choice is permitted to someone who has no personal interest, or who is believed not to look at persons. Thus, in Rome, the Consulship was common to everyone of a certain order; and it was permitted to seek it from the people, but not through bribery, lest the people be corrupted and the wealthy preferred over the poor. Although in this case, by tacit consent, virtue is respected, and the judgment regarding merit and well-deserving individuals is left to the people.

Conversely, just as in Geometry, the excesses of numbers are likened to the numbers themselves—so that a large number has a large excess and a small one a small excess—so in a Republic of the Aristocracy <term>Optimates | The "best men" or the nobility</term> persons are distinguished, and thus burdens, rewards, offices, and duties are also distinguished. The most excellent things are reserved for the Aristocrats, while the remainder is left to the common people. In this case, it is necessary that an arithmetic proportion be admitted separately within each faction: for among the things belonging to the people, all who are in the people shall take their share by lot; and among those of the Aristocrats, all the Aristocrats shall do the same. Unless this is done, there will be constant tiers even among the people, down to the lowest dregs, and constant tiers among the Aristocrats, up to the Prince of the State; by which reasoning it would not be a Republic, but a Royal type of city-state.

The Royal state, however, is most closely likened to Geometric proportion, because all rights of Majesty are reserved for the King, just as he himself surpasses all others either by noble lineage, by arms, or by virtues. Nevertheless, the method of governing in this state can most correctly be tempered from both types of proportion. For the one King, as arbiter of all—not by blind impulse like a lot, but by considerations of virtue, merit, order, and rank—dispenses all things between the Aristocrats and the people as far as is permitted. He executes all parts of distributive and commutative justice. This conjunction of both proportions is sufficient for Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher who argued that a "Harmonic" monarchy was the ideal state.</note> to establish a **Harmonic proportion**. Furthermore, he directs all counsels not so much toward individuals, or specific Orders, or men, as toward the whole body of the City and its safety, mutual charity, and concord. This is not unlike how, in numbers, proportions that deviate slightly from equality and similarity (destroying them if necessary) are referred back to the common harmony of all; in this manner, he will use my harmonic mediations <term>Harmonic Mean | A mathematical middle point that creates a specific musical or structural balance, used here as a metaphor for social stability</term>.

II. From the *Cyropaedia* <note>Xenophon’s "The Education of Cyrus," a semi-fictional biography of Cyrus the Great used as a manual for ideal leadership.</note>, Bodin proposes an example by which all three types of proportion can be explained. When Cyrus was a boy, since a man [of the nobles...]

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
<margin>The judgment of the boy Cyrus.</margin>
When the boy Cyrus <note>Referring to Cyrus the Great of Persia, often used in classical education as a model of leadership and judgment.</note> saw a tall boy wearing a short tunic and a small boy wearing a loose, oversized tunic, he judged that they should swap tunics so that each would have what was suitable for him. However, his teacher declared that each boy should be left with his own property. Now, if the tall boy had been ordered to pay some money to the small boy so that the exchange could finally be made, the teacher would have been perfectly reconciled with his pupil. In this case, Cyrus pushed for **Geometric proportion** <note>Geometric proportion here refers to "distributive justice," where things are assigned based on suitability or merit (the tunic fits the body).</note>, while the teacher protected each boy's own possessions <note>This represents **Arithmetic proportion**, or "commutative justice," where the focus is on strict equality and property rights regardless of fit.</note>. But a third person would have looked at both things at once—the physical need of the bodies and the preservation of each person’s wealth. Thus, he would have asserted **Harmonic proportion** in the sense of Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher who argued that the best state combines elements of both aristocracy and democracy.</note>, which is a mixture of the previous two. Indeed, it is also harmonic in my own sense; for such a person would not hesitate to take the excess cloth from one and money from the other so that both are provided for, because the common benefit of both is achieved through the sweetness of a "concert" or harmony. I have said, however, that it happens that sometimes a Geometric proportion is also harmonic (such as 1, 2, 4), just as it is suitable here for a tall man to have a long garment; but sometimes an Arithmetic proportion is also Harmonic (such as 2, 3, 4), just as it is suitable here that the small boy who owns the long garment should keep his own property, but have it converted into money, which he can use more rightly than a garment that is too large.

<margin>Types of Justice.</margin>
III. Since justice encompasses all methods of governing, he cites from Aristotle <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* defines justice as either "rectificatory" (arithmetic) or "distributive" (geometric).</note> its two parts: **commutative justice**, which deals with arithmetic equality, and **distributive justice**, which deals with geometric similarity. Bodin himself urges a third type of justice composed of both the former types. This type allows for goods to be sold at a lower price to certain people than to others, and it suggests that great things should not always be distributed to the great. Thus, both types of "just" treatment are set aside to some extent if the safety of the whole requires it, or if a public benefit arises from it. A proportion is not well-formed from two other types if it destroys them both. Therefore, this application is more suited to my own **Harmonic means**. For example, in the numbers 2, 3, 5, there is neither an arithmetic equality of differences nor a geometric progression, yet there is a Harmonic relationship between them.

At the end of his book, he applies this to the Poets, who imagine the three daughters of Themis (who is Justice): *Eunomia*, *Epieikeia*, and *Eirene* <note>original Greek: Εὐνομίαν, ἐπιείκειαν, εἰρήνην; translated as Orderly Law, Equity, and Peace.</note>—that is, Laws, Equity, and Peace—as if they were the guardians of the three proportions: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic.

<margin>Marriage laws.</margin>
IV. The laws of marriage, the primary bond of a city, provide a brilliant example of the three proportions. If Patricians <note>The hereditary nobility or upper class.</note> are ordered to marry Patricians, and Plebeians <note>The common people.</note> to marry Plebeians, this is a **Geometric similarity**. If, however, the law allows everyone to seek marriage indiscriminately, whether by chance, or by competing as much as possible for beauty, wealth, or virtue without regard for lineage, and no condition is forbidden: this would be **Arithmetic equality**. But in the former case, the hearts of the citizens are torn apart into factions; in the latter, the social orders are thrown into confusion. Both are ruinous to the Republic. Therefore, Bodin suggests that poor Patricians should sometimes be permitted to marry wealthy Plebeians, and rich Plebeians to marry poor Patricians. For this is beneficial to both orders: to the nobles, so that their increased wealth may protect the rank they hold and the women of that order may be married; and to the common people, so that with an entrance to honors opened to them, they may give to virtue...

# Harmonics Book III. 91

<margin>POLITICAL MATTERS</margin>
...apply themselves; finally to the State <note>original: "Reip." (Respublica), referring to the Commonwealth or organized political community.</note> itself, so that the Social Classes <note>original: "Ordines," referring to the distinct ranks of society such as the nobility and the commoners.</note> might embrace one another with mutual love.

Here again, he [Bodin] breaks the Geometric Analogy <note>A geometric progression (like 1, 2, 4, 8) maintains a constant ratio. In political terms, this usually represents an aristocratic system where rewards are strictly proportional to status.</note> to produce a Harmonic one, yet he does not reduce it to the mere equality of an Arithmetic progression <note>An arithmetic progression (like 1, 2, 3, 4) maintains a constant difference. In politics, this represents a democratic system where everyone receives an exactly equal share regardless of status.</note>. For example, if the Geometric series 1, 3, 9 is broken and becomes 1, 3, 8: just as much as this departs from 1, 3, 9, that much is taken away from the Patricians <note>The aristocrats or upper class.</note>. And insofar as the series 1, 3, 8—whose differences are 2 and 5 (where they were previously 2 and 6)—approaches the Arithmetic progression 1, 3, 5 (where the differences are equal at 2 and 2), that much is given to the Plebeians <note>The common people.</note>. Thus, in the numbers themselves, a "Concordance" <note>Kepler is using a musical term: the ratio 3:8 is a minor sixth plus an octave, a pleasing musical interval.</note> is established among 1, 3, 8; while in the State, a "Concord" <note>Social harmony.</note> is established between the Patricians and the Plebeians, while the distinction between the classes remains. This change of 1:9 into 1:8 will occur in Book V, even in the heavens themselves <note>A reference to Kepler's upcoming proof that planetary orbits follow these same harmonic ratios.</note>.

<margin>The Law of Banquets.</margin>
V. Arithmetic equality is foolish at Banquets <note>original: "Symposijs."</note> if everyone reclines together indiscriminately, with no consideration given to sex, condition, or age. Conversely, a mere Geometric similarity is tasteless. For if the learned are joined only to the learned, how will they benefit the unlearned? If women are only with women, what pleasure is there? If the loud are with the loud, who will model modesty for them? But if you admit neither a blind equality nor a stubborn similarity, but mix both moderately and with the judgment of reason, the proportion will be Harmonic. For you will ensure that the rows of youths and men enjoy the sight of the women; that the youths are governed by the wisdom of the elders; that the women are ruled by the authority of the men; and that the witty stir up the gloomy, while the gloomy in turn are respected, so that the wits do not pour themselves out into scurrility. Again, this is not a composition of perfect types, but a certain "violation" of them so that Harmony may exist.

<margin>Seating at the games.</margin>
VI. It pertains to Arithmetic equality that, in ancient times, the Fathers <note>The Senators or Patricians.</note> were accustomed to watch the games in a promiscuous seating arrangement with the plebeians. It pertains to Geometric proportion that later the Fathers were separated from the plebeians. This is certainly true if you consider the games alone. But if you hold all the benefits of the State in one grasp of the mind: since most of these were claimed for the Fathers by Geometric reason (with the people excluded), this very equalization of both classes at the games belonged to that "tempering" which is, in the sense of Bodin, the Harmonic form of the entire government. Indeed, by this, the plebeians were soothed—as children usually are by trivial things—and were invited to love the higher Classes, without anything being taken away from the dignity of those ranks. <margin><unclear>the same end</unclear></margin> This also fits my "Means" <note>Kepler's mathematical theory of the "Medietates" (Medial proportions).</note>, insofar as the proportion is not strictly kept so that concord may be kept. Previously, in certain persons of the Classes, the Analogy was set aside; now it is set aside in certain rewards.

<margin>Friendship.</margin>
VII. Harmonic tempering gives life to friendships. For what "Concordance" is in proportion, "Love" is in the whole scope of human life—and Love is the foundation of Friendship. But if a mere equality of duties is introduced by Arithmetic law, there will be no friendship except between equals. And if there is a mere and exquisite Geometric similarity of duties between unequals, there will be friendship in neither case. Instead, in the first case, there will be a perpetual haggling and "marketing" <note>original: "nundinatio," referring to a fair or marketplace exchange.</note> of duties for one's own advantage; in the second, a necessary association of Patron and Client, with no freedom to demonstrate Love and nothing spontaneous. Although friendship cannot stand with frequent injuries, it nevertheless rejects laws, and refers everything to the sober and healthy judgment of Love, now equalizing...

# ON PROPORTIONS
M
<meta>catchword: pro-</meta>

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
...now repaying such proportional things, there are places where neither are always such, which seem to happen for the preservation of Love <note>original: "Amoris"</note>: which, just as Harmony is stirred by dissonances, and as fire is stirred by an iron stylus, is poked by certain injuries, and through gracious forgiveness, it renews its strength.

<margin>The Lesbian Rules</margin>
VIII. Bodin beautifully compares **Arithmetic** equality to the iron **Rule of Polycletus** <note>Polycletus was a Greek sculptor who created a "Canon" or rule of perfect proportions for the human body; here it represents a rigid, unbending law.</note>, which would break before it could be bent; he compares **Geometric** similarity to the leaden **Lesbian Rule** <note>In antiquity, a leaden rule from Lesbos was famous for being flexible, allowing builders to measure curved surfaces; here it represents law that adapts to every circumstance.</note>, which was adapted to all angles. He himself sketches the **Harmonic** proportion of his own definition with a wooden Rule, which indeed bends, but returns to its shape immediately.

<margin>Laws and Equity</margin>
IX. In the governing of all kinds of states <note>original: "Politiarum"</note>, the rigor of the laws and the duty of the Judge are compared to **Arithmetic** equality, by which not only is each person given exactly what is theirs, but punishments are also imposed on offenders equally, without respect of persons. By this, Judges are bound to the laws and to what is alleged and proven, so that they may judge according to them, even if the laws seem unfair. Conversely, **Equity** <note>original: "Aequitas"</note> and the pure discretion of a Magistrate—provided he is good and acts from conscience—takes on the nature of a **Geometric Analogy**. But Bodin, using the example of a **Harmonic** tempering, places in the middle the duty of either the higher Courts, or all of them, or the supreme Magistrate. To these, it is not permitted to act out of pure discretion; yet they are allowed to bend the laws according to the logic of the circumstances, though not break them, and to interpret them in judgments according to equity, so long as nothing is taken away from the law through the specific rulings of the courts. He wants the laws to be held like his wooden Rule: that they may indeed yield to a bend, but immediately return. However, in this passage, Bodin has demonstrated by his own example what he had previously affirmed about legal experts: that they understand these **Mathematical** matters less because of their obscurity. For his discussion of **Numbers** does not fit the standard of our discipline; he says it is impossible for a **Geometric Proportion**, which exists between four terms, to be destroyed by any transposition of terms. He asserts that the same analogy exists in 6, 3, 4, 2 as in 3, 2, 4, 6. Not at all! 3 is to 2 as 4 is to 6 <note>Kepler is pointing out a mathematical error: 3 divided by 2 is 1.5, but 4 divided by 6 is 0.66. Bodin's claim that order doesn't matter in geometric proportions is incorrect.</note>. On the contrary, he thinks **Harmonic Proportion** is disturbed by transposition. Certainly, if he recognizes no proportion between two terms alone, he wins the argument.

<margin>What proportion means to me.</margin>
For this is the verbal subtlety of some people, joined with extreme obscurity, that they want to say *Reason* <note>original: "Rationem"</note> in Latin for what the Greeks call *logos* <note>original: "λόγον"</note>, but *Proportion* <note>original: "Proportionem"</note> for what the Greeks call *analogy* <note>original: "Αναλογίαν"</note>. I would certainly wish to be able to imitate that, as I remember having done before now; but the word *logos* among the Greeks is never used in common speech for the word "cause" <note>original: "αἴτιον"</note>, whereas for the Latins, *Ratio* very frequently sounds like "cause" or "method." It is therefore necessary to hold to the custom introduced by the "barbarian" <note>Kepler refers to the medieval Scholastic translators.</note> translators of Greek elements, and to use the word "proportion" for both *logos* and *analogy*; which I do frequently throughout this whole book.

Now, therefore, **Proportion** and **Concord** have been distinguished: the latter is, as it were, a certain quality of the former, and the former is the subject of the latter. Indeed, **Concord** is present in Proportions first and by itself, insofar as they are between two terms; not insofar as there is a certain continuity between several terms.

<summary>Kepler uses metaphors of different types of "rules" to explain how legal systems should balance rigid laws (Arithmetic) and flexible equity (Geometric) through a "Harmonic" middle ground. He also clarifies the mathematical and linguistic definitions of proportion and concord that he will use throughout the work.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Bodin, legal theory, equity, arithmetic proportion, geometric proportion, harmonic proportion, logos, analogy, ratio, Polycletus, Lesbian Rule, legal interpretation</keywords>

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS
### M 3

<margin>POLITICS.</margin>
...of proportion. And the two terms of a proportion are consonant not because of their position—in which one is first and the other second—but insofar as two strings are struck together at the same time. This concord is not changed by changing the position of the characters in writing, or even if the Lute <note>original: "Testudine," referring to a lute or stringed instrument with a vaulted back like a tortoise shell</note> is turned upside down. However, for a proportion that exists between three or more terms, a secondary concordance occurs because of the specific pairs of terms. In these, although the **Analogy** <note>In this context, "Analogy" refers to the specific mathematical relationship or ratio between numbers</note>—that is, the part of them mixed with **Geometric proportion**—can be changed by changing the position, the **Harmonic quality** cannot be changed at the same time. 

Therefore, Bodin argues that these four things—the Law, the Legal Action, Equity, and the Magistrate—are compared to four numbers joined by a **Harmonic proportion**. He claims that just as the harmony perishes if the numbers are transposed, so too is the harmony of the state disturbed if legal processes and execution are held as more important than the Laws, or if the Magistrate is placed before Equity. Yet, this argument should not be referred to what is truly "Harmonic" in proportions, but simply to the nature of proportions themselves (whether **Geometric** or **Arithmetic**). This is that genus of proportion tempered from both which the Ancients, by a certain weak persuasion, called "Harmonic." For it is common to all Analogies, whether simple or mixed—contrary to what Bodin teaches—that they are either changed into other species when the terms are transposed, or they are utterly destroyed. But I return to the matter at hand.

<margin>The necessity of laws.</margin>
If a Magistrate has mere arbitrary power of governing without laws, and neither observes the Law of Nature nor performs the duty of a good and innocent man, he will not be a magistrate, but a Tyrant. Since the number of good Princes is exceedingly small, it is not advisable for the State <note>original: "Reipublicæ"</note> to commit itself to this danger whenever a magistrate is renewed. Even if it happens that the state has a good magistrate for a time, that condition cannot be long-lasting; nor is it healthy for the State. For even if a Ruler is good, he will not always be prudent enough to see what is equitable without the standard of the laws. And even if he himself sees and follows what is right, the citizens will still find fault with even the best actions unless there are laws by which he can defend his deeds to the people. Citizens must be educated by the discipline of laws and deterred from evil deeds by the image of punishments <note>original: "pœnas"</note> prescribed by the laws. Therefore, a State cannot do without laws.

<margin>What equality is.</margin>
In turn, the laws—designated by the Greek word *Nomoi* <note>original: "Νόμοι," meaning both "laws" and "musical modes/melodies"</note>—signify the distributive part of justice, which in a popular state follows **Arithmetic equality**. But if everything were examined according to the rigor of the laws, an injury would be done to many. For laws decide on deeds without defining them by the variety of circumstances; yet individual deeds are described by their own circumstances, by which they are either mitigated or aggravated. Since there is such a variety of these, they can never be encompassed by any laws. Therefore, neither principle by itself alone protects the State; instead, Bodin teaches that they must be mixed, so that there are laws, but few of them (since a multitude of laws is a most fertile field for lawsuits), and many things are reserved for the Magistrate's discretion—not only individual deeds, but also some entire types of deeds and certain other matters of law, especially...

<summary>Kepler critiques Bodin’s musical-political analogies, arguing that political order relies on the inherent nature of proportion rather than literal musical harmony. He concludes that written laws are essential to prevent tyranny and educate citizens, though they must be balanced by a magistrate’s equity.</summary>

<keywords>Harmonic proportion, Jean Bodin, rule of law, tyranny, equity, Nomoi, arithmetic equality, justice, magistrate, political harmony</keywords>

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
...the intensifying and lessening of punishments, the interpretation of the laws themselves, and their application to the circumstances of a deed. Here we are not dealing with the triple form of a Republic <note>original: "Reipub." or "Respublica," referring to the state or commonwealth</note>, but with the triple form of governing within each one. A pure reasoning of equity, loosened from laws, is an aristocratic way of governing, even in a Popular or Royal state. The bonds of the laws create popular government, even in a Monarchy <note>original: "Regio," meaning a kingdom or royal state</note>. But if there are indeed Laws, but they are set aside in certain times and places at the whim of the governor appointed by the supreme power, that governor acts as a petty King <note>original: "Regulum"</note>, even if chosen by the people. Such are usually the Governors of Provinces. He, therefore, either observes the laws or judges based on equity, so long as the safety of the Republic allows; if otherwise, he does not hesitate to overstep. It is as if someone were to admit the types of proportions that create harmony, such as 2:3:4 or 1:2:4; but those that create dissonance, he disturbs and changes into consonants, such as 1:3:9 into 1:3:8 and 3:5:7 into 3:5:8. <note>Kepler compares the ruler's discretion to a musician tuning dissonant intervals into harmonious ones to maintain the "music" of the state.</note>

<margin>Fines.</margin>
X. In the laws themselves regarding monetary fines, *arithmetic* equality is mostly observed, so that whoever commits a crime pays the fine established by law, whether they are rich or poor. Yet one can see where there is also a *Geometric* similarity, such as if a fine is imposed on everyone in proportion to their wealth <note>original: "census," referring to a citizen's registered property or income</note>, or if a reckless litigant loses a certain portion of the valued lawsuit. But if a higher fine is named among all the wealthy, and a lighter one among the poor, and it is exacted equally from each member of that rank, this will be a tempering of proportion called *Harmonic* by *Bodin*. Here the types of proportions are not changed, but rather composed or distributed into distinct subjects belonging to the same whole.

<margin>Sumptuary laws.</margin>
XI. Laws regarding clothing <note>original: "Leges vestiariae," laws intended to restrain luxury or distinguish social classes by dress</note> have much of the *Geometric* proportion; so that the higher the rank of dignity one holds, the more precious the adornment of clothing permitted to him. *Arithmetic* equality is intolerable here. Because it is not only the variety of ranks that demands distinction in dress, but some consideration must be had for wealth and some for merit; nor can all ranks easily be declared under one law. Therefore, some tempering of both proportions is usually introduced into the laws themselves, or partly left to the judgment of the Moderators. Bodin considers this tempering to be *harmonic*, because he defines Harmonies by the joining of two types of proportion. To me [Kepler], it is not harmonic when another proportion is aimed for, and would be expressed perfectly if it could be.

<margin>Punishments.</margin>
XII. Almost the same must be said of those laws which, when they concern punishments, exempt distinguished persons from the danger of execution and Nobles from hanging, and change the type of punishment according to the custom received by many nations. For a defendant who loses the dignity he held is punished more severely by this disgrace (observing *Geometric* law) than if someone who had no dignity were publicly beaten with rods. And so there can be a certain equality of dissimilar punishments, and a *Harmonic* distribution in the sense of *Bodin*, who here rejects *Aristotle*. Aristotle had taught that *Geometric* proportion should be observed in rewards, but *Arithmetic* in punishments.

<margin>Satisfaction.</margin>
XIII. There is also another observable proportion in penal laws with the same tempering; which does not concern the offender, but the honor and vengeance of the injured person. For he who [injures] the Prince of the State is punished more severely...

<header>ON HARMONICS BOOK III.</header>

<margin>POLITICS.</margin>
...one who kills a member of the College of Electors <note>original: "Collegio Electorum," the high-ranking princes of the Holy Roman Empire who selected the Emperor</note> is punished more than one who kills a farmer; and more severely for a free man than a slave. For although this variety is to be referred to a Geometric similarity between the person and the vengeance for the injury inflicted upon them, it is rare. Conversely, in punishments for homicide, there is mostly an Arithmetic equality—especially among Christians, according to divine law, by which man is made equal to man and blood is repaid with blood. This confusion of both types of ratios belongs to what Bodin calls "Harmonic." Most notably, this is seen in the divine law where all assassins are punished with death by Arithmetic equality, yet the *type* of death is in the power of the judge, to be imposed as a Geometric response according to the deeds and the variety of circumstances, which differ widely; as Bodin reports, I believe, from the Rabbis.

Nor is this inequality of punishments granted so much to individual injured persons as to the safety of the entire Republic, which permits all enemies of the fatherland to be killed with impunity, and protects the safety of all citizens together in the safety of the Prince and the Nobles, and in the preservation of public tranquility. It has often been said that the "Public Good" has a certain resonance with the sweetness of a Harmonic concord. If this one supreme law, the mother of all laws, is observed—that whatever the safety of the Republic turns upon be ordered as sacred and legitimate—it is immediately clear that there is a similarity with Harmonic ratios (described according to my own opinion), even if that law contains nothing else similar to either Geometric or Arithmetic proportions. For neither do these numbers 15, 20, 24, 30, which contain a most sweet harmony <note>Kepler refers to the ratios of the Major Seventh chord. 15:20 is a Fourth, 20:24 is a Minor Third, and 24:30 is a Major Third. Together they form a complex but beautiful musical "state."</note>, observe one proportion or the other: for the differences between them are 5, 4, and 6, which are neither equal nor similar in ratio to the terms themselves, nor do they increase in the same order.

<margin>Estimation of a fine.</margin>
XIV. Bodin brings another example, more familiar to the Geometric discipline, in the interpretation of the laws regarding fines; namely, that pecuniary fines established in ancient times should be estimated according to the ratio of present public wealth or poverty. Here, an Arithmetic equality across all times <note>meaning, keeping the fine at the same numerical amount for centuries</note> would be intolerable; yet a Geometric proportion is not easy to observe in all things. Therefore, the judge, according to his prudence and the circumstances of the matters, will seek the **Harmonic mean**. He will take care lest he seem either to have violated the laws, or that through a malicious interpretation of the laws the poor are oppressed while the license to sin is given to the wealthy and more powerful. Indeed, out of a zeal for this same harmony, he will sometimes change a pecuniary punishment (which is Arithmetic) into a corporal one.

<margin>Punishment for theft.</margin>
XV. Bodin approves of the law that punishes thieves by hanging insofar as it rests on the reasoning that thieves should not increase—so that crimes which are likely to be frequent are punished more severely, which tastes of Geometric proportion. He criticizes the same law for its Arithmetic equality. For the legal action for theft is very frequent throughout all towns and villages, and mostly has common judges <note>original: "plebejos," meaning local or non-noble magistrates</note> who, while they hurry everyone equally to execution, do not understand that they are introducing a most unjust inequality of punishments, while they impose the same penalty for crimes that are most unequal in the variety of their circumstances. Most defendants lack the firmness of judgment by which they ought to guard themselves more against misfortune than against the magnitude of the crime: those whom opportunity, hun...

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>A DIGRESSIOIN.</margin>
Hunger, care for children, the hope of staying hidden, or the perception of another’s wealth makes thieves; yet the deed itself, when compared to others, is held in low esteem by natural judgment. This is even confirmed by divine law, which punishes theft only with fourfold restitution. <note>original: "quadrupli tantùm restitutione." This refers to the Mosaic Law in Exodus 22:1, where theft of property is compensated by a multiple of the value, rather than corporal or capital punishment.</note> Nevertheless, if it is just and holy that this class of men—born for deceit and darkness, reflecting the nature of mice, digging through walls—who disturb the public security not only of fortunes but of life itself, should be thinned out for the sake of the **Republic** <note>original: "Reip.," an abbreviation for "Respublica," the state or Commonwealth.</note> like other predatory beasts; certainly the regard for the **Republic**, as has often been said, corresponds to a **harmonic concord**. Nor should this question be handled without the most accurate **harmonic tempering**, lest, while providing for the **Republic**, life be snatched away recklessly for this kind of crime from many who could provide hope of being good citizens in the future.

<margin>Punishment of the excused.</margin>
XVI. Even in the imposition of punishments, it pertains to *Geometric* equity that the punishment of a child is lighter than that of an adult, a youth’s lighter than an old man’s, and a woman’s lighter than a man’s. Nothing here is more unjust than a perpetual *arithmetic* equality <note>Treating everyone exactly the same regardless of their age or status.</note>; yet if this is taken away from the prudence of the judge, to be used according to the situation, the *Harmonic* proportion will nonetheless be disturbed.

<margin>Recidivists.</margin>
XVII. *Bodin* <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher whom Kepler is critiquing/following here.</note> demonstrates *Harmonic* proportion in those laws which, when they first avenge a criminal act equally in all with a light fine—as a sort of warning—afterwards punish those who relapse [recidivists] more heavily, those who sin a third time more heavily still, and finally punish them with death. For there is a mixed *arithmetic* equality in the first act, and a *Geometric* proportion in the repetition, with a heavier punishment for a heavier crime. To *Bodin*, this composition of two into one seemed to constitute a *harmonic* proportion.

<margin>Of Retaliation.</margin>
XVIII. In general, punishments are dispensed either by laws or by the judge’s discretion according to the diversity and magnitude of crimes, and the entire law of *Retaliation* <note>term: "Jus Talionis" — the principle of "an eye for an eye," or equal retribution.</note> is to be attributed to *Geometric* analogy. As for the fact that some legislators avenge unequal types of sins equally: this *arithmetic* ratio has no place among men; in God, whose creatures we all are equally, it is not right for our complaints to find fault. But when legislators, for the sake of the **Republic**, equate certain crimes that are lighter in themselves with the gravest ones by the imposition of punishments; and when in the law of retaliation, not a "tooth for a tooth" but a price estimated in place of the tooth (upon which the litigants can agree) is repaid; and when a person who knocked out one of my two eyes is not inflicted with total blindness because he only had one eye himself—having his own remaining eye plucked out: this, according to *Bodin*, is part of *Harmonic* tempering. For in this way, individual sins have *arithmetically* equal punishments, and diverse sins are also distinguished by punishments.

<margin>Of intent.</margin>
XIX. Those who punish the <term>conatus animi</term> <gloss>attempts of the mind / criminal intent</gloss> with a punishment no lighter than if the effect followed the will, and those who punish an act from which the mind was absent [unintentional acts], establish a "plebeian" *arithmetic* equality with no small fault—the former in dissimilar mental attempts, the latter in dissimilar deeds. He who distinguishes here between the various forms of attempts—so that he who has done everything the mind could devise to bring it to an outcome receives the punishment for the crime, whether he perpetrated it or missed the mark; but he who merely lay in wait for opportunities does not—brings the matter...

He examines how this applies to theft, repeat offenders, and the "law of retaliation," suggesting that practical legal compromises (like fines instead of physical mutilation) represent a harmonic middle ground.</summary>

# ON HARMONICS. BOOK III.

<margin>POLITICS</margin>
...yet the event itself, by whose image a criminal could be deterred, did not occur: here he observes **geometric equity**. He punishes a mere persuasion to crime no less lightly than the crime itself in the perpetrator; and conversely, he punishes the author and instigator more severely than the servant, as one who carried out another's crime. Finally, he punishes more lightly the one whom a great force of lust or anger swept off course, than the one who, calmer than those, carried out everything with a premeditated mind. The same must be held regarding the variety of outcomes. He who robs a traveler of three obols <note>original: "triobolo," a small Greek coin of little value.</note> deserves the same punishment, if he gaped for a great prize in his mind, as he who snatched a talent <note>original: "talentum," a very large unit of currency; Kepler is contrasting intent with the actual amount stolen.</note>. On the contrary, he who took only a modest amount when he could have carried off the whole weight of gold deserves less punishment than he who snatched a purse containing only a few pennies <note>original: "pauculi asses," referring to the Roman *as*, a low-value copper coin.</note>. Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist who argued that the ideal state uses "Harmonic" justice to balance the needs of different social classes.</note> refers these **Geometric** distinctions to the philosophical estimation of crimes; but punishments, by which public examples are set for the sake of public tranquility, he exempts from that all-inclusive equality. Thus, public notice is taken more frequently of deeds that fall before the eyes of the citizens; more frequently, attempts that miss their mark, being generally inconspicuous to the common people, are passed over unpunished, or punished more lightly than was **geometrically** fair, so that less cruelty is found in the judge. So many considerations for the public good savor of something **Harmonic**.

<margin>The law of voting.</margin>
**XX.** In judgment and in consultations, the ratio is **Arithmetic** if votes are counted; it is **Geometric** if they are weighed, either by the weight of the person casting them or by the quality of the arguments. The **Harmonic** (in Bodin’s sense) was a mixture used among the Romans, where those of Consular rank explained their opinion in a speech, while the rest walked to the side of the opinion they approved. <note>original: "pedibus in eam ibant sententiam." This refers to the Roman *pedarii*, junior senators who voted by physically moving to one side of the house or the other without speaking.</note> To me, what was done by the law of necessity (for there would not have been enough time to hear everyone) does not seem comparable to **Harmonic** proportion.

<margin>Commutative justice</margin>
**XXI.** In **commutative justice** <note>Justice concerning the exchange of goods and services, ensuring that what is given is equal to what is received.</note>, Aristotle required **Arithmetic** equality. Bodin says even here **Geometric** analogy is not excluded, although the examples seem confusing. 1. For instance, if someone has harmed a private individual while also causing a public scandal: he will satisfy the private individual separately with **arithmetic equality**, and no more will be restored to him for his property from a nobleman than from a farmer. However, that nobleman will pay for the very bad example in one way, and the farmer in another, preserving the **Geometric** proportion of their social status. In this point, Aristotle is reconciled with Bodin.

<margin>Creditors.</margin>
2. But the fact that the assets of an insolvent debtor are distributed according to the size of each debt, without respect for the individuals, provided they were equal in the time and quality of the credit, is indeed done by purely **geometric** proportion. Aristotle did not deny this, but seems to have omitted it through thoughtlessness, and it is rightly supplied by Bodin. Although this is founded on the **arithmetic equality** of the payment and the debt, if the assets were sufficient. Yet a superior magistrate is not entirely forbidden from using a **harmonic** tempering, and preferring poor creditors to some extent and according to the circumstances <note>original: "pro renata," meaning as the situation arises.</note> over the wealthy ones.

<margin>Restitution for theft:</margin>
3. That also savors of something **harmonic** (in Bodin's sense); that by the custom of certain nations, things taken by theft are not compensated by a single amount, but by fourfold, and other things by fivefold. The rule applies equally to everyone, yet unequally to different things; in this, the different magnitude of the injury is estimated by a **geometric** ratio, not the bare price of the object.

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
DIGRESSION.
Damages.
</margin>

4. Harmonic proportion is more evident in the compensation for damages not caused by malice alone: in these cases, much depends on the circumstances of the actions of both parties in a contract. Sometimes—either by law or by the order of a Magistrate—these circumstances require an equal and arithmetic compensation; sometimes none at all; and there are instances where they require a moderate compensation based on fairness and goodness <note>original: "ex æquo et bono," a legal principle meaning "according to the right and good."</note>.

<margin>Arbitrators.</margin>
Of this kind also seems to be the fact that a superior magistrate does not allow everyone to try their case by the same law among themselves, nor in all causes. Instead, as the circumstances dictate, he either appoints arbitrators himself or permits the litigants to choose them; this is done so that either the interests of both parties or the interests of the State <note>original: "Reip:" short for *Respublica*.</note> may be served.

<margin>Interest.</margin>
5. Even interest <note>original: "usuræ," referring to the charging of interest on loans.</note> belongs to the commutative part of justice; yet legislators do not permit the same rates for every class of men. Instead, through a "geometric mixture," rates are unequal for persons of different social ranks, but equal for individuals within those ranks. Bodin calls this composition "harmonic."

<margin>
Remuneration.
</margin>

6. I shall quote an excellent exception to the arithmetic equality of exchange in Bodin's own words: *“A doctor often receives (indeed, demands) 500 gold coins <note>original: "aureos D."</note> for removing a stone <note>The "stone" refers to a bladder stone, a common and painful ailment requiring surgery in the early modern period.</note> from a wealthy man, but from a poor man only 10 or 5 (or indeed nothing, according to the formula of the Hippocratic oath). If they were to follow an arithmetic or geometric analogy in every respect, the one would perish from the stone and the other from hunger. But by harmonic proportion, wealth is provided to the one and health to the other (though not with the same certainty).”*

<margin>
The judge’s fee.
</margin>

7. According to this same reasoning, judges have also been accustomed to demand a fee and honorarium for their labor in deciding cases. For often the difficulty of the most trivial lawsuits is greater than if the matter concerned the weightiest things, yet they remain unprofitable for the judges. It is fair, therefore, that a slightly larger fee be demanded from the awarded claims of the most significant matters. This applies, specifically, if the judges do not receive a sufficient salary from the State, but—to reduce litigation—are ordered to seek compensation for their labor from the taxes of the litigants. However, I leave this "Harmonic harmony" to the author Bodin, the Frenchman; among us Germans, the courts in the principal cities and provinces are kept far from such filth; nor is it permitted to demand anything beyond what the law prescribes.

<margin>
Division of inheritances.
</margin>

8. The distribution of inheritances equally per capita for both sexes is carried out by arithmetic laws: so that those who are equal by birth may also be made equal in the proportions of the property left by the same father. But when the State's interests are considered, landed estates pass to the males, who are fit for necessary military service, while money passes to females and to persons consecrated to God. While the first-born are preferred over the others either by a larger portion or by possession of the whole estate <note>original: "totius assis," a Roman legal term for the entirety of an inheritance.</note>, the rest are provided for either with equal portions among themselves, or by a legacy, or by the right of use <term>usufruct<gloss>the right to enjoy the use and advantages of another's property short of destroying or wasting its substance</gloss></term> alone. This is done so that a certain image of leadership—useful to the state—may be established within families. This occurs by harmonic proportions, which are sometimes quite harsh and dissonant for individuals because arithmetic equality is disturbed; yet they conspire toward the preservation of the entire city.

<margin>
Forms of Government.
</margin>

XXII. In a popular government <note>democracy</note>, which is formed from Arithmetic equality, and in an aristocratic one, which comes from Geometric similarity; yet some method of blending is often maintained. As when the People themselves...

<summary>Kepler discusses how harmonic proportions allow for flexible justice in legal damages, medical fees, and inheritance, arguing that while these "proportions" may seem unfair to individuals, they preserve the stability of the state. He notably disagrees with Bodin regarding judges taking fees from litigants, calling the practice "filth" compared to the German system.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s exploration of Jean Bodin’s political theories, applying the mathematical concepts of arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic proportions to the structure of government and social classes.</meta>

### ON HARMONY, BOOK III.
N 2

<margin>POLITICS.</margin>
A ruler, being in control of affairs, of his own accord grants honors, magistracies, and priesthoods primarily to the patricians <note>The hereditary noble class in ancient Rome</note>; or, when the Aristocrats <note>original: "Optimates," the "best men" or traditionalist senatorial faction</note> allow the common people to share in some honors, they grant the most profitable duties to the commoners alone. They most severely avenge injuries inflicted upon the commoners by the Aristocrats and grant them the freedom to enjoy pleasures, which in itself suggests a "popular" or democratic state. They allow the common people a certain right of suffrage in naming a set number of candidates from among the aristocratic families; from this number, the Aristocrats themselves later entrust the magistracies to whomever they wish.

As long as this sharing of power exists by the free will of that Order which holds supreme command, a most sweet harmony <note>original: "concentus," a singing together or concord</note> of peace among the citizens endures. But if it is revoked, first the complaints of the penalized party emerge, then discords follow—as if the musical harmony were disturbed—and finally, either the command is transferred to others, or the entire state falls to its enemies. The same must be held regarding the Royal state, to which the <term>harmonic ratio</term> <note>A mathematical proportion where the middle term relates to the extremes in a way that mirrors musical intervals</note> is familiar: in a monarchy, the one King stands as far above all others as he alone possesses the supreme right of command; all others live beneath him in <term>arithmetic equality</term> <note>A state where everyone is treated exactly the same, regardless of status or merit</note>.

In this form of government, therefore, there can be three kinds of governing methods, which we touched upon above in Section IX; but there we dealt with the subject matter, and here we deal with the persons or Orders who are members of the Republic. For if a King communicates all duties equally, making no distinction between the nobility and the common people, the moderation will be popular and similar to an arithmetic proportion. This is not becoming of supreme majesty, for the highest person would be joined to the lowest dregs with no intermediate order placed between them—a thing which Nature, however, loves. Indeed, citizens of a noble character will leave the kingdom if there is no respect given to their lineage.

On the other hand, if the King bestows everything upon the nobility and excludes the common people entirely, this will be a <term>Geometric</term> <note>A proportion based on ratios rather than simple differences, often favoring those with higher status</note> form of commanding. This is dangerous and lacks "harmonic sweetness." For the people, being powerful in their great numbers, will eventually become offended and strip the Nobility of their magistracies and honors, and the King himself of his command. Even if a Governor distinguishes the Orders into many more levels and distinguishes their duties with great subtlety, if he still reserves for each order its own duties alone—such as in Rome where the <term>Tribunate</term> <note>An office representing the commoners</note> belonged to the common people alone, and the <term>Consulate</term> <note>The highest elected political office</note> belonged only to the patricians—the Orders will be alienated from one another and will not grow together into one body with firm concord. For the duties of the lower classes will be despised along with the order itself. This went so far in Rome that a patrician could not hold the Tribunate unless he renounced his nobility; and when the common people finally extorted the consulate for themselves, those few commoners who became Consuls began to despise the common people from then on.

Bodin proposes the idea of these disputes using numbers: first with these three: 4, 6, and 7. Here, 4 represents the King and 6 represents the Nobility, and he notes there is a harmony between them. But 7 represents the common people, a number which he rightly asserts is discordant with both of the former. He could have better used these: 4, 6, and 9. For just as 6 makes a harmony with 9, but 4 makes none with that same 9, so it is easier for the Nobility to associate with the common people than it is for the King. And just as 6 is the <term>Geometric mean</term> <note>The middle value in a geometric progression</note> between 4 and 9, harmonizing with both, so the Nobility is placed as a connecting link <note>original: "vinculo"</note> between the King and the lowest commoners.

He represents the Aristocratic form of governing a kingdom with the numbers of a "disjointed geometric proportion": 3, 6, 5, 10. He compares this "disjunction" to the dissensions in a State resulting from an over-accurate exclusion of the orders from one another.

<summary>Kepler applies musical and mathematical proportions to social classes, arguing that a stable state requires a "harmonic" middle ground (the nobility) to bridge the gap between the ruler and the common people.</summary>
