# ON PROPORTIONS
### V
<meta>Catchword: non</meta>

<margin>A DIGRESSIO.</margin>
[...] not ineptly. But this is poorly done, that he treats this disjunction <note>A "disjunction" in mathematics refers to a gap between two ratios, such as 3:6 and 5:10, which are equal in value but separate in their terms.</note> as if it were a matter of discord. For all these numbers—3, 6, 5, 10—create a common harmony. As has been said often, <term>Geometric Analogy</term> <note>The comparison of two equal ratios, e.g., A is to B as C is to D</note> has nothing to do with the quality of a Harmony, nor does the difference or disjunction within that analogy affect it. And even though, as if correcting himself on the same page, he provides another example of numbers in a disjoined proportion intended for the same purpose—namely 2, 4, 9, 18—in which the sounds denoted by 2 and 4 truly differ from the sounds 9 and 18, this musical discord does not arise from that geometric disjunction. Rather, it arises from its own proper causes: specifically, because the side of a Nonagon <note>original: "latus Nonanguli"; a nine-sided polygon. In Kepler’s theory, only shapes that can be constructed with a compass and straightedge are "harmonic." The nonagon is not, so the number 9 creates discord.</note> is not among the *Musical* ratios. Finally, consider the temperament of both 

<margin>
The Temperament of Royal Governance.
</margin>

forms of governing in a Royal state: for instance, that some commoners be mixed into the duties of the Nobility, but only a few, and those equal to the burden by their wealth, or recommended by virtue or some other quality; and that occasionally one of the poorer Nobles be placed in charge of a productive plebeian function, surrounding it with the honor of his lineage, so that it might become more commendable to the common people in the future. Or that a <term>Duumvirate</term> <note>A board of two officials</note> be established consisting of a Noble and a commoner, as a consolation to both orders; that a court be established from persons of all orders; that in deliberations concerning the public good, the poor be mixed with the wealthy; and that those who merely cultivate virtue and piety should not hold everything, but that some things be reserved for the brave, some for the ingenious, some for the prudent, and some for those powerful in experience. To each should be given those duties for which they bring fit talents and the greatest protection. This temperament, I say, is expressed by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist whose work Kepler is critiquing</note> with the Numbers 4, 6, 8, 12, believing that he is providing an example of what he calls a "containing Analogy," but what geometers call a <term>continuous proportion</term>. Here again he is mistaken: for 4 is not to 6 as 6 is to 8 <note>4:6 is a ratio of 2:3, while 6:8 is 3:4; therefore, they are not the same ratio</note>. Yet this much is true: among all four—4, 6, 8, 12 (or in their smallest terms 2, 3, 4, 6)—there is a common concord, regardless of the fact that 2 and 3 sound together in one way, 3 and 4 in another, and finally 2 and 4 or 3 and 6 in yet another. Therefore, whatever similarity exists between numbers and the Republic, it resides in them insofar as they are associated with geometric or arithmetic progressions (or a mixture of both) separately from Music. Or, conversely, if <term>Harmonic proportions</term> of Numbers bring any light to the understanding of Politics, they do so by themselves, apart from any consideration of geometric proportions.

<margin>
The true idea of a Harmonic Best Republic.
</margin>

And truly, if I had acquired a knowledge of the Republic and were acting as a Political philosopher in this book, I would use a distinction of matters to rewrite Bodin’s entire passage. In this way, Aristotle’s own decrees would remain unshaken, and Bodin would learn to philosophize better in politics from my "Harmonics," separately from Aristotle. I would say that the status of the State and its form of government is one thing, and the administration of justice is another; for they differ as a part differs from the whole. In the same way, in Mathematics, the Geometric and Arithmetic proportions of numbers are one thing, while musical concords expressed by numbers are another. Certainly, those who hold power—whether it be one, few, or all—establish the judgments. Yet those same people are occupied with the protection of the Republic and rarely exercise judgments themselves, except when it is permitted to use their own discretion, released from the laws. 

<margin>
Geometric and Arithmetic proportions do not pertain to the "Reason of State" as Harmonic ones do, but only to judgments.
</margin>

On the contrary, the higher duties are rarely entrusted to Judges; rather, laws are prescribed to which they are bound. Therefore, I would relegate Geometric and Arithmetic progressions to judgments along with Aristotle, without mixing in the respect for harmonic concords that happens to occur in them. For the "temperaments" in judgments that Bodin has desired up to this point are eventually devolved through appeals to the supreme moderator of the Republic himself. And it is then that he [the ruler] derogates from those proportions which Aristotle gave to Judgments and justice;

# BOOK III OF THE HARMONIES

<margin>POLITICS</margin>
[The ruler] no longer acts as a judge, but performs a higher duty, protecting the Republic and its individual members. To this Moderator, whether he be a king, the Nobles, or the whole People, I would certainly recommend **Harmonic proportions**—not through any <term>geometric Analogy</term> <note>The comparison of two equal ratios, such as 2:4 = 4:8</note>, nor through any <term>Arithmetic equality</term> <note>A sequence with equal differences, such as 2, 4, 6</note>, but through a simple regard for harmonies. I would command those subtle Analogies to give way to Harmonic harmonies, so that the rigid administration of both types of justice yields to the supreme commands and safety of the Republic. Oh God, what a harvest of disputes would arise here if someone wanted to go through each point by comparison! For consider the nature of each thing. Geometric analogy is common to Numbers and to continuous quantity, appearing in numbers only later, namely when the shaping of quantities allows them to be expressed by a number. Now it very often happens that the terms involved in a Geometric Analogy are <term>ineffable</term> <note>original: "ineffabiles"; in mathematics, these are irrational numbers that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction, which Kepler associates with the "rigid" and sometimes impractical nature of abstract law</note>, and the further we progress, the more they degenerate from expressibility. On the contrary, every **Harmonic proportion** can be expressed in numbers. What else does this mean when applied to politics, other than that the most just sentences of judges—exactly measured to the norm of the laws and equity through the subtle arguments of lawyers—must be precise; but on the other hand, the moderation of the Republic, which is free from such constraints, must be accommodated by the will of the ruler to the safety of all, according to the times and without much noise. Here the question should be divided into parts: how the crude ratio of **Arithmetic progression**, lacking any noble form and insisting only on the dimensions of matter, might be likened to commerce, crafts, and the commoners' way of life; and how **Geometric similarity** (observing only one law and caring nothing for whether the line it looks upon is the side of a pentagon or a triangle, or whether it is expressible or ineffable) might sketch out the simple office of judges. But **Harmonic ratios**, arising from many regular figures that can be known <note>Kepler refers to shapes that can be constructed with a compass and straightedge</note>, joined together from different kinds into one structure, represent the many distinct duties of the empire, for each of which there is its own proper law, separate from the others. Here, following Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist whose work Kepler studied deeply</note> (further below in the appendix to Book V), regarding the genres of harmonies and song:

<margin>Peace from the Soft Gen[re], War from the Hard G[enre]</margin>
The **Soft** <note>original: "Molle"; referring to the "soft" hexachord or minor-leaning scales, associated with sweetness and peace</note> would indeed be given to Peace, and the **Hard** <note>original: "Durum"; referring to the "hard" hexachord or major-leaning scales, associated with vigor and war</note> to War; and the disagreements of these genres would be the same as those of both times in the state. Truly, I leave these things to be cared for by others, to whose way of life they are more suited; I myself now hasten to the subsequent materials of my profession. Therefore, I will first finish with **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a famous French political philosopher who attempted to use musical ratios to describe the ideal state</note>. For I am arriving at the end of his book, and at the same time at the beginning of my third book.

<margin>The idea of a Kingdom in Numbers</margin>
XXIII. Now Bodin, passing over entirely to music as it has been described by me apart from Geometric proportions, and accommodating it to politics (as I also prefer), argues nothing more brilliantly in his whole book than what he says about the form of a Kingdom expressed by the numbers **1, 2, 3, 4**. Since these are the first in nature—and indeed Unity is the beginning of numbers—they are compared by a pleasant play of wit to the beginning of quantities, the **Point**, and from there to their three kinds: **2** to the line, **3** to the surface, and **4** to the body, in almost the same way I recounted from the Pythagoreans at the beginning of this third book. Then, for him, Unity is the **King**, the deputy of the almighty God in the Republic. **2** is the **Sacred order** [the Clergy], **3** is the **Military** or Knightly order, and **4** is the **People**, which is indeed fourfold: Farmers, Scholars, Merchants, and Artisans. Here he recounts the harmonies contained between these numbers in the same way I used above; however, he has a vain reason for fearing to proceed to the number five, as if harmony would be disturbed—which is clearly false from this entire book. Let there be other valid reasons for stopping at the **Quaternary** [the number 4]. Furthermore, he demonstrates that this form of the Republic is reflected in Man himself...

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION. The Soul.</margin>
...from Plato, in which he demonstrates that the faculties—1. The Mind, 2. The **Reasoning faculty**, which spreads itself into <term>syllogisms</term> <note>Logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>, 3. The **Spirited faculty**, and 4. The **Desiring faculty**—are located in the brain, the chest, and the belly, separated by harmonic intervals. These are likened to the parts of a state: the first to the **Empire** (the ruler), the second to the **Counsel**, the third to the **Military order**, and the fourth to the **Common people**, who possess the greatest share of it. From this arise the four pillars of the Republic: **Justice, Prudence, Fortitude, and Temperance**, truly called the "hinges" of the state, with each being especially entrusted to its own Order. Bodin has become so much a musician, having set aside Geometry and Arithmetic, that he has not even forgotten dissonances; under this image, he suggests that a magistrate may sometimes permit honors and other rewards of virtue to go to someone undeserving without being troubled. He argues that just as the rest of the harmony is better recognized and more greedily enjoyed by the opposition of a single dissonance, so too will everyone who sees and loathes the "fake" <note>original: "fucum," referring to a pretense or dye</note> version of such benefits in the Republic become more and more accustomed to fleeing similar vices and pursuing virtues.

<margin>The World.</margin>
XXIV. Finally, Bodin compares the State he has described to the world itself, showing how God the Creator adorned that work of His by joining the ratios of equal and similar things into one **Harmonic harmony**. In this premise, I agree with him most strongly. Indeed, the things that he and preceding philosophers did not even touch upon—concerning the most accurate harmonic tempering of certain motions—I supply in the following books and bring to light with the clearest demonstrations. However, I do not cease, even at the very end, to speak out against the wandering Bodin; for true Harmonies do not exist from the mixed ratios of equal and similar things, as has been said quite often. Therefore, Bodin, thinking he is demonstrating Harmonies in the world, instead demonstrates **geometric means**, equalities, and similarities: 
1. He demonstrates <margin>Namely, in each faculty, the very number that Bodin assigns to it.</margin> Harmonic ratios in the faculties of the Soul, but those are only symbolic, expressed without any evidence of proof in a solid form (as the Mathematical sciences prefer); for it cannot be understood how quantities, the next and immediate subject of harmonies, can exist within the Soul. 
2. Equality between the body of the World and the universal power of matter. 
3. Similarity (of quality based on shapes, rather than a relative similarity of quantitative terms) between the **Eternal Archetype** and the **Form of the World**; at this point, Bodin touches my heart, as he has—though through ignorance—touched upon the subject matter of my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>Kepler’s first major work (1596), which proposed that the distances between the planets were determined by the five Platonic solids</note>.

Yet, how much more plausibly is this mixture of equals and similars demonstrated regarding the primary parts of the World in Book IV of my *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy*—concerning the **Sun as the Mover**, the **Sphere of Fixed Stars as the Locator**, and the **Intermediary space** granted to the moving planets. For equality is established in the parts of matter, so that there is as much matter in the Sun as there is in either the circuit of the outermost sphere or in the intervening space. Indeed, to matter, as to the common people, **arithmetic equality** is due. Conversely, a **Geometric similarity** of proportion is found in the density of these three bodies; and again, another between the diameters of the moving Sun, the region of the Planets, and the ultimate, immobile, locating sphere of the stars. 4. Furthermore, he demonstrates **Geometric means** in a certain way: as between two kinds of motions, one toward the east and the other toward the west, a third, the **Trepida-**...

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS

<margin>FOR CHAPTER VI. ANIMALS.</margin>
The pious claim that they have produced the Harmony of Book III from five and two, with a thicker vertical line: of the squaring into a broad skin, **Leather**; the seal, between metals and minerals, **Stone**; **Fruit**; that which is Inspiration, and between breath and voice, **the Leap** <note>original: "Saltum"; here referring to a musical interval or a rhythmic jump</note>; that which is among quadrupeds and Amphibians, in the Airs, **the Bird**; prayers, between Men and Brutes, from the Stem, **the Shrub**; spirit, between Angels and Souls, from Wood, **Kindling** <note>original: "Fomentum"; literally tinder or fuel, used here metaphorically for the spark of life or spirit</note>; those who are conformed not only in mind but in body—do they also have access to the Harmonic melody? This same thing applies much from this point as the goal for this book, namely **Water**, **Air**, **Fire**, **Earth**, and the rest.

But it reminds us not a little, but a great deal, that just as in governance, retreating, it ascends by action into the animal virtue by a nod (which are claimed to be in human Bodies), powers seem to be added, quantities as they exist among themselves; it also kindles the way of proportion to the fitting proportions from these, and that is an example of divine reason; [fitting] to God, to death; the good body has its own proper mode and sings altogether rightly. It is distinguished by Harmonic song: but so the creature approaches, because it is prohibited by the nature of reason (for the mind has that determined), rather than by this vice; but He willed us to have a living soul of God among us, with which it might sing: I have spoken and I have lifted up my soul <note>original: "Dixi et animam levavi"; a play on the common phrase "Dixi et salvavi animam meam" (I have spoken and saved my soul)</note>.

# JOHANNES KEPLER’S
# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

# ON THE HARMONIC
## CONFIGURATIONS OF THE SIDEREAL RAYS
### in the Earth, and their effect in stirring up weather phenomena and other natural matters.

->**PROCLUS DIADOCHUS**<-
->Book I, Commentary on Book I of Euclid<-
->*On the use of Mathematics in Natural Philosophy and Politics: which chiefly concern that Harmonic part regarding Radiations.*<-

> For the contemplation of Nature, it supplies all the most important things, declaring the most beautiful order of Ratios, according to which this whole Universe was fabricated; and the Analogy of proportions, which connects all mundane things among themselves, as Timaeus <note>A reference to the character in Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, who describes the mathematical creation of the world</note> says somewhere, and which reconciles friendship among conflicting things, and response and mutual affection between those most distant. (And a little later) From there it is also possible, by reasoning, to hunt out favorable configurations <term>angulationes: The geometric angles formed between planets as seen from Earth, often called "aspects"</term>. (Again) This I think Timaeus also wished to signify, while everywhere through mathematical terms, he passes down the contemplation of the Nature of the whole universe, and depicts the origin of the elements with Numbers and Figures, and attributes their powers and affections, and even their effects, to these (figures); establishing acute or obtuse angles, rough or smooth sides, etc., as the causes of all kinds of changes.
> Truly, regarding the aforementioned doctrine of Politics, how could it be denied that it contributes many and wonderful things; while it measures out the opportunities for conducting affairs, and the various circuits of the whole universe, etc. And Harmonic numbers, as moderators of life, or authors of incongruity, and in general as helpers of impetus or relaxation, etc.

# Preamble & Rationale
## for the Order of the Work.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring floral patterns and scrolled leaves within a square border.</image-desc>

We have established Harmonic proportions, considered in the abstract, in the first three books. Of these, the first presented the geometric properties of individual figures; the second exhibited the congruences of joined figures; and the third derived the Harmonic proportions.

It remained for us to introduce the harmonic ratios described so far into the World in three other books. The first was to attribute harmonies to God, the Founder of the heavens; the second to Nature, the administrator of various motions; and the third to Man, who possesses a voice born of motion. However, the nature of the subjects to be discussed persuaded us not only to reverse the order—beginning with human song, moving from there to the works of Nature, and so finally to the work of Creation, which was the first and most perfect of all—but also to join the end of abstract speculation with the beginning of concrete harmonies in Song within that same third book. Therefore, having made the beginning of this introduction into the World in the preceding book, and having assigned the harmonies to human song (which others are accustomed to embrace with the general term "Art"), there now follows the fourth book, which in this reversed order assigns the second parts of concrete Harmony to Nature.

And although I touched upon the discussion of the essence of harmonies scattered throughout Book III, I nevertheless decided that the full treatment of this metaphysical discussion should be reserved for the beginning of this fourth book for the same reason. For since the common run of philosophers looks for Harmonies nowhere else but in song, and since for most people it is an unbelievable teaching <term>Acroama: literally 'a thing heard,' referring here to a profound philosophical doctrine or lecture</term> when it is taught that sounds are one thing and the Harmonies thought to be within the sounds are another, some allowance had to be made for the weakness of understanding. The origin of Harmonies had to be explained in musical terms commonly known, so as not to disturb the reader's eagerness with the untimely subtlety of metaphysical questions.

<margin>Yet Socrates in Plato, as cited by Proclus in Book I on Euclid, defines that musician as one who proceeds from those harmonies which are present in the senses to imperceptible harmonies and the investigation of their proportions. He eventually emerges as a Philosopher, having been awakened by both harmonies to contemplate the First True Being and truth itself.</margin>
But now, since the intention is to reveal Harmonies in Nature and in the motions of the Heavens, the common crowd of philosophers immediately conceives of the vocal music of the stars upon the first mention of Harmony, to be perceived by hearing. Like Cicero’s Scipio, they stand with ears pricked, ready to catch *so great and so sweet a sound* <note>original: "tantum & tam dulcem sonum"; a reference to the "Music of the Spheres" in Cicero's *Dream of Scipio*</note>. Since those unskilled in things are inclined to argue with that same dreamer Cicero that *such great motions cannot be stirred in silence* <note>original: "Non posse silentio tantos incitari motus"</note>, and with the Pythagoreans (following Aristotle) to give a reason why the heavenly sound is not heard on Earth—preconceived opinions which greatly hinder readers striving toward the inner secrets of Nature—they might even deter many who possess strong judgment and are followers of truth. Disdainful of these Pythagorean trifles <term>nugamenta: nonsense or trivialities</term> barely recognized from afar, they might throw the book aside unread. For these reasons, this very place seemed suitable for me to bring in this most necessary discussion.

<header>ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV.</header>

I was also moved by the example of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian polymath whose work on music theory and astronomy Kepler both admired and critiqued.</note>: who, when he had completed the harmonic doctrine concerning song in the first two books of his own *Harmonics*, and had undertaken to demonstrate in the third book that all perfect natures participate in harmonic power, began his own discussion with this very same question: *To what category of things should the Harmonic Nature or force, and its science, be referred?* <note>original: "Sub quod genus rerum referenda sit Natura seu vis Harmonica, ejusque scientia."</note> Therefore, although I have relegated my examination and critique of Ptolemy to the appendix of this work of mine, the question of what answer should be given to Ptolemy’s inquiry based on my own principles ought to be placed at the beginning of this fourth book for the reason stated. This serves not only to fortify the reader and turn away unfavorable opinions, but also to provide a fundamental explanation for the entire fourth book. Since we are about to speak concerning the <term>harmonies of the sidereal rays</term> <note>Kepler is referring to the light from planets and stars and the specific geometric angles—aspects—they form with one another as seen from Earth.</note>, of what kind and how many they are, and by what geometric principles they are formed, we must first know the essence of harmonies, apart from and outside of sounds (which do not exist here) and even outside the consideration of the rays themselves. We must ask: what is their proper subject; what are their boundaries; do they exist in things outside the intellect, or only in the soul; by what means are they perceived and received within; by what standard are they judged; and what effect follows this perception and recognition, and by what author or prime mover? Once these matters are explained, both in general and through a comparison of specific subjects, it will then be easy for us to discourse <term>Metaphysically</term> on the essence and properties of Souls and of <term>sublunary Nature</term> <note>The physical realm of Earth, situated "under the moon," which was traditionally thought to be the only place subject to change and decay.</note> itself, and to place the secrets of Nature in a greater light than they have been until now.

*Chapter VI. What kinship the Aspects have with Musical Consonances in their Number and causes.*
*Chapter VII. The Epilogue contains a contemplation of sublunary Nature and the lower faculties of the Soul.*

# CHAPTER I.
## On the essence of harmonic Proportions, both sensible and Intellectual.

As I prepare to dispute the essence of Harmonies, I find myself doubting whether it is clearer to first seek out the opinions of the ancients and then compare them with my own, or to begin with the exposition of my own opinion. The former method of philosophizing has been accepted by everyone and is frequently commended by Aristotle; the latter seems to better suit the present subject matter. For few have touched upon disputes concerning the *Essence of Harmonies* in their specific form. And if they have said anything about the subsistence of mathematical Genera and species—which could be applied to Harmonies specifically—that subject is necessarily full of obscurity in the philosophy of the Pagans <note>original: "philosophiâ Gentilium"</note>. Consequently, the reader’s mind fluctuates in doubt between a love for most beautiful dogmas and a suspicion of a fabricated thing. In the assemblies of Christians, if one embraces with firm faith the most holy Mystery of the Trinity and the origin of all things from the Mosaic history <note>Refers to the Book of Genesis.</note>, the main points of the dispute can be both more clearly proposed and find the minds of readers more inclined to believe. Therefore, so that we may unfold the method of what is to be said, we must begin with a division.

<margin>Division of Harmonies.</margin> For <term>sensible Harmony</term> <note>Harmony perceived through the senses, like hearing a chord or seeing a geometric alignment.</note> (or its analogue) is one thing, and <term>pure and secret Harmony</term> <note>Harmony that exists as a mathematical concept in the mind or in the divine plan, independent of physical objects.</note> apart from sensible things is another. Sensible harmonies are many, both by reason of their subjects (which differ in species) and by reason of individuals. But pure Harmony, separated from sensible subjects, is one and the same in every species. For example, there is one and the same species of Harmony that arises from a double proportion <note>A 2:1 ratio.</note>. If this is present in sounds, it is called a <term>Diapason</term> <note>The musical interval of an octave.</note>; if it is in radiations, it is called an <term>Opposite Aspect</term> <note>An astronomical "aspect" or angle of 180 degrees between two planets.</note>. In a musical system, it is either higher or lower, sharper or deeper, whether of human voices or of sounds from instruments. Nor is it less manifold in Meteorology; for it is either of Saturn and Jupiter or of another pair, and either from the equinoctial signs or from the Tropics.

<margin>Sensible Harmonies.</margin> We ask, therefore, concerning both kinds: how do they subsist? Does each exist through itself, or in other things? As far as sensible harmonies are concerned, four things concur for their *Being*: 1. Two sensible things of the same genus and quantity, so that they can be compared to each other on account of quantity; 2. A <term>comparing Soul</term> <note>original: "Anima comparans." A central concept for Kepler: harmony does not exist in the objects themselves, but is created by a mind recognizing the relationship between them.</note>; 3. The inward reception of the sensible things; 4. A suitable proportion, which is defined as Harmony. If any one of these is removed, the sensible Harmony is taken away. 

<margin>Order is required for the Being of Harmonies.</margin> For it is easy to understand that the Nature of Harmony is not to be defined by sensible things alone, such as by a sound or the ray of a star. For a sound is one thing, and a certain *order* between different sounds is another. I mean "order" in this place not because of a position in some physical location, nor because of time, but because of highness and lowness of pitch. Different sounds can exist, but unless there is a certain order between them—which is defined by certain proportions, a mathematical matter—there will be no Harmony between the voices. Conversely, if the sound is removed, what audible Harmony could be imagined? And if the rays of the planets are removed, what Harmony of con-

For the Order we are speaking of here is a relation, and things that are ordered are related to one another. Therefore, because harmonies are made of sounds, they are an **accident**, specifically

<margin>
Harmony is an accident of sensible things.
</margin>

one that exists within subjects and does not stand apart from them, and it can be absent without the destruction of the subjects themselves. <note>An "accident" in Aristotelian philosophy is a quality that can change or be removed (like the color of a shirt) without the object itself ceasing to exist.</note> Next, just as quantity in general cannot be separated from its own bodies, yet can certainly be increased or diminished along with those bodies while remaining an accident; so too this very Order of sounds—under which as a genus we have placed Harmony—cannot be taken away from sounds (provided there are more than one) that are distinguished from each other by the quantity of high and low pitch. For either they will cease to be "several," or if they are several, there will be an order between them according to excess and defect <note>original: "excessum & defectū," meaning the difference in pitch</note>; though that order is changeable if either of the related subjects is changed. Therefore, Order walks step-by-step with quantities, and specifically with number. Thirdly, just as Number is defined as a multitude built out of units—in which Aristotle recognizes something analogous to matter, namely its units, and something formal, namely the concept of the mind, which recognizes that multitude of individual units as a single thing separated from the rest in some respect—so the same philosopher says elsewhere that if the **counting Soul** were removed,

<margin>
The Soul is required for the existence of Harmony.
</margin>

all number would be removed, but not the individual units. Thus, number is in the things themselves *materially*, being nothing besides them, unless a **counting Mind** is added; for only then is number something apart from the things themselves and abstracted from them, a different thing altogether—namely, a concept in the mind of a plurality of individual things. In the same way, the order of sounds and other sensible things of which we treat here is nothing other than the several sounds themselves, unless a Mind is added to compare the sounds to each other as they differ in pitch. Indeed, in general, every relation is nothing without a Mind, except for the things it relates; for related things are not what they are called unless some mind is supposed which refers one to the other.

Therefore, what is true in general regarding order and relation must be applied most strongly to Harmony, which consists in proportion and in the counting of equal parts of quantity. That is to say: for any sensible harmony to subsist and be able to exist, besides the two sensible terms, there must also be a **comparing Soul**. For if this is removed, the terms will indeed be two sensible things, but they will not be one Harmony, which is a <term>being of reason</term> <note>original: "ens rationis," a philosophical term for something that exists only in the mind, like a concept or a memory.</note>.

<margin>
The existence of sensible Harmony requires the reception of external things into the Soul.
</margin>

We must now also look at the third point: the reception of sensible things into the soul, its necessity, and its manner.

Doubtless, Harmony is a single thing, but the sensible terms outside the Soul are not a single thing; nor can they be united anywhere except inside the soul. However, they cannot be inside unless they are received inwardly, which does not need to be proven with many words from experience. To be sure, a Musician, a creator of symphonies, can contemplate Harmony in his own mind between two or more voices which he has not yet received from the outside; but that harmony is not, in that act, *sensible*, and we are speaking of the essence of *sensible* harmony.

But what is the nature of that reception? Do not the sounds—to use a well-known example in place of all others—remain outside the ears in the air, and before the sounds, do not the movements of the bodies remain, according to whose quantity the sounds follow? Do they not remain in their own bodies? How then do they enter? I respond,

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>...partly by acting, and partly by being acted upon; acting, while they emit species <term>species: in 17th-century science, these were the "forms" or "images" that objects were thought to radiate so they could be perceived by the senses</term>; struck by their own motion, they emit sounds; bright things emit the rays of their light and color; and as we say when we describe objects "moving" the senses—for to move is indeed to act. Yet they are acted upon <note>original: "patiendo," the state of being passive or receiving an action</note> not as things in themselves, but through their species. When these species are felt, remembered, and compared, they must always, by common usage of speech, be said to "suffer" or be acted upon. And entirely this very unification of two terms in the Soul, through which the Essence of Sensible Harmony results—that is, the act of being related and compared—is for the things taken together something of the same sort as being seen or heard is for individual things, and even less than that. For all these things are certain "passions" <note>acts of receiving an external impression</note>, though the word is used equivocally <note>original: "æquivocè," meaning the word has multiple different meanings in different contexts</note>, covering a wide range of significance.

<margin>The degrees of the various meanings of "passion"</margin>But let us establish the degrees of these "passions." First, for the sake of example, Water is acted upon when, being cold, it grows warm from the application of fire. In a second sense, we say that moisture is acted upon even when it acts itself, namely by wetting dry things: for part of it is drawn into the dried-out passages and mixed with them, which is a form of being acted upon. Likewise, water is "acted upon" when it is tasted, for the thirsty person swallows and digests part of it. But in a third sense, water is acted upon in tasting when it is merely touched by the tongue—not only because it is warmed by the heat of the tongue while it cools the tongue with its own coldness, nor only because some water sticks to the tongue, but simply because it is touched by the tongue. This is like being very gently struck, or pulsed, or pushed, which results in the local motion of parts within the whole; and to be moved is to be acted upon.

Let there be a fourth sense in which water is said to be acted upon: when it emits vapor that strikes the nostrils and is perceived by smell. To be perceived is to be acted upon; and here, it is not the water itself that is acted upon, but its bodily outflow, by which "passion" some part of it is consumed. A fifth degree by which water is understood to be acted upon is when its noise is heard: first, the water itself is in motion; then the immaterial species of the water, as it is moved, is diffused from it in every direction and received into the passages of the ears. This reception is a "passion"—not of the water itself, but of its species or its immaterial outflow. In this reception, something is lost over time and through the frequency of the receptions. For a sound is duller when it strikes the ears or clothing of a great multitude, or when it is emitted amidst falling snow.

Sixthly, when water is seen, it also undergoes something: for it emits rays to the eye from its surface (or nearly so), specifically from its colors, insofar as it is colored. These rays are touched, reflected, refracted, and forced to a point; they are caught, once gathered, by the net-like membrane <note>the retina</note>. All these are "passions," not of the water itself, but of the immaterial species or the rays. And these rays, in this reception, lose nothing, neither in space nor in time: for if the thing touching them is removed, they continue further, entirely undiminished, which sound does not do.

Seventhly, after these species—and indeed the body of water itself—have first acted upon the bodily instruments of the senses, they affect those instruments to match themselves and make the instruments like them. Thus, the membranes of the tongue and skin perceive cold and flavor; the spirits of the nostrils perceive odor; the auditory spirits resound with its sound; and the visual spirits shine with its light. In this way, a sensory image and species is formed, which the eyes certainly carry around even after the object is removed, often against a person's will. Now, these sensible species from the thresholds of the senses

or openings [of the senses], they are received inwardly through a representative or imaginative power; they are recognized by the common sense; stored by the memory; brought forth by recollection; and judged by the superior faculty. All these things are understood to be "acted upon," <note>original: "pati," the passive state of receiving an impression</note> not in themselves, but in their sensible and mental species <term>species: the mental images or "forms" of objects that the soul uses for thought</term>. Then, therefore, even the supreme faculty of the soul—which presides over number and comparisons—takes one unified form for itself from many mental species of things, shaping it into a form of relation, order, and comparison. It compares the things existing outside with one another. This comparison, as we said above, occurs regarding the things themselves, but without their own effort; thus, it is understood to be a certain "passion" <note>a state of being acted upon</note> belonging to them. It is in much the same sense as when a legal judgment is made regarding the reputation of someone who is absent and unaware, or when someone is condemned to death or outlawed in their absence. This is an entirely fitting analogy; for just as such a person, even if they feel no harm at that moment and thus suffer nothing physically, will a little later experience the force of what they "suffered" in actual reality. In the same way, sounds—and anything that shares in congruence—are either continued or rejected, fled from, prohibited, hindered, suppressed, or ended, according to whether they have pleased the mind in this comparison. I do not say that the sounds are "acted upon" only in respect to this subsequent outcome, but in that very act when the mind compares them with one another. It is enough to have explained at length by what degree of equivocal meaning I call this mental comparison a "passion." But I have not been lengthy in listing these meanings in vain: for these <gloss>works</gloss> will henceforth wonderfully assist us in recognizing the Nature of the <gloss>Harmonic</gloss> Faculty and in completing this part of Metaphysics, which Aristotle did not even get a glimpse of.

<margin>
Are sensible
harmonies
concrete or
abstract?
</margin>

From these points it is also clear what I was contending before: namely, that the formal essence of sensible harmony, insofar as it is harmony, "happens" to sensible things, just as it happens to them to be seen or heard and so on. Secondly, it is clear that sensible harmonies are things in some way abstracted from the objects themselves, insofar as it is not the objects themselves outside, but the species of things entered through the senses and brought to the tribunal of the soul, which become the "terms" of the sensible harmonic proportion. Yet, conversely, these harmonies are still "concrete" <note>physical or tied to matter</note> for two reasons: first, because these species of sensible things are not images of their bare quantity alone, but also of their sensible quality—such as sound or light, etc. Second, because these sensible species, as sensations, cannot shine within the soul unless the things themselves of which they are species are also present and remain outside. For if those objects are removed, their species inside also cease—light, indeed, regarding its radiation, in an instant; sound, however, within a very brief moment of time. To be sure, some impression remains in the sensory instruments, as light does in the eye, but that is not the external thing itself, but rather a "species of a species" impressed into the body, having now become a momentary quality of the body. This is similar to what happens in optics, where colors—though the pure light of the sun is not colored at all—conceive the power of radiating color in every direction. And this is what we also contended at the beginning: that the sensible terms and the Soul must both be present and perform mutual works—the former by acting and moving the senses, the latter by being acted upon and comparing—so that the essence of Sensible Harmony may be established.

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>
CHAPTER I.
To what extent the Soul makes Harmonies and to what extent it finds them.
</margin>
...[to] find a suitable proportion: which was the fourth and formal principle of sensory harmony mentioned above: therefore, it might seem that the soul could be absent while the Essence of Harmony remains intact.

I respond by inversion: To find a suitable proportion in sensory things is to discover, recognize, and bring into the light the similarity of that proportion in sensory things with a certain archetype of the truest Harmony which is within the Soul. Just as the Athenians found a certain virtue in Zeno, they did not "find" the right of their Prytaneum <note>original: "Prytanei sui jus"; the Prytaneum was a public hall in Athens where distinguished citizens were honored at public expense</note> in him, but rather they conferred it upon him—an honor which Zeno could not have attained without the Athenians. In the same way, the Soul finds order and proportion in sounds and in rays (though it does not even find the proportion itself outside, but at least the terms <term>terms: the individual parts or numbers that make up a ratio</term>, as has been said). That this proportion is "harmonic" is something the Soul itself creates by comparing it with its own Archetype. It could not be called harmonic, nor would it possess any power to move souls, if this Archetype were not present. So much, then, for Sensory Harmonies.

<margin>
What is insensible Harmony?
</margin>
For we must now pass on to the pure and secret Harmonies, the other member of our division: namely, those which we have just now established as the Archetypes or Paradigms <note>original: "Paradigmata"</note> of sensory harmonies. For if these Archetypes had their own existence outside the Soul, I confess indeed that we would be deprived of a great argument for asserting the necessity of the Soul in constituting the essence of Harmony. But to establish them outside the Soul is a contradiction in terms <note>original: "oppositum in adjecto"</note>, as we shall hear.

<margin>
Its terms.
</margin>
For the principles of true and archetypal Harmony—which exists without being confused with any sensory appearance—are nonetheless divided and multiple in number. Since it too is a proportion, it therefore requires its own two terms. These terms, as we used in the previous books, are the whole Circle and its Part or parts—either an aliquot <term>aliquot: a part that fits into a whole an exact number of times, like 2 is an aliquot part of 6</term> or multiple parts—with the arc cut off by demonstration. This is the specific difference of harmonic proportion, by which not only is harmonic proportion distinguished from other proportions placed under the same category, but also the pure and archetypal is distinguished from the sensory—except insofar as by the most common popular usage, only the "Concord" of sounds is called Harmony. For in this very thing the clearest distinction appears between pure Harmony and sensory or "concrete" Harmony: in pure harmony, the terms are from mathematical categories—the Circle and the Arc—formed in a certain way. For the circle has its own formation or configuration from itself; the arc has its terms from the Subtense <note>original: "Subtensa"; a straight line or chord connecting the two ends of an arc</note> and its figure from the circle. In sensory Harmonies, however, there is no need for this special formation, for they can be either straight lines or other sensory quantities shaped differently, provided they are faithful examples of this archetypal Harmony of theirs in whatever quantity they possess. This is as much as there can be of faithful imitation in sensory things: because what is near to the truth in them, according to "more or less," is accepted as the truth itself. These, then, are the terms of archetypal harmony.

<margin>
For the BEING of abstract Harmony, Mind is required.
</margin>
Then, besides the terms—again, as was said before regarding sensory things—the Mind is also required, which compares the terms and judges whether they (namely, the arcs of the circle) are such that some side of a demonstrable figure would cut them off from the whole circle. Thus, there are in a sense three principles of Harmony...

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>Harmony is a qualitative Relation</margin>
Since every proportion—and thus also this proportion of a part of a circle to the whole—belongs to the category of Relation, this specific and defined form of proportion presents itself as a "quality of the fourth kind" <note>In Aristotelian logic, the fourth species of quality refers to form and figure.</note>. Indeed, Harmony is a somewhat qualitative or "figured" Relation, precisely because it is shaped by regular geometric figures.

If it was previously essential to the nature of sensory harmony that physical things should flow into the soul through a mental image, how much more necessary is it here for the terms of "secret harmony" we mentioned—the Circle and its Arc—to exist within the mind itself? Whether one says this happens through images received from the outside, or that these forms have endured alongside the Mind itself, present within before any sensory reception, is a question we must now examine with all our intellectual strength.

<margin>How the Genera and Species of Mathematical things exist in the Soul.</margin>
Now that we have reached this point, we cannot—without doing a great injustice to the reader eager for philosophy, as well as to the Ancients who walked this path before us—conceal their views on these same matters, at least as far as we understand them. I believe only one thing must be established first: we must distinguish between the mathematical "species" <term>species: here meaning the mental forms or "blueprints" of shapes like circles</term> themselves (the Circle and its Arc) and the comparison between them. I say this because if the species themselves, as the component parts, are to be placed inside the soul without being "received" from outside, then Harmony—which is the relationship between those parts—must even more so be placed in the mind. Its very nature does not exist outside the mind, since its essence consists in a specific action of the mind regarding those forms. The circle and its arcs are in the Soul in such a way that they are also, beyond controversy, in sensory objects; but Harmony, which exists between the circle and its part, is in its "formal" aspect <note>The "formal" aspect refers to the conceptual structure or definition of the harmony, rather than the physical sound.</note> in no way outside the soul, as was shown previously using the example of Number. The arguments of the ancients are chiefly concerned with the species themselves, which are simpler things; Harmony, however, is a more complex matter.

This is the point of difference between Aristotle, Plato, and Proclus on one side, and Ptolemy on the other. For the former group disputes the "Being" of the species, while Ptolemy disputes the "Being" of Harmony. But we shall relegate Ptolemy's text to the Appendix of this entire work, lest he stir up the confusion we feared at the start of this chapter; instead, we shall now listen to those who speak most pertinently to our current investigation.

<margin>Plato's doctrine on the existence of Mathematical things.</margin>
Plato's opinion regarding Mathematical things was this: that the human mind is self-taught regarding all species (figures), axioms, and conclusions; when the mind appears to be "taught," it is actually nothing other than being reminded by sensory diagrams of those things which it already knows within itself. He represents this with singular skill in his dialogues, introducing a young boy who, when questioned by a master, answers everything exactly as desired <note>Kepler refers to Plato's *Meno*, where a slave boy "recollects" geometric truths.</note>.

<margin>Aristotle's contrary doctrine.</margin>
Aristotle, on the other hand, in his *Metaphysics*, calls this invention a **fictional argument, forced to suit a hypothesis** <note>original Greek: "λόγον πλασματώδη, πρός τήν ὑπόθεσιν βεβιασμένον"</note>. For he argues that these Mathematical things never exist separately from sensory objects; nor do they have any other...

...where does such great certainty and such accuracy come from in these reasons (or definitions)? But it is impossible for it to come from sensible things; for is there not a much greater subtlety and exactness in these Reasons themselves? It must therefore come from the soul, which grants perfection to imperfect things and bestows that precise subtlety upon things that are not accurate at all.

For tell me, where among sensible things can be found the indivisible nature of a **point**, or a thing lacking width (**like a line**) or depth (**like a surface**)? Where is the equality of lines from a Center <note>The definition of a circle.</note>, or where are the ever-constant Proportions of sides (the subject of my Book I), or where are the perfections of right angles? Indeed, I do not see them, as all divisible things are mixed and confused among themselves; nothing is pure, nothing is free from its opposite; all things are divisible, whether they are separated in space or united. How then shall we grant a durable essence to unchangeable things derived from things that move and are constantly changing? For they themselves concede that whatever derives its existence from moving essences must have a changeable existence. And how shall we obtain accuracy for precise and certain forms <note>original: *species*</note> from those that are not accurate? For everything that is the cause of a constantly changing notion is itself even more so. It must therefore be supposed that the Soul itself is the progenitor <note>The source or "mother."</note> of mathematical forms and Reasons. <margin>The true essence of mathematical things is in the Soul.</margin> And if the soul, containing these within itself as first patterns or Paradigms <note>Ideal blueprints of reality.</note>, causes them to exist according to their essence—so that generations (the Christian understands this as the creation of sensible things) are nothing other than the propagation of forms that were already within it—then we shall agree with Plato. (For Christians know that the mathematical reasons for creating bodies were co-eternal with God, and that God is Soul and Mind in a super-excellent way; and that human souls are images of God the Creator, even in their essentials in their own way.) By saying these things, the true Essence of Mathematics will have been found by us. But if the Soul, while not possessing them nor having previously received Mathematical Reasons from elsewhere (as if they had not been created along with it), nevertheless wove this admirable immaterial adornment and labored at this most beautiful speculation—how then will it discern whether these things thus produced are stable and constant <note>original: *monima* (stable), I do not read it as *gonima* (productive/generated)</note>, or whether they vanish into the winds as phantoms rather than truths? For in this way, we would make their existence a matter of chance, tending toward no goal or limit. Therefore, mathematical forms are the offspring of the Soul itself, and it does not derive the Reasons it establishes from sensible things; rather, the latter are propagated from the former. These labors of the soul and these "births" <note>Kepler uses the metaphor of childbirth for intellectual creation.</note> are the evidence of permanent and perennial forms.

The Soul is the completion of all things; and this is a certain other adornment (beyond the sensible world) which both brings itself to things and is brought by a familiar and kindred principle; it fills itself with life and is filled by the Creator, in an incorporeal and non-local way. *And this Timaeus must be followed, who completes and perfects the Soul's entire origin and construction from Mathematical classes, and places the causes of all things within it. Again, the principles of Shapes are placed within the Soul in an architectural or craftsmanship-like manner; and the first and most principal of all motions, which surrounds and urges all other motions, existed together with it; for of all things that move, the principle is the circle and circular motion. Nor will it ever cease to generate and bring out one after another, while it strips its indivisible Ratios of their simplicity. For the Soul received all things beforehand, in the manner of principles and primary species; and according to its infinite power, from these anticipated principles, it builds the progressions of every kind of speculation. Thus far Proclus.*

I wanted to transcribe this entire passage because it not only establishes that the genuine terms of Harmonies—the Circles and arcs cut from shapes—exist essentially within the Soul and the mind among other mathematical things (so that these mathematical things become the Soul's own, and the Soul in turn becomes a kind of Essence for them, insofar as they are separated from individual objects), but also because for me, presenting similar arguments, it removes the resentment of having rejected Aristotle here and there; and it exceptionally commends this whole philosophy.

Regarding Numbers, I would hardly contend; indeed, Aristotle rightly refuted the Pythagoreans. For numbers are, in a way, "second intentions" <note>A logical term for concepts that exist only in the mind, abstracted from real objects.</note>—indeed, even third and fourth, and there is no limit to them. Nor do they have anything in themselves which they have not received either from quantities, or from other true and real beings, or even from various "intentions" of the Mind.

<margin>CHAPTER I. On Climacterics.</margin>
...[were to occur] <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page.</note>; and so I do not grant anything to the "Platonic Numbers" assigned to the revolutions of commonwealths <note>original: *Platonicis Numeris, conversioni Rerump. tributis*. Plato suggested in the *Republic* that certain numbers govern the timing of political change.</note>, which Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher who used numerology to explain history.</note> uses in his *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History*; nor do I grant anything to the so-called "Climacterics" <note>Critical or "dangerous" years in a person's life, traditionally multiples of 7 or 9, thought by ancient astrologers to be periods of major change.</note> for their own sake, except insofar as they count the revolutions of the stars and their configurations: as I clearly indicated recently in the *Prolegomena to the Ephemerides*.

But regarding continuous quantities, I completely agree with Proclus; although his speech flows like a torrent, overflowing its banks and hiding the dark shallows and whirlpools of doubt, while his mind, full of the majesty of such great things, struggles in the narrow straits of language, and his conclusion—never satisfying itself with the abundance of words—exceeds the simplicity of the propositions. I think, therefore, that if I now add my own reasons why I establish the "intellectual Circle" and its parts as the boundaries for insensible Harmonies (reasons conceived before I had read Proclus), I shall not only say things consistent with Proclus, but also provide a summary of the passage described, at least insofar as it serves my purpose.

<margin>The boundaries of insensible harmonies are abstract quantities.</margin>
I will not say among my reasons that those things being compared were first outside, then in the senses, and finally "abstracted" from things and from the sensible appearances of things—which is the meaning properly produced by the word "abstracting." For, as said above, this method of abstracting pertains to the sensible harmonies of sounds and rays, and it takes place only when sounds and rays are judged according to an Archetypal Harmony already present within, just as the good or bad deeds of citizens are judged by laws passed in antiquity.

But this is the reason why that which provides the boundaries for harmonic proportions is said to be an "intellectual quantity": because it is necessary for that quantity to be capable of a far more subtle demonstration. Indeed, that demonstration is never obtained from sensible diagrams, even if it is aided by them; nor does it arise from the collection of many individual sensible things into one Axiom, but is obtained *a priori* <note>Known through theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note>. Since Proclus previously and rightly objected this against Aristotle—regarding the intellect in general—I can make this point most secure in particular by the clearest arguments drawn from my first book. For the specific difference of the figures which cut off a harmonic arc of the circle, by which their essence is explained as part of the definition, is this: that they must be "knowable" <note>original: *scibiles*. In Kepler's geometry, this refers to shapes that can be constructed using only a compass and a straightedge.</note>. Now truly, what "knowability" is there without a Mind capable of knowledge? And do not say it is possible for a thing to exist while the knowledge of the thing does not; for knowledge consists in comparison, as when the side of a figure is equal to the radius. Now, equality that exists without a mind—especially in things separated by space—cannot be understood; and we are brought back to the argument already brought forward above even for sensible harmonies.

Nor is it enough for them to be "knowable"; they must also be *known*, so that the Archetypal Harmony might shine in actuality within the soul. For the mere possibility of knowing is not sufficient for us to judge sensible harmonies. Therefore, that thing whose essence is partly within the soul—and thus in its operation or energy—must itself be established within: namely, the boundaries of harmonies, the Circle, and its parts.

The soul possesses knowledge of mathematics by instinct.
</margin>
You may ask how there can be knowledge of a thing which the mind has never learned, and perhaps cannot learn, if it were deprived of the sensing of external things? To this, Proclus responded above in words well-worn in his philosophy; today, if I am not mistaken, we shall most correctly use the term **Instinct**. For quantity is known to the human mind and other souls by instinct, even if it were deprived of every sense for this purpose: the mind understands a straight line by its own nature, it understands an equal interval from a single point by its own nature, and by these it imagines a circle for itself. If it can do this, it can much more easily find a demonstration within it, and thus fulfill the office of the eye in looking at a diagram (if indeed it has need of one). Indeed, if the mind itself had never possessed any eye, it would demand an eye for itself for the comprehension of things placed outside of it, and it would prescribe the laws for forming it, sought from within itself (provided it were pure and healthy and without impediments—that is, if it were only that which it is). For the very recognition of quantities, innate to the mind, dictates what the eye ought to be: and therefore the eye was made as it is because the mind is as it is, and not the other way around. And why say more? Geometry, coeternal with the Divine Mind before the birth of things—God himself (for what is in God that is not God himself?)—supplied God with the patterns for creating the world, and passed into man with the image of God: it was not, after all, received within through the eyes.

<margin>
Proclus says almost the same thing a little after the place first cited: That mathematical essences are assimilated in truth to the gods, and that the Creator of the whole universe used mathematical archetypes, as coeternal things, in the conformation of the world.
</margin>
Since, therefore, "demonstrability" <note>The quality of being able to be proven through logic and geometry.</note> exists in quantities, not insofar as figures are subjected to the eyes, but insofar as they are open to the eyes of the mind—that is, insofar as they are not so much "abstracted" from sensible things as they were never "concrete" with them—we rightly establish abstract quantity as the boundaries for the Archetypal <term>harmonic proportions</term> <note>The fundamental ratios that Kepler believes govern the structure of the universe, based on the division of a circle.</note>, since these are derived from the demonstrable divisions of a circle.

There is another reason why I choose abstract quantities: because the circle, which is a figure—namely a species of the fourth quality—although it is a quantity, is nevertheless considered in this business purely as a figure, without distinction of large or small; so much so that it is in a way abstracted even from quantity itself (as if from its own subject), and its nature can be recognized even in the narrowness of a point. I believe Proclus intended this when he said that mathematical things exist in the soul in an incorporeal and non-extended way.

<margin>
The symbolism of divine and human things in quantities.
</margin>
Finally, there is this greatest and most fundamental reason: that there is a certain wonderful and plainly divine "polity" <note>An organized system or "government" of ideas.</note> of quantities, and a common symbolism in them of divine and human things. I have written here and there about the foreshadowing of the Holy Trinity in the sphere—in my *Optics*, in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Referring to his 1609 work *Astronomia Nova*.</note>, and in the doctrine of the sphere—which I wish to be repeated here. There follows, therefore, the straight line, which from the flow of a point in the center toward a single point on the surface, sketches the first rudiments of creation, emulating the eternal generation of the Son (the center's egress toward the infinite points of the whole surface, by infinite lines, under a most perfect equality for all, being figured and depicted), which straight line is the element, naturally, of corporeal form. This line, drawn in breadth, now foreshadows the corporeal Form itself, creating a Plane: but a sphere cut by a plane represents a Circle by its section, the genuine image of the created mind, which is set in charge of ruling the body: which is in that proportion to the sphere as the human mind is

to the divine—namely, like a line compared to a surface, though both are circular. Toward the plane in which it exists, however, it relates as the curved to the straight, which are <term>incommunicable and incommensurable</term> <note>original: "incommunicabilia & incommensurabilia" — meaning they do not share the same properties and cannot be measured by the same unit; a straight line cannot perfectly "measure" a curve</note>. The circle exists beautifully both in the cutting plane, circumscribing it, and in the sliced sphere, by the mutual meeting of both: just as the soul exists in the body, informing it and connected to the bodily shape, while also being sustained in God, like a kind of irradiation <note>A glow or beam of light</note> derived from the divine countenance into the body, drawing from there a more noble nature. This cause, just as it establishes the circle as the subject and source of terms for harmonic proportions, so it especially commends abstraction. This is because the sketch of the soul’s divinity exists neither in a circle of a specific size, nor in an imperfect one (such as material and sensible circles). Most importantly, it is fitting that the circle be as abstract from the physical and the sensible as the principles of the curve—the symbol of the Soul—are distinct and, as it were, abstracted from the straight line, which is the shadow of bodies. We are, therefore, sufficiently equipped to seek the terms for harmonic proportions (which are objects of the soul alone) primarily from abstract quantities.

To conclude this section, let us gather the main points together. Sensible harmonies <note>Harmonies we can hear or perceive with our physical senses</note> have this in common with <term>Archetypal harmonies</term> <note>The "original" or "blueprint" harmonies existing in the mind of God and the soul</note>: they both require terms, a comparison of those terms, and the energy of the Soul itself. In this comparison, the essence of both consists. However, the terms of sensible harmonies are themselves sensible, and must be present outside the Soul; the terms of Archetypal harmonies are already present within the Soul. Sensible harmonies, therefore, additionally require reception through an image <note>original: "speciem"</note> emitted from themselves, which reception is performed by the senses, the servants of the Soul. They also require another comparison: that of each sensible term with each Archetypal term (for instance, a physical circle with the mental concept of a circle). But the Archetypal harmony needs neither of these, since its terms are already present in the soul, born with it, and are indeed the Soul itself. Nor are they an image of their own true Paradigm <note>A perfect model</note>, but are, as it were, their own Paradigm. Thus, the simple comparison which the soul performs between its own parts, so to speak, completes the entire essence of the Archetypal Harmony. Finally, the Soul itself, engaged in this activity, is the Harmony we are proposing—just as, without regard to this activity, it is the circle and its parts (the terms of Harmony). In the end, Harmony is thoroughly given a soul, and even made divine.

Yet we do not yet seem to have touched upon the question most suited to our purpose, which lies not so much in the harmonic proportions themselves as in the harmonic faculty of the Soul—namely, the power of acting according to proportions. We have discussed proportions for the sake of their own Essence; now we must discuss them for the sake of the Soul itself.

<margin>
## CHAPTER II.
How many faculties of the Soul are occupied with Harmonies?
</margin>

There are two faculties concerning harmonic proportions: one is mental (or nearly so), operating through <term>discourse</term> <note>Latin: "discursum" — the step-by-step process of reasoning from one premise to another</note>, and the other is operative. The mental faculty is itself twofold: it is either *inventive*, finding proportions within abstract quantities, or *perceptive*, recognizing chosen proportions in sensible things <note>Objects that can be perceived by the senses</note>. Therefore, the faculty that investigates harmonic ratios is the same one that embraces all other sciences and arts: namely, the superior part of the human Soul. Regarding God, we say nothing here, for He does not investigate anything through discourse or study, but knows all things from eternity.

That faculty which perceives and recognizes noble proportions in sensible things (or in other things established outside itself) is an inferior faculty of the soul, which directly shapes the senses; or it is an even lower faculty, namely, the <term>vital soul</term> <note>The "anima vitalis," responsible for basic life functions like growth and instinct, rather than high reasoning</note>. This faculty does not "reason" as Philosophers do, nor does it use a formal method. It is present not only in humans, but also in wild beasts and cattle, and even in the <term>sublunary Soul</term> <note>The "Anima sublunaris," or the spirit of the Earth itself, which Kepler believed responded to planetary alignments</note>. 

<margin>Harmonic ratios are innate to souls.</margin> You might ask: if that faculty is not capable of reasoning, and thus cannot grasp the *science* of harmonic proportions, how does it recognize them when they are presented from the outside? For to "recognize" is to compare an external sensible object with internal Ideas, and to judge that they match. Proclus expresses this beautifully with the word *awakening*, as if from a sleep. For just as sensible things encountered outside make us remember those things we knew before, so too sensible mathematical objects, if they are recognized, draw out "intellectuals" <note>Inner concepts or archetypes</note> that were already present within. Thus, things which previously lay hidden in the Soul as if under a veil of potentiality now shine forth in the Soul as actualities. 

How, then, did they break inside? I respond: the Ideas or formal ratios of harmonies, as we discussed above, are entirely present in those things that possess this power of recognition. They are not received into the interior through reasoning; rather, they depend on a **natural instinct** and are born with the soul, just as the number of leaves in a flower or the cells in a fruit (an intellectual thing) is born with the forms of plants. This phenomenon in plants is similar to harmonic ratios (for number and proportion are kindred things, as shown above). This makes me feel I cannot confidently deny the faculty of recognizing the harmonic proportions of <term>sidereal rays</term> <note>The light or "influence" coming from the stars and planets</note> even to the vegetative faculty of the soul and to plants themselves; although I conclude nothing without my own experiments. 

Thus it happens that children, uneducated farmers, barbarians, and even wild beasts perceive the harmonies of voices, even if they know nothing of the science of harmony. If you ask where this instinct comes from, I shall either flee to God—who forms these shapes in bodies as images of Himself, according to more or less, and who makes you carry harmonic ratios within you just as He embraced them in His mind from eternity and expressed them in creation—or, which comes to the same thing, I will cite the kinship mentioned in Chapter I between these souls (even the inferior ones) and the **circle**. 

<margin>The Soul is in a way a circle. The foundation of astrological influences.</margin>
For souls are composed and shaped according to the circle as a rule and law. In adopting the circle and its "demonstrability," they have also put on the Idea of the harmonic proportions that depend upon it. Indeed, <term>Geneses</term> <note>Latin: "Geneses" — birth charts or horoscopes in natal astrology</note> strongly confirm this philosophy, when we see the character of the confluence of

<margin>Means by which the Soul perceives Harmonies</margin>
Furthermore, the means used by these inferior faculties of the Soul to perceive the harmonies of external things are the same means by which they receive the external objects themselves. If the objects are <term>sensible</term> <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses</note>, they are perceived by the senses—that is, by those faculties of the soul that give form to the senses. These faculties, no less than the superior one, are engaged in the comparison of certain things, but they do so by instinct, not by <term>discourse</term> <note>Latin: *discursu* — the step-by-step process of logical reasoning</note>. Thus, through the sense of hearing and the power presiding over it, consonant sounds are distinguished from dissonant ones. Likewise, architectural proportions are perceived by the eyes and by that faculty presiding over sight, and the beautiful and fitting are distinguished from the unfitting. If, however, the things themselves that contain a harmonic ratio are not sensible, but are perhaps perceivable by some other faculty, then those very proportions of things shine back into the soul: as is the case with the proportions of the stellar rays. How these are perceived by the <term>sublunary soul</term> <note>The "Spirit of the Earth," which Kepler believed responded to planetary alignments just as a human soul responds to music</note>, we shall investigate below in Chapter VII.

<margin>What kind of perception?</margin>
Yet, this perception of Harmonies in the inferior faculties of the Soul is obtuse and obscure, and in a way material, existing as if "under a cloud of ignorance." For these faculties do not know that they are perceiving; just as when we see something, but do not consciously notice that we are seeing it. Such are those movements and terrors celebrated by the Stoics <note>Ancient philosophers who taught that we should remain indifferent to external events</note>, which occur naturally without deliberation and even against the will. Such also is the natural affection of Hate or Love, which possesses a truly marvelous character.

<margin>The instinct of Love.</margin>
By judging the goodness or similarity of another’s soul to its own through the harmony of the limbs, the quality of the voice, and the temperament, this instinct wonderfully blazes up toward that person. Thus, a mad young man loves a girl; yet he does not know why, or what specifically he loves in her that any common prostitute could not provide (if it is an ignoble love) or any marriageable girl (if it is legitimate). But a <term>physiognomist</term> <note>A person who judges character by physical features</note>, arriving on the scene, finds in both persons some similarity of character. If these characters are vicious, they provide the occasion for perpetual quarrels in marriage; if good, for a peaceful life. Indeed, to this we must refer the entire

<margin>Physiognomic instinct.</margin>
physiognomic instinct; which, although it is "mute" and in some way "brute" (certainly not acquired by art, though it can be refined by it), is nevertheless the sole interpreter and arbiter of human affairs. For anyone obtains as much prosperity (naturally speaking) as his face, the harmony of his body, his gait, and the movement of his limbs appeal to those in power, and as much as he creeps into their favor. This happens even though those in power use no

<margin>Fascination of the Gaze.</margin>
deliberation on the matter, as if it were hidden; so that they often testify that they love or hate someone without knowing for what reason. Such, I say, in the inferior faculties of the Soul, is the sense of proportions without "sensing." Thus, they do not distinguish the proportion from its "Terms" or its subject (as when we hear a pleasant song, we think of nothing regarding the craftsmanship itself beyond the sounds), nor do they clearly distinguish between different Harmonies; they only notice that they exist, but they do not know what they are or how they vary. Indeed, even the <term>Ideas of Harmonies</term> <note>The pure mathematical patterns that exist in the mind of God and the human soul</note> which these inferior faculties possess within themselves are not instilled in them in a purely abstract form, but are wrapped in the "coverings" of the subject matter—that is, the specific object of each faculty. For example, the faculty of hearing (to use the example of musical chords for all the others), standing closest to the body, was too "thick" and therefore unsuitable to receive the purest Idea of proportion, as I will now immediately explain at greater length.
