<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
For now I come to the active faculties <note>original: *energeticas Facultates* — referring to the soul's power to take action or produce effects, rather than just passively receiving information</note>, which are occupied with harmonic proportions. This category is also twofold: for it is either active within itself, or in things outside of itself, in both cases either likening its works to proportions or introducing these proportions into those works. The former is similar to a passive state, while the latter is practiced, beyond controversy, in acting; the former is again the offspring of the lower faculties of the Soul, while the latter belongs to the higher. The former is subject to the forces of Nature; the latter to the human will. The former is certainly powerful in the motion of alteration which it inflicts upon its own body, so that it is entirely subject to the vital faculty.

<margin>How the Soul is affected according to Harmonies.</margin>
For the fact that we take delight in the harmonies of sounds has the appearance of a "passion" <note>In the philosophical sense of *passio*, meaning an effect produced by an external agent; a "feeling" or "undergoing"</note>, namely of being soothed and charmed. Hence, philosophers call this resonance of souls with song "sympathy" <note>original: *Sympathia* — literally "suffering together" or feeling in unison</note>, based on this idea of undergoing an effect. Yet, in truth, it is an operation of the soul, acting upon itself by a natural motion and stirring itself up. The soul is led to this not by deliberate counsel or will, but by natural instinct. It has, right from its very birth, ideas linked and fused together into one: both the ideas of the harmonies incorporated into sounds and the ideas of the corresponding affections of the soul. Thus, the Idea of Harmony is implanted in the soul specifically insofar as it brings joy and is something delightful, and insofar as it is entwined with the movement of the Idea. I believe this is what Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who deeply influenced Kepler’s mathematical mysticism</note> intended above when he affirmed that the Patterns of mathematical things (and thus even more so of Harmonies) exist in the Mind *intellectually*, but in the Soul *vitally*. For in this way, they will also exist in the faculty of hearing sonically, and in the vital faculty of sublunary things <note>The "Spirit of the Earth" which resides below the moon</note> radiantly and operatively; that is, they are not the pure internal Patterns themselves, but are Icons <note>Images or reflections</note> of them, derived outwardly.

<margin>How Souls act according to harmonic ratios.</margin>
Furthermore, we do not only take delight in the harmony of song, but we also adapt the movements of our fingers, mouth, feet, and body to it; this we perform by the animal faculty <note>The faculty responsible for movement and basic biological functions</note> joined with the will. But when we also adapt the voice to intelligible harmonies, meditating on a melodious song never heard before, here we use all faculties from the highest to the lowest: the highest because we will it and use judgment; the lower because we are able to, and because even without an intellectual understanding of proportions, we express through song the ideas of intervals implanted by nature, excluding all clashing sounds and wandering only through harmonious intervals.

<margin>From where the harmonic faculties of the Soul arise.</margin>
Therefore, the harmonic faculties explained thus far were breathed out during creation by that essential Harmony, GOD Himself, as He who is <term>being in activity</term> <note>original: *οὐσία ἐνεργείᾳ* — a Greek philosophical term for essence that is fully realized or active</note>. He inspired this small particle of His own image into absolutely all souls, though in varying degrees; with which emphasis I bring an end to this chapter.

# CHAPTER III.
## What are the Kinds of <term>harmonized things</term> <note>original: *τῶν ἡρμοσμένων* — things that have been put into a state of harmony</note>, that is, of things whether sensible or immaterial, in which Harmonies are expressed, either by God or by man, and in what way?

It is easily seen that the questions are distinct: 1. In whom do Harmonies exist as the Agent, Formative power, or Craftsman? 2. In whom do they exist as the formed work? We have dealt with the former until now; the latter must now be treated more accurately.

<header>ON CONFIGURATIONS</header>

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>1. In the Soul.</margin>Therefore, all things are either immaterial or they participate in matter. The Soul is immaterial (at least in respect to the body); and this, as we have maintained so far, is entirely in respect to its essence, inscribed by God into these Harmonic proportions. Those proportions which were previously in the Soul as a Craftsman <note>original: *Opifici* — referring to the soul's role in "building" or organizing life</note>—namely, as it is an Active Power <note>original: *Energia*</note>—now exist in the same Soul as a work of God. But those things that participate in matter participate in both Number and Magnitude. Position in space follows magnitude; and finally, local motion <note>The physical movement from one place to another</note> happens to these things.

<margin>2. Whether in the Number of the Planets.</margin>Number, therefore, is something naturally prior to Harmony, because the terms of any harmony must be more than one in number. However, the Number of the primary bodies of the World also has its causes in Geometry, which I repeat below in Book V from my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>Kepler’s first major work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596), where he proposed that the distances between planets correspond to the five Platonic solids</note>. Figure, its individual property, follows quantity; why a spherical shape should be granted to the stars and even to the World itself—namely, from the Archetype of the Sphere—is explained elsewhere in many places. A certain proportion immediately follows the figures of different bodies, and that is threefold: one of diameters, another of surfaces, and a third of space or volumes.

<margin>3. Whether in the movements of bodies.</margin>Therefore, if other causes for these Proportions were not available, we could probably assert that they were taken from the Harmonies. Whatever those causes are, the celestial Globes maintain them without any change, since they do not become larger or smaller through any motion or the passage of time. It is otherwise with those Proportions that are in bodies because of their position and because of their local motions: for these retain the character of Motion itself. Just as motion is in a state of continuous **BECOMING** <note>original: *FIERI*</note> and never in a state of **BEING** <note>original: *ESSE*</note>, so also the Proportions of motions are inconstant, being different at different times.

<margin>4. Whether in the intervals.</margin>It is indeed true that if the motion of the celestial bodies did not vary—that is, if their distances from the common goal or Base of the world never moved higher or deeper <note>Meaning if planets stayed in perfect circles rather than elliptical orbits</note>, but all stayed in a pure concentric circle—then not only would the proportion of the intervals be constant, but it would even have been purely Harmonic, if other causes had not been available.

<margin>5. Whether constantly in the speed of motions.</margin>The same must be said of motion by reason of its essence, that is, by reason of its speed through the ether: if this speed were constant and perpetual for each planet, there is no doubt that these various speeds and slownesses would have been tempered according to Harmonic laws.

<margin>6. Whether constantly in the apparent motions under the Zodiac.</margin>Finally, the same must be said of that same motion by reason of the space traversed, appearing under the Zodiac. For if all the planets had to move with the same apparent motion under the Zodiac, and never be separated further from one another: there is no doubt that God would have established such a position for them relative to each other under the Zodiac from the beginning (provided their arrangement was free and not bound by other laws of necessity) which would divide the Zodiac in every direction by Harmonic ratios.

<margin>7. Whether in their initial position appearing under the Zodiac.</margin>It is so consistent, even at the beginning of the motions (when the beginning of time is considered without time), that from a common position and Harmonic configuration (such as could appear either from the Earth or rather from the Sun), as if from the starting gates <note>original: *carceribus* — the starting barriers in a Roman chariot race</note>, each planet ran out into its own spaces or paths.

<margin>In many things not constant.</margin>But because the Planets move in altitude and depth <note>Coming closer to or moving further from the Sun</note>, changing the intervals of their position; and because a real intensification and slackening of motions by reason of speed follows this motion by physical necessity; and finally, because through the unequal apparent speeds of different bodies, the space of the Zodiac which they seem to traverse is divided differently at different times: for these three reasons, the same thing happens to positions as well as motions by reason of time, as happens to the quantities themselves without respect to time. In a whole circle, or on a straight line, the boundaries or marks of Harmonic ratios <note>original: *rationum Harmonicarum* — the mathematical relationships that create musical intervals</note> are not found at every single point, but only at certain specific ones. In the same way, Harmonies cannot exist throughout the entire duration of a motion, nor in every interval, nor in the varying speeds of the motions, nor in every space of the Zodiac intercepted between the planets. <margin>
10. In Song
The difference between celestial Harmonies and human song.
</margin>

Therefore, regarding the works of God known to us, the matter stands thus: if we now compare these to the things that Humans arrange according to harmonic laws, we must say they are partly the same and partly different. First, in Songs, although there is a continuous increase and decrease of quantity <note>The sliding of pitch or volume</note> no less than in the heavens, yet in the motions of the heavens this is necessary by fixed laws of nature. In the human voice, it is neither necessary nor even easy. For the throat is constructed with a distinction of circles for articulated voices; we reach from high to low, and vice versa, more easily through intervals of jumps <note>discrete musical notes</note>, as it were, than if we were ordered to use continuous tension <note>a "glissando" or continuous slide</note>. It is no wonder, then, that in celestial motions—given the continuous increase and decrease that could not be avoided—incongruous intervals remained mixed with the congruous and consonant ones. In human song, however, once all the incongruous ones are eliminated, only the congruous and consonant are observed. Nor does Song have any reason to boast over celestial motions for this reason; for another duty has been assigned to the planets to perform, and harmonic contemplation is only accessory to them. Song, on the other hand, has nothing to look toward except Harmonies; it requires nothing outside itself and is focused on the single end of delight.

<margin>
Why can the human voice not be stretched by continuous increases, like an instrument or a string?
Why are there not pure harmonic configurations [in the sky], as there are pure concords in song?
</margin>

<margin>
11. In the measure of the beat. See book III, page 14.
12. In Dancing.
13. Harmonies of poetic feet.
</margin>

There are also other human works into which the mind introduces harmonic proportions, though more obscurely and less nobly. This occurs when Song is shaped not only by the quality of high and low pitch, but also by the measure of the beat <note>original: *tactus* — the steady pulse or "touch" used to keep time</note>, participating in double and triple proportions. It also occurs in the motion of bodies when dancing in Choruses, first in the proportion of equality, and later in double proportion. Poets imitate this same thing by the arrangement of "feet" made of syllables, long and short, where the former is considered to be double the length of the latter. In this system:
*   The **Iambus** (short-long u-), **Trochee** (long-short -u), or **Tribrach** (short-short-short uuu)

*   Is as **3 to 4**.
*   Compared to the **Bacchiacs** (short-long-long u-- or long-long-short --u), the **Cretic** (long-short-long -u-), and the **Paeons** (long-short-short-short -uuu, short-long-short-short u-uu, short-short-long-short uu-u, short-short-short-long uuu-)
*   Is as **3 to 5**.
*   Compared to the **Molossus** (long-long-long ---) or **Choriamb** (long-short-short-long -uu-)...

<margin>
Whence the feet

</margin>
Poets and Grammarians take such delight even in the names of proportions that, using a terminology peculiar to them, they call four-syllable feet with one short syllable <term>Epitrites</term> <margin>The name Epitrite.</margin> <note>original: *Epitritos* — from the Greek meaning "one plus a third"</note>, which is to say, <term>Sesquitertials</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3</note>. They call them this because, just as in the proportion of 4 to 3 expressed by parallel lines, the first three units are represented by a double line while the fourth exceeds them by only a single line; so in this poetic foot, three syllables consist of two beats <note>or "times"</note> each, while the fourth has only one. And since the very word for "Feet" <note>original: *Pedum*</note> alludes to the Chorus, <margin>Theatrical harmonies.</margin> a part of Comedies and Tragedies, it seems that even the stage actors expressed all these proportions through the movement of their feet, no less than <term>double</term> and <term>triple</term> time <note>musical meters</note> are expressed today. <margin>Architectural [harmonies].</margin> In Architecture, whatever proportions of length to width or thickness are most highly approved—even by spectators who are not Mathematicians—are found to be those closest to the harmonic ratios. <margin>Why, among human harmonies, is singing the most exact?</margin> But the reason why the proportions of sounds are more exact than all these others, and why human Nature delights more intensely in expressing them, is because every living creature has the greatest power over sounds. Indeed, sounds are formed within the self, sent forth from the very depths of the chest, and are most ready to respond to every nod of the mind and every movement of the heart. Furthermore, as was said before, the soul has found a most suitable instrument: the Throat, stretched out in length like a string or rather like a flute, in whose straight length the voice wanders up and down most easily.

<margin>Why harmonies are not clearly present in the quantities of unmoving things.</margin>
Generally, however, in all things where quantity is found and where Harmonies can be sought according to that quantity, they are much more evident through motion than without motion. For although a half, a third, a fourth, a fifth, and a sixth part (and their multiples) exist within any single straight line, they remain hidden among the other parts that are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>having no common measure</note> to the whole. They are so buried in a single confusion with the whole that even if a second line, equal to one of those specific parts, stands right next to the whole—for example, a lintel beam of three feet next to a doorpost of five—its proportion to the whole is not so easily recognized as it would be if some motion were to discern, establish, and determine those comparable lengths. The cause is this: where quantity exists without motion, everything contained within that quantity is present simultaneously at the same time—namely, all the <margin>Why proportions shine brightest through motion.</margin> proportions of all the parts to the whole. But if a certain quantity is traversed by a motion, then (as is the essence of motion) the proportions that have been passed through no longer exist, and those not yet passed through do not yet exist; thus, any single proportion stands alone at the moment the motion reaches its mark. So it happens through the succession of movements that harmonic proportions are unshelled from the discordant ones and separated from the mixture, as if they were placed in pure light and offered up to be grasped by the senses. Thus, not even the mind itself can discern harmonic proportions from the infinite discordant ones standing before and after them in a given quantity without some "image of motion." For instance, when dealing with the infinite chords <note>straight lines connecting two points on a curve</note> in a circle, the mind is hard-pressed and seeks a demonstration to find the chord of a third or fourth part of the circle; it achieves through thought what the hand achieves by drawing a line: it separates that specific chord by this very act from the infinite others that were not thought of...

<margin>
CHAPTER II.
Why do proportions manifest most clearly in motion?
</margin>

The mind can indeed do this because it exercises its will and, at its own discretion, makes a cut in that infinite division of quantities which is entirely present to the mind for thinking. However, sensations and other natural perceptions—and finally the movements of bodies through which perceptions are aided—are not in the power of the living being in the same way. For instance, if infinite sounds, or the infinite angular relationships of two planets throughout the whole circuit of a circle, were confused together at the same time, the senses could not withdraw themselves from those that should be rejected and take refuge in only the pleasing ones. 

<margin>
This will, however, serve as an example for us below, to sketch out to some extent the Harmonies of rays.
</margin>

They therefore have need of motion, through which all those things that were confused by reason of quantity might be unrolled through successive intervals of time, so that individual things may strike the senses alone. If the eyes can do something similar to the mind—choosing the more excellent things from an infinite confusion of things present without motion (such as if, using the service of the hands, they were to choose and draw a chord equal to a third part of a circle, namely the side of a triangle, out of all infinite possible chords)—this very thing is to be judged as the work of the mind itself acting through the eyes, and not entirely without the motion of the hands, as I have said.

<margin>
How sensible things must be composed so that harmonies may exist in them.
</margin>

Therefore, to apply this observation to the prior pronouncements: if a thing is to be a genuine subject of harmonic proportion, it is necessary that quantity—namely length—be present in that thing. Furthermore, there must be at least two markers if the length is a circle, or three if it is a straight line; either one or all of these markers must traverse the length of the thing through some motion, becoming the boundaries of the parts of the length between which the proportion exists. This is the minimum requirement. And this occurs, in part, in the configurations which are the proper subject of this Fourth Book. For as will be said in the following chapter, Harmonies in the angles measured by the Zodiac are indeed considered without motion; yet the angles themselves, one after another, are established by the motion of the radiant bodies through the Zodiac. There are, however, more excellent modes tending toward the same end, as when bodies that have length are themselves determined by such signs wandering up and down, and the sections intercepted are moved at any given time. Thus, it is no longer the bodies, but the very motions of the bodies that are compared with each other, for the sake of length and shortness—not temporal, but bodily (since these are <gloss>forms</gloss> <note>original: *species* — in Kepler's physical theory, these are the formal images or emanations through which an object is perceived</note> of incorporeal motions, or of bodies established in motion). This is exactly how it is with sounds:

<margin>
How sounding things become the subject of harmonies.
</margin>

for sound is a form emitted from a body, both as a quantity, and as something shaped to some extent, and as it is established in motion: because both motion and sound exist according to the suitability of the shape.

<margin>
What the windpipe contributes to sounds for expressing Harmonies.
</margin>

And this is now a second and more evident reason why human nature is chiefly devoted to the harmonic proportions of sounds. This happens, again, because of the conformation of one's body: in which the throat is that body which is now long, now short, according to the constriction of the upper or lower cartilaginous ring in the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: *aspera Arteria* — literally "the rough artery," the standard anatomical term for the trachea in the 17th century</note>. When it is struck by the breath forced out from the bellows of the lungs, it produces a motion from its cavity (namely, its shape) similar to the form that reaches the ears. This sensation—of the windpipe itself as it is established in motion—is present to the perceiving soul. For it is the task of the <term>common sense</term> <note>The "sensus communis," a theoretical faculty that unified the data from the five individual senses</note> to perceive and enjoy the forms of the limbs of the body as they are affected and, as it were, shaped by various motions. These forms, as I explained in my **Dioptrics**, are carried from the members of the body...

<margin>CHAPTER III. How the human mind judges the quantity of sounding bodies through sound.</margin>

They can then examine these compared to one another according to the laws of harmonic proportions.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the difference between the Harmonies in this Fourth Book and those considered in the Third Book.

The importance of distinguishing the boundaries of things, comparing related things so they are not mistaken for the same, and contrasting opposites to bring them into light, is a matter of such weight for philosophizing well that it requires no long-winded introduction. Therefore, it will be worthwhile to bring under a single view everything useful that has been said so far—whether scattered, obscure, or in passing—and to clarify it further where necessary, specifically addressing the topic of this chapter. There is, then, a five-fold difference between the harmonic contemplations of this book and the preceding one. One lies in the harmonic matter itself, because of its scope; the second in its sensible terms; the third in the cause that grants harmony its essence; the fourth in its mode of existence; and the fifth in the order of causes that form the terms of the harmonic proportion.

<margin>Harmonies are more restricted in this book.</margin>
I. Regarding the matter itself, which is called **harmonic proportion** <note>original: *Harmonica proportio*</note>: in the third book, these first arose from sections of a circle demonstrated through regular plane figures, then were soon transferred to straight lines. When these were combined and joined together, they produced a significant abundance of harmonic parts—such as **harmonic sections**, **tones**, **genera**, **modes**, **systems**, and the like—and among them a certain admirable order. Almost that entire collection, in its full extent, will also be examined and applied below in Book V. But now, in this fourth book, although we begin from those same sections of the circle, we shall not proceed to straight lines; instead, we shall remain within the boundaries of the circle throughout the entire scope of the discussion. The reason for this was stated in the preceding chapter, and more will be said below in Chapter VI, where we will discuss the kinship and the effect of this distinction at greater length.

<margin>These are harmonies of angles.</margin>
II. Regarding the **terms** <note>the specific values or units being compared</note> of these harmonies or their sensible subject: in Book III, these were **sounds** <note>original: *Soni*</note> differing in pitch—the high and the low. Thus, they were categorized under the genus of motion, and were, in a sense, "figured" motions. In this fourth book, however, they are not voices—as said in the introduction—nor are they just any motions among which one might recognize harmonies; rather, they exist in **angles** which two planets, through the radiant rays of light they emit, form upon the Earth, insofar as such an angle meets at a single point with the four right angles <note>Kepler is referring to the 360 degrees of a circle surrounding the observer on Earth</note>...

<summary>Kepler distinguishes his study of planetary "aspects" (angles) from his previous study of musical tuning, noting that while both rely on the geometry of the circle, this book focuses strictly on the angular relationships perceived from Earth.</summary>

<header>ON HARMONICS BOOK IV. CHAPTER IV.</header>

...compared to those surrounding it. And here the reader needs a clear warning. I can explain these terms more clearly for your understanding, but I cannot do so without risking confusion in sound philosophy unless I carefully prepare the philosophical reader.

<margin>How the arcs of the Zodiac [act as terms].</margin>
Since the terms of a proportion must differ in quantity, and the quantity (or measure) of angles is an arc of a circle drawn from the point where the angles meet (as we are taught in Geometry); in the whole space of the world—which extends from the Earth to the very ends of things—we cannot describe or perceive any circle more suitable for measuring the angles of rays than that visible circle in the highest ether. This circle is defined by the crowded fixed stars and named the **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: the "circle of animals," a belt of the heavens extending about 8° on either side of the ecliptic</term> because those stars are grouped into certain animal shapes. The planets always move beneath this circle, and each planet appears to cover a single spot on it from our perspective. At the center of this circle, the Earth—our home—seems to be hidden, not just by its center (which is a mere point) but by the mass of its entire body, upon whose surface we humans are placed. Therefore, nothing is easier to understand than if we say (as in the previous chapter) that the harmonic proportions we will discuss in this book exist between the whole circle of the Zodiac and the arc of it which two planets appear to mark out or cut off by their visible positions.

<margin>Not truly celestial.</margin>
Even though this is the case, and is perfectly stated according to Geometrical and Astronomical principles, the philosophical reader must be extremely careful not to assume that this harmony (the subject of this fourth book) exists in the heavens themselves, in the Zodiac circle, or even in the planets. Not in the least! For this harmony exists in the parts of the Zodiac not for their own sake—since the radiating planets stand at an immense distance below this circle—but because those parts measure the angles of the rays meeting on Earth. Indeed, it is because they do not measure them by their own action, but instead an exact **Image** <note>original: *Icon*; Kepler uses this to mean a mental or spiritual representation</note> of the celestial Zodiac within the **sublunary Soul** <term>sublunary Soul: the animating spirit Kepler believed resided in the Earth or its atmosphere, which perceives and reacts to planetary configurations to produce weather and other natural effects</term> takes up this duty of measuring. The harmony exists in the rays of the planets, not insofar as they descend individually from their own planet or are offspring of light (though not without this), but insofar as the two rays of two planets, joined here on Earth, form a specific harmonic angle.

<margin>But Terrestrial.</margin>
On both counts, the subject of this harmony is **Terrestrial** (formally, and insofar as the rays become the **Terms** <note>original: *Termini*; the two quantities that make up a ratio or proportion</note> of the harmonic proportion). It is not celestial at all, except in a material sense regarding its own **Being**, without considering the Harmonies; that is, insofar as the rays of light—things originating in heaven but now fallen to Earth—shape the angles formed on Earth, which are the true subject of this harmony. We shall deal with truly celestial harmonies in Book V. Briefly: the terms of the harmonies in Book III were the work of Man or Art; in this Book IV, they will be the work of Nature; and finally, in Book V, they will be the work of God the Creator.

III. Now, as for the **Rational cause** which grants these harmonies their **Being**: there is generally no difference between the Third and Fourth books, except perhaps in their specific kind. For in Book III, the harmonies influenced things by reason of their sub-

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
...of their material subject (sounds) into the senses, they were received and judged by reason of their formal essence—insofar as they are harmonies—(that is, they were formed) by an instinct innate to the Mind, which shares in reason without needing long-winded argument. And up to this point, Harmonies were considered only in themselves.

But then, through a hidden yet acknowledged interaction of the soul’s faculties, the harmonies received within were poured into various emotions of the heart. Through certain similarities or images <note>original: "Icones"</note> of themselves, they were also poured into the locomotive faculty, so that a person might not only express the concept of harmony formed in the mind with their voice, but also imitate it with the movement of the body. In this way, Harmonies took on the role of a causative force.

Similarly, here too it is necessary to suppose a Soul, into which this standard of judgment <note>original: κριτηριον (kriterion)</note> for harmonic proportions has been instilled since the creation of things. This soul estimates the angle of two radiating stars within itself, however that angle is received (whether by something analogous to the senses, or by a property of its own essence as a soul, as discussed in the previous chapter and as will be discussed further in the following ones). It compares the angle to a full circle <note>literally "to four right angles," referring to the 360 degrees of the Zodiac</note>, distinguishes the harmonic from the non-harmonic, and thus grants these harmonies their intellectual Existence—which these angles did not yet possess while they were outside the thresholds of the mind.

<margin>
These Harmonies shine forth: 1. In the human Soul.
</margin>
If it is asked what kind of soul this is, or where or in what body it is located: I answer, first, that the souls of all humans are of this kind. However, in the third book, we discussed the faculty that presides over hearing and thus the senses; here, we are not speaking of a sensory faculty. For the eyes—whose objects are Light and luminous rays—do not provide an adequate judgment of the harmonic radiation of two planets. Nor is it a Reasoning faculty; for although reason finds and computes which aspects exist at any given time based on Astronomical Observations managed through the eyes, it does not do so naturally (since it is not done by all people indiscriminately), but voluntarily, by the few dedicated specifically to astronomy. Rather, human souls are the subject of these harmonies, first by reason of natural instinct—insofar as souls are patterns of the Creator, as said in Chapter IV—and secondly by reason of the Vital and Natural faculties and their vital and natural movements. In the Platonic style, these are the Desiring and Spirited parts <term>Concupiscibilis & Irascibilis: terms from Platonic philosophy referring to the parts of the soul driven by desire/appetite and by anger/courage</term>. Harmonies affect the former insofar as they *are* harmonies, but they affect the latter insofar as the "species" or forms of the Harmonies are imprinted on these faculties, becoming the driving and stimulating causes of the works of Nature, both in the mind and in the body.

<margin>
2. In sublunary Nature or the soul of the Earth.
</margin>
Furthermore, the primary soul into which these Harmonies of radiation flow is that which philosophers call "Sublunary Nature." This nature is diffused through the entire body of the Earth, our foster-mother, and is rooted in a certain specific part of it, just as the human soul is rooted in the heart. From this center—whether we call it a hearth, a source, or an inner sanctuary—it goes out by its own form into the Ocean surrounding the Earth and the Air poured over both.

Just as a person listening to a singer sweetly performing a Melody testifies—by a joyful expression, by voice, or by the clapping of hands or feet timed to the measure of the Melody—that they perceive and approve of the harmony within it; in the same way, Sublunary Nature reacts with significant and evi...

This testifies to what we have already established: that the Earth, by a certain natural instinct, is no less capable of perceiving the harmonic proportions of angles than it is powerful in its natural faculty—similar to our own vital faculty—to heat and stir up the body of the Earth and the subterranean workshops in the mountains at specific harmonic times. It does this so that they may exhale a great abundance of vapors and mists, from which, through the **antiperistasis** <term>antiperistasis: a process where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating when surrounded by cold</term> of the upper cold, all kinds of meteorological phenomena <note>original: "meteora," referring to rain, wind, and storms rather than falling stars</note> are formed.

<margin>See Chapter VII.</margin>
For this soul must be placed within the body of the Earth, because harmonic angles of rays do not exist in any other part of the world except on the Earth; and the works of Nature that follow these configurations of rays take their origin from the bowels of the Earth and the caverns of the mountains.

## IV. The fourth distinction consists in the ways in which different Harmonies exist within their subjects.

<margin>The difference between these harmonies and Musical ones, in their continuity.</margin>
In Book III, when harmonies were present in Song, they were present throughout the whole—that is, for the entire time the song lasted. And although the intervals of the voices, like all things participating in quantity, allow for continuous division, there was nevertheless no transition in the song from a lower sound through infinite intermediates to that which was first consonant or melodic. Instead, all intermediates were passed over with a leap and with silence; indeed, every vocal pause was on sounds that were harmonious with one another. In the same way, in a Concert <note>original: "Concentu," referring to polyphony or harmony</note>, although infinite intervals lie between the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> and the Sixth <note>original: "Dihex"</note>, there was no continuous stretching of the voices through all the intermediates until the Octave became a Sixth. Instead, the voices were carried by a leap from a pure Octave into a pure Sixth, with all intermediates passed over in silence. In organs, one leaped from one pipe to another; in stringed instruments like the Lute or Harp, from one string to another. Or, if strings producing many sounds were used—as in the Clavichord, the Pandura, the Lute <note>original: "Chely"</note>, or the Cittern <note>original: "Cythara"</note>—from one fret to another; or in the human throat, from one ring of the windpipe to another.

It is not so in Book IV. For the harmonies we shall consider here, as we began to say in the preceding chapter, do not always exist between the angle of two planetary rays and the four right angles <note>meaning the 360 degrees of the full circle</note>. Instead, there is a continuous separation of the planets (to whom this movement is given beneath the circle of the Zodiac) through all unharmonious <note>original: "ἀνάϱμοσα" (anarmosa)</note> intervals toward the harmonic ones—the furthest of which is two right angles, the semicircle or "opposition." From there, they move in a retrograde order through all the unmelodic and dissonant intervals again, until they reach a conjunction. No leap is made here from one harmonic angle to another—for example, from a Trine <note>120 degrees</note> to a Square <note>90 degrees</note>—but the transition from the former to the latter is continuous, through all intermediates. Therefore, unharmonious configurations of rays occupy the entire time of celestial motions; 

<margin>They are momentary.</margin>
whereas harmonic configurations of two, or sometimes three or even four planets, mark off only certain specific moments, while the others continue in their state of incongruity. It is as if seven organ pipes were to emit as many dissonant sounds through a continuous alteration of tension, and there occurred a mutual meeting of tensions, so that occasionally...

<summary>Kepler argues that the Earth is a living entity that reacts to planetary alignments to create weather, and distinguishes celestial harmony (which is a fleeting moment in a continuous motion) from musical harmony (which consists of discrete, intentional leaps).</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>

...two or three [rays] harmonize while the others are dissonant. Thus, truly and properly speaking, these harmonic configurations themselves do not exist in time, but are perfected in indivisible moments <note>Kepler means that a precise geometric angle, such as exactly 90 degrees, occurs at a specific instant rather than over a duration of time</note>. Yet it is also true that the stirrings that arise in the Souls from these harmonies are not momentary; for the harmonic configurations move the soul as they are coming into being, and at the very moment they become perfect, their stimulus slackens. However, the works of Nature, which are stirred by these stimuli, take the measure of their own time from the conditions of matter, and they often last far beyond the moment when the radiation is perfected. 

Thus, a brass machine <note>original: "machina ænea," referring here to a cannon</note> that has been fired—if it catches fire from the ignited gunpowder <note>original: "pulveris pyrij"</note>—does not immediately lose its heat once the fuel of the fire is consumed. Likewise, the body of an animal—to use a more fitting example—when tossed by a fit of fever <note>original: "febrili paroxysmo"</note>; although the vital faculty of the soul, which is the author of the inflammation, relaxes its effort once its task is done and the febrile matter is either melted down or ejected from the innermost parts toward the exterior, the body is not immediately freed from all heat. For that heat clings for a long time to the matter of the body—the flesh, bones, and nerves—until it too expires in the passage of time.

<margin>Their effect, however, is not momentary.</margin>

<margin>Fol. 124. They are mixed with incongruous and ineffective ones.</margin>

Therefore, these Harmonies are among those which we said above in Chapter II are not subject to free providence, but are mixed by the necessity of motions with infinite incongruous <note>unfitting or non-harmonic</note> ones of their own kind. God ordained minds that would recognize these harmonies when they occur. And yet, sublunary Nature <note>The natural world of the Earth, beneath the moon</note> is far more successful in distinguishing these than the ears are in song. For the sense of hearing is not greatly delighted by the Harmony of two voices if five other dissonant ones are making a noise. Sublunary Nature, accustomed to perpetual incongruous configurations, treats them as nothing because it notices nothing new; but it is so intent on a harmonic angle as if it were the only one. Just as when a Prognostication <note>A weather forecast or astrological prediction</note> fails a thousand times, it is nevertheless ignored; but if it hits the mark once, it is deemed worthy of memory, and is celebrated in the talk of all.

<margin>They are necessary, not procured.</margin>

From these things, therefore, one may understand that Harmonies in voices are established by the choice and plan of the singer; but in the radiant angles, they arise from no plan of sublunary nature, but by the sheer geometric necessity of motions. For because two Planets must be separated through the length of the entire semicircle or 180 Degrees, it necessarily happens that at their specific moments they are also distant by its harmonic parts, namely 30, 60, 90, 120, etc. degrees. Therefore, harmonies of song are sought from within by the singer, while harmonies of rays are expected from without by sublunary Nature; they are observed when they occur, distinguished from non-harmonic ones (and thus receive their **Being** <note>original: "Esse"</note> from it), and are received and applied. In short, the configurations lead the song, and sublunary Nature dances to the laws of this melody.

<margin>Dissimilarity in the order of causes.</margin>

### V. 

The fifth distinction is in some way to be attached to the first. For the Harmonies of this book and the preceding one differ not only in latitude, but also in the order of different respects by which Geometric Figures produce both kinds of Harmonic proportions: for in the third book, the respect of **Scibility** <term>Scibility: (from "scibilis") the capacity for a thing to be known or constructed by the mind</term> was more important, while in this fourth book, **Congruence** <term>Congruence: the property of geometric figures fitting together to fill a space or create a solid</term> will be more important. But concerning this fifth distinction, we shall deal with it expressly in Chapter V, in the explanation of the Axioms.

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
# CHAPTER V.
## On the causes of effective Configurations; their Number and the order of their degrees.
### DEFINITION I.

The term **Configuration** <note>Also known as an "aspect" in astrology</note> is used for that angle formed by two rays, each descending from its own Planet, where those rays meet here on Earth (which, for this purpose, is considered a single point). Or, what amounts to the same thing, it is used for the arc of a great circle described in the Zodiac which serves as the measurement of that angle—the arc that the two Planets seem to mark out and, as it were, cut off for us inhabitants of Earth by the positioning of their bodies.

*Regarding the name, it should first be noted that Ptolemy, in his four-part work <note>The Tetrabiblos</note>, in his Great Work <note>The Almagest</note>, and in his Harmonics, calls these **Schematisms** <note>original Greek: $\Sigma\chi\eta\mu\alpha\tau\iota\sigma\mu\omicron\grave{\upsilon}\varsigma$</note>. The Arabic authors translated this as **Aspects**, as if "Schema" were the same as "countenance" or "face." This is also found in our German tongue, which is accustomed to calling the face **das Angesicht**, while **Aspect** and the **Schemata** of masked performers—the coverings of the face—are called **Gesichter**, which the Italians call **Mascaras** <note>masks</note>. However, one also finds the term **prosblypseis** <note>original Greek: $\pi\rho\omicron\sigma\beta\lambda\acute{\epsilon}\psi\epsilon\iota\varsigma$</note>, which we translate as "Aspects" from the Arabic, but which good Latin authors are also accustomed to call **Intuitus** <note>gazes or lookings</note> and **Intuientia** <note>gazing signs</note>. Yet in this sense, the term does not apply so much to the planets as to the signs or <term>Dodecatemoria</term> <note>the twelve 30-degree divisions of the Zodiac</note>; since these have length, they can be turned toward one another more or less through their hollow curves. For adjacent signs cannot "gaze" at one another, since their faces are not turned toward each other, but are turned side-by-side toward the same region.*

*Next, note that at the same time two Planets form an Angle on Earth, they also form other angles in other places in the world; but nowhere are they so great as in the arc of the circle drawn through their bodies and the body of the Earth, or around the line that connects their bodies, like a rotation around an axis. Outside of these locations, their radiations meet at far different angles, whether they are also Harmonic or incongruous, as occurs throughout almost the rest of the world. Note especially that no angle is formed within either of the planetary bodies themselves. For an angle requires two rays: yet every ray is outside the body; there is no ray within the body itself. This must be noted because an effect on Earth follows the formation of an angle on Earth; for at the time of these Aspects, the matter for rain and other <term>meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to all atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and clouds</note> is exhaled. Thus, we can argue regarding the seat of the cause that moves the meteors: that it is not in one or the other Planet, nor in some other empty place in the world, but in the Earth itself.*

*Thirdly, it was not without reason that I added the mention of the Earth being considered as a point. From this it follows that even though the living beings on Earth are innumerable, and the rays from any Planet onto them and other points on the Earth are infinite, the angle of the rays coming from two Planets at the same time is effectively the same through all points of the Earth—whether at the center, on the surface, or in the caverns of the mountains. All those aspects, though infinite in number, are held as a single aspect; for they are all effectively equal to one another.*

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

## DEFINITION II.

An **effective configuration** is said to be when the rays of two Planets form such an angle that it is fit to stimulate sublunary Nature <term>Natura sublunaris: the life-force or "soul" of the Earth and the environment below the moon</term> and the lower faculties of Living Creatures, so that each becomes more active in its own work around the time of the configuration.

Efficacy is attributed to the configuration—which is formally a "being of reason" <note>original: *Ens rationis*; a conceptual or geometric relationship rather than a physical object</note>—but it is not an immediate efficacy upon the thing itself. It is not as if rain and similar things fall from heaven itself, namely from the configured planets, which is a foolish persuasion of the common people. Rather, the efficacy is mediated and objective. For just as objects move the senses—sound moving the hearing but not the eyes, and color moving the sight but not the hearing—so also here, a certain quality of this Relation called a "configuration" moves not the senses of the body, but the animal faculty, which is capable of receiving Instinct without discourse <note>In this context, "discourse" refers to logical, step-by-step reasoning; Kepler argues the Earth's soul recognizes geometry instinctively, without having to "think" about it</note>. 

Therefore, the Configuration does this not by its own power, but by the power of the Soul, which is said to receive the influence, though in truth it rather acts upon itself. Afterward, the soul or sublunary Nature, having been así moved or stimulated by the aspect and reminded of itself, rouses itself to draw out from the bowels of the earth the material for every kind of weather. If there were no Soul in the Earth, which we call sublunary Nature, the planets themselves could achieve nothing on Earth, neither by themselves nor by a favorable aspect. For it is an absurd thought, and similar to a poetic joke, to think that from the harmonic union of two rays—as if from the coupling of a male and female—a vapor (the matter of wind or rain) is conceived. It is as if moisture and the other things which evaporate from the earth were made from the substance of the Harmony (which is a relation), or the Angle (which is a qualitative quantity), or even Light itself (which is a quality, but by no means a physical substance), just as a seed is from the substance of the parents. Just as we say nothing is made from nothing, so also from something immaterial, nothing material can be naturally drawn out. See more in Chapter VII.

## Axiom I.

The arc of the Zodiac circle, which is cut off by the side of a congruent and knowable figure or star <note>Kepler uses "figure" or "star" to refer to regular polygons, like a triangle or square, which can be inscribed in the circle of the Zodiac</note>, measures the angle of an effective Configuration.

## Axiom II.

The angle of a knowable and congruent figure or star is the measure of the angle of an effective Configuration.

The entire business rests upon these two Axioms. I have made them two because there are two probable ways by which Souls and sublunary Natures can come to know the Configurations that exist at any time.

For they perceive either that figure whose side cuts an arc from the Zodiac circle (which serves as the measurement of the Configuration or the radiant angle), or they perceive that figure whose element is that very angle of the configuration. What the difference is between these figures, and what their mutual relationship is, will be seen from these diagrams, compared here with one another in order—

For there are two <term>reciprocally related schemas</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀντιπεπονθότα* (antipeponthota), a geometric term for figures where the parts of one correspond to the parts of the other</note>. First, the diameter is reciprocal to itself, whether it bisects the circle by being drawn through the center, or whether it touches it, where two rays forming an angle make two right angles or rather no angle at all, being arranged into a single straight line. The same must be thought regarding the **Conjunction** ☌ of the planets, which is improperly called a "configuration." <margin>Figure II</margin> For if two planets are under the same point of the Zodiac, then there is no angle at the center, while there are infinite angles on the circumference, and the sides of the figure are mere points; the circle is, as it were, an **Infinite-angled Figure**. This configuration had no need for a visual representation.

<margin>Figure II.</margin>
Next, the **Square** <note>original: *Tetragonus*; the 90-degree aspect</note> is also <term>reciprocally related</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀντιπέπονθε*</note> to itself, because the angle which two sides form on the circumference is equal to the angle at the center which one side subtends. Because of this, the **Trine** <note>Triangle/120-degree aspect</note>, **Sextile** <note>Hexagon/60-degree aspect</note>, the **Pentagon** of the five-pointed star, the **Octagon** of the eight-pointed star, the **Decagon** of the ten-pointed star, and the **Dodeca-gon** of the twelve-pointed star are all <term>reciprocally related</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀντιπεπονθασιν*</note>; so that if all the angles of one of the pair are inscribed in the circumference, its side subtends one angle of the other placed at the center.

The centers of all these circles represent the **Earth**, as if located in the middle; the circles themselves represent either the **Zodiac**, as imagined from the Earth, or any other circle subordinate to the Zodiac, imagined for the sake of measuring angles. Such circles are, in potentiality, the **souls** themselves, which are moved by the "aspects" <note>the geometric alignments of planets</note>; these are circles, as it were, abstracted from physical quantity and reduced into the narrowness of a qualitative point, yet capable of perceiving the different regions and directions of the sky.

I have placed two radiating stars outside this circle, one higher than the other, so that I might warn through this visual representation that it makes no difference to the Configuration on Earth whether a Planet is high or low in the heavens; one can be many times higher than the other while the same Configuration remains on Earth.

Furthermore, the fact that in the first axiom the word *congruent* precedes, and in the second the word *knowable* precedes, was not done by chance but by design. For the fact that a certain Aspect is effective is caused by both figures: both the one inscribed in the circumference and the one whose single angle is formed by the rays at the center. This is due to both **Knowability** and **Congruence**, though not equally so. All of these matters require a somewhat more lengthy explanation; the reason the subject is so thorny is for this one purpose: that the number of Aspects may be reduced through philosophical reasoning, or at least categorized into certain degrees...

## Proposition I.

The kinship of <term>Radiations</term> <note>original: *Radiationum*; the rays of light or influence emitted by planets</note> with the Circle and its arcs is greater than that of <term>Consonances</term> <note>original: *Consonantiarum*; musical harmonies</note>.

The foundations of this were laid down in Book III and should now rightly be transferred to Book IV as an axiom; however, it is proven thus: 1. Consonances belong to sounds, and sounds consist in motions; and their high and low pitches, by which Consonances are expressed, arise from the speed and slowness of motions, according to what was demonstrated in Book III. But fast and slow sounds are drawn from stretched strings that are plucked, not only if the tension is circular, but also, and much more so, if it is rectilinear <note>Kepler is pointing out that you can hear a harmony on a straight guitar string, so the "circle" isn't strictly necessary for music</note>. Therefore, consonances do not immediately regard the circle and its arcs because of its circular shape, but because of the length of the parts—that is, their mutual proportion. They possess what they possess from the circle even if the circle is destroyed and stretched out into a straight line. **Aspects**, on the contrary, by Definition I, are angles which the circle measures with its arcs; they cannot exist otherwise unless that which is said to exist remains—insofar, that is, as it possesses a circular shape and retains it whole.

The opposite is true in Aspects: for the measurement of that which corresponds only to a circle can in no way have a regard for straightness.

Therefore, figures are more familiar to <term>Aspects</term> <note>original: *Aspectibus*; the specific geometric angles between planets, such as a square or trine</note> than to Consonances.

# Proposition III.

**The <term>congruence</term> <note>original: *congruentia*; Kepler's term for the ability of shapes to fit together perfectly, like tiles, which he uses to rank their "harmonic" perfection</note> of figures has more power in establishing effective Configurations than in Consonances.**

Many arguments for this matter are available. 1. *Congruence is a property of the figure insofar as the figure is a whole and has a particular form:* but a figure, insofar as it possesses this whole form, is first of all more naturally related to <term>configurations</term> <note>original: *configurationibus*; the arrangement of planets in the sky</note> than to Consonances, according to Proposition II. Secondly, it divides the circle harmonically as a whole, and the circle itself is also more closely related to configurations than to consonances, according to Proposition I. Therefore, for both reasons—the specific nature of the figure and the shared nature of the figure and circle—the Congruence of figures carries greater weight in configurations than in consonances.

2. *From the number of figures.* For we have established this, through the preceding axioms: that figures are effective through their properties. Therefore, where the number of efficient [factors] corresponds more...

## Proposition IV.

->**For the efficacy of configurations, the Congruence of figures is more powerful than Knowability.**<-

This is proven from the condition of the <term>sublunary Soul</term> <note>original: *Animæ sublunaris*; in Kepler's view, the "soul" or vital force of the Earth that responds to the heavens</note>, and also from the faculties of the human soul which perceive the aspects. Indeed, its instinct—as we said in Chapter III—is as much duller than human instinct as the body of the Earth is cruder than the body of man. Yet even Congruence is something subsequent to Knowability, and as it were extended outward into something

...body, which holds the Idea of sensible works. It is therefore reasonable to believe that these animate faculties are moved and affected by the **Congruence** <note>original: *Congruentiâ*; the property of shapes fitting together to fill a space</note> rather than by the **Knowability** <note>original: *Scibilitate*; the mathematical possibility of a shape being constructed or known</note> of figures.

Congruence and Knowledge were contrasted within the same class of Configurations. Now, two figures are contrasted with each other: first, by the cause of Congruence alone, and then by the cause of Configuration.

## Proposition V.

Congruence is a property more of the **Circumferential** figure than of the **Central** one.

*For it holds a more powerful place in that figure which can be made whole by reason of the place from which it is named; because congruence belongs to whole figures, as appears from Book II. But of the Central figure, no more than one angle can stand in the center, by the first definition. In the circumference, however, it can be entirely Circumferential: therefore [the proposition holds].*

## Proposition VI.

Of the two figures which each **Aspect** <note>An astrological relationship between planets based on their angular distance</note> claims for itself, the Circumferential is more powerful than the Central.

For in this business, Congruence is more powerful than Knowability, according to Proposition IV. And that [Congruence] is more powerful in the circumferential figure, according to Proposition V. Therefore, that in which the prevailing quality exists more strongly also makes that thing prevail—namely, <margin>Figure IX</margin> the circumferential figure.

The same is also proven from the innermost properties of the **Soul**, touched upon in Chapter III. For since it is the Soul that provides the formal **Being** <note>original: *Esse formale*</note> to the **Harmonic** <note>original: *Harmonik*</note> Configurations, surely by the same distinction that the soul is either a circle or a point (the center of the circle), those familiar figures—the Circumferential and the Central—will also be distinguished.

Even though every Soul carries a certain Idea of a circle—abstracted indeed not only from matter but also in a way from magnitude, as said in Chapter III—and thus the circle and <margin>Figure X</margin> center here almost coincide, and the soul itself can be called either a potential circle or a more distinct point, and thus in a way qualitative; nevertheless, this distinction seems to be observed: that some faculties of the soul are to be considered rather as a circle, and others rather as a point. For just as a circle cannot be thought of without a center, every...

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
...in turn, the point has around itself a region for drawing a circle; so also in the **Soul** <note>original: *Anima*; the animating principle of a living being</note> there is no operation without an imaginative impression. Conversely, every internal reception or meditation exists for the sake of external movement; every interior faculty of the soul exists for the sake of those further outward. The sovereign and supreme faculty of the Soul itself, called the **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*; the highest, intuitive part of the soul</note>, what is it but the **Center**? What is the **Reasoning** faculty <note>original: *Ratiocinativa*; the part of the mind that processes information step-by-step</note>, if not the **Circle**? For just as the center is within and the circle is without, so the Mind remains within itself, while reasoning weaves a kind of external web. And just as the center is the basis of the circle, so the Mind is the basis, fount, and origin of reasonings.

<margin>Figure XI.</margin>
<image-desc>A circular diagram containing a five-pointed star (pentagram) inscribed within it. Lines connect the vertices, and asterisks mark two points: one at the top vertex and one at the bottom-left vertex. There is a smaller polygonal area delineated in the center of the star.</image-desc>
Furthermore, all these faculties of the Soul—the **Intellect** as much as **Discourse** <note>linear, logical thought</note>, and finally even the **Sensitive** faculty—are a kind of **Center**; but the motive faculties of the Soul are the **Circle**. This is because, just as the external circle is placed around the center, so action is directed outward, while knowledge and meditation are perfected within. As the circle is to the point, so in a certain way is external **Action** to internal **Contemplation**, and animal motion to sensation. For the point, because it is opposed to the circumference from every side, is naturally suited for representing to the recipient; and the sensitive Soul (or here, the faculty that perceives **Radiations** <note>The light and influence reaching Earth from the planets</note>), what else is it doing in sensing and perceiving than being acted upon? Namely, because it is moved by objects.

<margin>Figure XII.</margin>
<image-desc>A circular diagram depicting an inscribed octagon. Within the octagon, lines radiate from a small central five-pointed star toward the vertices and sides of the octagon. Comparing both relationships: just as the center is the same on both sides, so also the form of knowledge is in a certain way the same, whether it be the sovereign mental form or the sensitive (or its analog, the perceptive faculty of Radiations). Neither, insofar as it is such, uses discourse within itself, but knows without it. Thus, this nature—I mean the **sublunary Nature** <note>The "soul" of the Earth or the atmosphere that responds to planetary aspects</note>, or even the sensitive faculty—is a certain thin image of the sovereign human Mind: just as that discourse of reason is an image of these actions or operations of the soul; both are a circle.

Insofar, therefore, as Souls perceive celestial radiations, and are thus moved by them within themselves, let them be as **points** to us. But insofar as they in turn move—that is, insofar as they transfer the perceived harmonies of the radiations into their own works and are stimulated by them to act—they ought to be considered as a **circle**.

It follows, therefore, that in the degree that it knows the **Harmonies** of the rays, the soul is occupied chiefly with the **central figure**; but in the degree that it operates, stirring up **meteors** <note>original: *meteora*; in the 17th century, this referred to all atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, or lightning</note> (and similar things in man), it accommodates itself to the **circumferential** figure. And indeed, in an **aspect** <note>the angular relationship between planets</note>, our first concern is for its efficacy rather than the manner in which it is perceived by the operating Soul; therefore, the consideration of the circumferential figure is prior to that of the central.

# ON HARMONICS, BOOK IV.

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

In the previous section, the relationship of one figure to another was compared within a single aspect. In the following "twin" proposition, assuming the same figure, its Congruence will be compared against its Knowability.

## Proposition VII.

**IN** a circumferential figure <note>A geometric shape whose sides are chords along the edge of a circle.</note>, Congruence <note>The property of shapes fitting together without gaps, like floor tiles.</note> takes precedence over the Knowability of the side; conversely, in a central figure <note>A shape formed by rays meeting at the center point of a circle, such as the angles formed by planets at the Earth.</note>, the Knowability of the side takes precedence over the Congruence of the figure.

*This proposition serves to complete the work begun in Proposition III. For although Congruence is more powerful in Book IV than in Book III, "demonstrability" (or the ability to be proven) was also more significant in Book III. However, this must not be entirely separated from the formation of the Aspects <note>The specific angular distances between planets that create astrological "harmonies."</note>. Since no Congruence lacks its own scientific determination, it depends upon that determination—both of the side and especially of the area contained by the figure's sides. For the demonstration is drawn from the angles, in which the "fitness" for congruence resides.*

*Regarding this specific proposition, it might seem that the opposite is true for both cases. For as far as the central figure is concerned, one of its angles is actually expressed by the rays themselves. In a circumferential figure, no angle is expressed, but only the side, to a certain extent. Yet Congruence is a property of angles; therefore, it seems Congruence should primarily be looked for in the Central figure. For if the sublunary nature <note>original: *natura sublunaris*; the animating spirit or soul of the Earth and its inhabitants which Kepler believed responded to celestial harmonies.</note> perceives the size of the angle formed at the Earth by the rays of two planets, it seems it should also be able to perceive that angle’s "fitness" or aptitude for fitting together with others.*

*On the other hand, the reason why the Knowability <term>Scibilitas</term> <note>The degree to which a shape can be constructed and understood using geometric logic (constructability).</note> of the side should be considered more important than the Congruence of the figure in a circumferential shape seems to be as follows. For the knowledge by which a figure is known (as demonstrated in the first book) consists in the equality of either the side with a rational <term>effable</term> <note>original: *effabilis*; a technical term for a length that can be expressed as a rational ratio to the diameter.</note> part of the diameter, or the square of the side with a rational part of the square of the diameter, or the area of the figure with the same, or in some other connection and determination of the side, its square, or its area, to the diameter or its square. Now, granted that the sublunary Nature has a sense of the Zodiac circle—that is, the sensible circle standing outside, which it compares to the idea of an abstract, intellectual circle innate or co-created within itself—it follows that, in the order of nature, it first senses how large an arc of the Zodiac is marked off by two planets. It then senses how large a straight line is stretched under that arc (the chord), and what its quality is: whether it is of an "effable" length, or only so in the "power" of its square <note>meaning the square of the line is a rational proportion of the square of the diameter, even if the line itself is not.</note>, or whether, with some other part, it makes an effable sum of squares and an effable rectangle (upon which property the Effability of the area is founded). These things, I say, seem to become known to the sublunary Nature first in the order of nature, because the side exists before the figure described by the multiplication of that side. Only later, when the whole figure has been described in the Zodiac circle, do its angles and their sizes become clear—whether they are of a "fitting" type, whether the figure concurs in all its angles toward the same kind of congruence, and whether that congruence can be continued. In short: congruence is a property of the angles, while knowability is a property of the sides. Therefore, where the angle of a figure becomes known before the side, the roles of Congruence seem prior and more important than those of Knowability; where it becomes known later, they are less important. But in a figure reaching to the center, the angle is known first; whereas in a figure described on the surface (formed, say, by only two planets), the side is known first. It therefore seems right that in a central figure, Congruence is given more weight, and in a superficial figure, Knowability.*

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

These arguments brought against our proposition must therefore be refuted; and by the same effort, the order of properties—*Congruence and Knowability*—must be strengthened with true arguments.

First, then, even if it is true that in a central figure <note>A "central figure" is a geometric shape formed by planetary rays meeting at the Earth, which acts as the center point. See Figure III mentioned in the margin.</note>, one angle is formed by the rays of two planets, it does not follow that the mind perceiving the size of that angle perceives the *Congruence* <note>Congruence refers to the property of shapes fitting together perfectly to fill a space, like tiles on a floor.</note> of the figure to which that angle belongs as being prior in nature or order. The reason is clear: because Congruence, insofar as it belongs to a single angle and a few of its equals meeting at one point on a plane, is too general. There are infinite forms of angles that fit together in this way, and the smaller each individual angle is, the greater the number of them required to fill the space. Therefore, this is not that specific *Congruence* which we discussed in Book II, which does not apply to angles in isolation, but to entire figures because of their angles—nor does it apply to single figures, but to several joined together.

Thus, the objection is not only dissolved but even turned back against itself. For what the opponent used regarding the circumferential figure <note>A "circumferential figure" is one whose sides are chords drawn along the outer edge of a circle, connecting the positions of the planets themselves.</note>, we can just as rightly claim for the central figure: that the Congruence proposed here is secondary to *Knowability* <note>original: "Scibilitas"; the property of a shape being mathematically definable or constructible by a geometer.</note>. Therefore, the role of Knowability must be more important than the role of Congruence, even by the opponent's own admission. For a figure must first be formed before the whole can fit together. Now, unless the side of the figure is "knowable," the figure cannot be formed. For even if it is true that, given one angle of a figure (formed by the rays of two planets at the center), the total number of sides is implied, and through them the fitness of the whole figure for congruence—and that the nature of the side does not enter into this specific proof—yet that single angle of the figure is not "given" (that is, it is not recognized as the angle of a fitting figure) except through a knowable side. Therefore, in the order of nature, the Soul <note>Kepler believes the "Soul of the World" or the human mind has an innate geometric instinct that "recognizes" these harmonies.</note> knows the side before it recognizes that a fitting angle is being presented to it.

But if we compare both figures here, the side or area of the central figure is actually less "given" by the act of radiation itself than the side of the circumferential figure. For the rays themselves always determine the latter, but they do not always determine the former, except in certain figures—such as in the Triangle <note>original: "Trigono"; a 120-degree aspect.</note>, because the individual sides of the circumferential angle subtend an arc equal to the intercepted arc. Therefore, the central figure is further from the act of knowing than the circumferential one; thus, the notification of Congruence is also further removed. Yet the objection relied on the opposite, as if Central Congruence were closer to our knowledge than Circumferential Congruence.

Furthermore, if the size of an angle is perceived, by what means will it be perceived if not by its own measure? That is, by the arc of that circle which is described from the point of the proposed angle—which is the Earth. It is not perceived primarily by the circle that circumscribes the central figure and passes through the Earth. Therefore, in perceiving the size of an angle in a central figure, the Soul must exert that power by which it is a circle <note>Kepler views the Soul as a geometric entity that reflects the structure of the circle.</note>, not that power by which it is a tiny point where the angle meets. And by this same pattern of its circular essence, it also perceives the side of the circumferential figure and its arc, and does so first. Only later, by doubling this arc, does the arc of the smaller circle emerge (which circumscribes the central figure and is drawn through the center of the first circle). This arc serves the inscription of the central figure into the circle. For the same order found in reasoning is also found in instinct. Thus, it is demonstrated once more that the path to perceiving the central figure is longer, and so also is the path to its Congruence. Therefore, the objection subverts itself by placing superiority in "prior perception."

Regarding the reasons for the other part, the answer is as follows: it is indeed true even in the circumferential figure that the Knowability of the side is prior to the Congruence of the whole figure, due to the arguments mentioned, which also apply here. But it does not follow that from two things...

# BOOK IV OF THE HARMONICS

...things, where one is the cause of the other; that which is the cause should, in turn, move a third thing even more strongly. For according to the capacity of the soul which must be moved, the cause often has less power over it than the effect: just as here, the <term>Sublunary Soul</term> <note>Kepler’s term for the soul of the Earth or the human soul living beneath the moon, which responds to planetary alignments.</note>, insofar as it is perceptive, is moved more by the <term>knowability</term> <note>original: "scibilitas"; the property of a geometric figure being rational and mathematically definable.</note> of the central figure; but insofar as it is operative, it is moved more by the <term>congruence</term> <note>original: "congruentia"; the property of shapes fitting together perfectly to tile a plane, discussed in Book II.</note> of the circumferential figure.

<margin>Previously Prop. VI.</margin>
<margin>Prop: VI. <gloss>for we used it earlier</gloss></margin>
My own arguments for proving this proposition are these: the center is a certain idea of the Theoretical mind, or intellect; the circumference is an idea of the Practical or operative faculty: because just as the center of a circle is the base and origin, so is meditation the origin of action. Therefore, a figure which extends an angle to the center—that is, to the Earth where the Soul sits—being the perceiver of the figure, extends itself as if for knowing and judging, since the center represents the tribunal of knowledge. Therefore, in a <term>central figure</term> <note>A geometric figure formed by the rays of two planets meeting at the Earth (the center).</note>, knowledge should be considered more highly; regardless of the fact that it is compared through the circle as an instrument, as was said a little earlier.

On the contrary, a figure that arranges its angles on the circumference applies itself more toward imitating and expressing in the Soul's work, as if concurring with the idea of the works. And yet, congruence rather than knowability possesses the idea of sensible works and buildings, because it follows the figures as wholes, whereas the side—by which a figure is known—is merely its element. For this reason, in a <term>circumferential figure</term> <note>A figure whose vertices lie on the circle formed by the planetary orbits.</note>, congruence is to be regarded more than knowability.

The second argument for this second part rests on the same consideration of the Soul. That for the sake of which other things exist is superior. But for the sake of the work of Sublunary Nature, and thus also of the human Soul and its lower faculties, configurations are perceived; that is, they are perceived so that they may be expressed in work. Therefore, the dignity of the motor faculty is greater in this business. But since the knowability of the Circumferential figure serves perception, and Congruence serves operation (as stated), then the congruence of the circumferential figure is superior to its own knowability.

## Proposition VIII.

An arc of a circle formed by an <term>incongruous figure</term> <note>A shape that cannot tile a surface perfectly, such as a heptagon.</note> grants no Efficacy to the radiations of the two planets that mark the ends of that arc.

For if congruence is the most powerful cause of Efficacy (according to Propositions III, IV, and VII), then when this is lacking, knowability—which is a lesser cause in this context—will not be sufficient. For even if knowability prevails over congruence in the Central figure (by the other part of Proposition VII), the circumferential figure is in turn more powerful than the central one (by Proposition VI). And in that circumferential figure, congruence is more powerful (by the first part of Proposition VII). Thus, the congruence of the circumferential figure still outweighs the knowability of the central figure.

Behold the reason why, although knowable figures are infinite (granted, of different degrees), the <term>Aspects</term> <note>The specific angular relationships between planets (like 90° or 120°) that are believed to have physical or astrological effects.</note> are nevertheless few.

## AXIOM III.

Arcs of a circle whose figures possess more and better degrees of congruence and knowability also receive more effective configurations.
