*If the first two axioms are consistent with the truth, then this shall also be: that for whatever reason a thing is of a certain nature, when that reason is intensified, the thing itself will be even more so. Understand it thus: that in a circumferential figure <note>A geometric shape defined by its relation to the outer edge of a circle.</note>, the comparison of degrees of **Congruence** <note>original: "Congruentiae"; the property of shapes to fit together perfectly without gaps, like floor tiles.</note> is primary; in a central figure, the degrees of **Knowability** <note>original: "Scibilitatis"; the ease with which a shape can be constructed using only a compass and straightedge.</note> are primary; and finally, the parts of the circumferential figure are more potent.*

## Proposition IX.

**E**ffective configurations <note>Often called "aspects" in astrology; the specific angles between planets that Kepler believed influenced the Earth.</note> are those which intercept the following arcs of the Zodiac circle:
180 Degrees: **Opposition** ☍, from the **Diameter** of the circle: as in Figure I.

45 Degrees: **Octile** or **Sesquiquadrate**, and 135 Degrees: **Trioctile** or **Sesquiquadrate** ⚎ from the **Octagon** and its **Star-shape**: as in Figure V and VI.
30 Degrees: **Semisextile** ✳, and 150 Degrees: **Quincunx**, from the **Dodecagon** <note>A twelve-sided polygon.</note> and its **Star-shape**: as in Figure VII and VIII.
72 Degrees: **Quintile** ♈, and 108 Degrees: **Tridecile** or **Sesquiquintile**: from the **Pentagon** and the **Decagonal Star**: as in Figure IX and X.
144 Degrees: **Biquintile** ♊, and 36 Degrees: **Semiquintile** or **Decile**: from the **Pentagonal Star** and the **Decagon**: as in Figure XI and XII.

*That these figures are **Knowable** and can be demonstrated was shown in Book I; that they are also **Congruent** was shown in Book II. That the configurations of the arcs expressed by such shapes are indeed effective is held by the previously mentioned Axioms I and II.*

## Proposition X.

**T**he first and strongest degree of effectiveness among the Aspects is that of the **Conjunction** ☌ and the **Opposition** ☍.

<margin>Commonly used symbols.</margin>
*For in a **Conjunction**, two rays coincide into the same line and descend from the same direction; in an **Opposition** ☍, though they descend from different directions, they are nonetheless parts of one continuous line. This is truly the most perfect **Congruity** and a kind of starting point for all congruence. Thus, while the conjunction is represented by a point marked on the circumference of the circle, and the opposition by the **Diameter**; these are certainly the principles—the former the starting point and the latter the measure—of all knowledge in this branch of science. This is because every straight line within a circle is contained by a scientific, demonstrative determination through either the length or the "power" <note>In geometry, "power" often refers to the square of a line's length.</note> of the Diameter: as shown in Book*

### Proposition XI.

#### The second degree in the Efficacy of Aspects belongs to the Square □.

*For in the Square many prerogatives concur. The first is that the central figure <note>The shape formed inside the circle by connecting the points of the aspect.</note> is similar to the circumferential figure <note>The divisions of the circle's edge.</note>: therefore, whatever degrees it obtains in **Congruence** <note>The ability of shapes to fit together without gaps.</note> and **Knowability** <note>original: "Scibilitate"; how easily a shape can be constructed geometrically using a compass and straightedge.</note>, these are understood to be, in a sense, doubled compared to the other Aspects. For just as the Square is the first after the Opposition to expand from the thinness of a line into a certain width or superficial magnitude of a four-sided area: so the other Aspects depart from the identity of the Square's shapes into a certain variation of shapes. Since, therefore, in other physical matters a united force is stronger, there will also be a greater degree of strength in this ideal and objective impression, where the figures in distinct locations—namely, the central and the circumferential—are of the same species.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the properties of the square (Tetragon) within a circle. It features a circle with an inscribed square, and within that, another square rotated by 45 degrees. Lines connect the center of the circle to the vertices and midpoints, forming various triangles and demonstrating the symmetry and congruency discussed in the text.</image-desc>

<margin>□</margin>
*Next, as far as Congruence is concerned, it is most perfect and all-encompassing in the **Tetragon** <note>A square.</note>. For this figure fits with itself in a solid to form a **cube**; which is the measure of all solidity. It fits most simply, with only three angles joined at a point. It also fits with itself in a plane, with four angles meeting. Furthermore, in solid form, it fits variously with the **Triangle**, **Pentagon**, **Hexagon**, **Octagon**, and **Decagon** to form solid figures <note>Referring to the Platonic and Archimedean solids, such as the cuboctahedron or the rhombicuboctahedron.</note>. It fits with all of these, and additionally with the **Dodecagon** <note>12-sided figure</note> and **Icosagon** <note>20-sided figure</note> to some extent, to tile a flat surface: in which property it is surpassed by no other.*

*Thirdly, the area of the Tetragon is **effable** <note>original: "effabilis"; a technical term meaning the area can be expressed as a rational proportion of the square of the circle's diameter.</note>, which is a principle of a certain singular and distinguished Congruence in a plane: such that a certain number of areas of this figure equals a certain number of squares of the diameter. Thus, the figures do not only fit together by their angles and sides, but also, in a way, through their specific lines, they fit with the sides of the square of the diameter. In this property, the Square aspect shares a partial kinship only with the **Semisextile** <note>The 30-degree aspect.</note>. See Book II.*

*Fourthly, the degree of knowledge of the side is not ignoble, as it is **expressible in power** <note>original: "effabile potentiâ"; meaning that while the side itself might be an irrational number, its square is a rational number relative to the circle.</note>: in which degree it excels all other figures, except for the Hexagon. Yet it does not yield its place to the Hexagon for that reason; since Knowability is not to be compared to Congruence, as explained above: truly the accumulation of prerogatives is effective in increasing Efficacy, by Axiom III of this book.*

### Proposition XII.

#### The third degree of Efficacy belongs to the Trine △, the Sextile ✳, and the Semisextile ⚺.

*The reason I place the Trine, Sextile, and Semisextile in the same degree...*

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin> ...it is not the identity of properties, but their **Equipollence** <note>original: "æquipollentia"; the state of having equal power or weight in a system, even if the forms differ.</note> that creates this effect. First, their primary figures offer mutual assistance in **Plane Congruence** <note>original: "congruentia plana"; how shapes tile a flat surface without gaps.</note>: for they fit together in various ways both among themselves and with others, such as the Square. Here, the **Triangle** <note>The Trine aspect (120°).</note> and the **Hexagon** <note>The Sextile aspect (60°).</note> excel because their individual types can tile a plane on their own; however, the Hexagon excels the Triangle because it achieves the most perfect congruence in a plane, namely with only three angles meeting at a single point. Both excel the **Dodecagon** <note>The Semisextile aspect (30°).</note> because they also fit together with other figures to form solid bodies, which the Dodecagon cannot do.

<margin>Δ <note>The symbol for the Trine aspect.</note></margin>
<image-desc>A circular diagram showing an equilateral triangle inscribed within a circle, with a smaller hexagon positioned inside the triangle.</image-desc>

But in turn, the Dodecagon excels the others in its **Effability** <note>original: "effabilitate"; the degree to which a geometric value can be expressed as a rational number or a specific type of square root.</note>, since the areas of the Triangle and Hexagon are "medial" and thus less "noble" <note>In Euclidean geometry, "medial" areas involve irrational square roots that are considered less "knowable" than more direct proportions.</note>. This difference in areas, as just mentioned, flows back into the perfection of their congruence.

Similarly, the Triangle again excels the Hexagon because the triangular form fits with itself in various ways to create solid shapes, giving rise to three **Regular Bodies** <note>The Tetrahedron, Octahedron, and Icosahedron, which are built from triangles.</note>; the Hexagon, however, only fits together with other types of figures to form solids. Thus, by weighing the importance of these diverse properties against each other, **Congruence**—which is the first and most important element of **Efficacy** <note>The power of the aspect to affect the soul.</note>—is brought to a nearly equal balance among these three.

In terms of **Knowability** <note>original: "scibilitate"; how easily the shape can be constructed with a compass and straightedge.</note>, the Hexagon holds the first rank because its side is "effable" <note>The side of a hexagon is equal to the radius of the circle, a simple 1:1 ratio.</note>. The Triangle holds the second rank, occupying the same level as the Square, having a side that is "effable in power" <note>The side of an equilateral triangle is the square root of 3 times the radius.</note> but in a less prestigious proportion. Last here is the Dodecagon, which has an "ineffable" side.

<margin>*</margin>
<image-desc>A circular diagram featuring an inscribed hexagon. Inside the hexagon, additional lines form a smaller central triangle or geometric construction.</image-desc>

However, "knowability" is neither the primary argument for Efficacy, nor is it considered in the "primary" figure—that is, the one on the circumference. Instead, it is only considered in the "central" figure, which is less primary. If this property has any power, it makes the **Trine** slightly more effective than the **Sextile**, because a Trine forms the angle of a Hexagon at the center; it makes the **Semisextile** (measured by the angle of a **Twelve-pointed Star** at the center) slightly less effective than both. Nevertheless, the "science" or definition of the Semisextile is more noble than those that follow it.

<margin>*</margin>
<image-desc>A circular diagram containing a complex twelve-pointed star, identified as a "Stella Dodecagonica," at its center, surrounded by concentric circles.</image-desc>

This is because the side of its central figure is of the most noble species among "Ineffables"—namely, a **Binomial** <note>original: "Binomium"; a specific mathematical term from Euclid's Book X for a line segment composed of two rational parts that are only commensurable in square.</note>. In the case of its double division, it always holds the higher rank, so much so that when paired with its partner (the side of the circumferential figure), it forms an "effable rectangle." This is a mark of almost absolute perfection. Thus, this weight of its "ineffability" allows this figure to compete in "knowability" with the Triangle and Hexagon.

## Proposition XIII.

The Fourth Degree in the Efficacy of Configurations is the **Quintile**, the **Biquintile**, and the **Quincunx**.

<image-desc>Three circular geometric diagrams representing the fourth-degree aspects. The top circle contains a regular pentagon with a small five-pointed star (pentagram) at its center. The middle circle contains a large, bold pentagram whose points touch the edge of the circle. The bottom circle contains a complex, twelve-pointed star (dodecagram) formed by intersecting lines.</image-desc>

For these share a common **Congruence** <note>original: "congruentia"; refers to how geometric shapes tile a surface or fit together.</note> of their primary figures in a plane, although the individual species do not tile the plane on their own. Instead, the first two <note>The pentagon and pentagram.</note> fit together with one another, while the last <note>The dodecagonal star.</note> fits with others related to it. The first two aspects excel because their figures—the **Pentagon** and its **Star** <note>The pentagram.</note>—also fit together in three dimensions to form two regular solid bodies <note>The dodecahedron and the icosahedron, two of the five "Platonic Solids."</note>. Because of this "nobility," they are ranked almost as high as the **Trine** and the **Square**. The **Dodecagonal Star** <note>Associated here with the Quincunx (150°), or 5/12 of a circle.</note> does not fit together to form a solid body. However, in turn, the Dodecagonal Star excels in its **Plane Congruence**, which can be continued infinitely <note>A reference to how twelve-sided symmetry can create repeating patterns on a flat surface.</note>; whereas the pentagonal shapes cannot be extended very far without resulting in an irregular mixture. See all of these demonstrations in Book II.

As far as the **Knowability** <term>Knowability|original: "scibilitas"; a concept from Book I regarding whether a shape's dimensions can be expressed through rational numbers or square roots—a measure of "harmony" for Kepler.</term> of the sides in the central figures is concerned: here also, the sides of the **Decagon** <note>A 10-sided figure, related to the 36° aspect.</note>, the **Tridecile** <note>An aspect of 108°, or 3/10 of the circle.</note>, and the **Dodecagon** <note>A 12-sided figure, related to the 30° aspect.</note> occupy a middle ground. In this class, they stand between the side of the preceding **Trine** <note>120° aspect.</note> and the sides of the **Pentagon** and **Pentagonal Star**, which are the central figures in the following class. For it was demonstrated in Book I that the side of the Decagon is "prior in knowledge" <note>Meaning it is more fundamentally constructible or geometrically "simpler."</note> to the side of the Pentagon, and the Tridecile is prior to the Pentagonal Star. Therefore, **Knowability** leads to the same ranking as **Congruence**, according to Proposition VII. This was the primary reason that Proposition VII had to be presented first: to prevent the **Decile** <note>36° aspect.</note> or **Tridecile** from being ranked higher than the **Quintile** <note>72° aspect.</note> and **Biquintile** <note>144° aspect.</note>. If, however, someone ignores the central figure and prefers to seek Knowability in the outer circumference (just as one seeks Congruence)—even though it must be admitted that, in this way, the Decile would be preferred over the Quintile, and the Tridecile over the Biquintile—let him remember that the most important parts of Congruence are...

Therefore, these degrees are not only weighed against each other, but the side of the **Decagon** <note>the 10-sided figure</note> actually excels somewhat. Rightly, then, was it done that I placed the **Quincunx** aspect (150 degrees) in the same rank as the **Quintile** (72 degrees) and **Biquintile** (144 degrees), though the primary seat was given to these latter two.

### Proposition XIV.

**The Fifth**, last, and weakest degree of aspects consists of the **Decile** and **Tridecile**, the **Octile** and **Trioctile**.
*I have assigned the fifth place to the Decile and Tridecile (Maestlin <note>Michael Maestlin, Kepler's university professor and mentor</note> calls them the Semi-quintile and Sesqui-quintile), which I have omitted from my Ephemerides <note>astronomical tables predicting the positions of celestial bodies</note> until now. With these I have associated the Octile and Trioctile (or the Semi-square and Sesqui-square), which calendar-makers have seized upon too hotly and thoughtlessly, though indeed at my suggestion and with some authority from Ptolemy. Therefore, both points must be proven: first, that these four aspects are weaker than the Quintile and Biquintile; and second, that the Decile and Tridecile are only very slightly stronger than the Octile and Trioctile.*

<image-desc>A circular diagram showing an inscribed decagon (ten-sided polygon) with a five-pointed star (pentagram) drawn inside it, connecting every second vertex. There are small tick marks at the 12 o'clock and 2 o'clock positions on the circle's circumference.</image-desc>

<margin>
Since, therefore, our Propositions place the chief weight of Efficacy in the **congruence** <note>the ability of shapes to fit together without gaps, like floor tiles</note> of the primary figure (that is, the one on the circumference), it is manifest that the **Pentagon** and its star fit together with figures of their own kind to form a perfect solid, as has just been said. They also fit together beautifully to pave a plane surface. Conversely, the **Decagon** and the **Octagon** <note>8-sided figure</note> with their stars cannot fit together with others of their kind to form a solid. To be sure, the Decagon and Octagon do fit together, but not with all others

### Proposition XV.

**There are some configurations that waver between being effective and ineffective: namely, the Arc of 24 Degrees from the Pentadecagon <note>A 15-sided polygon</note>, and the Arc of 18 Degrees from the Icosagon <note>A 20-sided polygon</note>.**

For these figures are <term>knowable</term> <note>original: "scibiles." In Kepler’s geometry, this means they can be constructed using only a straightedge and compass according to Euclidean rules.</note>, but the former only improperly, and the latter at a remote degree, as demonstrated in Book I. And they are congruent <note>capable of tiling a flat surface</note>, but the former is not equal in all its angles within the same form of **Congruence**; while the latter has all angles, but with a Congruence that clearly cannot be continued, as shown in Book II. Therefore, there is a certain beginning of Effectiveness, a sort of attempt; but the effect is either non-existent or imperfect.

These figures have many stars; the former [the 15-sided figure] indeed has five, whose sides subtend these arcs of the circle: 48°, 96°, 112°, 156°, and 168° <note>These arcs are generated by the various star-polygons that can be drawn within a 15-sided figure. Some values in the OCR, like 112 and 156, may be slight transcription errors for 120 and 144.</note>. The latter [the 20-sided figure] has four, whose sides subtend arcs of the circle of 54°, 126°, 162°, and 171°. But since these stars have hollow angles into which other congruent angles are not received—just as in the hollow angles of the **Pentagonal** and **Decagonal** figures, Pentagonal angles are received; in the **Octagonal**, the angle of the **Tetragon** <note>Square</note>; in the **Dodecagonal**, the angle of the **Trigon** <note>Triangle</note>—there remains for them only the congruence of the acute angles, which we call Rays. Thus, they are more base than their own primary figures.

# CHAPTER VI.

## What the kinship of the Aspects with Musical Consonances is, in Number and its causes.

On what occasions the effective Configurations were detected, and their number increased: it is not the place here to recount, for this pertains to **Astrology**. I dealt with that matter twelve years ago in my book on the *New Star* and the *Fiery Trigon* <note>original: "de stellâ novâ & Trigono igneo." Referring to Kepler's 1606 work *De Stella Nova*, which discussed the supernova of 1604 and the astrological significance of planets meeting in the "fiery" zodiac signs (Aries, Leo, Sagittarius).</note>, chapters VIII, IX, and X. There I showed not only the huge difference between **Aspects** and other...

<summary>Kepler concludes his geometric analysis of astrological aspects, arguing that while many angles are theoretically possible, experience and geometric "purity" (congruence) should limit the number of active aspects. He then begins a new chapter linking these geometric aspects to the mathematical laws of musical harmony.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s defense of his reformed astrology. He is moving from a purely geometric justification of planetary aspects (the angles between planets) to a comparison with musical harmonies, while referencing his previous debates with contemporary scholars.</meta>

<header>BOOK IV OF THE HARMONIES</header>

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>...comments, which are truly Astrological vanities; but I have also solidly dissolved, in my opinion, the philosophical reasons of Count Johannes Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a famous Italian humanist who wrote a massive critique of astrology, which Kepler here claims to have refuted.</note> which were opposed even to this part of Astrology, where they required dissolving and refuting.

And when, nine years ago, Helisaeus Röslin, a Doctor of Medicine and a philosopher of no small renown, took it upon himself to attack this new philosophy in a book published in the German language—being himself devoted to the old style of Astrology—and likewise when another physician, Philippus Feselius, attacked all the parts of Astrology indiscriminately from the opposite side, including the doctrine of configurations <note>original: "configurationibus," referring to the "aspects" or geometric angles between planets</note>; I resisted them both by publishing two small German booklets. The title of one was *Answer to Röslin’s Objections*; the other was *The Third Party Intervening* <note>original: "Tertius Interveniens," a famous work where Kepler sought a middle ground between total belief in astrology and total rejection</note>. In the latter, I defended the truth of the Aspects, while in the former, I asserted the manner of the cause by which the Aspects are effective. Thus, learned men have testified in letters written to me that, finally, a purer philosophy is being taught to Astrologers by me. In all these booklets, I mentioned the kinship that exists between Musical consonances and the Aspects. However, in the first one, I still hesitated regarding the number of Aspects, observing some as spurious—or certainly weak—among the principal ones, while entirely neglecting some stronger ones. In the German works, I began to uncover these defects in my speculation; I decided to repeat this with a somewhat fuller declaration here, as the topic demands, just as I did recently in the *Prolegomena to the Ephemerides* <note>An "Ephemeris" is a table showing the predicted positions of celestial bodies</note>, pages 33, 34, 35, and 36. What could not be explained more extensively there due to intended brevity, I shall now supply here, as the order of the work brings us to it. 

The Axiom which I adopted in the year 1606, and took up for examination and refutation in the cited place of the *Ephemerides*, was this: *That God the Creator either took the laws for ordering the Aspects from the Harmonies of Song below the Octave, described in Book III; or that He attuned the ears of man, the judges of those Chords, to the celestial Aspects.* If this Axiom were true in every respect, it would be necessary for there to be exactly as many aspects as there are Chords up to the Octave <note>original: "Diapason," the Greek musical term for an octave</note>. For the **Sextile** corresponds to the **Minor Third**, the **Quintile** to the **Major Third**, the **Square** to the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, the **Trine** to the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, the **Sesquiquadrate** to the **Minor Sixth**, the **Biquintile** to the **Major Sixth**, and the **Opposition** to the **Octave**. This is because if you subtract from a string a portion as large as the portion of the circle that any aspect takes away, the remainder of the string makes that Consonance with the whole which is assigned to each Aspect here. Therefore, since that seven-fold number of Chords—or rather of harmonic sections, which each Chord follows below the Octave—is certain and demonstrative (no less than the five-fold number of Regular bodies <note>The five "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note> is in Geometry, as was shown in Book III, Chapter II), the method for demonstrating the number of Aspects would be easy and ready through this adopted Axiom. There would have been no need for that laborious apparatus of new Axioms in Book IV.

And indeed, if Meteorological observations had fully supported this seven-fold set of Aspects, I would have rested content with the axiom stated above; nor would I have been greatly worried about the objections that could be raised from the origin of Harmonic ratios or from the consideration of metaphysical causes. But because it has been frequently discovered that sublunary Nature <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which were thought to be influenced by the heavens</note> is also stimulated by the **Semisextile**, which intercepts a twelfth part of the circle—even though when a twelfth portion is taken from a string, the remainder, of the parts...

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>...[the eleventh] does not harmonize with the whole; and because the stimulations of the weather <note>Kepler believed that planetary aspects "stimulated" the Earth's "soul," causing changes in weather.</note> were found to be unreliable through the Sesquadrate <note>original: "Sesquadrum," referring here to the sesquiquadrate or trioctile aspect, which is 135 degrees</note>, which marks off three eighths of the circle; yet when three eighths are removed from a string, the remaining five eighths harmonize perfectly with the whole octave; for this reason, the necessity arose for me to investigate more deeply the causes of this disagreement and diversity in this fourth book. Even though I consider this to have been correctly accomplished and the clearest causes unearthed, it will not hurt to repeatedly emphasize the main point of the whole dispute: since the explanation of those things which were stated more concisely in the *Introduction to the Ephemeris* requires it in this place.

<margin>
1. In forming a concordance, the Remainder of the circle is valid; it is not valid in forming an Aspect.
</margin>The cause, therefore, why there are not as many Aspects as there are harmonic sections in Music—as I had believed up until the year 1608—is this: because Music draws some of its principles of the number seven from the very straightness of the string; whereas the circle, in which we mark the Aspects, returns into itself; nor can another circle be made from the Remainder of the Zodiac, as can be done from a string. These are the words of the said *Prolegomena* on page 35, which are to be explained thus: for as was said in Chapter IV of this book, harmonic sections arise in one way, and Aspects in another, even though both arise from the same circle. For in Book III, the Axioms were arranged such that any string and any part of a string, whether long or short, could be compared again to the whole circle, no less than the whole or longest string was compared to the same circle. But in this Book IV, an arc of a circle, whether larger than a semicircle or smaller, could not be compared to the whole. 

I will speak more clearly: in whatever ways a circle is divided demonstrably <note>meaning by geometric proof using a compass and straightedge</note>, all those ways can be transferred onto a straight line—that is, a string—and any part of it. But it is not the case that a demonstrative division of the whole circle (for example, into three or five) can therefore also be transferred into any arc of it; this was sufficiently demonstrated in the final propositions of Book I. The cause lies in the figure; for a straight line remains a straight line, whether it is cut short or lengthened; but a truncated circle does not remain a circle. Therefore, a proportional <term>SECTION</term> <note>original: "sectio," the division of a line or arc into specific ratios</note> of any two straight lines is possible, and a proportional section of any two circles is possible, but a proportional section of any two arcs of one circle is not possible.

These things are adapted to the proposal in this way: if a string is divided into eight parts by the demonstrative division of a circle, one eighth <note>original: "Octava," used here for a division of 1/8th</note> harmonizes with the whole, and three eighths also harmonize, because one eighth of a circle can be geometrically carved out, as can three eighths. This same demonstrative determination is also among the reasons why the Octile <note>an aspect of 45 degrees</note> and Trioctile <note>an aspect of 135 degrees</note> are effective. But this is the difference: in the former case, a harmonic <term>SECTION</term> is not yet established unless the Remainder—the seven eighths and five eighths—also harmonize both with the whole (of eight parts) and with the carved-out parts (7 with 1, and 5 with 3). And yet, the demonstrative determination of part 1 and part 3 does not grant to their remainders, 7 and 5, that they themselves be consonant: for while 5 is indeed consonant, 7 is dissonant. Therefore, the section of the whole 8 into 5 and 3 is harmonic, but the section into 7 and 1 is not harmonic. From where, then, does the Remainder 5 get its consonance with the whole 8, and the Remainder 7 get its dissonance from it? Doubtless from this: because a circle divided into 5 has a side subtending two-fifths that is geometric; hence it is that a string divided into five (as is the part proposed here from the string of 8) harmonizes with the part that is 2 portions long; wherefore also with...

4 and 8, which are related to 2 in a continuous double proportion <note>These are octaves: 1:2, 1:4, 1:8.</note>. On the other hand, a circle divided into 7 does not produce a chord that can be geometrically demonstrated as a single seventh part; therefore, that Remainder of the chord which contains 7 is dissonant with 1, and thus also with 2, 4, and 8. Observe how a harmonic section of the whole 8 into 3 and 5 <note>A division of a string into 3/8 and 5/8 creates musical intervals.</note> produces only one consonance from the Octagon, and another from the Pentagon. Indeed, it even has a third from another figure: the Decagon. For Part 3 would not be consonant with the Remainder 5, unless it were first consonant with its double, 10; and this is because, in a circle divided into 10, the line subtending three-tenths is demonstrable. However, this coupling of multiple figures has no place in a circle and its parts. For if you first inscribed a regular Octagon in the whole circle, and assumed that you could divide an arc consisting of three-eighths into five parts (although it is impossible to do so by geometric demonstration): certainly, a Pentagon could not be inscribed within those divisions; it would become highly irregular, and more like a hexagon, since the arc already has two endpoints before its division. Since, therefore, there is a vast difference between Remainders—of the chord on one hand, and the circle on the other—it is clear that unless we progress from the circle to the straight line, the ratio of the Remainder cannot be accounted for. Yet an Aspect is an angle, the measure of which is not a straight line, but an arc of a circle described from the meeting of rays at a point. Therefore, the circle does not measure the Aspect, nor form it, nor make it effective by reason of the Remainder, but only by reason of the arc intercepted by the aspect. If not by reason of the Remainder, then it is not by reason of the harmonic section of the chord arising from that division of the circle; because a harmonic section cannot be defined without the Remainder.

† See Emendations on page 255.
</margin>

And thus, that axiom—that the harmonic proportions of song are the causes of the Aspects—is overthrown. Nor does it follow that because the Trioctile or Sesquadrate <note>An astrological aspect of 135 degrees, or 3/8 of a circle.</note> corresponds to the harmonic section that produces a minor third and is effective, that its efficacy therefore comes from the harmonic section of the circle as such. But this much is true, as stated in the *Introduction*: there is a *great* kinship between Harmonies and Aspects, both genres having the same origin from "noble" figures that can be inscribed in a circle. That is to say, the geometric knowability <note>Kepler’s term "scibilitas" refers to whether a shape can be constructed using only a straightedge and compass.</note> of the line subtending three-eighths of a circle is among the elements from which both the harmonic section in Music and the effective Aspect in Physics are constituted.

<margin>
The nature of the knowledge of Harmonic Sections compared with Aspects.
</margin>

I speak here from a hypothesis, as if the mere "knowability" of a figure were enough for efficacy, just as it suffices for the simple consonance of a Part with the Whole. For if we are to be precise, there is also this distinction: in Consonances, "Knowability" carries the most weight; but in Aspects, the "Congruence" <note>Congruence here refers to "tessellation"—the ability of shapes to fit together perfectly to fill a space.</note> of the figures excels. The Semisquare <note>45 degrees.</note> and Sesquadrate are effective not only because the side of the Octagon and its star-form are knowable, but also, and most importantly, because the Octagon and its star are congruent figures.

This is precisely the reason why the Dodecagon <note>A 12-sided figure.</note> primarily produces a strong Aspect, but does not produce a harmonic section—that is, a triple consonance—even though it produces a simple one.

<margin>
The correspondence of minor concords and Aspects is not true, but only a matter of opinion.
</margin>

For the Remainder 11, which is left when one-twelfth is removed, hinders the harmonic section, but it does not hinder the efficacy of the twelfth part itself. But I shall say more on this shortly.

For if a true, mathematical, and causal comparison of Concords with Aspects is to exist, we must utterly overturn the axiom—

...because it is not only insufficient, but even diametrically opposed to the truth. For no aspect properly corresponds to any minor consonance <note>original: "concordantiæ minori"</note>, except for the Opposition <note>The 180° aspect</note>, which corresponds to the Octave consonance <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. Instead, each aspect corresponds to the major consonances—the partners of the minor ones—arising from the triad of each section. Namely, Aspects are defined by the same segments of the circle as the major consonances; however, the minor consonances are defined by the circle's Remainders. For example, the Trine <note>120°</note> aspect does not correspond to the consonance of the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, but to the Octave-plus-Fifth <note>original: "Diapason & epidiapente," a ratio of 3:1</note>. The Square <note>90°</note> does not correspond to the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessarô"</note>, but to the Double Octave <note>original: "Disdiapasôn," a ratio of 4:1</note>. The Quintile <note>72°</note> does not correspond to the Major Third <note>original: "Tertiæ duræ"</note>, but to a compound of that Third and a Double Octave <note>a ratio of 5:1</note>. The Sextile <note>60°</note> does not correspond to the Minor Third <note>original: "Tertiæ molli"</note>, but to the Double Octave plus a Fifth <note>a ratio of 6:1</note>. The Biquintile <note>144°</note> does not correspond to the Major Sixth <note>original: "Sextæ duræ"</note>, as we previously thought, but to a compound of the Major Third and the Octave <note>a ratio of 5:2</note>. The Sesquiquadrate <note>135°</note> does not correspond to the Minor Sixth <note>original: "Sextæ molli"</note>, but to a compound of the Fourth and the Octave <note>a ratio of 8:3</note>, as is evident from the same proportion of the part to the Whole on both sides.

<margin>
3. The true correspondence of major consonances with Aspects does not determine their number.
</margin>

->In this correspondence, therefore, there would be no limit to the aspects;<-
since major consonances are infinite. Those who rely solely on this reason to establish the Semiquadrate aspect <note>45°</note>—because it corresponds to a Triple Octave consonance <note>original: "Trisdiapasôn"</note>—have no excuse for not also accepting the Decile <note>36°</note>, the Tridecile <note>approx. 27.7°</note>, the Vigintile <note>18°</note>, and many others which they nevertheless reject. For these also correspond to their own major consonances, which pile up another Octave every time the division of the circle doubles the number of portions.

<margin>
Hence correct the Book on the New Star <note>original: "Libro de stella nova"</note>, Chapter IX, pages 38 and 40, using this book, which you see promised there on page 41. Hence also supplement my *Tertius Interveniens* <note>A 1610 work by Kepler on astrology</note>, number 59, near the end.
</margin>

What, then, is it that sets a boundary to the number of Aspects? And why is no Semiquadrate or Octile, no Decile or Tridecile introduced, except as secondary principles? Why is the Sesquiquadrate—ennobled by its musical kinship—either omitted or held in low esteem, while the Semisextile <note>30°</note>—a stranger to Music—is not only included but displayed among the primary aspects? It is because Music does not form the Aspects; rather, Geometry forms both types, though by different laws for the one and the other. For whatever comes from a noble figure—which possesses certain unique privileges in Geometry—is both "Harmonic" in Music and "Effective" in Weather <note>original: "Meteoris"</note>. But Meteorology <note>Here meaning the study of celestial influence on Earth's atmosphere</note> and Music are like different nations originating from the same homeland of Geometry. One of them, that is, the Harmonic proportions discussed in Book III, acknowledged the circle as its homeland and traced its origin to it, no less than the Aspects do here. Yet, those proportions emigrated, as it were, from the circle and established their own colony, propagating themselves by their own laws. The Aspects, remaining within the circle of their homeland, use no laws other than those prescribed by the roundness of the circle, derived from the Regular Plane Figures that are Congruent <note>term: Congruent <gloss>Meaning shapes that can tile a surface or fit together perfectly</gloss></note> and inscribed in the circle.

<margin>
4. The primary cause for forming aspects is the Congruence of Figures.
</margin>

For in Music, that "council of seven" sections is constituted from certain marriages, even including the females. For example, the line subtending three Octaves—the eight-angled star <note>The octagram</note>—is indeed among the citizens of Geometry and the class of regular figures, but it is not of the highest nobility. In Music, however, its arc (three-eighths of the circle) found a place because it was born from a marriage in which a commoner woman named the Remainder (that is, three-fourths of the circle) was joined to a Noble (the fourth part of the circle), whose nobility in Geometry comes from the Square <note>original: "Tetragono"</note>. For from this mother (three...

...fourths), through musical generation (by the addition of one Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>) a Part is born, three octaves; to which, with due respect to its senatorial honor, it is allowed to marry another plebeian named "five octaves." The condition of its birth is the same: for its mother is also a Remainder—namely, four-fifths—while its father is patrician, a single fifth, whose geometric nobility is derived from the Pentagon <note>A five-sided figure</note>.

Indeed, the twelfth part of the circle, although it has the right of citizenship in Music—since its chord <term>subtensa: the straight line segment connecting two points on a circle</term> is of the highest geometric nobility in its own right (due to Congruence <note>The ability of shapes to fit together without gaps</note>) and inherited from its parents (for the Hexagon and Triangle are noble figures, from the doubling of whose sides the Dodecagon is formed, more excellent than them because of its expressible area)—yet because this twelfth part has a wife, the Remainder of eleven-twelfths, who in Music and thus also in Geometry is of foreign origin (tracing its lineage to the Hendecagon, a non-demonstrable eleven-sided figure), she cannot attain the right of citizenship. Therefore, the husband has no seat on the council of seven <note>original: "septemviratus"; here referring to the seven divisions of the musical scale</note> in Music to establish the number of divisions of the monochord <note>A one-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</note>.

In Meteorology <note>In Kepler’s time, this included the study of how planets influence the Earth's atmosphere</note>, however, the custom is different. For as each part is noble either by birth or by merit (namely, by its "Knowability" or Congruence), so it holds the greatest authority; the rest flit about like shadows, and no account is taken of the "females" <note>In Kepler’s metaphor, the "female" is the Remainder of the circle that completes the whole</note>.

Thus here the Octile <note>A 45° aspect</note> or Sesquiquadrate <note>A 135° aspect</note>, and the Sesquiquadrate, setting aside their rights in Music because they have "ignoble" chords, are of the common people. They possess no power unless the primary magistrates are absent and the weight of business is pressing. That is, if for a long time there were no primary Aspects, perhaps even these minor Aspects would produce an effect, especially if the earth were full of moisture, in which case it relieves itself sometimes without any stimulus from planetary configurations. But because the primary aspects are usually at hand, sublunary Nature <note>The realm of Earth, located beneath the moon</note>, exhausted by them, does not feel these minor stimuli.

The Decile <note>A 36° aspect</note> and Tridecile <note>A 108° aspect</note> are indeed from an illustrious family, the ten-fold division of the circle which uses the Divine Proportion <term>Divine Proportion: The Golden Ratio</term>; yet they have not illustrated their lineage with deeds (because they do not fit together in every way in a solid three-dimensional shape); nor are they heads of the family. And if they can do anything at all (fitting together to some extent in a flat plane, or even with others in a solid), all of that power is snatched away from them by the aristocrats of other families; or their glory is overshadowed by a greater splendor. For if nature has been sufficiently exercised by an Aspect of 30 degrees, and the earth sufficiently exhausted by it, little strength is left for the neighboring, weaker aspect of 36 degrees to do any work.

Finally, for the Semi-sextile <note>A 30° aspect</note>, there is preeminent nobility from the Dodecagon <note>A 12-sided figure</note>, which is exceptionally Knowable and Congruent. Nor does the "foreign marriage"—which in Music had blocked its path to honors—stand in its way at all in Meteorology. After this Dodecagon, the figures that follow, both in the three "secret" families (the Square, the Triangle, and the Pentagon) and in the fifteen-sided mixture, are all of inferior nobility. Furthermore, they have no clear merits of their own regarding Congruence. Therefore, by the inviolable law of the state, they are barred from the honors and the power of establishing Aspects.

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s mathematical and metaphysical justification for why certain planetary angles (aspects) influence human life and nature. Having previously compared these angles to musical intervals and social classes, he now explains the hierarchy of these aspects based on the geometric "nobility" of the shapes they represent.</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER VI</margin>

From these things it is apparent what I said in the *Prolegomena* <note>The introductory preface</note> of the *Ephemerides* <note>Kepler’s published tables of predicted planetary positions</note>: that in the *establishment of the Aspects <term>Aspect: a specific angular distance between planets, like 90° or 120°, believed to have astrological influence</term>, various causes are at work, and they act together*. I also stated that *Nature makes a selection of those which are provided with more privileges*, and that the *Semisextile <note>An aspect of 30°</note> shares certain rights with the Square <note>An aspect of 90°</note>*; namely, the "effability" <term>effability: the mathematical ability to express a shape's area or side length as a rational ratio of the circle</term> of the area within the figure. It also shares certain rights with the Sextile <note>An aspect of 60°</note>, specifically a multifaceted "congruence" <term>congruence: the ability of geometric shapes to fit together perfectly to fill a flat surface or form a solid</term> on a plane. With these forces joined together, the semisextile emerges as somehow more powerful than the sextile itself, insofar as the mathematical expressibility of the Dodecagonal <note>12-sided figure</note> area is superior to the expressibility of the Hexagonal <note>6-sided figure</note> side; this is because a more perfect fitting-together (congruence) on the plane follows from it. And yet, in this Book IV, I have directed the Semisextile to follow the Sextile, though I place them in the same rank.

In the preface to my tables, I also categorized the Trine <note>120°</note>, the Square, the Quintile <note>72°</note>, and the Biquintile <note>144°</note> as equals in the first and most powerful cause—namely, their pure congruence in three dimensions, used to build the Regular Solids <note>The five Platonic solids, which Kepler believed were the blueprints of the universe</note>. *I stated that the Trine and Square add a second cause, which is not much less significant*: understand this as the pure congruence of figures on a flat plane. This quality is indeed also shared by the Sextile; however, the Sextile does not add this to the first cause, but possesses it as a separate trait. Just as *the Square is said to add a third cause*, namely the mathematical expressibility of the plane; it is not that the Semisextile does not also participate in this, but rather that those qualities which are found individually in other shapes are all accumulated in the Square, so that it becomes the most powerful of all aspects.

Thus, when gathering the "votes" to rank the Sextile, I said that *it shares a certain nobility with the Opposition <note>180°</note>*, referring to the expressibility of the side of the figure, because it is exactly half of the circle's diameter. Again, the Sextile *shares some nobility with the Trine and the Square*; specifically, the pure congruence on a flat plane mentioned earlier. For *only a small portion of that quality*—that is, the ability to fit together with figures of other types—belongs to the *Semisextile* and other more "ignoble" <note>lower-ranked or less mathematically perfect</note> angles. In this *small category of congruence, the figures of the Semisextile and the Octile <note>45°</note> hold the first rank*: the star-shape of the Semisextile could also be grouped here because the tiling they begin can be continued infinitely without mixing in different types of shapes.

The *second rank* is held by the Quintile and Biquintile—though these have a nobler congruence in three-dimensional solids—along with the *Trioctile <note>135°</note>, Decile <note>36°</note>, and Tridecile <note>108°</note>*, because their figures do continue by congruence, but only by mixing different shapes together. All of these also correspond to some extent in solid geometry, to a greater or lesser degree, except for the *Quincunx <note>150°</note>* (the Dodecagonal star-shape); it is therefore relegated to the *third rank*. To this rank, the *Sesquiquadrate <note>135°</note>, or the star of the Octagon*, can also be added, due to the obscurity of the science regarding it.

I have indeed extended these ranks even further, to the *Vigintile <note>18°</note> and Quindecile <note>24°</note>*, which correspond to figures with fifteen and twenty angles. I gave them the *fourth rank* (based only on that small portion of congruence mentioned); the reasoning for this is found in Proposition III of this book. For their star-shapes, a *fifth rank* was assigned; while they are equal to the primary figures in terms of "knowability" <note>original: "scibilitate"; the ease with which they can be understood or constructed</note>, they are far inferior in congruence, as they only touch at single points. Truly, it was not strictly necessary for me to go that far; since even down to the third rank, the aspects produced are not entirely certain. We could elegantly set a limit to these budding aspects at the point where solid congruence and perfect mathematical expressibility of the side or plane end. Therefore, let the ranks of "nobility" for these geometric figures be sought from the conclusions of Books I and II; it is from those that the ranks of the astrological Aspects have been distinguished in this book.

<header>ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV.</header>

# CHAPTER VII.

## Epilogue, on the Sublunary <term>Sublunary: referring to the Earth and its atmosphere, literally "below the moon," which was traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</term> Nature, and the Lower Faculties of the Soul, especially those upon which Astrology depends.

Much has been said regarding this contemplation in the second chapter, much throughout this fourth book, and some even in the third book. I also wrote on this topic a year ago in the *Prolegomena to the Ephemerides* <note>original: "Prolegomenis Ephemeridum"; Kepler's introduction to his astronomical tables</note>, and in the first book of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* on page 125; again in the year 1610 in *The Third Intervening Party* <note>original: "Tertio interveniente"; a work where Kepler mediated between those who believed in astrology and those who rejected it entirely</note>, at numbers 40 to 43, and 59 to 72, and 113, etc.; as well as in my *Response to the Objections of Roeslin*; and in the year 1606 in my book *On the New Star* <note>original: "De stella nova"</note>, chapters 8, 9, 10, and 24, 28, especially from page 171 to 175; and in the year 1604 <note>The OCR reads 1064, but this is a typo for 1604, the publication date of the work mentioned</note> in the *Optical Part of Astronomy* <note>original: "Astronomiæ parte Opticâ"</note> on pages 26, 27, and 224. For I deliberately omit the prognostications <note>predictions</note>, in which I have occasionally prefaced or interjected regarding the more certain foundations of Astrology, as they are not widely scattered.

However, since I have seemed to some very famous professors of Philosophy and Medicine to be establishing a "new philosophy"—and a most true one at that—this tender little plant (as all new things are) must be nourished and raised with every care, so that it may take root in the minds of those who practice philosophy. It must not be suffocated by the excessive moisture of vain sophistries, nor washed away by the torrents of common opinions, nor grow stiff in the cold of public neglect. If I happen to be careful in this regard, I do not fear anything from the winds of calumny <note>slander</note>—lest it be broken—nor from the scorching Sun of solid criticism—lest it be burned up.

Therefore, since in Chapter I, I touched upon the essence of the Soul, but only for the sake of the Harmonies; and since in the second Chapter I did not speak of the Soul as my main subject, but of the Harmonies for the sake of the Soul; it is now pleasing in this chapter to discourse on the Soul for its own sake, a little more generally. It is my pleasure to make a collection <note>original: "Syllogum"</note> in this Epilogue of all things which pertain to the present matter; those things which were said scatteringly, or in passing, or latently; here to bring them under a single view, and to explain the whole nature of the matter in a continuous thread of discourse.

<margin>Pages 11 and 117.</margin>
Timaeus of Locri, following Pythagorean teachings in the works of Plato, defended the idea that there is some Soul of the entire universe, set over the motions of the stars, the generation of the elements, the conservation of living things and plants, and finally the mutual sympathy of the higher and lower things. Furthermore, Proclus established this, both elsewhere and especially in the words transcribed in the first chapter of this fourth book. They made this Soul distinct from the Mind; both because the Mind was simple, while this Soul was manifold in its faculties; and because the Ideas <note>Ideal forms</note> of all sensible things existed in the Mind first through themselves, pure and identical; but in the Soul secondarily, for the sake of the Mind and received from it, leaning more toward matter. Because of this, they also used a distinction of names, calling the Intellectual or Mental ones **PARADIGMS** <note>original Greek-derived: "PARADIGMATA"; original models or patterns</note>, while the Animal <note>soul-based</note> ones were the **ICONS** <note>original Greek-derived: "ICONES"; images or reflections</note> of those Paradigms. The sum of it comes to this: that any Christian could very easily understand God the Creator in place of the Platonic Mind, and the Nature of things in place of the Soul.

He distinguishes between the divine Mind (the source of perfect patterns) and the Soul of Nature (which mirrors those patterns in the material world).</summary>

<margin>
The negligence of the Astrologers.

This is the primary source of the foulest astrological superstitions. Yet I do not wonder much at the prognosticators, a class of men who are for the most part vulgar, childish, and dreamers; it is the famous professors of Philosophy who seem more worthy of rebuke. While they accept from their Aristotle that the life of animals and plants is nourished by the power of the Sun, they do

How much more alert than these philosophers, and how much wiser, was the poet Virgil? All these are signs of LIFE and suppose a Soul in the body that is receiving the influence. <margin>
*Beware of ambiguity: Among the causes for Meteorological Effects, Aspects generally concur; however, daily Aspects do not cause the long-term quality of the year or its continuous and general nature, but act only on the specific days on which they fall. See below.
</margin>
Before everything else, I decided that I must read the fourteen books <note>original: "libros XIV"; although Pico's *Disputationes* is usually divided into twelve books, Kepler refers to fourteen here</note> of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, against Astrology, and that the arguments he set against each chapter must be examined. By doing so, I was not only confirmed in my condemnation of many superstitions, but a new light also dawned on me regarding certain matters; for while I was dismantling the force of his objections through an intense struggle of the mind, I began to see the matter itself more deeply. Ultimately, that book succeeded in making me believe in some things by refuting them—things that the astrologers, by defending them, had previously made me doubt. Such was the case with the Aspects. For on one hand, I looked at most constant experience—not specifically watching for snow, or winds, or thunder, and other things that astrologers are accustomed to predict, but *generally* noticing that the state of the air is stirred in whatever way whenever there are aspects (for example, if Mars and Jupiter were in conjunction), and at rest if there were none. On the other hand, I heard the man of Mirandola asking: why should one believe that Jupiter and Mars do more when they are seen together than when they are separate? He argued that light is not increased by conjunction; for whatever light they possessed when separate, they bring just as much to the meeting. And if planets of different qualities were to meet, it would seem that one would rather be hindered by the other. Here, I say, while seeking a response to defend the Aspects—following which I saw the Weather <note>original: "Meteora"</note> occur—I began to consider more diligently first the Aspects as the cause, and then the weather as the effect.

<margin>
Consideration of the cause of Storms.
</margin>
For the form of an Aspect, which creates an "Aspect" from a shared configuration or angling, was a qualitative quantity—or rather, it was a Relation of such quantities, an entity of reason <note>original: "ens rationis"; a philosophical term for something that exists in the mind/intellect rather than as a physical object</note>. Therefore, in order to stir the air, it was necessary for it first to move some Reason <note>Kepler implies a vital, sensing "soul" of the Earth</note> which has power over either the air or that by which the air is disturbed. At the same time, I kept before my eyes the comparison of Aspects with Musical Harmonies <note>original: "Concordantijs Musicis"</note>, handed down by Ptolemy, explained by Cardano, but too rashly exploded by the man of Mirandola. I was greatly helped by this analogy in the investigation of causes. For I saw that most of the things Pico objected against the aspects could also be objected against the contemplation of two voices. Truly, even in sounds, a triple proportion or a *sesquialtera* <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a 3:2 ratio, known in music as a perfect fifth</note> achieves nothing by reason of its pitch alone; and yet the sounds are pleasing if they are in a triple or *sesquialtera* ratio; conversely, they are shrunk from if they are in a *septupla* <note>7:1 ratio</note> or a *sesquisexta* <note>7:6 ratio</note>. Since, therefore, there must be something Rational to judge between the triple and the seventh—namely, the Soul presiding over the sense of hearing—it must also be that in the business of celestial Radiations, there is a Rational creature <note>The "Sublunary Nature" or Earth-Soul</note> that discerns between the chords <note>original: "subtensas"</note> of 60 degrees and those of 59 or 61. Whether that creature uses reasoning for this (like a human understanding Geometry), or whether it possesses this from a co-created instinct alone (like the forms of plants, which guard a certain number of leaves entrusted to them since the beginning of things and always build according to that architecture). There is no force of "mixing" here, as if according to exact medical measurements, nor any physical instrument; nor do sounds delight or rays animate because they are so blended that, like mixing hot and cold until a quality results suitable for a body about to bathe, they produce a physical effect. For in such mixtures, there is usually only one unique "best" temperature, while all others approach it by being more or less close. But among configurations,

Here, he provides a series of anatomical analogies to prove that the Earth possesses a "Soul" (Anima) capable of responding to the geometric harmonies of the planets.</meta>

### ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV
X
<meta>catchword: Because</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
I was searching, even comparing the bodies of living beings with the body of the Earth: I saw that almost everything that comes from the body of a living creature, witnessing the soul within it, also comes from the body of the Earth. <margin>Works of the Earthly Soul.</margin> For just as the body produces hair on the surface of the skin, so the Earth produces plants and trees; and just as lice are born there, here caterpillars, locusts, various insects, and sea monsters are born. And as the body produces tears, mucus <note>original: "blennam"</note>, and earwax, and sometimes even gum from facial pustules, so the Earth produces amber and bitumen. As the bladder pours out urine, so the mountains pour out rivers; and as the body produces excrement of a sulfurous odor and flatulence <note>original: "crepitus"</note>, which can even be set on fire, so the Earth produces sulfur, subterranean fires, thunder, and lightning. And as blood is generated in the veins of a living creature, and with it sweat, which is ejected outside the body; so in the veins of the Earth are generated metals and minerals <note>original: "fossilia"; in this period, this referred to anything "dug up" from the ground</note>, and the vapor that becomes rain.

<margin>The Earth's nourishment.</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, that just as other living creatures draw in food and drink, so also the Earth, through certain channels, should draw in some matter from which it "cooks" such a variety of things—for nothing comes from nothing. It draws in and swallows sea water; this is the reason why the sea never overflows despite the eternal pouring in of so many rivers. From what has been said, you can gather how absurd those people are who attribute the creation of metals solely to the operation of the Sun, without the effort of the Earth.

<margin>What kind of Soul the Earth has.</margin>
In my book on the "New Star" <note>original: *De Stella Nova* (1606), where Kepler discussed the supernova of 1604</note>, I also responded to that common objection: that if the Earth had a soul, it would seem it ought to grow and have limbs fit for movement. For as the body is, so the soul and its faculties correspond to it; since this soul exists for the sake of the Earth's body, and not this body for the soul—just as the human body exists for the sake of the Mind <note>original: "Mens"</note>, the primary faculty of the Soul. Therefore, if the Earth had needed growth, or if it had needed nourishment other than what I mentioned (as if by hunting), then those duties would have been entrusted to this Soul, and suitable instruments would have been given. This was the philosophy of the dying Socrates in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul and its immortality</note>, attributing all things to a governing Mind, and everything to deliberation about what is best. Therefore, if anyone argues that there are only four faculties of the Soul, none of which fit this Earthly Soul, and that there is therefore no soul in the Earth, I shall bid him add this fifth one to the number—following the same example and the same laws of reasoning by which those four were found in man.

<margin>The imagination of the Earthly Soul.</margin>
But so that I might attribute a Soul to the Earth with even greater confidence, I was also moved by other things which I have emphasized throughout my other books, and collected in a bundle in the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy*, page 125. Chiefly this: that there is a formative faculty <note>original: "formatrix facultas"; also known as the *vis plastica* or the power to give shape to matter</note> in the bowels of the Earth, which—in the manner of a pregnant woman—expresses in split stones human affairs occurring outside, as if it had seen them: such as soldiers, monks, popes, kings, and whatever else is on men’s lips, including new and unusual fashions. <margin>Geometry in gems.</margin> This happens rarely, but the following happens perpetually: it expresses the five regular geometric solids in gems and minerals. For the work testifies to the craftsman. <margin>Movement of its body.</margin> To these things, whoever follows Copernicus may add the daily rotation of the Earth’s globe, which is perpetual and most uniform; he will most rightly count this among the duties of this Soul.

### ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>
<margin>The sense of Touch in the Earth.</margin>
Moreover, does it not seem that a certain sense of touch or even hearing exists within the globe of the Earth? This is supported by the consistent tradition of many provinces: if someone climbs the peaks of the highest mountains and casts a small stone into those deepest chasms they possess, a sound is usually provoked; or if one throws it into a mountain lake (which undoubtedly lacks a bottom), storms are stirred up on the spot. This is exactly how animals react; if one inserts something tickling into the tender passages of the ears or nostrils, they are seized by a shiver, shake their head, or throw themselves into a run.

<margin>Diseases of the Earth.</margin>
There are also particular illnesses in certain regions of the Earth, and internal changes of the "entrails." For sometimes they abound with too much moisture; at other times they suffer from "crudity" <note>An old medical term for indigestion or unconcocted humors</note> or imperfect digestion—as when sheer winds arise instead of timely rains. Sometimes, as if seized by a burning fever <note>original: "causo correpta"</note>, they produce no moisture, but instead sweat out sulfurous vapors or pestilential dampness. Therefore, I did not wrongly advise in my book *On the New Star* <note>Kepler's *De Stella Nova*, published in 1606</note>, on page 173, that all the faculties of digestion—the **Attractive**, the **Retentive**, and the **Expulsive**—are to be sought in the Earth, since those "diseases" are actually affections of these faculties.

<margin>The respiration of the Earth.</margin>
Indeed, what is more similar to the respiration of terrestrial animals—and especially to that reciprocal breathing of fish, who swallow water with the mouth and press it out again through the gills—than that wonderful semi-diurnal ebb and flow of the Ocean? It is true that this motion accommodates itself to the movements of the Moon, so much so that it seemed probable to me in the *Preface to the Commentaries on Mars* <note>This refers to Kepler’s famous 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*</note> that the waves are pulled by the Moon as iron is by a magnet, through a corporeal faculty of the union of bodies; I repeated this recently in the introduction to the *Ephemerides*, where I examine the opinion of David Fabricius. Nevertheless, if one were to argue 

<margin>From where does the ebb and flow of the Ocean come?</margin>
that the Earth accommodates its own respiration (as it were) to the movement of the Sun and Moon—just as animals have the same cycles of sleep and waking as the day and night—I believe such a person should be heard with a fair ear in philosophy. This is especially true if some evidence were found of flexible parts in the depths of the Earth that could perform the role of lungs or gills. For if their nature were something like our air, capable of being condensed and extended, there would no longer be a need for a movement of the Earth's surface for this respiration, analogous to the movement of the diaphragm muscles in a breathing human body.

Indeed, what more suitable reason could there be for the receiving of sea waters into the "kitchen" of metals, as it were, than this very process through these perpetual semi-diurnal channels <note>original: "Euripos," referring to the Euripus Strait known for its strong currents</note>? What else does that marvelous event make us suspect, when—a few years before the crowds of merchants deserted Antwerp—the ebb and flow deserted the Ocean for a single day (terrifying the city no small amount), yet the Moon did not desert her course? Surely the Earth itself, being the master of this reciprocation, even if it participates in it by a natural motion, "held its breath" for that one day; just as living beings sometimes hold their breath, even though the movement of the diaphragm is itself mixed with the natural [involuntary] motion.

Though perhaps we shall prove more rightly that some respiration is necessary for the Earth because of the presence of the Soul, rather than proving the Soul because of the respiration.

### ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV

#### CHAPTER VII.
<margin>The Soul of the Earth is like a flame.</margin>
For now, as if it were a settled matter that there is a soul in the Earth, let us come to the contemplation of its essence. Indeed, that soul is not merely some light, such as that of fires or glow-worms, depending on itself and not on illumination from the sun; the proof of this is that it perceives the luminous rays of the planets in some way. Rather, it clearly seems to be a kind of flame (to be fostered, of course, by respiration or absorption), as evidenced by the 
<margin>The source of subterranean heat.</margin>
perpetual and sensible subterranean heat. No such heat persists in naked matter indefinitely without a soul; in fact, it does not even exist potentially in things coming from the substance of animals and plants unless it is produced by a Soul and by Forms, which are something igneous <note>fiery or fire-like</note>. See my *Optics*, pages 25, 26, 27.

<margin>pages 115, 119, 121. The Soul of the Earth is a kind of Zodiac.</margin>
We shall assign this "flame" as the "matter," so to speak, of the Soul of the Earth. Into this matter, in place of a form, the image of the divine face has been impressed, along with the Ideas of both the Circle and all its ratios, as well as the Ideas of its own sensible body over which it is appointed to rule, and indeed of the whole World in which its body was to exist. For God possesses within Himself not only geometric models but also the concepts of all sensible things to be created; all of these pass simultaneously into Souls—the patterns of God—according to each soul's capacity or use. Therefore, there shines in the Soul of the Earth a certain image of the 
<margin>pages 129, 141. The cause of sympathy between Heaven and Earth. pages 122, 123. The soul is activity.</margin>
sensible Zodiac circle, and indeed of the entire firmament, which is the bond of sympathy <note>a shared resonance or connection</note> between celestial and terrestrial things. Much more strongly does there shine within it the Archetype <note>the original pattern or blueprint</note> of all its own duties and all the movements by which it moves its body in any sense. This, others might call <term>dynamis</term> <note>original Greek: δυνάμιν; meaning "power" or "potential"</note>, but I would more willingly call <term>energeia</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνέργειαν; meaning "activity" or "actualization"</note>. For this is the essence of souls; these flames have a kind of <term>physis</term> <note>original Greek: φύσις; meaning "nature" or "internal principle of growth"</note>, in that the souls themselves are always so composed within as if they were performing that for which they were made to perform, whether they actually possess the instruments of the body or are hindered from using them. 
<margin>page 123.</margin>
For God is substantial Activity, and He subsists by this very activity (if I may stammer about divine things in a human way). Therefore, the essence of the divine image consists <term>in acting</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ ἐνεργεῖν</note>, just as the essence of a flame consists <term>in bringing forth</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ φύειν; referring to the act of burning or producing growth</note>. ...for the sake of which that Soul is like a kind of operative circle); it is always carried along in its own works within that circle. However, this happens more notably if these three circles concur and conspire into one—that is, if the soul, prompted by its own **Aspects** <note>Harmonious angles between planets</note>, persists in its work with some excess. It never ceases from "cooking" <note>original: *coquendo*; this refers to the Aristotelian concept of "concoction," the process by which internal heat transforms matter</note>, nor is this "cooking" ever without smoke and vapor. Indeed, fossils are made from smoke (just as arsenic consists of the smoke from metallic furnaces); but from the warm vapor, cooled inside the stony crusts of the Earth and gathered into drops, rivers distill at their origins. From that same vapor breathing out onto the Earth's surface, the breathable air—which had fallen by night, coming together into dews—is daily renewed.

<margin>
Why there are excesses through the Aspects.
</margin>
Truly, although this work of the Earth's Soul is perpetual, there was a need for certain excesses in evaporation—not continuous for some length of time, but reduced to certain days. This ensures that from the abundance of vapors sent outside, timely rains might be supplied (with sunshiny periods occurring in between) for the sake of refreshing and moistening the Earth's surface, from which crops and fodder for animals might grow.

<margin>
That the Sun also stirs up vapors even without aspects.
</margin>
Someone might object to me concerning the deepest parts of Africa and Peru, situated under the equinoctial line <note>the Equator</note>, where continuous rains fall throughout the whole summer. In those places, where is this distinction of **Aspects** from "ineffective configurations"? Where is the alternation of sunshine and rain? And does not the course of the Sun—a solitary planet—alone do everything without regard for configuration with others? And does it not do so as a natural cause, rather than a "being of reason" <note>original: *Ens rationis*; a conceptual entity as opposed to a physical one</note>, insofar as it directs its heat and fire to those parts, so that from the parched parts of the earth's innards, thinned moisture might expire? I answer that this natural action must not be denied to the Sun; but it is not unique to the Torrid Zone <note>the Tropics</note>, but can also be observed among us. For when the Sun is present in our hemisphere during the summer, more abundant rains generally fall than during the winter, when snow usually falls in the sun's absence.

<margin>
That rivers are increased.
</margin>
As for the fact that our rivers are increased by melting snows, which do not seem to be increased so much by falling rains—certainly not by such long-lasting increments—that happens partly because the individual layers of the falling snow accumulate little by little and are preserved in a storehouse for many months by the force of the cold. In contrast, the earth, parched by suns, immediately drinks up most of the summer rains, even the heaviest ones. Partly, however, it happens because the snow in the Alps cannot be dissolved except by the heaviest falling summer rains; thus, those continuous increases of the rivers are not from the snows alone, but also from the joined rains. Therefore, if you weigh everything, a greater abundance of moisture usually exudes even among us during the summer than during the winter. Thus, the objection achieves this: that there is a concurrence of celestial causes, of which one is natural (the heat of the Sun) and the other is rational (the **Aspects**). There is also a concurrence of sublunary causes, so that not only does one Zone have more moisture than another, but even within the same climate, one region has more than another for its own reasons. Meanwhile, even in the Torrid Zone, it can rain more at the time of the **Aspects** than on days free from aspects.

Truly, regarding this characterization of the Earthly Soul which I mentioned in the second place—derived from the sensible Zodiac and the entire sphere of the fixed stars—that...

For this is the Nature of all things that are kin to light: that being stirred by the light of the Sun, or at least of the day, they conceive a certain affection that lasts for a certain time. Thus, in the eyes, the visual spirits <note>In 17th-century physiology, "spirits" were subtle fluids thought to carry sensory information</note>—the offspring of light—having been imbued by a sudden sight of the Sun, carry and move this image around wherever the eyes are turned, even against one's will. Likewise, among the secrets of the Chymists <note>Alchemists or early chemists</note> is this wonderful and especially memorable experiment: they prepare gems (as I recently learned from a certain <term>autoptē</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτόπτῃ, meaning an eyewitness</note>) which, although they lie hidden in darkness like other things devoid of light, yet if someone exposes them to the light of the sun or day, they are kindled by it like candles. They carry that splendor with them even into the darkness, shining like the eyes of cats; yet this light is extinguished again in a short time. Something of this sort happens to this soul, which I have called kin to light and fire: in that region (for it is a point distinguished by regions, or a potential Zodiac circle) in which the superior planets met or an Eclipse appeared, it conceives a "character" <note>An imprint or lasting impression</note> of the conjunction, which lasts for some time. Therefore, as often as any of the planets—especially the Sun or Moon—crosses that place, the soul itself exerts its power, just as it would exert it at the actual stimulation of the conjunction. This entire business, I say, is similar to the memory of animals. For having once seen a man, I carry his image in my mind, yet I do not always have him present in my thoughts; but when he or someone similar appears again, that former image is drawn out anew and placed into the act of thinking through reminiscence. Yet the memory of man is more noble in this regard, because I am not only reminded of the remembered thing by an external encounter, but I also remind myself as often as I wish; because, of course, the faculty of discourse <note>The ability to reason and move from one thought to another</note> is present in man, which is lacking in this Soul. But these things will be more evident in the contemplation of the human Soul.

There still remains a question, not yet discussed by the Physicists to whom I have appealed: how is the picture of the thing to be seen—which I have shown is formed on the retiform tunic—then received further inward through the opaque parts of the body to the "inner sanctum" of the Soul? Does the soul perhaps travel outward to meet it? And other questions connected to these. And I, to confess frankly, am more stuck on the nature of vision than on this perception of the angle of rays: for I feel I can stammer something not altogether foolish about the latter, while on the former I am entirely mute.

I could, of course, avoid the labor of speculation without harming the main point of the argument, and answer anyone asking with what eyes the Soul of the Earth sees the rays of the stars: "With the same eyes by which it saw the soldier with the tattered leggings, whose image it planted in the fissile stone <note>Kepler believed the Earth's soul had a formative power that created patterns, such as fossils or mineral formations that resembled soldiers or plants, in rocks</note>." But inertia is the death of philosophy: let us live and exercise our minds.

<margin>
