How the Soul of the Earth regulates its own body.
</margin>
First, the soul has obtained the character of a point in actuality (at least by reason of its attachment to its body), and the shape of a circle in potentiality. Since the soul is Energy <note>Aristotelian *energeia* or active power</note>, it spreads itself from that seat in the point into a circle. For whether it must sense external things, those things surround it in a spherical fashion; or whether it must govern its body, it also has the body surrounding it. The soul itself lies hidden within, rooted in a certain point of the body, from which it goes out by a "species" <note>An image or radiation of its own essence</note> of itself into the rest of the body. But how should it go out, except by straight lines? For this is truly what it means to "go out." What other way of going out could there be for a soul that is itself both light and flame, than the way other lights go out from their sources—namely, in straight lines? It therefore moves outward toward the exterior of the body by the same laws as the surrounding lights of the firmament move inward toward the soul residing in that point. Now, since the entire surface of the terrestrial hemisphere—and indeed all the points on the surface of the air with which it is clothed—is irradiated by infinite rays from one and the same Planet, only one of all those rays tends toward the seat of the soul. Conversely, since the Soul goes out into all points of the surface of its body in infinite lines (like the rays of the Sun, because the soul itself is a kind of light, and the spirits <note>Subtle physiological fluids thought to carry life and sensation</note> commonly celebrated by physicians seem to be nothing other than these rectilinear rays and these species of the soul): yet there is only one line among them all which tends from the center to that point on the surface which is struck by that single ray of the Planet tending toward the seat of the Soul. Let us suppose, therefore, that the perception of the rays of a single planet consists in this: when the inward rush of the planet and the outward meeting of the soul coincide in one single geometric straight line. This is very similar to the example of vision, which is perfect and accurate only in the single perpendicular ray in the middle of the whole eye. For the Soul, through those outflows of its own "species" <note>original: "specierum sui"; in 17th-century physics, a "species" was a non-material image or power transmitted from an object</note>, has a faithful knowledge of all the members of its body, and of those things which occur anew in each of them at any time. Given these facts, it follows that if such an impression is made by a planet upon some point in the air, which does not tend toward the seat of the soul but passes by it to the side, the soul may receive the species of that affected point through the return of its own species; yet it would disregard it as a thing of no consequence. 

But if an impression is made upon some point on the surface of the air that tends toward the seat of the Soul, then this affected point is announced to the Soul. This sensation is then judged as pertaining to the Soul and is distinguished from the others; therefore, the Soul imagines the star to be in that single point alone, and not at all in the others mentioned. For the "ray" of the Soul is activated and, as it were, illuminated by the ray of the star when they coincide on the same straight line—just as the color of visible things is activated by the arrival of light, and as vision is activated when we gather ourselves and realize that we are seeing. 

Since this is the case not only for one planet, but for two, the soul will find two signs in two parts of its body. Whether its body is round, or irregular and rough, the Soul has it surrounding itself (sitting in a single point) in the manner of a sphere. By its rays, or the "species" of its immaterial nature—or, as others say, by its "second acts" <note>original: "actib' secundis"; a philosophical term referring to the active exercise of a faculty</note> emitted around itself—the soul breathes out a sort of perfect sphere as far as its body extends. Therefore, it evaluates that body according to the idea of a circle—specifically the circle of the Zodiac—described around its seat as a center, and measures its distinct parts. Thus, there is no need to grant that the Earth is transparent all the way to its center, nor that the soul must travel out to the stars; nevertheless, the way in which the angles of the configurations <note>The geometric aspects/angles between planets</note> are perceived by the Soul is now clear.

<margin>
Optical deceptions apply to the Soul of the Earth and its works.
</margin>
By this supposition, all the arguments that Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology</note> brought forward to overturn the doctrine of "Great Conjunctions" <note>Alignments of Jupiter and Saturn</note> and of aspects are dissolved. For because the Soul (by imagining) arranges all the bodies of the world around the point of its seat into the form of a sphere, and all planets into the form of a circle, and does so by the law of straight lines leading from a single point; it therefore does not matter whether a star is large or small, whether it completes a long or short journey in the sky, or whether it is high or near to the Earth. For all these things move the Soul just as they are perceived; and they are perceived by the same laws by which they are seen by us—namely, all as if they were equally high, and as if they lacked a "second motion" <note>The planets' individual orbits</note>, but were equally swift in their "first diurnal motion" <note>The daily rotation of the sky</note>, and without a great difference in visible size. As for other answers to Pico’s arguments, look in the frequently cited place in my book *On the New Star* <note>original: "de stella nova"; Kepler's 1606 work *De Stella Nova in Pede Serpentarii*</note>. This is enough for now concerning the Soul of the Earth, which they call "Sublunary Nature" <note>original: "Naturam sublunarem"; the realm of change below the Moon</note>.

This figure becomes deeply ingrained within it (even though the heavens move on to other configurations immediately after the moment of birth). Within this "animal idea" of the circle, the Zodiac marks all the positions that the Planets held among the fixed stars, as well as the points of the rising, the setting, or the midheaven.

Why the birth chart is used rather than the chart of conception.
</margin>
Now, the vital faculty begins to act and is brought into reality specifically when it is "inflamed" within the lamp of the heart through the act of birth, such that from then on it requires respiration to foster the flame of life. Therefore, when it begins to be what it is—namely, when it "architects" the Harmonies—it is at that moment that the perceptible radiant Harmony of the Planets flows most strongly into it.

<margin>
What Aspects can do in a Birth Chart.
</margin>
This is the very reason why those who are born at a time when there are many **Aspects** between the planets usually turn out to be both hardworking and industrious. This is true whether they are accustomed to accumulating wealth from childhood, or are chosen as leaders of public affairs, or finally, whether they have devoted themselves to studies. If I seem to anyone to be an example in this latter kind of life, I have not begrudged them the knowledge of my own **genesis** <note>birth chart/horoscope</note> in my book *On the New Star* <note>original: "De stella nova" (1606), folio 43</note>, which it is also convenient to explain on this occasion. I do not care about the charge of boasting; let them complain if they wish—those who condemn this whole genre of writing as folly, whether they be the unlearned, the half-educated, or the peddlers of titles and trappings meant to deceive the public. Even "plebeian theologians," as **Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a philosopher who famously attacked astrology</note> calls them, may object. Among true lovers of wisdom of any rank, I easily wash away this charge by the utility I provide to my reader; for I have explored no one's birth chart, nor the internal disposition of their mind, as certainly as my own. Jupiter, therefore, was very near the "ninetieth" <note>the Midheaven or a square aspect</note>, being four degrees over...

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
</margin>
...the **trine** <note>an aspect of 120 degrees</note> of Saturn had passed, and the Sun and Venus, joined together, were moving away from it and moving toward the other planet, forming **Sextiles** <note>aspects of 60 degrees</note> on both sides. They were also moving away from a **square** <note>an aspect of 90 degrees</note> with Mars, which Mercury was then closely approaching; the Moon was heading toward a trine with the same planet, positioned very near the **Eye of the Bull** <note>The star Aldebaran</note>, even in its latitude. At that time, Gemini was rising at 25 degrees, and Aquarius was at the midheaven at 22 degrees. A change in the weather revealed the triple **partile configuration** <note>an aspect precise to the exact degree</note> of that day—the Sextile of Saturn and the Sun, the Sextile of Jupiter and Venus, and the Square of Mercury and Mars; for after several days of frost, on that very day a warmth arose, melting the ice and bringing rain.

<margin>
An objection against Astrology.
</margin>
However, I do not wish to defend and confirm all the aphorisms of the Astrologers with this single example; nor do I assign the steering of human affairs to the heavens. This philosophical observation is immensely far removed from that folly—or rather, I should say, madness. To follow the footsteps of this very example: I know a woman born under almost the same aspects, who possesses an incredibly restless spirit. Yet, not only has she gained nothing from literature (which is not surprising for a woman), but she also disturbs her entire town and is the author of her own deplorable misery. Therefore, first, alongside the aspects of the Planets, one must consider the long-lasting imagination of my pregnant mother; she had a great admiration for my grandmother, who was a practitioner of folk medicine—a craft also practiced by my father. Second, there is the fact that I was born a man and not a woman; a distinction of sex that Astrologers seek in the heavens in vain. Third, I inherit a temperament of body from my mother that is more suited for study than for other ways of life. Fourth, my parents' circumstances were not wealthy; there was no plot of land, so to speak, for me to be born into or to be tied down to. Fifth, there were Schools available, and examples of the generosity of the Magistrates toward boys suited for study.

<margin>
Things produced by sublunary circumstances are not to be attributed to the stars.
</margin>
<margin>
The qualities of the Soul mostly agree with the qualities of the planets.
</margin>
Insert here, again from my *On the New Star* <note>original: "ex Genesi," likely referring to his 1606 work *De Stella Nova in pede Serpentarii*</note>, the distinctions of the Planets in their qualities. For if the Soul is a kind of light, it will distinguish the redness of Mars from the brightness of Jupiter and the lividness of Saturn. Thus, it must be admitted that great help comes from Mars—not just for industry, as mentioned before, but also for the sharpness of wit, which consists of a fiery power. You may see that the most prominent experts in natural Philosophy and Medicine are born under suitable aspects of Mars with the Sun and Mercury; because, clearly, a greater sharpness and greater skill are required to unearth the secrets of Nature than for the remaining business of life and the studies serving them. I will even grant something more: that it is because of Jupiter being elevated in the Midheaven that I take more delight in Geometry expressed in physical things than in that which is abstract and shows the dryness of Saturn. I mean, I delight more in Physics than in pure Geometry. And I grant that the **gibbous Moon** <note>more than half but not fully illuminated</note> in the bright constellation of the Bull’s forehead fills the Imaginative faculty of my Soul with images; many of these I have actually found to be consistent with the nature of things, as if they had fallen from the **Paradigms of Proclus** <note>referring to the Neoplatonic philosopher Proclus, who believed mathematical forms were innate to the soul</note>.

<margin>
* A small coin here for our Satirists. For, as it appears, poverty presses upon those who have already chewed over my one joke similar to this from the book on the new star several times within the course of twelve years.
</margin>
But if I speak now of the outcome of my studies, what further do I find in the heavens, I ask, that alludes to it even slightly? Experts admit that significant parts of Philosophy have been either unearthed anew, or corrected, or clearly perfected by me. But here, my "stars" were not Mercury rising in the angle of the seventh house in square to Mars, but **Copernicus** and **Tycho Brahe**. Without Tycho's books of Observations, everything that has now been placed in the clearest light by me would lie buried in darkness. My lords were not Saturn, the ruler of Mercury, but the August Emperors, **Rudolph and Matthias**. My home was not the "house" of Saturn in Capricorn, but the house of the Emperor in Upper Austria, and...

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.
</margin>
...and finally, the prompt generosity of the Nobles toward my request was of an uncommon example. This is that "Corner"—not the western Angle of a birth chart <note>original: "Thematis occiduus"; in astrology, an 'angle' is a significant point in a chart, but Kepler is punning on his physical relocation</note>, but a corner of the Earth—into which I have withdrawn with the consent of the Emperor, my Master, from an overly restless court. In this place, during these years now verging toward the sunset of my life, I strive to complete these *Harmonies* and whatever other works I have at hand. In vain will the Astrologer seek in my birth chart <note>original: "Themate Genethliaco"</note> the causes for my discovery of the proportions between the celestial spheres in the year 1596; the causes for my discovery of the way of seeing <note>his work on optics</note> in the year 1604; or the causes, in this year 1618, for why each Planet happened to have exactly such an eccentricity, neither smaller nor larger. Nor will they find there the causes for the demonstration of celestial physics, the ways in which the planets are moved, and their true motions, discovered in the intervening years; nor, finally, the metaphysical foundations for why the heavens have an effect on these lower things. These things did not flow into me from the character of the heavens into that little flame of the vital faculty when it was recently kindled and brought into action; rather, they partly lay hidden within the innermost essence of the Soul, according to the Platonic doctrine <note>the theory of reminiscence, where knowledge is innate</note> cited above from Proclus. Partly, they were received inward through another path, namely through the eyes. The sole and unique work of the Birth Chart was that it both sharpened those little sparks of genius and judgment, and incited the mind to tireless labor, and increased the desire for knowledge. In short, the stars did not inspire my mind, nor any of the faculties mentioned here, but they summoned them forth.

<margin>
No individual events come from the stars.
</margin>

<margin>
Folio 117. General effect of the stars.
</margin>

<margin>
Vain topics of Astrology.
</margin>
From this example, it is easily apparent to anyone how far Astrology is from being able to answer exactly from a single birth chart those topics commonly proposed: concerning Parents, Sex, Wealth, Children, the number of Wives, Religion, Career, Friends, Enemies, Inheritances, Family, Regions, and infinite other matters.

Regarding the length of life, insofar as an Astrologer can pronounce upon it—that is, what the power of "directions" <note>a technical method of predicting timing in astrology</note> might be—I shall speak a little later. But concerning the Fortune of the person born, I see I must now say something separately, in agreement with what was said above.

<margin>
On what things and by what means does a man's fortune depend to some extent on the stars?
</margin>
There are three things upon which a man's fortune seems to rest, regarding natural factors: the Mind <note>original: "Animus"</note>, the Physiognomy <note>physical appearance/features</note> of the body, and the Guardian Spirit <note>original: "Genius tutelaris"</note>. No one doubts the first; the second is more hidden and not as well known to the common people; regarding the third, I can offer nothing but conjectures. We have dealt with the first so far—namely, the Mind—from which character <note>original: "Mores"</note> depends. Regarding this, there is a well-worn common proverb: *Each person is the architect of their own fortune* <note>original: "Quilibet sit fortunæ suæ faber"</note>. In this saying, the sum of this whole part of philosophy is contained. Come now, let us place before our eyes one type of action and character as an example for all, previously touched upon in the example of the woman. For human affairs are so arranged that there is always a great abundance of thick-headed and "popularly wise" men, not only among the common folk, but also among Magistrates and in the sacred order. To these men, those who are discerning, critical, and reformers are annoying, and are regarded as nothing but litigious men. Therefore, for someone to enjoy prosperous fortune—that which comes from social gatherings—he certainly needs a right judgment of morals and labor and industry in his own affairs (which are hidden from the common folk); yet it is also necessary that his mind have some "thickness" <note>original: "pinguedinis," meaning a lack of over-sensitivity or intellectual sharpness</note> mixed in. His character must be popular and his way of acting must be such that it pleases the thick-headed public. Minds that are too subtle and restless, unless they withdraw into some seclusion of studies (and are thereby looked down upon and despised), usually create misfortunes for themselves.

<margin>
Character is the architect of fortune.
</margin>

IT IS THEREFORE... <note>catchword from original: "Itaque"</note>

Therefore, if one draws sufficient conjectures from the birth figure <note>original: "figurâ coeli Genethliacâ"; a horoscope cast for the moment of birth</note> regarding the qualities of the Mind, that person can also make a fairly sensible conjecture about a man’s fortune in general. However, it is only a conjecture and nothing more; indeed, even that person can be deceived due to the intervention of many causes, both supernatural and natural.

<margin>Page 122. The fascination of the face.</margin>
For, to bring in another foundation of human fortune from my earlier writings—namely, the dignity of the countenance—it is true that the imagination of Mothers contributes a great deal to this in the fetus during the entire time of pregnancy. Thus, the face, character, and the fortune resting on those foundations are often transferred to the fetus, resembling those of unfortunate parents (or even other people or animals frequently and vividly appearing before the pregnant woman). But nevertheless—just as <margin>Page 117. The Nativity expressed in the face.</margin> the mental paradigms of <term>Proclus</term><note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher whom Kepler admired for his mathematical and mystical views on geometry</note> were multiplied into living, mobile, and complex animals, intertwined with the ideas of life and motion—so too here, the character of the birth-sky is immersed into the appearance of the face through the hidden power of the <term>formative faculty</term><note>original: "facultatis formatricis"; the biological force then believed to shape the body in the womb according to an internal blueprint</note>. It is recognized in the face of the one born by an even more hidden instinct in those who look upon them. You may see that for those who are born under the conjunctions of several planets before the Sun <margin>Whence the power of the "Bodyguard" Planets.</margin> (which Astrologers call <term>doryphoria</term><note>original: "δορυφορίας"; literally "spear-bearing" or "bodyguarding," a configuration where planets flank the Sun or Moon like a royal guard</note>), crowds of common people are joined to them as if by some fascination. 

An example of this matter, commended to the memory of all posterity, can be seen in <term>Girolamo Cardano</term><note>A famous 16th-century Italian polymath and astrologer</note> regarding the birth chart of Luther, although many other causes for that public movement converged. Those who are born in this way (though no single certain form can be prescribed) often possess great authority among the people, great influence in councils, and great favor among the Princes of the State; indeed, their nature corresponds to this. Thus, fortune often stands on the side of the undeserving, or those not endowed with other suitable virtues of the mind. <margin>Page 122.</margin> Refer back here to the remaining things I have said above regarding <term>Physiognomy</term><note>The practice of judging character from facial features</note>, and which could be said further.

<margin>The protection of Guardians. Job 33. Matthew 18. Luke 15.</margin>
Regarding the <term>Guardian Spirit</term><note>original: "Genio tutelari"; the idea of a personal guiding angel or spirit</note>, the divine oracles testify that a specific guardianship is attributed to each individual person, and that they are given both admonition and intercession at the tribunal of God's providence. Here, the nature of sensory things has no possession. If, however, astrologers can predict from a birth chart events that are clearly accidental (speaking naturally)—that is, those which happen neither because of a man's bad character, nor from recklessness, nor from an intemperance of anger or lust, and which do not depend on the dignity of the face (the two foundations of fortune explained so far)—it raises a question. For example: a tile falling from a roof strikes a passerby; a stray bullet or arrow strikes someone crawling in the woods; a sunken ship leaves miserable travelers in the middle of the waves; one man is caught in flames and extinguished, another is crushed by the ruin of a house or a mountain; and conversely, one person enters into an unexpected inheritance, while another finds a treasure by chance. If, I say, the birth chart contains the signs of these events—which belong without controversy to the duties of the Guardian Angel—then it must follow that obstacles to this guardianship, <margin>Do clearly accidental evils depend on the stars?</margin> as well as contrary promotions, proceed from the birth-star. Whether this contains an impious opinion within itself, let the Theologians see, especially those who write nativities and prognostications in great numbers. 

I myself have an experience—I know not what to call it—of two men who, since they were born under the most violent constellations and followed a similar character, to the point that for one of them, it was a game...

...it would be as if someone, in a leap, were carried headlong over a precipice and caught a rope in mid-flight, but if he missed it, his life would already be over. Yet, they did not seem to have brought destruction upon themselves by their own recklessness: for one of them was struck by a lightning bolt, and the other by a lead bullet from a hunter who, lying in wait for wild beasts, had been deceived in his sight and hearing. Nor do I see how the heavens could do such things to a man, <margin>Sins are often the causes of accidents.</margin> apart from the <term>Genii</term><note>In Kepler’s time, 'Genii' referred to guardian spirits or intermediary spiritual beings thought to influence human life and the natural world.</note>; for everything else the heavens can do is found to be possible only through a man’s Mind or body (within which there is no inherent force for such "accidental" events). It has happened to me more than once that after I had tormented myself for a long time with pity for certain people who perished by chance and seemed to me most innocent, I finally learned from trustworthy sources that their lives had been such that a good angel would easily be driven away—as bees are driven off by smoke—and the man would typically be left to blind chance, like a chariot without a driver. It is as if he were emancipated from the paternal power of God his Creator and left to his own judgment, or rather, to the tyranny of Satan. Whether something of this sort should also be determined regarding the examples previously mentioned, and those "accidents" attributed to divine Nemesis <note>original: "Nemesi divinæ"; the Greek goddess of retribution, here used to mean divine justice or punishment.</note>, is known only to Him who searches hearts, who "visits the iniquity of fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation." But as for all who perish by chance, far be it from me to pass the same judgment. <margin>The deeds of men are not from heaven.</margin> However, astrologers cannot see such impiety of life from the stars. For divine assistance against the wicked inclinations of the mind is not described in the figure of the heavens—inclinations into which the influence of the heavens degenerates after the Fall <note>Referring to the original sin in Christian theology</note>, not by corrupting the mind itself, but by inciting a mind already corrupted. Much less are the types of punishment owed for individual sins inscribed in the "lividness" of Saturn or the "redness" of Mars, as if in the <term>Pandects</term><note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* was a vast compendium of Roman law; Kepler uses it here as a metaphor for a universal legal code or ledger of punishments.</note>. Therefore, since there is no immediate natural connection of these things <margin>Does the guardian spirit have business with the client's birth chart?</margin> with the heavens, I have once and again over these twenty years offered this for public consideration: whether, just as those spiritual overseers of provinces and peoples complain in the ninth chapter of Daniel that they are hindered by "adversary spirits," so too the <term>Genii</term> of individual men might be naturally hindered by the stars. This would prevent them from conveniently resisting the "powers of the air" that lie in wait for us <term>in a mass</term><note>original: "πανδημεί" (pandēmēi); meaning all together, or as a whole population.</note>. Perhaps these hindrances might be foreseen from the birth theme <note>The horoscope</note>, which perhaps influenced the Guardian Spirit no less than the mind of the one being born. From this follows some general misfortune for the person born, which is the origin of the proverb: <margin>Admonitions of the spirits</margin> *No calamity comes alone.* Yet God does not frequently hinder this course of the nature of invisible things, because He knows how to procure some good even from that hindrance of protection, which might turn out well for the one in danger if he is pleasing to God, or if he is displeasing, might fulfill the measure of just vengeance. Surely, if the guardian Angel cannot prevent an imminent evil, he at least warns the client in hidden ways so that he does not allow him to perish unprepared. Such were the forebodings and warnings that preceded that recent collapse of the mountain among the <term>Rhaetians</term><note>original: "Rhetis"; referring to the catastrophic landslide in Piuro (Grisons, modern-day Switzerland) in 1618 which killed thousands.</note>.

<margin>What is the beginning of a man's life in the womb, and of what kind?</margin>
Let this, therefore, be a third foundation for a man’s fortune, at least as a conjecture, for I affirm nothing. We must now return to the consideration of the Essence of the Faculty of the Vital Soul. For it may be asked: if the character of the heavens only exerts influence at the exact point of Birth, does the fetus then only conceive the vital faculty of the soul during labor? Should I say it was soulless before birth? It altogether conceives its own proper, energetic, vital faculty only when it is separated from the mother. Before then, it was illuminated by the rays of the mother’s "vital flame" through the umbilical vein and artery...

<meta>This page continues Chapter VII of Book IV. ### ON THE CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
<margin>How does the fetus live before birth?</margin>
...the vessel is inserted into the heart of the fetus, with a passage separate from those two through which it later, nourishing its own flame of life within, draws blood from one side and air from the lungs on the other. This separate passage of the heart collapses on the first day of life and completely vanishes; as Georgius Horstius <note>Georgius Horstius (1578–1636) was a prominent German physician. Kepler often consulted with medical contemporaries to ground his theories in physical anatomy.</note>, Physician to the Landgrave of Hesse and a most expert consultant on all nature, demonstrated to me in Prague using a newly born piglet. From this, therefore, I draw arguments that the heart of the fetus, while it is in the womb, lacks those movements of **systole and diastole** <note>original: "systolês & diastolês"; the contraction and expansion of the heart</note> as much as it lacks respiration, and therefore the flame of its own life is not yet kindled within it. And to insist more firmly on a most faithful analogy: just as the smoke of a wooden roof, scorched by a fire, relates to the flame that suddenly seizes it, so does that which precedes in the fetus relate to the **vital faculty** <note>The 'vital faculty' was considered the biological force that governed involuntary functions like heartbeat and breathing.</note>, kindled at the birth itself, or shortly before.

<margin>Whence comes the force of the Transit of Planets through the places of the Nativity?</margin>
In this vital faculty of Man, thus kindled at birth, there shines out especially that likeness of **Memory** which I also showed above to exist in the Soul of the Earth. For so great is the constancy of the celestial character—and of all parts of the **Birth Chart** <note>original: "Thematis Genethliaci"</note>—and so great is its durability in the Soul, that it is not laid down before the end of life. For this faculty is moved by all the **transits** <note>The movement of planets in the sky as they cross over the specific degrees they occupied at the moment of a person's birth.</note> of the planets through the primary places of the chart, exactly as if those places were not mere empty images surviving in the soul of things that passed long ago, but were true stars. Thus it is as if there were not one, but for example, two Suns in the sky, meeting as one; and by that meeting, the nature of the vital faculty is moved in the manner described above.

<margin>Why are the birth charts of parents and children related?</margin>
The clearest evidence of this matter, beyond all exception, is found in the kinship of the birth charts under which parents are born and those under which their children are born. For when the fetus is mature, the **formative faculty** of the soul, which is in charge of generation, then especially prepares itself to expel the fetus and to kindle the new vital faculty of the soul by that expulsion; this occurs when the stars have returned to the seats of the maternal or paternal birth chart, or to the same configurations, and thus remind the Soul of itself and its own celestial character. See the book *On the New Star*, page 43. <note>Kepler refers to his 1606 work *De Stella Nova*, where he discussed the Great Conjunction and its astrological implications.</note>

<margin>Note the natural foundation of Directions.</margin>
What of the fact that this faculty observes not only the true transits of the planets through the places of the birth chart, but also the successions of the parts of heaven? These parts, which held planets at the Nativity, move into the primary places of the charts that are established when whole days have passed from birth; the faculty observes the proportion of a Day to a Year (since Copernicus attributes both revolutions of the Earth to it). <note>Kepler is explaining 'Directions' or 'Progressions'—an astrological technique where each day after birth symbolizes one year of life. He links this to the Copernican model of the Earth's daily rotation and annual orbit.</note> By this proportion, the soul dispenses its works through the whole life of a Man, so that as much as a Year is longer than a Day, so much later does the **Effect** follow the **Sign** in the "direction" than the Sign follows the birth in the direction. Thus, this celestial impression does not merely endure while resting, but by enduring, it propagates itself through a motion of extension into the longer spans of life. Truly, this faculty is not just a circle, but an "ideal" circular motion, and a twin one at that; it is, finally, through motion, also "ideal Time." See the words of Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose work on geometry and the soul deeply influenced Kepler.</note> quoted above on page 117. We can seek an example of this matter again from Memory, which is a slightly higher faculty. For on a tablet, things are painted only with the circumstance of place; but in the memory, deeds are preserved even with the character of time. Finally, in this business of **Directions**, the character of positions and motions in time...

### ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV.

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
...the time of things past is multiplied into operations, while observing the sensible worldly proportion of the diurnal revolution to the annual movement under the Zodiac; so that the operations are now separated by an interval of time from their original stimuli. You might say that along with the body of the Born person itself, the time of the **Genethliacal** <note>Related to a birth or natal chart; from the Greek 'genethlios,' pertaining to birth.</note> character of the movements also grows.

<margin>Can the length of life or the year of death be predicted from the stars?</margin>
<margin>What a "Direction" is physically.</margin>
<margin>Genuine causes of death.</margin>
Whatever astrologers presume to predict about the length of life from a natal theme, all of it is condensed into this chapter: the preludes of **Directions** <note>A "direction" is an astrological timing technique where the movement of planets in the hours or days following birth is used to predict events in the years of a person’s life.</note>, acting as if from the pulpit of the natal theme, inform the vital faculty as to which year of life one or another redundant humor <note>The "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were believed in Kepler's time to govern health and temperament.</note> ought to be expelled from the body or stirred up. This is a stimulus of Nature to perform its extraordinary work, which may result in the prolongation of life. Death is not in the stars, nor in any Direction, nor are the various forms of death found there. It is the matter of the body that either smothers the flame of life by overflowing or abandons it by failing; it is matter that hinders the efforts of nature and twists them toward destruction. It is sin that deprived the human race of the remedy of immortality once granted; it is sin that even now drives away, hinders, and repels the Guardian Angel from protecting life against the assaults of demons, men, and the elements. But this matter should be dealt with more extensively in Astrology; I have treated it not too briefly in the book *On the New Star* <note>Kepler's *De Stella Nova* (1606) discussed the supernova of 1604 and its astrological implications.</note> on page 43, and in *The Third Intervener* <note>Kepler's *Tertio Interveniente* (1610) was a defense of astrology's "middle ground" against both skeptics and superstitious practitioners.</note> at Number 65 and following. And perhaps it will happen that I shall publish the books of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** <note>Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) wrote a famous critique of astrology; Kepler intended to harmonize Pico's criticisms with his own reformed astrology.</note> with a commentary, if I understand that I would be doing something pleasing to students of philosophy and if I am not destitute of the necessary means.

<margin>The reasoning and power of the Horoscope or the degree of the Ascendant in Birth.</margin>
Now, because I hasten toward the end, I will subjoin a comparison of the vital faculty in man with the **Soul of the Earth** <note>Kepler's "Anima Telluris"—the idea that the Earth itself is a living being that responds to the harmonies of the planets.</note>, regarding the influence of the heavens. It seems to be this: the Soul of the Earth is like a circle that has no beginning or end anywhere, nor is it bound by any part of itself. But the vital faculty of man is compared to a circle bound as if by many points. The cause is that the Soul of the Earth has no "character of birth," since it always remains the same and is never born or kindled; but a man's birth, being recent and close to death, receives the character of its origin, which marks the Zodiac with certain points of beginning and end.
<margin>Genesis of the World.</margin>
And even if you attribute a Genethliacal character to the Earth from the first day of Creation, the entire space of the sky is still always accessible to it; nothing in it has the nature of a beginning or end, rising or setting. To a human, the surface of the Earth hides half of the sky and distinguishes the signs of rising and setting. Thus the reason for the comparison is clear.

<margin>The foundation of Crises.</margin>
And so true is this comparison of the vital faculty (once established in action) with a circle bound by certain points, that even at the beginning of a disease 
<margin>What disease is.</margin>
(which is, as it were, a new life—namely, a new energy of the vital faculty, or its extraordinary action, natural yet outside the usual state of the constitution, striving to expel harmful humors from the body), the place which the Moon possessed influences the Soul and conceives a power like that of some "true Moon," immobile in this degree of its own. If the true Moon in the sky reaches the square or opposite positions to this place, the Nature of the man is stimulated to struggle <note>original: "agonisandum"; to enter a 'crisis' or contest against the illness.</note> with the disease. On this matter rests the doctrine of **Crises** <note>The "critical days" in medicine when a patient's condition was expected to either improve or worsen, traditionally calculated by the Moon's movement.</note>, which I have treated accurately enough in *The Third Intervener*, Number 70 and following.

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
Let enough have been said for the present regarding even the lower faculty <note>The "lower faculty" refers to the biological or vegetative part of the soul responsible for growth and involuntary vital functions, which Kepler believes reacts to planetary aspects.</note> of the human Soul, and regarding this entire subject matter.

Furthermore, I have discussed these matters concerning the Soul thus far, not indeed with the intention of calling students of divine philosophy away from the reading of Metaphysical authors; nor to shut the eyes <note>original: "oculos configerem" — literally "to transfix the eyes," here meaning to silence or challenge the authority of.</note> of so many interpreters of Plato and Aristotle of the deepest insight—Greek, Arabic, and Latin: Plotinus, Themistius, Simplicius, Porphyry, Alexander, Averroes <note>Averroes (1126–1198) was a medieval Andalusian polymath whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western thought.</note>, and those not a few of his own nation whom he cites, as well as Boethius, and the most recent and subtle J. C. Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a Renaissance scholar whose work on the soul and nature Kepler highly respected.</note>—who dispute concerning the Soul and the Intelligences. Rather, my purpose was to add these things, drawn from my own profession <note>Kepler refers here to his role as a mathematician and astronomer.</note> and from the inner storehouse of this Harmonic work, as a kind of supplement, since they have not yet been touched upon by those authors in their considerations (as far as I know). Thus, by those who after me shall devote themselves to this Metaphysical contemplation and read the aforementioned authors, these "experiments" of ours may be compared with their reasonings. By testing both against the other with the most free judgment of reason (which I confess has been done by me very little on this occasion), this part of the Metaphysical science may finally be established more clearly, more richly, and more perfectly in every respect. That this may yield to the glory of the most blessed Name, God the Creator of things Visible and Invisible, and to the increase of holiness and innocence of life in those who contemplate it, and finally to the eternal salvation of many Souls, to that same

## Preface.

What I suspected twenty-two years ago, as soon as I discovered the five solid figures <note>Kepler refers to the five Platonic solids, which he used in his 1596 work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, to explain the spacing between planetary spheres.</note> between the celestial spheres; what I firmly persuaded myself of before I had seen Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*; what I promised to my friends in the title of this fifth book before I was certain of the matter itself; what I urged should be sought in a public writing sixteen years ago; for the sake of which I spent the best part of my life on astronomical contemplations, visited Tycho Brahe, <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was the greatest observational astronomer of the age; Kepler used Tycho's precise data to prove his theories.</note> and chose Prague as my residence: that, at last, I have brought to light. 

By the grace of God the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deo Opt. Maximo"</note>—who inspired my mind, excited this great longing, and prolonged my life and mental strength—and through the generosity of two Emperors and the leaders of this province of Upper Austria <note>original: "Austriæ Supr-Anisanæ"</note> who provided the other means; having first completed the astronomical task as much as was sufficient, I have finally, I say, brought it to light. And I found it to be truer than I could ever have hoped: that the entire nature of Harmony, in all its magnitude, with all its parts explained in Book III, is found among the celestial motions. This was found not indeed in the way I had first imagined (this part of my joy is not the least), but in a very different way, which is both most excellent and most perfect.

During this middle time, while the very laborious restoration of the motions <note>Kepler refers to the years of grueling calculations required to fix the orbits of the planets, particularly Mars.</note> held me in suspense, there came a major increase to my desire and incentive for the project: the reading of Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*. These were sent to me in manuscript by an eminent man, born to promote philosophy and every kind of learning, Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, Chancellor of Bavaria. There, beyond expectation and with the greatest admiration, I found that almost his entire third book was spent on that same contemplation of celestial harmony, fifteen hundred years ago. 

But at that age, much was still missing from Astronomy; and Ptolemy, having tried the matter unsuccessfully, could have caused others to despair—looking like one who, alongside Cicero’s Scipio, <note>Referring to the "Dream of Scipio" (*Somnium Scipionis*) by Cicero, which describes the "Music of the Spheres" as a beautiful but perhaps imaginary concept.</note> had recited a sweet Pythagorean dream rather than aiding philosophy. But I was strongly confirmed in pursuing my purpose, both by the roughness of that ancient astronomy and by this very agreement between our meditations—exact to a hair's breadth—across an interval of fifteen centuries. 

For why use many words? Nature herself was going to reveal herself to humans through different interpreters across the centuries. It was the *finger of God* <note>original: "digitus Dei"</note> (to speak with the Hebrews) that the same concept of the world’s structure should be in the minds of two men who had dedicated themselves entirely to the contemplation of Nature, though neither had been the other's guide on this path. 

Now, since eighteen months ago the first light dawned, three months ago the proper day, and only a few days ago the pure Sun itself shone forth upon this most admirable contemplation; nothing holds me back. I am glad to indulge in sacred frenzy, I am glad to taunt mortals with the honest confession that I...

## The chapters of this book are as follows:

*I. Concerning the five regular solid figures.* <note>The Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>

*IV. In which things pertaining to the motions of the Planets the simple Harmonies are expressed; and that all those harmonies found in Song are present in the Heavens.*
*V. That the keys of the Musical Scale, or the positions of the System, and the Genera of Harmonies—the Major and Minor—are expressed by certain motions.* <note>original: "Durum & Molle," referring to the hard/major and soft/minor scales.</note>
*VI. That the Musical Tones or Modes are each expressed in some way by the individual planets.*
*VII. That universal Counterpoints, or Harmonies of all the Planets, can exist, and that they are diverse, one following from another.*
*VIII. That the natures of the four voices—Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass—are expressed in the Planets.*
*IX. A demonstration that, to obtain this harmonic arrangement, the Eccentricities of the Planets had to be exactly what they are for each one, and no others.*
*X. An epilogue concerning the Sun, based on most fruitful conjectures.*

*The Appendix contains: I. A version of the third book of Ptolemy’s Harmonics, starting from chapter III, which treats the same subject.*
*II. A supplement to the Ptolemaic text in the last three chapters of Ptolemy, for which Ptolemy provided only the headings.*
*III. Notes on this part of the Harmonics, in which I explain and refute the author, and compare either his discoveries or his attempts with my own.*

Kepler quotes from Plato's *Timaeus* 27c.</note>

# CHAPTER I.
## Concerning the five regular solid figures.

<margin>
The circles circumscribed around the angles sketch out the Spheres, but those spheres should be conceived as slightly larger than these circles—except in figure 5—so that all the figures truly touch the angles. The ratio of magnitude observed in this diagram was this: so that the sphere of figure 1 can be inscribed in figure 4 of this; again the sphere in figure 3, and the sphere of that in 2, and finally the sphere of that in 1. The Cube touches all its six planes at their centers.
</margin>

How the regular plane figures <note>Two-dimensional shapes like the equilateral triangle, square, and pentagon.</note> agree to form solids was stated in the second book; indeed, we spoke there concerning the five solids (among others) for the sake of the planes. However, the five-fold number of those was demonstrated there; and it was added why they were called "Cosmic" <note>Also known as the Platonic solids.</note> by the Platonists, and to which Element <note>The classical elements: Earth (cube), Air (octahedron), Fire (tetrahedron), Water (icosahedron), and the Aether or Universe (dodecahedron).</note> each is compared, and for what property. Now, in the entrance to this book, we must again deal with these figures for their own sake, not for the sake of the planes; at least as much as suffices for the Harmony of the Heavens. The reader will find the rest in the second part of the *Epitome of Astronomy*, book four.

Therefore, from the *Mysterium Cosmographicum* <note>Kepler’s first major work (1596), in which he proposed that the distances between the planets were determined by these five solids nested within one another.</note>, I briefly repeat here the Order of the five figures in the World, of which three are primary and two are secondary. For the **Cube (1)** is the outermost and most ample, because it is first-born, and contains the ratio of the Whole by the very form of its generation. The **Tetrahedron (2)** follows, as a Part established by the section of the Cube, yet it is also primary, having a three-lined solid angle just like the Cube. Within the Tetrahedron is the **Dodecahedron (3)**, the last of the primaries; it is similar to a shape composed from the parts of a Cube which are themselves similar to a Tetrahedron, that is, from tetrahe-

...is added one that is like a celibate or <term>Androgynos</term> <note>original: Androgynos. Kepler uses this Greek-derived term (hermaphrodite) to describe the Tetrahedron because it is the only Platonic solid that is its own dual—it fits perfectly inside another tetrahedron of the same proportions.</note>, the Tetrahedron; for it is inscribed in itself, just as those little females are inscribed in and, as it were, subjected to the males. They have the signs of the female sex opposite to the male—namely, they have angles where the males have planes.

<image-desc>Two diagrams at the bottom left. The left diagram shows a tetrahedron with internal lines connecting to a central point. The right diagram shows a tetrahedron with an inverted tetrahedron inside it, illustrating nesting or proportional relationships.</image-desc>

Furthermore, just as the Tetrahedron is the element, the internal organs, and as it were the rib of the Male Cube; so the Female Octahedron is the element and part of the Tetrahedron, in another way: thus the Tetrahedron acts as a mediator in this marriage.

The principal difference between these unions or families consists in this: that the proportion of the Cubic union is indeed **Expressible** <note>original: Effabilis. In the mathematical language of Kepler's time, "effable" or expressible meant a rational ratio, or one that can be described using whole numbers or their square roots.</note>; for the Tetrahedron is a third of the cubic body, and the Octahedron is half of the tetrahedral body, or one-sixth of the Cube. But the proportion of the Dodecahedral marriage is indeed **Inexpressible** <note>original: Ineffabilis. This refers to irrational ratios, specifically the "Golden Ratio" or "Divine Proportion" required to construct pentagons and dodecahedrons.</note>, yet **Divine**.

The coupling of these two words warns the reader to be careful about their meaning. For the word **Inexpressible** here does not denote by itself any nobility, as it otherwise does in Theology and divine matters; but it denotes the condition...

<meta>This page continues Kepler's geometric analysis of the Platonic solids, specifically focusing on the Dodecahedron and its "divine proportion." He transitions from the pure geometry of the shapes to their "kinship" with musical harmonies, which is the core thesis of this book.</meta>

<page-num>182</page-num>

...no worse: for in Geometry, as stated in the first book, there are many **ineffable** <note>original: "ineffabilia." In Kepler’s time, this referred to what we now call irrational numbers—lengths that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of whole numbers.</note> things which do not, for that reason, participate in the **divine** proportion. What the divine proportion is (though it should rather be called the "sectional" proportion) must be sought from the first book. For while other proportions are supplied by their own four terms, and **Continuous** proportions by three, the **divine** proportion requires a singular relationship of terms beyond the proportion itself: namely, that the two smaller terms, as **parts**, constitute the larger term, as the **whole**. <note>Kepler is describing the Golden Ratio, where the ratio of the whole line to the larger segment is the same as the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller one.</note>

Therefore, as much as this Dodecahedral Marriage loses because it employs an **ineffable** proportion, it gains back in turn because that ineffable quality advances into the **divine**.

This marriage also possesses a **solid star**, the origin of which comes from the continuation of the five planes of the Dodecahedron until they all meet at a single point: see its origin in Book II.

Finally, one must note the proportion of the Orbs circumscribed around them to those inscribed within them. In the Tetrahedron, this is **effable** <note>meaning "rational" or expressible as a ratio of whole numbers.</note>, as 100,000 to 33,333, or as 3 to 1. In the Cubic marriage, it is ineffable, yet the semidiameter of the inscribed orb is **effable in power** <note>original: "potentiâ effabilis." This means the square of the number is rational—in this case, the square root of one-third of the square of the diameter.</note>, being the square root of one-third the power of the diameter, namely as 100,000 to 57,735. In the Dodecahedral marriage, it is plainly ineffable, as 100,000 to 79,465; and in the star, as 100,000 to 52,573.

## CHAPTER II.
# On the Kinship of Harmonic Proportions
### with the Five Regular Figures.

This kinship is varied and manifold; however, there are four primary degrees. For either the sign of kinship is taken from the external appearance alone which the figures possess; or the same proportions are born along with the construction of the side itself, which are also harmonic; or they result from the figures already constructed, either individually or joined; or finally, they are either equal to or near the proportions of the orbs of the Figure.

In the first degree, Proportions whose character or greater term is 3 have a familiarity with the Triangular plane of the Tetrahedron, Octahedron, and Icosahedron; those whose greater term is 4 have a familiarity with the Square plane of the Cube; and those whose term is 5 with the Pentagonal plane of the Dodecahedron.

This similarity of the plane can even be extended to the smaller term of the proportion, so that wherever a three is found next to one of the continuous doubles, 그 proportion is held to be familiar to the three figures first

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
The kinship is similar because of the external appearance of the **solid angle**, which in the primary bodies is **trilinear** <note>original: "trilinearis"; an angle formed by three lines or faces meeting at a point, such as the corners of a cube.</note>, in the Octahedron **quadrilinear** (four-lined), and in the Icosahedron **quinquelinear** (five-lined). Therefore, if one term of the proportion shares a relationship with the number three, the proportion will be related to the primary bodies; if with four, to the Octahedron; and finally, if with five, to the Icosahedron. But in the **female forms** <note>Kepler categorized the Platonic solids into "masculine" (Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron) and "feminine" (Octahedron, Icosahedron) based on their geometric properties.</note> this kinship is more distinct, because the characteristic shape follows the appearance of the angle, lying hidden within: in the Octahedron it is a **Square**, in the Icosahedron a **Pentagon**. Thus 3:5, because of both reasons, would belong to the Icosahedral sect.

The second degree of kinship, which consists in the origin, is to be conceived as follows. First, there are certain **Harmonic** proportions of numbers familiar to a single marriage or family—namely, the individual perfect proportions belonging to the Cubic family. Conversely, there is a proportion which is never expressed in whole numbers, nor is it demonstrated through numbers in any other way except by a long series of them gradually approaching it. This is called the ***Divine*** proportion <note>The Golden Ratio.</note> when it is perfect, and it reigns in various ways through the Dodecahedral marriage. Therefore, those Harmonies—1:2, 2:3, 3:5, and 5:8—begin to foreshadow that proportion; for it is most imperfect in 1:2 and most perfect in 5:8, and would be even more perfect if we placed 8 over the sum of 5 and 8 (which is 13), were it not that this would cease to be Harmonic.

Furthermore, to establish the side of a figure, the diameter of the Sphere must be divided. The Octahedron requires its **bisection**, the Cube and Tetrahedron **trisection**, and the Dodecahedral marriage **quinquesection** (division into five). Therefore, the Proportions are distributed among the figures according to these numbers which express them. Indeed, the square of the diameter is also divided—or rather, the square of the figure's side is formed from a certain part of it. When the squares of the sides are compared with the square of the diameter, they constitute these proportions: Cubic 1:3, Tetrahedral 2:3, Octahedral 1:2. For this reason, when joined in pairs, the Cubic and Tetrahedral make 1:2, the Cubic and Octahedral make 2:3, and the Octahedral and Tetrahedral make 3:4. The sides of the Dodecahedral marriage are **ineffable**. <note>original: "ineffabilia"; Kepler means they are irrational numbers that cannot be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers.</note>

Thirdly, Harmonic proportions follow the already established figures in various ways. For either the **Number of sides of a face** is compared with the number of sides of the whole figure: and these proportions arise: Cubic 4:12 (or 1:3), Tetrahedral 3:6 (or 1:2), Octahedral 3:12 (or 1:4), Dodecahedral 5:30 (or 1:6), Icosahedral 3:30 (or 1:10). Or the number of sides of a face is compared with the **number of faces**: then the Cube gives 4:6 (or 2:3), the Tetrahedron 3:4, the Octahedron 3:8, the Dodecahedron 5:12, the Icosahedron 3:20. Or the number of sides or angles of a face is compared with the **number of solid angles**: and the Cube gives 4:8 (or 1:2), the Tetrahedron 3:4, the Octahedron 3:6 (or 1:2), the Dodecahedron with its partner 5:20 and 3:12 (that is, 1:4). Or the **number of Faces** is compared with the **number of solid angles**: and it gives for the Cubic marriage 6:8 (or 3:4), for the Tetrahedron...

Or, consider the number of all sides compared with the number of solid angles: the **Cube** gives 8 to 12, or 2 to 3; the **Tetrahedron** 4 to 6, or 2 to 3; the **Octahedron** 6 to 12, or 1 to 2; the **Dodecahedron** 20 to 30, or 2 to 3; and the **Icosahedron** 12 to 30, or 2 to 5.

Furthermore, the bodies themselves are compared to one another if the Tetrahedron is hidden within the Cube, and the Octahedron within the Tetrahedron and the Cube, by geometric inscription. The Tetrahedron is one-third of the Cube; the Octahedron is half of the Tetrahedron and a sixth part of the Cube. Just as that Octahedron which is inscribed in a globe <note>original: "globo"; here meaning a sphere.</note> is a sixth part of the Cube that circumscribes the same globe. The volumes of the remaining bodies are **inexpressible** <note>original: "ineffabilia"; in a geometric context, this refers to irrational numbers or proportions that cannot be expressed as simple whole-number ratios.</note>.

The fourth species or degree of kinship is more specific to this work; it is where the proportion is sought between the **orbs** <note>The celestial spheres believed to carry the planets.</note> inscribed within the shapes and the orbs circumscribed around them, and it is considered which **Harmonic proportions** <note>Musical intervals expressed as mathematical ratios.</note> most closely approximate them. But in the **Cubic marriage** <note>The relationship between the Cube and the Octahedron.</note>, the proportion (which is unique there) is like lines that are expressible only by their power <note>original: "solâ potentiâ effabilibus"; meaning the squares of the lines are rational, but the lines themselves are square roots (irrational).</note>. In the Dodecahedral marriage, the proportion of the orbs is again unique, but inexpressible, slightly larger than 4 to 5. Therefore, for the **Cuboctahedral** <note>Referring to the Cube and Octahedron pair.</note> proportion of orbs, these Harmonies are approximate: 1 to 2 as the nearest larger, and 3 to 5 as the nearest smaller. For the Dodecahedral proportion of orbs, the Harmonies 4 to 5 and 5 to 6 are the nearest smaller, while 3 to 4 and 5 to 8 are the nearest larger.

But if, for certain reasons, 1 to 2 and 1 to 3 are claimed for the Cube, then just as the proportion of Cubic orbs is to the proportion of Tetrahedral orbs, so will these Harmonies—1 to 2 and 1 to 3 assigned to the Cube—be to 1 to 4 and 1 to 9, which would be assigned to the Tetrahedron, if this analogy is to be used. For these proportions are indeed the doubles of those Harmonies. And because 1 to 9 is not harmonic, the nearest harmony, 1 to 8, will take its place for the Tetrahedron. For the Dodecahedral marriage, by this same analogy, there will come roughly 4 to 5 and 3 to 4. For just as the proportion of Cubic orbs is nearly triple that of the Dodecahedral orbs, so also the Cubic harmonies 1 to 2 and 1 to 3 are nearly triple the harmonies 4 to 5 and 3 to 4. For 4 to 5 tripled <note>In musical ratios, "tripling" an interval means cubing the ratio: $(4/5)^3$.</note> becomes 64 to 125, and 1 to 2 is 64 to 128. Likewise, 3 to 4 tripled becomes 27 to 64, and 1 to 3 is 27 to 81.

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin>
<margin>The Hypotheses of *Copernicus*.</margin>
In their place—although I cannot do otherwise than substitute the opinion of *Copernicus* alone regarding the world and, if it were possible, persuade everyone of it—but because the matter is still new to the common sort of students, and to many a most absurd dogma to hear, that the Earth is one of the planets and is carried among the stars around a motionless Sun: let those who are offended by the strangeness <note>original: "insolentiâ"; literally "unusualness" or "novelty"</note> of this opinion know: these harmonic speculations also find a place within the hypotheses of *Tycho Brahe*. 
<margin>The Hypotheses of *Tycho Brahe*.</margin>
This is because that author has all other things in common with *Copernicus* which pertain to the arrangement of bodies and the contemplation of motions; he himself merely transfers the annual *Copernican* motion of the Earth into the whole system of the planetary spheres and into the Sun, which occupies its center, by the agreement of both authors. 
<margin>A comparison of both:</margin>
For from this transfer of motion, it nevertheless happens that the Earth—if not in that vast and immense space of the sphere of the fixed stars, then at least in the system of the planetary world—obtains at any time the same place according to *Brahe* that *Copernicus* gives it. Therefore, just as someone who draws a circle on paper moves the writing leg of the compass around, while someone who attaches the paper or tablet to a spinning lathe <note>original: "torno volubili"</note> describes the same circle with a stationary leg or stylus as the tablet runs beneath it; so also here, for *Copernicus* the Earth measures out a circle by the real motion of its body, walking in the middle between the outer circle of *Mars* and the inner circle of *Venus*; but for *Tycho Brahe*, the whole planetary system (in which, among the rest, are the circles of *Mars* and *Venus*) is turned like a tablet on a lathe, applying to the stationary Earth—as if to the turner's stylus—the gap between the circles of *Mars* and *Venus*. And by this motion of the system, it happens that the Earth marks the same circle in it around the Sun, intermediate between those of *Mars* and *Venus*, while remaining stationary herself; just as she marks it in *Copernicus* by the motion of her body while the system remains at rest. Since, therefore, harmonic contemplation considers the eccentric <term>eccentric: an orbital path that is not a perfect circle centered on the sun, but shifted</term> motions of the planets as if seen from the Sun, it is easily understood that if any observer were in the Sun— 
<margin>Harmonic contemplation is valid within the hypotheses of *Brahe*.</margin>
however much it might be in motion—the Earth, though stationary (as is now granted to *Brahe*), would nevertheless appear to that observer to run through an annual circle, in the middle between the planets, and also in the middle space of time. Therefore, even if there is a man of weak faith who cannot grasp the motion of the Earth among the stars, he can nevertheless enjoy the most excellent contemplation of this most divine mechanism; if he applies whatever he hears about the daily motions of the Earth in its eccentric to their appearance in the Sun—the kind of appearance that *Tycho Brahe* also exhibits, with the Earth at rest.

<margin>It is much more valid in the *Copernican* system.</margin>
Nor, however, do the true followers of the Samian philosophy <note>The philosophy of Pythagoras (who was from the island of Samos), who famously associated the movements of the heavens with musical intervals.</note> have a just cause to grudge such people the sharing of this most delightful speculation: as those whose joy will be many times more perfect, namely from the finished perfection of the speculation, if they also accept the immobility of the Sun and the motion of the Earth.

First, therefore, let readers hold this fast: it is a matter of absolute certainty among all astronomers today that all the planets orbit the Sun, with the exception of the Moon, which alone has the Earth for its center. The size of the Moon's orbit or path is not so great that it can be drawn on this page in proper proportion to the others. Therefore, the Earth is added to the other five as a sixth planet; whether by its own motion while the Sun remains still, or being itself unmoved while the entire system of planets is turned around <note>Kepler is acknowledging both the Copernican and Tychonic views here</note>, the Earth also describes a sixth circle around the Sun.

Second, it is also certain that all planets are eccentric—that is, they change their distances from the Sun, so that in one part of their circle they become most distant from the Sun, and in the opposite part they come very close to the Sun. In the attached diagram <note>original: "schemate"; referring to a visual plate included in the original printing</note>, three circles are drawn for each planet. The actual orbit (such as AD) touches the upper of the three circles, AF, at one region (A), and the lower circle, CD, at the opposite region (D). <margin>Refer here to the diagram of Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Sun ☉, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿.</margin> The circle GH, shaded with dots and drawn through the center of the Sun, indicates the path of the Sun according to Tycho Brahe. If the Sun moves along this path, every single point of the entire planetary system depicted here moves along an equal path, each following its own. And when one of its points—namely the center of the Sun—stands at one part of its circle (as here at the lowest), every single point of the system will stand in the lowest parts of their respective circles. Due to the narrowness of the space, the three circles for Venus have also merged into one, contrary to my intention.

Euclid wrote a book about these many centuries ago called the *Elements*, because it is constructed from a series of propositions. Furthermore, it was made clear in the second book of this current work that there cannot be more regular bodies—that is, regular plane figures cannot fit together to form a solid more than five times.

However, the proportions are not perfectly equal, as I once dared to promise regarding a final, perfected astronomy. <margin>CHAPTER III</margin>
From this it is clear that the very proportions of the planetary intervals from the Sun are not taken from the Regular solids alone; for the Creator, the very source of Geometry and—as Plato wrote—*the one who practices eternal Geometry*, does not stray from His own **Archetype** <note>The divine blueprint or original model of the universe</note>. Indeed, this could be gathered from the fact that all planets change their intervals over certain periods of time, so that each one has two notable distances from the Sun: a Maximum and a Minimum. Between any two planets, there is a fourfold comparison of intervals from the Sun: either both maximums, both minimums, or the extremes of being furthest apart or closest together. Thus, for every pair of neighboring planets, there are twenty such comparisons, whereas, conversely, there are only five solid figures. It is, however, consistent that the Creator, if He cared for the proportion of the spheres in general, also cared for the proportion that exists between the varying intervals of each specifically, and that this care was the same for both, with one being linked to the other. Having weighed this, we will surely find that to establish the diameters and the eccentricities of the spheres together, more principles are needed beyond the five regular solids.

<margin>Astronomical axioms of true motions.</margin>
Fifthly, to come to the motions among which the **Harmonies** are established, I again remind the reader that it has been demonstrated by me in my commentaries on Mars <note>referring to his 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*</note>, based on the most certain observations of **Tycho Brahe**, that *equal daily arcs on one and the same eccentric orbit are not traversed with equal speed; but that these varying delays in equal parts of the eccentric orbit follow the proportion of their intervals from the Sun*, the source of motion. # ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

Given equal times—for example, one natural day on both sides—the corresponding true daily arcs of the eccentric **orbit of a single planet** have an inverse proportion to the two distances from the Sun. At the same time, I have demonstrated that *the orbit of a planet is elliptical*, and that the Sun, the source of motion, is in one of the foci of this ellipse. Thus it happens that when a planet has completed a quadrant <note>A quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees</note> of its total circuit from its aphelion <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun</note>, it is at precisely the middle distance from the Sun, between the maximum distance at aphelion and the minimum at perihelion <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun</note>. From these two axioms, it is concluded that the *mean motion* <note>The theoretical average speed if the planet moved in a perfect circle</note> of a planet in its eccentric orbit is the same as the true daily arc of that eccentric orbit at those moments when the planet is at the end of the quadrant of the orbit calculated from the aphelion—even though that true quadrant may still appear smaller than a proper quadrant. It follows further that *any two* truest daily eccentric arcs, situated at equal distances—one from the aphelion and the other from the perihelion—when joined together, equal two mean daily arcs. Consequently, since the proportion of circles is the same as that of their diameters, the proportion of one mean daily arc to the sum of all mean arcs (which are all equal to each other throughout the circuit) is the same as the proportion of one mean daily arc to the sum of all the true eccentric arcs, which are equal in number but unequal to each other. These facts regarding the true daily arcs of the eccentric and the true motions must be understood beforehand, so that from them we may now understand the apparent motions as seen from the eye placed at the Sun.

<margin>
VI. Astronomical Axiom of the apparent motions from the Sun, or the angles formed at the center of the Sun by the lines encompassing the daily motions.
2.
</margin>
Sixth, as far as the apparent arcs as seen from the Sun are concerned, it has been known even from ancient astronomy that among true motions—even if they were equal to each other—the one which has receded further from the center of the world (such as at aphelion) appears smaller to an observer at that center, while the one which is nearer (such as at perihelion) appears larger. Since, moreover, the true daily arcs are also physically larger when near the Sun due to faster motion, and smaller at the remote aphelion due to the slowness of motion, I have demonstrated in my **Commentaries on Mars** <note>original: "Martialibus"; referring to his 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*, which focused on the orbit of Mars</note> that *the proportion of the apparent daily arcs of a single eccentric orbit is quite precisely the inverse square of the proportion of their distances from the Sun*. For example, if a planet on one of its days, when at aphelion, were at a distance of 10 parts from the Sun (by any measure), and on the opposite day, when at perihelion, at 9 similar parts: it is certain that its apparent advancement as seen from the Sun at aphelion will be to the apparent advancement at perihelion as 81 is to 100 <note>Kepler is explaining that because the planet is both physically slower and further away, the "apparent" speed decreases by the square of the distance: 9 squared is 81, 10 squared is 100</note>.

<margin>
3.
4.
5.
6.
7.
</margin>
However, this is true with these cautions: first, *that the eccentric arcs are not large*, lest they span different distances that vary too much (that is, they should not cause a sensible variation in the distance of their endpoints from the apsides <note>The points of greatest or least distance in an orbit</note>). Next, *that the eccentricity is not excessively great*; for the greater the eccentricity (that is, the larger the arc), the more the angle of its appearance increases beyond the measure of its approach to the Sun, *according to Theorem 8 of Euclid’s Optics*. This, however, is of no consequence in small arcs and at great distances, as I noted in Chapter XI of my own *Optics*. But there is another reason why I mention this. For *the eccentric arcs near the Mean Anomalies are viewed obliquely from the center of the Sun*, and this obliquity diminishes the magnitude of the appearance; whereas by contrast, the *arcs near the apsides* are presented directly to the view, as if from a person stationed in the Sun. Therefore, when the eccentricity is very great, the proportion of the motions is sensibly harmed...

<margin>VII. Rejection of the motions which appear to those looking out from the Earth.</margin>
Seventhly, if anyone should happen to encounter those daily motions that appear not as if from the Sun, but to those viewing from the Earth; of which Book VI of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* treats: let him know that no account of them is taken in this business. Truly, it neither ought to be, since the Earth is not the source of their motion; nor can it be, since those motions degenerate not only into mere rest or apparent station, but clearly into retrogradation <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky, which Kepler correctly identifies as an optical illusion caused by the Earth's own movement</note>, according to deceptive appearance; by which means an infinity of proportions is attributed to all planets simultaneously and equally. Therefore, so that we may have certainty as to what proper proportions the daily motions of the individual true eccentric orbits constitute (even though they themselves are still apparent, as if to one looking from the Sun, the source of motion): first, this "fantasy" of the annual motion, which is common to all five [planets], must be removed from these proper motions; whether that arises from the motion of the Earth itself, according to Copernicus; or from the annual motion of the entire system, according to Tycho Brahe; and the proper, clarified motions of each planet must be subjected to view.

<margin>VIII. What is the proportion of the periodic times to the intervals of any two from the Sun? 2. 3. 4.</margin>
Eighthly, thus far we have dealt with the different motions or arcs of one and the same planet. Now we must also deal with the motions of two planets compared with each other. Here, note the definition of terms that will be necessary for us. We shall call the *nearest apsides* <note>Apsides are the points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the center of motion</note> of two planets the perihelion <note>Closest point to the Sun</note> of the superior <note>outer</note> one and the aphelion <note>farthest point from the Sun</note> of the inferior <note>inner</note> one; notwithstanding that they do not point to the same region of the world, but to different and perhaps opposite ones. By *extreme motions*, understand the slowest and the fastest of the whole planetary circuit. *Converging or converted* [motions] are those at the two nearest apsides, namely at the perihelion of the superior and the aphelion of the inferior; *diverging or diverse* [motions] are those at the opposite apsides, namely at the aphelion of the superior and the perihelion of the inferior. Again, therefore, some part of my *Cosmographic Mystery*, suspended 22 years ago because it was not yet clear, must be completed here and introduced. For once the true intervals of the orbits were found through the observations of Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe, the master observational astronomer whose data Kepler used</note>, by the continuous labor of a very long time; at last, at last, the genuine proportion of the periodic times to the proportion of the orbits—*it looked back upon the idle one, though late*— <note>Kepler quotes Virgil’s Eclogues here, personifying his discovery as a goddess who finally visited him after years of waiting.</note>
