### IX. Proposition.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

**T**he individual proportions of the extreme motions <note>The "extreme motions" refer to the planet's speed at its slowest point (aphelion) and fastest point (perihelion).</note> of Saturn and Jupiter, when joined together, ought to have become approximately a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"; a musical interval with a ratio of 2:3.</note>.

<gloss>
This follows from the preceding proposition: for if the motion of Jupiter at its closest point to the sun is triple the motion of Saturn at its farthest point, and conversely, Jupiter’s motion at its farthest is double Saturn’s at its closest, then by taking away the ratio of 1:2 from 1:3, there remains 2:3.
</gloss>

---

### X. Axiom.

**W**hen the choice is otherwise free, the superior planet is entitled to a proper proportion of motions that is prior by nature, or of a more excellent kind, or even larger in scale.

---

### XI. Proposition.

**T**he proportion of Saturn’s motion from its farthest point to its closest point ought to have been a Major Third <note>original: "Tertia major"; a ratio of 4:5.</note>, while that of Jupiter’s ought to have been a Minor Third <note>original: "Tertia minor"; a ratio of 5:6.</note>.

For because they possess a Fifth (2:3) when joined together, and this interval is not divided harmonically in any other way than into a Major Third (4:5) and a Minor Third (5:6); therefore, God the Arranger <note>original: "Harmostes"; a Greek term for one who fits things together or a tuner.</note> divided the harmony of the Fifth harmonically, according to Axiom I. Following Axiom X, He gave the larger harmonic part—which is of the more excellent "Hard" <note>original: "Duri"; in music, "Dur" refers to the Major key, which Kepler associates here with a more masculine or "harder" character.</note> kind and is masculine—to the larger and higher planet, Saturn; and He gave the smaller part, 5:6, to the lower planet, Jupiter.

---

### XII. Proposition.

**T**o Venus and Mercury was owed the Greater Harmony of a Double Octave <note>original: "Disdiapason"; a ratio of 1:4.</note>.

<margin>
Remember that the terms "Double," "Triple," "Half-triple," etc., sometimes name individual proportions considered absolutely as a certain quantity, and at other times express a proportion derived from comparing two other proportions to one another.
</margin>

For just as the Cube is the first of the primary figures, so the Octahedron is the first of the secondary figures, according to Chapter I of this book. And just as the Cube, considered geometrically, is on the outside while the Octahedron is on the inside (since the latter can be inscribed within the former); so too in the World, Saturn and Jupiter are the beginning of the superior and outer planets, or those seen from the outside; while Venus and Mercury are the beginning of the interior planets, or those seen from within. The Octahedron is placed between their paths: see Chapter III. Therefore, Venus and Mercury are owed some harmony from the primary class that is related to the Octahedron.

Furthermore, in the natural order of harmonies, after the Octave (1:2) and the Twelfth (1:3) follows the Double Octave (1:4). This is related to the cubic ratio of 1:2 because it arises from the same family of figures—namely, the tetragonal <note>referring to four-sided or square-based geometry</note>—and it is commensurable with it, being its double. The Octahedron is also related and commensurable to the Cube. The 1:4 ratio is also related specifically to the Octahedron because of the number four within it, and the square figure hidden within the Octahedron <note>A square can be formed by the four middle vertices of an octahedron.</note>, the ratio of whose spheres is called a "half-double" <note>original: "Semidupla"; likely referring to the ratio of the square root of 2.</note>. Therefore, the name of that proportion is the harmony of 1:4, a continuous multiple in a double proportion—that is, a "quadruple half-double." See Chapter II.

Therefore, 1:4 was owed to Venus and Mercury. And because the 1:2 ratio in the Cube was made the "minor" harmony of the pair (since its position fell on the outermost part), in the Octahedron this 1:4 will now be the "major" harmony of the pair, as its position fell on the innermost part. But there is also this reason why 1:4 is given here as the major harmony and not the minor: since the proportion of the Octahedron’s spheres is "half-triple" <note>original: "Semitripla"; the ratio of 1 to the square root of 3.</note>, even assuming the Octahedron is perfectly inscribed between the planets (though it is not perfect, but penetrates Venus somewhat, which is to our advantage), the proportion of the convergent motions must be smaller than the "one-and-a-half" power <note>original: "sesquialtera"</note> of that half-triple ratio. Yet even 1:3 is clearly a double half-triple, and thus larger than what is right; how much larger than right will 1:4 be, which is even greater than 1:3? Therefore, not even half of 1:4 can be tolerated between the convergent motions. Thus, 1:4 cannot be the minor "Octahedrical" harmony; it must therefore be the Major.

larger. Furthermore, 1:4 is related to the Octahedral square in the same way, as the ratio of its spheres is the sub-double <note>original: "Semidupla"; Kepler is referring to the ratio of the radii of the spheres inscribed in and circumscribed around the solid.</note>: just as 1:3 is related to the Cube, as the ratio of its spheres is the sub-triple <note>original: "Semitripla"</note>. For just as 1:3 is a multiple of the sub-triple, namely its double; so also here 1:4 is a multiple of the sub-double, namely its double, which is to say quadruple. Therefore, if 1:3 ought to have become the major Harmony of the Cube, by Proposition VII; then 1:4 also ought to become the major Harmony of its Octahedron.

## XIII. Proposition.

To the extreme motions of Jupiter and Mars, there were due Harmonies: a Major one of approximately 1:8 (a Triple Octave <note>original: "Trisdiapason"</note>), and a Minor one of 5:24 (a Minor Third above a Double Octave <note>original: "Tertia minor supra Difdiapason"</note>).

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
*For because the Cube was assigned 1:2 and 1:3, but the ratio of the spheres of the Tetrahedron—which is situated between Jupiter <note>♃</note> and Mars <note>♂</note>—called "Triple," is the double of the ratio of the spheres of the Cube, called "Sub-triple": therefore it was fitting that the proportions of the motions accommodated to the Tetrahedron should also be the doubles of the cubic proportions. Now, the doubles of 1:2 and 1:3 are these proportions: 1:4 and 1:9. But 1:9 is not Harmonic, and 1:4 has already been used up for the Octahedron. Therefore, the Harmonies neighboring these proportions had to be chosen, by Axiom I. Now, the first neighbors to 1:9 are the smaller 1:8 and the larger 1:10. Between these, the choice is made by kinship with the Tetrahedron; it has nothing in common with the Pentagon, whereas 1:10 is a pentagonal division <note>Kepler associates the number 5 and its ratios with the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, which have pentagonal faces or symmetry.</note>. However, the Tetrahedron has a greater kinship with 1:8 for many reasons, which you may seek in Chapter II. Further supporting 1:8 is this: just as 1:3 is the major harmony of the Cube, and 1:4 the major of the Octahedron, because they are multiples of the proportions between the figured spheres; so also 1:8 ought to become the major of the Tetrahedron. For as the body of this solid is double that of the Octahedron inscribed within it, as stated in Chapter I, so also the term 8 of this Tetrahedral proportion is the double of the term 4 of the Octahedral proportion. Furthermore, just as 1:2, the minor of the Cube, is one Octave <note>Diapason</note>, and 1:4, the major of the Octave, is two Octaves: so now 1:8, the major of the Tetrahedron, ought to have become three Octaves. Moreover, more Octaves were due to this solid than to those, because since the minor Tetrahedral Harmony is necessarily the greatest of all the minor harmonies in the other figures (since the ratio of the Tetrahedral spheres is also the greatest of all the figures), the major Tetrahedral Harmony also ought to exceed the others in the number of its Octaves. Finally, the triple interval of Octaves has a familiarity with the Trilateral <note>Trigonicâ</note> species of the Tetrahedron, and possesses a certain perfection, according to the saying: "Everything in threes is perfect" <note>original: "Omne trinum perfectum"</note>; since even the number Eight, its term, is the first of the Cubic numbers of perfect quantity, namely, of three dimensions.*

II. Neighboring 1:4 (or 6:24) are the Harmonies: the major 5:24 and the minor 6:20 (or 3:10). But again, 3:10 is a Pentagonal division, which has nothing in common with the Tetrahedron. But 5:24, on account of the numbers 3 and 4 (from which the numbers 12 and 24 are descended), has a familiarity with the Tetrahedron. For we here neglect the other smaller terms, namely 5 and 3, because they have the slightest degree of kinship with the figures, as can be seen in Chapter II. Besides, the ratio of the spheres of the Tetrahedron is Triple; and approximately that great also ought to be the ratio of the converging intervals, by Axiom II. But by Chapter III, the ratio of the converging motions approaches the inverse of the ratio of the intervals raised to the power of three-halves <note>Kepler is referencing the mathematical relationship between a planet's distance and its orbital speed.</note>; and the three-halves power of the Triple ratio is approximately between 1000 and 193. Therefore, in a system where the aphelion <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the sun.</note> motion of Jupiter is 1000, Jupiter's motion will be a little greater than 193, and much less than 333 (which is a third part of it). Therefore, not the Harmony 10:3 (which is 1000:333), but the Harmony 24:5 (which is 1000:208) has a place between the converging motions of Jupiter and Mars.

# XIV. Proposition.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin> The proper ratio of the extreme motions of Mars <note>The "proper ratio" refers to the relationship between a single planet's fastest speed at perihelion and its slowest speed at aphelion.</note> ought to have been made larger than a Fourth (3:4) and approximately 18:25.

For let the precise Harmonies already attributed to Jupiter and Mars in common (from Proposition XIII) be 5:24 and 1:8—the latter expressed as 3:24. Subtract the smaller ratio (5:24) from the larger (3:24); there remains 3:5, which is the sum of the proper ratios of both planets together. However, the proper ratio of Jupiter alone was found above in Proposition XI to be 5:6. Therefore, subtract this from the sum of the proper ratios (3:5). That is, subtract 25:30 from 18:30 <note>Kepler is using a common denominator to subtract the ratios: 3/5 is 18/30 and 5/6 is 25/30. In terms of division of ratios: (3/5) ÷ (5/6) = 18/25.</note>; there remains the proper ratio of Mars, 18:25. This is larger than 18:24 (which is a Fourth, 3:4). It will become even larger if the common major ratio of 1:8 is increased through the following arguments.

# XV. Proposition.

Among the convergent motions <term>convergent motions<gloss>The ratio between the fastest speed of an outer planet and the slowest speed of the planet immediately interior to it.</gloss></term> of Mars and the Earth, the Earth and Venus, and Venus and Mercury, the following Harmonies had to be distributed: the Fifth (2:3), the Minor Sixth (5:8), and the Major Sixth (3:5), in that specific order.

*For the Dodecahedron <note>A 12-sided solid.</note> and the Icosahedron <note>A 20-sided solid.</note>, which are the figures located between Mars, the Earth, and Venus, have the smallest proportion between their circumscribed and inscribed spheres. Therefore, the smallest of the possible Harmonies are owed to them, being related for this very reason, and so that Axiom II may hold true. However, the smallest Harmonies of all—namely 5:6 and 4:5—are not possible according to Proposition VI. Therefore, the Harmonies next largest to these are owed to the said figures: namely either 3:4, 2:3, 5:8, or 3:5.*

*Again, the figure located between Venus and Mercury, namely the Octahedron <note>An 8-sided solid.</note>, has the same proportion of its spheres as the Cube. To the Cube, by Proposition VII, there fell an Octave (1:2) to be the prominent Harmony between its convergent motions. Therefore, by analogy, such a great interval—namely a 1:2 Octave—would also be owed to the Octahedron if no other difference were introduced. But a difference does arise: for in the case of the "Cubic" planets (Saturn and Jupiter), the sum of their individual proper ratios did not exceed 2:3. Here, however, for the "Octahedral" planets (Venus and Mercury), the sum of their individual proper ratios will exceed 2:3, as is easily shown. For suppose that the analogy between the Cube and Octahedron required the Minor Octahedral ratio to be larger than what is prescribed here; let it be exactly as large as the Cubic ratio was, namely 1:2. The Major ratio was 1:4 by Proposition XII. If we subtract the Minor (1:2) from this, there still remains 1:2 for the sum of the proper ratios of Venus and Mercury. But 1:2 is more than the sum (2:3) of the proper ratios of Saturn and Jupiter. Indeed, a greater eccentricity follows from this greater sum (by Chapter III), and a smaller ratio of convergent motions follows from that greater eccentricity (by the same Chapter III). Therefore, by adding greater eccentricity to the analogy between the Cube and Octahedron, a smaller proportion of convergent motions is required for Venus and Mercury than 1:2. This was also consistent with Axiom I: that since the Octave (1:2) was used up by the Cubic planets, another nearby Harmony should be reconciled to the Octahedral planets—and by the previous demonstration, one smaller than 1:2. The next smallest is 3:5, which as...*

# ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK V.

The larger of the three [ratios] was assigned to the figure with the larger proportion between its [circumscribed and inscribed] spheres, namely the **Octahedron**. Therefore, the smaller ratios of 5:8 and 2:3 (or 3:4) were left to the **Icosahedron** and the **Dodecahedron**, which are figures with smaller proportions between their spheres.

These remaining ratios, however, are distributed between the two remaining pairs in this way: For just as among the figures, even though they may have equal proportions between their spheres, the **Cube** was assigned the Harmony 1:2 while the **Octahedron** was assigned the smaller 3:5—because the sum of the proper motions of Venus and Mercury exceeded the sum of the proper motions of Saturn and Jupiter—so also here, the **Dodecahedron** (although it creates the same proportion of its spheres as the **Icosahedron**) was due a smaller ratio than the **Icosahedron**. Yet, for a similar reason, it is very close to it; specifically, because this figure lies between **Earth** and **Mars**, where a large <term>eccentricity<gloss>The degree to which a planet's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</gloss></term> was established in the previous sections. In contrast, the eccentricities of **Venus** and **Earth** are the smallest, as we shall hear in what follows. And since the Octahedron has a 3:5 ratio, the Icosahedron (whose orbital proportion is smaller) follows it with a slightly smaller ratio, namely 5:8. This left the Dodecahedron with either the remaining 2:3 or 3:4; but the former (2:3) is preferred, as it is closer to the Icosahedral 5:8, because these two figures are similar <note>Kepler refers to the geometric "duality" between the Icosahedron and Dodecahedron.</note>.

But the 3:4 ratio was not even possible. For although the proper ratio of the extreme motions of **Mars** was large enough in the previous sections, **Earth** (as has been said and will be clear in the following) contributed a proper ratio too small for the sum of both to exceed a <term>Fifth<gloss>original: Diapente (a musical interval with a 2:3 ratio).</gloss></term>. Therefore, 3:4 could not take that place, according to Proposition VII. This is even more certain because, as follows in Proposition XLVII, the proportion of the convergent intervals had to be larger than 1000:795.

### XVI. Proposition.

The proper ratios of the motions of **Venus** and **Mercury**, when joined together, ought to have produced approximately 5:12.

Subtract the smaller harmony of 3:5 (which was commonly assigned to this pair in Proposition XV) from their larger harmony of 1:4 (or 3:12); according to Proposition XII, there remains 5:12 as the sum of the proper motions of both. Therefore, the proper ratio of the extreme motions of **Mercury** alone is smaller than 5:12 by the amount of the proper ratio of **Venus**. Understand this regarding these primary calculations. For later, through secondary calculations, once a certain "ferment" <note>Kepler uses the term "fermentum" to describe the slight mathematical adjustments or "leavening" required to tune the ideal ratios to the observed physical reality of the heavens.</note> is added to the common harmonies of both, it will be brought about that the proper ratio of Mercury alone perfectly obtains the 5:12 interval.

The Harmony of the <term>divergent motions<gloss>The ratio between the slowest speed of an outer planet and the fastest speed of the planet immediately interior to it.</gloss></term> of **Mars** and **Earth** could not be less than 5:12.

For **Mars** alone obtained more than a <term>Fourth<gloss>original: Diatessaron (a 3:4 ratio).</gloss></term> in its own proper ratio of motions, and more than 18:25 according to Proposition XIV. Their smaller Harmony is a Fifth, 2:3, according to Proposition XV. Therefore, these two parts joined together make 12:25. But according to Axiom IV, **Earth** must also have its own proper ratio. Therefore, since the Divergent Harmony consists of these three elements <note>The three elements are: the proper ratio of the outer planet, the convergent harmony between the two, and the proper ratio of the inner planet.</note>, it will be larger than 12:25. But the harmony immediately larger than 12:25 (which is 60:125) is 5:12 (that is, 60:144). Therefore, if there is need of a Harmony for this greater ratio of the two planets...

So far, then, all the remaining pairs of planets have obtained their two harmonies through necessary reasons; only the pair of **Earth** and **Venus** has thus far been allotted a single harmony, 5:8, by the axioms used up to this point. Should we therefore now seek out its remaining harmony—namely the Major, or the harmony of the divergent motions—by making a new beginning?

# XVIII. Axiom.

Universal harmonies of the motions had to be established by the tempering together of the six motions, especially through the extreme motions.
->*Proven by Axiom I.*<-

# XIX. Axiom.

Universal harmonies had to occur within a certain range <note>original: "latitudinem", referring to a breadth or latitude of values rather than a single fixed point</note> of motions, so that they might happen more frequently.
> *For if they had been restricted to individual points of motion, it could have happened that they never occurred, or certainly only very rarely.*

# XX. Axiom.

Just as the distinction of the <term>Types of Harmonies<gloss>Generum Harmoniarum</gloss></term> into "Hard" and "Soft" <note>original: "Durum & Molle"; in Kepler's time, these terms were the precursors to our modern "Major" and "Minor" keys.</note> is most natural, as proven in Book III, so universal harmonies of both types had to be provided between the extreme motions of the planets.

# XXI. Axiom.

Different species of harmonies of both types had to be established, so that the beauty of the world might be composed of all possible members of variety; and this through the extreme motions, at least some of them.
->*By Axiom I.*<-

# XXII. Proposition.

The extreme motions of the planets had to mark the places or "strings" of the <term>diapason<gloss>The Greek term for an octave; here Kepler uses it to mean the full span of the musical system.</gloss></term> system, or the keys of the musical scale.

# BOOK V OF THE HARMONIES

For the origin and comparison of the Harmonies begun from a single common term produced the Musical scale, or the division of the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> into its proper places or sounds, as proven in Book III. Since, therefore, various Harmonies are required between the extremes of the motions, by Axiom I, XX, and XXI: it follows that a real distinction of some celestial system or Harmonic scale is required through the extremes of the motions.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

## Proposition XXIII.

It was necessary that there be one pair of Planets between whose motions no Harmonies could exist except two Sixths, the Major (4:5) and the Minor (5:6). <note>While Kepler writes 4:5 and 5:6 here as "Sixths," these ratios usually define the Major and Minor Thirds; he correctly identifies the Sixths as 3:5 and 5:8 in the following paragraph. He likely names them here because they produce the same "Diesis" difference.</note>

For since the distinction of the <term>Types of Harmonies<gloss>Genera Harmoniarum</gloss></term> was necessary (by Axiom XX), and this distinction must occur through the extremes of the motions at the <term>Apsides<gloss>the points where a planet is closest to or farthest from the sun</gloss></term> (by Axiom XXII); and because only the extremes—the slowest and the fastest motions—require the definition of an arranger and orderer (the intermediate tensions occur spontaneously as the planet passes from slowest to fastest motion without special care), this ordering could not happen in any other way than by the extremes of two planetary motions defining a <term>Diesis<gloss>the small mathematical interval—ratio 24:25—that separates a Major harmony from a Minor one</gloss></term>. This is because the Types of Harmonies are distinguished by a Diesis, as explained in Book III.

But the Diesis is the difference either between two Thirds (4:5 and 5:6) or between two Sixths (3:5 and 5:8), or between the same intervals increased by one or more Octaves. Now, two Thirds (4:5 and 5:6) found no place between any pair of Planets (by Proposition VI), nor were Thirds or Sixths increased by an Octave found anywhere, except for the 5:12 ratio in the pair of Mars and Earth; however, even that was only found in company with the 2:3 ratio (the Fifth). Therefore, it remains that two Sixths, 3:5 and 5:8, had to be given to one pair of Planets.

But if only these Sixths were to be granted to the variation of those motions, they had to be arranged so that they neither dilated their terms to include the next largest interval, the **Octave** (1:2), nor contracted them to the narrowness of the next smallest, the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note> (2:3). For even though it is true that two planets making a Fifth at their converging extremes and an Octave at their diverging extremes could also make Sixths—and thus pass through the Diesis—this would not savor of the singular providence of the <term>Orderer of motions<gloss>Kepler’s term for God as a geometer/architect</gloss></term>. For the Diesis, the smallest of intervals, exists latently in all larger intervals encompassed by the extreme motions, and it is passed through by the intermediate motions as they vary in continuous tension; but it is not *determined* by their extremes, since the part (the Diesis) is always smaller than the whole—namely, the interval of a **Fourth** (3:4) which lies between a Fifth (2:3) and an Octave (1:2), which would be the "whole" determined by the motions' extremes in such a case.

## Proposition XXIV.

The two Planets that change the type of Harmony must have the difference of their own proportions <note>the ratio of a single planet's fastest motion to its slowest motion</note> between the extremes of their motions equal to a Diesis, and the proportion of one of them must be greater than a Diesis: and they must produce one of the Sixths with their <term>Aphelion<gloss>farthest from the sun, slowest</gloss></term> motions and the other with their <term>Perihelion<gloss>closest to the sun, fastest</gloss></term> motions.

For since the extremes of the motions produce two Harmonies differing by a single ...

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS
<meta>catchword: XXVI. Pro-</meta>

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...the variations, this can happen in three ways: either so that the motion of one Planet remains constant while the other is varied by a <term>Diesis<gloss>a small musical interval, specifically the ratio 24:25, which distinguishes a major scale from a minor one</gloss></term>; or so that both are varied by half a Diesis, creating a 3 : 5 **Major Sixth** when the superior planet is at <term>Aphelion<gloss>the point in orbit furthest from the sun</gloss></term> and the inferior is at <term>Perihelion<gloss>the point in orbit closest to the sun</gloss></term>; and then, having moved through those spaces and meeting each other—the superior moving toward perihelion and the inferior toward aphelion—they create a 5 : 8 **Minor Sixth**. Or, finally, so that one varies its motion more than the other from aphelion to perihelion, and the excess of one is a Diesis; thus, the Major Sixth exists between both aphelia, and the Minor Sixth between both perihelia. 

However, the first method is not legitimate, for then one of these Planets would be without <term>Eccentricity<gloss>the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</gloss></term>, which contradicts Axiom IV. The second method was less beautiful and less convenient. It was less beautiful because it was less Harmonic; for the proportions of the proper motions of the two Planets would have been <note>original: "inconcinnae"</note> unmusical or "clashing," because anything smaller than a Diesis is unmusical. It is better for only one Planet to suffer from this unmusical smallness. Indeed, it could not even happen, because in this way the extreme motions would have strayed from the "places" of the system, or the keys of the Musical scale, contrary to Axiom XXII. It would also have been less convenient, because those Sixths would have occurred only at the moments when the planets were at opposite <term>apsides<gloss>the extreme points of an orbit</gloss></term>. There would have been no "latitude" or range through which these Sixths—and thus the universal Harmonies according to them—could occur. Universal Harmonies would therefore have been extremely rare, with the positions of all the Planets reduced to the narrow constraints of certain single points in their Orbits, contrary to Axiom XIX. There remains, therefore, the third method: that both Planets indeed vary their own proper motion, but one varies more than the other by at least one perfect Diesis.

## Proposition XXV.

Of the Planets that change the type <note>or "Genus"</note> of Harmony, the superior must have a proportion of its own motions smaller than a **Minor Tone** (9 : 10), while the inferior must have one smaller than a **Semitone** (15 : 16).

For they will create either the 3 : 5 ratio with their aphelion motions or with their perihelion motions, according to the previous premise. Not with the perihelia: for then the ratio of the aphelion motions would be 5 : 8, and the inferior planet would thus have a proper proportion one Diesis greater than the superior, by the same premise. But that is against Axiom X. They therefore form a 3 : 5 at aphelion, and 5 : 8 at perihelion—which is less than the former by the ratio 24 : 25 <note>the Diesis</note>. 

Now, if the aphelion motions create a **Major Sixth** (3 : 5), then the aphelion of the superior with the perihelion of the inferior will create more than a Major Sixth, for the inferior will add its entire proper proportion. In the same way, if the perihelion motions create a **Minor Sixth** (5 : 8), the perihelion of the superior and the aphelion of the inferior will create less than a Minor Sixth, for the inferior subtracts its entire proper proportion. But if the proper proportion of the inferior planet equaled a **Semitone** (15 : 16), then in addition to the Sixths, a <term>Fifth<gloss>Diapente</gloss></term> (3 : 2) could also occur, because a Minor Sixth (5 : 8) diminished by a semitone becomes a Fifth. This, however, is against Proposition XXIII <note>which states this pair only forms sixths</note>. Therefore, the inferior planet has an interval smaller than a semitone in its own proper range. And because the proper proportion of the superior planet is larger than the proper proportion of the inferior by one Diesis—and a Diesis added to a Semitone makes a **Minor Tone** (9 : 10)—the superior's proper proportion is therefore smaller than a Minor Tone.

## XXVI. Proposition.

The **P**lanets that change the genus of Harmony: the superior ought to have either a double <term>Diesis<gloss>a small musical interval, specifically the ratio 24:25; a "double diesis" is the square of this ratio, approx. 12:13</gloss></term> 576 : 625 (that is, approximately 12 : 13) for the interval of its extreme motions, or a <term>Semitone<gloss>the interval 15:16</gloss></term> 15 : 16, or something intermediate, differing from one or the other by a <term>Comma<gloss>the syntonic comma, a very small interval of 80:81</gloss></term> 80 : 81. The inferior, however, should have either a simple Diesis 24 : 25, or the difference between a Semitone and a Diesis, which is 125 : 128 (that is, approximately 42 : 43); or finally, similarly something intermediate, differing by a Comma 80 : 81 from one or the other: namely, the former a double Diesis and the latter a simple Diesis, with both intervals diminished by a Comma.

> *For the superior planet's proper interval <note>Kepler refers to the ratio between the planet's fastest and slowest speeds</note> must be larger than a Diesis, by Proposition 25, but smaller than a <term>Tone<gloss>the whole tone ratio 9:10</gloss></term> 9 : 10, by the preceding proposition. Moreover, the superior must exceed the inferior by one Diesis, by Proposition 24. And Harmonic beauty suggests that their proper intervals—if they cannot be perfectly Harmonic due to their smallness—should at least be from the <term>Concinnous<gloss>musical intervals that are pleasing to the ear but not primary harmonies</gloss></term> intervals, if this can be done, by Axiom I. Yet there are only two Concinnous intervals smaller than a Tone 9 : 10: the Semitone and the Diesis. However, these do not differ from one another by a Diesis, but by a smaller interval 125 : 128. Therefore, the superior cannot have a Semitone while the inferior has a Diesis simultaneously. Instead, either the superior will have a Semitone 15 : 16 and the inferior 125 : 128 (that is, 42 : 43), or the inferior will have a Diesis 24 : 25 and the superior a double Diesis, roughly 12 : 13. Since the rights of both Planets are equal, if the nature of the Concinnous had to be violated in their proper intervals, it should have been violated equally in both; so that the difference of their proper intervals could remain an exact Diesis, which is necessary for distinguishing the genera of Harmonies, by Proposition 24. Now, the nature of the Concinnous was violated equally in both if the superior's proper proportion fell short of a double Diesis (or exceeded a Semitone) by as much as the inferior's proper proportion fell short of a simple Diesis (or exceeded the interval 125 : 128).*

---

> *Furthermore, this excess or defect ought to be a Comma 80 : 81, because again no other interval was demonstrated by Harmonic proportions; and so that the Comma might be expressed among the celestial motions just as it is expressed in Harmonics—namely, only by the excess and defect between intervals. For in Harmonics, the Comma distinguishes between the Tones, the major and the minor, and is not known in any other way.*

---

> *It remains for us to investigate which of the proposed intervals are better: whether the Diesis (simple for the inferior planet, double for the superior) or rather the Semitone for the superior and 125 : 128 for the inferior. And the Dieses win by these arguments: For although the Semitone is expressed in various ways in the Musical scale, its companion 125 : 128 is not. On the other hand, the Diesis is expressed in various ways, and the double Diesis in a certain way, namely in the resolution of Tones into Dieses, Semitones, and <term>Limmata<gloss>the remainder of a tone after a semitone is removed</gloss></term>. For then, as said in Book III, Chapter VIII, two Dieses succeed each other closely in two places. Another argument is that in the distinction of genera, the rights belong to the Diesis, and none to the Semitone; therefore, greater respect had to be paid to the Dieses than to the Semitone. The conclusion from all this is: the superior's proper interval ought to be 2916 : 3125, or approximately 14 : 15; the inferior's proper interval 243 : 250, or approximately 35 : 36.*

It is asked whether the highest creative wisdom was occupied in seeking out these tiny calculations? I respond, it is possible that many reasons are hidden from me. But if the nature of Harmonics did not allow for weightier ones,

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

...indeed, in these proportions, which fall below the quantity of all <term>concinnous<gloss>musically pleasing or harmonious</gloss></term> intervals: it is not absurd that God followed even these, however thin they may appear, since He ordained nothing without a cause. For it would be far more absurd to affirm that God snatched up these quantities by chance below the prescribed limit of the <term>Minor Tone<gloss>the musical ratio 9:10</gloss></term>. Nor is it enough to say: "He chose such great ones because such great ones pleased Him." For in geometric matters, though subject to the freedom of choice, nothing pleased God without some geometric cause, as is apparent in the edges of leaves, in the scales of fish, in the pelts of wild beasts and their spots, and the order of those spots, and other such things.

## XXVII. Proposition.

The Major ratio of the motions of the Earth and Venus ought to have been a <term>Major Sixth<gloss>the ratio 3:5; "Sexta dura" refers to the "hard" or major interval</gloss></term> between their <term>aphelion<gloss>the point in orbit furthest from the sun, where the planet moves slowest</gloss></term> motions; and the Minor ratio, a <term>Minor Sixth<gloss>the ratio 5:8; "Sexta mollis" refers to the "soft" or minor interval</gloss></term>, between their <term>perihelion<gloss>the point in orbit closest to the sun, where the planet moves fastest</gloss></term> motions.

*For it was necessary to distinguish the genera of Harmonies <note>major and minor keys</note>, according to Axiom 20. This, however, could not be done otherwise than through Sixths, according to Proposition 23. Therefore, since the Earth and Venus—the closest planets and those associated with the <term>Icosahedron<gloss>a 20-sided Platonic solid</gloss></term>—received one of these [the 5:8 ratio], according to Proposition 15, it was also necessary that the other [the 3:5 ratio] be distributed. Truly, this was not between the extremes, whether converging or diverging; but between the extremes of the same region: one between the aphelia, the other between the perihelia, according to Proposition 24. Furthermore, the 5:8 Harmony is cognate to the Icosahedron, seeing as both are divided according to a pentagonal ratio. See Chapter 2.*

Behold the cause why precisely the Harmonies between the motions of these two are found at the aphelia and perihelia, rather than between the converging motions as in the cases above.

## XXIIX. Proposition.

For the Earth, a proper ratio of motions of about 14 : 15 was appropriate; for Venus, about 35 : 36.

*For these two had to distinguish the genera of Harmonies, according to the preceding proposition: therefore, by Proposition 26, the Earth, as the superior, ought to have obtained the interval 2916 : 3125—that is, nearly 14 : 15. Venus, however, as the inferior, ought to have the interval 243 : 250—that is, very nearly 35 : 36.*

Behold the cause why these two planets have such small <term>eccentricities<gloss>the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</gloss></term>, and accordingly, small intervals or proper ratios of their extreme motions; even though Mars, immediately above the former, and Mercury, immediately below the latter, have significant eccentricities, the largest of all. That this is true, Astronomy confirms; for in Chapter 4, the Earth clearly had 14 : 15, while Venus had 34 : 35, which astronomical certainty can scarcely distinguish from 35 : 36 in this planet.

## XXIX. Proposition.

The Major Harmony of the motions of Mars and the Earth, when diverging, could not be greater than 5 : 12.

*Above, in Proposition 17, it was not one of the smaller intervals; now, however, it is not one of the larger ones either. For the other ratio common to these, or the Minor 2 : 3, along with the proper ratio of Mars, which by Proposition 14 exceeds...*

## XXX. Proposition.

Mercury’s proper proportion of motions ought to have been made greater than all other proper [proportions].

This, indeed, was not specifically sought after, nor taken from any separate and singular archetype of beauty; but it comes forth of its own accord, by the necessity of the causes linked through the Harmonies established thus far.

## XXXI. Proposition.

The aphelion motion of the Earth ought to have agreed with the aphelion of Saturn through some number of <term>Diapasons<gloss>octaves</gloss></term>.

For it was necessary that there be universal Harmonies, by Proposition XVIII: therefore also of Saturn with the Earth and Venus. But if neither of the extreme motions of Saturn agreed with either of these, it would have been less harmonic than if each of its extremes agreed with these planets, by Axiom I. Therefore Saturn ought to have agreed by both its extremes: the aphelion with one of these two planets, and the perihelion with the other, since nothing stood in the way, as it is the first planet. These Harmonies will therefore be either <term>Unisons<gloss>identical in sound across different octaves</gloss></term> or <term>Dissonant<gloss>different in sound</gloss></term>, that is, of a ratio either continuously double [2:1] or otherwise. But they cannot both be of another proportion: for between the terms 3:5 (defining the Major Harmony between the <term>aphelia<gloss>furthest points from the sun</gloss></term> of Earth and Venus, by Proposition XXVII) two Harmonic means cannot exist: for a Sixth cannot be divided into three Harmonic intervals. See Book III. Therefore Saturn could not make an octave with both its motions relative to the Harmonic means between 3 and 5; but in order for its motions to agree with both the 3 of the Earth and the 5 of Venus, it is necessary that one of them agree identically with one of the terms, namely with one of the said planets themselves, or...

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>...by several <term>Octaves<gloss>Diapason</gloss></term>. However, since identical harmonies <note>Kepler refers to octaves and unisons as "identical" because the notes share the same name and character.</note> are superior, they must also be established between the superior extremes of the motions—namely, between the <term>aphelia<gloss>the points in an orbit farthest from the sun, where motion is slowest</gloss></term>. This is because they hold the place of the beginning due to the elevation of the planets, and they claim for themselves a certain prerogative over the <term>Major Sixth<gloss>the ratio 3:5</gloss></term> harmony—which we are now treating as the major harmony of the Earth and Venus. For although that harmony also applies to the perihelion of Venus and a certain intermediate point of the Earth, according to Proposition XXII, the start is made from the extremes of motions; intermediate motions follow after the beginnings. 

Now, since on one side we have the aphelion motion of Saturn, the highest planet, on the other side the aphelion of the Earth rather than that of Venus must be coupled with it; because of these two, which distinguish the genus of harmony, the Earth's is again higher. There is also another closer cause: that the later ratios, which we are now dealing with, do indeed detract from the earlier ones, but only regarding the smallest [intervals], which in <term>harmonics<gloss>Harmonice</gloss></term> is regarding intervals smaller than all concordant ones. But by the earlier ratios, it was the aphelion of the Earth, not Venus, that approached a harmony of several octaves to be established with the aphelion of Saturn. 

For if you collect into one sum: 
1. First, Saturn's own proportion of motions, 4:5 (that is, from the aphelion to the perihelion of Saturn, from XI); 
2. Second, the converging motions of Saturn and Jupiter, 1:2 (that is, from the perihelion of Saturn to the aphelion of Jupiter, from VIII); 
3. Third, the diverging motions of Jupiter and Mars, 1:8 (from the aphelion of Jupiter to the perihelion of Mars, from XIV); 
4. Fourth, the converging motions of Mars and the Earth, 2:3 (from the perihelion of Mars to the aphelion of the Earth, from XV);

—you will accumulate between the aphelion of Saturn and the aphelion of the Earth a proportion of 1:30. This lacks no more than 30:32 (that is, 15:16 or a <term>Semitone<gloss>the interval of a half-step</gloss></term>) to be 1:32 or <term>Five Octaves<gloss>Pentakis Diapason</gloss></term>. Therefore, if a semitone—divided into particles smaller than the smallest concord—is added to these four elements, the harmony of Five Octaves will be perfect between the proposed aphelia of Saturn and the Earth. 

But for that same aphelion of Saturn to make several octaves with the aphelion of Venus, it would have been necessary to take away almost an entire <term>Fourth<gloss>Diatessaron</gloss></term> from the earlier ratios. For if 3:5, which is between the aphelia of the Earth and Venus, is added to the sum of 1:30 gathered from the four previous elements, the result between the aphelia of Saturn and Venus is 1:50. This interval differs from 1:32 (Five Octaves) by 32:50 (that is, 16:25, which is a <term>Fifth<gloss>Diapente</gloss></term> with a <term>Diesis<gloss>a very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</gloss></term>); and from <term>Six Octaves<gloss>Hexakisdiapason</gloss></term> or 1:64, it differs by 50:64 (which is 25:32, or a Fourth minus one Diesis). Thus, an identical harmony ought to have been established not between the aphelia of Venus and Saturn, but between the aphelia of the Earth and Saturn, so that a harmony of different sounds remained for Saturn with Venus.

### XXXII. Proposition.

**I**n the universal harmonies of the planets of the <term>Soft Genus<gloss>the minor mode or scale</gloss></term>, the clearly aphelion motion of Saturn could not exactly harmonize with the other planets.

For the Earth, by its aphelion motion, does not concur in the universal harmony of the soft genus, because the aphelia of the Earth and Venus make an interval of 3:5, which is of the <term>Hard Genus<gloss>the major mode or scale</gloss></term>, by Proposition XXVII. But Saturn, by its aphelion, makes an identical harmony with the aphelion of the Earth, by Proposition XXXI. Therefore, Saturn also does not concur by its aphelion motion. Nevertheless, a somewhat more intense motion of Saturn, very close to the aphelion, succeeds in its place even for the soft genus, as appeared in Chapter VII.

### XXXIII. Proposition.

The <term>Hard<gloss>Durum</gloss></term> genus of Harmonies and the Musical Scale is natural to <term>aphelion<gloss>the point where a planet is furthest from the sun and moves slowest</gloss></term> motions; the <term>Soft<gloss>Molle</gloss></term> genus is natural to <term>perihelion<gloss>the point where a planet is closest to the sun and moves fastest</gloss></term> motions.

*For although a Hard Harmony is established not only between the aphelion of the Earth and the aphelion of Venus, but also between the motions of the Earth below its aphelion and the lower motions of Venus, even down to its perihelion; and conversely, a Soft Harmony is established not only between the perihelion of Venus and the perihelion of the Earth, but also between the higher motions of Venus up to its aphelion and the higher motions of the Earth, according to Proposition XXVII; nevertheless, the proper and evident designation of the genus is made only by the extremes of both, according to Propositions XX and XXIV. Therefore, the proper designation of the Hard genus exists only in the aphelion motions, and the proper designation of the Soft only in the perihelion motions.* <note>Kepler is defining "Hard" and "Soft" as what we would now call Major and Minor modes. He argues that the planetary "scales" are defined by their slowest and fastest speeds.</note>

### XXXIV. Proposition.

The Hard genus is more natural to the higher of two compared planets; the Soft genus to the lower.

*For because the Hard genus is proper to aphelion motions and the Soft to perihelion motions (by the preceding proposition), and aphelion motions are slower and <term>lower in pitch<gloss>graviores</gloss></term> than perihelion motions, the Hard genus therefore belongs to slower motions and the Soft to faster ones. But the higher of two planets is more naturally disposed toward slow motions, and the lower toward fast motions, because in the System of the World, slowness of proper motion always follows height <note>original: "altitudinem"</note>. Therefore, the higher planet also relates more naturally to the Hard genus of the scale, and the lower to the Soft, among those two which accommodate themselves to both genera. Furthermore, the Hard genus uses the larger intervals—the <term>Major Third<gloss>the ratio 4:5</gloss></term> and the <term>Major Sixth<gloss>the ratio 3:5</gloss></term>—while the Soft uses the smaller—the <term>Minor Third<gloss>5:6</gloss></term> and the <term>Minor Sixth<gloss>5:8</gloss></term>. And indeed, a higher planet has both a larger orbit and slower (that is, larger) motions and a more extended circuit; since great things suit both sides, they unite with one another more naturally.*

### XXXV. Proposition.

Saturn and the Earth embrace the Hard genus more naturally; Jupiter and Venus, the Soft genus.

*For first, the Earth, when compared with Venus and designating both genera with her, is the higher planet; therefore the Earth chiefly embraces the Hard genus, and Venus the Soft genus, by the preceding proposition. Saturn, however, in its aphelion, accords through an <term>Octave<gloss>Diapason</gloss></term> with the aphelion of the Earth, by Proposition XXXI. Wherefore Saturn also, by XXXIII, embraces the Hard genus. Furthermore, Saturn in its aphelion motion favors the Hard genus more and rejects the Soft genus, by XXXII. It therefore conducts itself more naturally toward the Hard genus than the Soft, because the genera are properly designated by the Extreme motions.*

*Now, as far as Jupiter is concerned: he is lower in comparison with Saturn; therefore, just as the Hard genus is owed to Saturn, so the Soft genus is owed to Jupiter, by the preceding proposition.*

<summary>Kepler assigns the "Hard" (Major) musical mode to planets at their slowest points (aphelia) and the "Soft" (Minor) mode to planets at their fastest (perihelia). He further categorizes Saturn and Earth as Major-oriented and Jupiter and Venus as Minor-oriented based on their relative positions and speeds.</summary>

## Proposition XXXVI

The perihelion <gloss>fastest</gloss> motion of Jupiter had to agree with the perihelion of Venus in one Musical Scale, but not also in the same Harmony; and much less so with the perihelion of the Earth.

> *For because Jupiter was chiefly assigned to the <term>Soft genus<gloss>the Minor mode</gloss></term>, by the preceding proposition; and to those planets, perihelion motions are indeed familiar, by Proposition XXX: Jupiter therefore by its perihelion ought to designate the Scale of the Soft genus, namely its certain location or <term>pitch<gloss>original: phthongum, a Greek term for a musical note</gloss></term>. But both the perihelia of Venus and the Earth designate the same Scale, by Proposition XXVII. Therefore, when these planets are at their perihelia, Jupiter’s perihelion had to be associated in the same pitch <gloss>tension</gloss>. Yet it could not establish a Harmony <gloss>a perfect musical interval</gloss> with the perihelion of Venus. For because by Proposition VIII it had to make about 1:3 <note>a compound perfect fifth</note> with the aphelion of Saturn, that is, the key **d** of that system, in which the aphelion of Saturn made the key **G**, and the aphelion of Venus the key **e**: therefore it approached the key **e** within the space of the smallest Harmony: For that is 5:6 <gloss>a minor third</gloss>, but between **d** and **e** is a much smaller interval, namely the 9:10 Tone <gloss>a minor whole tone</gloss>. And although in the perihelion pitch, Venus is raised from the **d** of the aphelion pitch; yet this elevation is less than a <term>diesis<gloss>a very small interval, less than a semitone</gloss></term>, by Proposition XXVIII. A diesis indeed (and something less than it) joined to a minor Tone does not yet equal the interval of the smallest Harmony 5:6. Therefore, the perihelion of Jupiter could not maintain approximately 1:3 with the aphelion of Saturn and simultaneously harmonize with Venus. Nor even with the Earth. For if the perihelion of Jupiter were adjusted to the scale of Venus's perihelion in the same pitch, so that it maintains an interval with the aphelion of Saturn of 1:3 below the quantity of the smallest concord, namely distant from the perihelion of Venus by a minor Tone (9:10 or 36:40) (beyond some <term>Octaves<gloss>original: Diapason</gloss></term>) toward the Bass; indeed, the perihelion of the Earth is distant from that same perihelion of Venus by 5:8 <gloss>a minor sixth</gloss>, that is, by 25:40. Thus the perihelia of the Earth and Jupiter will be distant by 25:36, beyond some Octaves. That, however, is not Harmonic: being indeed double 5:6 <gloss>the minor third</gloss>, or the <term>Fifth<gloss>original: Diapente</gloss></term>, diminished by one diesis.*

## Proposition XXXVIII.

**The addition** of 243:250 to the sum of the proper <gloss>individual</gloss> motions of Saturn and Jupiter—which was previously established by the primary ratios as 2:3—was to be distributed between the planets in such a way that a **Comma** (80:81) would be added to Saturn, and the Remainder (19683:20000, or roughly 62:63) to Jupiter.

> *It follows from Proposition XIX that this addition had to be distributed between both planets so that each could coincide within a certain range to the universal Harmonies of their familiar <term>genus<gloss>the major or minor mode</gloss></term>. Yet the interval 243:250 is smaller than all <term>concinnous<gloss>musically pleasing or "fitting"</gloss></term> intervals. Therefore, no harmonic laws remain by which it may be divided into two concinnous parts, except only those used above in Proposition XXVI for the division of the **Diesis** (24:25): namely, that it should depart into a Comma 80:81 (which is one of the primary intervals serving the concinnous ones) and into a Remainder of 19683:20000, which is slightly larger than a Comma, roughly 62:63. However, not two but one Comma had to be cut off, lest the parts become too unequal, since the proper motions of Saturn and Jupiter are nearly equal. This follows Axiom X, extended even to the concinnous and their smaller parts. At the same time, it is because a Comma is defined by the intervals of a Major Tone and a Minor Tone, whereas two Commas are not so defined. Furthermore, to Saturn, as the higher and more powerful planet, belonged not the larger of these parts (even though it had a larger proper motion of 4:5), but rather that part which is prior and more beautiful—that is, more Harmonic. For in Axiom X, the consideration of priority and harmonic perfection takes precedence; the consideration of quantity holds the last place, because there is no beauty in quantity by itself. Thus, the motions of Saturn become 64:81, an <term>adulterine Major Third<gloss>original: Tertia major adulterina; a musical third that is slightly out of tune compared to the pure 4:5 ratio</gloss></term>, as we called it in Book III, Chapter XII; while those of Jupiter become 6561:8000.*

I do not know whether it should be counted among the causes of the Comma being added to Saturn that the extreme intervals of Saturn might thereby constitute the ratio 8:9, a **Major Tone**; or whether that instead resulted spontaneously from the preceding causes of the Motions. You have here, therefore, in place of a corollary, the reason why above in Chapter IV, page 195, the intervals of Saturn were found to closely encompass the ratio of a Major Tone.

## Proposition XL.

**T**o the common Harmony of Jupiter and Mars when their motions are diverging <gloss>moving toward their slowest and fastest extremes respectively</gloss>, established by earlier reasons as 1:8 (a triple Octave), the Platonic Limma <note>a small musical interval of 243:256</note> had to be added.

For because the ratio between the aphelia <gloss>slowest points</gloss> of Saturn and the Earth had to be 1:32 (that is, 12:384) per Proposition XXXI; and from the aphelion of the Earth to the perihelion <gloss>fastest point</gloss> of Mars had to be 3:2 (that is, 384:256) per Proposition XV; and from the aphelion of Saturn to its own perihelion 4:5 (or 12:15) with an addition, per Proposition XXXVIII; and finally, from the perihelion of Saturn to the aphelion of Jupiter 1:2 (or 15:30) per Proposition VIII: there remains, therefore, from the aphelion of Jupiter to the perihelion of Mars a ratio of 30:256, once the addition for Saturn is removed. But 30:256 exceeds 32:256 (which is 1:8) by the amount 30:32 (which is 15:16 or 240:256), which is a **Semitone**. Therefore, the addition for Saturn—which according to Proposition XXXVIII had to be 80:81 (or 240:243)—when subtracted from that 240:256, leaves 243:256. That is the **Platonic Limma**, which is roughly 19:20; see Book III. Therefore, the Platonic Limma had to be added to the 1:8 ratio.

Thus, the larger proportion of Jupiter and Mars (that of their diverging motions) must be 243:2048. This is a sort of middle ground between 243:2387 and 243:1944—that is, between 1:9 and 1:8. The former was required by Proportion <gloss>analogy</gloss>, while the latter was closer to Harmonic fittingness.

<margin>CHAPTER IX</margin>
If, between the aphelion <gloss>the point in orbit furthest from the sun, where the planet moves slowest</gloss> of Mars, there is a perfect minor sixth <note>original: "Sexta mollis", a musical interval with a ratio of 5:8</note> above a double octave <note>original: "Disdiapason", an interval spanning two octaves</note>, rather than a deficient one (as per Proposition XIII): it follows that Mars, in its aphelion motion, marks a position that is one **comma** <note>a very small musical interval, roughly a 1/9th of a whole tone</note> higher than the natural key. Therefore, it will obtain nothing but a "false f" <note>original: "f. adulterinũ", a note slightly out of tune with the standard scale</note>; and even then, it does not fit fully, but agrees with this scale only through a certain "jump." Indeed, it enters into a universal harmony that is neither pure nor "false." For the perihelion <gloss>the point in orbit closest to the sun, where the planet moves fastest</gloss> of Venus occupies the position of *e* in this tuning. But between *e* and *f* there is a dissonance because of their proximity <note>they are a semitone apart, which Kepler considers dissonant in this specific cosmic arrangement</note>. Therefore Mars (♂) is dissonant from all the planets—specifically from the perihelion of Venus (♀). But it also dissonances from the other motions of Venus, for they are lowered by one **Comma** less than a **Diesis** <note>a small interval, often 24:25</note>. Wherefore, since between the perihelion of Venus and the aphelion of Mars there is a Semitone and a Comma, there will therefore be a Semitone and a Diesis between the aphelion of Venus and the aphelion of Mars (disregarding the octaves), which is a minor Tone; this is still a dissonant interval. Thus, the aphelion of Mars agrees only with the Scale of the Soft Genus <note>the Minor scale</note>, and not with the Hard <note>the Major scale</note>. For since the aphelion of Venus coincides with the *e* of the Hard Genus, and the aphelion of Mars (disregarding octaves) is made higher than *e* by a minor Tone; therefore, the aphelion of Mars in this tuning would necessarily fall between *f* and *f#*, creating with *g* (which the aphelion of the Earth occupies in this tuning) an interval of 25:27—clearly an unmusical <term>inconcinnum|an interval that does not fit into the standard harmonic ratios</term> interval, specifically a major Tone from which a Diesis has been taken away.

In the same way, it will be proven that the aphelion of Mars also disagrees with the motions of the Earth <note>original: "Telluris"</note>. For because it makes a Semitone and a Comma with the perihelion of Venus, as stated (that is, 14:15), but the perihelia of the Earth and Venus make a Minor Sixth (8:15 or 15:24 per Proposition XXVII); the aphelion of Mars will therefore make with the perihelion of the Earth (adding octaves to it) a ratio of 14:24 or 7:12—an unmusical interval, let alone a Harmonic one, such as 7:6. For whatever lies between 5:6 and 8:9 is dissonant and unmusical, as is 6:7 here. But neither can any other motion of the Earth harmonize with the aphelion of Mars. For it was said above that it makes an unmusical 25:27 with the aphelion of the Earth (disregarding octaves): and now from 6:7 or 24:28 up to 25:27, all are smaller than the smallest Harmonic interval.

## XLVI. Corollary.

It is clear therefore from this Proposition XLIII concerning Jupiter and Mars, and from XXXIX concerning Saturn and Jupiter, and from XXXVI concerning Jupiter and the Earth, and from XXXII concerning Saturn: why, above in Chapter V, it was found that the extreme motions of the planets were neither all perfectly adjusted to one natural system or musical scale, nor did all those which were adjusted to the system of the same tuning divide those locations by a natural proportion, or produce a purely natural succession of musical intervals. For the prior causes are those by which individual planets obtained individual Harmonies, by which all the planets also obtained universal Harmonies, and by which, finally, the universal Harmonies obtained two genera, the Hard and the Soft <note>Major and Minor</note>. Once these are established, a total adjustment to a single natural system is now hindered. But if those causes had not necessarily preceded it: there is no doubt that either a single system and its one tuning would have embraced the extreme motions of all the Planets; or, if two systems were needed for the two kinds of song, the Hard and the Soft, the very order of the natural scale would have been expressed not only in the one of the Hard genus, but also in the remaining one of the Soft genus. You have here, therefore, the causes of the disagreements by the smallest amounts—smaller than all musical intervals—which were promised in the said Chapter V.

## XLV. Proposition.

To the common double octave <gloss>an interval of two octaves, or a 1:4 ratio</gloss> of Venus and Mercury, as well as to Mercury’s own specific ratio—both established by earlier calculations in Propositions XII and XVI—it was necessary to add an interval equal to the interval of Venus’s own motion. This was done so that Mercury’s own motion would become a perfect minor tenth <note>original: "5. 12," a ratio of 5:12, which in music is an octave plus a minor third</note>, and thus Mercury, at both extremes of its motion, would harmonize with the single perihelion <gloss>the point closest to the sun</gloss> of Venus.

*For because the aphelion <gloss>the point furthest from the sun</gloss> of Saturn had to harmonize with the aphelion of Earth—as the outermost planet, circumscribed by its specific geometric figure and the highest in the heavens, must agree with the highest point of Earth, which distinguishes the classes of geometric figures—it follows by the laws of opposites that the perihelion of Mercury must harmonize with the perihelion of Earth. Mercury is the innermost planet, inscribed within its geometric figure and the lowest, closest to the Sun; its lowest motion thus aligns with the lowest motion of Earth, which serves as a common boundary. The former (Saturn/Earth aphelia) are designed for the "Hard" <term>Major</term> genus of harmonies, while the latter (Mercury/Earth perihelia) are for the "Soft" <term>Minor</term> genus, according to Propositions XXXIII and XXXIV. But the perihelion of Venus had to harmonize with the perihelion of Earth in a minor sixth harmony <note>ratio 5:8</note> per Proposition XXVII. Therefore, the perihelion of Mercury also had to be tuned into the same scale along with the perihelion of Venus. Now, in Proposition XII, the diverging harmony of Venus and Mercury was defined as a perfect fourth <note>ratio 3:4</note> based on those earlier calculations. That ratio now had to be "fermented" <note>Kepler uses "fermented" to mean adjusted or tempered through mathematical refinement</note> by the addition of the entire interval of Venus’s motion. Consequently, it is no longer from the aphelion, but from the perihelion of Venus to the perihelion of Mercury that a perfect double octave is formed. Furthermore, the converging harmony is now a perfect major sixth <note>ratio 3:5</note>, according to Proposition XV. When that is subtracted from the double octave <note>ratio 1:4</note>, there remains for Mercury alone a ratio of 5:12, which is also perfect, rather than being diminished by Venus’s own proportion (as was the case in Proposition XVI under the earlier calculations).*

*Another reason: Just as the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, which are paired figures, do not touch Saturn and Jupiter at all on their outer sides, so too these same figures do not touch Mercury on its inner side. For they touch Mars, Earth, and Venus—Mars on the inside, Venus on the outside, and Earth, the middle one, on both sides. Therefore, just as a portion equal to the motion of Venus was distributed into the specific proportions of the motions of Saturn and Jupiter (which are supported by the Cube and Tetrahedron), so now an equal amount had to be added to the specific motion of solitary Mercury, which is contained by the Octahedron—a figure associated with the Cube and Tetrahedron. For just as the Octahedron, the only figure among the Secondary solids, takes the place of two (the Cube and Tetrahedron) among the Primary solids (on which see Chapter I), so also among the lower planets, Mercury alone stands in the place of two of the upper planets, namely Saturn and Jupiter.*

*Thirdly, just as Saturn, the highest planet, had to harmonize its aphelion motion across several octaves (that is, in a continuous doubling of the 1:32 ratio) with the aphelion motion of the two planets that change the harmonic genus <note>Earth and Venus</note>, which are higher and prior to it, according to Proposition XXXI; so conversely, Mercury, the lowest planet, also across several octaves (that is, in a continuous doubling of the 1:4 ratio), had to harmonize its perihelion motion with the perihelion motion of the two planets that change the harmonic genus, which are lower and similarly nearer to it. Fourthly, among the upper three (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars), only the extreme motions harmonize in the universal harmonies; therefore, for the lower and unique planet, Mercury, both of its extremes had to harmonize with them. For the middle planets, Earth and Venus, had to change the genus of the harmonies, according to Propositions XXXIII and XXXIV. Finally, in the three pairs of upper planets, perfect harmonies were found between converging motions, while the diverging motions and the specific motions of each were "fermented." In the two pairs of lower planets, conversely, perfect harmonies were to be found not primarily between converging or diverging motions, but between motions on the same side <note>e.g., perihelion to perihelion</note>. And because two perfect harmonies were owed to Earth and Venus, two perfect ones were also owed to Venus and Mercury. And indeed, those two planets required a perfect harmony between their aphelia even more strongly than between their perihelia, because they had to change the genus of the harmony.*

## XLVI. Axiom.

The arrangement of the solid figures <term>Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</term> between the planetary spheres—if it is free and not hindered by the necessity of preceding causes—ought to follow the analogy of geometric inscriptions <gloss>fitting one shape inside another</gloss> and circumscriptions <gloss>fitting a shape around another</gloss> in their perfection; and likewise the conditions of the ratio of the inscribed shapes to the circumscribed ones.

For nothing is more consistent than that a physical inscription should exactly represent a geometric one, just as a finished work represents its own archetype.

***

## XLVII. Proposition.

If the inscription of the figures between the planets was free, the **Tetrahedron** <gloss>a four-sided pyramid</gloss> ought to have touched the perihelion sphere of Jupiter exactly with its corners at the top, and the aphelion of Mars exactly with the centers of its faces at the bottom. The **Cube** and **Octahedron**, however, standing with their corners on the perihelion sphere of their respective planets, ought to have penetrated the sphere of the interior planet with the centers of their faces, so that those centers are positioned between the aphelion and perihelion spheres. On the other hand, the **Dodecahedron** <gloss>a twelve-sided figure</gloss> and **Icosahedron** <gloss>a twenty-sided figure</gloss>, touching the perihelion spheres of their planets with their corners on the outside, ought not to have fully reached the aphelion spheres of their interior planets with the centers of their faces. Finally, the **Dodecahedral Star** <note>original: "Echinus Dodecaëdricus," literally "Dodecahedral Hedgehog." This refers to the small stellated dodecahedron, a figure Kepler himself was among the first to describe.</note>, standing with its corners on the perihelion sphere of Mars, ought to have come very close to the aphelion sphere of Venus with the middle points of its inverted sides (the two solid rays that distinguish it).

For the Tetrahedron is the middle figure of the primary solids, both by its origin and its position in the world; therefore, if nothing hindered it, it ought to have pushed apart the two regions of Jupiter (♃) and Mars (♂) equally. Because the Cube was above it and further out, and the Dodecahedron was below it and further in, it was fitting that their inscriptions should take on a variation of that middle position held by the Tetrahedron. One of them would create an excess in the inscription, and the other a deficit; that is, one would penetrate the interior sphere to some extent, while the other would not reach it. # THE HARMONIES OF THE WORLD, BOOK V, CHAPTER IX.

The Octahedron is akin to the Cube, having an equal proportion of its spheres; likewise, the Icosahedron is akin to the Dodecahedron. Therefore, whatever the Cube possesses regarding the perfection of its inscription <gloss>the way a sphere fits inside it</gloss>, the same was also owed to the Octahedron; and what the Dodecahedron possesses, the same was owed to the Icosahedron. Furthermore, the placement of the Octahedron is similar to the placement of the Cube, while that of the Icosahedron is similar to the placement of the Dodecahedron. For just as the Cube holds one boundary toward the exterior of the world, so the Octahedron holds the remaining extreme toward the interior; the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, however, act as mediators. Therefore, a similar type of inscription is appropriate: in the former case, one that penetrates the inner planetary sphere; in the latter, one that falls short of it.

The **Echinus** <note>original: "Echinus" (sea urchin). Kepler uses this term for the Great Stellated Dodecahedron, a star-shaped polyhedron with twenty points.</note>, however—which represents the Icosahedron by the tips of its angles and the Dodecahedron by its bases—ought to fill, embrace, or arrange both regions: both the region between Mars and the Earth (assigned to the Dodecahedron) and the region between the Earth and Venus (assigned to the Icosahedron). Which of the two opposites fits which partnership is made clear by the preceding axiom.

For the **Tetrahedron**, having an inscribed sphere that is expressible <note>original: "effabilem." In the context of Euclidean geometry, this refers to a ratio that can be expressed in rational numbers or square roots; it implies a "cleaner" geometric relationship.</note>, has been allotted a middle position among the Primary figures, flanked on both sides by figures of incommensurable spheres—the outer being the Cube and the inner the Dodecahedron, according to Chapter I of this book. This geometric quality (the "expressibility" of the inscribed sphere) represents, in Nature, the perfect inscription of a planetary sphere.

The **Cube**, therefore, along with its partner <note>The Octahedron</note>, has inscribed spheres that are at least half-expressible (that is, only in power <gloss>meaning their squares are rational, even if the lengths are not</gloss>); they ought, therefore, to represent a semi-perfect inscription. In this case, even if the very boundary of the planetary sphere is not reached, at least something further inward—specifically the midpoint between the spheres of the aphelion <gloss>farthest point from the sun</gloss> and perihelion <gloss>closest point to the sun</gloss>—should be touched by the centers of the figure's faces, if this can be achieved by other means.

The **Dodecahedron**, by contrast, along with its partner <note>The Icosahedron</note>, has inscribed spheres that are plainly inexpressible, both in the length of the radius and in power. They ought, therefore, to represent a plainly imperfect inscription, touching absolutely nothing of the planetary sphere—that is, failing to even reach the aphelion sphere of the planet with the centers of their faces.

The **Echinus**, although it is related to the Dodecahedron and its partner, nevertheless possesses something similar to the Tetrahedron. For the radius of the sphere inscribed by its inverted sides is indeed incommensurable with the radius of its circumscribed sphere, yet it is meanwhile commensurable in length with the distance between two neighboring angles. Thus, the perfection of the commensurability of its radii is almost as great as the Tetrahedron's, while its internal imperfection is as great as the Dodecahedron's and its partner's.

It is therefore consistent that a physical inscription should also suit it—one that is not plainly Tetrahedral, nor plainly Dodecahedral, but of an intermediate kind. Since the Tetrahedron ought to reach the highest point of the sphere with its faces, and the Dodecahedron ought not to reach it by a certain space, this "spiny" figure <note>the Echinus</note>, with its inverted sides, should stand between the Icosahedral space and the top of the inscribed sphere, reaching very close to this summit—provided that this figure was also to be admitted into the society of the other five, and that these laws could be tolerated alongside the laws of those others.

Indeed, why do I say "could be tolerated"? Those others could not do without these! For if a loose inscription that does not touch the sphere was appropriate for the Dodecahedron, what else could restrain that undefined looseness within the boundaries of a certain quantity, other than this subsidiary figure? Related as it is to the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, its own inscription reaches very close, failing no more (if indeed it fails at all) than the Tetrahedron exceeds and penetrates. We shall deal with this quantity in the following section.

This cause for the Echinus being associated with the two related figures (namely, to determine the proportion of the spheres of Mars and Venus, which the others had left undefined) is rendered very likely by the fact that the semi-diameter of the Earth's sphere is found to be 1000, which is almost exactly the proportional midpoint...

## Proposition XLVIII.

**The inscription of the regular solid figures between the planetary spheres was not a matter of absolute freedom: for it was hindered in the smallest details by the Harmonies established between the extreme motions.**

For according to Axioms I and II, the proportion of the spheres of each Figure ought not to have been expressed immediately through itself, but first had to be sought through that proportion, and the Harmonies—which are most closely related to the proportions of the spheres themselves—had to be accommodated to the extreme motions.

Next, so that according to Axioms XVIII and XX, the universal Harmonies could be of two kinds, it was necessary to add a bit of "leaven" <note>original: "fermenti," used here metaphorically to mean a small adjustment or tempering agent</note> to the Major Harmonies of the individual pairs through subsequent ratios. Therefore, so that these could stand and rely upon their own proper ratios, they required intervals differing somewhat from those that result from the perfect inscription of the figures between the spheres, according to the laws of motions explained in Chapter III. To prove this, and to show how much is taken away from each figure by the Harmonies established by their own ratios: come, let us construct from them the intervals of the planets from the Sun, using a new form of calculation never before attempted by anyone.

<margin>
Calculation of the planetary intervals emerging from the Harmonic policy.
</margin>
*There will be three heads of this inquiry: First, from the two extreme motions of each planet, its extreme intervals from the Sun will likewise be sought, and from these, the Radius of the orbit in that dimension of the extreme intervals proper to each planet. Second, from the same extreme motions, in that same common dimension, the mean motions and their proportion will be sought. Third, from the proportion of the mean motions now revealed, the proportion of the Spheres or Mean intervals will be investigated, and with them also that of the extremes; and these will be compared with the proportions of the figures.*

*Regarding the first point: it must be repeated from Chapter III, number VI, that the proportion of the extreme motions is the double of the inverse proportion of the corresponding intervals from the Sun. Since, therefore, the proportion of squares is also double the proportion of their sides: the numbers by which the extreme motions of each are expressed will be considered as Squares, and the sought roots of those numbers will give the extreme intervals, of which it is easy to take the arithmetic mean for the semi-diameter of the Orbit and the Eccentricity <term>Eccentricity: the measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term>. Therefore, the Harmonies established thus far have prescribed:*

Then, by subtracting half of the difference between these two means from the geometric mean, the value of the Mean Motion is established in the proper dimension of each planet's extreme motions; this value is then easily transformed into a common dimension by the rule of proportions.*

*Therefore, from the prescribed Harmonies, the proportion of the mean daily motions has been found—that is, the ratio between the numbers of degrees, minutes, etc., of each planet compared to one another. It is easy to explore how closely this approaches the findings of Astronomy.*

*The third point of the proposals requires Chapter 3, number 8. For the proportion of the mean motions is the inverse sesquialter <term>sesquialter: A 3:2 ratio. Kepler is describing what we now call his Third Law: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance from the Sun.</term> of the proportion of the Orbs. Furthermore, the proportion of cubic numbers is the sesquialter of the proportion of the squares assigned to the same roots in the Table of Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician whose "Practical Geometry" included tables of squares and cubes.</note>, which he appended to his Practical Geometry. Then, the Eccentricities previously assigned to each, in the dimension of their own individual semidiameters, will be easily transposed into a dimension common to all by the rule of proportions. Thus, by adding these to and subtracting them from the semidiameters of the orbs, the extreme intervals of each planet from the Sun may be established. We shall give the semidiameter of the Earth's Orb a round dimension of 100,000, as is customary in Astronomy. This is done with the intention that since this number, whether multiplied as a square or a cube, always consists of mere zeros, we shall also express the mean motion of the Earth by the number 1,000,000,000, using the rule of proportions so that the number of the mean motion of each planet relates to the number of the mean motion of the Earth just as...*
