But first, I cannot defend that reduction by harmonic reasons; for the aphelion <note>The point in a planet's orbit furthest from the sun.</note> of Mercury will not fit into any musical scale; nor is the full ratio of opposition for all conditions maintained in the planets that are opposite in the world. Furthermore, the mean daily motion of Mercury becomes too large, and therefore the periodic time of Mercury—which is the most certain thing in all of astronomy—is shortened too much. Therefore, I abide by the harmonic system of motions, employed here and confirmed throughout the whole of Chapter IX. <margin>A Challenge</margin> However, by this example, I challenge all of you who may come across the reading of this book, you who are steeped in the mathematical disciplines and the knowledge of the highest philosophy: act vigorously, tear away even one of the harmonies applied throughout, exchange it with some other; and test whether you will come as close to the astronomy prescribed in Chapter IV. Or, strive by reasoning whether you can build something better and more convenient for the celestial motions, and whether you can destroy the arrangement used by me in part or in whole. Whatever pertains to the glory of our Creator and Lord; let that be equally permitted to you through this book of mine, just as I have taken the liberty for myself up to this hour of changing throughout those things which, in previous days, I could detect as having been conceived perversely due to drowsy care or hastening passion.

## II. Epiphonema <note term="Epiphonema">A striking concluding sentence or exclamation that summarizes a previous argument with force or flair.</note>.

**I**t was good that the solid figures <note>The five Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> in the generation of intervals gave way to harmonic ratios, and the greater harmonies of pairs gave way to the universal harmonies of all, as much as was necessary for this purpose.

*By a beautiful chance, we have arrived at the second square of seven <note>Reference to the 49th proposition or axiom in his sequence.</note>; so that this might succeed as a kind of Sabbath, following the six solid octonaries <note>Groups of eight.</note> of axioms concerning the work of the heavens. Rightly also have I made an Epiphonema, which could have been placed among the Axioms at the start: because even God, having finished the work of Creation, saw all things that He had made, and behold, they were very good.*

*There are two parts to the Epiphonema: the first concerns harmonies in general, demonstrated thus: For where there is a choice between diverse things that do not exactly fit one another, the more excellent things are to be preferred, and the cheaper things must be diminished as much as is necessary—the very word "cosmos" <note>original: τõ κόσμος (tou kosmou)</note>, which signifies ornament, seems to argue this. But by as much as life excels the body, and form excels matter, by so much does harmonic ornament excel simple geometry.*

<margin>see book IV, page 163.</margin>
*For as life perfects the bodies of living things, because they were born to lead this life—which follows from the Archetype <note term="Archetype">The original divine blueprint or "idea" in the mind of God.</note> of the World, which is the very divine essence—so the regions assigned to the planets measure the motions of each of their stars: because so that a star could be moved, its own region was assigned to it. <margin>see book IV.</margin> But the five solid figures, by the force of the word itself, pertain to the spaces of the regions, and to the number of them and of the bodies; whereas Harmony pertains to the motions. Again, as Matter is diffused and indefinite in itself, and Form is definite, united, and the limit of that matter: so also there are infinite geometric proportions, but few harmonies. For although even among the geometric proportions there are certain degrees of definitions, formations, and restrictions, and no more than three can exist from the inscription of spheres to regular figures; yet these also follow a common accident with all the rest: that an infinite possible division of quantities is presupposed, which those whose boundaries...*

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...are incommensurable <note term="Incommensurable">Magnitudes that have no common measure, such as the relationship between the side and the diagonal of a square; they cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</note> with one another. But *Harmonic* proportions are all expressible, and the terms of all of them are commensurable; and these are taken from a certain and finite species of plane figures. For infinity represents the material of a division, while commensurability or "Expressibility" of the terms represents the Form. Therefore, just as matter desires Form—like a rough stone of the right size desires the Idea of a human body—so *Geometric Figural* proportions desire *Harmonies*. They do not do so to invent or create them, but because this *Matter* fits this *Harmony* more aptly; so that they may be shaped and formed further: the *Matter* by its *Form* (as stone is shaped by a sculptor <note>original: "Colapte"</note> into the likeness of a living being), and the proportion of the figural orbits by its own Form—that is, by a nearby and fitting *Harmony*.

*What has been said so far will become clearer from the history of my discoveries.* When I happened upon this contemplation 24 years ago, I first inquired whether the individual orbits of the planets were distant from each other by equal intervals (for the orbits in *Copernicus* <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), who first proposed the Sun-centered model Kepler is refining.</note> are distant and do not touch each other). Indeed, I recognized nothing more beautiful than the principle of equality. But that idea had neither head nor tail: for this material equality provided no fixed number of moving bodies and no fixed quantity for the intervals. I thought, therefore, about the similarity of the intervals to the orbits—that is, about Proportion. But the same complaint followed: for although the intervals between the orbits did indeed turn out to be unequal, they were not "unequally unequal" as *Copernicus* requires, nor was the quantity of the proportion or the number of orbits established. I moved on to regular plane figures; intervals were formed from them by the inscription of circles, but still with no fixed number. I came to the five solids <note term="Five solids">The Platonic Solids: the Cube, Tetrahedron, Octahedron, Dodecahedron, and Icosahedron. Kepler famously proposed they acted as spacers between planetary orbits.</note>; here, both the number of bodies and the magnitude of the intervals appeared nearly true—so much so that I appealed to the rest of the discrepancy for the perfection of *Astronomy*. *Astronomy* was perfected during these 20 years; and behold, the intervals still differed from the solid figures, and the causes of the *Eccentricities* <note term="Eccentricity">A measure of how much a planet's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, which are most unequally distributed among the *Planets*, were not yet clear. To be sure, in this house of the *World*, I was seeking nothing but stones of a more elegant form, but of the kind that would suit stones; I was ignorant that the *Architect* <note>Meaning God, as the creator-architect of the universe.</note> had shaped them into the most articulated likeness of a living body. Thus gradually, especially in these last 3 years, I have come to the *Harmonies*, having abandoned the *Solid figures* regarding the smallest details. This was partly because the harmonies stood on the side of the *Form* which the final hand would impose, while the figures stood on the side of *Matter* (which in the *World* is the number of bodies and the raw size of the spaces). It was also because the harmonies gave the *Eccentricities*, which the figures did not even promise: the harmonies, you see, reconciled the nose, eyes, and remaining limbs to the statue, for which the figures had prescribed only the external quantity of the raw mass.

*Therefore, just as the bodies of living beings are not made, nor is a mass of stone usually made, according to the pure rule of some geometric figure; but rather the external round shape—no matter how elegant—is reduced (while the proper size of the mass remains) so that the body can obtain the organs necessary for life, or the stone can obtain the likeness of a living being: so also the proportion which the solid figures were to prescribe for the planetary orbits (as something inferior and looking only to the body and matter) had to yield to the Harmonies, as much as was necessary for them to stand together and for the motions of the spheres to be adorned.*

<margin>Above, number XVIII, among the Axioms assumed from Part I.</margin>
The other part of the concluding exclamation, regarding *Universal Harmonies*, has a proof related to the first. For the final hand of perfection is owed rather to that which perfects the *World* more; conversely, that which holds a secondary role here must be diminished (if either must be diminished). But the universal *Harmony* of all [planets] perfects the *World* more than the singular harmonies of pairs and neighboring...

# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, BOOK V.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...are twin. For Harmony is a certain principle of unity: they are more unified, therefore, if all of them harmonize together into one, rather than if pairs individually agree on two separate harmonies. Therefore, in a conflict between the two, the individual harmonies of planetary pairs had to give way so that the universal harmonies of all could stand. Furthermore, the *Greater* harmonies of divergent motions <note term="Divergent motion">Calculated using the slowest speed of an inner planet and the fastest speed of an outer planet.</note> had to give way, rather than the *Lesser* harmonies of convergent motions <note term="Convergent motion">Calculated using the fastest speed of an inner planet and the slowest speed of an outer planet; these are the points where the planets' speeds are most similar.</note>. For if those motions diverge, they look toward neighboring planets rather than the proposed pair; but if they converge, the motions of each planet lean toward the motion of the other, interchangeably. 

For example, in the pair of Jupiter and Mars: Jupiter’s aphelion <note term="Aphelion">The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun, where the planet moves at its slowest speed.</note> leans toward Saturn, and Mars's perihelion <note term="Perihelion">The point in an orbit closest to the Sun, where the planet moves at its fastest speed.</note> leans toward the Earth; but Jupiter’s perihelion leans toward Mars, and Mars's aphelion toward Jupiter. Therefore, the Harmony of these latter motions is more specific to Jupiter and Mars, while the Harmony of the divergent motions is, in a sense, more foreign to them. The principle of unity—which binds neighbors together in pairs—was less harmed if a more foreign and distant Harmony was "fermented" <note>Kepler uses the word *fermentaretur* to describe the "leavening" or slight adjustment of an interval to make it fit a larger musical scale.</note> than if the Harmony proper to them (the one between the closer motions of neighboring planets) were altered. 

Yet this fermentation was not very great. For a system was found by which the universal harmonies of all the planets could stand—and these of two distinct types—with a certain breadth of tension that would at least equal a *Comma* <note term="Comma">A very small musical interval, specifically the difference between a major and minor tone.</note>; and the individual harmonies of two neighbors are also maintained as twin harmonies. Indeed, the harmonies of the convergent motions in four planetary pairs are perfect; those of the aphelia in one pair and the perihelia in two pairs are likewise perfect; while those of the divergent motions in four pairs differ by less than one *Diesis* <note term="Diesis">The smallest interval used in ancient Greek music theory, even smaller than a semitone.</note>—the smallest interval by which the human voice almost constantly errs in polyphonic singing. In the single pair of Jupiter and Mars, the difference is between a *Diesis* and a *Semitone*. It is clear, then, that this mutual yielding is in every respect very good.

***

Thus far, then, we have provided an *epiphonema* <note>original: "ἐπεφώνησω" (epiphonēsis) – a concluding summary or exclamation.</note> regarding the work of God the Creator. Now it remains that, having at last removed my eyes and hands from the table of demonstrations and lifted them up to heaven, I may pray as a devout suppliant to the Father of Lights:

"O You, who through the light of Nature foster in us a longing for the light of Grace, so that through it You may transport us into the light of Glory; I give thanks to You, Lord Creator, because You have delighted me in Your creation, and I have exulted in the works of Your hands. Behold, I have now completed the work of my profession, using as much strength of intellect as You have given me. I have manifested the glory of Your works to the men who will read these demonstrations, as much as the narrowness of my mind could grasp of Your infinity. My mind was ready to philosophize with the utmost correctness: if anything unworthy of Your designs has been uttered by me—a little worm, born and nourished in the wallowing-place of sins—which You would wish men to know, inspire me also to amend it. If I have been enticed into rashness by the admirable beauty of Your works, or if I have loved my own glory among men while progressing in a work destined for Your glory; be gentle and merciful, and forgive me. Finally, may You deign to 

->graciously bring it to pass<-

that these demonstrations may serve Your glory and the salvation of souls, and in no way hinder them."

## CHAPTER X.

### A Conjectural Epilogue Concerning the Sun.

From celestial music to the listener; from the Muses to Apollo the Master of the Choir; from the six circling planets making harmonies, to the Sun at the center of all their circuits, immobile in its place, yet revolving upon itself. For the most perfect harmonic system exists between the extreme motions of the planets—not according to their actual speeds through the ethereal air, but according to the angles formed by the ends of their daily arcs relative to the center of the Sun. Harmony, however, does not adorn the individual parts (that is, the motions on their own), except insofar as they are joined and compared to one another and become the object of some Mind. 

And since no object is arranged in vain without some being existing to be moved by it, these angles seem to presuppose some action similar to our sight, or certainly that sensation by which (as described in Book IV) the nature of the sublunary world <note term="Sublunary nature">Kepler believed the Earth possessed a "soul" or animating force that sensed the geometric alignments of planets (astrological aspects) and responded to them, much like a person responds to music.</note> perceived the angles of the rays from the planets formed upon the Earth. Indeed, what kind of sight exists in the Sun, what eyes there are, or what other instinct there might be for perceiving these angles even without eyes and for judging the harmonies of the motions—which enter the vestibule of the mind through whatever gate—and finally, what that Mind in the Sun might be, is not easy for us inhabitants of Earth to guess. 

However these things may be, certainly that arrangement of the six primary orbits around the Sun, honoring it with perpetual revolutions and, as it were, adoring it (just as four moons circle the globe of Jupiter, two Saturn, and as a single Moon circles, honors, cherishes, and serves us and the Earth), and now adding this special harmonic business to that consideration—a most evident trace of the highest providence regarding the Sun—extort this confession from me: Not only does Light go out into the whole world from the Sun, as from a hearth or the eye of the world; and life and heat as from a heart; and all motion as from a king and prime mover; but conversely, there are gathered into the Sun from every province of the world, by royal right, these "tax-returns" of most desirable harmony. Indeed, the species <note term="Species">In the Aristotelian sense, the 'form' or 'image' of an object that travels through space to the observer.</note> of both motions flow together there, bound into one harmony by the work of some mind, just as coins are struck into money from raw silver and gold. 

Finally, in the Sun there is the **COURT**, the Palace, and the Headquarters or Royal Residence of the entire kingdom of Nature; whatever Chancellors, Palatines, or Prefects the Creator has given it, and for whomever He prepared those seats, whether created right from the beginning or to be transferred there one day. For even this terrestrial finery lacked for a very long time the observers and users for whom it was intended, and the seats were empty. Therefore, the thought enters the mind: what did the ancient Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that the universe was ordered according to mathematical and musical principles.</note> (mentioned in Aristotle) mean when they used to call the center of the world (where they placed Fire, but understood the Sun) the **WATCHTOWER** of Jove, <note>original: ΔΙΟ'Σ ΦΥΛΑΚΗ'Ν (*Dios Phylakēn*), meaning the Guard-post of Zeus.</note>; and what was the ancient interpreter thinking when he [mentions the verse] from...

<header>ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK V.</header>

<margin>
CHAPTER X
Which was mentioned many times in the earlier books.
</margin>
...would render that verse from the Psalms in this way: **HE HAS SET HIS TABERNACLE IN THE SUN.** <note>Psalm 19:4. Kepler is discussing how ancient interpreters and philosophers viewed the Sun as the dwelling place of God or the "seat" of the cosmic soul.</note> I also recently came across a *Hymn to the Sun* by the Platonic philosopher Proclus, which is filled with venerable mysteries—provided you remove that one word, "Hearken" <note>original: κλῦθι (*klythi*), a prayerful invocation to the Sun as a deity.</note>. Yet even this was somewhat excused by the ancient interpreter I just cited: he argued that by invoking the Sun, Proclus really meant to address the One who "placed his tabernacle in the Sun."

<margin>During the time of Constantine, Maxentius, and Julian the Apostate.</margin>
For Proclus lived at a time when it was considered a crime to profess that Jesus of Nazareth, our Savior, was God, or to despise the gods of the pagan poets—a crime punished with every kind of torture by the monarchs of the world and even by the common people themselves. 

<margin>
The ancient judgment of his book *On the Mother of the Gods* <note>original: Μητρὸς θεῶν</note> was this: that in it, the doctrine of the unity of God was explained not without a divine rapture; and that by the tears of the author appearing throughout it, all suspicion was removed from the listeners. Yet this same man wrote 18 "Arguments" against the Christians, which John Philoponus opposed, reproaching Proclus for his ignorance of Greek matters which he had nevertheless undertaken to defend. It is clear that Proclus ignored those things which did not fit his own philosophy.
</margin>
Therefore Proclus—who through his Platonic philosophy and the natural light of the mind had caught a glimpse from afar of the Son of God, that "True Light which enlightens every man coming into this world"—knew well that divinity was by no means to be sought in physical things alongside the superstitious commoners. Nevertheless, he preferred to appear to seek God in the Sun rather than in the man Christ. He did this partly to deceive the pagans by honoring the Titan <note term="Titan">A poetic name for the Sun god (Helios/Apollo).</note> of the poets in name only, and partly to serve his own philosophy. He intended to lead both pagans and Christians away from physical things: the former from the visible Sun, and the latter from the Son of Mary. He did this because he rejected the Mystery of the Incarnation, trusting too much in the natural light of the Mind. Finally, he sought to adopt into his own philosophy those most divine concepts held by the Christians—concepts which were highly consistent with Platonic philosophy—by claiming them as his own.

Therefore, a claim is here made on behalf of the Gospel doctrine concerning Christ against this Hymn of Proclus. Let that Titan keep his physical properties: his "golden reins" <note>original: χρυσήνια</note> and his "storehouse of light" <note>original: ταμιῖον φάος</note>, and "placed in the center, the seat of the world, the heart-like circle of ever-shining light" <note>original: μέσσατι ϊωαῖος δ’ ἔδραν κόσμε κραδιαῖον ἀεὶ φεγγέα κύκλον</note>—a description that even Copernicus grants to the Sun. Let him even keep his "returning chariots" <note>original: παλιννόσος διφρείας</note>, though he does not possess them according to the ancient Pythagoreans; in their place, they put "the center, the Prison of Zeus" <note term="Prison of Zeus">A Pythagorean term for the central fire of the universe, which Proclus, according to Kepler, had forgotten or misunderstood over the centuries.</note>. Let him have the "offspring sprouting from you" <note>original: γενέθλην ἐκ σέ βλασήσασαν</note> and whatever else is natural. 

But in turn, let the philosophy of Proclus yield to Christian dogmas; let the visible Sun yield to the Son of Mary. It is the Son of God whom Proclus actually addresses under the name of Titan: "O King, you who hold the key to the life-sustaining source" <note>original: ζωαρκέος, ὦ ἄνα, πηγῆς αὐτὸς ἔχων κληῖδα</note>, and "You filled everything with your mind-awakening providence" <note>original: πάντα τεῆς ἔπλησας ἐγερσινόοio προνοίης</note>. This includes that immense power over the Fates <note>original: μοιράων</note>, and things that were read in no philosophy before the proclamation of the Gospel: demons fearing his "menacing lash," demons lying in wait for souls, "lest they should forget the high-reaching hall of the ever-shining Father" <note>original: ὄφρα ὑψιτενὲς λάθοιντο πατρὸς ἀειφεγγέος αὐλῆς</note>. And who is this but the Word of the Father, that "Image of the All-Begetting God" <note>original: εἰκὼν παγγενέταο θεῶ</note>, "at whose appearance from the unutterable Father, the roar of the elements rushing against one another ceased" <note>original: ὦ φανέντος ἀπ’ ἀρρήτε γενετῆρος παύσατο σοιχείων ὀρυμαγδὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντων</note>.

and in whose choir Pæan <note>Apollo as the god of healing.</note> is a partner, **having filled the wide world with all-healing harmony.** <note>original: Πλήσας ἁρμονίης παναπήμονος εὐρέα κόσμον</note> By this beginning, he indicates what the Pythagoreans understood by the name "Fire"—so that it is a wonder that the disciple <note>Proclus</note> should disagree with his masters <note>The Pythagoreans</note> regarding the location of the Center, which they assigned to the Sun itself. At the same time, he transfers the entire *Hymn* from the physical body of the Sun and its sensible light to intellectual things. To that "intellectual fire" of his (perhaps the "artisan fire" of the Stoics), and to that "created God" of his master Plato—the leading Mind or **Self-Mind** <note>original: Αὐτόνῳ</note>—he assigned a royal seat in the body of the Sun, confusing the Creature with the One through whom all things were created. 

But we Christians, taught to distinguish better, know that the eternal and uncreated **Word** <note>original: *Logos*</note>—who was **with God** <note>original: πρὸς τὸν Θεόν</note> and who is contained by no dwelling place, though He is within all things and excluded by none, though He is outside all things—took on flesh from the womb of the most glorious Virgin Mary into the unity of His Person. And we know that when the ministry of the flesh was completed, He occupied a royal seat in the heavens—where the heavenly Father is also recognized to dwell in a manner more excellent than in other parts of the world, namely through glory and majesty. He also promised that in that house of His Father, there are mansions for His faithful. For the rest, we consider it superfluous to inquire too curiously into that seat, or to summon our senses and natural reasoning to investigate what "eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man." We rightly subject the created mind, however great its excellence, to its Creator; we do not introduce "Intelligent Gods" with Aristotle and the pagan philosophers, nor innumerable armies of planetary spirits with the Magi, to be worshiped, or...

# FIFTH BOOK ON HARMONIES

<margin>
CHAPTER X.
</margin>

...or proposing that we should summon spirits through **theurgic** <note>Theurgy refers to ancient rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods or spirits; Kepler is clarifying that his investigation is scientific and philosophical, not magical.</note> superstitions for mutual communication. Guarding diligently against this, we now freely investigate through natural reasoning what the nature of each **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*</note> might be—especially if there is one in the heart of the World acting in place of the **Soul of the World** <note>original: *anima mundi*</note>, bound closely to the Nature of things (or if perhaps some intelligent creatures, of a different nature than humans, inhabit or will inhabit a globe so animated). 

<margin>
See Chapter XXIV of my book *On the New Star* regarding the **Soul of the World** and some of its duties.
</margin>

But if it is permitted to follow the thread of analogy to pass through the labyrinths of Nature’s mysteries, one might, I think, argue not foolishly as follows: that the relationship of the six orbits to their common center—and thus to the center of the whole world—is the same as the relationship of **discursive reason** <note>original: *τῆς διανοίας* (dianoia)—the step-by-step process of logical thinking</note> to **pure intellect** <note>original: *τὸν νοῦν* (nous)—instantaneous, direct understanding or intuition</note>, as these faculties are distinguished by Aristotle, Plato, Proclus, and others. Furthermore, the relationship of the local revolutions of the individual planets around the Sun to the rotation of the Sun itself, which remains **unmoved** <note>original: *ἀμεταθέτῳ*</note> in the central space of the whole system, is the same as the relationship of **the reasoning process** <note>original: *διανοητικῆς*</note> to **the intellectual faculty** <note>original: *τὸ νοερὸν*</note>—that is, the manifold wandering of logic compared to the simplest mental understanding. 

<margin>
Concerning this, the **sunspots** remain; this was demonstrated in the commentaries on the **motion of Mars**. See page 117, Book IV.
</margin>

For just as the Sun, rotating within itself, moves all the planets by means of a **species** <note>Kepler used the term "species" to describe a physical force or influence, like light or gravity, emanating from a body.</note> sent out from itself, so also the mind—as philosophers teach—by understanding itself and all things within itself, stimulates reasonings; and by spreading and unfolding its own simplicity into those reasonings, it causes all things to be understood. Indeed, the motions of the planets around the Sun at their center and the discourse of reasoning are so connected and bound together that if the Earth, our dwelling place, did not measure out its annual circle between the other orbits—changing its position from place to place and station to station—human reasoning would never have been able to struggle toward the true distances of the planets and the other things depending on them, and would never have established the science of **Astronomy**.

<margin>
See the **Optical Part of Astronomy**, CHAPTER IX.
</margin>

Conversely, the simplicity of pure understanding follows from the stillness of the Sun in the center of the world by a beautiful correspondence. This is because we have always maintained that those solar Harmonies of motions are defined neither by a diversity of regions nor by the vastness of the spaces of the World. Doubtless, if any mind looks out from the Sun, it lacks those aids of motion and diverse stations for its seat, from which it might weave the reasonings and discourses necessary for measuring the intervals of the planets. Therefore, it compares the daily motions of each planet not as they are in their own orbits, but as they flow toward the center of the Sun through angles. Thus, if it has knowledge of the size of the spheres, this knowledge must be present in it **from the beginning** <note>original: *à priori*</note>, without the labor of reasoning; it has already been shown above from Plato and Proclus that this is true, to some extent, of both human minds and sublunary nature.

<margin>
Allow me to imitate Plato’s **Atlantis** by storytelling, and Cicero’s **Scipio** by dreaming.
</margin>

Since these things are so, it would not be surprising if someone—having taken a generous draft from this **bowl of Pythagoras** <note>original: *Pythagoræ cratere*—a reference to the vessel used by the Creator in Plato's *Timaeus* to mix the soul of the world.</note> which Proclus offers in the very first verse of his *Hymn*, and having been warmed by it and lulled to sleep by the sweetest harmony of the choir of planets—should begin to dream: that through the remaining globes moving from place to place around the Sun, the discursive or reasoning faculties are scattered (the most excellent and perfect of which must be considered that which is in the middle of those globes, namely the human faculty on Earth); but that in the Sun dwells the simple **Intellect**, the **intellectual fire** <note>original: *πῦρ νοερὸν*</note> or **Mind** <note>original: *νοῦν*</note>, the source of all Harmony, whoever that may be.

For... <note>catchword: *Nam*</note>

<meta>This page concludes Chapter X of Book V. Kepler shifts from abstract harmonic theory to a grand theological and physical speculation: if the universe is designed with such harmonic precision, it must be inhabited. He argues by analogy from Earth's diverse biomes that other planets—and even the Sun—contain life suited to their conditions, ending the work with a prayer of praise.</meta>

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>

For if even Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was the preeminent observational astronomer whose data Kepler used to derive his laws of planetary motion.</note> believed that those vast, bare globes were not uselessly placed in the world but were filled with inhabitants, how much more likely is it that we should draw a conclusion about the other globes from the variety of God’s works and plans that we see on this globe of Earth? For He who created species to inhabit the waters (where there is no air for living things to breathe); He who sent birds supported by wings into the vastness of the air; He who gave white bears and white foxes to the snowy regions of the North, providing whales as food for the former and birds' eggs for the latter; He who gave lions to the deserts of sweltering Libya and camels to the vast plains of Syria, granting them endurance against hunger and thirst—would this same Creator consume all His art on the globe of Earth so that He could not, and all His goodness so that He would not, adorn the other globes with suitable creatures? Such adornment is suggested by the long or short periods of their revolutions, their proximity to or distance from the Sun, the variety of their **eccentricities** <note>The degree to which a planet's orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, the brightness or darkness of their bodies, or the properties of the geometric figures upon which each region is supported.

For behold: just as the generations of living beings on this globe of Earth bear the image of the **Dodecahedron** <note>A 12-sided Platonic solid made of pentagons.</note> for the male and the **Icosahedron** <note>A 20-sided Platonic solid made of triangles.</note> for the female (the former of which supports the Earth's sphere from the outside, the latter from the inside), and finally the image of generation itself in the divine proportion of their marriage and its **ineffability** <note>original: *ineffabilitate*; Kepler refers to the "Golden Ratio" or "Divine Proportion" found in these solids, which involves irrational numbers that cannot be expressed as simple fractions.</note>—what shall we suppose the other globes have from the other geometric figures? To what end do four Moons circle Jupiter and two circle Saturn <note>At the time of writing (1619), only four moons of Jupiter (the Galilean moons) and two of Saturn (Titan and Rhea) had been identified.</note>, just as this single Moon of ours circles our home?

In the same way, we shall also reason about the globe of the Sun. We shall incorporate conjectures drawn from the **Harmonies** <note>The musical and mathematical ratios Kepler believed governed the universe.</note>—which are weightiest in themselves—with other conjectures that lean more toward physical bodies and are better suited to the common understanding. Is that globe empty while the others are full, even though everything else corresponds so closely? If the Earth exhales clouds, and the Sun exhales "black soot" <note>Kepler is interpreting sunspots as a kind of solar "soot" or atmospheric phenomenon.</note>; if the Earth is moistened and turns green with rain, and the Sun shines with those scorched spots of its own, while brighter little flames flash forth upon its body, which is entirely fiery—then to what use is all this preparation if the globe is empty? Do not the senses themselves cry out that fiery bodies dwell here, capable of **simple Minds** <note>original: *Mentium simplicium*; Kepler suggests these solar beings might possess a more direct, intuitive intelligence than humans.</note>, and that the Sun is truly an **intellectual fire** <note>original: *πυρὸς νοερὸν* (pyros noeron)</note>, if not the King, then at least the Royal Palace?

I purposely break off both this dream and this most vast speculation, crying out only this with the **Royal Psalmist** <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms.</note>:

> Great is our Lord, and great is His virtue, and of His wisdom there is no number; praise Him, O heavens; praise Him, O Sun, Moon, and Planets, whatever sense you use for perceiving, whatever tongue for speaking of your Creator.

<margin>
And you above
all, Maestlin,
in your happy
old age, for
you used to
animate these
concerns with 
your words.
<note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631) was Kepler's university professor and mentor who first introduced him to Copernicanism.</note>
</margin>

Praise Him, O celestial Harmonies; praise Him, you who are the judges of the Harmonies now discovered. And you, my soul, praise the Lord your Creator as long as I shall live; for from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things, **both the sensible and the intelligible** <note>original: *καὶ τὰ αἰσθητὰ, καὶ τὰ νοερά* (kai ta aisthēta, kai ta noera)</note>—those things which we are entirely ignorant of as well as those things we know, which are the smallest part of them, because there is still always more beyond. To Him be praise, honor, and glory forever and ever. **AMEN**.

# APPENDIX
## TO BOOK V OF THE HARMONICS.

Regarding the Appendix that I promised earlier in the Table of Contents of Book V: the reader should not expect it here. A wine jar began to be formed;

->the wheel turns, but a pitcher comes out.<-
<note>original: "Amphora cæpit / Institui, currente rotâ verùm urceus exit." This is a famous quote from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, used to describe a project that starts with grand intentions but ends up much smaller or different in nature.</note>

I will state the reasons briefly: I was about to navigate a great and overflowing river, when suddenly, as the volume of water subsided into a thin stream, a ford appeared that I could cross on foot, leaving the ship at its station for more necessary uses. This is what I mean: **Ptolemy’s three books on Harmonics**, of which I possess Greek manuscripts along with the commentaries of the profound philosopher **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote an extensive commentary on Ptolemy's musical theory.</note>—likewise in Greek, from the beginning up to Book II, Chapter VII—always seemed worthy to me to be published in full in a Greek-Latin edition. For that reason, ten years ago, I began to translate them into the Latin language; that version proceeded until the middle of Porphyry’s codex. My move to a different location, combined with many troubles, hindered me from proceeding further. After I came to Linz <note>Kepler moved to Linz, Austria, in 1612 to serve as the provincial mathematician after the death of Emperor Rudolf II.</note>, there was a new beginning of astronomical studies. 

However, when I proposed a year ago to publish my own five books of Harmonics, I saw that immense importance lay in comparing my work with that of Ptolemy—especially my Book V with the final chapters of Ptolemy’s Book III, the last three of which contain nothing but headings or titles provided by Ptolemy. Thus, with a reluctant spirit, I decided to pluck out only one part of a work that was already incomplete in itself, which most suited my subject matter. To this end, I translated Ptolemy’s Book III from Chapter III to the end; and for the three empty titles, I supplied their own texts, composed with as much skill as possible based on the principles of Ptolemaic astronomy and the author's intent. Finally, I added commentaries or Notes, by which the lack of Porphyry's commentary (which breaks off at Book II, Chapter VII) is supplied in this third book. In these, Ptolemy’s discoveries are compared with my own, and the distinction is shown between Ptolemy’s **symbolisms** and my own legitimate demonstrations. From this, the weakness and imperfection of those symbolisms—and the primary cause of this, namely the falsity of the principles of Ptolemaic astronomy—becomes clear. 

Since this appendix alone would have occupied thirty pages of the book, behold: in the meantime, the nearby **Bohemian War** <note>The "bellum Bohemicum" refers to the early stages of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648). The conflict caused massive disruptions to travel, trade, and printing across Central Europe.</note> broke out, by which travel was hindered and many workmen enlisted for military service. Thus, first we ran out of paper, and then the laborers who manage the press failed us; finally, the time was stretched out by the most tiresome delays. Driven by these obstacles, I finally reconsidered and cut short my plan. I did not want to expose—and almost ruin—the book of that excellent author Ptolemy and his commentator Porphyry by publishing it in such a mutilated fragment. Would it not be better, then, to spend the remaining half of the labor on finishing the translation of Porphyry’s exposition; to write Notes on the remaining chapters of Books II and III; and to join them with those I have already written for nearly all of Book III? In this way, the work would be made whole and published as a Greek-Latin edition where it exists. For such an edition, another time and another place are required, as well as a suitable printer.

However, so that the reader does not feel completely deprived of what I promised above, or so that nothing is missing from this final part regarding the integrity or easier understanding of my work on Harmonics, come: I shall transcribe the titles of the chapters of Ptolemy’s Book III and compare them with the relevant places in my own work; and I shall record in a summary fashion what is contained in my Notes.

First, those things which Ptolemy taught in Books I, II, and the beginning of III concerning the discipline of Harmonics, I have encompassed in my Book III using another method, which is not a little different. For while Ptolemy seeks the principles of harmonies from abstract numbers, following the ancients; I, on the contrary, denying that power resides in numbers as counters, for them numbers...

# APPENDIX.
¶ A

...the numbered [objects], that is, the things themselves subjected to those numbers—namely, regular plane figures and the divisions of the circle to be managed by them—establishing the principles of Harmonies, I necessarily prefixed Books I and II concerning Harmonic figures to my Book III.

Now **Ptolemy**, in Book III, Chapter 3 of his work, prescribed this title: *Under what genus of things the nature or force of Harmony, and the science of it, should be referred; showing that there is some causal, formal, mental, and therefore divine principle, which unites Harmonies to things.* Chapter IV: *That the force of Harmonic tempering is present in all things whose natures consist of a higher degree of perfection: and that this is most apparent in human Souls and in celestial revolutions.* Here you see the division of those topics that remained for Ptolemy to discuss: first, <note>original: "de Harmonijs in Animis existentibus"</note> *concerning Harmonies existing in Souls*, and second, <note>original: "de Harmonijs in cæli motibus"</note> *concerning Harmonies in the motions of the heavens*. And regarding the first, three chapters follow; *regarding the second, nine remaining chapters.* Chapter V: *He compares individual consonances <term>consonance: a combination of notes that sound pleasant or stable together</term> with the individual faculties of the rational Soul, and does so concisely, through subdivisions of both things compared.* Chapter VI: *He compares individual genera of Harmonies with individual genera or classes of virtues.* Chapter VII: *He compares the changes of Tones <note>Original: "Tonorum," referring to musical modes or scales.</note> with the changes of public pursuits over different times; and likewise even with the sudden changes of emotions in Souls.*

In this part, I dispute many things against **Ptolemy**, primarily that those symbolisms are for the most part not necessary, nor causal, nor natural, but rather poetic and oratorical; for those special faculties and virtues that reside in souls do not receive either the Idea or the numbers of their constitution from Harmonies as if from an Archetype <note>An "Archetype" is an original pattern or model from which things are copied; Kepler argues that the soul's structure is not merely a byproduct of musical numbers.</note>, but have other acknowledged or evident causes. Indeed, they do not even correspond to the number [of the harmonies], but are reconciled to them by a far-fetched or poorly-aimed appearance of equal-multiple division: many excesses or, conversely, defects are disguised; certain things that succeed less are "dragged by the hair" <note>A Latin idiom meaning forced or strained logic.</note>: finally, those things that most precisely and skillfully correspond to one another are nevertheless not made according to any proportion of quantities of the same kind; yet Harmony cannot exist except in comparisons of quantities.

But that Musical Tones are compared to public emotions and customs, I have shown to be most natural and to have the character of a cause: where, on the occasion of Ptolemy's text, I have brought forward the opinions of various philosophers concerning the kinship of Souls, Numbers, and harmonies among themselves, to which I have also added the Epilogue of my Book V. And what specifically pertains to the effect of tones in moving souls in various ways: I have encompassed that material in the specific Chapter XV of my Book III. Likewise, what pertains to Commutative and Distributive Justice <note>Commutative justice deals with fairness in exchange; distributive justice deals with the fair allocation of resources in a community.</note>, and Friendship, and Economics and Politics: on this subject, insofar as Musical proportions prevail in them, I made a Digression at the end of my Book III. Finally, the material of the already mentioned Chapters III and IV, and what could truly be said in general about V, VI, and VII; I have encompassed in the first three and again in the seventh chapter of my Book IV: where, having explained the nature of Souls, I showed that since a circle, geometrically cut by the inscription of plane figures, truly and properly defines Harmonic proportions by the comparison of the parts with the whole: therefore, in souls, by a certain essential reason, there exists a circle, formally and abstractly, not only from matter but even in a way from quantity itself, considered materially. Wherefore, since the circle—and thus Harmonies—resides in souls, this is the reason why Souls are moved by Harmonies: but all these things are only in general; no consequent causation of the distribution of the Soul into special faculties follows. This, then, is how the matter stands with human Souls.

As for celestial motions, **Ptolemy** in Chapter VIII of his Book III compares the Zodiac with the system or scale of Music: in Chapter IX, he compares the consonances themselves with the Aspects <note>In astrology, "Aspects" are the specific angular distances between planets (like 60°, 90°, or 120°) that Kepler believed corresponded to musical intervals.</note>.

### li 2

...of the Planets. Here I have shown in which parts the doctrine of **Aspects** <term>Aspects: The specific angles (like 90° or 180°) that planets make with each other, believed in astrology to influence the world.</term> in the work of **Ptolemy** is lacking, and how through the integration of numbers—on one hand of the Aspects, and on the other of the **Consonances** <term>Consonances: Musical intervals that sound harmonious and stable.</term>—a natural and causal connection of these things finally appears. This is, moreover, the genuine subject matter of my Book IV, especially chapters IV, V, and VI.

In Chapter X, **Ptolemy** creates a certain melody from the motion of a Planet from its rising to its setting; in Chapter XI, from the motion of the Planets in height and depth <note>original: "in altum & profundum," referring to the planet's distance from the Earth.</note>, he creates the genera of song. In Chapter XII, from the motion along the side of the equator, he creates the variety of musical Tones. In Chapter XIII, from the various configurations of the planets with the Sun, he creates the various **Tetrachords** <term>Tetrachord: A musical scale of four notes, the building block of ancient Greek music.</term> of the system. In these four chapters, I have shown that **Ptolemy** indulges in an exercise of poetic or oratorical comparison; for the things he compares are not real in the heavens—except for a small portion of Chapter XI, which I wish to set aside for the last three chapters because of the kinship of the subject matter. I have also shown that here, partly, things are compared that cannot be compared because the nature of the things compared cries out against it, and partly that those things which do correspond in all their parts do so at least accidentally, rather than cohering out of the necessity of some cause. Thus, so far, there is nothing or very little that agrees with my celestial Harmonies.

But indeed, the following Chapter XIV of **Ptolemy** proposes to inquire according to which prime numbers the sounds of the system or musical scale can be compared with the primary spheres in the Planetary system. Here I have shown that the comparison made by **Ptolemy** and the **Pythagoreans** in their accustomed Astronomy was impossible—though I have tried to devise something consistent with **Ptolemy's** principles so that his text might be supported by more than just a bare title. I have also shown that, since the primary spheres are defined by their quantities just as strings are defined by their lengths, the comparison ought to have been established according to quantities; yet the proportion of the spheres differs greatly from the proportion of consonant strings. I have, however, repeated the corrected and causal (or Archetypal) connection of the spheres of the World with the **regular bodies** <term>Regular bodies: Also known as the five Platonic solids, which Kepler believed dictated the spacing of the planetary orbits.</term> from the beginning of my Book V, drawn from my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>original: "Mysterio Cosmographico," Kepler's first major work published in 1596.</note>.

Chapter XV of **Ptolemy** seeks how the proportions of proper motions can be taken through numbers, but the text is missing. I have therefore shown the same things as in the preceding chapter. For the rest, I have given this for consideration: that here, 1300 years ago, **Ptolemy** began to treat the proper subject of my Book V, if only he had been able to do so through his own astronomy. I, therefore, in my emended Astronomy—which retains the true and simple motions of the planets, having eliminated the appearances that consist of deceptions of the eyes—have shown that in the heavens, according to a true and genuine quantitative and measurable reason, and not through a mere flimsy symbolization, there exist all the Harmonic proportions, the genera of Harmonies, the system or musical scale and most of its keys, the varieties of Tones, the planets as rivals of the voices of figured <note>or polyphonic</note> music, and finally the universal counterpoints of the primary planets, varied both in genera and in tones. 

In Chapter XVI and last, **Ptolemy** promises that he wants to investigate by what reason the "familiarities" of the **Wanderers** <note>original: "Erronum," an old term for the planets.</note> can be compared with the familiarities of sounds: namely, he busied himself with demonstrating the principles of astrology—concerning planets that are beneficial or harmful, or friends or enemies to each other—through celestial Harmonies. And because the text for this chapter is also missing, I have reconstructed it as best I could, especially from **Macrobius** <note>Macrobius: A 5th-century Roman writer who preserved much Pythagorean lore.</note>; and at the same time, I have shown in the notes what is lacking in this business that prevents it from succeeding according to ancient astronomy. In my own work, however, I have no part corresponding to Chapter XVI, except for a small portion from the Epilogue of Book V. For astrology deals with the effects of the stars on the Earth, but my celestial Harmonies are not formed by rays on the Earth, but in the Sun. And here is the end of **Ptolemy's** work; with which I would also finish the summary of the Appendix promised in the entrance to Book V, were I not invited by the affinity of things to also satisfy those who have urged me, such as **Mr. Robert Fludd** <note>original: "D. Roberti de Fluctibus," refers to the English physician and occultist Robert Fludd.</note>...

# APPENDIX.

I should not omit mention in my work on Harmony of the Oxford Physician <note>referring to Robert Fludd (1574–1637), a prominent English Paracelsian physician and mystic</note>, who a year ago published a book on the **Microcosm** and **Macrocosm** <term>Microcosm and Macrocosm: The Renaissance idea that the human being (microcosm) is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (macrocosm).</term> filled with harmonic contemplations. Rather, I should show the reader in a few words the matters in which he and I agree, and those in which we conversely disagree.

# APPENDIX.

<margin>
On the World Music of Mr. Robert Fludd, Physician of Oxford.
</margin>

Therefore, that author promised two volumes; the one titled *On the Macrocosm* is already published, while the other on the *Microcosm* is still awaited. The first volume, comprising two treatises, appeared at different times. I saw the first treatise, *On the Triple World*, after the Frankfurt autumn book fair of 1617; the second, *On the Arts* (which he calls the *Ape of Nature* <note>original: "Naturae Simia," Fludd's title for his work on the arts and sciences as imitations of divine creation</note>), I saw at the Easter fair of the following year, 1618. In the second treatise, he placed Music among the arts, covering to some extent the material of my third book. In the first treatise, however, which is completed in seven books, he destined the third book for **World Music** <term>World Music: Known in Latin as *Musica Mundana*, the ancient theory that the movements of the stars and planets create a form of unspoken music or harmony.</term>, using the same title that I prefixed to my entire work; there, he touched upon the subject matter of my fourth and fifth books.

Let us therefore begin with his "artificial music" <note>Music created by human art and instruments, as opposed to the music of the spheres.</note>. He treats this in seven books: in the first, he reviews authors and nomenclatures, and the power of music over the souls of men. Regarding authors or the history of the invention, I say nothing, or certainly very little, because my intent is to reveal the causes of natural things. I have included necessary nomenclatures throughout my definitions and omitted the superfluous ones. I deal with the power of music over the Soul in Book III, chapter 15, and throughout Book IV.

In the second book, the author approaches the subjects themselves, which he calls *Intervals* and *Times*. Again, I have said almost nothing about "Times" (the length or brevity of sounds), for these are arbitrary and do not require an inquiry into their causes. He calls certain intervals "simple," which to me are the "fitting" <note>original: "concinna," meaning melodic intervals that are not quite dissonant but not fully consonant</note> and least dissonant ones: the major Tone, minor Tone, semitone, and **diesis** <term>Diesis: A very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone, common in ancient Greek tuning.</term>. He wishes others to be composed from these, which I call **Consonances**. Yet, I expressly refuted this opinion of the ancients—that consonances are composed of smaller intervals as if they were prior by nature—in Chapter IV of my third book, showing that, on the contrary, the smaller intervals arise from the consonances that are larger than themselves.

In the third book, he explains the system or the musical scale, which is the principal part of my third book from Chapter IV to IX. The remaining four books of the author deal with practice, which I do not even touch upon. For in Book IV, he teaches about the measurement of the **tactus** <term>Tactus: The basic rhythmic beat or pulse in Renaissance music.</term>, its various modes, and the value of notes through them, about which I say very little in Book III, chapter 15, and Book IV, chapter 3. In Book V, he has instructions for the composer of **figured song** <term>Figured song: Complex, polyphonic music with multiple independent voices.</term>, an art which I do not profess. In Book VI, he even wanders into various musical instruments, which I have not even thought about. Finally, in Book VII, he reveals a new instrument of his own.

In these last four books, therefore, he differs from me as a Practitioner differs from a Theorist. For while he teaches about instruments, I inquire into the causes of things or consonances; and while he teaches how to compose a melody for many voices, I arrange mathematical demonstrations for those things that are naturally present in both Choral and Figured song. Because of this, there are many pictures in his work; in mine, there are mathematical diagrams marked with letters. You may also see that he delights greatly in the dark riddles of things <note>referring to Fludd’s use of complex, symbolic illustrations</note>, whereas I strive to bring things wrapped in obscurity into the light of the intellect. The former is a familiar habit of the **Chemists**, **Hermeticists**, and **Paracelsians** <term>Chemists/Hermeticists/Paracelsians: Various schools of occult philosophy and alchemy that sought hidden, mystical relationships between the heavens and the earth.</term>; the latter is the specific task of the **Mathematicians**.

And so, even in Books II and III, where he treats the same subject matter as I, there is this difference between us: what he takes over from the ancients, I dig out from the nature of things and establish from the very foundations. What he has received, he presents in a confused manner (because of...

# APPENDIX

...varying opinions of those who pass down traditions, and uses them incorrectly; I proceed by a natural order, so that all things may be corrected according to the laws of Nature, and confusion may be avoided; thus, I do not even apply my findings to the decrees of the ancients, except where no confusion follows. So, where I expressly refute the ancients when discussing the causes of harmonies, he [Fludd] follows the ancients without a moment's doubt; he does not even think of more truthful causes. In a single word, in the discipline of Harmony, one [Fludd] acts as a vocal and instrumental Musician; the other [Kepler] as a philosopher and Mathematician.

Now let us pass to another section of the author, where he introduces Music into the World. Here, indeed, there is a massive difference between us. First, those harmonies he intends to teach are mere symbolisms <note>original: "meri Symbolismi"</note>, about which I say the same as I did regarding the symbols in Ptolemy: they are poetic or rhetorical rather than philosophical or mathematical. This is the very soul of that whole Work, as is clear even from the title *Macrocosm and Microcosm*. For in the second volume, he undoubtedly intends to demonstrate that noble theme: that the Ideas of the whole great world, and of all its parts, are found in man. This is the same soul found in the first volume: because he distributes the whole world into three regions; where, according to that most celebrated axiom of Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus and the Hermetic axiom "As above, so below"</note>, he makes the things above similar or analogous to the things below. But for this analogy to succeed in all things, those things which are compared on both sides must often be "pulled by the hair" <note>a Latin idiom, *crinibus trahenda*, meaning to force a connection or use a strained argument</note>. My opinion on analogies is clear from the digression at the end of my Book III: namely, that although the analogy of proportions in geometric forms is something "formal" in respect to the indefinite and indeterminate quantity of matter itself, yet in respect to harmonic proportions, it can be considered a "material" affection. This is because, while harmonic proportions define a certain quantity, analogies conversely are suited to run out into infinity by themselves, and thus they assume a material state of infinity.

And although I also treat some things similar to those Macrocosmic matters in my work—such as in Book IV where I make the Earth a living being <note>original: "Terram animal facio"</note>—I do so for a far different reason. For I do not contend that there is a mere analogy between the Earth and animals, nor do I wish the archetype of the animal to be taken from the Earth itself; rather, I simply have it as my proposed goal to demonstrate that those works which are observed in the globe of the Earth cannot proceed from the motions of elements or from the solitary qualities of matter, but testify to the presence of a Soul. Now, for my arguments to be understood, it was necessary to cite various functions of the soul in the body of an animal. To come closer to the foundations upon which <term>Robert Fludd</term> <note>original: "Robertus de Fluctibus"</note> builds his World Music: first, he occupies the whole world and all three of its parts—the Empyrean, the Celestial, and the Elemental; I occupy only the celestial, and not even all of that, but only the motions of the planets as if beneath the Zodiac. He, trusting in the ancients who believed the power of Harmonies resided in abstract numbers, is satisfied if he can demonstrate some concord between parts by grasping them in numbers in whatever way possible, with no care as to what kind of units are accumulated in that number. I nowhere teach the seeking of Harmonies where the things between which the Harmonies exist cannot be measured by the same measure of quantity—so that, by reason of quantity, the same proportion exists between them as between two strings of the same tension by reason of length. Therefore, he divides the whole World into three equal parts by reason of its semi-diameter, knowing full well that those parts are not at all equal; but he does so only because the first unit is the Elemental world, the second the Aethereal world, and the third the Empyrean. And indeed, units cannot be depicted otherwise than by the equality of lines. But I, unless astronomy testifies to the same quantitative measure of units, never use them as units for the purpose of numbering...

# A P P E N D I X.

...calculating Harmonic proportions. He [Fludd], however, insisting on his own principles and drawing out a pyramid from its base—the great circle of the Earth—places its vertex at the very peak of the empyrean heaven <note>The highest part of heaven, believed in ancient and medieval cosmology to be occupied by the element of fire or the presence of God</note>; and having divided its height into three equal parts (as if he possessed units that were truly equal), he counts how many parts fall to the Empyrean, how many to the Celestial, and how many to the Elementary region. For in this way, the top of the Elementary region is twice as far from the top of the Celestial as it is from the top of the Empyrean. In the division of the pyramid, regarding the axis, the three regions receive three equal parts; however, regarding the triangle through the axis, one unit goes to the Empyrean, three to the Celestial, and five units to the Elementary. Finally, regarding the space or bulk of the figure, one unit goes to the Empyrean, seven to the Celestial, and nineteen units to the Elementary. 

What shall I say now of the other, opposite Pyramid of light, whose base he makes the adorable Trinity itself at the highest peak of the Empyrean heaven, while placing its vertex on the Earth itself? When he mingles these two pyramids together and elicits musical proportions from that mixture, he attempts something very different from the purpose of my work. For he compares light (the giver of *form* and *soul*) and *matter*—two things most different from one another—to which quantities are by no means present in the same respect. I, however, for the purpose of establishing the terms of Harmonic proportion in the world, do not admit anything except those things which receive quantities in the same respect; for example, the daily motions <note>original: "diurnos"</note> of *Mars* and *Jupiter*. 

Nor does the difference between us consist in less than this: that he assigns four degrees of obscurity and darkness to the Elementary region, because whatever thing nourishes has four fourths, certainly no less than three thirds and five fifths <note>Kepler is mocking Fludd’s arbitrary use of numbers; Fludd argues that because a thing can be divided into fourths, it must have "four degrees."</note>; and now he says all four are in the Earth, three in water (and that it is already translucent), two in air, and one in fire. Again elsewhere, he subdivides any region, whether of an element or of the heavens, into three spaces: the highest, the middle, and the lowest—not everywhere following the probability of the senses. You see, his units are again arbitrary. 

He continues, therefore, to establish a fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron," a musical interval of a perfect fourth</note> between Earth and water, and to apply its three intervals—tone, tone, and semitone—to the three spaces (highest, middle, lowest); whereas the former [the musical intervals] have certain quantities from their own causes, while the latter [the elemental spaces] have not even boundaries from nature, and their measures according to these most general principles are plainly indeterminate. And so it goes for the rest. 

But for me, the natural units—namely the two extreme motions of the planets (whether daily or hourly, it makes no difference) expressed by nature in their own certain quantities—are the objects in which I seek Harmonies. He seeks Harmonic proportions in degrees of darkness and light, without respect to any motion; I *seek Harmonies only in motions*. He tastes a few small concords and elicits them from the mixture of his pyramids—by which he carries about the World painted privately in his own mind—or proves they are represented by it. I have demonstrated that the whole body of Harmonic tempering, with all its parts, exists in the extreme proper motions of the planets, according to certain measures demonstrated by Astronomy. Therefore, his subject of *World Harmony* <note>original: "Harmoniæ Mundanæ"</note> is his own concept of the World, while mine is the World itself, or the real motions of the planets within it. 

From these few points, I think it is clear that although a knowledge of harmonic proportions is absolutely necessary to understand the mysteries packed into the very deep philosophy which *Robert* [Fludd] passes down, nevertheless, he who has learned even my entire work will still be a good deal further from those most perplexing mysteries than those mysteries themselves have receded from the most accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations. 

And here now let there also be the **END** of the Appendix.

# THINGS TO BE AMENDED IN THE WORK.

First, you should know that the first two books, which were printed last, have their own separate sequence of page numbers. Therefore, correct these numbers: Book I, page 41. And Book III, pages 58, 63, 112, 150, 161, 200, 212, 228, 229, 236, 237. Correct the remaining errors as follows. Book I, page 2, the third line from the bottom: **from every side** <note>original: "undique"</note>. Page 66, in the margin at conclusion 29, let page 150 be cited; and at conclusion 30, page 82 of Book III.

Pages 33, 34, and 35: The text was collected from sheets written at different times, but it was not assembled quite aptly; although everything in it is true, it has acquired some obscurity from a confusion of things that should be distinguished and from a repetition of propositions. The distinct questions are these:

**Question I.** Do Consonances <note>In music theory, a consonance is a combination of notes that sounds pleasant or "stable" to the ear</note> have parts which are themselves also consonances, or at least fitting intervals? The answer is this: In consonances, there are distinct elements: first, the proportion (a geometric matter), and second, the quality of the proportion (the consonance itself). Insofar as they are proportions, one is exceeded by another, the smaller by the larger, and thus one can be a part of the other. However, insofar as each of them receives the quality of consonance from its own demonstrable figure, they do not undergo composition <note>Kepler argues that musical harmony comes from geometric shapes like triangles; you cannot simply add shapes together to get a new "pure" shape in the same way you add numbers</note>. The arguments are these: 1. A species, as a species, is indivisible and one. 2. A species is constituted by its cause; but the causes of the individual harmonies are distinct from one another. Therefore, the harmonies themselves are distinct from one another in species; nor can one be dissolved, as a larger one, into others of its own species as parts, though it can well be dissolved into smaller ones of a different species. 3. If a fitting or consonant part of a consonance increased the consonance or fitness of the whole (as a multiplied part increases quantity), then dissonance and unfitness would not eventually be produced by the accumulation of parts.

**Question II.** Do consonances have one common measure, such as a **Tone**, a **Diesis**, a **Comma**, etc.? <term>Tone, Diesis, Comma</term> <note>These are technical terms for small musical intervals used as building blocks in various tuning systems</note> The answer is no. This is not the case even as they are proportions, because in that sense they are incommensurable—that is, they lack a common measure. Nor is it the case as they are species, because they are distinct from one another by the causes from which they arise and by which they are defined. For they have, in a way, the nature of figures; now, a triangle <note>original: "Trigonus"</note> and a pentagon inscribed in the same circle have side lengths that are incommensurable. Finally, a measure is prior to the things measured; but fitting intervals like the Tone or Diesis, etc., are posterior to the consonances. And note, those parts—the Major Tone, Minor Tone, semitone, etc.—are common to the consonances, but not all of them to all consonances; nor is there any one of them which alone can measure the consonances.

# Plate 4

**Dd** and **Ee**: Two variations of planar <term>tilings</term> <note>patterns of shapes that fit together without gaps or overlaps</note>. **Dd** shows an octagonal arrangement, while **Ee** shows a tiling made of octagons and squares.

**Ff**: A central star polygon surrounded by triangles and other smaller polygons, creating a radiant effect.

**Gg**: A circular, crown-like arrangement featuring twelve star polygons linked together.

**Ii**: A tiling pattern composed of large dodecagons and small triangles, showing how large and small shapes can share edges to fill a space.

**Kk** and **Ll**: A cluster of polygons—including hexagons, squares, and triangles—arranged into a larger triangular structure, illustrating a more varied combination of shapes.

**Mm**: A large circular arrangement composed of twelve <term>decagons</term> <note>polygons with ten equal sides</note>.

# Plate 5

Following his study of flat patterns, Kepler here illustrates various three-dimensional solids. This plate is historically significant for depicting "star polyhedra," which were a breakthrough in geometric theory.

**Mm** and **Nn**: These large, intricate circular forms are complex polyhedra with many facets. They represent the transition from simple shapes to near-spherical geometric solids.

**Oo**: A regular <term>octahedron</term> <note>a solid with eight triangular faces; one of the five "Platonic solids"</note>.

**Pp**: A series of multi-faceted solids demonstrating how edges can be truncated or modified to create more complex forms.

**Rr**: A collection of faceted prisms and elongated solids, exploring how symmetry is maintained across different axes.

**Qq**: A sequence of cubes and rectangular blocks. Notably, some of these cubes contain detailed internal illustrations of "trees." These represent <term>dendrites</term> <note>branch-like mineral crystallizations, often found in nature, that Kepler used to show how geometric growth occurs in the natural world</note>.

**Ss** and **Tt**: Two large, magnificent <term>stellated polyhedra</term> <note>three-dimensional star shapes created by extending the planes of a polyhedron's faces until they intersect to form new points</note>. These specific figures—the small stellated dodecahedron and the great stellated dodecahedron—are now known as "Kepler Solids" in his honor.

**Vu**: A multifaceted solid showing an advanced arrangement of triangular and quadrilateral faces.

**Xx**: A series of faceted ovals. These shapes bridge the gap between pure mathematical geometry and the practical art of <term>lapidary</term> <note>the cutting and polishing of gemstones</note>, illustrating how light and symmetry interact in crystals.

<summary>This plate illustrates Kepler's move from two-dimensional tilings to three-dimensional solids, featuring his landmark discovery of stellated polyhedra and the geometric patterns found in natural crystals.</summary>
<keywords>polyhedra, Kepler Solids, geometry, stellation, dendrites, octahedron, crystallography, Platonic solids</keywords>

# Plate 3

Following his study of flat patterns, Kepler here illustrates various three-dimensional solids. This plate is historically significant for depicting "star polyhedra," which were a breakthrough in geometric theory.

<gloss>PP</gloss> <gloss>QQ</gloss> <gloss>GG</gloss>
<note>Labels for multi-faceted solids and cubes. **Pp** and **Qq** show how edges can be modified or truncated to create more complex forms. **Gg** refers to the structural arrangement of these edges.</note>

<gloss>M</gloss> <gloss>N</gloss>
<note>These large, intricate circular forms are complex polyhedra with many facets. They represent the transition from simple shapes to near-spherical geometric solids.</note>

**Oo**: A regular <term>octahedron</term> <note>a solid with eight triangular faces; one of the five "Platonic solids"</note>.

<gloss>RR</gloss> <gloss>SS</gloss> <gloss>II</gloss> <gloss>HH</gloss>
<note>**Rr** and **Ss** are two large, magnificent <term>stellated polyhedra</term> <note>three-dimensional star shapes created by extending the planes of a polyhedron's faces until they intersect to form new points</note>. These specific figures—the small stellated dodecahedron and the great stellated dodecahedron—are now known as "Kepler Solids" in his honor. **Ii** and **Hh** label the internal vertices and intersection lines.</note>

<gloss>VV</gloss> <gloss>FF</gloss>
<note>**Vv** depicts a multifaceted solid showing an advanced arrangement of triangular faces. **Ff** labels the perspective of the surrounding faces.</note>

<gloss>LL</gloss> <gloss>II</gloss>
<note>These labels refer to the <term>nets</term> <note>unfolded two-dimensional patterns that can be folded to create a three-dimensional solid</note> shown at the top of the diagram, specifically for a truncated tetrahedron.</note>

<gloss>XX</gloss>
<note>A label for the complex stellated polygons on the right side of the plate, showing the progression of intersecting lines.</note>

---

<summary>This plate illustrates Kepler's groundbreaking work on three-dimensional geometry, including the first formal depiction of stellated polyhedra (Kepler Solids) and the relationship between solid shapes and their flat nets.</summary>

<keywords>polyhedra, Kepler Solids, stellated dodecahedron, Platonic solids, geometry, nets, truncation, University of Copenhagen</keywords>

--- Page 350 ---
<meta>This page continues the illustration of Johannes Kepler's "Mysterium Cosmographicum" theory as presented in his 1619 work, "The Harmony of the World." Having established the geometric properties of three-dimensional solids on the previous page, Kepler now applies those shapes to the structure of the universe itself.</meta>

## THE CUBE
<note>Kepler theorized that a cube, if placed between the spheres of Saturn and Jupiter, would perfectly account for the distance between their orbits.</note>

<summary>This diagram illustrates Kepler’s famous "Nested Solids" model, where the distances between the planetary orbits are determined by the five Platonic solids (cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron, and dodecahedron).</summary>
